A student claims: "The force between two parallel currents is proportional to 1/d² because the magnetic field of a wire falls as 1/d and the force on the other wire also falls as 1/d, so together it's 1/d²." Identify the error in this reasoning and give the correct dependence.

In a current balance experiment to define the ampere, two parallel wires are 1.00 m apart in vacuum. One wire carries a known current of 2.00 A. The measured force per unit length on the other wire is 8.00 × 10⁻⁷N/m. The student calculates the unknown current as 1.00 A. Is this correct? If not, find the correct value and explain the student's mistake.

A circular coil of 50 turns and radius 5 cm carries a current of 2 A. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T such that the plane of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the field direction. Calculate the magnitude of the torque on the coil.

Two identical circular loops carry the same current. Loop A has its magnetic moment parallel to B; Loop B has its magnetic moment at 45° to B. Compare the torques on the two loops. Which loop is in stable equilibrium?

A moving coil galvanometer has 100 turns, each of area 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m². It is placed in a radial magnetic field of 0.2 T. The torsional constant of the suspension spring is 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ N·m/rad. Calculate the current sensitivity in rad/A and in mm/μA if the pointer length is 5 cm. (Assume small angle approximation: deflection in mm ≈ pointer length × φ in rad).

Two moving coil galvanometers M1 and M2 have identical spring constants and magnetic fields. M1 has N1 = 30, A1 = 3.6 × 10⁻³ m², R1 = 10 Ω. M2 has N2 = 42, A2 = 1.8 × 10⁻³ m², R2 = 14 Ω. Determine the ratio of (a) current sensitivity and (b) voltage sensitivity of M2 to M1.
A galvanometer has a resistance of 50 Ω and gives full-scale deflection for 1 mA. What is the shunt resistance required to convert it into an ammeter of range 0–5 A?
A galvanometer of resistance 20 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 2 mA. Calculate the series resistance needed to convert it into a voltmeter of range 0–10 V.

Two students convert the same galvanometer (G = 100 Ω, Ig = 1 mA) into an ammeter of range 0–1 A. Student A uses a shunt of 0.1 Ω. Student B uses a shunt of 1 Ω. Which ammeter will have higher accuracy for measuring currents near 0.5 A? Explain using the concept of equivalent resistance and circuit loading.

A galvanometer is converted into a voltmeter of range 0–5 V using a series resistance of 4950 Ω. The galvanometer resistance is 50 Ω. A student claims: "The voltage sensitivity of this voltmeter is 1 division per volt because the full-scale deflection is 5 V and the scale has 5 divisions." Evaluate this claim.

Design a multi-range ammeter using a single galvanometer (G = 60 Ω, Ig = 1 mA) that can measure 0–0.1 A, 0–1 A, and 0–10 A. Specify the shunt resistances needed and explain how the range selector switch should be wired to avoid damaging the galvanometer when switching ranges.
Fill in the blank: Observe a school laboratory ammeter and ______ — both have multiple range settings (e.g., 0-1 A, 0-3 A, 0-5 V, 0-15 V).
Fill in the blank: Observe a school ______ ammeter and voltmeter — both have multiple range settings (e.g., 0-1 A, 0-3 A, 0-5 V, 0-15 V).

Two identical bar magnets are placed with their north poles facing each other, separated by 10 cm. A student claims the magnetic field at the exact midpoint is zero because the fields from the two magnets cancel. Is this correct? Explain using the direction of magnetic field lines.

A bar magnet of magnetic moment m = 0.50 A·m² is placed in a uniform magnetic field B = 0.20 T. The magnet's axis makes an angle of 30° with the field direction. Calculate (a) the torque acting on the magnet, and (b) the potential energy of the magnet (taking zero potential energy at θ = 90°). Give answers in SI units.

A bar magnet of magnetic moment 0.5 A·m² is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. The magnet’s axis makes an angle of 30° with the field. Calculate the torque on the magnet. Explain why the torque is maximum at 90° and zero at 0°.

A closely wound solenoid of 500 turns, cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², carries a current of 1.5 A. Calculate its magnetic moment. If this solenoid is suspended freely in a uniform horizontal magnetic field of 0.3 T, what is the maximum torque it can experience?

Compare the potential energy of a magnetic dipole in a uniform field at orientations 𝜃 = 0°, 90°, 180°. Which orientation is stable equilibrium? Which is unstable? Justify using the expression 𝑈 = −𝐦·𝐁.

A short bar magnet has magnetic moment 0.48 J/T. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance of 10 cm from the centre on (a) the axial line, (b) the equatorial line. Use μ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ T·m/A.
Fill in the blank: Observe iron ______ on a sheet of paper placed over a bar magnet (a common Class 12 lab activity).
Fill in the blank: Observe iron filings on a sheet of paper placed over a bar magnet (a common Class 12 lab ______).

A magnetic needle free to rotate in a vertical plane aligns itself at an angle of 60° with the horizontal. What is the angle of dip at that location? If the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field is 0.4 G, calculate the total magnetic field.

The magnetic declination at Delhi is 0° 58' E. A compass needle shows a bearing of N 30° E. What is the true geographic bearing? If the angle of dip is 42° and H_E = 0.35 G, find the vertical component and total field.

Two places A and B have the same horizontal component H_E = 0.3 G. At A, δ = 30°; at B, δ = 60°. Compare the total magnetic field and vertical component at the two places. Which place has stronger total field? Why does H_E remain constant while δ changes?
A student solves: "Given δ = 45°, H_E = 0.4 G, find B_E." They write: B_E = H_E × cos 45° = 0.4 × 0.707 = 0.283 G. Identify the error and give the correct solution. Why is this error common?

Fill in the blank: Earth's magnetic field at any location is completely described by three ______ elements: (1) Magnetic Declination (D) — the angle between the geographic meridian and the magnetic meridian, measured in degrees east or west; (2) Angle of Dip or Inclination (δ) — the angle made by the total Earth's magnetic field vector with the horizontal plane in the magnetic meridian, positive downward in the northern hemisphere; (3) Horizontal Component (H_E) — the component of Earth's total magnetic field along the horizontal direction in the magnetic meridian, measured in tesla (T) or gauss (1 G = 10⁻⁴ T).

A student measures the magnetisation M of a material placed in a uniform magnetic intensity H = 500 A/m and finds M = -0.005 A/m. What is the magnetic susceptibility χ, and how would you classify this material?

A solenoid of 1000 turns/m carries a current of 2 A. Its core is a material with relative permeability μᵣ = 400. Calculate: (a) H, (b) B, (c) M, and (d) the magnetising current Iₘ that would produce the same B without the core.

A paramagnetic salt follows Curie's law: χ = C/T. At T = 300 K, its susceptibility is 2×10⁻³. The salt is placed in a solenoid with H = 10⁴ A/m. If the temperature is lowered to 150 K while keeping H constant, by what factor does the magnetisation M change?

A solenoid of length 0.5 m has 1000 turns and carries a current of 2 A. Its core is made of soft iron with relative permeability μᵣ = 5000. Calculate the magnetic field B inside the core. (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A)

A ferromagnetic rod placed in a solenoid of 1500 turns/m carrying 0.8 A acquires a magnetisation M = 1.2 × 10⁶ A/m. Calculate (a) H, (b) χ, (c) relative permeability μr, and (d) the magnetic field B inside the rod. (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A)
A circular coil of radius 5 cm has 100 turns and is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. What is the magnetic flux linked with the coil? State the SI unit of magnetic flux.

In Faraday's Experiment 6.3 (two stationary coils, one connected to battery via tapping key), the galvanometer shows a momentary deflection when the key is pressed and released, but zero deflection when held pressed. Explain WHY this happens using the concept of magnetic flux and its rate of change.

A square loop of side 20 cm and resistance 2 Ω is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The field is reduced to zero uniformly in 0.4 s. Calculate the magnitude of induced emf and the induced current in the loop.

A student solves Example 6.2 from NCERT but writes: "Initial flux = BA = 0.1 × 0.01 = 0.001 Wb" (using side 10 cm = 0.1 m, area = 0.01 m², but forgetting cos45°). They get ε = 1.43 mV instead of 1.0 mV. Identify the error and explain why the angle between area vector and magnetic field matters.

A rectangular loop of wire (width w = 0.20 m, length l = 0.40 m) is pulled at constant velocity v = 0.10 m/s out of a region of uniform magnetic field B = 0.50 T directed into the page. The loop's plane is perpendicular to the field. At the instant when half the loop is still in the field, find (a) the magnitude of the induced emf, and (b) the direction of the induced current.

A student argues: "In Experiment 6.1 (NCERT), when the north pole of a magnet is pushed toward a coil, the induced current creates a north pole facing the magnet. This *attracts* the magnet, so the magnet accelerates *toward* the coil without any external work. This violates conservation of energy, so Lenz's law must be wrong." Identify the flaw in this argument and explain what actually happens.

A horizontal rod of length 1.0 m moves horizontally at 5 m/s in a region where Earth's magnetic field has a horizontal component of 0.3 G and a vertical component of 0.4 G. The rod is oriented east-west and moves northward. Which component of Earth's field produces a motional EMF across the rod? Explain why the other component does not contribute.

A metal rod of length 0.8 m rotates in a horizontal plane about one end with an angular speed of 12 rad/s. A uniform vertical magnetic field of 0.5 T exists. Calculate the motional EMF induced between the fixed end and the free end of the rod.

Two identical rods of length l move with the same speed v in the same uniform magnetic field B . Rod A moves perpendicular to B with its length also perpendicular to both v and B . Rod B moves at 45° to B , but its length is adjusted to be perpendicular to both v and B . Compare the motional EMF induced across the two rods.

Design a simple classroom demonstration of motional EMF using only a strong neodymium magnet, a 30 cm aluminium ruler, a sensitive galvanometer (or a phone with a magnetic sensor app), and connecting wires. Describe the procedure, the expected observation, and how you would verify the mathcalE ∝ v relationship.

A long solenoid of length 0.5 m, cross-sectional area 10 cm², and 1000 turns carries a current of 2.0 A. The current is reduced uniformly to zero in 0.1 s. Calculate (a) the self-inductance of the solenoid, (b) the magnitude of the average induced emf, and (c) the magnetic energy initially stored. (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m)

Two concentric circular coils of radii r₁ = 2 cm and r₂ = 20 cm (r₁ ≪ r₂) are placed coaxially. The larger coil carries a current I₂ = 5.0 A. Calculate the mutual inductance M and the flux through the smaller coil. If the current in the larger coil is reversed in 0.01 s, find the average induced emf in the smaller coil. (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m)

A student solves a problem: "Self-inductance of a solenoid is 5 mH. Current changes from 2 A to 4 A in 0.1 s. Find induced emf." The student writes ε = -L(I_f - I_i)/Δt = -5 × 10⁻³ × (4-2)/0.1 = -0.1 V, then says "magnitude is 0.1 V, direction opposes the increase in current." Is the solution fully correct? Identify any missing step or conceptual gap.
A coil of 200 turns and area 0.15 m² rotates at 60 revolutions per second in a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. Calculate the maximum emf generated. (Use π = 3.14)
In an AC generator, the coil rotates at 50 Hz. The induced emf is ε = ε₀ sin(ωt). At what time after t=0 does the emf first reach half its maximum value? (Give answer in milliseconds.)
A solenoid of self-inductance 40 mH carries a steady current of 2.5 A . Calculate the magnetic energy stored. If the current is doubled, by what factor does the stored energy change?

An induction furnace uses a high-frequency alternating magnetic field (f = 10 kHz) to melt a cylindrical iron ingot (radius r = 5 cm, height h = 20 cm, resistivity ρ = 10⁻⁷ Ω·m). Estimate the order of magnitude of the eddy current power loss per unit volume if the peak magnetic field is B₀ = 0.5 T. Use the approximate formula for a long cylinder: P/V ≈ (π² B₀² f² r²)/(8ρ).
What is the RMS value of a sinusoidal AC voltage whose peak value is 300 V? State the formula used and the final answer with units.

The voltage across a household socket is rated as 220 V AC. A student says, "The voltage reaches 220 V at its peak." Is this statement correct? Explain why or why not, and state what the actual peak voltage is.

A 60 W incandescent bulb is designed for a 220 V RMS AC supply. Calculate: (a) the resistance of the bulb filament (assume constant), (b) the peak voltage across the filament, and (c) the RMS current through the bulb. Show all steps with units.
Two AC sources produce sinusoidal voltages: Source A has vm = 200 V, Source B has Vrms = 150 V. Which source delivers more average power to an identical 100 Ω resistive load? Justify quantitatively.

A student solves Example 7.1 from NCERT (100 W bulb, 220 V supply) and writes: "Peak current im = P/vm = 100 W / 311 V = 0.322 A." Identify the error in this reasoning and provide the correct calculation for peak current.
Fill in the blank: Observe the ceiling fan in your classroom — it runs on the 220 V AC mains ______.
Fill in the blank: Observe the ceiling fan in your ______ — it runs on the 220 V AC mains supply.

State the phase relationship between voltage and current in a purely resistive AC circuit. What is the phase angle φ? Write the expression for instantaneous current if the applied voltage is v = 300 sin(100πt) volt and resistance is 50 Ω.

An electric heater rated at 1500 W, 240 V (RMS) is connected to a 240 V, 50 Hz AC mains supply. Calculate: (a) the resistance of the heater element, (b) the peak voltage across it, (c) the RMS current through it, and (d) the peak current through it.

The voltage across a pure resistor is given by v = 200 sin(314t) V. The average power dissipated is measured to be 50 W. Determine the resistance R and the RMS current Irms. Sketch the phasor diagram showing V and I phasors at an instant when ωt = π/4.
Fill in the blank: Observe an ______ bulb in your home — it glows steadily when connected to the 220 V, 50 Hz mains supply, even though the current reverses direction 100 times per second.

A pure inductor of 40 mH is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz AC supply. Calculate (a) the inductive reactance, (b) the rms current, (c) the peak current, and (d) write the instantaneous current equation if the voltage is v = 311 sin(100π t) volts.

Two identical inductors are connected to AC sources of different frequencies: f₁ = 50 Hz and f₂ = 200 Hz. The rms voltage is the same in both cases. Compare the reactances, rms currents, and the phase differences. Explain the trend.
A student calculates the average power in a pure inductive circuit as P = V_(rms) I_(rms) = 220 × 5 = 1100 W. Identify the error and state the correct average power with justification.

Design a simple experiment using a function generator, an inductor, a dual-trace CRO, and a current-measuring resistor to demonstrate that the current through an inductor lags the voltage by 90°. Describe the connections, what you would observe on the CRO, and how you would measure the phase difference.
In a pure capacitive AC circuit, the current leads the voltage by 90°. Explain physically why this phase lead occurs, using the concept of charging and discharging of the capacitor.
A 20 µF capacitor is connected to a 240 V (rms), 50 Hz AC supply. Calculate: (a) the capacitive reactance, (b) the rms current, and (c) the peak current.
A series LCR circuit has R = 40 Ω, L = 0.12 H, C = 25 μF, and is connected to a 230 V, 50 Hz AC supply. Calculate (a) the impedance Z, (b) the rms current I, and (c) the phase angle φ.

At resonance in a series LCR circuit, the voltage across the inductor is measured as 150 V (rms) and the voltage across the capacitor is also 150 V (rms). The source voltage is 20 V (rms). Explain how the source voltage can be smaller than the individual voltages across L and C.

Fill in the blank: In a series LCR circuit connected to an AC source, impedance (Z) is the total effective ______ to current flow, combining resistance (R), inductive reactance (Xₗ = ωL), and capacitive reactance (X꜀ = 1/ωC) as a phasor sum: Z = √[R² + (Xₗ - X꜀)²].
What is the resonant angular frequency ω₀ of a series LCR circuit with L = 2.0 H and C = 50 μF? State the formula and compute the numerical value in rad/s.

In a series LCR circuit at resonance, the voltage across the inductor is measured as 300 V (rms) while the source voltage is only 50 V (rms). A student claims this violates Kirchhoff's voltage law. Explain why the student is wrong using phasor concepts.

A series LCR circuit has R = 20 Ω, L = 1.5 H, C = 35 μF. It is connected to a 200 V (rms), variable-frequency AC supply. Calculate: (a) the resonant frequency f₀ in Hz, (b) the rms current at resonance, (c) the rms voltage across the inductor at resonance, (d) the quality factor Q.

Two series LCR circuits have identical L and C but different resistances: Circuit A has R = 10 Ω, Circuit B has R = 100 Ω. Both are driven at their resonant frequency by the same voltage amplitude vm. Compare: (i) the peak current in each circuit, (ii) the quality factor Q, (iii) the bandwidth Δω, (iv) the voltage across the capacitor at resonance.

A student solves a resonance problem and writes: "At resonance, XL = XC = 0, so Z = R." Evaluate this statement. Is it correct? If not, what is the correct condition and why is the student's version wrong?

Design a simple experiment using a function generator, an oscilloscope, a resistor (100 Ω), an inductor (10 mH), and a capacitor (0.1 μF) to demonstrate resonance in a series LCR circuit. Describe the procedure, what to measure, and how to identify the resonant frequency from the oscilloscope display.

Fill in the blank: Resonance in a series LCR circuit occurs when the inductive reactance (XL = ωL) equals the ______ reactance (XC = 1/ωC), causing the impedance to become purely resistive (Z = R) and minimum, the current amplitude to reach its maximum value (im = vm/R), and the phase difference between voltage and current to become zero.

In a series LCR circuit, the voltage across the inductor is 120 V, across the capacitor is 80 V, and across the resistor is 60 V (all RMS). The source voltage is 100 V RMS. A student claims the power factor is 0.6 because V_R/V_source = 60/100 = 0.6. Is this reasoning correct? Explain why or why not.

A series LCR circuit has R = 40 Ω, X_L = 70 Ω, X_C = 30 Ω, and is connected to a 230 V, 50 Hz RMS supply. Calculate: (a) the impedance Z, (b) the RMS current, (c) the power factor, and (d) the average power dissipated.

Two circuits are connected to the same 220 V, 50 Hz RMS supply. Circuit A: pure resistance 50 Ω. Circuit B: resistance 30 Ω in series with inductive reactance 40 Ω. Compare the power factor, RMS current, and average power in both circuits. Which circuit draws more current from the supply for the same real power output? Explain the practical implication for transmission lines.

A factory operates at 400 V RMS, 50 Hz with an inductive load drawing 100 A RMS at a power factor of 0.7 lagging. The management installs a capacitor bank in parallel to improve the power factor to 0.95 lagging. A student calculates the required capacitive reactance as X_C = V² / (P tan φ) and gets 12.5 Ω. Evaluate this calculation: identify the error and compute the correct X_C.

In an LC circuit, the capacitor is initially fully charged. When the capacitor discharges completely (q = 0), a student claims the current must also be zero because "no charge means no current." Is this correct? Explain using energy conservation.

A step-down transformer has 500 turns on the primary and 50 turns on the secondary. If the primary is connected to 230 V (rms) mains, what is the secondary voltage? Explain why the secondary current is larger than the primary current for a resistive load.

A transformer draws 0.5 A (rms) from a 220 V (rms) supply and delivers 12 V (rms) to a load drawing 8 A (rms). Calculate (a) the turns ratio Np:Ns, (b) the input power, (c) the output power, and (d) the efficiency.

Design a simple experiment using a low-voltage AC source (e.g., 6 V from a lab transformer), two coils of different turns, and a multimeter to verify the turns-ratio voltage relationship. List the steps, measurements, and how you would account for non-idealities.
Fill in the blank: Observe a phone charger: it plugs into 230 V ______ but outputs 5 V for the battery.
Fill in the blank: ______ a phone charger: it plugs into 230 V mains but outputs 5 V for the battery.
A parallel plate capacitor with circular plates of radius 10 cm is being charged by a steady current of 0.5 A. What is the displacement current between the plates? (Assume no edge effects.)

A parallel plate capacitor of plate area A = 2.0 × 10⁻² m² has a time-varying electric field E(t) = (3.0 × 10⁴ V/m) sin(2π × 10⁶ t) between its plates. Calculate the displacement current at t = 0 . (Given varepsilon₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m .)

In a charging capacitor, the conduction current i꜀ in the connecting wires is 2.0 A. At a point P outside the capacitor but near the wire, the magnetic field is measured. At a point M between the plates, at the same radial distance from the axis, the magnetic field is also measured. How do the two magnetic fields compare? Explain using the Ampere-Maxwell law.

A plane electromagnetic wave propagates in vacuum along the +z direction. At a given instant, the electric field is along +x and has magnitude E₀ = 100 V/m. Using the relation from Maxwell's equations, calculate the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field at that instant.

Why are microwaves (λ ~ 1 mm – 30 cm) used in radar for aircraft navigation, while radio waves (λ > 1 m) are not suitable for precise distance measurement? Explain using the relationship between wavelength and resolution.
A microwave oven operates at 2.45 GHz. Calculate: (a) the wavelength in cm, (b) the photon energy in eV. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

Design a simple experiment using household items to demonstrate that UV radiation is blocked by ordinary glass but visible light passes through. Specify: (1) UV source, (2) detector/indicator, (3) control, (4) expected observation.
A plane EM wave in vacuum has electric field amplitude E₀ = 120 N/C. Without calculating, explain why the magnetic field amplitude must be B₀ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ T. What physical principle fixes this ratio?

A radio station broadcasts at f = 98.3 MHz with an average intensity I = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ W/m² at a certain distance. Calculate (a) the wavelength λ, (b) the electric field amplitude E₀, and (c) the radiation pressure on a perfectly absorbing surface at that location.

Compare the average electric energy density ⟨ u_E ⟩ and average magnetic energy density ⟨ u_B ⟩ in a plane EM wave in vacuum. If the wave enters a dielectric with varepsilon_r = 4, μ_r = 1, how do ⟨ u_E ⟩ and ⟨ u_B ⟩ change relative to each other? Justify.

A student argues: “Since light carries momentum, a flashlight should recoil like a gun when turned on. Why don’t we observe this?” Evaluate this statement quantitatively. Estimate the recoil force of a 5 W flashlight and compare it to the weight of a mosquito (mg ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁵ N).
State the frequency range and production mechanism for radio waves as per NCERT Class 12. What is the wavelength range corresponding to the FM radio band (88–108 MHz)?
A microwave oven operates at 2.45 GHz. Explain why this specific frequency is chosen, referencing the interaction with water molecules. Why don't radio waves at 100 MHz heat food effectively?

An X-ray tube operates at 50 kV. Calculate the minimum wavelength of X-rays produced (in nm). If the tube current is 10 mA, how many photons per second are produced assuming all electron kinetic energy converts to X-ray photons of this minimum wavelength? (Use h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3×10⁸ m/s, e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C)

Compare the penetration ability of radio waves (λ = 10 m), microwaves (λ = 3 cm), and X-rays (λ = 0.1 nm) through: (a) a brick wall, (b) human soft tissue, (c) a metal sheet. Explain each case using the relationship between wavelength and interaction with matter.

Fill in the blank: ______ waves are self-propagating oscillations of mutually perpendicular electric and magnetic fields that travel through vacuum at speed c = 3×10⁸ m/s; their applications exploit specific wavelength/frequency bands — radio waves (λ > 0.1 m) for communication via accelerated charges in antennas, microwaves (λ = 1 mm to 0.1 m) for radar and dielectric heating via resonant molecular excitation, and X-rays (λ = 10⁻⁸ m to 10⁻¹³ m) for medical imaging and therapy via high-energy photon interactions with matter.
A concave mirror of radius of curvature 30 cm is used. A student writes the focal length as f = +15 cm. Is this correct? Explain using the sign convention.
An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. Using the Cartesian sign convention, write the values of u and f with correct signs and units.

Fill in the blank: Reflection of light is the ______ where a light ray, incident on a smooth surface, bounces back into the same medium following two laws: (1) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r), and (2) the incident ray, reflected ray, and the normal to the surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

A concave mirror of focal length 15 cm forms a real image three times the size of the object. Explain why the object distance must be negative and calculate its value. Why does the magnification formula have a negative sign?

An object of height 4.0 cm is placed 25 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature 30 cm. Calculate: (a) the focal length, (b) the image distance, (c) the magnification, (d) the image height, and (e) state the nature of the image. Show all steps with units.

A convex mirror of focal length 20 cm forms an image of a car located 10 m behind the mirror. Compare the image distance and magnification when the car is at 10 m versus at 5 m. Explain the trend without calculation, then verify numerically.

Design a simple experiment using a concave mirror, a screen, and a metre scale to verify the mirror formula. Specify how you would choose at least 5 object positions, what measurements to take, and how to plot a graph to determine the focal length. Include how to handle sign convention in your data table.

Fill in the blank: The mirror formula relates the object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) of a spherical mirror through the equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, where distances are measured from the pole using the Cartesian sign ______.

A ray of light travels from water (n = 1.33) into crown glass (n = 1.52). Will the ray bend towards the normal or away from the normal? Explain using the concept of optical density and the speed of light in the two media.
A light ray in air (n = 1.00) strikes a glass slab (n = 1.50) at an angle of incidence of 35°. Calculate the angle of refraction inside the glass. Give your answer in degrees to one decimal place.

A student performs the glass slab experiment and obtains the following data for sin i and sin r: | sin i | 0.20 | 0.40 | 0.60 | 0.80 | | sin r | 0.13 | 0.26 | 0.39 | 0.52 | Plot sin i vs sin r mentally. What does the slope represent? If the student accidentally swapped the axes (plotting sin r on y-axis and sin i on x-axis), what would the slope represent then?

A ray of light passes from medium A (n = 1.6) to medium B (n = 1.2). The angle of incidence is 40°. A student calculates the angle of refraction as 60°. Evaluate this answer. Is it physically possible? If not, what phenomenon occurs instead?
A ray of light travels from glass (n = 1.5) to air (n = 1.0). The angle of incidence is 40°. Will total internal reflection occur? Justify your answer by calculating the critical angle and comparing.

Calculate the critical angle for a diamond-air interface (refractive index of diamond = 2.42). If a light ray inside diamond strikes the diamond-air interface at an angle of incidence of 30°, what is the angle of refraction in air? Explain why this property makes diamonds sparkle.

An optical fiber has a core of refractive index 1.68 and cladding of refractive index 1.44. (a) Calculate the critical angle for the core-cladding interface. (b) A ray enters the fiber from air at the maximum acceptance angle such that it undergoes TIR at the core-cladding interface. Derive the expression for the numerical aperture (NA) of the fiber in terms of n_core and n_cladding, and compute its value.

A plano-convex lens has its plane surface facing the object. The curved surface has radius of curvature R = 20 cm. The lens material has refractive index n = 1.5. Calculate the focal length of the lens in air. Use Cartesian sign convention.

A biconvex lens of focal length 20 cm in air is cut into two identical plano-convex lenses by a plane through its principal axis. Each plano-convex lens is then placed with its plane side facing the object. What is the focal length of each plano-convex lens? Justify your answer.

Fill in the blank: The lens maker's formula relates the focal length (f) of a thin lens to the refractive index of its material (n₂) relative to the ______ medium (n₁) and the radii of curvature (R₁, R₂) of its two spherical surfaces: 1/f = (n₂/n₁ - 1)(1/R₁ - 1/R₂).

A student writes the lens formula as (1)/(v) + (1)/(u) = (1)/(f) and uses it for a convex lens with object at 30 cm (u = -30 cm) and f = 10 cm. They get v = 7.5 cm. Explain why the formula and sign usage are incorrect. What is the correct image distance and nature?

A convex lens of focal length 20 cm forms a real image of an object placed 30 cm from the lens. Calculate the image distance, magnification, and image height if the object height is 4 cm. State the nature of the image.

A concave lens of focal length -15 cm is used to view an object placed 10 cm from it. Without calculation, predict: (a) sign of image distance v, (b) sign of magnification m, (c) whether image is real or virtual, (d) whether image is magnified or diminished. Justify using the lens formula qualitatively.

Two thin lenses of focal lengths +20 cm and –30 cm are placed in contact. An object is placed 40 cm from the combination. Find the position and nature of the final image. (Use Cartesian sign convention: u = -40cm.)

Two combinations are made: (A) a convex lens of focal length 10 cm and a concave lens of focal length 20 cm; (B) two convex lenses each of focal length 20 cm. Compare the effective focal lengths and powers. Which combination has greater converging ability?

A student solves a problem: "Two lenses of powers +3 D and –1 D are in contact. Find the focal length of the combination." Their working: P = 3 + 1 = 4D, F = 1/4 = 0.25m. Identify the error and give the correct answer.

A ray of light is incident on one face of a prism of refracting angle A = 60° at an angle of incidence i = 45°. The ray emerges from the other face at an angle of emergence e = 55°. What is the angle of deviation δ? (Recall the formula relating δ, i, e, and A.)

A prism of refracting angle A = 60° and refractive index n = 1.5 is placed in air. Calculate the angle of minimum deviation Dm. Then find the angle of incidence i required to achieve this minimum deviation.

A ray of light is incident at an angle i = 30° on one face of a prism with A = 60° and n = 1.6. The ray undergoes total internal reflection at the second face. Determine whether this is possible. If yes, find the angle of refraction r1 at the first face and the angle of incidence r2 at the second face. (Critical angle for glass-air interface: sin ic = 1/n.)

A thin prism of angle A = 4° is made of crown glass (n_y = 1.52, n_v = 1.53, n_r = 1.51). Calculate the angular dispersion (δ_v - δ_r) and the dispersive power ω. A student calculates ω = (n_v - n_r)/n_y. Is this correct? Justify.
What is the magnifying power of a simple microscope when the final image is formed at the near point (D = 25 cm) in terms of its focal length f?
Why does a simple microscope provide angular magnification even though the angular size of the object equals the angular size of the image (as stated in NCERT Points to Ponder 5)?
A student uses a convex lens of focal length 5 cm as a simple microscope. Calculate the magnifying power when (a) the image is at the near point (25 cm) and (b) the image is at infinity.

Compare the magnifying power of two simple microscopes: one with f = 2 cm and another with f = 10 cm, both used with the final image at the near point. Which gives higher magnification and why? Discuss the practical limitation of very short focal lengths.
A student claims that if they use a simple microscope with f = 4 cm and place the object at 3 cm from the lens, the magnifying power will be m = v/u (linear magnification). Evaluate this claim.

What is the approximate formula for the magnifying power of a compound microscope when the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision (D = 25 cm)? State the meaning of each symbol.

A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 1.0 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 2.5 cm. The tube length is 16 cm. Calculate the magnifying power when the final image is formed at (a) the near point (25 cm) and (b) at infinity.

A student sets up a compound microscope with fo = 4 mm, fe = 2 cm, and tube length L = 16 cm. She claims the magnifying power is 2000 when the final image is at infinity. Evaluate her claim and identify the error.

Design a compound microscope to achieve a magnifying power of 400 with the final image at infinity. You have available objective lenses of focal lengths 2 mm, 4 mm, 8 mm, and eyepieces of focal lengths 1 cm, 2 cm, 4 cm. The tube length is fixed at 16 cm. Choose the combination that gives exactly 400 and justify your choice.
What is the magnifying power of an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment if the focal length of the objective is 100 cm and that of the eyepiece is 2 cm? State the formula used.

A telescope has an objective of focal length 140 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5.0 cm. Find the separation between the lenses (tube length) when (a) the final image is at infinity, and (b) the final image is at the least distance of distinct vision (25 cm). Also compute the magnifying power in each case.

An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has a magnifying power of 50 and a tube length of 102 cm. Find the focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece. If the same telescope is used to view an object at a finite distance (say 1 km), will the magnifying power change? Explain qualitatively.

Design a simple experiment using two convex lenses (one of focal length 50 cm, another of focal length 2 cm) to build an astronomical telescope. Describe how you would adjust it for normal adjustment and for viewing at the near point. What measurements would you take to verify the magnifying power experimentally?

A plane wavefront is incident on a glass slab (refractive index 1.5) at an angle of 30° to the normal. Using Huygens' construction, find the angle of the refracted wavefront inside the glass. Speed of light in vacuum = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Show the geometric steps.

In the Huygens' construction for refraction (Fig. 10.4 of NCERT), why is the refracted wavefront CE drawn as a tangent from point C to the sphere centered at A with radius v₂t, and not as the backwave? What physical assumption justifies ignoring the backwave?

A plane wave of wavelength 500 nm in air (n = 1.00) enters a glass slab (n = 1.50) at an angle of incidence 30°. Calculate (a) the angle of refraction, (b) the speed of light in glass, and (c) the wavelength of light in glass. (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s)

A hydrogen spectral line has a rest wavelength of 656.3 nm (Hα). In a distant galaxy's spectrum, this line is observed at 660.0 nm. Is the galaxy moving towards or away from us? Explain how you know without calculating the velocity.
Calculate the radial velocity of the galaxy in Question 2 using the non-relativistic approximation. Express your answer in km/s.

A radar gun emits microwaves of frequency 10 GHz. A car approaches the gun at 30 m/s. The waves reflect off the car and return to the gun. What is the beat frequency between the emitted and received signals? (Hint: The car acts as a moving observer then a moving source.)
Design a simple thought experiment using a spaceship moving at 0.8c towards a star emitting yellow light (λ₀ = 580 nm). What colour would the astronaut see? Justify using the relativistic formula.

Two identical tuning forks of frequency 512 Hz are struck simultaneously. Fork A is at x = 0 m, Fork B is at x = 1.5 m. A microphone at x = 3.0 m detects sound. Speed of sound = 340 m/s. Are the two sources coherent? What is the phase difference at the microphone?

In a Young's double slit experiment, the two slits are illuminated by a single sodium lamp (λ = 589 nm). A student covers one slit with a thin mica sheet of thickness 2 μm and refractive index 1.58. Explain whether the central fringe shifts, and if so, in which direction and by how many fringes.

Two coherent sources S₁ and S₂ emit light of wavelength 600 nm with equal intensity I₀ = 4 W/m². At point P on a screen, the path difference S₂P - S₁P = 450 nm. Calculate the resultant intensity at P. If the sources were incoherent, what would be the intensity at P?

A student sets up Young's double slit with slit separation d = 0.5 mm, screen distance D = 1.2 m, using a He-Ne laser (λ = 632.8 nm). They observe clear fringes. Then they replace the laser with a white light LED bulb placed at the same position. The fringes disappear. Explain why, using the concept of temporal coherence and spectral width. Calculate the coherence length of the LED if its spectral width Δλ = 30 nm at λ = 600 nm.

Evaluate the following statement: "Two independent laser pointers of the same wavelength (650 nm) can produce a stable interference pattern on a screen because lasers are highly coherent sources." Identify the error and explain the correct physics.

In a YDSE, the slits are separated by 0.5 mm and the screen is placed 2 m away. The distance between the central bright fringe and the fourth bright fringe is measured as 2.4 mm. Calculate the wavelength of light used. Express your answer in nanometres.

Two wavelengths λ₁ = 600 nm and λ₂ = 450 nm are used in a YDSE with d = 0.3 mm and D = 1.5 m. Find the least distance from the central maximum where the bright fringes of the two wavelengths coincide.
A student performs YDSE with λ = 500 nm, d = 0.4 mm, D = 1 m. They claim the 10th dark fringe is at x = 11.25 mm. Is this correct? Justify your answer.
In a Young's double slit experiment, λ = 600 nm, d = 0.5 mm, D = 2.0 m. Calculate (a) the fringe width β, and (b) the distance of the 3rd bright fringe from the central maximum.

State Malus's law in words and give the mathematical formula with SI units for each quantity. What is the transmitted intensity when the angle between the pass-axes is 60° if the incident polarized intensity is 10 W/m²?

Unpolarized light of intensity I_(inc) falls on a polaroid P1. The transmitted light then passes through a second polaroid P2 whose pass-axis is at 30° to that of P1. A student claims the final intensity is I_(inc) cos² 30°. Is this correct? Explain why or why not, and give the correct expression.

Two polaroids P1 and P2 are crossed (pass-axes at 90°). A third polaroid P3 is inserted between them with its pass-axis at 45° to both P1 and P2. If unpolarized light of intensity 32 W/m² is incident on P1, calculate the intensity emerging from P2. Show all steps with units.

In an experiment, a student uses two polaroids and measures transmitted intensity at various angles. The data shows I = 0 at θ = 90° and I = I_(max) at θ = 0°, but at θ = 30° the measured intensity is 0.6 I_(max) instead of the theoretical 0.75 I_(max). Evaluate possible reasons for this discrepancy. Which reason is most likely in a typical school lab?
In the photoelectric effect experimental setup (NCERT Fig. 11.1), what is the function of the commutator connected to the battery? State the SI unit of the quantity measured by the microammeter.

A student claims: "If we increase the intensity of incident light, the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons increases because more energy is delivered to the surface." Using the experimental results from Fig. 11.2 and Fig. 11.3, explain why this statement is incorrect. What does the stopping potential actually depend on?

Monochromatic light of frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz is incident on a caesium surface (work function φ₀ = 2.14 eV). The stopping potential measured is 0.95 V. (a) Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons in joules. (b) If the intensity of light is doubled while keeping frequency constant, what will be the new stopping potential? (c) How does the saturation current change? Use e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

An experimentalist reports: "For a certain metal, when green light (λ = 530 nm) is used, the stopping potential is 0.8 V. When the same metal is illuminated with yellow light (λ = 580 nm) at the same intensity, the stopping potential is 1.2 V." Evaluate this claim. Is it physically possible? Justify using the relationship between stopping potential and frequency.

Light of wavelength 400 nm is incident on a caesium surface (work function φ₀ = 2.14 eV). Calculate: (a) the energy of each photon in eV, (b) the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons in eV, (c) the stopping potential in volts. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

The graph of stopping potential V₀ versus frequency ν for two metals A and B are straight lines with the same slope but different intercepts on the frequency axis. Metal A has intercept ν_(0A) = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz, metal B has ν_(0B) = 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (a) Which metal has the larger work function? (b) If light of frequency 7.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz is incident on both, which metal will emit photoelectrons? (c) What is the ratio of their work functions φ_(0B)/φ_(0A)?

In a photoelectric experiment, a student plots V₀ vs ν and obtains a straight line with slope 4.12 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s and ν-intercept 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The student calculates Planck's constant as h = slope × e = (4.12 × 10⁻¹⁵)(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.59 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Is this calculation correct? If not, identify the error and give the correct value.

Imagine a massive reserve of high-grade iron ore is discovered 5 kilometers deep beneath a dense forest in Central India. The cost of digging a 5-km-deep shaft and restoring the forest is estimated at ₹10,000 per ton, while the market price of iron ore is ₹4,000 per ton. Apply the resource criteria to determine if this iron ore can currently be classified as an economic resource.

Compare the wind blowing across the Thar Desert of Rajasthan 200 years ago with the wind blowing there today. Analyze how the status of wind changed from a mere natural phenomenon to an important resource.

Propose a 3-step framework or checklist that a local government in Ladakh should use to decide whether the hot springs (geothermal energy) in the region should be developed into a sustainable energy resource.

A thermal power station in West Bengal consumes 15,000 tonnes of Gondwana coal per day. A nearby geological survey identifies a local reserve of 54.75 million tonnes. Assuming no other consumers and uniform daily consumption, calculate the lifespan of this coal reserve in years (take 1 year = 365 days).
Evaluate the geographical and economic consequence if an industrial region depends 100% on imported petroleum for its transport and thermal energy needs.
Propose a spatial transition plan for an Indian industrial district currently running entirely on coal from the Raniganj basin to systematically reduce non-renewable depletion over a 20-year period.

A residential community in Bengaluru uses 50,000 liters of water daily. By installing rooftop rainwater harvesting and greywater recycling systems, they save 40% of their daily fresh water requirement. Calculate the total volume of fresh water conserved by the community in a 30-day month.
Design a 3-step action plan for a school situated in a drought-prone region of Maharashtra to achieve self-sufficiency in non-potable water use through individual and community actions.

A degraded agricultural block of 100 hectares in Rajasthan receives 400 mm of annual rainfall, but 70% of it is lost as surface runoff, leaving soil moisture depleted. A urban development board proposes building a paved industrial zone over an urban wetland, offering to offset it by planting 5,000 ornamental trees along roadsides. Evaluate this plan from a regenerative geography perspective.

Evaluate whether calling groundwater "unlimited renewable energy" in this village's master plan is geographically accurate, and justify your answer.

A timber cooperative harvests 1,500 cubic meters per square kilometer annually from this zone. An industrial district plans to meet its rising energy and water demands by clearing 200 hectares of mangrove forests along the Odisha coast to build coal yards and desalination intake pipes, arguing this brings economic growth. Evaluate this proposal from the perspective of long-term sustainable resource management.

A district in Rajasthan has an annual groundwater recharge rate of 120 million cubic meters (mcm). The agricultural sector pumps out 150 mcm annually, while domestic use requires 20 mcm. Calculate the annual groundwater deficit and predict the long-term physical impact on the local aquifer.

Propose a 3-step community-level land management plan for a hilly village in Uttarakhand facing severe soil erosion due to overgrazing and deforestation.

A development board must select a site for a 500 MW solar plant. Site A is a flat desert region in western Rajasthan with 320 sunny days annually. Site B is a dense valley in Meghalaya with heavy forest canopy and high yearly monsoon rainfall. Which site should be chosen, and why?
