If a patient sample gives 50 % inhibition, what is the drug concentration in the sample? (1 mark)

**APPLICATION:** A biotech startup wants to produce the flavonoid quercetin in Escherichia coli. They have cloned the plant phenylpropanoid pathway (PAL, C4H, 4CL) and the flavonoid pathway (CHS, CHI, F3H, FLS). However, quercetin titre is < 5 mg/L. Suggest three metabolic engineering interventions to improve yield, explaining the biochemical rationale for each.
A researcher isolates a *Bacillus* mutant that forms spores but they are killed by 80 °C for 10 min, whereas wild‑type spores survive. Propose the most likely genetic lesion and justify.

**Application:** You are given a set of 20 clinical *E. coli* isolates. All are resistant to ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin. Design a workflow to determine whether resistance is plasmid‑mediated and, if so, whether the plasmids are conjugative.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** (a) Define “R plasmid” and list two features that distinguish it from a typical cryptic plasmid. (2 marks) (b) Explain how the *tra* operon facilitates conjugative transfer. (3 marks) (c) A hospital isolates *P. aeruginosa* resistant to meropenem, gentamicin, and ciprofloxacin. The resistance genes are located on a 120 kb plasmid that transfers to *E. coli* at 10⁻⁴ per donor. Discuss the clinical implications. (5 marks)
State Mendel’s law of segregation and explain how his monohybrid cross data supports it. (3 marks)
Describe Mendel’s law of segregation. Explain how the behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis provides a physical basis for this law. (4 marks)

A farmer observes that in his wheat field, plant height ranges from 60 cm to 110 cm with a bell‑shaped distribution. Propose the most likely genetic architecture of this trait and justify your answer.

A researcher studies a trait in Drosophila where the phenotype is “curly wings”. The trait appears in both sexes equally, and when a curly‑winged fly is crossed with a normal fly, all F1 progeny have curly wings. In the F2 generation, the ratio is 3 curly : 1 normal. (a) Identify the mode of inheritance. (b) State the genotypes of the parental, F1, and F2 generations using appropriate symbols. (c) Explain why this trait is classified as a qualitative trait.

An ISC 2023 Biotechnology paper asked: “A couple, both phenotypically normal, have a daughter with a rare autosomal recessive disorder. They are planning a second child. (a) What is the probability that the second child will be affected? (b) If the second child is a son, what is the probability he will be a carrier? (c) Explain how you would construct a pedigree for this family up to the second child.”
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Define gene. Explain how the concept of allele arises from the structure of a gene.” (3 marks)

A past CISCE ISC paper asked: “Explain how the concept of multiple alleles is illustrated by the ABO blood group system. Why does an individual still have only two alleles?” Write a model answer suitable for 4 marks.

In a pedigree, an autosomal dominant disease shows 70 % penetrance. If a heterozygous affected parent has four children, what is the probability that exactly two children display the disease phenotype?

A farmer grows a drought‑tolerant maize variety (genotype DD) and a susceptible variety (dd) in the same field. In a dry year, the DD plants yield 5 t/ha, dd yield 1 t/ha. In a wet year, both yield 6 t/ha. Calculate the genotype‑by‑environment interaction effect for the DD genotype.

(a) Define penetrance and expressivity. (b) A dominant allele for polydactyly has 60 % penetrance and variable expressivity (extra digit on one hand to both hands and feet). In a family, an affected heterozygous parent has three children, all genotypically heterozygous. What is the probability that exactly two children show any polydactyly? (c) If the two affected children each have a 70 % chance of expressing the trait on both hands, what is the probability that both show bilateral expression?

A past CISCE ISC paper asked: “Define genotype. How does it differ from phenotype? Give one example where two different genotypes produce the same phenotype.” Provide a model answer structured for 4 marks.

**APPLICATION:** A couple undergoes pre‑implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) for an autosomal dominant disorder (allele *D*). The father is heterozygous (*Dd*), the mother is homozygous normal (*dd*). They produce 8 embryos. How many embryos are expected to be heterozygous, and what is the zygosity of the unaffected embryos?

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Define hemizygosity. (b) A male child is born with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X‑linked recessive). His mother is phenotypically normal. What is the mother’s genotype and zygosity? (c) If the couple has another son, what is the probability he will be affected? (Marks: 1+2+1)

A couple seeks genetic counselling. The man has an autosomal dominant condition (Aa) with 90 % penetrance; the woman is unaffected (aa). They want to know the probability that their first child will be phenotypically affected. Calculate this probability.

(a) Draw a pedigree for three generations showing an autosomal dominant trait with complete penetrance, indicating genotypes. (b) If the trait shows 70 % penetrance, how does the pedigree interpretation change? (c) Calculate the recurrence risk for a grandchild of an affected individual, assuming the intermediate parent is phenotypically normal.
In an ISC exam, a question asks: “Explain why the ABO blood‑group system is an example of co‑dominance and not incomplete dominance.” Write a concise answer suitable for 3 marks.

An ISC 2023 paper asked: “In a cross between a man of blood group A (genotype IAi) and a woman of blood group AB, what is the probability of having a child with blood group B? Show the genetic cross.” Provide the answer with a Punnett square.

A past ISC paper asks: “In a monohybrid cross involving a recessive allele, the F₂ phenotypic ratio is 3:1. If 1600 F₂ individuals are observed, how many are expected to show the recessive phenotype? If the observed number is 380, perform a chi‑square test at 5 % significance level and state your conclusion.”

In a human population, height is a polygenic trait influenced by at least 10 additive loci. If you randomly sample 1000 individuals, describe the expected shape of the height distribution histogram and explain why.
A CISCE ISC question asks: “Explain why polygenic inheritance leads to continuous variation in a population.” Write a concise answer that would earn full marks (3 marks).

(a) Define “transgressive segregation” in the context of polygenic inheritance. (2 marks) (b) Give a genetic explanation for why transgressive segregation can occur in the F₂ of a cross between two pure‑line parents. (3 marks) (c) How would a breeder exploit transgressive segregation to develop a new variety? (2 marks)

A past ISC paper asks: “Explain how polygenic inheritance and environmental factors together produce the continuous variation observed in human skin colour.” Provide a structured answer suitable for 5 marks.

**HOTS:** A novel gene *X* is discovered in a plant. Knock‑out mutants show (1) dwarf stature, (2) early flowering, and (3) altered leaf morphology. Overexpression lines show the opposite phenotypes. Propose a molecular mechanism that could explain how a single gene produces these three distinct developmental effects.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “In a certain plant, a single gene controls both flower colour (purple dominant to white) and seed texture (smooth dominant to wrinkled). A plant heterozygous for both traits is self‑pollinated. What is the expected phenotypic ratio in the progeny?” (Adapted from ISC 2018)
In a pedigree, a woman carries a heteroplasmic mitochondrial mutation at 60 % mutant load. She has three children. Predict the mitochondrial mutant load in each child.

(a) Define heteroplasmy and homoplasmy in the context of mitochondrial genetics. (b) A woman has a heteroplasmic mutation at 40 % mutant load. The disease threshold is 60 %. She has a daughter who, due to the mitochondrial bottleneck, inherits a mutant load of 65 %. Will the daughter be affected? (c) Explain why the bottleneck can cause such a shift in mutant load between generations.
In a population, the frequency of the haemophilia A allele (q) is 0.001. Assuming Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium, calculate the expected frequency of affected males and carrier females.
A test cross of a dihybrid (AaBb) with a double recessive (aabb) yields 420 progeny: 190 AB, 185 ab, 22 Ab, 23 aB. Calculate the recombination frequency and state whether the genes are linked.
Explain why a recombination frequency of 50 % does not prove that two genes are on different chromosomes.
In a test cross, the observed phenotypic ratio is 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. What does this indicate about linkage and crossing over?

A CISCE ISC question: “In a dihybrid test cross, 800 progeny are obtained. 380 show parental phenotype 1, 370 show parental phenotype 2, 30 show recombinant phenotype 1, and 20 show recombinant phenotype 2. Calculate the map distance between the genes in centiMorgans.”

A geneticist observes a recombination frequency of 12 % between genes *M* and *N* in maize. She then performs a three‑point cross adding gene *O* and finds the order M‑O‑N with distances M‑O = 7 cM and O‑N = 6 cM. Explain why the sum of the two intervals (13 cM) exceeds the direct M‑N distance (12 cM).

A past CISCE ISC paper asks: “In a test cross involving two linked genes, 1600 progeny are obtained. The recombinant phenotypes together constitute 8 % of the total. How many progeny show each parental phenotype if the parental phenotypes are equally frequent?”
In a test cross of a dihybrid *AaBb* (coupling) × *aabb*, 500 progeny are obtained: 210 *AB*, 190 *ab*, 50 *Ab*, 50 *aB*. What is the COV between genes *A* and *B*?
Why does a raw COV of 25 % underestimate the true genetic distance between two loci?

A three‑point test cross yields the following progeny numbers (parental classes in bold): **ABC** 320, **abc** 310, **Abc** 45, **aBC** 40, **ABc** 12, **abC** 10, **AbC** 3, **aBc** 2. Determine the gene order.
Create a small dataset (≤200 total progeny) for a dihybrid test cross that would give a COV of exactly 12.5 cM. Show the numbers for each phenotypic class.

A CISCE ISC 2023 paper asked: “If the recombination frequency between genes X and Y is 0.35, what is the map distance in centimorgans using Haldane’s mapping function?” Provide the answer with calculation.
A student argues that “since COV is a percentage, it can never exceed 50 %.” Is this statement correct? Justify your answer with reference to the biology of crossing over.

A plant breeder performs a test cross and obtains 1200 progeny. The recombinant classes total 180. The breeder wants to know if the genes are linked at the 1 % significance level using a chi‑square test for independence (expected 1:1:1:1 ratio). Calculate the chi‑square value and state the conclusion.

A past CISCE ISC question: “In a three‑point test cross, the double‑recombinant frequency is 0.02. The single‑recombinant frequencies for intervals A‑B and B‑C are 0.12 and 0.08 respectively. Calculate the coefficient of coincidence and interference.”

A radiology technician receives an average occupational dose of 2 mSv per year from scattered X‑rays. Using the linear no‑threshold (LNT) model, estimate the excess lifetime cancer risk if the technician works for 30 years, given a risk coefficient of 5 % per Sv.

**Application:** A hospital plans to install a new CT scanner. The radiation safety officer must estimate the collective effective dose to the radiology staff who will be in the control room (shielded by 2 mm lead glass) during 2000 scans per year. Each scan delivers 0.02 mSv at the operator position without shielding. Lead glass attenuates 99 % of scattered radiation. Calculate the annual collective dose for 5 staff members.

A factory worker in a dye‑manufacturing unit develops bladder cancer after 15 years of exposure to benzidine‑based dyes. Identify the IARC group of benzidine, the likely metabolic activation pathway, and the characteristic DNA adduct formed.

In an ISC‑style question, a student is asked: “Distinguish between initiation and promotion in chemical carcinogenesis, giving one example of each.” Write a model answer that would earn full marks (4 marks).

**ISC Past‑Paper Pattern (10 marks)** **(a)** Define “tumour promoter” and give one example of a chemical tumour promoter. (2 marks) **(b)** Explain why tumour promoters are not detected in the standard Ames test without modification. (3 marks) **(c)** A researcher treats initiated mouse skin cells with a promoter and observes increased tumour yield. Design a **control experiment** to confirm that the promoter does not cause additional mutations. (5 marks)

A researcher sequences a tumour and finds a single nucleotide substitution in KRAS at codon 12 (GGT → GTT). Explain why this alteration is classified as an oncogenic activation and not a tumour‑suppressor inactivation.
A breast tumour biopsy shows HER2/ERBB2 copy number of 12 per nucleus (normal = 2). Which oncogenic mechanism is operating, and what diagnostic test would confirm it clinically?
In a CISCE ISC exam, a question asks: “Explain how a chromosomal translocation can create an oncogene. Use a named example.” Write a concise answer that would earn full marks (3 marks).
A biopsy report states “invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, ER 80 %, PR 60 %, HER2 1+ (negative), Ki‑67 25 %”. Evaluate the therapeutic implications of this profile.
Apply the TNM system: a 3 cm breast tumour with 2 positive axillary nodes and no distant metastasis. State the stage group.
Design a diagnostic algorithm for a 60‑year‑old male with an elevated PSA of 12 ng/mL and a normal digital rectal exam.
CISCE exam‑style: “A 35‑year‑old woman presents with post‑coital bleeding. Pap smear shows HSIL. Colposcopy‑directed biopsy confirms CIN 3. What is the next appropriate management step?”

**HOTS:** A 50‑year‑old man presents with painless haematuria. CT urography shows a 3 cm enhancing lesion in the left renal pelvis. Urine cytology is negative. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic procedure and why?
**Application:** A hospital introduces a liquid‑biopsy NGS panel (50 genes) for advanced NSCLC. List three pre‑analytical variables that must be controlled to ensure reliable ctDNA detection.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** (a) Define “tumour marker” and give two examples with their associated cancers. (2 marks) (b) Explain the principle of immunohistochemistry (IHC) in cancer diagnosis. (3 marks) (c) A 45‑year‑old female has a 2.5 cm breast tumour, 1 positive axillary node, and bone scan negative. Assign TNM and stage group. (3 marks)

A patient with metastatic EGFR exon‑19 deletion NSCLC is started on osimertinib. After 14 months, CT shows progression. A liquid biopsy detects EGFR T790M and MET amplification. Which next‑line strategy is most appropriate?

**HOTS:** A phase III trial compares adjuvant osimertinib vs. placebo in completely resected EGFR‑mutated (exon 19 del/L858R) stage IB‑IIIA NSCLC (ADAURA). The hazard ratio for disease‑free survival is 0.20 (95% CI 0.14‑0.30). (a) Interpret the hazard ratio and confidence interval in clinical terms. (b) Discuss two potential biases that could exaggerate the benefit. (c) If the 5‑year DFS in the placebo arm is 55%, estimate the 5‑year DFS in the osimertinib arm assuming proportional hazards.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern (Multi‑part):** A 62‑year‑old male with locally advanced rectal cancer (cT3N1M0) undergoes neoadjuvant chemoradiation (CAPOX + 50.4 Gy/28 fractions) followed by total mesorectal excision. Pathology shows ypT2N0 with tumour regression grade 2. (a) Define “tumour regression grade (TRG) 2” in the Mandard system. (b) State the recommended adjuvant chemotherapy regimen and duration per current guidelines. (c) Explain why adjuvant radiotherapy is generally omitted after neoadjuvant chemoradiation in rectal cancer.
If a population has allele frequencies *p = 0.6* and *q = 0.4* for a biallelic locus, what genotype frequencies does the Hardy‑Weinberg law predict?

A researcher observes that a tribal population in Central India has an *FST* value of 0.12 relative to a neighboring caste group for a set of neutral SNPs. Explain what this *FST* indicates about gene flow and genetic differentiation, and discuss one implication for pharmacogenomic studies.

A clinical trial in Mumbai tests a new anti‑diabetic drug. Participants are genotyped for *TCF7L2* rs7903146 (C/T). The observed genotype counts: 180 CC, 150 CT, 20 TT (total 350). (a) Compute allele frequencies. (b) Test Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium. (c) If the T allele is associated with higher drug response, propose how the trial design could incorporate this pharmacogenomic information.

An ISC past‑paper question: “A population of 500 individuals is screened for a recessive disease allele *d*. 45 individuals are affected (dd). Assuming Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium, (i) calculate the frequency of the *d* allele, (ii) estimate the number of carriers, (iii) discuss one limitation of applying HWE to this disease in a real Indian population.”

A village of 200 diploid individuals is fixed for allele *B* at a locus (frequency = 1). Ten migrants arrive, each heterozygous *B/b*. Calculate the new allele frequency of *b* after migration, assuming random mating and no selection.
Create a short scenario (3–4 sentences) illustrating how a new mutation can expand a gene pool and later be acted on by natural selection.

**HOTS:** A population of 1 000 individuals has allele *M* at frequency 0.6. A new mutation creates allele *m* at a rate of 1 × 10⁻⁵ per generation per allele. Assuming no other forces, estimate the number of *m* alleles after 10 generations. Show your reasoning.

**APPLICATION:** In a breeding program, a herd of 200 cattle is fixed for allele *B* (frequency = 1). To introduce allele *b* for heat tolerance, 20 heterozygous *B/b* bulls are added. After one generation of random mating, what is the expected frequency of *b*? Provide the calculation steps.

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE (multi‑part):** (a) A student claims: “If a population is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, its gene pool cannot change.” Critique this statement. (2 marks) (b) Give one real‑world scenario where a population appears to be in HWE but its gene pool is actually changing. (2 marks) (c) Explain why the gene‑pool concept is still useful even when HWE assumptions are violated. (2 marks)

**COMPARISON (multi‑part):** Compare the effects of **mutation** and **migration** on a population’s gene pool by completing the table below. (4 marks) | Feature | Mutation | Migration | |---|---|---| | Source of new alleles | | | | Typical magnitude of allele‑frequency change per generation | | | | Directionality (predictable vs random) | | | | Dependence on population size | | |

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN (multi‑part):** A conservation biologist studies a fragmented population of an endangered frog. Subpopulation A (N = 50) and Subpopulation B (N = 500) are isolated. Both start with allele *F* frequency 0.4. After 15 generations, Subpopulation A shows *F* = 0.65, Subpopulation B shows *F* = 0.42. (a) Which evolutionary force most likely explains the larger shift in Subpopulation A? (1 mark) (b) Calculate the approximate variance in allele frequency due to drift for Subpopulation A after 15 generations, using the formula Var(p) ≈ p₀q₀[1 − (1 − 1/(2N))^t]. (2 marks) (c) Suggest one management action to counteract the loss of genetic diversity in Subpopulation A. (1 mark)
A population of 500 individuals is genotyped for a biallelic locus with alleles *M* and *m*. The observed genotype counts are: *MM* = 180, *Mm* = 240, *mm* = 80. What is the allele frequency of *M*?
Why must the sum of allele frequencies at a locus always equal 1 in a diploid population?
Evaluate the statement: “If allele *A* frequency is 0.7 in a population, then 70 % of individuals must show the dominant phenotype.”

A researcher samples 100 individuals from a village and finds allele *T* frequency = 0.4. She then samples another 100 individuals from a neighbouring village and finds *T* frequency = 0.6. If the two villages merge into a single population of 200, what is the new *T* frequency assuming equal contribution?

Create a hypothetical scenario (with numbers) where allele frequency of a recessive disease allele *d* is 0.02 in a population of 10 000, but the observed number of affected individuals (*dd*) is 5. Explain the discrepancy.

A researcher wants to estimate the allele frequency of a rare variant (*v*) in a large city. She sequences 500 randomly chosen individuals and finds 3 heterozygotes (*Vv*) and no homozygotes (*vv*). Provide a point estimate and a 95 % confidence interval for the allele frequency using the Wilson score interval (you may approximate).
Evaluate the suitability of using allele frequency data from a 1990s Indian census to design a 2025 pharmacogenomic dosing guideline for warfarin.

A past CISCE ISC paper asked: “In a population of 1000 individuals, the frequency of allele *A* is 0.6. Calculate the expected number of heterozygous individuals under Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium.” Provide the answer with steps.
If the frequency of the dominant allele *p* = 0.7 in a population at Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium, what is the expected frequency of heterozygotes? Show your working.
A population has observed genotype frequencies: AA = 0.5, Aa = 0.4, aa = 0.1. Is this population in Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium? Evaluate with calculations.
In a village, 1 in 100 individuals expresses an autosomal recessive disorder. Assuming Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium, estimate the carrier frequency in this village.

A community in Maharashtra has a carrier frequency of 1 in 20 for β‑thalassaemia (autosomal recessive). Assuming Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium, calculate: (a) the allele frequency *q* of the thalassaemia allele, (b) the expected incidence of affected newborns, (c) the number of affected babies expected per 10,000 births.

A research article claims: “Our sample of 50 individuals from an isolated tribe shows genotype frequencies exactly matching Hardy‑Weinberg expectations, proving the tribe is not evolving.” Critique this claim in three points.

An ISC 2023 Biotechnology paper (Section B, Question 4) asked: “In a population of 1000 individuals, the genotype counts for a gene with two alleles are: AA = 490, Aa = 420, aa = 90. (a) Calculate the allele frequencies *p* and *q*. (b) Determine the expected genotype counts under Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium. (c) Perform a chi‑square test to assess whether the population is in equilibrium (use α = 0.05). State the degrees of freedom and critical value. (d) If the population is not in equilibrium, suggest two possible biological reasons.” Provide a complete solution with all steps and final conclusions.

A researcher claims that because the CYP2C19*2 allele frequency is 0.30 in Population A and 0.10 in Population B, a uniform clopidogrel dosing guideline can be applied to both. Critique this claim using pharmacogenomic principles.

A hospital introduces pre‑emptive CYP2C19 genotyping for all cardiac patients. After one year, stent‑thrombosis rates drop from 2.5 % to 1.2 %. Calculate the absolute risk reduction and number needed to genotype (NNG) to prevent one stent thrombosis, assuming 1 000 patients were genotyped.

(a) Explain why HLA‑B*58:01 screening is recommended before allopurinol in South Asians but not universally in all ethnic groups. (b) If the allele frequency in a European cohort is 0.001, compute the expected number of carriers in 10 000 individuals. (c) Discuss the cost‑effectiveness implication of the frequency difference.

An ISC past‑paper style question: “A 55‑year‑old Indian male with coronary artery disease is genotyped as CYP2C19*1/*2 and VKORC1 AA. He is prescribed clopidogrel 75 mg daily and warfarin 5 mg daily. (a) Predict the likely pharmacodynamic outcome for each drug. (b) Propose evidence‑based dose or drug modifications. (c) Justify your recommendations using allele‑frequency considerations for the Indian population.”

A small population of 20 individuals loses a rare allele after a flood kills 15 members randomly. Which evolutionary force is primarily responsible, and why does it have a stronger effect in small populations?

A researcher observes a new allele at frequency 0.001 in a population of 10,000. Assuming no selection, migration, or drift, which force generated this allele, and what is its expected fate over many generations?

A population of 500 individuals has allele frequencies p = 0.5, q = 0.5 at a neutral locus. (a) Calculate the expected heterozygosity under Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium. (b) If the population experiences a bottleneck to 20 individuals for one generation and then recovers to 500, what is the expected heterozygosity after the bottleneck? (c) Explain why heterozygosity declines more than allele‑frequency variance in a bottleneck.

A new allele arises by mutation in a population of effective size N_e = 1000. The mutation rate at this locus is μ = 1 × 10⁻⁶ per generation. (a) What is the expected number of new mutant alleles entering the population each generation? (b) If the allele is neutral, what is its probability of eventual fixation? (c) How would the fixation probability change if the allele were beneficial with s = 0.01?

Critique the following statement: "In a large population, genetic drift is negligible, so we can ignore it when modelling allele‑frequency change over 100 generations." Provide a quantitative argument using the variance effective population size.
In a population with allele frequencies p = 0.6 (A) and q = 0.4 (a), complete positive assortative mating for the trait occurs. What happens to heterozygosity after one generation?
Design a simple computer simulation to show how a forward mutation rate of 10⁻⁵ per generation changes the frequency of a neutral allele over 1,000 generations in a population of 10,000 individuals.

**HOTS:** A researcher observes that in a large, randomly mating population, the frequency of a deleterious recessive allele remains constant at q = 0.02 over many generations despite strong selection against homozygotes (s = 0.9). Propose a mechanism that could maintain this equilibrium and derive the approximate mutation rate required.

**APPLICATION:** In a plant breeding program, a recessive allele for dwarfism (d) is desired. The current frequency of d is 0.1. The breeder enforces strict self‑fertilization (F = 0.5) for two generations. What will be the frequency of dwarf (dd) plants after two generations? Assume no selection.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “In a population, the frequency of allele A is 0.8 and allele a is 0.2. If the inbreeding coefficient F is 0.2, what is the frequency of heterozygotes?” (2 marks)
If the frequency of allele A is 0.6 in a population at Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium, what are the expected genotype frequencies? Show the calculation.
A researcher observes genotype frequencies AA = 0.5, Aa = 0.3, aa = 0.2 in a population. Evaluate whether this population is in Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium.
Explain how allele‑frequency data for the CYP2C19*2 variant in Indian sub‑populations can guide clopidogrel dosing.

A population geneticist samples 500 individuals from an isolated island community and finds genotype counts: AA = 245, Aa = 210, aa = 45. (a) Calculate allele frequencies. (b) Compute expected genotype counts under Hardy‑Weinberg. (c) Perform a chi‑square test (α = 0.01) and state whether the population deviates from equilibrium. (d) Suggest one evolutionary mechanism that could explain a significant deviation.

A pharmacogenomic guideline recommends genotyping CYP2C9*2 and *3 before warfarin dosing. In a cohort, *2 allele frequency = 0.12, *3 allele frequency = 0.08 (assume linkage equilibrium). (a) Calculate the expected frequency of individuals carrying at least one reduced‑function allele (*2 or *3). (b) If the cohort size is 2,000, how many individuals would need dose adjustment? (c) Explain why assuming linkage equilibrium is critical here.

ISC 2023 Paper 2, Question 12 (6 marks): “A researcher studies the ACE I/D polymorphism in two Indian populations. In Population A, the D allele frequency is 0.55; in Population B, it is 0.35. (i) Calculate the expected genotype frequencies for each population assuming Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium. (ii) If the observed DD genotype frequency in Population A is 0.40, discuss two possible reasons for the deviation. (iii) Explain how this polymorphism could influence response to ACE‑inhibitor therapy.”
List the seven characteristics of living organisms as defined in the ISC Class 11 syllabus.

A researcher discovers a new microscopic organism in a hot spring (85 °C, pH 2). It has a cell membrane, ribosomes, and a circular DNA chromosome, but no nucleus or membrane‑bound organelles. **(a)** Which domain does it likely belong to? **(b)** List two characteristics of life it clearly exhibits. **(c)** Suggest one experiment to test if it performs metabolism. **(Marks: a‑1, b‑2, c‑2)**
A culture of Escherichia coli starts with 500 cells. If the generation time is 20 minutes, how many cells will be present after 2 hours? Use the formula N = N₀ × 2^(t/g).
In the ISC 2023 paper, a question asked: “Name the group of bacteria that oxidise ammonia to nitrite.” Write the correct answer and the metabolic category it belongs to.

Application: A water sample from a hot spring (80 °C, pH 2) is cultured. After 48 hours, microscopic examination shows rod‑shaped cells without a nucleus. Which group of Monera is most likely present, and what adaptation allows survival?

A pond sample contains *Euglena* (length 50 µm, flagellum 30 µm) and *Phacus* (length 40 µm, no emergent flagellum). Calculate the ratio of flagellum length to total cell length for *Euglena* and express it as a percentage.
Describe the life cycle of a plasmodial slime mould (e.g., *Physarum*) with reference to spore formation, germination, and plasmodium formation. (5 marks)
Describe the life cycle of a cellular slime mould (*Dictyostelium*) with labelled diagram description. (5 marks)
A culture of *Paramecium caudatum* doubles every 4 hours. Starting with 50 cells, how many cells will be present after 24 hours? (Assume unlimited resources and no death.)
You observe an unknown amoeba under a calibrated eyepiece micrometer. The cell spans 40 divisions, and each division equals 2.5 µm. Calculate the cell diameter.
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Describe the process of conjugation in *Paramecium* and explain its genetic significance.” (5 marks)

A fungal colony on an agar plate expands radially at a constant rate of 2.5 mm per day. If the colony starts as a 3 mm diameter inoculum, how many days will it take to reach a diameter of 90 mm? Show your calculation.

In a laboratory experiment, a single basidiospore of a mushroom germinates and undergoes five successive generations of spore production. If each generation each spore produces exactly 10 new spores, how many total spores will exist after the fifth generation? Assume no spore death.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain the term ‘dikaryophase’ in the life cycle of Basidiomycetes. Why is it considered a unique feature?” (3 marks)

A researcher discovers a new microscopic animal with the following traits: multicellular, no cell walls, heterotrophic, exhibits a blastula stage, has true tissues but no organs, and shows radial symmetry. (a) Assign this organism to the correct level of organization. (b) Identify its likely germ layer condition. (c) Name the phylum it most probably belongs to. (1 mark each)

An animal shows the following: bilateral symmetry, three germ layers, a body cavity that is not fully lined by mesoderm, and a complete digestive tract with two openings. (a) Classify its coelom type. (b) Predict its likely excretory structure. (c) Suggest one phylum it could belong to. (1 mark each)

Compare and contrast the body plans of Phylum Platyhelminthes and Phylum Nematoda using the following criteria: (a) Symmetry, (b) Germ layers, (c) Body cavity, (d) Digestive tract, (e) Segmentation. Present your answer as a table. (5 marks)

Critically evaluate the statement: “The presence of a notochord is the single most important character for classifying an animal as a chordate.” Discuss with reference to subphyla and exceptions. (3 marks)
Past ISC Paper 2023, Question 4(b): “Distinguish between diploblastic and triploblastic organization. Give one example of each.” (3 marks)
A culture of *Chlamydomonas* starts with 150 cells and doubles every 5 hours. How many cells will be present after 20 hours? Show the calculation.

**HOTS:** A researcher isolates a novel unicellular alga from a hot spring (pH 2.5, 55 °C). It has a single chloroplast with a pyrenoid, a cell wall of glycoprotein, and two equal flagella. Based on these traits, propose its likely division and justify your reasoning. Discuss one additional biochemical test that could confirm the classification.

**APPLICATION:** A coastal community plans to cultivate *Gracilaria* (a red alga) for agar production. They have two sites: Site X with high nitrate (30 µM) and low phosphate (0.2 µM), and Site Y with low nitrate (2 µM) and high phosphate (5 µM). Which site is more suitable for rapid *Gracilaria* growth, and why? Include the concept of limiting nutrients.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Name the type of life cycle exhibited by *Polysiphonia* and state the ploidy of its three distinct phases. (2 marks) (b) Draw a labelled diagram of the carposporophyte of *Polysiphonia* showing its attachment to the female gametophyte. (3 marks) (c) Explain why the carposporophyte is considered a parasitic phase. (2 marks)
A moss capsule produces 2.5 × 10⁶ spores. If only 0.02 % of these spores successfully germinate and establish a new gametophyte, how many new gametophytes are expected? Show your calculation.

Design a simple numerical model to estimate the number of spores a liverwort thallus must produce to ensure at least 1 000 successful gametophytes, assuming a germination success rate of 0.05 %. Provide the formula and compute the required spore number.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Describe the structure of a mature moss capsule and explain the mechanism of spore dispersal.” (5 marks)
Given a fern with 2n = 24 chromosomes in the sporophyte, determine the chromosome number in the gametophyte and in the zygote.
In a CISCE ISC exam, a question asks: “Compare the seed coat origin in gymnosperms and angiosperms.” Write a concise answer that would earn full marks (3 marks).

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Draw a labelled diagram of the longitudinal section of a *Pinus* ovule showing the micropyle, nucellus, megagametophyte, archegonia, and integument. Write two functions of the micropyle.” (5 marks)
A flower has 5 sepals, 5 petals, 10 stamens, and 2 fused carpels. Predict whether it is a monocot or dicot and justify using at least two floral criteria.

**HOTS:** A fossilised flower from the Early Cretaceous shows 5 sepals, 5 petals, numerous stamens, and an inferior ovary with many ovules. Based on these features, argue whether it is more likely a basal angiosperm or a derived eudicot.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Describe the process of double fertilisation in angiosperms. Mention the ploidy of the structures formed.” (3 marks)
If the animal kingdom has 36 recognized phyla and 30 of them are invertebrate phyla, how many vertebrate phyla are there? Show your calculation.

A student measures the length of the elongation zone in a maize seedling as 4.2 mm and the meristematic zone as 0.8 mm. If the total root tip length (cap + meristematic + elongation + maturation) is 12.5 mm, calculate the combined length of the root cap and maturation zone. Show all steps.

A sweet potato tuberous root stores 180 g of starch. If the dry mass of the root is 250 g and starch constitutes 72 % of the dry mass, verify whether the given starch mass is consistent with the percentage. Show calculations.

Application: A botanist discovers a new mangrove species with pencil‑like roots emerging 30 cm above the waterline. Design a simple field experiment to test whether these structures function as pneumatophores for gas exchange.
A plant has 120 leaves each with an average area of 25 cm². The ground area covered by the plant is 0.5 m². Calculate the Leaf Area Index (LAI).
A flower has 5 sepals, 5 petals, 10 stamens, and 1 pistil. Is it a complete flower? Justify your answer.

Design a floral diagram description (in words) for a hypothetical flower that is zygomorphic, with 5 sepals (two fused), 5 petals (one large standard, two wings, two keel), 10 stamens (diadelphous – 9 fused, 1 free), and a single carpel. Include the arrangement of whorls.
Write the floral formula for a flower that is bisexual, actinomorphic, with 5 free sepals, 5 free petals, 10 free stamens, and a superior ovary of 5 fused carpels with axile placentation.
Write the floral formula for a bisexual, zygomorphic flower with 5 sepals (gamosepalous), 5 petals (polypetalous, papilionaceous), 10 stamens (diadelphous), and a monocarpellary superior ovary.

A farmer collects 120 mango fruits from a tree. Each fruit weighs on average 250 g, and the seed (stone + kernel) accounts for 15 % of the fruit mass. Calculate the total mass of edible mesocarp harvested.
In the ISC 2023 paper, a diagram shows a fruit with a hard stony endocarp, a thick fleshy mesocarp, and a thin epicarp. Identify the fruit type and give one Indian example.

An ISC 2022 question showed a longitudinal section of a fruit with a single seed, a fleshy mesocarp, and a hard endocarp. The question asked: “Identify the fruit type and name the plant family it typically belongs to.” Provide the answer and justify.
A dicot seed weighs 0.60 g. Its embryo (radicle + plumule + cotyledons) weighs 0.12 g. Calculate the percentage of the total seed mass contributed by the embryo.

Design a simple laboratory experiment to compare the effect of two constant temperatures (20 °C and 30 °C) on the germination rate of mung bean (*Vigna radiata*) seeds over 7 days. Outline the setup, variables, and the data you would record.

A microscopic measurement shows that a xylem vessel element in a maize stem is 120 µm long and 30 µm wide, while a tracheid in the same stem is 2 mm long and 20 µm wide. Calculate the ratio of the length of the tracheid to the length of the vessel element. Express your answer as a simplified whole‑number ratio.

A student measures the cross‑sectional area of xylem vessels in a stem segment: 12 vessels with diameters (µm): 20, 22, 18, 24, 20, 26, 18, 22, 20, 24, 20, 22. Calculate the mean hydraulic diameter (using the formula for hydraulic diameter of a circular tube, Dh = 4 × area / perimeter = diameter) and the standard deviation of the diameters.

A transverse section of a dicot root shows a vascular cylinder of radius 0.5 mm. The central xylem occupies a circular region of radius 0.2 mm. Assuming the phloem forms a uniform ring around the xylem, calculate the cross‑sectional area of the phloem region. Use π = 3.14.

Design a simple experiment to compare the vascular bundle density (bundles mm⁻²) in a 1 cm² cross‑section of maize (monocot) stem versus mango (dicot) stem. Outline the steps, measurements, and calculation.
Draw a labelled diagram of a transverse section of a dicot leaf showing upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, lower epidermis, vascular bundle, and stomata. (5 marks)
A frog’s vertebral column has 9 vertebrae. If each vertebra averages 0.6 cm in length, calculate the approximate length of the vertebral column.
Design a simple experiment to measure the rate of oxygen consumption in a frog at rest. If the frog consumes 0.5 mL O₂ per gram per hour and weighs 30 g, calculate total O₂ consumption in 2 hours.

**HOTS:** A frog is placed in a sealed container with water and air. Over time, the oxygen concentration in the air drops while carbon dioxide rises. Explain how the frog’s three respiratory surfaces contribute to this gas exchange, and predict which surface would dominate if the water temperature rises to 30 °C.
A plant cell has a radius of 20 µm. Calculate its surface‑area‑to‑volume ratio (SA/V) assuming a spherical shape. Express the answer in µm⁻¹.
In a CISCE ISC 2023 paper, a question asked: “Explain why mitochondria are called the powerhouse of the cell.” Write a concise answer (≤ 50 words) that would earn full marks.
**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “Describe the structure and function of the nucleolus. (3 marks)” Write a model answer aligned with ISC marking scheme.
A bacterial culture doubles every 20 minutes. Starting with 100 cells, how many cells will be present after 2 hours? Show calculation.
A culture of Escherichia coli doubles every 30 minutes. If the initial population is 250 cells, calculate the population after 3 hours. Show all steps.

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** Critique the following statement: “Because prokaryotes lack a nucleus, they cannot regulate gene expression in response to environmental signals.” Provide a structured answer with (a) your judgement, (b) two supporting arguments, (c) one counter‑example, and (d) a concluding remark. (4 marks)

**COMPARISON:** Compare and contrast the mechanisms of chromosome segregation in prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Present your answer as a table with three rows: (i) Structural basis, (ii) Motor proteins, (iii) Checkpoint control. (3 marks)

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Define “nucleoid”. (b) State two differences between the nucleoid and a true nucleus. (c) Explain why the presence of a nucleoid does not violate the cell theory. (5 marks)
A student places a red blood cell in a solution of 0.9 % NaCl (isotonic) and another in distilled water. Predict the net water movement in each case and explain the outcome using osmosis principles.

A plant cell has a cytoplasmic solute concentration of 0.3 M. It is placed in a 0.5 M sucrose solution. Calculate the osmotic pressure difference (Δπ) across the plasma membrane at 25 °C. Use the van’t Hoff equation π = iCRT, where i = 1 for sucrose, R = 0.0831 L·bar·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹, T = 298 K.
Calculate the surface‑area‑to‑volume ratio of a spherical mitochondrion with radius 0.5 µm. How does this ratio support its function?
**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** A textbook states: “Mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell because they produce 95 % of the cell’s ATP.” Critique this statement for accuracy and completeness.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Describe the structure of a mitochondrion as seen under an electron microscope. Explain how its structure is adapted for its function.” (5 marks)
A spherical plant cell has a radius of 10 µm. Calculate its surface‑area‑to‑volume ratio. Express the answer in µm⁻¹.
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Describe the structure of the plant cell wall and explain how its composition contributes to both mechanical strength and controlled permeability.” (5 marks)
A light microscope uses a 40× objective and a 10× eyepiece. The image of a cell measures 8 mm on the retina. Calculate the actual size of the cell in micrometres.

An ISC 2023 paper asked: “Draw a labelled diagram of a typical animal cell as seen under an electron microscope. Indicate the nucleolus, rough ER, smooth ER, Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, lysosome, centrioles, and plasma membrane.” List the marking scheme (1 mark per correct label + 1 mark for correct relative positioning).

**Application:** A student prepares a temporary mount of cheek epithelial cells and observes them under 400× total magnification. The nucleus appears 0.8 mm wide in the field of view. Estimate the actual nuclear diameter in µm.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** An ISC 2022 long‑answer question (5 marks) read: “Explain how the endomembrane system contributes to the synthesis and secretion of insulin in pancreatic β‑cells.” Outline a model answer with marking points.
Calculate the molecular formula of a linear polysaccharide made of 150 glucose units linked by α‑1,4‑glycosidic bonds.
In the ISC 2023 paper, a question asked: “Name the glycosidic bond present in maltose and state its configuration.” Write the exact answer expected.
An ISC 2022 question: “Write the Haworth projection of β‑D‑fructofuranose and indicate the anomeric carbon.” Provide the drawing description and the carbon number.

Calculate the approximate molecular mass of a polypeptide containing 150 amino‑acid residues, assuming an average residue mass of 110 Da and that each peptide bond formation loses one water molecule (18 Da).
If a protein of 300 residues has 12 cysteine residues forming 6 disulfide bridges, how many fewer hydrogen atoms does the oxidised protein have compared to the fully reduced form?

In a CISCE ISC practical, a student adds 6 M urea to an enzyme solution and observes complete loss of activity. After dialysis to remove urea, activity partially returns. Explain the observation in terms of protein structure.

A past ISC paper asked: “Explain why the substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the β‑globin chain causes sickle‑cell anaemia.” Write a concise answer covering structural and physiological consequences.

Calculate the iodine value of an oil sample if 0.500 g of oil consumes 12.5 mL of 0.100 N sodium thiosulphate in the Wijs method. (Iodine value = (V × N × 12.69) / mass of oil, where V in mL, N in normality, mass in g.)

Determine the saponification value of a fat if 2.00 g requires 25.0 mL of 0.500 N HCl for back‑titration after saponification with excess 0.500 N KOH (blank = 30.0 mL). (Saponification value = (V_blank − V_sample) × N × 56.1 / mass of fat.)

In an ISC practical, a student obtains an acid value of 2.5 mg KOH g⁻¹ for a fresh oil sample. The FSSAI limit for refined edible oil is ≤0.5 mg KOH g⁻¹. What does this indicate about the oil quality, and what chemical change does the acid value measure?

(a) Define “iodine value” and state its unit. (b) A 0.300 g oil sample gives an iodine value of 95.0 g I₂ 100 g⁻¹. Calculate the volume of 0.100 N Na₂S₂O₃ required in the Wijs titration. (c) Explain why the iodine value of a fat decreases after hydrogenation.

A student prepares a phospholipid vesicle (liposome) using phosphatidylcholine with two saturated C₁₆:₀ chains and another using one C₁₆:₀ and one C₁₈:₁ (cis) chain. Predict which vesicle will have higher membrane fluidity at 25 °C and justify using the concept of lipid packing.

(a) Write the balanced chemical equation for the saponification of a simple triglyceride (tripalmitin, C₅₁H₉₈O₆) with aqueous KOH. (b) If 1.00 g of tripalmitin is saponified, calculate the theoretical mass of KOH consumed (molar mass KOH = 56.1 g mol⁻¹). (c) Discuss how the saponification value would differ for a triglyceride containing three lauric acid (C₁₂:₀) chains instead of palmitic acid.

An ISC 2023 question: “A 0.500 g sample of an unknown oil is analysed. The Wijs titration consumes 15.0 mL of 0.100 N Na₂S₂O₃. The saponification value determined by back‑titration is 195 mg KOH g⁻¹. (a) Calculate the iodine value. (b) Based on these two values, suggest whether the oil is more likely a drying oil (e.g., linseed) or a non‑drying oil (e.g., olive). Justify.”
A DNA sample from a plant shows 22 % adenine. Using Chargaff’s rules, calculate the percentages of thymine, guanine, and cytosine. Show all steps.

The molecular weight of a double‑stranded DNA fragment is 1.3 × 10⁶ Da. Assuming an average molecular weight of 650 Da per base pair, estimate the number of base pairs in the fragment. Show the calculation.
A past CISCE ISC question: “The percentage of guanine in a DNA sample is 24 %. What is the percentage of adenine?” Provide the answer with a brief justification.
In the CISCE ISC 2023 paper, a question asked: “Explain why the enzyme carbonic anhydrase requires Zn²⁺ for catalytic activity.” Provide a concise answer suitable for full marks.
An enzyme has Vmax = 120 µmol min⁻¹ and Km = 0.5 mM. Calculate the initial velocity when [S] = 1.0 mM.
A student plots 1/v versus 1/[S] and obtains a straight line with y‑intercept 0.02 min µmol⁻¹ and slope 0.5 mM min µmol⁻¹. Determine Vmax and Km.
An enzyme exhibits Vmax = 200 µmol min⁻¹ and Km = 0.2 mM. If the substrate concentration is 0.05 mM, what percentage of Vmax is the initial velocity?

Critique the following experimental design: “To determine Km, I will measure the reaction rate at a single substrate concentration of 1 mM and use the Michaelis–Menten equation assuming Vmax = 100 µmol min⁻¹.”
Compare the catalytic efficiencies of two enzymes: Enzyme A has kcat = 500 s⁻¹, Km = 5 mM; Enzyme B has kcat = 50 s⁻¹, Km = 0.05 mM. Which enzyme is more efficient at low substrate concentrations?
An enzyme shows maximum activity at pH 8.0. Predict the effect on *K_m* and *V_max* if the assay pH is shifted to 6.0, assuming the catalytic residue is a histidine with pK_a ≈ 6.5.

Given the following initial‑rate data for an enzyme at 37 °C, pH 7.4: | [S] (mM) | v (µmol min⁻¹) | |----------|----------------| | 0.5 | 12 | | 1.0 | 20 | | 2.0 | 30 | | 5.0 | 40 | | 10.0 | 45 | Construct a Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v vs 1/[S]) and determine *K_m* and *V_max*.
Explain why the temperature coefficient Q₁₀ ≈ 2 for many enzymes between 0 °C and 40 °C, but the Arrhenius plot (ln k vs 1/T) deviates from linearity above 40 °C.

A researcher claims that “since Q₁₀ ≈ 2, raising the temperature from 20 °C to 40 °C will quadruple the enzyme rate.” Critically evaluate this statement using the concept of temperature optimum and denaturation.

You are given an enzyme that loses 50 % activity after 10 min at 50 °C but retains full activity at 37 °C. Propose a practical protocol to determine its thermal inactivation half‑life (t₁/₂) at 45 °C.

Critique the following experimental design: “To test pH effect on enzyme X, the student prepares buffers at pH 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 using the same buffer species (phosphate) and measures initial rates at 37 °C with saturating substrate.” Identify two potential confounding factors.

A past ISC paper asked: “An enzyme follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics. In the presence of 0.2 mM inhibitor, the apparent K_m becomes 4 mM while V_max remains 80 µmol min⁻¹. If the original K_m is 1 mM, calculate the inhibitor constant K_i.” Provide the full solution.

A plant root tip cell spends 12 hours in interphase and 1 hour in M‑phase. If the total cell‑cycle duration is 13 hours, calculate the percentage of time the cell spends in each major phase (interphase vs. M‑phase). Show your work.
A CISCE ISC 2023 question: “Describe the significance of the G₂/M checkpoint in preventing genomic instability.” Provide a model answer structured for 3 marks.

A researcher measures the total cell cycle time of a cultured human cell line as 20 hours. Flow cytometry shows 45 % of cells in G1, 35 % in S, 15 % in G2, and 5 % in M. Assuming an asynchronous population, calculate the average duration of each phase.

In a typical human somatic cell, the G1 phase lasts about 11 hours, S phase 8 hours, G2 phase 4 hours, and M phase 1 hour. If a mutation causes the G2/M checkpoint to fail, which phase(s) would be most directly affected and what would be the likely consequence for the daughter cells?

**HOTS:** A cancer cell line shows a shortened G1 phase of 3 hours while S, G2, and M remain unchanged. Propose a molecular mechanism that could cause this specific shortening and predict its effect on the cell’s sensitivity to a DNA‑damaging agent administered during G1.

**Application:** You are given a population of human fibroblasts with a known doubling time of 24 hours. Design a protocol using a thymidine block‑release method to synchronise the cells at the G1/S boundary, and explain how you would verify synchrony.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** In a certain human cell type, the G1 phase occupies 55 % of the total cell‑cycle time. If the S phase lasts 7 hours and the combined G2 + M phases last 5 hours, calculate the total cell‑cycle time and the duration of G1.
A diploid plant cell has 2n = 24 chromosomes. Calculate the chromosome number in each daughter cell after (a) mitosis, (b) meiosis I, and (c) meiosis II.
Design a table showing chromosome number and DNA content (C-value) at each major stage of meiosis for a cell with 2n = 10, assuming the haploid (1C) DNA content is 2 pg.
CISCE past-paper pattern: “Draw a labelled diagram of a cell in metaphase I of meiosis, showing a bivalent with chiasmata. Explain how this arrangement leads to genetic variation.” (5 marks)
If a human somatic cell undergoes 10 successive mitotic divisions without any cell death, how many cells will be produced from the original single cell? Show your calculation.
In a CISCE ISC paper, a question asks: “Explain how independent assortment during meiosis I contributes to genetic diversity.” Write a concise answer worth 3 marks.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain how the significance of meiosis is reflected in the genetic diversity of offspring.” (3 marks)

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** ISC 2022 Question: “Describe the molecular events at the G2/M checkpoint that lead to the activation of MPF. Include the roles of cyclin B, Cdk1, Wee1, and Cdc25.” (5 marks)

In a root‑tip squash of Allium cepa, you count 300 cells: 12 in prophase, 6 in metaphase, 4 in anaphase, 2 in telophase, and the rest in interphase. If the total cell‑cycle time is 20 hours, calculate the average duration of mitosis (M phase).
A past ISC question: “Explain how loss of p53 function can lead to uncontrolled cell proliferation.” Provide a concise answer structured for 3 marks.

A researcher uses siRNA to knock down p21 in a p53‑wildtype cell line, then exposes cells to ionising radiation. Predict the cell‑cycle profile 6 hours post‑irradiation compared to a control siRNA treatment, and explain the molecular basis.
In a root tip squash, 300 cells are counted. 45 cells are in various stages of mitosis. Calculate the mitotic index.
A single yeast cell undergoes mitotic division every 90 minutes. How many cells will be present after 6 hours, assuming no cell death?
Application: A pathology report states “high mitotic index (25%) and loss of p53 immunostaining” in a breast biopsy. What does this imply about tumour behaviour and prognosis?

Apply (numerical): A diploid somatic cell of a flowering plant has 2n = 24 chromosomes. Calculate the number of chromosomes and DNA molecules in a cell at (a) G1 phase, (b) metaphase of mitosis, (c) metaphase I of meiosis, (d) metaphase II of meiosis. Show all steps.

Create (numerical): Design a short‑answer question (2 marks) that tests the ability to calculate the duration of M phase given the total cell‑cycle time and the durations of G1, S, and G2. Provide the question, the model answer, and the marking scheme.

Application: A horticulturist observes that a certain ornamental plant produces pollen grains with 12 chromosomes, while its somatic cells have 24 chromosomes. Explain how this observation confirms the occurrence of meiosis and not mitosis in pollen formation.
Name the three major physiological processes covered in Chapter 06 and give one primary product or outcome of each.
In an ISC practical, a student measures the respiratory quotient (RQ) of germinating groundnut seeds and obtains 0.71. Interpret this value in terms of substrate utilisation.

**(a)** Define photosynthetic quotient (PQ) and respiratory quotient (RQ). **(b)** A C₃ plant leaf under high light shows PQ = 1.2. Propose a physiological explanation. **(c)** If the same leaf is darkened, predict the change in gas exchange and RQ.

A researcher treats dwarf pea seedlings with 10⁻⁵ M GA₃ and measures internode elongation after 72 h. The control grows 2 mm; treated grows 12 mm. **(a)** Calculate the fold increase. **(b)** Suggest a molecular mechanism for GA‑induced elongation. **(c)** Design a control to test whether the effect is due to GA perception or downstream signalling.

**(a)** In an ISC 2023 practical, students measured O₂ evolution from Hydrilla sprigs at three light intensities (50, 200, 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹). The data: 0.12, 0.45, 0.78 mmol O₂ m⁻² min⁻¹. Plot the light‑response curve and estimate the light saturation point. **(b)** Explain why the curve plateaus. **(c)** If the experiment is repeated at 35 °C, predict the effect on the saturation point and justify.

In an experiment, a leaf disc assay shows that 0.025 mol of O₂ is evolved in 10 minutes under saturating light. Calculate the amount of CO₂ fixed (in moles) during the same period, assuming the overall stoichiometry holds.

A researcher measures the quantum yield of PSII (ΦPSII) in a C₃ plant under increasing light intensities. At low light, ΦPSII ≈ 0.8; at high light, ΦPSII drops to 0.3. Explain the physiological mechanisms causing this decline, referencing non‑photochemical quenching and photoinhibition.

Design an experiment using a Clark‑type oxygen electrode to compare the light‑saturated photosynthetic rate of a C₃ plant (e.g., wheat) and a C₄ plant (e.g., maize) at 25 °C and 35 °C. State the expected trend and the biochemical basis.

A past CISCE ISC paper asked: “Explain how the light‑dependent reactions of photosynthesis are affected when a herbicide blocks electron flow from QA to QB in Photosystem II.” Provide a model answer for 4 marks.
Explain why the respiratory quotient (RQ) for glucose is 1.0 while for a typical fat such as tripalmitin it is about 0.7.
Calculate the RQ for the oxidation of palmitic acid (C₁₆H₃₂O₂) given the balanced equation: C₁₆H₃₂O₂ + 23 O₂ → 16 CO₂ + 16 H₂O.

In a tissue‑culture experiment, a callus is cultured on medium containing 2 mg L⁻¹ auxin (NAA) and 0.5 mg L⁻¹ cytokinin (BAP). After four weeks, roots dominate. If the cytokinin concentration is increased to 2 mg L⁻¹ while auxin stays at 2 mg L⁻¹, what organogenic outcome is expected? Provide a quantitative justification using the auxin : cytokinin ratio concept.

A mango orchard uses ethylene gas at 100 ppm for 24 h to ripen 500 kg of mature green mangoes. If the ripening chamber volume is 10 m³, calculate the mass of ethylene (C₂H₄, molar mass 28 g mol⁻¹) required, assuming ideal gas behaviour at 25 °C and 1 atm. (R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)

A student measures a seedling’s fresh mass as 0.8 g on day 2 and 1.4 g on day 5. Calculate the absolute growth rate (AGR) and relative growth rate (RGR) assuming the mean mass over the interval is 1.1 g. Show units.
In an ISC practical, you are given a table of fresh mass (g) of maize seedlings at days 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Outline the steps to plot the sigmoid growth curve and determine the day of maximum AGR.

**APPLICATION:** You are given a dataset of fresh mass (g) of soybean seedlings at days 0, 5, 10, 15, 20: 0.3, 1.2, 5.8, 12.5, 14.0. (a) Compute AGR for each interval. (b) Identify the interval of maximum AGR. (c) Estimate the day of peak AGR. (d) Sketch the expected sigmoid curve labeling the three growth phases.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Define absolute growth rate (AGR) and relative growth rate (RGR) with units. (b) A pea seedling’s fresh mass increases from 0.6 g to 1.5 g in 4 days. Calculate AGR and RGR (use mean mass). (c) Explain how a deficiency in gibberellins would alter the sigmoid growth curve of the seedling.
Evaluate the statement: “All plants flower when day length exceeds 12 hours.” Provide a counter‑example and explain the underlying principle.
A short‑day plant has a critical night length of 13 hours. It is grown under a 10‑hour day / 14‑hour night regime. Will it flower? Show your calculation.

Application: A horticulturist wants to force chrysanthemum (SDP) to flower in summer (long days). She uses blackout cloth to extend the night to 14 hours. If the natural day length is 15 hours, how many hours of blackout must she apply each evening? Show calculation.

CISCE past‑paper pattern: “Explain why a short‑day plant fails to flower if a brief flash of red light is given during the long night, but flowers if the red flash is followed by a far‑red flash.” (3 marks)
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Describe the sequence of events leading to leaf abscission, emphasizing the role of the abscission zone and the hormonal regulation involved.” (5 marks)
Calculate the respiratory quotient (RQ) for a plant tissue that consumes 0.018 mol O₂ and releases 0.018 mol CO₂ in 20 minutes. State the substrate likely being oxidised.
In a CISCE ISC 2023 paper, a question asked: “Explain the role of gibberellins in breaking seed dormancy.” Provide a concise answer as per the marking scheme (3 marks).

In the ISC 2022 Biology paper, a question asked: “Describe the role of the Calvin cycle in carbon fixation and explain how the cycle is regulated by light.” Provide a structured answer covering the three phases and light‑dependent regulation.
If the partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar air is 104 mmHg and in pulmonary capillary blood is 40 mmHg, calculate the net diffusion gradient for O₂ and state its direction.
A person has a tidal volume of 500 mL and respiratory rate of 12 breaths min⁻¹. Dead space volume is 150 mL. Calculate the alveolar ventilation per minute.

( CISCE exam‑style ) Using the alveolar gas equation, calculate the arterial PCO₂ (PaCO₂) if PAO₂ = 100 mmHg, FiO₂ = 0.21, Patm = 760 mmHg, PH₂O = 47 mmHg and the respiratory exchange ratio (R) = 0.8.

During heavy exercise, a student’s tidal volume increases to 3000 mL and respiratory rate to 30 breaths min⁻¹. Dead space remains 150 mL. Calculate alveolar ventilation and comment on whether it meets the estimated metabolic demand of ~250 mL O₂ min⁻¹ (assuming 5 % O₂ extraction).

(a) State Fick’s law of diffusion for a gas across a membrane. (b) Calculate the rate of O₂ diffusion (V) given: diffusion coefficient D = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ cm² s⁻¹, alveolar‑capillary surface area A = 70 m², partial pressure difference ΔP = 13 kPa, membrane thickness T = 0.5 µm. Express V in mL s⁻¹. (c) Explain how chronic smoking alters each term in Fick’s law and the overall impact on V.
A patient’s CBC shows: Hct = 0.36, RBC = 3.0 × 10¹² L⁻¹, Hb = 100 g L⁻¹. Calculate MCV, MCH, and MCHC. Classify the anaemia morphologically.
If a person’s plasma volume is 3.0 L and haematocrit is 0.45, compute the total blood volume.

A patient with severe burns loses 2 L of plasma (mostly water and electrolytes) but retains red cells. Initial blood volume = 5 L, Hct = 0.45. Assuming no immediate fluid replacement, calculate the new haematocrit and discuss the physiological consequence on blood viscosity.

Compare the oxygen‑carrying capacity of 1 L of blood with Hb = 150 g L⁻¹ versus 1 L of a haemoglobin‑based oxygen carrier (HBOC) solution containing 100 g L⁻¹ of polymerised Hb (P50 = 30 mmHg, Hill coefficient n = 2.5). Assume arterial PO₂ = 100 mmHg, venous PO₂ = 40 mmHg, and that each gram of Hb binds 1.34 mL O₂. Which delivers more O₂ to tissues per litre of fluid?
Calculate the cardiac output (in L/min) for a person with a heart rate of 80 beats/min and a stroke volume of 65 mL/beat.
**Application:** A patient has a heart rate of 110 beats/min and a stroke volume of 55 mL/beat. Calculate cardiac output and state whether this suggests adequate perfusion at rest.
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Draw a labelled diagram of the human heart showing the internal structure. Indicate the direction of blood flow with arrows.” (5 marks)
State the typical duration of one complete cardiac cycle at a resting heart rate of 75 beats min⁻¹.
Given a stroke volume of 70 mL and a heart rate of 80 beats min⁻¹, calculate the cardiac output in L min⁻¹.

(a) Define “stroke volume” and state its typical value in a healthy adult at rest. (b) If end‑diastolic volume is 130 mL and end‑systolic volume is 55 mL, compute stroke volume. (c) Explain how a decrease in venous return would affect stroke volume, referencing the Frank‑Starling mechanism.

A patient with aortic stenosis has a peak left ventricular pressure of 25 kPa during systole while aortic pressure is 13 kPa. (a) Calculate the pressure gradient across the aortic valve. (b) Discuss how this gradient influences the work of the left ventricle. (c) Predict the effect on the pressure‑volume loop shape.

Compare the cardiac cycle of a trained endurance athlete (resting HR 50 bpm, SV 100 mL) with that of a sedentary individual (resting HR 75 bpm, SV 70 mL). Discuss differences in (a) diastolic filling time, (b) atrial kick contribution, and (c) cardiac output at rest.
Given: renal plasma flow (RPF) = 600 mL min⁻¹, filtration fraction (FF) = 0.20. Calculate the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in mL min⁻¹.

Tetany is a syndrome of involuntary, sustained muscle contractions caused by acute hypocalcaemia (serum ionised Ca²⁺ < 1.0 mmol L⁻¹). The low free calcium reduces the electrical screening of negative charges on voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, lowering the depolarisation threshold and causing spontaneous nerve-muscle firing. A wrong answer (e.g., “tetany is caused by high potassium”) reveals the misconception that any electrolyte imbalance produces similar spasms, confusing hypalaemic muscle weakness with hypocalcaemic hyperexcitability.

Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism causes the findings because removal or devascularisation of parathyroid glands leads to decreased PTH, decreased renal 1α-hydroxylase, decreased 1,25-(OH)₂D, decreased intestinal calcium absorption, and decreased renal calcium reabsorption that produce hypocalcaemia. Immediate management requires IV calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 10 minutes with cardiac monitoring, then oral calcium carbonate 1 g TDS and calcitriol 0.25 µg daily. A wrong answer (e.g., “give IV magnesium”) reveals confusion between hypomagnesaemia-induced PTH resistance and primary hypoparathyroidism; magnesium is adjunctive, not first-line for acute tetany.

186 mg of elemental calcium is delivered because 10% w/v means 10 g calcium gluconate per 100 mL, yielding 1 g per 10 mL, which equals 0.00233 moles of calcium gluconate (1 g / 430 g mol⁻¹), containing 0.00465 moles of Ca²⁺ since each mole contains 2 moles of Ca²⁺, resulting in a mass of 0.186 g (0.00465 mol × 40 g mol⁻¹). A wrong answer (e.g., “90 mg”) usually stems from assuming one Ca per molecule or using the wrong molecular weight, showing misunderstanding of the salt’s stoichiometry.

The emergency department clinical algorithm for acute tetany follows a strict sequence: assess ABCs for airway security and oxygen, confirm tetany via Chvostek’s and Trousseau’s signs, draw blood for ionised calcium, total calcium, magnesium, phosphate, PTH, 25-OH-vitamin D, and ABG, administer IV calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 10 minutes with cardiac monitoring, re-check ionised calcium after 15 minutes and repeat bolus if below 1.0 mmol L⁻¹, start oral calcium and calcitriol once stable, and treat the underlying cause. A wrong answer (e.g., “give IV calcium chloride first”) reveals the misconception that calcium chloride is preferred; it is more tissue-irritant and reserved for central line administration, not peripheral ED use.

The claim is partially true because severe hypomagnesaemia (< 0.5 mmol L⁻¹) impairs PTH release from parathyroid chief cells and causes end-organ resistance to PTH, which leads to secondary hypocalcaemia that then produces tetany, while isolated hypomagnesaemia does not directly lower the Na⁺ channel threshold because magnesium does not screen surface charges like calcium. A wrong answer (e.g., “Mg²⁺ directly blocks Na⁺ channels”) reveals the misconception that magnesium mimics calcium’s electrostatic role, ignoring its distinct enzymatic cofactor functions.

Nutritional rickets / vitamin D deficiency is the diagnosis because low 25-OH-D causes decreased intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption leading to hypocalcaemia and hypophosphataemia, while high phosphate reflects renal secondary hyperparathyroidism conserving phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase reflects increased osteoblastic activity from high PTH, and resulting hypocalcaemia triggers tetany. A wrong answer (e.g., “hypoparathyroidism”) would show low PTH, normal/high phosphate, normal alkaline phosphatase — not matching the labs.

Reduced 1α-hydroxylase activity lowers 1,25-(OH)₂D to decrease intestinal calcium absorption, simultaneous phosphate retention complexes calcium, and metabolic acidosis alters albumin binding to decrease the ionised fraction, keeping total calcium appearing normal because the bound pool is maintained while physiologically active ionised calcium falls below the Na⁺ channel stability threshold to precipitate tetany. **Marking points (ISC style):** - Mention impaired 1,25-(OH)₂D synthesis (1 mark) - Phosphate-calcium precipitation (1 mark) - Altered ionised vs. total calcium due to pH/albumin (1 mark) - Link to Na⁺ channel threshold (1 mark) A wrong answer (e.g., “renal failure causes hypercalcaemia”) shows confusion between renal osteodystrophy phases and the acute electrolyte picture.

A small manufacturing unit in Gujarat that produces plastic containers has been using the same mould design for ten years. Recently, a competitor launched a lighter, stackable design that reduced material cost by 15% and gained rapid market acceptance. The Gujarat unit’s manager evaluates the new design, calculates that switching would require ₹8 lakhs investment in new moulds, and decides to wait for another six months to see if the trend persists before making a decision. Identify the entrepreneurial type shown by the manager’s behaviour and justify your answer by distinguishing it from a drone entrepreneur.

Compare the likelihood of a drone entrepreneur versus an imitating entrepreneur to adopt a new GST‑compliant e‑invoicing system after the government mandates its use for businesses with turnover above ₹50 lakhs. Support your answer with reference to their core behavioural traits.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern (multi‑part):** (a) Define entrepreneurship in not more than 30 words, using the three core elements. (b) Give one example of a social entrepreneur from India and state which core element is most prominent in their work. (c) Explain why a person who merely inherits a family business and runs it without change is not considered an entrepreneur under this meaning.

Which of the following best captures the core of the entrepreneurship definition? A) Any person who works for themselves. B) A process of identifying an opportunity, mobilising resources, bearing risk, and creating value. C) Registering a company under the Companies Act, 2013. D) Receiving a government subsidy for a small shop.

A startup founder in Pune has identified a gap in last‑mile delivery for perishable goods, secured a ₹50 lakh seed round, and launched a pilot with three delivery vans. Map each of the four definition elements to this scenario.
Create a one‑sentence definition of entrepreneurship that incorporates the MSME Act, 2006 threshold for investment in plant and machinery.
In an ISC‑style short‑answer question, a student writes: “Entrepreneurship is starting a business.” Award marks out of 3 and justify.

(a) Define entrepreneurship in your own words, ensuring all four core elements appear. (b) Explain why the MSME Act, 2006 investment threshold alone cannot serve as a complete definition. (c) Give one Indian example of a venture that meets the legal MSME criteria but fails the entrepreneurial definition.

A startup in Kochi plans to launch a biodegradable packaging line. They have identified a corporate client ready to sign a 3‑year contract, but need ₹1 crore for machinery. The founders have ₹20 lakh personal savings and approach a bank for the rest. (a) Identify which definition elements are already satisfied and which remain uncertain. (b) Suggest two risk‑mitigation strategies the founders could adopt before committing the bank loan.
ISC 2023 Paper – Short Answer (3 marks): “State the four elements of the entrepreneurship definition as per the ISC Business Studies syllabus and give one Indian example for each element.”

**Application:** A rural entrepreneur in Odisha wants to start a cold‑storage unit for mangoes. She has ₹8 lakh savings, can access a 12 % MUDRA loan, and the state offers a 25 % capital subsidy. Identify which entrepreneurial characteristics she must employ to structure the financing and justify each.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** (a) Define *risk‑bearing* in entrepreneurship. (b) A start‑up founder invests ₹15 lakh of personal savings and raises ₹35 lakh from angel investors for a new AI‑based agritech platform. Explain how this illustrates risk‑bearing. (c) State one limitation of risk‑bearing as a sole indicator of entrepreneurship.

**APPLICATION:** An aspiring entrepreneur plans to launch a solar‑panel installation service in Rajasthan. Using the eight success characteristics, draft a one‑page action plan (bullet points) showing how she will demonstrate each trait in the first 12 months.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain how the characteristics of successful entrepreneurs contribute to the sustainability of a start‑up in the Indian regulatory environment. Use two real‑life Indian examples.” (6 marks)
Explain how a reduction in corporate tax rate from 30 % to 22 % for new manufacturing units influences entrepreneurial decisions.
Create a brief policy brief (max 150 words) recommending two political reforms to boost social entrepreneurship in India.
In the ISC 2023 Business Studies paper, a 4‑mark question asked: “Explain how political stability and policy continuity influence entrepreneurial risk perception.” Write a model answer.

A startup founder reads that “India’s Ease of Doing Business rank improved from 142 to 63.” She concludes that all political barriers to entrepreneurship have been removed. Critique this conclusion using at least three specific political factors.

(a) Define “policy continuity” in the context of entrepreneurship. (2 marks) (b) Explain how a lack of policy continuity affected the solar energy sector in India between 2014‑2019. (4 marks) (c) Suggest one institutional mechanism to improve policy continuity for emerging sectors. (2 marks)
ISC 2022 Past Paper Style: “Political factors are the most critical determinants of entrepreneurial success in India.” Discuss. (12 marks)
A startup’s aggregate turnover in FY 2023‑24 is ₹18 lakh. It operates in a normal‑category state. Is GST registration compulsory?
A food‑processing unit in Tamil Nadu employs 30 workers. Which labour statutes apply, and what is the key compliance each imposes?
Explain how a rise in the GST rate on a product from 12 % to 18 % affects the break‑even volume of a startup with fixed costs ₹5 lakh, variable cost ₹200/unit, and selling price ₹500/unit (pre‑GST).

A new ed‑tech platform plans to offer online courses across India. (a) Identify the central statutes that apply to its operations. (b) Explain whether the platform needs a separate licence from each state. (c) Discuss the impact of the Consumer Protection (E‑Commerce) Rules 2020 on its refund policy.

Compare the statutory entry barriers for (i) a small‑scale food‑processing unit (investment ₹50 lakh) and (ii) a scalable fintech startup (investment ₹5 crore) in India. Structure your answer under: (a) Incorporation & capital requirements, (b) Sector‑specific licences, (c) Ongoing compliance frequency, (d) Penalty exposure.

Critically evaluate the statement: “The introduction of the four Labour Codes (2020) has simplified statutory compliance for entrepreneurs.” Provide three arguments for and three against, referencing specific provisions.

Past‑paper style: “A startup incorporated in 2022 as a private limited company has not filed its annual return for FY 2022‑23. The Registrar of Companies issues a notice under Section 92(4) of the Companies Act 2013. (a) What is the maximum penalty that can be imposed on the company? (b) What is the penalty for each officer in default? (c) Suggest two remedial steps the startup should take immediately.”
A startup estimates fixed capital of ₹40 lakh and working capital of ₹15 lakh. Calculate total capital requirement and suggest two suitable Indian sources for each component.

**Application:** A young entrepreneur in Jaipur wants to launch a mobile‑app based tutoring platform. She has ₹8 lakh personal savings and can access a MUDRA Shishu loan up to ₹50 000. Estimate the maximum fixed and working capital she can allocate if she follows a 70:30 fixed‑to‑working capital ratio, and discuss whether this capital base is realistic for a tech startup.

**Comparison:** Compare the suitability of **venture capital** versus **bank term loan** for a biotech startup requiring ₹5 crore for R&D and pilot manufacturing. Structure your answer under (i) risk profile, (ii) repayment flexibility, (iii) strategic value addition.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** (a) Define ‘working capital’ and state its two components. (2 marks) (b) Explain how an increase in the credit period allowed to customers affects the working capital requirement of a trading firm. (3 marks) (c) A firm’s current assets are ₹40 lakh and current liabilities ₹25 lakh. Calculate its net working capital and comment on its liquidity position. (3 marks)

A food‑delivery startup plans to hire 200 delivery partners in Mumbai. The applicable minimum wage for unskilled workers is ₹ 450 per day (8‑hour shift). The startup offers a fixed daily pay of ₹ 500 plus a performance bonus of ₹ 50 per 10 deliveries. Calculate the total daily labour cost if each partner completes 30 deliveries on average.
Create a brief labour‑strategy outline for a new organic‑farming venture in Punjab that intends to employ 50 seasonal workers. Include recruitment, training, compliance, and retention elements.
A CISCE ISC 2023 paper asked: “Discuss how labour laws influence the choice of business organisation for a manufacturing startup.” Provide a concise answer structured for 4 marks.

A venture capitalist evaluates two early‑stage startups: Startup A (AI‑based analytics) and Startup B (handloom weaving). Both seek ₹ 2 crore funding. Discuss how labour‑factor analysis would differ in the due‑diligence for each. (Answer in 150 words)

An entrepreneur in Jaipur wants to set up a blue‑pottery unit employing 40 artisans. The state offers a 25% wage subsidy for the first year under the Mukhyamantri Yuva Swavalamban Yojana. If the market wage is ₹ 350/day, calculate the effective daily wage cost per artisan after subsidy, and the total annual subsidy amount for the unit (assume 300 working days).

Past‑paper style (ISC 2022, 6 marks): “Explain how the following labour‑related factors influence entrepreneurial decisions: (a) Availability of skilled labour, (b) Labour legislation, (c) Industrial relations climate.”
A cotton‑spinning startup in Gujarat faces a 20 % rise in global cotton prices. Evaluate two mitigation strategies it could adopt.

**HOTS:** A tea‑estate entrepreneur in Darjeeling considers two options: (i) continue buying green leaf from small growers at auction, (ii) lease 200 ha to cultivate own leaf. Using the raw‑material factor framework, compare the options on risk, control, and capital intensity.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** (a) Define “raw material” as a factor affecting entrepreneurship. (2 marks) (b) Explain how **price volatility** and **regulatory constraints** jointly influence an entrepreneur’s location decision. (4 marks) (c) Suggest two mitigation strategies for a startup facing both high price volatility and stringent environmental clearance for its key raw material. (4 marks)
