A student selects a 12 V DC motor rated 0.5 Nm continuous torque for a joint that requires 0.45 Nm at 30 rad/s. The motor’s no‑load speed is 40 rad/s. Explain whether this motor meets the 1.5× speed margin rule.
Given a PID controller tuned by Ziegler‑Nichols with ultimate gain Ku = 8 and ultimate period Tu = 0.4 s, compute Kp, Ki, and Kd. Show the formulas used.

A robot uses a 3‑cell Li‑Po pack (11.1 V nominal, 2200 mAh, 25 C rating). The motor draws 15 A peak, the controller board 0.8 A, and sensors 0.3 A. Determine if the pack can supply the peak current and estimate the maximum run time at an average draw of 5 A.

Design a complete power‑train for a line‑following robot that must carry a 500 g payload at 0.3 m/s on a 10 % incline. Provide motor torque, gear ratio, battery capacity (choose a standard 2‑cell Li‑Po), and a PID gain set using Ziegler‑Nichols (assume Ku = 6, Tu = 0.5 s). Show all steps.

A robotics team claims that “using a higher voltage battery always makes the robot faster.” Evaluate this claim for a 12 V DC motor with a fixed gear ratio, considering motor voltage limit, driver rating, and thermal constraints. (a) State the conditions under which the claim holds. (b) Explain two scenarios where increasing voltage degrades performance or damages hardware. (c) Relate your answer to the ISC marking emphasis on balanced design.

A line‑follower robot uses a PID controller with Kp=5, Ki=2, Kd=0.5. During a sharp 90° turn, the robot overshoots the line and oscillates. Propose a step‑by‑step gain adjustment plan, explaining the effect of each gain on overshoot and settling time. Include a sketch description of the expected root‑locus movement (no drawing required).

Compare the following two power‑train options for a 3 kg robot required to climb a 15° incline at 0.2 m/s. Option A: 12 V 100 W brushed motor, 20:1 gearbox, 3‑cell Li‑Po 2200 mAh 25 C. Option B: 24 V 150 W brushless motor with ESC, 15:1 gearbox, 6‑cell Li‑Po 5000 mAh 20 C. (a) Compute the required wheel torque for each option. (b) Determine which option provides longer run time. (c) Discuss the trade‑offs in complexity, cost, and control difficulty relevant to an ISC project.

An ISC past‑paper question (2023) asks: “Design a closed‑loop speed control for a 12 V DC motor using a microcontroller PWM output, an H‑bridge driver, and a quadrature encoder. Provide a block diagram, list the signals, and write the PID update equation in discrete time with a 1 kHz sampling period.” Produce a concise answer that would earn full marks.
In the ISC Robotics exam, a question asks: “Describe how the design‑thinking process aligns with the systems‑engineering V‑model.” Provide a structured answer suitable for 6 marks.

A multi‑part question: (a) List four sectors where collaborative robots (cobots) are increasingly adopted in India. (b) For each sector, state one safety standard that governs human‑robot interaction. (c) Explain why the design‑thinking “test” stage must include a risk‑assessment per ISO 12100.

Application scenario: A logistics company in Mumbai wants to automate loading of 20 kg cartons onto 12 m trailers using a robot. The dock height varies ± 50 mm. Propose a robot system architecture (topology, sensors, end‑effector) and map each element to a design‑thinking stage where it was decided.

Compare the suitability of a SCARA robot versus a 6‑axis articulated robot for the task of inserting a 5 mm diameter pin into a 5.1 mm hole on a moving conveyor (speed 0.5 m/s). Discuss kinematic, dynamic, and economic factors.

Past‑paper style: (a) Define “design thinking” in the context of robotic system development. (b) A student project uses design thinking to create a robot for cleaning solar panels on rooftops in Rajasthan. Outline the “empathise” and “define” outputs for this project. (c) Explain how the “prototype” stage would differ for a low‑fidelity vs. high‑fidelity prototype in this context. (Marks: 2+4+4 = 10)

A warehouse in Chennai wants to replace forklifts with AMRs for pallet transport. The floor has expansion joints every 6 m, and the building vibrates from nearby railway. List three technical challenges and one mitigation per challenge.

ISC 2023 Paper Question (adapted): "A robotic system is to be designed for automated harvesting of tomatoes in a polyhouse. (a) List three environmental constraints specific to polyhouse tomato farming. (b) For each constraint, specify a robot design feature. (c) Explain why a wheeled mobile base with a 6-DOF arm is preferred over a tracked base."

A prototype weeding robot runs for 2 h on a 12 V 7 Ah lead‑acid battery. The team wants 4 h runtime without increasing battery mass. Suggest two design‑thinking‑consistent strategies and explain how each would be validated in the Test phase.

Compare the design‑thinking approach with a traditional waterfall engineering process for a robotic project. Structure your answer as a table with at least five comparison dimensions (e.g., stakeholder involvement, iteration, documentation, risk handling, delivery). For each dimension, state which approach better serves a Class 11 ISC robotics project and why.

Design a minimal interface specification for a 6‑axis robot that must mount on a 50 mm pitch conveyor frame, run on 48 V DC, and exchange position data with a PLC every 1 ms. List the three interface categories and one concrete parameter for each.

An integration engineer observes that the robot’s actual cycle time during SAT is 1.3 s, exceeding the 1.0 s target. Propose two systematic troubleshooting steps that address communication and mechanical domains respectively.

A robotic cell uses a safety‑rated light curtain (Type 4) connected to a safety PLC. The light curtain’s OSSD outputs are wired to the safety PLC’s safe inputs. During validation, the safety PLC reports a “cross‑circuit fault” on the OSSD channels. (a) Explain what a cross‑circuit fault indicates in this context. (b) List two wiring errors that could cause it. (c) Describe the test procedure to locate the fault.

An integration engineer must choose between PROFINET IRT and EtherCAT for a new robot cell requiring 0.5 ms cycle time with 16 axes. (a) Compare the two protocols on determinism, topology flexibility, and vendor ecosystem. (b) Recommend one for this application and justify.

A deployment team records the following SAT data for a robot cell: 8‑hour run, 28 800 cycles planned, 27 500 cycles completed, 3 unplanned stops totaling 45 min, 2 quality rejects. (a) Calculate Availability, Performance, Quality, and OEE. (b) If the target OEE is 85 %, does the cell meet it? (c) Suggest one improvement for each OEE component.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern Question:** A manufacturing plant plans to deploy a robotic palletizing cell. The robot must handle 20 kg boxes at 8 cycles/min, interface with a stretch‑wrapper and a conveyor, and comply with ISO 10218‑1. (a) List four essential clauses from ISO 10218‑1 that the integration must address. (b) Draw a block diagram (text description acceptable) showing the safety‑related parts of the control system (SRP/CS) including emergency stop, safety PLC, robot controller, and light curtain. (c) Explain how the validation of the SRP/CS differs from functional testing of the robot’s motion.

Design a basic specification for a hospital logistics robot that must carry 30 kg of medicines, navigate 2 m wide corridors, and operate 12 hours on battery. List three key subsystems and one safety feature.
An ISC exam question asks: “List two functional safety requirements for a rehabilitation exoskeleton per ISO 13482 and describe a test method for each.” Provide a concise answer.

(a) Define “Physical Assistant Robot” per ISO 13482. (b) Give two examples from healthcare robotics. (c) State the minimum Performance Level required for a PAR that can exert 50 Nm at the user’s knee joint during gait training.

A rehabilitation robot uses a series elastic actuator (SEA) with spring constant k = 500 Nm/rad. The motor encoder reads 0.02 rad deflection during a therapy session. (a) Calculate the output torque. (b) If the control loop runs at 1 kHz and the torque command updates every 2 ms, what is the maximum torque ripple due to discretisation assuming a linear ramp? (c) Explain why SEA is preferred over rigid actuation for human‑robot interaction.

An ISC 2023 paper asked: “A team is developing a robot‑assisted needle insertion system for biopsy. The needle must be inserted to a depth of 80 mm with ±1 mm accuracy. The robot uses a linear stage with a 5 µm resolution encoder and a 0.5 mm pitch ballscrew. (a) Calculate the theoretical positioning resolution in mm. (b) Identify two error sources that could degrade accuracy below the requirement. (c) Propose a closed‑loop control strategy to achieve the required accuracy, naming the sensor modality.”

During field trials, a weeding robot achieves 78 % weed detection accuracy. The team decides to iterate by retraining the vision model with more labeled images. Which metric should they monitor to decide if the iteration was successful?
Design a three‑step test plan for a line‑following robot that must complete a 10 m track with sharp 90° turns. Specify the test type, objective, and pass criterion for each step.
Create a one‑page iteration log template that a Class 11 robotics team could use after each prototype cycle. List the essential fields.

In an ISC practical exam, you are asked to demonstrate the iteration cycle for a robotic arm that must pick objects of varying weight. Outline the steps you would perform in 30 minutes, including how you would record results.

(a) Define “unit test”, “integration test”, and “field test” in the context of a robotic system. (2 marks) (b) For a drone that must deliver a 500 g medical kit to a remote village, propose one specific test case for each test type, including the pass criterion. (4 marks) (c) Explain why the order of these tests matters for risk reduction. (2 marks)

Compare the iteration approach for a software‑only robot (e.g., a chatbot) versus a hardware‑intensive robot (e.g., a robotic arm). Discuss two key differences in prototype fidelity, test cost, and iteration speed. (6 marks)

An ISC 2023 practical paper asked: “You have built a line‑following robot. After three iterations, the robot still loses the line at sharp curves. Describe a systematic method to diagnose the root cause and decide the next design change.” Provide a step‑by‑step answer with marks allocation. (8 marks)
Evaluate the statement: “If a robot’s uptime is 95%, its Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) must also be 95%.”
A pick‑and‑place robot shows a sudden increase in mis‑pick rate from 0.2% to 2.5% after a software update. Using the 5 Whys technique, outline the first three “why” questions you would ask.
Design a one‑week PDCA cycle to test a new gripper material that claims 20% longer life. Specify the Plan, Do, Check, and Act steps with measurable criteria.

A robotic inspection cell uses a camera to detect surface scratches. The defect‑detection rate over 10 batches (each 200 parts) is: 98%, 97%, 99%, 96%, 98%, 97%, 98%, 99%, 97%, 98%. The specification requires ≥97.5% detection with 95% confidence. (a) Compute the mean detection rate and its 95% confidence interval. (b) Does the cell meet the specification? (c) If the next batch drops to 94%, which run rule is triggered?

A logistics robot fleet manager wants to reduce energy consumption per delivery. Current average: 1.85 kWh/delivery (σ=0.12, n=50). A new routing algorithm is tested on 30 deliveries, yielding mean 1.78 kWh (σ=0.10). (a) Perform a two‑sample t‑test (α=0.05, unequal variances) to evaluate improvement. (b) State the practical significance if the cost of electricity is ₹8/kWh and the fleet makes 10,000 deliveries/month.

A collaborative robot (cobot) is deployed for machine tending. The safety standard requires that the protective stop activates within 200 ms of a human entering the safeguarded zone. During validation, 15 stop‑time measurements (ms) are recorded: 185, 190, 188, 192, 187, 195, 189, 191, 186, 193, 188, 190, 187, 194, 189. (a) Test at α=0.01 whether the mean stop time exceeds 200 ms. (b) Compute the process capability index Cpk assuming specification limit USL=200 ms, LSL=0. (c) If the validation fails, propose two design‑thinking‑inspired modifications to reduce stop time.

Compare the use of a p‑chart versus an np‑chart for monitoring the defect rate of a robotic welding process where the number of welds inspected per shift varies between 80 and 120. (a) Which chart is appropriate and why? (b) If the process average defect rate is 2%, calculate the control limits for the appropriate chart for a shift with 100 welds. (c) Explain how varying sample size affects the control limits on the chosen chart.

ISC 2023 Robotics Paper, Question 4 (10 marks): “A robotic packaging line must achieve an OEE of at least 85%. Current data: Availability 92%, Performance 88%, Quality 96%. (a) Calculate the current OEE. (b) The plant manager proposes to increase Performance to 95% by reducing minor stops. Assuming Availability and Quality remain unchanged, what will be the new OEE? (c) If the target is still not met, suggest two specific improvement actions for Availability and two for Quality, justifying each with a robotic‑system example.”

(c) Explain why “one week” is an insufficient test duration (1 mark).

Comparison (multi‑part): Compare the design‑thinking approach for a “hospital logistics robot” versus a “search‑and‑rescue drone” across the Define and Ideate stages. (a) List two Define‑stage differences (1 mark each). (b) List two Ideate‑stage differences (1 mark each). (c) Which project would benefit more from rapid‑prototyping with 3D‑printed parts? Justify (2 marks).

CISCE past‑paper pattern (multi‑part): The 2022 ISC Robotics paper included a 5‑mark question: “Design a robotic system for automated sorting of mixed municipal waste. (c) Sketch an Ideate selection matrix with three concepts and four criteria (weights sum to 100 %) (2 marks).

Answer the following as per ISC 2023 pattern: (a) Define sociology. (2 marks) (b) Name two founding fathers of sociology. (2 marks) (c) Explain the relevance of studying the origin of sociology for understanding contemporary Indian society. (4 marks)

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Define “social fact” as per Durkheim. (2 marks) (b) Give one example of a social fact in contemporary Indian society. (2 marks) (c) Explain why Durkheim insisted that social facts must be treated as things. (4 marks)
ISC‑style: “Anthropology is the most humanistic of the sciences and the most scientific of the humanities.” Discuss with reference to its nature and scope. (10 marks)
(Evaluation/Critique) Critique the concept of “anthropology at home” as practiced in India. Does it dilute the discipline’s comparative edge? (Answer in 150 words with three distinct points.)

(Comparison) Compare the role of fieldwork in Malinowski’s *Argonauts of the Western Pacific* (1922) and S.C. Dube’s *Indian Village* (1955). Highlight two similarities and two differences in their fieldwork practice and theoretical payoff.

(CISCE past‑paper pattern) (a) Define “holism” in anthropology. (2 marks) (b) Explain how the four‑field approach operationalizes holism. (4 marks) (c) Give one example from Indian anthropology where holism was crucial to the research design. (4 marks)
Name the anthropologist who wrote *Primitive Culture* (1871) and the theoretical school he founded.

**HOTS:** “If evolutionism had never been challenged, how might contemporary anthropology’s ethical stance toward indigenous peoples differ? Discuss in 150 words.”

**Evaluation/Critique (multi‑part):** (a) State one major criticism of **diffusionism** from a **functionalist** perspective. (2 marks) (b) State one major criticism of **functionalism** from a **structuralist** perspective. (2 marks) (c) Which school, in your view, best explains the persistence of **caste endogamy** in modern India? Justify in 80 words. (4 marks)

**Comparison (multi‑part):** Compare **evolutionism** and **structuralism** on the following dimensions: (i) Unit of analysis (1 mark) (ii) Role of history (1 mark) (iii) View of cultural diversity (1 mark) (iv) Methodological implication (1 mark)

**CISCE past‑paper pattern (multi‑part, 6 marks):** “Read the extract and answer: ‘The kula ring is not merely an economic exchange; it is a vast inter‑tribal network that binds men together in a system of mutual obligations and prestige.’ — *Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific* (a) Identify the theoretical school represented. (1 mark) (b) Name the key concept Malinowski uses to explain the kula’s persistence. (1 mark) (c) Explain how Radcliffe‑Brown would reinterpret the same phenomenon. Explain the role of the Indian Sociological Society in institutionalizing sociology in India. (4 marks)
Discuss the impact of the “Delhi School” on the development of sociological theory in India. (6 marks)

(a) Identify two Enlightenment ideas that influenced the birth of sociology. (2 marks) (b) Explain how each idea shaped early sociological thought. (4 marks) (c) Evaluate whether these ideas remain relevant in contemporary sociology. (4 marks)

A researcher wants to study the impact of digital media on village youth in Rajasthan. (a) Which discipline — sociology or anthropology — is more appropriate, and why? (3 marks) (b) Suggest one quantitative and one qualitative method suitable for this study. (4 marks) (c) Discuss one ethical concern specific to this context. (3 marks)

Critically assess the statement: “The scope of sociology is limited to the study of social institutions.” (a) Present two arguments supporting the statement. (4 marks) (b) Present two arguments refuting the statement. (4 marks) (c) Conclude with your reasoned position. (2 marks)
Compare the origin of sociology and anthropology using the following criteria: (a) Historical context (3 marks), (b) Key founding figures (3 marks), (c) Primary methodological legacy (4 marks).

Past‑paper style (ISC 2022, 10 marks): “Trace the development of sociology in India and highlight its major theoretical orientations.” (a) Outline the three phases of Indian sociology’s development. In an ISC‑style short answer (3 marks), explain how Spencer’s idea of “survival of the fittest” differs from Darwin’s natural selection.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “Herbert Spencer’s theory of social evolution has been criticised for being ‘a biological metaphor stretched beyond its limits.’ Discuss with reference to (i) the organic analogy, (ii) the concept of ‘survival of the fittest’, and (iii) the Indian experience of planned development.” (12 marks)
Explain Social Darwinism and discuss two major criticisms. (10 marks)

Evaluate whether Spencer’s organic analogy can adequately explain the rapid social transformation during India’s 1991 economic liberalisation.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** The following question appeared in ISC 2022 Sociology Paper 1 (4 marks): “Explain two ways in which Herbert Spencer’s organic analogy differs from Durkheim’s structural functionalism.” Provide a model answer with mark allocation.
**APPLICATION:** Design a 5‑minute classroom activity that lets Class 11 students experience the sacred/profane shift using a familiar Indian school ritual.
**APPLICATION:** Design a short survey (3 questions) to test whether employees in a Mumbai call centre experience anomie related to their specialised roles.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern Question:** “Durkheim argues that the transition from mechanical to organic solidarity is driven by the increasing division of labour. (a) Explain the term ‘dynamic density’ and its role in this transition. (3 marks) (b) Using an Indian example, illustrate how a rise in dynamic density can lead to anomie. (4 marks) (c) Briefly evaluate whether the concept of organic solidarity adequately captures the social cohesion of a contemporary Indian metropolitan city. (3 marks)”
In an ISC‑style question, explain how Weber’s concept of the “iron cage” relates to the rationalisation of modern Indian administration. (4 marks)

(a) List the three components of Weber’s definition of rational‑legal authority. (b) Explain how each component supports bureaucratic predictability. (c) Give one Indian example where a component is weakened. (3+3+2 marks)

Apply Weber’s bureaucracy to the functioning of a large Indian private corporation (e.g., Tata Steel). Identify two features that align with the ideal‑type and two that differ because of corporate culture. (4 marks)

Critically evaluate the statement: “Weber’s ideal‑type of bureaucracy is irrelevant for understanding 21st‑century Indian start‑ups.” Structure your answer with (a) two arguments for relevance, (b) two arguments against relevance, (c) a balanced conclusion. (2+2+2 marks)
Compare Weber’s bureaucracy with Durkheim’s organic solidarity in terms of (a) basis of social cohesion, (b) role of rules, (c) view of individual autonomy. (2+2+2 marks)
Past‑paper style: “Explain how Max Weber’s concept of ‘Verstehen’ informs his analysis of bureaucracy.” (6 marks)
Given a scenario: “A municipal commissioner issues an order to demolish illegal constructions under the Municipal Corporation Act, 1957.” Identify the type of authority.
Write a short note (150 words) on Weber’s classification of authority, highlighting the basis of legitimacy for each type.

**Application – Multi‑part** A new religious sect, **“Ananda Marga”**, is founded by **Guru Anand** who claims direct divine revelation. After his death, a **Council of Disciples** codifies his teachings into a **“Book of Discipline”**, establishes **regional centres** with appointed **coordinators**, and registers the organisation under the **Societies Registration Act, 1860**. (a) Identify the authority type during Guru Anand’s leadership. (b) Identify the authority type after the Council’s actions. (c) Explain which routinization pathway this illustrates.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern – Multi‑part** Answer the following: (a) State **two features** of charismatic authority. (2 marks) (b) Explain **why legal‑rational authority is considered the most stable** in modern societies. (3 marks) (c) Give **one Indian example** of each authority type. (3 marks)
ISC‑style: “Explain how Marx’s concept of alienation operates in the contemporary Indian gig economy (e.g., food‑delivery riders).” (6 marks)

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN (multi‑part):** “Read the excerpt: ‘The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.’ (Marx & Engels, *Communist Manifesto*, 1848) (a) Identify the **historical materialist** assumption underlying this statement. List the six social sciences that Chapter 3 relates to sociology.

**Application – Multi‑part** (a) Choose two disciplines from this chapter to study urban homelessness in Delhi. (b) Outline a research design integrating them. (c) Identify one ethical concern. *Marks: (a) 2, (b) 5, (c) 2*

**Evaluation/Critique – Multi‑part** (a) Critique the view that anthropology’s focus on “culture” makes it irrelevant for studying modern Indian corporations. (b) Provide a counterexample. (c) Suggest how sociology can incorporate anthropological insights. *Marks: (a) 3, (b) 3, (c) 2*

**Comparison – Multi‑part** (a) Contrast the primary data sources used by history and sociology when studying the 1857 Revolt. (b) Explain how each discipline’s temporal focus shapes its research questions. (c) Assess which discipline better captures subaltern voices. *Marks: (a) 3, (b) 3, (c) 2*

What is the minimum age defined as “senior citizen” under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007?

Evaluate the statement: “The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 has solved accessibility problems in India.”

**COMPARISON:** Compare the barrier‑removal approach of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 with the earlier Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995, focusing on (a) definition of disability, (b) obligation for universal design, (c) enforcement mechanism.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Discuss how attitudinal barriers and built‑environment barriers interact to exclude differently‑abled students from higher education in India. Support your answer with two concrete examples.” (6 marks)
Explain why a 70% luminance contrast ratio is specified for visual signage in the Harmonised Guidelines.

In an ISC exam, a question asks: “Discuss the role of signage in promoting social inclusion of persons with disabilities, citing the RPwD Act 2016 and Harmonised Guidelines.” Outline a structured answer (introduction, body, conclusion) with mark allocation.

(2 marks) (c) Conclude whether the criticism invalidates the framework for studying Indian villages. (2 marks)

**CISCE past‑paper pattern (structured):** “Read the excerpt: ‘The village is an ecological unit where the physical environment, the technique of production and the social structure are in constant interaction.’ (Mukherjee, *Social Ecology*, 1930) (a) Identify the three interacting elements. (2 marks)”
Write a short note (150 words) on Ghurye’s contribution to the study of caste, highlighting his methodological approach.

In an ISC‑style short‑answer question, a student writes: “Sanskritization means lower castes become Brahmins.” How would you correct this answer to reflect Srinivas’s precise meaning? (2 marks)

**HOTS Multi-part:** (a) Identify one common theme across the works of Mukherjee, Bose, and Karve. (b) Explain how each scholar addresses social change within that theme. (c) Critique the adequacy of their combined frameworks for studying urban India today. (3+3+4 = 10 marks)

**Comparison Multi-part:** Compare the treatment of tribe in N.K. Bose and Radha Kamal Mukherjee. (a) Identify each scholar’s primary unit of analysis for tribe. **CISCE Past-Paper Pattern Multi-part:** “Discuss the contributions of Indian sociologists to the development of sociology in India.” (15 marks) Structure your answer with introduction, body (thematic), and conclusion. Indicate mark allocation per section.

(CISCE past‑paper pattern) A 2023 ISC question asked: “Explain how the concept of ‘Sanskritization’ can be used to analyse the changing status of a tribal community that has recently been included in the Scheduled Tribes list.” Provide a model answer with mark allocation.
What is the default profit‑sharing ratio prescribed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 when the partnership deed is silent?

Calculate the amount of interest on capital to be charged to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.

(a) Compute interest on drawings for P assuming 6 % p.a. and average period 6 months. (b) Prepare the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account. (c) If the firm decides to create a reserve of 10 % of profit after all appropriations, show the reserve amount.

Prepare the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and show the final capital balances assuming fluctuating capital method and no drawings.” (10 marks)
Which section of the Indian Partnership Act 1932 defines a partnership?

Compare the mutual agency principle under the Indian Partnership Act 1932 with the concept of “apparent authority” in agency law. Highlight one similarity and one difference relevant to partnership accounting.
A past ISC question: “State any three consequences of non‑registration of a partnership firm under the Indian Partnership Act 1932.” Provide the answer with section references.
State the default profit‑sharing ratio under the Indian Partnership Act 1932 when the partnership deed is silent.
A firm has three partners and no deed. Partner A contributed ₹5,00,000 capital, B ₹3,00,000, C ₹2,00,000. Explain why the profit share is still equal.
Calculate each partner’s share of a ₹9,00,000 profit for a four‑partner firm with no deed.

In the absence of a partnership deed, which of the following is NOT a default provision under the Indian Partnership Act 1932? (a) Equal profit sharing (b) No interest on capital (c) Interest on drawings @ 6 % p.a. (d) No salary to partners.

**HOTS – Multi‑part:** A four‑partner firm (A, B, C, D) has no deed. During the year: (a) A advanced a loan of ₹2,00,000 to the firm. (b) B withdrew ₹1,50,000 as drawings. Compute: (i) Interest on A’s loan, (ii) Interest on B’s drawings, (iii) Profit available for distribution, (iv) Each partner’s final share.

(c) What default rule governs the new partner’s profit share?

**Comparison – Multi‑part:** Compare the default rules for (i) interest on capital, (ii) interest on drawings, (iii) partner’s salary under the Indian Partnership Act 1932 with those under the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008 (LLP Act). Highlight two key differences.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern – Multi‑part:** (a) State the default profit‑sharing ratio when a partnership deed is absent. (b) A firm with three partners (no deed) earns ₹18,00,000 profit. Create a scenario where a partnership deed is silent on interest on capital. Using the Indian Partnership Act 1932, state the treatment in the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account.

A firm’s deed provides “12 % commission on profit after charging such commission.” Net profit before commission is ₹5,00,000. Compute the commission.

Partner X is entitled to a commission of 8 % on profit after commission. The firm also guarantees Partner Y a minimum profit of ₹40,000. Net profit before commission is ₹4,00,000. Profit‑sharing ratio (excluding commission) is 3:2. Show the Appropriation Account.

An ISC 2022 question: “A partnership firm earned a profit of ₹6,00,000 before charging commission to partner B at 15 % on profit after commission. Calculate B’s commission and the profit available for distribution.”

**HOTS:** A partnership deed provides “Partner A gets 20 % commission on profit after commission.” The firm also agrees to transfer 10 % of profit **before** commission to a reserve. Net profit before any appropriation is ₹20,00,000. Compute commission, reserve transfer, and profit left for distribution.

**Application:** A firm’s deed: “Partner B receives a fixed commission of ₹50,000 per annum plus 5 % on profit after commission.” Net profit before commission ₹6,00,000. Calculate total commission to B.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern (2023):** “A partnership firm earned a profit of ₹9,00,000 before charging commission to Partner C at 12 % on profit after commission. The deed also provides for a transfer of 5 % of profit before commission to General Reserve. Profit‑sharing ratio (excluding commission) is 2:1 between C and D. Prepare the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.”
A partnership deed is silent about reserves. The partners decide to retain 15 % of profit as a General Reserve. Which account is debited to create this reserve?

A firm’s Profit and Loss Appropriation Account shows a net profit of ₹5,00,000 before appropriations. Partners agree to allocate 8 % of profit to a Workmen Compensation Reserve and 5 % to an Investment Fluctuation Reserve. Calculate the amount transferred to each reserve and the balance available for distribution after these reserves.

A firm’s Profit and Loss Account shows a net profit of ₹9,00,000. Partners agree to allocate 8 % to a General Reserve, 5 % to an Investment Fluctuation Reserve, and the remaining profit is to be shared equally. Calculate (a) the amount transferred to each reserve, (b) the profit available for distribution, and (c) each partner’s share of profit.

(a) List the steps to prepare the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account when a partnership has interest on capital, salary to a partner, commission, and a reserve to be created. (b) Using the following data, prepare the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account: Net profit before appropriations ₹5,50,000; Interest on capital ₹44,000; Salary to partner A ₹60,000; Commission to partner B ₹33,000; Reserve to be created 10 % of net profit. (c) State the journal entry for the reserve and show how the reserve affects the partners’ Capital Accounts under the fluctuating capital method, assuming profit sharing ratio 3:2 and opening capitals A ₹4,00,000, B ₹2,50,000.
In a firm where partners X, Y, Z share profits 4:3:2, Z is guaranteed ₹50,000 by X and Y in the ratio 3:2. If net profit after all appropriations is ₹1,20,000, what is the deficiency borne by X?

A partnership deed states: “Partner M shall receive a minimum profit of ₹40,000 per annum, guaranteed by partners N and O equally.” Net profit after appropriations is ₹90,000. Profit‑sharing ratio is M:N:O = 5:3:2. Prepare the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account showing the guarantee adjustment.
A CISCE ISC 2023 question: “Partners A, B, C share profits 3:2:1. C is guaranteed ₹30,000 by the firm. Net profit ₹1,20,000. Show the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account.” Provide the full account.

**HOTS:** A partnership deed provides that Partner X shall receive a guaranteed profit of ₹80,000 per annum, guaranteed by the firm. The profit‑sharing ratio is X:Y:Z = 3:2:1. In a year, the firm incurs a net loss of ₹20,000 after charging interest on capital and salaries. The deed is silent on guarantee in case of loss. Discuss whether X is entitled to the guaranteed amount and how the loss should be allocated.

**APPLICATION:** Partners P, Q, R share profits 5:3:2. R is guaranteed ₹70,000 by P and Q in the ratio 4:1. Net profit after all appropriations is ₹2,50,000. However, the deed also provides that the guarantee shall not exceed 20% of the net profit. Compute the actual guarantee payable to R and the deficiency borne by P and Q.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN (multi‑part):** (a) Partners L, M, N share profits 3:2:1. N is guaranteed ₹60,000 by L and M in the ratio 2:1. Net profit after all appropriations is ₹1,80,000. Compute the amount credited to each partner’s capital account. (4 marks) (b) If instead the guarantee is by the firm, recompute the credits. (3 marks) (c) State one disclosure requirement for profit guarantee in the notes to accounts. (1 mark)
State the default profit‑sharing ratio under the Indian Partnership Act 1932 when the deed is silent.
Evaluate the impact on partners’ capital accounts if interest on capital was omitted for three years and the deed provides 10 % p.a. on fixed capitals of ₹5,00,000 (A) and ₹3,00,000 (B).

Apply the past‑adjustment procedure: Partners P and Q share profits 2:1. The deed is amended to 3:2 retrospectively for the last two years. Profits were ₹6,00,000 (Year 1) and ₹8,00,000 (Year 2). Compute the adjustment for each partner.
Create a journal entry for the past adjustment in Question 4, assuming the firm uses fluctuating capital accounts.

A CISCE ISC past‑paper style question: “M/s Gupta & Co. discovered that partner’s salary of ₹20,000 p.a. was not recorded for 2021‑22 and 2022‑23. The deed provides salary to partner R only. Pass the adjusting entry on 31 March 2024.”

**HOTS:** A partnership firm discovers that for the past three years, partner’s commission was calculated on net profit before charging such commission, whereas the deed specifies commission on net profit after charging commission. Explain the conceptual error and compute the adjustment for Year 3 if net profit before commission was ₹10,00,000 and commission rate is 5 %.

**Application:** Partners R and S share profits 4:1. The deed is amended to 3:2 retrospectively for two years. Profits: Year 1 ₹5,00,000; Year 2 ₹7,00,000. The firm uses fixed capitals with current accounts. Prepare the adjustment entry.

**Evaluation/Critique (multi‑part):** (a) Critique the practice of passing past‑adjustment entries through the Profit & Loss Account instead of the Appropriation Account. (2 marks) (b) If a firm has both fixed and fluctuating capitals, explain how the adjustment entry differs. (3 marks) (c) A partner argues that past adjustments should be disclosed as a prior‑period item in the Statement of Profit & Loss. Evaluate this view per ISC guidelines. (2 marks)

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern (multi‑part):** M/s Singh & Co. (partners A, B, C) shared profits 2:2:1. On 1 April 2023 they admitted D with 1/5th share, and retrospectively revised the old partners’ ratio to 3:2:1 for 2021‑22 and 2022‑23. Profits: 2021‑22 ₹6,00,000; 2022‑23 ₹8,00,000. (a) Compute the past adjustment for each old partner. (4 marks) (b) Pass the journal entry on 31 March 2024 assuming fluctuating capitals. (3 marks) (c) State how the adjustment will be disclosed in the financial statements. (2 marks)
A firm’s goodwill is valued at ₹1,00,000 but does not appear in the books. Partners A and B change their PSR from 3:2 to 1:1. Pass the journal entry for goodwill adjustment.

Draft the journal entries for the following on change in PSR: (i) Goodwill valued ₹50,000 not in books; (ii) General Reserve ₹20,000; (iii) Revaluation loss ₹5,000. Old ratio 2:1, new ratio 1:1. Partners X and Y.

CISCE exam-style: A, B, C share 5:3:2. They change to 2:2:1. Goodwill ₹90,000 (not in books). General Reserve ₹45,000. Revaluation profit ₹15,000. Pass necessary journal entries and show Partners’ Capital Accounts. (10 marks)

**HOTS:** Partners P, Q, R share 3:2:1. They change to 1:1:1. Goodwill ₹1,80,000 (not in books). General Reserve ₹60,000. Revaluation loss ₹30,000. After adjustments, they decide to adjust capitals to the new ratio by opening current accounts. Show the full working for sacrificing/gaining ratios, goodwill adjustment, reserve distribution, revaluation, and final capital/current account balances. (12 marks)

**Application:** A firm’s partners L and M share 4:1. They change to 3:2. Goodwill ₹2,50,000 (not in books). Workmen Compensation Fund ₹50,000. Investment Fluctuation Fund ₹30,000. Revaluation profit ₹40,000. Capitals: L ₹5,00,000, M ₹3,00,000. Partners agree to adjust capitals to new ratio by cash. Pass journal entries and compute cash brought/withdrawn. (10 marks)

**Evaluation/Critique:** “When goodwill is not recorded in books, it is always better to raise goodwill at full value and then write it off in the old ratio rather than adjusting directly through capital accounts in gaining/sacrificing ratio.” Critically evaluate this statement with reference to accounting standards and partnership practice. (8 marks)

**Comparison:** Compare and contrast the accounting treatment of a change in profit‑sharing ratio with the admission of a new partner, focusing on (a) sacrificing/gaining ratio computation, (b) goodwill treatment, (c) distribution of reserves, (d) capital adjustment. (10 marks)

**CISCE Past-Paper Pattern:** (a) A, B, C share 5:3:2. They change to 2:2:1. Goodwill ₹1,50,000 (not in books). General Reserve ₹75,000. Revaluation loss ₹25,000. Pass journal entries. (6 marks) (b) After the above, partners decide to adjust capitals to the new ratio by bringing/withdrawing cash. Capitals before adjustment: A ₹4,00,000, B ₹3,00,000, C ₹2,00,000. Show the cash transactions. (4 marks)

A firm has average profit of ₹2,40,000. The normal rate of return in the industry is 12%. The total capital employed (fixed assets + current assets – current liabilities) is ₹15,00,000. Calculate goodwill using the super profit method with 3 years’ purchase.

From the following information, calculate goodwill using the capitalisation method and state the journal entry if the goodwill is to be written off immediately: Average profit = ₹3,00,000; Normal rate of return = 10%; Total assets (excluding goodwill) = ₹22,00,000; Outside liabilities = ₹4,00,000.

(a) Define super profit. (b) Explain why the number of years’ purchase is a matter of agreement between partners. (c) If a firm’s average profit is ₹5,00,000, normal profit is ₹3,20,000, and partners agree on 2 years’ purchase, compute goodwill.

A firm has capital employed of ₹8,00,000 and a normal rate of return of 15%. Its average profit for the last four years is ₹1,50,000, ₹1,70,000, ₹1,60,000, and ₹1,80,000. Compute goodwill using the average profit method with 2 years’ purchase.

A partnership firm’s Balance Sheet shows: Capital Accounts (fixed): A – ₹4,00,000; B – ₹2,50,000. Reserves: General Reserve – ₹1,00,000; Workmen Compensation Fund – ₹50,000. Average profit of the last three years – ₹2,20,000. Normal rate of return in the industry – 10%. The partners decide to admit C for 1/4 share, bringing ₹3,00,000 as capital. Goodwill is to be valued by the super profit method with 2 years’ purchase and raised in the books. Required: (i) Calculate the value of goodwill. (ii) Determine the sacrificing ratio of A and B. (iii) Pass the necessary journal entries for admission of C including goodwill, capital, and reserves.
State the default profit‑sharing ratio and interest‑on‑capital rate prescribed by the Indian Partnership Act 1932 when the partnership deed is silent.

A partnership deed provides for interest on capital @ 10 % p.a. but is silent on interest on drawings. Partner A withdrew ₹ 50,000 on 1 July 2023 and ₹ 30,000 on 1 January 2024. The accounting year ends 31 March 2024. Compute interest on drawings at the statutory rate.

Prepare the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account for the year ended 31 March 2024 for partners X, Y, Z (profit‑sharing ratio 3:2:1). Net profit before appropriation ₹ 6,00,000. Deed provides: interest on capital @ 12 % p.a. on opening capitals (X ₹ 5,00,000, Y ₹ 3,00,000, Z ₹ 2,00,000); salary to X ₹ 24,000 p.a.; commission to Y @ 5 % of net profit after charging such commission; transfer 10 % of divisible profit to General Reserve. No interest on drawings. Show workings.

Create a journal entry for past adjustment: It was discovered that interest on capital @ 10 % p.a. on Partner A’s capital of ₹ 4,00,000 for 2022‑23 was omitted. The profit for 2022‑23 was shared equally between A and B. Pass the adjustment entry on 1 April 2023.

An ISC 2023 8‑mark question: “P, Q, R are partners sharing profits 4:3:2. The deed provides for interest on capital @ 9 % p.a., salary to P ₹ 30,000, commission to Q @ 10 % of net profit after charging such commission, and a guarantee to R that his share shall not be less than ₹ 1,20,000. Net profit before appropriation ₹ 9,00,000. Capitals: P ₹ 6,00,000, Q ₹ 4,00,000, R ₹ 2,00,000. Prepare the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account.” Outline the steps and final profit shares.

**HOTS:** A partnership deed provides for interest on capital @ 10 % p.a. and interest on drawings @ 6 % p.a. Partner A’s capital is ₹ 6,00,000 throughout the year. He draws ₹ 20,000 at the beginning of each quarter. The firm’s net profit before appropriation is ₹ 5,00,000. The deed is silent on salary, commission, and reserves. Compute the net amount credited to A’s Current Account for the year, assuming fixed capital method.

**APPLICATION:** A firm’s deed states: “Commission to managing partner @ 12 % of net profit before charging such commission.” Net profit before any appropriation is ₹ 8,00,000. The managing partner also receives salary ₹ 48,000 and interest on capital ₹ 72,000. Compute the commission amount and the divisible profit after commission.

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE (multi‑part):** (a) A partnership deed provides for a guarantee to Partner Z that his share of profit shall not be less than ₹ 2,00,000. The profit‑sharing ratio is 4:3:2 (X:Y:Z). Net divisible profit is ₹ 9,00,000. The accountant allocates the guarantee deficit equally between X and Y. Critique this treatment. (b) If the guarantee is instead given by X alone, how does the allocation change? (c) Show the journal entry for the guarantee adjustment in both cases.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN (2022, 8 marks):** “P, Q, R are partners sharing profits 5:3:2. Their fixed capitals on 1 April 2021: P ₹ 10,00,000, Q ₹ 6,00,000, R ₹ 4,00,000. Deed: interest on capital @ 9 % p.a.; salary to P ₹ 60,000 p.a.; commission to Q @ 10 % of net profit after charging such commission; transfer 10 % of divisible profit to General Reserve. Net profit before appropriation for year ended 31 March 2022 ₹ 15,00,000. Prepare Profit & Loss Appropriation Account and Partners’ Current Accounts.”
A partnership firm purchases another firm for ₹2 crore. The fair value of net identifiable assets acquired is ₹1.6 crore. Calculate goodwill and state the journal entry.

**HOTS:** A firm acquires another for ₹5 crore. The fair value of net identifiable assets is ₹4.2 crore. The acquirer’s management argues that because the target has a strong brand, the goodwill should be split into “brand goodwill” ₹50 lakh and “remaining goodwill” ₹30 lakh. Is this permissible under AS 26? Justify.

**APPLICATION:** In a partnership, Partner A retires. The firm’s goodwill is valued at ₹60 lakh (not previously recorded). The continuing partners decide to raise goodwill in the books at full value and then write it off. Show the journal entries.
**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** “Goodwill should be amortised over 10 years because it provides benefits for a limited period.” Critically evaluate this statement with reference to AS 26.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Define goodwill. (2 marks) (b) State two reasons why internally generated goodwill is not recognised. (2 marks) (c) A firm purchases another for ₹8 crore. Net identifiable assets fair value ₹6.5 crore. Calculate goodwill and pass the journal entry. (4 marks)
A firm purchases another business for ₹25 crore. The fair value of identifiable net assets acquired is ₹18 crore. Compute the goodwill recognised and classify it as purchased or internally generated.
In an ISC board question, a student writes: “Goodwill is amortised over 10 years like other intangible assets.” Critique this statement.

A firm’s balance sheet shows “Goodwill ₹12 lakh” acquired two years ago. The management believes the brand value has increased due to a successful marketing campaign and wants to revalue goodwill upward by ₹3 lakh. Is this permissible under ISC standards? Justify.

A company acquires a subsidiary and recognises goodwill of ₹40 lakh. At year‑end, the recoverable amount of the cash‑generating unit (CGU) to which goodwill is allocated is ₹35 lakh, while its carrying amount (including goodwill) is ₹45 lakh. Compute the impairment loss and explain its allocation.

(a) Define “purchased goodwill” and “internally generated goodwill”. (b) Explain why ISC prohibits recognition of internally generated goodwill. (c) If a firm spends ₹5 lakh on advertising to build brand awareness, how is this treated?

**ISC 2023 Paper – Question 4 (a)** “M/s. Gupta Ltd. acquired M/s. Singh Ltd. for ₹1,20,00,000. The fair value of Singh Ltd.’s identifiable net assets was ₹85,00,000. The directors of Gupta Ltd. believe that the goodwill of ₹35,00,000 should be amortised over 7 years because the industry average life of goodwill is 7 years.” (i) State whether the directors’ view is correct. (ii) Describe the correct accounting treatment for the goodwill recognised. (iii) If at the end of Year 1 the recoverable amount of the CGU is ₹1,10,00,000 and its carrying amount (including goodwill) is ₹1,18,00,000, calculate the impairment loss and its allocation.
A firm’s identifiable net assets are ₹50 lakh. Its average profit is ₹12 lakh and the normal rate of return is 15 %. Identify whether goodwill exists and name the feature that explains this.

A firm’s goodwill is valued using the capitalisation of average profit method. The average profit is ₹25 lakh and the normal rate of return is 10 %. Compute goodwill and explain which feature of goodwill makes this method appropriate.

During admission of a partner, the firm’s goodwill is ₹40 lakh. The new partner brings ₹20 lakh as capital for a 1/5th share. Show the journal entry for goodwill adjustment and state the feature that necessitates this entry.

(a) Explain why goodwill is not recognised for internally generated brands. (b) If a firm purchases another firm and pays ₹5 crore over net assets, how is this treated? (c) What feature of goodwill justifies the difference?

Given two firms A and B with following details: Firm A – average profit ₹10 lakh, strong brand, good location; Firm B – average profit ₹12 lakh, weak brand, remote location. Which firm likely has higher goodwill? Justify.

(a) Identify three internal factors and two external factors that affect goodwill value. (b) For a firm operating in a highly cyclical industry, explain how industry cyclicality interacts with management quality to influence goodwill. (c) If the firm’s average profit is ₹20 lakh and the appropriate years’ purchase is determined as 2.5 due to high cyclicality but strong management, compute goodwill.

A partnership firm “Mehta & Associates” provides CA services in Mumbai. It has a stable client base, partners with 15 years’ experience, and operates from a prestigious address. The firm’s average profit is ₹25 lakh. The industry norm for years’ purchase is 3. However, a new regulation mandates mandatory rotation of audit partners every 5 years. Assess the impact on goodwill valuation and compute the revised goodwill if the years’ purchase drops to 2.5.
A firm’s profits for three years are ₹1,00,000, ₹1,20,000 and ₹1,40,000. No adjustments are needed. If goodwill is valued at 2 years’ purchase, what is the goodwill amount?
Evaluate whether the simple average profit method is appropriate for a firm whose profits have risen sharply each year: ₹80,000, ₹1,20,000, ₹1,80,000.
A partnership earned ₹2,50,000, ₹2,70,000 and ₹2,90,000 before partner’s salary of ₹30,000 per year. The deed provides for salary to be charged against profit. Compute goodwill at 3 years’ purchase.
In an ISC 2023 paper, a question gave profits for 5 years and asked for goodwill at 2.5 years’ purchase using simple average profit. Outline the steps a student must follow to secure full marks.

**HOTS:** A partnership firm has adjusted profits of ₹1,00,000, ₹1,20,000, ₹1,40,000 and ₹1,60,000 for four years. The partners agree on a years’ purchase of 2.5. However, the industry norm for similar firms is 3 years’ purchase. Discuss the implications of using 2.5 versus 3 years’ purchase on goodwill and on the admitting partner’s capital contribution.

**Application:** A firm’s profits for three years are ₹2,00,000, ₹2,50,000 and ₹3,00,000. The partnership deed provides for interest on capital at 12 % on ₹10,00,000 capital, which has not been charged. Compute goodwill at 2 years’ purchase after proper adjustment.

**Evaluation/Critique (multi‑part):** (a) Explain why the simple average profit method may undervalue goodwill for a start‑up partnership with profits ₹50,000, ₹80,000, ₹1,20,000 over three years. (b) Calculate goodwill using simple average profit at 2 years’ purchase. (c) Suggest an alternative method and justify its suitability.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern (multi‑part):** The following data relate to a partnership firm for the last four years: Year 1: Profit ₹2,00,000 (includes abnormal gain ₹30,000) Year 2: Profit ₹2,20,000 (after charging partner’s salary ₹40,000) Year 3: Profit ₹2,50,000 (includes abnormal loss ₹20,000) Year 4: Profit ₹2,80,000 (no adjustments) Goodwill is to be valued at 3 years’ purchase using simple average profit. (a) Compute the adjusted profit for each year. (b) Determine the average profit. (c) Calculate goodwill. (d) State one limitation of this method for the given data.

A firm’s adjusted profits for 2019‑2022 are ₹1,20,000, ₹1,50,000, ₹1,80,000, ₹2,10,000. The partnership deed assigns weights 1,2,3,4 respectively. Explain why the weighted average profit will be higher than the simple average profit.
Compute goodwill for a firm with adjusted profits ₹2,00,000 (2020), ₹2,40,000 (2021), ₹2,80,000 (2022), ₹3,20,000 (2023). Weights are 1,2,3,4. Years’ purchase = 2.5.

A CISCE ISC 2023 question: “The profits of a firm for the last four years are ₹1,00,000, ₹1,20,000, ₹1,40,000 and ₹1,60,000. The weights assigned are 1, 2, 3 and 4 respectively. Goodwill is valued at 2 years’ purchase of weighted average profit. Calculate goodwill.” Provide the full working.

A firm’s profits for four years are ₹1,00,000, ₹1,20,000, ₹1,40,000, ₹1,60,000. The weights are 1,2,3,4. The accountant mistakenly uses the simple average profit to compute goodwill at 3 years’ purchase. (a) Compute the goodwill using the correct weighted average method. (b) Compute the goodwill using the erroneous simple average method. (c) Quantify the difference and comment on its significance for a partner admission.

A partnership firm has adjusted profits: Year 1 ₹2,50,000; Year 2 ₹2,80,000; Year 3 ₹3,10,000; Year 4 ₹3,40,000. The deed prescribes weights 2,3,4,5 and goodwill at 2 years’ purchase. However, the accountant discovers that Year 3 profit includes a non‑recurring gain of ₹40,000. (a) Re‑compute goodwill after adjusting Year 3 profit. (b) Explain why the adjustment has a larger effect under weighted average than under simple average.

ISC 2022 Past Paper Style: “The profits of a firm for the last five years are: ₹2,00,000; ₹2,20,000; ₹2,50,000; ₹2,80,000; ₹3,00,000. The partnership deed provides that goodwill shall be valued at 3 years’ purchase of the weighted average profit, assigning weights 1,2,3,4,5 respectively. However, the profit of the third year includes a non‑recurring gain of ₹50,000. Calculate the value of goodwill after making the necessary adjustment.” Show all workings.
A firm’s capital employed is ₹8,00,000 and the normal rate of return is 10 %. Its adjusted average profit is ₹1,00,000. Calculate super profit.
A partnership has the following data: Capital employed ₹12,00,000; Normal rate of return 12 %; Adjusted average profit (weighted) ₹2,00,000; Years’ purchase 4. Compute goodwill.

A CISCE ISC 2023 question: “X Ltd. has capital employed ₹15,00,000, normal rate of return 10 %, average profit ₹2,00,000 (after all adjustments). Goodwill is valued at 3 years’ purchase of super profit. Compute goodwill.” Provide the answer with steps.

**HOTS:** A firm’s capital employed is ₹30,00,000. The normal rate of return is 10 %. The adjusted average profit is ₹4,00,000. The partners agree on 2.5 years’ purchase. However, the firm expects a major contract next year that will increase profit by ₹1,00,000 annually for three years. Should this future increment be included in super profit calculation? Justify.

**Application:** A partnership firm has the following data: Capital employed ₹18,00,000; Normal rate 12 %; Profits for last 4 years (after adjustments) ₹2,00,000, ₹2,20,000, ₹2,40,000, ₹2,60,000. Goodwill is to be valued at 3 years’ purchase of super profit using weighted average (weights 1,2,3,4). Compute goodwill.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern (2022):** A firm’s capital employed is ₹25,00,000. Normal rate of return is 10 %. The average profit (after adjustments) is ₹3,50,000. Goodwill is valued at 4 years’ purchase of super profit. (a) Compute normal profit. (b) Compute super profit. (c) Compute goodwill. (d) If the normal rate changes to 12 %, recompute goodwill and comment on the impact.
A firm’s average maintainable profit is ₹3,00,000 and the industry NRR is 15 %. Compute goodwill by capitalization of average profit.
A partnership has capital employed ₹40,00,000, average maintainable profit ₹6,00,000, and NRR 12 %. Compute goodwill by capitalization of super profit.
In an ISC 2023 paper, a question gave: “Capital employed ₹25,00,000; average profit ₹4,00,000; NRR 10 %. Compute goodwill by capitalization of super profit.” Provide the answer with working.

**HOTS:** A firm’s average profit is ₹8,00,000. Capital employed is ₹60,00,000. NRR is 10 %. (a) Compute goodwill by both capitalization methods. (b) If the firm’s assets are revalued upward by ₹10,00,000, how does each goodwill figure change? (c) Which method better reflects the economic reality of goodwill?

**APPLICATION:** A partnership deed states goodwill shall be valued at 3 years’ purchase of super profit. The firm’s super profit is ₹1,50,000 and NRR is 12 %. The partners instead decide to use capitalization of super profit. Compute goodwill under both methods and state which yields a higher value.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) A firm’s capital employed is ₹25,00,000. Its average profit after all adjustments is ₹3,75,000. The normal rate of return is 12 %. Calculate goodwill by capitalization of super profit. (b) If the firm’s goodwill is to be shared between two partners in the ratio 3:2, determine each partner’s share. (c) Pass the journal entry to record goodwill in the books when a new partner is admitted and brings his share of goodwill in cash.

**(HOTS)** A firm with old PSR 8:5:3 admits a new partner for 1/4 share. The new partner acquires his share 2/4 from the first partner, 1/4 from the second, and 1/4 from the third. If the total capital of the firm after admission is ₹2,00,000, calculate the capital balance of each partner assuming capitals are maintained in the new profit‑sharing ratio.

**(Application)** A partnership’s old PSR is 4:3:2. A new partner is admitted for 1/5 share, which he acquires 2/5 from the first partner and 3/5 equally from the second and third. If the firm’s total profit for the year is ₹1,50,000, compute the profit share of each partner after admission.

**(CISCE past‑paper pattern)** In the admission of a partner, the old profit‑sharing ratio of Ram, Lal and Mohan is 5:3:2. They admit Sohan for 3/10 share, which he acquires 2/10 from Ram, 1/10 from Lal, and the remaining from Mohan. If the firm’s total reserves before admission amount to ₹1,20,000, calculate the amount of reserves to be credited to each partner’s capital account after admission, assuming reserves are distributed in the new profit‑sharing ratio.
P and Q share profits in the ratio 7:3. They admit R for a 1/5 share, bringing ₹40,000 as goodwill premium. Calculate the amount of goodwill credited to P’s capital account.
(From ISC specimen) A and B are partners sharing profits 3:2. They admit C for 1/6 share. C brings ₹30,000 as goodwill. Journalise the treatment of goodwill.

A firm’s old profit‑sharing ratio among partners L, M, N is 3:2:1. They admit O for 1/3 share, but the partnership deed states that L’s share will be reduced by exactly 0.05 (absolute) while M and N adjust proportionally. Calculate the sacrificing ratio of L, M, N.
X and Y share profits 5:3. They admit Z for 3/10 share. Z brings ₹80,000 as goodwill. Calculate the amount of goodwill credited to Y’s capital.

(From ISC 2022 paper) A, B, and C are partners sharing profits in the ratio 5:3:2. They admit D for 1/4 share. D brings ₹90,000 as goodwill. The partners agree that A’s share will not change. (i) Calculate the new profit‑sharing ratio of A, B, C, D. (ii) Determine the sacrificing ratio of B and C. (iii) Pass the journal entry for the treatment of goodwill.
Create a scenario where two existing partners have equal gaining ratios after the admission of a third partner, and show how a goodwill premium of ₹1,20,000 would be allocated.

(a) A firm’s old profit‑sharing ratio among partners L, M, N is 5:3:2. They admit O for 1/4 share, and the new ratio becomes 15:9:6:4. Verify the new ratio is correct. (b) Calculate the gaining ratio for each partner. (c) If O brings goodwill worth ₹2,00,000, journalise the allocation of goodwill to the existing partners’ capital accounts.
A firm admits a partner who brings ₹50,000 goodwill cash. Old partners sacrifice 3:2. The accountant debits Goodwill Account ₹50,000 and credits old partners 3:2. Evaluate this treatment.
Journalise: New partner brings ₹1,00,000 goodwill cash. Old partners A and B sacrifice 2:1.

CISCE‑style: P and Q share profits 4:1. They admit R for 1/4th share, which he acquires 1/8 from P and 1/8 from Q. R brings ₹80,000 goodwill cash. (a) Compute sacrificing ratio. (b) Allocate goodwill. (c) Pass journal entries if the premium is fully retained.

**HOTS:** M and N share profits 3:2. They admit O for 1/5th share. O acquires his share 1/10 from M and 1/10 from N. O brings ₹1,20,000 goodwill cash. (a) Calculate sacrificing ratio. (b) Allocate goodwill. (c) Pass journal entries if 25% of the premium is withdrawn by M and N. (d) Show the capital accounts after all entries assuming opening capitals M ₹3,00,000, N ₹2,00,000, O ₹1,50,000.

**Application:** A new partner brings goodwill premium partly in cash (₹50,000) and partly by taking over a liability of the firm (₹20,000). The sacrificing ratio of old partners is 3:2. How should the total premium of ₹70,000 be recorded? **Answer:** Total premium ₹70,000 is allocated 3:2 → Old Partner A ₹42,000, B ₹28,000. Journal: Bank Dr. ₹50,000, Liability (creditors) Dr. ₹20,000 → A’s Capital Cr. ₹42,000, B’s Capital Cr. ₹28,000. The liability taken over is treated as cash equivalent. A wrong answer (e.g., crediting only cash portion) reveals misconception that only cash constitutes premium — AS‑26 recognises any consideration given for goodwill.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** P, Q, R share profits 4:3:2. They admit S for 1/5th share. S acquires 1/10 from P, 1/20 from Q, and 1/20 from R. S brings ₹2,00,000 goodwill cash. (a) Compute sacrificing ratio of P, Q, R. (b) Allocate goodwill. (c) Pass journal entry for goodwill premium if it is fully retained. (d) If P withdraws ₹30,000 of his share, give the entry. (4+4+2+2 = 12 marks)
A firm has two partners, X and Y, with capitals ₹1,20,000 and ₹80,000. They admit Z for 1/4 share. Z brings ₹60,000. Calculate hidden goodwill.
Pass the journal entry for hidden goodwill of ₹30,000 when old partners A and B sacrifice in ratio 3:2 and new partner C is admitted.

A CISCE ISC 2023 question: “X and Y share profits 3:2. They admit Z for 1/5 share. Z brings ₹40,000. Capitals after revaluation: X ₹1,50,000, Y ₹1,00,000. Calculate hidden goodwill and pass entry.” Solve.

**HOTS:** A partnership firm admits two new partners simultaneously. Partner M gets 1/6 share and brings ₹80,000. Partner N gets 1/8 share and brings ₹60,000. Old partners’ combined capital after revaluation is ₹6,00,000. Calculate hidden goodwill, if any, and explain how it should be allocated among old partners if their sacrificing ratio is 3:2.

**Application:** A firm’s old partners have capitals ₹4,00,000 and ₹2,00,000. They admit a new partner for 1/5 share. The new partner brings ₹1,50,000. The accountant records hidden goodwill of ₹50,000 and credits old partners equally. Identify the mistakes and pass the correct entry.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** (a) X and Y share profits 4:1. Capitals: X ₹5,00,000, Y ₹2,00,000. They admit Z for 1/5 share. Z brings ₹2,00,000. Calculate hidden goodwill. (3 marks) (b) Pass the journal entry for hidden goodwill adjustment assuming sacrificing ratio = old ratio. (2 marks) (c) State why hidden goodwill is not debited to Goodwill Account. (1 mark)
A firm’s Revaluation Account shows a credit balance of ₹50,000. The old partners share profits 4:1. How much will each old partner’s capital account be credited?

During admission, the following adjustments are made: (i) Machinery depreciated by ₹25,000; (ii) Investment valued up by ₹40,000; (iii) Provision for legal claims increased by ₹10,000. Show the Revaluation Account and state the net result.
A partnership admits a new partner. The Revaluation Account shows a loss of ₹18,000. The old PSR is 2:3. Pass the journal entry to transfer the loss.

Create a Revaluation Account for the following scenario and compute each old partner’s share: Old PSR = 5:3. Adjustments: (a) Building appreciated ₹2,00,000; (b) Stock written down ₹50,000; (c) Outstanding rent ₹20,000 recognised; (d) Prepaid insurance ₹10,000 written off.

In an ISC 2023 paper, a question gave: “On admission of Z, the following revaluations were agreed: Land increased by ₹3,00,000; Furniture decreased by ₹40,000; Provision for doubtful debts increased from ₹30,000 to ₹45,000.” The student wrote the Revaluation Account with Land and Furniture correct but credited Provision for Doubtful Debts ₹15,000. Identify the error and correct it.

**HOTS:** A partnership firm admits a new partner. The Revaluation Account shows a profit of ₹2,00,000. The old PSR is 3:2. However, the partnership deed states that any revaluation profit shall be shared equally irrespective of PSR. Is the deed clause valid under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932? Justify and show the correct allocation.

**Application:** A firm’s Revaluation Account includes the following: (a) Building appreciated ₹5,00,000; (b) Stock written down ₹80,000; (c) Provision for tax increased ₹30,000; (d) Prepaid advertising ₹20,000 written off. The old PSR is 4:1. Compute the net revaluation profit/loss and each old partner’s share.

**Comparison (multi‑part):** Compare the Revaluation Account with the **Memorandum Revaluation Account** used when partners decide **not** to alter book values but only to record the effect for capital adjustment. (a) List two key differences in purpose. (b) Show how the journal entries differ for a building appreciation of ₹2,00,000.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern (multi‑part):** The following information relates to the admission of **D** into the firm of **A, B, C** (old PSR 5:3:2). - Land & Building (book ₹12,00,000) revalued at ₹15,00,000. - Stock (book ₹3,00,000) revalued at ₹2,70,000. - Provision for Doubtful Debts (₹40,000) increased to ₹55,000. - Outstanding expenses ₹25,000 not recorded. - Unrecorded investment ₹1,00,000 discovered. **Required:** (i) Prepare the Revaluation Account. (ii) Compute each old partner’s share of revaluation profit/loss. (iii) Pass the journal entry for transfer.

A firm has General Reserve ₹90,000 and Profit & Loss Account (credit) ₹30,000. Old partners X and Y share profits 4:1. They admit Z. Calculate the amount credited to X’s and Y’s capital accounts from these reserves.
Pass the journal entry for distribution of Workmen Compensation Fund ₹50,000 (credit balance) between old partners P and Q sharing profits 2:3 on admission of R.

**CISCE exam‑style:** “A, B and C are partners sharing profits 5:3:2. They admit D for 1/4th share. The Balance Sheet shows General Reserve ₹1,20,000 and Profit & Loss Account (debit) ₹40,000. Pass necessary journal entries for adjustment of reserves on D’s admission.”

**HOTS:** A firm has a Contingency Reserve ₹1,00,000 (credit) and a debit balance in Profit & Loss Account ₹60,000. Old partners share profits 3:2. On admission, the partners decide to **net off** the debit balance against the reserve before distribution. Is this permissible? Justify with accounting principles.

**Application:** The Balance Sheet of X & Y (profit‑sharing 4:1) shows: General Reserve ₹2,00,000; Investment Fluctuation Fund ₹50,000; Investments book value ₹10,00,000, market value ₹9,80,000. They admit Z. Show the ledger accounts for General Reserve, Investment Fluctuation Fund, Investments, and Partners’ Capital Accounts after admission adjustments.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern (multi‑part):** A firm’s Balance Sheet as on 31‑Mar‑2025 shows: - General Reserve ₹3,00,000 - Profit & Loss Account (credit) ₹1,20,000 - Investment Fluctuation Fund ₹80,000 - Investments (book value) ₹20,00,000; Market value ₹19,50,000 Old partners A & B share profits 3:2. They admit C for 1/5th share. **(a)** Calculate the amount of fall in investment value and the journal entry to write it off. **(b)** Determine the balance of Investment Fluctuation Fund after write‑off and its distribution between A and B. **(c)** Pass the journal entries for distribution of General Reserve and Profit & Loss Account. **(d)** Show the final capital account balances of A and B if their opening capitals were ₹10,00,000 and ₹6,00,000 respectively.

A firm has partners X and Y sharing 3:2. They admit Z for 1/5 share. New PSR = 3:2:1. After goodwill and revaluation, adjusted capitals are X ₹2,70,000, Y ₹1,80,000. Z brings ₹1,00,000 cash as capital. Compute the capital adjustment required for X and Y under the proportionate capital method.
Create a journal entry for the following: Partner A’s capital after goodwill and revaluation is ₹4,00,000; target capital as per new PSR is ₹4,50,000. A brings the shortfall in cash.

In an ISC 2023 question, a firm admits a partner and decides to adjust capitals through current accounts without any cash movement. The old partners’ capitals after all adjustments are ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,00,000; new partner brings ₹1,00,000. New PSR = 3:2:1. Pass the necessary adjustment entries.

A firm admits a partner and decides to adjust capitals by the proportionate capital method. The new partner brings ₹2,00,000 as capital for a 1/4 share. Old partners’ capitals after all adjustments are ₹6,00,000 and ₹4,00,000. The accountant computes total capital as ₹8,00,000 (old) + ₹2,00,000 = ₹10,00,000 and then sets target capitals as 3/4, 1/4 of total for old partners and 1/4 for new partner. Identify the error and compute correct target capitals.

During admission, goodwill is valued at ₹80,000. The new partner brings ₹50,000 as goodwill premium in cash and the balance ₹30,000 is raised as hidden goodwill. Old partners’ sacrificing ratio is 2:1. Show the journal entries for goodwill treatment and explain how this affects capital adjustment.

(a) A partnership firm has partners M and N sharing 3:2. They admit O for 1/5 share. New PSR = 3:2:1. After goodwill (premium ₹40,000 cash), revaluation profit ₹20,000, and reserve distribution ₹30,000, the capitals are M ₹4,00,000, N ₹2,50,000. O brings ₹1,50,000 as capital. Compute the capital adjustment required under proportionate capital method. (b) If instead the firm decides to adjust capitals through current accounts only, show the current account entries.

**ISC 2022 Style Question:** P and Q are partners sharing profits 4:1. They admit R for 1/5 share. New PSR = 4:1:1. Goodwill valued at ₹1,00,000. R brings ₹1,00,000 as goodwill premium and ₹2,00,000 as capital. Revaluation loss ₹30,000. General Reserve ₹50,000. Capitals before admission: P ₹5,00,000, Q ₹1,00,000. (i) Prepare Revaluation Account, Partners’ Capital Accounts, and Cash/Bank Account. (ii) Calculate the amount of capital adjustment required for each partner under proportionate capital method.

A firm’s partners change PSR from 5:3:2 to 2:2:1. The revaluation profit is ₹1,20,000. General reserve stands at ₹80,000. Goodwill is valued at ₹2,00,000. Pass the necessary journal entries for revaluation, reserve distribution, and goodwill adjustment (premium method) assuming the sacrificing partners are compensated.

**APPLICATION:** Partners M and N share 3:2. They admit O for 1/5 share. O brings ₹3,00,000 capital. The firm’s net assets are ₹12,00,000. Goodwill is to be valued at 2 years’ purchase of average profits ₹4,00,000. Pass journal entries for goodwill (premium method) and capital adjustment if the new ratio is 3:2:1.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Partners A, B, C share 4:3:3. They admit D for 1/5 share. New ratio 3:2:2:3. Goodwill valued at ₹2,00,000. D brings ₹1,50,000 capital and ₹50,000 goodwill cash. Revaluation profit ₹60,000. Reserve ₹40,000. Pass journal entries for goodwill (premium), revaluation, reserve, and D’s capital. (b) Show the sacrificing ratio calculation. (c) If the firm decides to write off goodwill immediately after admission, give the entry.

Create a scenario with three partners P, Q, R sharing profits 5:3:2. Q retires. P and R agree to gain Q’s share in the ratio of their existing capitals, which are ₹6,00,000 and ₹4,00,000 respectively. Compute the new PSR of P and R.

A firm’s partners D, E, F share profits 5:3:2. E retires. D and F agree to gain E’s share in the ratio of their existing capitals, which are ₹9,00,000 and ₹3,00,000 respectively. Calculate the new profit‑sharing ratio of D and F.

In the retirement of partner G, the old PSR of H, I, J was 2:2:1. The gaining ratio of H and I is 1:1, and J does not gain any share. (a) Calculate the new PSR of H, I, and J. (b) If the firm’s total goodwill (including hidden goodwill) is ₹1,20,000, show how it is distributed among H, I, and J using the new PSR. (c) State the journal entry for distributing the goodwill.

(a) A firm’s partners A, B, C share profits 3:2:1. B retires. A and C agree to gain B’s share in the ratio of their existing capitals, which are ₹6,00,000 and ₹4,00,000 respectively. Calculate the new PSR of A and C. (b) If the firm’s revaluation profit on retirement is ₹30,000, show how it is allocated between A and C using the new PSR. (c) State why the revaluation profit must be allocated in the new PSR and not the old PSR.
On retirement of partner D, the firm’s goodwill is valued at ₹1,80,000. The gaining ratio of the remaining partners A, B and C is 2:1:1. Show the journal entry for goodwill adjustment.

On 31 March 2023, partners L, M and N shared profits in the ratio 5:3:2. M retired on that date. The goodwill of the firm was valued at ₹1,50,000. The new profit‑sharing ratio between L and N is 3:2. (a) Calculate the gaining ratio of L and N. (b) Pass the journal entry for goodwill adjustment.

A firm’s goodwill is valued at ₹3,60,000 on retirement of partner D. The gaining ratio of the remaining partners A, B and C is 3:2:1. Show the journal entry for goodwill adjustment and compute the amount debited to each partner’s capital account.

On 1 April 2022, partners X, Y and Z shared profits in the ratio 4:3:3. Y retired on 30 September 2022. The goodwill of the firm was valued at ₹2,40,000. The new profit‑sharing ratio between X and Z is 3:2. (a) Calculate the gaining ratio of X and Z. (b) Pass the journal entry for goodwill adjustment, assuming the adjustment is made through capital accounts. (c) Show how the profit from 1 April 2022 to 30 September 2022 (₹60,000) is distributed to X and Z using the gaining ratio.

**Case‑based:** A partnership of L, M, and N shares profits in the ratio 6:4:1. N retires and is paid ₹2,00,000 for his share of goodwill. The remaining partners agree to share future profits in the ratio 3:2. Calculate the sacrificing ratio of L and M and show how the goodwill amount will be debited to their capital accounts.

**(CISCE exam‑style)** In the firm of X, Y, and Z, the profit‑sharing ratio is 5:3:2. Z retires and is paid ₹1,50,000 for his share of goodwill. The remaining partners decide to share future profits equally. Journalise the treatment of goodwill.

**(HOTS)** A firm’s old profit‑sharing ratio among A, B, and C is 7:2:1. C retires and the remaining partners agree to share future profits in the ratio 4:3. If the firm has hidden goodwill valued at ₹1,80,000 (not recorded in the books), calculate the sacrificing ratio of A and B and show how the hidden goodwill will be adjusted in the partners’ capital accounts.

**(Application)** In the firm of P, Q, and R, the profit‑sharing ratio is 8:4:3. Q retires and is paid ₹3,60,000 for his share of goodwill. The remaining partners decide to share future profits in the ratio 5:2. Compute the sacrificing ratio of P and R and allocate the goodwill amount accordingly.

**(CISCE past‑paper pattern)** In the firm of A, B, and C, the profit‑sharing ratio is 6:5:4. B retires and is paid ₹5,00,000 for his share of goodwill. The remaining partners agree to share future profits in the ratio 2:1. Pass the necessary journal entry for the treatment of goodwill, showing all workings.
A firm’s average profit is ₹2,00,000, normal rate of return 10%, net tangible assets ₹15,00,000. Compute hidden goodwill.
Partners X, Y, Z share profits 5:3:2. Z retires. Goodwill valued ₹1,20,000. Gaining ratio of X and Y is 5:3. Pass journal entries if goodwill is not raised.

CISCE exam-style: “A, B, C are partners sharing 4:3:2. B retires. Goodwill appears at ₹80,000. The firm’s goodwill is valued at ₹1,40,000. Pass necessary entries assuming goodwill is raised and written off.”

**HOTS:** A firm has three partners A, B, C sharing 5:3:2. C retires. The firm’s goodwill is valued at ₹1,50,000. The partnership deed is silent on goodwill treatment. The continuing partners decide to raise goodwill to its full value and then write it off. However, they mistakenly write it off in the old ratio. (a) Compute the correct gaining ratio. (b) Show the correct journal entries for raising and writing off goodwill. (c) Quantify the error in capital accounts caused by writing off in old ratio.

**APPLICATION:** A partnership firm’s balance sheet shows goodwill ₹40,000. On retirement of partner D (share 1/4), the firm’s goodwill is revalued at ₹1,00,000. The partners agree to adjust goodwill without raising it. Pass the necessary journal entries.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** Partners L, M, N share profits 4:3:2. N retires on 31‑Mar‑2025. The Balance Sheet shows Goodwill ₹60,000. The firm’s goodwill is valued at ₹1,80,000. The partnership deed provides that goodwill shall not appear in the books. (a) Calculate N’s share of goodwill. (b) Pass journal entries for goodwill adjustment. (c) If the gaining ratio of L and M is 4:3, show the effect on their capital accounts.

A firm has undistributed profits of ₹2,00,000. Partners A, B, C share profits 3:2:1. B retires. The firm decides to distribute undistributed profits in the new ratio 2:1 between A and C. Evaluate this decision.
Calculate each partner’s share of undistributed profits of ₹1,80,000 for partners X, Y, Z sharing profits 5:3:2.
Draft the journal entry to distribute undistributed profits of ₹3,00,000 among partners P, Q, R in ratio 4:3:2.

A partnership firm’s Balance Sheet shows General Reserve ₹1,20,000 and Profit & Loss Account (Cr.) ₹80,000. Partners A and B share profits equally. A retires. Pass necessary journal entries for distribution of undistributed profits.

A firm has undistributed profits of ₹5,00,000 (General Reserve ₹3,00,000, P&L Cr. ₹2,00,000). Partners A, B, C share 3:2:1. B retires. The firm decides to distribute only the General Reserve and keep P&L (Cr.) for future. (a) Is this treatment correct? Justify. (b) Calculate the correct share of each partner if the correct treatment is followed. (c) State the impact on B’s capital if the incorrect treatment is followed.

Partners X, Y, Z share profits 4:3:2. On 30‑Sep‑2025, Z retires. The Balance Sheet shows: General Reserve ₹2,70,000; Investment Fluctuation Reserve ₹90,000 (investment market value equals book value); Profit & Loss (Dr.) ₹30,000. (a) Determine the net undistributed profit/loss. (b) Pass the journal entry for distribution. (c) If the firm instead transfers the Investment Fluctuation Reserve to a separate “Reserve for Future” account and does not distribute it, explain the error.

From the following Balance Sheet of M/s Gupta & Co. as on 31‑Mar‑2026, pass journal entries for distribution of undistributed profits on the retirement of partner C. Partners A, B, C share profits 5:3:2. Liabilities: Capital A ₹4,00,000; B ₹3,00,000; C ₹2,00,000 General Reserve ₹1,80,000 Profit & Loss (Cr.) ₹1,20,000 Workmen Compensation Reserve ₹60,000 (actual liability ₹40,000) Assets: (details not needed) **Required:** (a) Calculate total undistributed profits. (b) Determine each partner’s share. (c) Write the journal entry. (d) Show the Capital Accounts after distribution (only the effect of this distribution).

A firm’s profit for the year ended 31‑Mar‑2024 was ₹18,00,000. Partner X (PSR 2/5) dies on 31‑Dec‑2024. The partners decide to use the previous year’s profit as the estimate for the current year. Calculate X’s profit share to date of death.

Partner Y (PSR 3/8) dies on 15‑Oct‑2025. The firm’s profit for 2024‑25 was ₹16,00,000. The partnership deed provides for a salary of ₹2,00,000 per annum to Y, payable before profit distribution. Using the previous year’s profit as estimate, compute Y’s profit share to date of death.

Create a journal entry for the following: Firm “Mehta & Co.” has partners P, Q, R sharing 4:3:3. R dies on 30‑Jun‑2025. Estimated profit for 2025‑26 (based on 2024‑25) is ₹24,00,000. No salary or interest. Record R’s profit share to date of death.
