**HOTS:** A company issues an appointment letter with a clause: “The employee shall not join any competitor for 24 months after resignation, anywhere in India.” The employee resigns after 10 months and joins a competitor in a different state. The company sues for injunction. Discuss the likely court outcome, referencing relevant case law principles.

**APPLICATION:** You are HR manager of a manufacturing unit in Tamil Nadu with 120 workers. Draft the statutory clauses that must appear in every appointment letter to comply with the Tamil Nadu Shops and Establishments Act, 1947 (as amended). List at least five clauses with section references.

**COMPARISON:** Compare the appointment letter requirements for a “workman” under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 with those for a “managerial employee” excluded from the Act. Highlight three key differences.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain the essential elements of a valid appointment letter under Indian law. (6 marks)” Provide a structured answer with mark allocation.
A sole proprietor starts with capital ₹4,00,000. During the year he earns profit ₹1,50,000 and withdraws ₹40,000 for personal use. Calculate his closing capital.

A sole proprietor, Ravi, has a business loan of ₹12 lakh secured by a charge on his business premises. He also has a personal home loan of ₹30 lakh. The business fails and the premises are sold for ₹8 lakh. Explain the order of settlement of claims and the impact on Ravi’s personal assets.

An ISC past‑paper question: “Explain the concept of ‘unlimited liability’ in the context of a sole proprietorship. Illustrate with an example how it affects the proprietor’s personal assets.” (4 marks)
State the four essential elements required for a partnership under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

A partnership deed provides for 10% interest on capital and a monthly salary of ₹25,000 to a working partner. The firm earns a profit of ₹12,00,000 before these appropriations. Capital balances are: Partner X ₹40,00,000, Partner Y ₹20,00,000. Compute the amount of profit transferred to each partner’s current account after appropriations.
Partner A, without consulting B, signs a contract to purchase machinery worth ₹15 lakh for the firm. The purchase is within the firm’s usual line of business. Is the firm bound? Justify.

In an ISC 2023 paper, a question asked: “Distinguish between a partnership and a private limited company on the basis of (i) legal status, (ii) liability of members, (iii) minimum number of members, (iv) transferability of interest.” Provide the four-point distinction.

(HOTS) A partnership firm suffers a loss of ₹8,00,000 in a year. The deed provides for interest on capital at 12% p.a. on opening capitals of ₹30,00,000 (A) and ₹20,00,000 (B). No salary or commission. Show the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and explain the treatment of interest on capital when profits are insufficient.

(Application) A partnership deed is silent on interest on drawings. Partner C draws ₹50,000 per month at the beginning of each month. The firm’s accounting year ends 31 March. Compute interest on drawings at 10% p.a. for the year.
(Comparison) Compare the dissolution of a partnership by agreement with dissolution by court order under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. List at least three procedural differences.

(CISCE past‑paper pattern) The following data relates to a partnership firm for the year ended 31‑03‑2024: Capital (01‑04‑2023): P ₹10,00,000; Q ₹6,00,000. Drawings: P ₹1,20,000 (evenly throughout the year); Q ₹80,000 (at the end of each quarter). Profit before appropriations: ₹5,00,000. Deed provides: Interest on capital 10% p.a.; Interest on drawings 12% p.a.; Salary to P ₹2,000 per month; Profit sharing ratio 3:2. Prepare the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and Partners’ Capital Accounts (fixed capital method).
State the four statutory restrictions that define a private limited company under Section 2(68) of the Companies Act 2013.
A private limited company has 195 members. It issues 10 new shares to an employee who already holds shares. Does this breach the member limit? Justify.
Apply the concept: “GreenFields Agro Private Limited” wants to raise ₹5 crore by issuing a prospectus to the public. Identify the legal obstacle and the remedy.

CISCE exam‑style: “Section 2(68) of the Companies Act 2013 defines a private company. List any three features that flow from this definition and explain their impact on the company’s governance.” (6 marks)

**HOTS:** (a) Explain how the “member cap of 200” interacts with the “restriction on share transfer” to preserve the private character of the company. (b) If a private limited company inadvertently exceeds 200 members due to a clerical error in the register of members, what statutory remedy exists?

**Application:** “Quantum Analytics Private Limited” plans to issue 5,000 equity shares of ₹10 each to its 10 existing members on a rights basis. The company’s authorised capital is ₹1 crore (10 lakh shares). After the issue, the paid‑up capital will be ₹80 lakh. Calculate the new authorised capital utilisation percentage and state whether any RoC filing is required for the increase in paid‑up capital.

**Evaluation/Critique:** Critically assess the statement: “The Companies (Amendment) Act 2015 removed the minimum paid‑up capital requirement for private companies, making incorporation cost‑free.” Provide at least three points.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Section 2(68) of the Companies Act 2013 defines a private company. (i) List any three restrictions imposed on a private company. (ii) Explain the consequence if a private company invites the public to subscribe to its shares. (iii) State the maximum number of members a private company can have, and the exception to this limit.” (8 marks)
State the minimum number of members required to form a public limited company under the Companies Act 2013.
Assess the impact of the removal of minimum paid‑up capital requirement (2015 amendment) on the ease of incorporating a public limited company.

Section 2(71) of the Companies Act 2013 defines a public company. (a) Quote the essential words of the definition. (b) Identify two consequences if a private company inadvertently invites the public to subscribe its shares.

**HOTS:** A public limited company proposes to issue bonus shares. (a) State the condition under Section 63 of the Companies Act 2013 for issuing bonus shares. (b) Explain the effect on the company’s share capital structure. (c) Discuss one advantage for existing shareholders.
**APPLICATION:** A company with 8 members and 3 directors wants to list on the NSE. List the additional requirements beyond the Companies Act 2013 that it must satisfy.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** As per ISC 2023 Business Studies paper, answer: (a) Define public company as per Section 2(71). (b) State two privileges of a private company over a public company.
Evaluate the statement: “A public limited company can have a maximum of 200 members.”
Apply the definitions: “GreenTech Innovations” has 150 shareholders, shares are freely transferable, and it has issued a prospectus to the public. Identify the entity type and justify.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** (a) Define “Private Company” as per Section 2(68) of the Companies Act, 2013. (2 marks) (b) State two privileges enjoyed by a private company over a public company. (2 marks) (c) Explain why a private company cannot invite the public to subscribe to its securities. (2 marks)
A sole proprietor with a turnover of ₹1.5 crore wants limited liability and the ability to add investors without losing control. Recommend the most appropriate entity and justify.

**HOTS:** A private limited company with 180 members wishes to admit 30 new investors. Explain whether it can do so without converting to a public limited company, and analyse the implications if it exceeds the 200‑member ceiling.

**Application:** Calculate the minimum number of directors required for each entity type if the business is (i) a private limited company with paid‑up capital ₹8 crore, (ii) a public limited company with paid‑up capital ₹12 crore, (iii) a One Person Company (OPC) — note OPC is outside this node’s scope but test awareness.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern (Multi‑part):** (a) Define “private company” as per Section 2(68) of the Companies Act, 2013. (2 marks) (b) State two privileges enjoyed by a private company over a public company. (2 marks) (c) A private company has 190 members (including 15 employees holding shares under ESOP). It proposes to allot shares to 20 new investors. Advise whether the allotment can proceed without conversion. (3 marks)
State the statutory maximum redemption period for redeemable preference shares under the Companies Act 2013, except for infrastructure projects.
A company issues 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹5 per share. Show the journal entry for receipt of application money of ₹3 per share (including premium) for 80,000 shares.

GreenTech Ltd. proposes to issue 5,00,000 convertible preference shares of ₹100 each, convertible into equity at a ratio of 1:1 after 5 years. The current equity share price is ₹150. Advise whether conversion is beneficial for a preference shareholder.
An ISC 2023 question: “Distinguish between ‘calls in arrears’ and ‘calls in advance’ in the context of share capital accounting.” Provide a concise answer with ledger treatment.

**HOTS:** A company’s articles authorise “participating preference shares” with a right to share surplus profits after a 10 % fixed dividend and after equity dividend of 12 %. In a year, profit after tax is ₹5 crore. Equity capital ₹20 crore (₹10 face), preference capital ₹5 crore (₹100 face). Compute the total dividend payable to each class.

**Application:** Draft the board resolution excerpt for issuing 2,00,000 9 % cumulative redeemable preference shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2, redeemable after 8 years, as per Section 55 Companies Act 2013.
**Comparison:** Compare the accounting treatment of “calls in arrears” and “calls in advance” under Schedule III of the Companies Act 2013. Present in a two‑column table.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern (2022):** (a) Define “equity share” as per Section 43 of the Companies Act 2013. (2 marks) (b) State two differences between “cumulative” and “non‑cumulative” preference shares. (2 marks) (c) A company issued 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹3. Applications received for 60,000 shares. Allotment made pro‑rata. Excess application money adjusted towards allotment. Allotment money ₹5 (including ₹2 premium). Pass journal entries for application and allotment. (6 marks)

A company issues 12% secured debentures of ₹100 each at a 5% discount, redeemable at par after 5 years. Issue expenses are 2% of face value. Corporate tax rate is 30%. Compute the **after‑tax cost of debenture (Kd)** using the approximate formula.

Vikram Engineering Ltd. issues 10,000, 9% debentures of ₹1,000 each at par, redeemable at a 10% premium after 6 years. The company creates a Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) as per Section 71(4). Show the journal entries for (a) issue, (b) annual interest payment, (c) creation of DRR, and (d) redemption.
In an ISC 2023 paper, a case study described a listed company issuing NCDs with a **call option** after 3 years. Explain the advantage to the issuer and the risk to the investor.

**HOTS:** A company issues zero‑coupon debentures (ZCDs) at ₹600, redeemable at ₹1,000 after 5 years. No periodic interest is paid. The corporate tax rate is 30%. Compute the **effective annual yield (YTM)** for the investor and the **after‑tax cost of debt** for the issuer. Discuss why the tax treatment differs from coupon‑bearing debentures.

**APPLICATION:** PQR Ltd. plans to raise ₹200 crore via NCDs. It can choose between (A) 8% secured NCDs, 7‑year tenure, issue expenses 1.5%, or (B) 7.5% unsecured NCDs, 5‑year tenure, issue expenses 1%. Tax rate 25%. Assuming both are issued at par and redeemed at par, which option has lower after‑tax cost? Show calculations.

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE (multi‑part):** A company issues 10% convertible debentures with a conversion price set at a 20% premium to the current market price. The conversion option is exercisable anytime after 18 months up to maturity (5 years). (a) Explain how the conversion premium affects the **conversion value** and the **investor’s decision**. (b) If the share price rises 50% in 2 years, calculate the **conversion value per debenture** (face value ₹1,000, conversion ratio 20 shares). (c) Critically assess whether the company benefits more from conversion or redemption, considering dilution and cash outflow.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN (multi‑part):** “XYZ Ltd. issued 50,000, 9% debentures of ₹100 each at a discount of 10%, redeemable at a premium of 5% after 5 years. Issue expenses were 2% of face value. The company decided to create a Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) as per the Companies Act, 2013. (a) Calculate the amount of DRR to be created before redemption. (b) Pass the journal entry for creation of DRR in the first year. (c) If the company’s profit before tax for the year is ₹2 crore and tax rate is 30%, determine whether the profit is sufficient to create the required DRR.”
A company reports net profit after tax of ₹15 lakh and declares a dividend of ₹4 lakh. Calculate the retained profits and state how this amount will be shown in the balance sheet.

**Application:** Given: Net profit after tax ₹25 lakh, dividend payout ratio 40 %. Compute retained profits. The firm intends to invest the retained amount in a project with expected IRR 14 %. The firm’s current WACC is 12 %. Should the firm accept the project? Justify.

**Evaluation/Critique (multi‑part):** (a) Critically assess the statement: “Retained profits are always the best source of finance for expansion.” (3 marks) (b) Identify two situations where retained profits may be unsuitable. (2 marks) (c) Suggest an alternative source for each situation. (2 marks)

**Comparison (multi‑part):** Compare retained profits and equity shares on the following dimensions: (a) Cost of capital, (b) Control dilution, (c) Obligation to pay returns, (d) Impact on leverage ratios. (4 marks)

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern (multi‑part):** A company earned net profit after tax of ₹25 lakh for the year ended 31 March 2024. The board declared a dividend of 30 % on the paid‑up equity share capital of ₹50 lakh. (a) Calculate the amount of dividend paid. (1 mark) (b) Determine the retained profits for the year. (1 mark) (c) Show how the retained profits will appear in the Balance Sheet under “Shareholders’ Funds”. (2 marks) (d) Explain one advantage and one limitation of using these retained profits for financing a new project. (2 marks)
What is the maximum limit of public deposits a non‑NBFC company can accept under the Companies Act 2013?

A company with paid‑up capital ₹8 crore and free reserves ₹4 crore wants to raise public deposits at 10 % p.a. for 3 years. Calculate the maximum deposit it can accept and the annual interest outgo at that maximum.
In an ISC‑style question: “State two regulatory conditions a company must satisfy before accepting public deposits under the Companies Act 2013.”

A company with paid‑up capital ₹15 crore and free reserves ₹5 crore has already accepted public deposits of ₹4 crore. It now wants to accept more deposits. (a) What is the statutory maximum deposit limit? (b) How much additional deposit can it accept? (c) If it accepts the additional amount at 9 % p.a. for 2 years, compute the total interest payable over the tenure.

A firm is deciding between public deposits and a bank term loan for ₹2 crore working‑capital need. The deposit rate is 10 % p.a., the bank loan rate is 11 % p.a., but the bank requires a 20 % margin on inventory. The firm’s inventory is ₹10 crore. (a) Calculate the effective amount the firm can draw from the bank loan after margin. (b) Compare the annual interest cost of the two options for the required ₹2 crore. (c) State one non‑cost factor that may tilt the decision toward public deposits.

(a) List three eligibility criteria a non‑NBFC company must meet to accept public deposits under the Companies Act 2013. (b) Explain why a credit rating is mandatory. (c) If a company fails to repay deposits on maturity, what penalty does Section 76A prescribe?
A company borrows ₹10 lakh at 12% p.a. for 3 years with monthly rests. Explain how the effective annual rate (EAR) differs from the nominal rate.
Evaluate the impact of a negative covenant restricting dividend payout to 30% of PAT on a firm’s financial flexibility.
Calculate the EMI for a ₹25 lakh term loan at 10% p.a. for 7 years (monthly rests).
Design a loan proposal for a startup seeking ₹50 lakh for equipment, specifying collateral, tenure, and two covenants you would include.
In an ISC board question, a firm’s loan of ₹1 crore at 9% becomes NPA after 95 days overdue. State the RBI classification and its provisioning requirement.

**HOTS:** A firm is considering two loan structures for ₹30 crore: (A) 8% fixed for 5 years, (B) floating at MCLR (currently 7.5%) + 0.5% spread, reset annually. Assuming MCLR follows a mean‑reverting process with long‑term mean 8% and volatility 0.5%, discuss qualitatively which structure minimises expected interest cost and risk.

**APPLICATION:** A textile exporter avails a pre‑shipment credit (packing credit) of ₹2 crore at 6% p.a. (subsidised rate under RBI’s Interest Equalisation Scheme) for 180 days. Compute the interest cost and compare with a regular working capital loan at 10% p.a. for the same period.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “A company takes a loan of ₹50 lakh at 12% p.a. for 4 years. The loan agreement stipulates a moratorium of 6 months during which only interest is payable. After moratorium, the principal is repaid in 7 equal half‑yearly instalments. Calculate the half‑yearly instalment amount.”
A supplier offers terms “3/15 net 45”. Explain what these terms mean and calculate the effective annual cost of not taking the discount.
A firm purchases goods worth ₹5,00,000 on terms “2/10 net 30”. It pays on the 25th day. Compute the amount paid and the implicit cost of forgoing the discount for the extra 15 days.
Create a short journal entry sequence for a company that buys inventory on credit terms “1/10 net 30”, avails the discount, and records the payment.

**HOTS:** A firm’s average payable period is 45 days, but its suppliers offer “2/10 net 30”. The finance manager proposes to pay all suppliers on the 10th day using a short‑term loan at 10 % p.a. Critically assess this proposal.

**APPLICATION:** A company purchases goods worth ₹12,00,000 on terms “1.5/15 net 45”. It has a bank overdraft facility at 11 % p.a. Determine whether the company should use the overdraft to pay within the discount period. Show calculations.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Define trade credit. (b) State two advantages and two limitations of trade credit as a source of finance. (c) A firm buys goods on terms “2/10 net 30” and pays on the 20th day. Calculate the effective annual rate of interest implicit in this transaction.
A bill of ₹2,00,000 is discounted 60 days before maturity at 10 % p.a. The drawer records a discount of ₹3,288. Is this correct? Justify.
A company discounts a ₹3,00,000 bill at 11 % p.a., 45 days before maturity. Pass the journal entry in the company’s books.

ISC 2023 style: “A bill of ₹4,00,000 drawn on 1 Jan 2024, payable 90 days after date, is discounted on 15 Feb 2024 at 12 % p.a. Calculate the discount and the amount received. Show the journal entry in the drawer’s books.”
A firm discounts a bill of ₹6,00,000 at 11 % p.a. on 20 April 2024. The bill was drawn on 1 April 2024 for 90 days. Calculate the discount using the exact number of unexpired days.

A company has the option to either discount a ₹4,00,000 bill at 10 % p.a. for 50 days or take a 50‑day loan at 10.5 % p.a. with a processing fee of 0.25 % of the loan amount. Determine the cheaper option and the savings.

ISC 2022 past‑paper pattern (multi‑part): (a) Define “discounting of a bill of exchange”. (2 marks) (b) A bill of ₹5,00,000 drawn on 15 Jan 2024 for 90 days is discounted on 1 Mar 2024 at 12 % p.a. Calculate the discount and the amount credited to the bank account. (4 marks) (c) Pass the journal entry for the discounting in the drawer’s books. (2 marks) (d) If the bill is dishonoured on maturity and the bank pays ₹200 as noting charges, give the rectifying entry. (2 marks)
TechNova Ltd. issues 200,000 GDRs at $50 each. Each GDR represents 5 equity shares. The exchange rate is ₹83/$. Calculate the rupee proceeds before expenses.

**HOTS:** (a) Explain how a change in the rupee‑dollar exchange rate after a GDR issue affects the Indian company’s reported earnings. (b) If the rupee depreciates by 5 % post‑issue, quantify the impact on the rupee value of a $10 million GDR proceeds.

**Application:** A mid‑size pharmaceutical firm wants to raise ₹500 crore via GDRs. The current share price is ₹250, conversion ratio 1 GDR = 5 shares, and the expected GDR issue price is $30. The exchange rate is ₹83/$. Determine the number of GDRs needed and check feasibility.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “XYZ Ltd. issued 2,00,000 GDRs at $40 each. Each GDR represents 6 equity shares of face value ₹10. The issue expenses were 3 % of gross proceeds. The exchange rate at the time of issue was ₹84/$. (i) Calculate the gross proceeds in US $. (ii) Calculate the net proceeds in ₹. (iii) If the company declares a dividend of ₹5 per share, compute the dividend per GDR in US $ (exchange rate ₹85/$ at dividend date).”
A start‑up valued at ₹8 crore pre‑money receives ₹1.6 crore from an angel. Calculate the post‑money valuation and the angel’s equity percentage.
In an ISC board question, a case study describes a start‑up that received ₹50 lakh from a friend who expects a fixed 12 % annual return. Classify this source of finance.

An angel invests ₹50 lakh in a start‑up at a ₹5 crore pre‑money valuation. Six months later, the start‑up raises a Series A at ₹20 crore pre‑money from a VC. Calculate the angel’s paper return multiple and percentage gain assuming no further dilution.

Past‑paper style: “A start‑up in the renewable energy sector seeks ₹3 crore for 15 % equity. An angel offers the amount but insists on a 2× liquidation preference. Discuss the implications for the founder and for a subsequent VC investor.”
A start‑up raises ₹15 crore in Series A at a ₹60 crore pre‑money valuation. The term sheet includes a 10 % ESOP pool created pre‑investment. Calculate the VC’s equity percentage after the round.
Design a one‑page term‑sheet outline for a Series B investment of ₹50 crore in a health‑tech start‑up valued at ₹200 crore pre‑money. Include at least five key clauses.

**HOTS:** A VC fund has a ₹500 crore corpus, 2 % management fee, 20 % carried interest after 8 % hurdle. In Year 1 it deploys ₹100 crore across five start‑ups. By Year 5, three fail (total loss), one returns 3×, one returns 10×. Calculate the fund’s net IRR to LPs assuming no further investments.

**Application:** A start‑up founder wants to negotiate a lower liquidation preference (1× non‑participating) but the VC insists on 1.5× participating with a 3× cap. Using a scenario where the exit valuation is ₹500 crore and the VC holds 25 % equity, show the payout difference and advise the founder.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** (a) Define “venture capitalist” as per the ISC Business Studies syllabus. (2 marks) (b) State two differences between venture capital and bank loan. (2 marks) (c) A start‑up raises ₹20 crore at a pre‑money valuation of ₹80 crore. Calculate the percentage of equity diluted for the founders if an ESOP pool of 10 % is created *before* the investment. (3 marks)
A startup raises ₹80 lakh through an equity crowd funding platform in India. The platform charges a 6 % fee. How much net capital does the startup receive?

A food‑delivery startup wants to raise ₹30 lakh via reward‑based crowd funding. It plans to offer a “lifetime free delivery” perk to each backer who contributes ₹500. How many backers are needed to meet the target?
Create a brief pitch (max 50 words) for a crowd funding campaign for a solar‑powered water purifier targeted at rural households in Maharashtra.

**HOTS:** A startup considers two options: (i) equity crowd funding raising ₹5 crore for 10 % equity on a platform charging 6 % fee; (ii) a bank term loan of ₹5 crore at 11 % p.a. for 5 years with a 1 % processing fee. Assuming the startup’s projected EBITDA is ₹2 crore per year, analyse which option is more cost‑effective over 5 years, ignoring tax.

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE (a)/(b)/(c):** (a) Critique the statement: “SEBI’s ₹10 crore cap on equity crowd funding is too low for growth‑stage startups.” (b) Propose one regulatory change that could balance investor protection and startup needs. (c) Explain how the cap affects a startup planning a ₹15 crore raise.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN (a)/(b)/(c):** (a) Define “crowd funding” as per the ISC Business Studies syllabus. (b) State two advantages of crowd funding for a first‑time entrepreneur. (c) A startup raises ₹50 lakh via equity crowd funding at a post‑money valuation of ₹5 crore. If the platform fee is 5 %, calculate the effective pre‑money valuation after fees.
Explain why a P2P platform must maintain a contingency fund of at least 1 % of its outstanding portfolio.

A borrower takes a ₹5 lakh P2P loan at a nominal 15 % p.a. for 24 months. The platform charges a 2 % upfront processing fee on the principal. Calculate the effective annual interest rate (APR) assuming monthly reducing balance repayments.
Design a P2P loan structure for a women‑led handicraft cooperative in Rajasthan needing ₹9 lakh for inventory, ensuring compliance with RBI exposure limits and maximizing lender participation.

In the ISC 2023 Business Studies paper, a 4‑mark question asked: “Distinguish between Peer‑to‑Peer lending and Crowd funding on the basis of (i) nature of return, (ii) regulatory authority, (iii) investor protection, (iv) suitability for start‑ups.” Provide a concise answer.

**HOTS:** A fintech startup proposes a “P2P‑plus” model where the platform **co‑lends** 20 % of each loan from its own NBFC balance sheet while 80 % comes from retail lenders. Discuss whether this structure complies with the RBI NBFC‑P2P Master Direction.

**APPLICATION:** A borrower takes a ₹4 lakh P2P loan at 14 % p.a. for 24 months with a 2 % upfront fee. The platform offers an **early‑repayment option** after 12 months with a 1 % prepayment penalty on outstanding principal. Calculate the total cost if the borrower repays early.

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** Critically assess the RBI’s **₹10 lakh aggregate borrower cap** for P2P lending. Does it adequately protect borrowers from over‑indebtedness, or does it hinder genuine MSME funding needs? Support with two arguments each side.
“Explain the term ‘globalisation’ and state two opportunities it offers to Indian firms.” (ISC 2023, 4 marks)
In the ISC 2023 Business Studies paper, a 4‑mark question asked: “Distinguish between globalisation and internationalisation with two points.” Provide a model answer.

**ISC 2022 Past‑Paper Style (6 marks):** “Globalisation has transformed the way Indian businesses operate.” **(a)** Explain the meaning of globalisation. **(b)** Discuss two ways in which globalisation has changed business operations in India. **(c)** State one challenge Indian firms face due to globalisation.

In the ISC 2023 Business Studies paper, a 4‑mark question asked: “Describe the nature of globalisation with reference to any two features.” Outline a model answer structure that would secure full marks.

(a) Define “interconnectedness” in the context of globalisation’s nature. (1 mark) (b) Give one Indian example where a supply‑chain disruption abroad affected a domestic firm. (2 marks) (c) Explain why interconnectedness makes risk management a strategic priority. (2 marks)

An Indian renewable‑energy firm wants to raise $50 million via green bonds listed on the London Stock Exchange. Identify the two nature attributes most critical for this plan and describe one concrete action for each.

Critically assess the view that “globalisation’s nature inevitably leads to cultural homogenisation, eroding India’s diverse business practices.” Structure your answer in three parts: (i) argument for homogenisation, (ii) counter‑argument with Indian evidence, (iii) synthesis. (6 marks)

Compare the nature of globalisation as experienced by (a) a traditional handicraft exporter from Rajasthan and (b) a cloud‑native SaaS start‑up from Hyderabad. Highlight two similarities and two differences in how the five attributes manifest. (6 marks)

ISC 2022 Business Studies Paper – 5‑mark question: “Explain how the nature of globalisation influences the strategic choices of an Indian pharmaceutical company planning to enter the US generic market.” Provide a concise model answer with mark allocation.

Application: A Chennai‑based automotive ancillary firm (turnover ₹500 cr) receives an RFQ from a German OEM requiring IATF 16949 certification and just‑in‑time delivery to a plant in Bavaria. Using the opportunity‑threat lens, decide whether the firm should (i) export from India, (ii) set up a warehouse in Germany, or (iii) form a JV with a local Tier‑1 supplier. Justify with two factors per option.

Evaluation/Critique: “Critically assess the view that the Production‑Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for electronics manufacturing fully neutralises the threats of globalisation for Indian firms.” Answer in three parts: (a) Identify two threats the PLI addresses. (b) Identify two threats it does not address. (c) Conclude with a balanced judgement (4 marks total: a‑1, b‑1, c‑2).

CISCE past‑paper pattern: “Explain how globalisation influences the strategic choice between exporting, licensing, and foreign direct investment (FDI) for an Indian pharmaceutical company.” (10 marks) Provide a model answer structured as: Introduction (1 mark), Four decision criteria with explanation (4 marks), Application to pharma context (3 marks), Conclusion (2 marks).
Create a brief strategic plan (max 150 words) for a mid‑size Indian auto‑component manufacturer to globalise its operations over the next three years.
In the ISC 2023 Business Studies paper, a 6‑mark question asked: “Discuss how globalisation transforms the organisational structure of a firm.” Provide a model answer outline with mark allocation.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern (10 marks):** “Globalisation transforms the way businesses organise their activities.” Discuss this statement with reference to (i) organisational structure, (ii) supply‑chain management, (iii) financial management, and (iv) human‑resource practices. Provide Indian examples for each.

In an ISC‑style case, a Mumbai‑based auto‑ancillary firm evaluates three entry modes for the Mexican market: (a) exporting, (b) joint venture with a local Tier‑1 supplier, (c) wholly owned subsidiary. The firm has limited capital but strong proprietary technology. Which mode should it choose and why? (3 marks)

**HOTS:** A Chennai‑based EV‑component startup holds a patented battery‑thermal‑management system. It must choose between (a) licensing to a Chinese Tier‑1 supplier, (b) forming a joint venture with a German OEM, (c) setting up a wholly owned subsidiary in Mexico for USMCA access. The startup has ₹30 cr cash, strong IP, and aims for global scale in 5 years. Analyse each option on IP protection, scale‑up speed, and capital efficiency. Recommend a sequenced strategy. (6 marks)

**Application:** A Kolkata‑based tea exporter (annual export ₹40 cr) faces a 15% US tariff on bulk tea but zero tariff on value‑added packaged tea under a trade agreement. The firm can either (i) continue bulk export, (ii) invest ₹8 cr in a packaging unit in a US Foreign‑Trade Zone (FTZ), or (iii) form a joint venture with a US specialty‑food brand to co‑pack. Using the concept of global value‑chain upgrading, recommend the best option and justify with cost‑benefit reasoning. (5 marks)

**Evaluation/Critique:** Critically assess the statement: “For Indian services firms, the global delivery model (offshore development + onsite client teams) is merely a cost‑arbitrage play and does not create sustainable competitive advantage.” Structure your answer as (a) arguments supporting the statement, (b) arguments refuting it, (c) your synthesis with an Indian example. (8 marks)

**Comparison:** Compare the entry‑mode decision framework for a **manufacturing firm** (capital‑intensive, tangible assets) versus a **knowledge‑intensive services firm** (asset‑light, human‑capital‑intensive) entering a developed market. Highlight at least three dimensions where the optimal mode diverges and explain why. (6 marks)

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “Globalisation has compelled Indian firms to rethink their market‑entry strategies. With reference to any two Indian companies, discuss how the choice of entry mode reflects the firm’s resource base, risk appetite, and the target market’s institutional environment.” (10 marks)

CISCE exam‑style: “Distinguish between symmetric and asymmetric encryption in the context of e‑business. Give one example of each used in a typical online transaction.” (4 marks)

**Evaluation/Critique:** (a) Critically assess the statement: “The IT Act, 2000 is sufficient to address all cyber‑security concerns of Indian e‑businesses today.” (b) Identify two gaps that the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 fills. (c) Propose one amendment to the IT Act that would strengthen e‑business security.

**Comparison:** Compare the security architecture of **UPI** (Unified Payments Interface) and **credit‑card 3D Secure 2.0** in terms of (a) authentication factors, (b) liability allocation for fraud, (c) regulatory oversight body. Present as a table.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** (a) Define “digital signature” as per the Information Technology Act, 2000. (2 marks) (b) Explain how a Certifying Authority (CA) contributes to the trust model in e‑business. (3 marks) (c) A company’s DSC expires on 31 March 2025. ISC 2023 Paper: “Explain how e‑business reduces information asymmetry between buyer and seller.” Provide a model answer structured for 4 marks.

**(a)** List the five nature characteristics of e‑business as per the ISC syllabus. (2 marks) **(b)** For any three, give one distinct buyer benefit and one distinct seller benefit. (6 marks) **(c)** Why is “information density” considered a double‑edged sword for buyers? (2 marks)

A traditional bookstore in Kolkata decides to launch an e‑commerce website. They estimate monthly fixed costs of ₹2,00,000 (website, warehousing, staff). ISC 2022 Paper (adapted): “E‑business has transformed the buyer‑seller relationship.” **(a)** Explain how *interactivity* and *information density* have shifted power toward buyers. (4 marks) **(c)** Give one example of an Indian company that has successfully used such tools. (2 marks)

A Mumbai‑based media house outsources its video‑editing to a boutique post‑production firm. The SLA specifies “delivery of edited episodes within 48 hours of raw footage upload.” During a major sports event, raw footage volume triples and the provider misses deadlines. (a) Identify the SLA deficiency. (b) Suggest a clause to handle volume spikes. (c) Explain how this clause protects both parties.
Compare BPO and KPO on the dimensions of (a) nature of work, (b) skill requirement, (c) typical Indian hub cities, and (d) value‑addition level. Present as a 2 × 4 table.
**ISC Past‑Paper Pattern (4 marks):** “Explain the role of a Service Level Agreement (SLA) in outsourcing. Give two essential components of an SLA.” Provide a model answer structured for full marks.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN (Multi‑part):** **(a)** Define “outsourcer” in the context of Business Process Outsourcing. (2 marks) **(b)** Explain two reasons why a company may choose to outsource its finance‑and‑accounting function. (3 marks) **(c)** State two key clauses that must appear in the Service Level Agreement to protect the outsourcer’s interests. (3 marks) **(d)** Briefly describe the outsourcer’s responsibility under RBI’s outsourcing guidelines for banks. (2 marks)

The RBI’s Master Direction on Outsourcing (2017) requires the bank to retain “effective oversight”. (b) Recommend **two** additional contractual safeguards GreenFields should insist upon. (c) If the BPO commits a systematic error causing ₹12 lakh GST penalty, outline the **step‑by‑step** recovery process GreenFields should follow.
A Bengaluru‑based IT firm signs an SLA promising 99.9 % uptime for a client’s cloud infrastructure. In a month, uptime falls to 99.2 %. Apply the SLA concept to determine the likely consequence.

In an ISC‑style case, a company outsources its customer‑support to a provider in Tier‑2 city. The provider’s agents lack product knowledge, causing a 15 % drop in CSAT. Identify the root cause and propose a contractual remedy.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Define “service provider” in the context of outsourcing. (2 marks) (b) State two essential elements of a Service Level Agreement. (2 marks) (c) Explain one advantage and one risk of engaging an offshore service provider for an Indian firm. (3 marks)

Identify the BPO type and design a vendor‑selection scorecard with four weighted criteria.

**ISC 2022 Past‑Paper Style:** A case study describes “GreenFields Agri Ltd., a Punjab‑based agri‑input company, outsourcing its farmer‑helpline (IVR + live agents) to a Mohali BPO. **CISCE exam‑style:** “Distinguish between KPO and LPO on the basis of (a) nature of work, (b) skill set required, (c) typical client industry.” (3 marks)

(3 marks) (c) Suggest one contractual safeguard the client should include in the SLA. (1 mark)

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern (Multi‑part):** “Read the case and answer: **Case:** *GreenPower Ltd*, a renewable‑energy firm, outsources **solar‑plant performance monitoring** (real‑time SCADA data analysis) to a KPO and **payroll processing** to a BPO. (b) Explain how the platform can comply with the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 for rental disputes. (c) Identify one GST implication for the platform’s commission income.

(c) Suggest one India Stack component GreenCart should integrate for seamless onboarding of resident sellers.

(1 mark) (b) Explain why the platform must collect TCS under Section 52 of CGST Act. (2 marks) (c) State one benefit to farmers from UPI‑based 48‑hour payment. (1 mark) (d) If the platform also allowed farmers to sell directly to urban households, name the new model introduced. (1 mark)

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** “Mandatory e‑invoicing for turnover above ₹5 cr has forced all firms to adopt full ERP suites.” Critique this statement with reference to the actual compliance options available to Indian businesses.

Determine whether the issue meets the 75 % QIB allocation rule and state the consequence if it does not.

A merchant banker is managing a ₹1,000 crore IPO. The issuer wants to allocate 60 % of the issue to anchor investors before the book‑building opens. Is this permissible under current SEBI regulations? Justify with the relevant regulation.

“Delta Ltd.” has appointed a Category III merchant banker for its ₹40 crore rights issue. The merchant banker’s net worth is ₹3 crore. Identify the regulatory violation and the corrective action SEBI can take.

(a) State two differences between a merchant banker’s due‑diligence certificate and an auditor’s report on the financial statements included in the offer document. (2 marks) (b) Explain why the merchant banker’s certificate is critical for investor protection in a book‑built issue. (3 marks)

A past ISC paper asked: “Discuss the regulatory framework governing merchant bankers in India and outline their obligations during a public issue.” Provide a concise answer plan that would secure 8 marks.
An investor holds 500 shares of Tata Motors in a demat account with DP A. She sells 200 shares through a broker who uses DP B. Describe the depository‑level steps for this transaction.
In the ISC 2023 Business Studies paper, a question asked: “State two advantages of the depository system for investors.” Provide the answer with mark allocation.
**Application:** An investor wants to pledge 1,000 shares held in a demat account with DP Axis Bank to obtain a loan. Outline the depository‑level steps for creating the pledge.
**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “State any three functions of a depository as per SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 2018.” Provide the answer with mark allocation.

An investor buys 500 units of a debt fund at NAV ₹22.40. After three months the NAV is ₹23.10 and the fund declares a dividend of ₹0.60 per unit under the dividend payout option. Compute the investor’s total gain if she reinvests the dividend at the ex‑dividend NAV of ₹22.50.

HOTS: “A mutual fund scheme’s risk‑o‑meter shows ‘Moderately High’. The fund manager proposes to increase allocation to unrated corporate bonds from 10 % to 25 % of portfolio. Analyse the impact on the scheme’s risk profile, NAV volatility, and regulatory compliance.”
Application: “An investor wants to invest ₹5 lakh for 18 months with minimal capital erosion. Recommend a suitable mutual fund category and justify using SEBI classification and risk‑o‑meter.”

CISCE past‑paper pattern: “(a) Define Net Asset Value (NAV) of a mutual fund. (b) A scheme’s portfolio value is ₹120 cr, liabilities ₹2 cr, units outstanding 4 cr. Calculate NAV. (c) Explain how expense ratio affects NAV.”
XYZ Ltd issues commercial paper (CP) rated “A1+” by CRISIL. If the prevailing 91‑day Treasury bill yield is 6.50 %, estimate a plausible yield for the CP and justify your estimate.

**APPLICATION:** A corporate treasurer is evaluating two funding options for a ₹200 crore capex: (i) 5‑year bank loan at 8.50 % p.a. floating, (ii) 5‑year NCDs rated ‘AA‑’ with a fixed coupon of 8.20 % p.a. The current 5‑year G‑sec yield is 7.10 % and the ‘AA‑’ spread is 90 bps. Advise the treasurer, considering interest‑rate risk and credit‑risk perception.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Define “Credit Rating Agency” as per SEBI regulations. (2 marks) (b) List any three obligations of a CRA under the SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999. (3 marks) (c) Explain how a rating outlook “Negative” differs from a rating “Watch Negative”. (2 marks)
In the ISC 2023 Business Studies paper, a 4‑mark question asked: “State two functions of IRDAI related to policyholder protection.” Provide a model answer with mark allocation.

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** Critically assess whether IRDAI’s current commission cap structure (e.g., 15 % first‑year for life, 10 % renewal) adequately prevents mis‑selling while ensuring intermediary viability.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Define “solvency margin” as per IRDAI regulations. (b) A life insurer’s available solvency capital is ₹300 crore and required solvency capital is ₹200 crore. Compute the solvency ratio and comment on compliance. (c) State two consequences if the insurer’s solvency ratio falls below 150 %.
An individual agent sells a health policy with a first‑year premium of ₹40,000. The IRDA commission cap for general insurance is 15 %. Calculate the maximum commission the agent can legally earn.

**APPLICATION:** A corporate agent sells a health policy (first‑year premium ₹60,000) and a motor policy (first‑year premium ₹30,000) to the same client. IRDA caps: health 15 %, motor 15 %. The agent receives ₹10,000 total commission from the insurers. Determine if the agent is compliant. Show calculations.

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** (a) Critically assess the effectiveness of the 25 % first‑year commission cap for life insurance in curbing churning. (b) Suggest two complementary measures IRDA could adopt. (c) Discuss any potential unintended consequences of those measures.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** Answer the following as per ISC 2023 Business Studies paper style (marks indicated). (a) Define ‘insurance agent’ as per IRDA regulations. (2 marks) (b) State two differences between an insurance agent and an insurance broker. (2 marks) (c) Explain the term ‘churning’ in insurance distribution and state one penalty IRDA can impose for it. (3 marks)
Calculate the brokerage commission earned by a direct broker who places a fire insurance policy with a premium of ₹2,00,000 at a commission rate of 7.5 %.

**APPLICATION:** A broker places a marine cargo policy for an exporter. The premium is ₹8,00,000 and the brokerage rate is 8 %. The insurer pays the broker directly. Show the journal entries in the broker’s books for (a) receipt of commission, (b) payment of professional indemnity insurance premium of ₹25,000.
**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** “The IRDAI’s net‑worth requirement for direct brokers (₹50 lakh) is too low to ensure financial stability.” Critique this statement with two arguments for and two against.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) State the meaning of “insurance broker” as per IRDAI. (2 marks) (b) List any three conditions for grant of a direct broker licence. (3 marks) (c) Explain the broker’s obligation regarding disclosure of commission. (2 marks)
A food processor with an annual turnover of ₹25 crore operates in two states. Which category of FSSAI licence must it obtain, and why?

A small spice grinding unit in Kerala has an annual turnover of ₹8 lakh and sells only within the district. It has not applied for any FSSAI authorisation. Identify the correct authorisation it requires and outline the key steps to obtain it.

In an ISC Board exam, a question asks: “Explain the role of FSSAI in regulating food processors with reference to licensing, standards, and enforcement.” Outline a structured answer that would earn full marks (6 marks).

A food processor in Punjab (turnover ₹18 crore, single state) holds a State Licence. It plans to start exporting its products to the UAE. Explain the additional FSSAI requirements for export‑oriented units and the role of the **Export Inspection Council (EIC)**.

**(a)** Compare the enforcement powers of FSSAI (under the FSS Act, 2006) with those of SEBI (under the SEBI Act, 1992) in respect of **licence suspension** and **penalty imposition**. **(b)** Which regulator has a broader scope for **criminal prosecution**? Justify.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern Question (6 marks):** “Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) plays a pivotal role in regulating food processors. Discuss the **licensing framework**, **key compliance requirements**, and **enforcement mechanisms** of FSSAI with respect to food processors.”
A packer with an annual turnover of ₹25 crore applies for an FSSAI licence. Which licence category should it obtain, and why?
A packer with a state licence expands operations and its turnover crosses ₹22 crore mid‑year. What must the packer do regarding its licence?

(a) List the three categories of food‑business operators under FSSAI that require a licence. (b) For each, state the turnover threshold that decides central vs. state licence. (c) Explain why a packer falling in the “manufacturer” category still needs to meet packaging‑specific Schedule 4 requirements.
A company producing steel re‑bars wants to use the ISI mark. The relevant standard is IS 1786. Outline the three main stages the company must complete to obtain the licence.

A manufacturer of **plastic water tanks** (voluntary IS 12701) obtains an ISI licence. After two years, the government issues a notification making IS 12701 mandatory. **(a)** What immediate obligations arise for the manufacturer? **(b)** How does the surveillance regime change? **(c)** What steps should the manufacturer take to remain compliant?
**Past‑paper style:** “Explain the role of BIS‑accredited laboratories in the ISI certification scheme. (4 marks)”
Calculate the mole fraction of O₂ dissolved in water at 298 K when the partial pressure of O₂ is 0.21 atm. Henry’s constant for O₂ at 298 K is k_H = 4.4 × 10⁴ atm (mole‑fraction basis).

An ISC 2023 question: “The Henry’s law constant for N₂ in water at 298 K is 6.1 × 10⁴ atm. Calculate the molar concentration of N₂ in water exposed to air at 1 atm (assume air is 78 % N₂ by volume).” Provide the answer with units.

**HOTS:** (a) Derive the relationship between the mole‑fraction‑based Henry’s constant k_H (Pa) and the concentration‑based constant k_H' (mol·m⁻³·Pa⁻¹) for a dilute aqueous solution, assuming the molar density of water is 55.5 mol·L⁻¹. (b) Using this relationship, convert k_H = 4.4 × 10⁴ atm for O₂ at 298 K to k_H' in mol·L⁻¹·atm⁻¹. (c) Discuss why the two constants have different temperature dependencies.

**Application:** A deep‑sea diver breathes a gas mixture containing 2 % O₂ by volume at a total pressure of 20 atm. Calculate the molar concentration of O₂ dissolved in the diver’s blood plasma (assume plasma behaves like water) at 310 K. Henry’s constant for O₂ at 310 K (concentration basis) is k_H' = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol·L⁻¹·atm⁻¹. (a) Find p_O₂. (b) Find C_O₂. (c) If the diver ascends rapidly to 1 atm, what is the new equilibrium C_O₂? (d) Explain the risk of decompression sickness in terms of Henry’s law.

**Evaluation/Critique:** A research paper claims: “Henry’s law constant for CO₂ in seawater at 298 K is 3.3 × 10⁻² mol·kg⁻¹·atm⁻¹, which is 10 % lower than in pure water, proving that salinity enhances CO₂ solubility.” Critique this statement using the concepts of Henry’s law and solution non‑ideality. (a) Identify the correct interpretation of the constant’s units. (b) Explain whether a lower constant means higher or lower solubility. (c) Discuss the effect of salinity on gas solubility (salting‑out effect).

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** (a) Define Henry’s law and give its mathematical expression. (b) The Henry’s law constant for CH₄ in water at 298 K is 4.1 × 10⁴ atm (mole‑fraction basis). Calculate the mole fraction of CH₄ dissolved in water when the partial pressure of CH₄ is 0.5 atm. (c) If the temperature is raised to 308 K, the constant becomes 5.2 × 10⁴ atm. Calculate the new mole fraction at the same partial pressure. (d) Explain the trend in terms of gas solubility and temperature.
Calculate the vapour pressure of a solution prepared by dissolving 0.1 mol of non‑volatile urea in 0.9 mol of water at 298 K, given pure water vapour pressure = 3.17 kPa.

Design a binary mixture of two volatile liquids A and B such that the total vapour pressure at a given composition is 80 kPa, given \(P_A^0 = 100\) kPa, \(P_B^0 = 50\) kPa. Find the required mole fraction of A.

A solution of two volatile liquids X and Y obeys Raoult’s law. At 300 K, pure X has vapour pressure 60 kPa, pure Y 40 kPa. If the vapour phase contains 0.5 mole fraction of X, find the liquid composition.

(a) Derive the expression for the total vapour pressure of a binary solution of two volatile liquids A and B that obeys Raoult’s law. (b) Show mathematically that the vapour phase is always richer in the more volatile component. (c) If the same system exhibits a positive deviation from Raoult’s law, how does the actual total vapour pressure compare with the Raoult’s law prediction? (3 marks total: a=1, b=1, c=1)

A perfume contains ethanol (volatile) and a non‑volatile fragrance oil. As the perfume sits on skin, ethanol evaporates. Using Raoult’s law, explain why the scent intensity changes over time. (4 marks)
Critique the use of Raoult’s law for calculating the vapour pressure of a solution of acetone and chloroform, which exhibits negative deviation. (4 marks)
Compare Raoult’s law for volatile solutes with Henry’s law for gas solubility. Highlight two similarities and two differences. (4 marks)

(a) Define Raoult’s law for a non‑volatile solute. (b) A solution of 0.02 mol non‑volatile solute in 0.98 mol water at 298 K has a vapour pressure of 3.10 kPa. Calculate the vapour pressure of pure water. (c) Explain why the relative lowering of vapour pressure is a colligative property. (5 marks: a=1, b=2, c=2)

For a binary mixture of components 1 and 2 at 298 K, pure vapour pressures are \(P_1^0 = 40\ \text{kPa}\) and \(P_2^0 = 10\ \text{kPa}\). At \(x_1 = 0.3\), the measured partial pressures are \(P_1 = 13.2\ \text{kPa}\) and \(P_2 = 7.0\ \text{kPa}\). Calculate the activity coefficients \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) and state the deviation type.

In an ISC 2023 paper, a question asked: “A binary mixture of liquids X and Y forms a minimum‑boiling azeotrope. Sketch the \(P\)–\(x\) and \(T\)–\(x\) diagrams at constant pressure, labelling the azeotropic point.” Describe the expected shapes and labels.

**HOTS:** A binary mixture of A and B forms a minimum‑boiling azeotrope at \(x_A = 0.4\) and 350 K. The pure‑component boiling points at 1 atm are \(T_A^0 = 340\ \text{K}\) and \(T_B^0 = 360\ \text{K}\). Sketch the \(T\)–\(x\) diagram at 1 atm, labelling the azeotropic point. Then explain why the azeotrope composition does not correspond to the maximum of the \(P\)–\(x\) curve at 350 K.

**Application:** A perfume manufacturer mixes essential oil (component E) with ethanol (component Et) to make a fragrance. At 298 K, \(P_E^0 = 0.5\ \text{kPa}\), \(P_{Et}^0 = 8\ \text{kPa}\). For a mixture with \(x_E = 0.1\), the measured total vapour pressure is \(7.5\ \text{kPa}\). The manufacturer wants the fragrance to evaporate slowly (low vapour pressure). Should they increase or decrease \(x_E\)? Calculate the ideal pressure at \(x_E = 0.1\) and at \(x_E = 0.2\) to support your recommendation.

**Evaluation/Critique:** A textbook states: “For any binary mixture, if the activity coefficient of one component is greater than 1, the other component’s activity coefficient must also be greater than 1.” Critique this statement using the Gibbs‑Duhem equation.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** (a) Define an ideal solution. (1 mark) (b) State two thermodynamic criteria for ideality. (2 marks) (c) A binary mixture of liquids P and Q at 300 K has pure vapour pressures \(P_P^0 = 60\ \text{kPa}\) and \(P_Q^0 = 20\ \text{kPa}\). At \(x_P = 0.3\), the measured total vapour pressure is \(30\ \text{kPa}\). Determine whether the mixture shows positive or negative deviation. (2 marks) (d) If the mixture in (c) forms an azeotrope, predict whether it will be minimum‑boiling or maximum‑boiling. (1 mark)

A student measures the vapour pressure of pure benzene at 25 °C as 12.4 kPa and finds it drops to 11.2 kPa after dissolving a non‑volatile solute. Evaluate whether the solution can be considered ideal based on the data.
Calculate the vapour pressure of a solution containing 0.020 mol of urea in 0.180 mol of water at 298 K, given that the vapour pressure of pure water at this temperature is 23.8 mm Hg.

A CISCE exam paper asks: “The vapour pressure of pure ethanol at 293 K is 5.95 kPa. After adding 2.0 g of a solute to 50.0 g of ethanol, the vapour pressure falls to 5.70 kPa. Calculate the molar mass of the solute.” Provide the answer with correct significant figures.

(a) State the expression for relative lowering of vapour pressure in terms of the masses of solute (\(w_2\)) and solvent (\(w_1\)) and their molar masses (\(M_2\), \(M_1\)). (b) Using this expression, calculate the molar mass of a solute if 1.50 g dissolved in 50.0 g of water lowers the vapour pressure from 23.8 mm Hg to 22.9 mm Hg at 298 K. (c) Discuss one assumption made in part (b) that could lead to error if the solute is an electrolyte.

(a) Explain why the relative lowering of vapour pressure is independent of temperature for an ideal solution. (b) If the vapour pressure of pure benzene at 300 K is 12.4 kPa and at 310 K is 16.2 kPa, calculate the relative lowering at each temperature for a solution whose mole fraction of solute is 0.020. (c) Comment on whether the observed change in lowering with temperature indicates ideality or non‑ideality.

(a) Derive the relation between relative lowering of vapour pressure and the elevation of boiling point (\(\Delta T_b\)) using the Clausius‑Clapeyron equation. (b) For water, \(K_b = 0.512 K kg mol^{-1}\). If a solution shows a relative lowering of 0.015, calculate \(\Delta T_b\). (c) Identify one limitation of using this relation for concentrated solutions.

Compare the relative lowering of vapour pressure for two solutions at the same temperature: Solution X contains 0.010 mol of urea in 0.990 mol of water; Solution Y contains 0.010 mol of NaCl in 0.990 mol of water (assuming complete dissociation). Which solution shows a greater lowering and why?

A CISCE past‑paper question: “The vapour pressure of pure acetone at 293 K is 24.5 kPa. After adding 3.00 g of a solute to 40.0 g of acetone, the vapour pressure drops to 23.2 kPa. (i) Calculate the molar mass of the solute. (ii) If the solute is known to be a non‑electrolyte, comment on the reliability of the result. (iii) Suggest one experimental improvement to reduce error.”
Explain why a 0.1 mol kg⁻¹ NaCl solution shows a larger boiling‑point elevation than a 0.1 mol kg⁻¹ glucose solution.

A student measures ΔTb = 0.30 K for a solution of 1.00 g of an unknown non‑electrolyte in 20.0 g of water (Kb = 0.512 K kg mol⁻¹). The student calculates the molar mass as 85 g mol⁻¹. Evaluate whether this result is plausible and identify any error.

An ISC 2023 question: “0.5 g of a non‑volatile solute dissolved in 25 g of benzene (Kb = 2.53 K kg mol⁻¹) raises the boiling point by 0.28 K. Calculate the molar mass of the solute.” Provide the full solution with units.

A 0.05 mol kg⁻¹ solution of a weak electrolyte HA (Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵) in water shows ΔTb = 0.026 K. Kb = 0.512 K kg mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the apparent van’t Hoff factor i. (b) Determine the degree of dissociation α of HA. (c) Comment on whether the assumption of negligible volume change is justified.

An industrial process uses a 30 % by mass ethylene glycol (C₂H₆O₂, M = 62.07 g mol⁻¹) solution in water as a coolant. (a) Calculate the molality of the solution. (b) Determine the boiling‑point elevation at 1 atm. (c) If the system operates at 1.5 atm, estimate the boiling point of the solution (pure water boils at 111.4 °C at 1.5 atm).

A student is given the following data for an unknown solute X in benzene (Kb = 2.53 K kg mol⁻¹): mass of X = 1.20 g, mass of benzene = 25.0 g, ΔTb = 0.45 K. (a) Calculate the molar mass of X assuming it is a non‑electrolyte. (b) If the same mass of X is dissolved in 25.0 g of water (Kb = 0.512 K kg mol⁻¹) and ΔTb = 0.12 K, calculate the molar mass again. (c) Explain any discrepancy between the two results and what it implies about the behaviour of X in the two solvents.

Compare the boiling‑point elevation produced by 0.1 mol kg⁻¹ solutions of (i) urea (non‑electrolyte), (ii) NaCl (strong electrolyte), and (iii) CaCl₂ (strong electrolyte) in water. Use Kb = 0.512 K kg mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate ΔTb for each assuming complete dissociation. (b) Rank them from smallest to largest ΔTb. (c) Discuss why the experimental ΔTb for CaCl₂ might be slightly lower than the theoretical value.

ISC 2022 pattern: “A solution containing 0.5 g of a non‑volatile solute in 20 g of water boils at 100.15 °C. The ebullioscopic constant of water is 0.512 K kg mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the molar mass of the solute. (b) If the solute is known to be a dimer in the solid state but monomeric in solution, what would be the effect on the calculated molar mass if the student mistakenly used i = 2? (c) State one experimental precaution to minimise error in ΔTb measurement.”
Calculate the freezing point of a solution containing 10 g of urea (NH₂CONH₂, molar mass 60 g mol⁻¹) dissolved in 200 g of water. Kf for water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹.

A 0.2 molal aqueous solution of a non‑electrolyte shows a freezing‑point depression of 0.372 K. The cryoscopic constant of water is 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹. Determine the van’t Hoff factor and comment on the nature of the solute.

(a) Derive the relationship between freezing‑point depression (ΔTf) and the molar mass (M₂) of a non‑volatile, non‑electrolyte solute, starting from ΔTf = Kf m. (b) If the solute dissociates into three ions (i = 3), how does the observed ΔTf change for the same mass concentration? (c) Discuss two limitations of using freezing‑point depression to determine molar masses of macromolecules (e.g., proteins).

A car radiator uses ethylene glycol (C₂H₆O₂) as antifreeze. If 500 g of ethylene glycol (molar mass 62 g mol⁻¹) is added to 4 kg of water, calculate the freezing point of the mixture. Kf = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹. Assume i = 1.

(a) Define cryoscopic constant. (b) A solution of 2.00 g of a non‑electrolyte in 50.0 g of water freezes at 272.85 K. Calculate the molar mass of the solute. (c) If the same mass of solute is dissolved in 50.0 g of benzene (Kf = 5.12 K kg mol⁻¹), what would be the freezing‑point depression? (Freezing point of pure benzene = 278.65 K.)
A 0.05 mol L⁻¹ aqueous solution of glucose (non‑electrolyte) at 300 K shows an osmotic pressure of 1.24 × 10⁵ Pa. Verify whether this value is consistent with the ideal‑solution equation.
A solution contains 0.02 mol L⁻¹ NaCl (assume complete dissociation, i = 2) at 298 K. Calculate its osmotic pressure in kPa.
In an ISC exam, a student writes π = CRT for a 0.1 M MgCl₂ solution and obtains 2.48 × 10⁵ Pa at 298 K. Identify the error and give the correct π.

**HOTS:** A solution of a weak electrolyte HA (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) at 0.01 M and 298 K shows an osmotic pressure of 2.45 × 10⁵ Pa. Assuming the van’t Hoff factor i = 1 + α (where α is degree of dissociation), calculate α and comment on the consistency with Ka.

**APPLICATION:** A food technologist wants to concentrate fruit juice by reverse osmosis. The juice has an effective solute concentration of 0.30 mol L⁻¹ (assume i = 1) at 293 K. What minimum applied pressure (in bar) is required to achieve net solvent flux from juice to pure water side? (1 bar = 10⁵ Pa)
**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** A research paper claims that “osmotic pressure of a 0.001 M protein solution at 298 K is 2.48 × 10³ Pa, proving that proteins behave as ideal solutes.” Critique this claim.

**COMPARISON:** Compare the magnitude of osmotic pressure (π) and boiling‑point elevation (ΔT_b) for a 0.1 M sucrose solution at 298 K. Use K_b = 0.512 K kg mol⁻¹ and assume density ≈ 1 kg L⁻¹. Which colligative property gives a more easily measurable change?

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** (a) Define osmotic pressure and state its SI unit. (b) Derive the relationship π = CRT for a dilute solution starting from the equality of chemical potentials of solvent in solution and pure solvent. (c) A 0.2 g sample of a non‑electrolyte solute is dissolved in 100 mL of water at 300 K. The osmotic pressure is found to be 4.95 × 10³ Pa. Calculate the molar mass of the solute.

An aqueous solution of 0.20 mol kg⁻¹ of a substance X shows an elevation of boiling point of 0.12 K at 373 K. Given \(K_b\) for water = 0.512 K kg mol⁻¹, calculate the van’t Hoff factor and comment on whether X associates or dissociates.

In an ISC examination, a question states: “A 0.15 mol kg⁻¹ solution of a substance Y in water gives an osmotic pressure of 3.00 atm at 300 K. Calculate the abnormal molar mass of Y if its normal molar mass is 120 g mol⁻¹.” Provide the answer with correct units.

(a) State the van’t Hoff factor for a solution of calcium chloride that is 70 % dissociated into Ca²⁺ and 2 Cl⁻ ions. (b) If the normal molar mass of CaCl₂ is 111 g mol⁻¹, calculate the abnormal molar mass. (c) Explain how the abnormal molar mass would change if the temperature were increased, assuming dissociation increases with temperature.

A 0.12 mol kg⁻¹ solution of a weak acid HA in water gives a boiling‑point elevation of 0.058 K at 373 K. \(K_b\) = 0.512 K kg mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the van’t Hoff factor. (b) Determine the degree of dissociation α of HA. (c) If the normal molar mass of HA is 80 g mol⁻¹, find the abnormal molar mass.

Compare the abnormal molar mass obtained from (i) elevation of boiling point and (ii) osmotic pressure for a 0.05 mol kg⁻¹ solution of a solute that dissociates into two ions with a degree of dissociation of 0.40. Assume the normal molar mass is 150 g mol⁻¹, \(K_b\) = 0.512 K kg mol⁻¹, and use \(R\) = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ at 300 K. Show all steps and state whether the two methods give the same abnormal molar mass; if not, explain why.

A student measures the freezing‑point depression of a 0.20 mol kg⁻¹ solution of an unknown substance and obtains ΔTf = 0.30 K. Using \(K_f\) = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹, they calculate an abnormal molar mass of 124 g mol⁻¹. The normal molar mass of the substance, determined independently by mass spectrometry, is 180 g mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the van’t Hoff factor implied by the freezing‑point data. (b) State whether the substance associates or dissociates. (c) Suggest a plausible molecular explanation for the observed abnormality.

In an ISC‑style question, a 0.10 mol kg⁻¹ solution of a solid X in water shows an osmotic pressure of 2.20 atm at 298 K. The normal molar mass of X is 130 g mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the van’t Hoff factor. (b) Determine the abnormal molar mass. (c) If X is known to be a weak acid HA that dissociates as HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, find the degree of dissociation α. (d) Discuss how the value of α would change if the same experiment were repeated at 310 K, assuming the dissociation constant increases with temperature.
A 0.05 mol kg⁻¹ solution of CaCl₂ shows a freezing point depression of 0.279 K. Calculate the van’t Hoff factor and comment on the extent of dissociation. (Kf for water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹).
Explain why a solution of ethanoic acid in benzene shows a van’t Hoff factor less than 1, and what this indicates about the solute.
A 0.2 mol kg⁻¹ solution of a non‑volatile solute in water elevates the boiling point by 0.102 K. Calculate the van’t Hoff factor. (Kb for water = 0.512 K kg mol⁻¹).

In an ISC examination, a student calculates i for a 0.1 M KCl solution from osmotic pressure data as 1.8. The teacher marks it incorrect. Identify the most likely error and give the correct value of i (assume complete dissociation).

A 0.02 mol kg⁻¹ solution of Al₂(SO₄)₃ shows a freezing point depression of 0.372 K. (a) Calculate the van’t Hoff factor. (b) If the salt dissociates completely into 2 Al³⁺ + 3 SO₄²⁻, what is the expected i? (c) Suggest one reason why the experimental i might differ from the theoretical value.

The osmotic pressure of a 0.005 M urea solution at 298 K is measured as 0.122 atm. (a) Calculate the van’t Hoff factor. (b) Urea is a non‑electrolyte; what does the obtained i tell you about the solution? (c) If the measured pressure were 0.244 atm, what would i be and how would you interpret it?

A student prepares three solutions each containing 0.10 mol of solute X in 1 kg of water: (i) X = glucose, (ii) X = NaCl, (iii) X = CH₃COOH. The measured freezing point depressions are 0.186 K, 0.350 K, and 0.200 K respectively. (a) Calculate the van’t Hoff factor for each solute. (b) Using the values, deduce the degree of dissociation of NaCl and CH₃COOH. (c) Explain why the depression for CH₃COOH is only slightly larger than that for glucose despite being a weak acid.

Compare the van’t Hoff factor for a 0.01 M solution of BaCl₂ and a 0.01 M solution of sucrose under identical conditions. State which solution exhibits a greater colligative effect and why, referencing the particle count contributed by each solute.

In an ISC board paper, a question states: “0.2 g of a solid Y dissolved in 50 g of water gives a freezing point of –0.186 °C. Calculate the molecular weight of Y assuming it does not dissociate. If the experimental molecular weight is found to be half of this value, what is the van’t Hoff factor and what does it indicate about Y?” (a) Calculate the assumed molecular weight of Y. (b) Determine the van’t Hoff factor from the observed and assumed molecular weights. Write the ground‑state electronic configuration of a neutral manganese (Mn) atom (Z = 25) using noble‑gas core notation.

**HOTS:** (a) Predict the magnetic moment of [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ and [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺. (b) Explain the difference in terms of ligand field strength. (c) If the measured μ for [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ is 2.3 BM, what does this indicate about the spin state?

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** (a) Write the electronic configuration of Cr³⁺ and Mn²⁺. (b) Calculate the spin‑only magnetic moment for each. (c) Which ion would you expect to show a more intense colour in aqueous solution and why? (Marks: 2+2+1)
Calculate the mass of KMnO₄ required to prepare 250 mL of a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution. (Atomic masses: K = 39.10, Mn = 54.94, O = 16.00 g mol⁻¹)

Write the balanced half‑reaction for the reduction of MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺ and calculate the amount (in moles) of Fe²⁺ oxidised. (Assume the reaction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O; Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻)

ISC 2023 Paper 2, Question 4(b): “Draw the shape of the permanganate ion and indicate the bond angle. State the hybridisation of manganese.” Provide a complete answer as per marking scheme.

Calculate the volume of 0.100 N K₂Cr₂O₇ solution required to oxidise 0.250 g of oxalic acid dihydrate (H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O, M = 126.07 g mol⁻¹) in acidic medium. Reaction: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3H₂C₂O₄ + 8H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6CO₂ + 7H₂O.

A sample of potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇) is used in a redox titration where 0.025 mol of K₂Cr₂O₇ reacts with Fe²⁺ ions. Calculate the moles of Fe²⁺ oxidized, given the balanced equation: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6 Fe²⁺ + 14 H⁺ → 2 Cr³⁺ + 6 Fe³⁺ + 7 H₂O.

(a) State one use of uranium‑235 in nuclear reactors. (b) Explain why the isotope U‑235 is preferred over U‑238 for sustaining a chain reaction. An ISC 2022 question asked: “Explain why the +3 oxidation state is most common for lanthanoids but actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states.” Provide a concise answer.

A researcher measures the magnetic moment of a lanthanoid(III) complex and obtains 3.5 BM. Which lanthanoid ion is most likely present, and why might the measured value deviate from the spin‑only prediction?

An ISC 2021 paper asked: “(a) Write the electronic configuration of the Pm³⁺ ion. (b) Explain why promethium has no stable isotopes. (c) Predict the magnetic moment of Pm³⁺ using the spin‑only formula.” Provide the complete answer with marks allocation.

In the ISC 2023 paper, a question asked: “Write the formula of the coordination sphere for a complex of Cr(III) with three chloride ions and three ammonia molecules.” Provide the correct formula with charge.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern (multi‑part):** (a) Define the term “chelate effect”. (1 mark) (b) For the complex [Co(en)₃]³⁺, calculate the coordination number and the overall charge. (2 marks) (c) Explain why [Co(en)₃]³⁺ is more stable than [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺. (2 marks)
Explain why the coordination number of [Co(en)₃]³⁺ is 6 even though only three ligand molecules are present.
A student writes the formula of a complex as [Ni(NH₃)₄]Cl₂ and claims the coordination number of Ni is 2 because there are two chloride ions outside the bracket. Evaluate this claim.
Design a coordination entity with a central metal ion of your choice that has coordination number 5. Write its formula and name the geometry.
In the ISC 2023 paper, a question gave the complex [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂. State the coordination number of cobalt and the number of ionisable chloride ions.
ISC 2022 question: “The coordination number of the central metal ion in [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] is ___.” Fill the blank and justify your answer with reference to ligand denticity.

In an ISC practical, a student measures the molar conductivity of a 0.01 M solution of \([Pt(NH_3)_4]Cl_2\) and obtains a value consistent with a 1:2 electrolyte. Does this observation support the proposed formula? Justify.

ISC 2023 Paper 2, Question 4 (adapted): (a) Write the IUPAC name of the complex [Cr(NH₃)₂Cl₂(en)]Cl. (b) Draw all possible geometrical isomers for this complex, indicating which are chiral. (c) If the complex is dissolved in water, how many ions per formula unit are produced?

An ISC 2023 question: “A coordination compound of formula [M(AA)₂B₂] (AA = bidentate, B = monodentate) shows optical isomerism. Using Werner’s theory, explain why a tetrahedral geometry cannot exhibit this isomerism for the given composition.”

(a) For the complex [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺, state the d‑electron count, predict high‑spin or low‑spin, and give the number of unpaired electrons. (b) Calculate its spin‑only magnetic moment. (c) If the absorption maximum is at 450 nm, compute Δ₀ in cm⁻¹.

A researcher prepares [Fe(phen)₃]²⁺ (phen = 1,10‑phenanthroline) and finds it is low‑spin with μ = 0 BM. (a) Explain why phenanthroline causes low‑spin configuration. (b) Predict the geometry and hybridisation. (c) Suggest a ligand substitution that would convert it to high‑spin and justify.

Calculate the turnover frequency (TOF) of Wilkinson’s catalyst, RhCl(PPh₃)₃, if 0.002 mol of catalyst hydrogenates 0.50 mol of H₂ in 10.0 minutes.

An ISC 2023 question asked: “Write the structure of the major product when chlorobenzene is treated with NaNH₂ in liquid NH₃.” Provide the answer and mechanism name.

(a) Compare the rate of SN1 reaction of 2‑bromo‑2‑methylbutane vs 1‑bromo‑2‑methylbutane in aqueous ethanol. (b) Predict the effect of adding a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone) on each rate. (c) Explain using carbocation stability. (4 marks)

(a) Write the balanced equation for the Wurtz reaction of 1‑bromopropane. (b) Name the product. (c) State one limitation of the Wurtz reaction. (d) Suggest an alternative method to prepare the same alkane. (4 marks)
