Evaluate the effectiveness of India’s National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) in advancing sustainable development. Structure your answer in three parts: (a) mitigation, (b) adaptation, (c) equity. (6 marks)
Explain the three pillars of sustainable development and give one Indian example for each. (6 marks)
CISCE past‑paper pattern: “Explain, with two Indian examples, how development policies can generate unintended social consequences that necessitate further policy intervention.” (10 marks)

(a) Define “environmental justice” in one sentence. (b) Give one Indian example where environmental injustice is evident. (c) Explain why addressing environmental justice is essential for sustainable development. (2+2+2 marks)

Apply the “tragedy of the commons” framework to the over‑extraction of groundwater in Punjab’s rice‑wheat belt. Identify the actors, the common‑pool resource, and two institutional solutions. (3+2+3 marks)

Critique the claim: “India’s National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) adequately addresses ecological issues arising from industrialization.” Structure your critique in three points: (i) mitigation focus, (ii) adaptation gaps, (iii) equity concerns. (3+3+3 marks)

Compare the ecological impacts of “green revolution” agriculture in Punjab with “contract farming” for export crops in Maharashtra. Use a table with three criteria: (a) soil health, (b) water use, (c) biodiversity. (3+3+3 marks)
Past‑paper style: “Discuss how ecological issues arising from globalization have influenced social movements in India. Illustrate with two movements.” (12 marks)
**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** “Theoretical frameworks like Resource Mobilisation Theory explain all aspects of social movements.” Critique this claim in 150 words, referencing Indian examples.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain the term ‘social movement’ and distinguish it from a ‘pressure group’. (6 marks)” Provide a model answer structured for the ISC marking scheme.
**APPLICATION:** “Design a brief research plan to test whether relative deprivation or political opportunity better explains the 2011 Anna Hazare anti‑corruption movement.”

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Answer the following in about 150 words: ‘Examine the view that social movements are caused by a combination of structural strain, cultural framing, and resource mobilisation. Illustrate with reference to any two Indian movements.’”

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** Assess the extent to which digital media has transformed the *repertoire of contention* of Indian social movements since 2010. Structure your answer in three parts: (a) new tactics, (b) amplified reach, (c) new vulnerabilities.
**COMPARISON:** Compare the role of *frame resonance* in the Chipko Movement (1970s) and the Pink Chaddi Campaign (2009) in building cross‑class alliances.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain how social movements contribute to sustainable development in India. Give two examples.” (4 marks)

Comparison: Build a three-row comparison of the cell wall and the cell membrane covering: (1) living or non-living, (2) what it allows to pass, (3) its main job. Then add one line: which single word pair (armour/gate or gate/armour) correctly summarises wall-and-membrane, and why.

Create: Design a two-column poster titled "Same house, different walls" that teaches a Class 5 child the difference between plant and animal cells. Write the poster text: at least four similarity lines and three difference lines, each in child-friendly words.
Create: Design the marking scheme (rubric) your teacher should use for the model project: five assessment points with marks totalling 10, and one line explaining why each point is included.

Evaluation/Critique: A parent volunteer suggests: "Models are a waste of two periods — the children already have the textbook diagram; drawing it twice teaches the same thing." Critique this claim: state what a 3-D model builds that a repeated drawing cannot, and concede the one respect in which the parent is right.

Create: Your school is placing a plaque under its microscope display: "THE INSTRUMENT THAT GAVE BIOLOGY ITS EYES". Compose the two-line subtext for the plaque — written for Class 6 visitors — that captures what the naked eye could not do and what the microscope revealed.

Create: Design a "first-slide guide card" — five numbered instructions a Class 5 student should follow to OBSERVE (not prepare) a permanent onion-peel slide properly — and one warning line about the commonest observer error.

Create: Design a three-line "wanted poster" series for the classroom wall — one poster per blood component — each with the component's NAME, its physical DESCRIPTION as seen under the microscope, and its JOB line, written so a Class 4 student could match each poster to the right worker instantly.

Create: Your school's lab needs a one-page "Microscope Rules" card for Class 5's first visit. Write six rules — two about carrying, two about lenses, two about focusing — each rule in under ten words, each with a three-word reason in brackets.

Application: Your principal offers the Chapter 01 classroom one permanent display, and students will vote between "The Cell Wall of Fame" (a chart of one giant plant cell) and "The Two Cells Side by Side" (one poster with BOTH cells half-size each). As the biology monitor, analyse which display better serves a YEAR of daily pass-by exposure: use the persistence property and the comparison principle of the chapter, decide, and state the one design feature (size, position, or annotation) you would insist on for the winner.

Create: Your teacher asks you to plan a five-minute "cell cinema" lesson for Class 6 using this chapter's structures. Design the running order: choose THREE clips, set each clip's length, write the one-line purpose of each, and state the one rule you would enforce so the video supports — not replaces — the hands-on aids.

Evaluation: Two Class 6 videos of the cell are offered. Video P: a real microscope film of live onion cells with visible cytoplasmic streaming — slightly blurry, no labels. Video Q: a bright animation of a plant cell with smiling organelles, accurate shapes, permanent captions — but it shows a "stomach vacuole digesting food" in a plant cell and draws the animal cell with a cell wall. Judge which video belongs in the lesson and justify with three criteria.

Comparison: Compare the video (previous node) and the E.M. photograph as the two "extreme" aids of this chapter — one shows life in motion at visible scale, the other shows death-still detail at invisible scale. Fill this comparison: which aid shows movement, which shows finer structure, which shows the living state, which a Class 6 student could operate personally — and what single purpose do both serve together?

Reasoning: A runner finishes a 100-metre race breathing hard and sweating. Using only knowledge revisited in this node, explain BOTH observations as the body meeting its needs — and state what each observation hints at about systems inside the body.

Create: Build a two-column table titled "Known / Askable" — list four body facts a Class 6 student certainly KNOWS, and beside each, the question this chapter will answer about it. Then state which single known-fact opens the widest door into the chapter, with your reason.

HOTS: Two Class 6 sections revise differently before the same chapter. Section A re-reads its junior-class notes silently for ten minutes. Section B spends the ten minutes answering rapid recall questions aloud, sorting foods into groups, and writing one "I want to know" question each. Predict which section will learn the digestive chapter better, justify with what revisiting is FOR, and note one situation where Section A's method would win.

Evaluation: Two Class 6 textbooks present the digestive system. Book A starts with the glands (liver, pancreas, salivary glands) in detail, then introduces the canal. Book B starts with the canal stations in order, then introduces the glands as helpers. Judge which order teaches better, with two reasons from this node's assembly-line principle, and name one situation where Book A's order would actually be better.
If pancreatic lipase acts on fat at a rate of 0.8 g min⁻¹, how many grams of fat are digested in 12 minutes? (Use the formula Amount = rate × time.)

A student measures that 5 g of starch yields 4.2 g of maltose after salivary amylase action. Calculate the percentage conversion of starch to maltose. (Percentage = (mass of product ÷ mass of substrate) × 100.)

Create: Design a "Respiratory Relay" floor activity for a class of 44 — the air is a runner (one volunteer), and each of the main parts is a station manned by students who must STATE their function while performing one physical action on the runner. Write the seven stations (nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchus, bronchiole-branch, air sac), each with its action and its stated line, plus the return-leg rule that teaches two-way traffic.

Application: Your school is planning a dust-pollution awareness march. Write four slogan-ready lines, each carrying one true respiratory defence fact (nose filtering, mucus-cilia escalator, epiglottis/air-road guarding is irrelevant to pollution — so choose defence facts, not food facts), and design one 30-second demonstration your team can perform showing why a wet cloth over the nose helps on a dusty day.

If the length of the pharynx in an adult is about 12 cm and air moves through it at 0.5 m/s during quiet breathing, calculate the time taken for air to travel the length of the pharynx. (Given: 1 m = 100 cm)
Design a simple calculation to find the volume of a cylindrical model of the pharynx if its length is 12 cm and average diameter is 3 cm. Use π ≈ 3.14. Show the steps.

Why is the voice of a Class 6 girl usually shriller (higher-pitched) than the voice of her father? Give the reason in terms of the vocal cords, and name the visible feature on a man's neck that marks this difference.
Name the organ: "A tube about 10–12 cm long, held open by C-shaped cartilage rings, which runs from the larynx into the chest and divides into two bronchi." State its one cargo.
If the trachea (diameter 2 cm) splits into two primary bronchi each of diameter 1.5 cm, calculate the percentage increase in total cross‑sectional area at this first branching.

A Class 6 student counts 16 breaths per minute sitting at her desk. After one minute of skipping, her friend counts 26 breaths per minute. Explain the rise using what the exercising muscles need, and predict what happens after she rests five minutes.

A student's table shows: Grandmother — 3 meals, 8 glasses of water, vegetables daily, no digestive complaints. Friend — skips breakfast, 3 glasses of water, weekly vegetables, frequent acidity. Vendor uncle — irregular meals, 5 glasses of water, vegetables most days, occasional gas. Write two habit–health links visible in the data and state the one comparison this small sample cannot support.

Application: Your friend returns from her interviews having forgotten to note the water intake of one interviewee. She suggests writing "about 6 glasses" because "that is normal". What is wrong with this, and what should she do instead?

Past-paper pattern: Your school asks for a one-page project report on "Food Habits of Three People". (a) State, in order, the four sections your report must contain. (b) Write two complete sentences that could open your conclusion, using the sample data: grandmother (regular meals, 8 glasses water, no complaints), friend (skips breakfast, 3 glasses, frequent acidity), vendor (irregular meals, 5 glasses, occasional gas). (c) State one limitation you must mention for honesty.
What is the primary purpose of asking Class 6 students to draw the digestive system after they have built a working model?
Compare the use of children’s drawings versus multiple‑choice questions for assessing organ‑system knowledge in Class 6. Which provides richer diagnostic information and why?
A past CISCE Class 6 Biology paper asked: “Draw a labelled diagram of the human respiratory system. Mention the function of each part.” Outline the key elements a full‑mark answer must include.

Apply: Write the six-question instrument for a 10-minute interview with the school nurse about staying healthy in the monsoon: label each question closed or open, order them from easiest to most personal, and state why the instrument works for later comparison with two more interviewees.

Create: Design the one-page "Interviewer's Kit" card a Class 6 student can carry to the field. Write its five sections with their exact contents — and the one emergency instruction for the moment the interviewee says "I don't want to answer that."

Evaluation: A company offers schools a "Survey App": students tap answers on a tablet after the interviewee taps THEIR answers on the screen — no paper, no writing, instant charts. Evaluate it for the Class 6 field visit: two genuine advantages, two things it would quietly remove from the students' learning (name the skills), and the verdict with the reason.

Apply: You hold the raw materials — a question sheet, three field tables (one with two "declined" cells), the model photograph, the drawings, and a note reading "monitor: habit self-made, since class 4". State which of the six sections each material belongs to, in which form (original or recopied, and why), and where the "declined" cells go.

Application: The school archive wants your report to be usable by next year's Class 6 without a guide. Add the "re-use apparatus": state the four additions to the submitted report — each with the exact next-year use it enables — and the one line you would add at the very end of the report addressed to next year's readers.

In the ICSE Class 6 exam, a question asks: “Draw a labelled diagram of the human digestive system and indicate where protein digestion begins.” Explain how a model and a chart would each help answer this.

Application: Your school's annual health record shows, for your class of 40: 6 children anaemic, 4 with frequent colds, 2 with dust allergy, 1 diabetic (childhood), 1 recovered from typhoid in June. The school nurse asks you to draft the class health plan with one line per child-group: family of disease, the school's correct action, and what the class should NOT do for each group.
A culture of *Vibrio cholerae* starts with 200 cells and doubles every 30 minutes. How many cells will be present after 2 hours?

Design a simple experiment to show bacterial growth on agar plates. If you inoculate a plate with 10 cells of a bacterium that doubles every 20 minutes, how many colonies would you expect after 24 hours assuming each cell forms one colony?
If a village reports 120 malaria cases in a month and the population at risk is 3,000, calculate the monthly incidence rate per 1,000 population.

**Application:** A district health officer plans to distribute long‑lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) to reduce malaria. If each net protects 2.5 persons on average and the target population is 50,000, how many nets are needed? Show calculation.
If a village has 500 children and 12 % are infected with roundworm, how many children are infected? Show calculation.

Apply: In one monsoon week, four households of one ward take these risks: (1) family A fills pots from the flooded street where drain and rain mix; (2) family B boils water but stores it in a wide open pot with a common mug dipped by all; (3) family C's hand-pump sits beside a soak-pit that overflows in the rain; (4) family D drinks boiled water but washes salad and chutney ingredients in tap-water of doubtful source. For each, state the unguarded link of the faecal-oral chain and the one correction.

Application: A district school (500 students, one borewell, one overhead tank, 12 classrooms, two water coolers, one mid-day meal kitchen) asks you, as health captain, for its monsoon water-safety plan: one line each for (1) the source, (2) the tank, (3) the coolers, (4) the kitchen, (5) the classroom habit, and (6) the sick-student rule.

Evaluate: After a wedding, 80 of 400 guests fall ill overnight with vomiting and cramps. The cook says, "I cooked everything fully — my food cannot be at fault." The caterer says, "Then it must be the water." The butler says, "It must be the cold salad." Evaluate all three claims and design the two-question investigation that finds the true door.

Apply: At one monsoon wedding: (1) the halwai with a bandaged finger finishes the kheer by hand; (2) the paneer tray sits uncovered through the evening breeze; (3) the gol-gappa water is mixed from a hand-pump can; (4) the leftover biryani is cooled in a deep vessel and served at breakfast. For each, name the open door, the germ most likely riding it, and the one correction.

HOTS: At a school fate, two stalls sell identical sandwiches. Stall 1 makes 100 sandwiches at dawn and stacks them under a cloth; Stall 2 makes them on demand in batches of six, each grilled hot on order, served on tongs-paper. By evening, Stall 1 has sold out; Stall 2 has 20 unsold sandwiches and a queue complaining of the wait. A student concludes: "Stall 1's system is obviously better — zero waste, no waiting." Test the conclusion with the route's economics: what the stack-and-cloth system costs invisibly, what the batch system's "waste" actually is, and the one number that would settle which stall fed germs.

Application: You are made "Feast Captain" for the school's annual day lunch for 600. Write the one-line rule for each of the seven checkpoints: (1) menu choice, (2) the cooking shift, (3) water and ice, (4) serving line, (5) the waiting window, (6) leftovers, (7) the sick-handler rule.

Apply: Match each scene to its disease-risk, its vector and the one immediate action: (1) a labourer with fever that returns every evening with shivering, after a month at a canal-side site; (2) a schoolgirl with sudden high fever, pain behind the eyes and aching joints, in a colony with a dry-week campaign underway; (3) a night watchman with recurring evening fevers who refuses to sleep under the society's nets; (4) a toddler with fever and swollen legs, in a lane where the drain is clogged for months.

HOTS: A housing society boasts: "We have no mosquitoes — we have an electric zapper lamp, ultrasonic repeller plugs and coil smoke every evening; our outbreak proves nothing about us." After 14 dengue cases, test the boast: classify each gadget by what it claims to kill or repel, why none touches the life-cycle, and the one reformulation of the boast that would be true.

Apply: One monsoon week, one household must run the full programme. Match each event to its shield in action: (1) the daughter's school reports three measles cases in her class; (2) the father's typhoid is confirmed and his medicine begins; (3) the municipal tank supply turns cloudy after pipe repair work; (4) the balcony cooler tray holds water from last week's rain; (5) the baby's DPT booster is due at the clinic; (6) grandfather, recovering, shares the family plate.

Application: A new residential school (300 boarders, own borewell, own kitchen, one medical room) asks you for its one-page Prevention Constitution — five articles, one per support, each with two enforceable clauses: articles for (1) water, (2) food, (3) air-and-bite, (4) sick-students and treatment, (5) armour-and-records.

Apply: Match each case to its branch of the non-communicable family, its cause and one next step: (1) a Class 4 boy who cannot see the blackboard at dusk but sees well in daylight; (2) a woman, pale and breathless after one flight of stairs, whose diet is mostly tea and rice; (3) a man of 42, thirsty all day, urinating often, wounds healing slowly; (4) a child who sneezes and wheezes every time the storeroom is opened; (5) a toddler with bowed legs who has never walked, raised in a dark one-room home.

HOTS: A town's blood-donation camp finds 30 per cent of donors anaemic; a newspaper headlines "Anaemia outbreak in the town — is it contagious?" Write the correction the health office must publish: what the 30 per cent actually measures, the two tests that settle contagious-versus-shared, and the headline the office would prefer.

Application: A Class 6 section drafts its "Over-Reaction Corner" plan for the dusty season: (1) the storeroom opposite two students' desks; (2) the class's three sneezers seated scattered; (3) the ceiling fan over a week of chalk-dust; (4) one asthmatic student's inhaler kept in the principal's office "for safety"; (5) a classmate's claim that the sneezers "are spreading their allergy." Give the one-line correction for each, and the two-line class notice that ends the season.

Apply: Match each prevention to its branch and state one way it could fail if done carelessly: (1) iodised salt kept in an open dish near the stove; (2) a daily evening walk with the family; (3) an asthmatic child's inhaler locked in the school office; (4) fruit juice in sealed sweetened packets as the "vitamin C source"; (5) the family's yearly weight-and-blood-pressure check.

Create: Design the "Default Week" planner — a one-page tool a Class 6 student runs for their own household: state the seven daily rows (one per prevention rule in action), the tick-rule that keeps ticks honest, the two "storm days" the planner must survive (festival week, exam week), and the family-meeting question that closes the week.

Application: A district school-sports meet is coming, and the Class 6 coach asks you for the "Train-and-Stay-Well" card — one line each for: (1) the week's plate during training; (2) the water habit at practice; (3) the sleep line during the season; (4) the dust-and-pollen morning for the team's two wheezy runners; (5) the snack table at the meet itself.

Apply: Match each practice to the carrier or route it blocks, and state the disease risk it removes: (1) food always kept covered; (2) weekly scrubbing of the cooler tray; (3) mesh screens on windows; (4) covered, never-overflowing bin; (5) drinking water stored in a clean, lidded pot and drawn with a dedicated utensil; (6) daily flushing and disinfecting of the toilet.

HOTS: A municipal billboard reads: "CLEANLINESS WEEK — Prize for the Tidiest Lane! Judged on appearance, Sunday 10 a.m." A health teacher rewrites the notice. Test the prize: what the appearance-judging actually measures, the three ways a lane can WIN while still breeding disease, and the rewritten notice with its new judging rule.

Application: Your school is hosting 400 visitors for its annual day. The Class 6 brigade is asked for the "Visitor-Day Sanitation Card" — one line each for: (1) the extra bins plan; (2) the water-point plan; (3) the tiffin-shed protocol for the day; (4) the toilet protocol; (5) the next-morning reset that makes the day a one-day event, not a week-long outbreak.

A family produces 2 kg of wet waste daily. If composting reduces the mass by 60 %, how much compost is produced in a week? (Use the formula Compost mass = Initial wet waste mass × Decomposition efficiency.)
A school collects 150 kg of dry recyclable waste per month. If 30 % is paper, 20 % plastic, and the rest metal, calculate the mass of metal waste.
Design a simple waste segregation chart for a classroom that a Class 6 student can follow.

A municipality proposes to replace all community compost pits with a single large mechanised composting plant. Critically assess one advantage and one disadvantage of this centralised approach for a Class 6 student’s neighbourhood.
Explain why washing hands with soap for at least 20 seconds is more effective than rinsing with water alone.
Design a daily hygiene checklist for a Class 6 student living in a tropical Indian city.
Application: Design a one‑week “Hygiene Hero” challenge for a Class 6 class, specifying daily tasks, a tracking method, and a reward that reinforces intrinsic motivation.
CISCE past‑paper pattern: “Explain how regular personal hygiene and proper waste disposal together reduce the incidence of diarrhoeal diseases in a community.” (3 marks)
Design a three‑step daily routine for a Class 6 student that addresses air, water, and insect transmission routes.
**Application:** Design a one‑page “Health Passport” for a Class 6 student that tracks daily hygiene actions for a week. List the columns you would include.
**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “Explain how safe disposal of garbage helps in the prevention of communicable diseases.” (3 marks)

Apply: Choose and justify the correct chart-type for each job, and state its one making-warning: (1) showing how typhoid travels from a carrier's hands to a family's lunch; (2) comparing the two disease families for the corridor wall; (3) keeping the class's daily hygiene duties running all month; (4) showing the soap-survey result — 30 of 40 children wash with soap.

Application: The Class 6 quiz team must prepare a wall of FIVE charts that together revise the whole Health-and-Hygiene chapter for the school's open day, when parents will walk the corridor. Write the "Five-Chart Spine Wall" plan — one line each for: (1) chart one and its type; (2) chart two; (3) chart three; (4) chart four; (5) chart five and the walking order that makes the five argue as one.

Apply: For each element of the parents'-meet talk, state which channel it belongs to — slide, speech, or handout — and why: (1) the photograph of the lane's flooded cooler tray; (2) the explanation that standing water breeds mosquito larvae in about a week; (3) the six handwash appointments list; (4) the story of the glitter handshake done with a volunteer; (5) the request to turn over one bucket tonight.

Create: Design the "Presenter's Card" — the single cue-card a Class 6 presenter holds during a health talk: state the five zones of the card, the one line written in red, the three questions the card's margin asks during questions-time, and the rule about what must NOT be written on it.

Application: The class's health talk must be delivered TWICE in one day — once to Class 4 children (age 9) in the morning, once to the parents' association in the evening. The spine is the same. Write the "Two-Audience Card" — one line each for: (1) what stays identical; (2) the hook swap for the two rooms; (3) the language swap; (4) the ask swap; (5) the one thing that must never be swapped.

Apply: For each organism, name its habitat group, one biotic and one abiotic component it depends on there, and one body feature that answers an abiotic condition: (1) the pond fish; (2) the mountain goat; (3) the water hyacinth or lotus of a pond; (4) the camel; (5) the pigeon.

Application: The class plans a one-hour 'Habitat Safari' within the school's own compound. Write the "Mini-Safari Card" — one line each for: (1) the three habitats the compound itself contains; (2) the observation question asked at each; (3) the two tools carried; (4) the recording rule that keeps the safari science and not a stroll; (5) the return-and-enter step that feeds the Address Book.

Apply: Match each feature to the bill it pays at the pond surface, naming the organism it belongs to: (1) the swollen, spongy leaf-stalk; (2) the oiled feather-coat; (3) the flat, sieving bill; (4) the long, spread legs on the surface film; (5) the hanging feathery root tassel; (6) the waxy upper leaf face with stomata on top.

Create: Design the "Surface Line Survey" — a Class 6 one-period study of the school pond's floating community: state the four stations of the survey, the tool and record-line at each, the two safety-and-honesty rules, and the closing calculation the class performs about their own pond.

Application: The class must keep a water hyacinth healthy through the two-month school holiday with no visitors. Write the "Holiday Bucket Protocol" — one line each for: (1) the pre-holiday set-up; (2) the water plan; (3) the light plan; (4) the population plan; (5) the reopening inspection and what its findings will teach.

Reasoning: A flood muddies the school pond for two weeks — the water turns opaque brown and light barely reaches a hand's depth below. Using this node's adaptations, predict what happens to (1) the submerged plants, (2) the lotus at the edge, and (3) the fish, and give the reason for each prediction.

Apply: Match each feature to the bill it pays and the organism it belongs to: (1) the ribbon-like flexible leaf; (2) the hollow, air-filled stalk; (3) the feathery red gills; (4) the streamlined spindle body; (5) the broad waxy leaf floating flat; (6) the small anchoring roots.

Create: Design the "Under-Water Line Survey" — the companion of the surface survey from the last node — a Class 6 one-period study of the pond's submerged and fixed residents: the four stations, the tool and record-line at each, the two safety rules, and the closing comparison the class writes between its two survey lines.

Application: The class must design a "Monsoon Watch" for the pond's under-water lines — a three-day observation protocol for the first flood days: one line each for (1) what to measure about the water, (2) which resident is watched first and why, (3) what the fish's behaviour will tell, (4) the single comparison entry against the dry-day survey, and (5) the safety change from the fair-weather rule.

Apply: Match each situation to the specimen form it needs (fresh / preserved / herbarium), with the one-line reason: (1) tomorrow's lesson on how a vallisneria leaf bends; (2) a monsoon-term study of a fish's gill combs, to be repeated next year; (3) a wall display comparing leaf designs from pond, desert and mountain; (4) recording which plants flower around the school lake in July without picking any; (5) measuring the exact root length of a week-old seedling.

Application: The class must plan a single herbarium submission for an inter-school exhibit: "One habitat, one story, one sheet" — using the pond. Write the plan, one line each: (1) which plant is collected and the quota logic; (2) the collection-day steps in order; (3) the week of processing; (4) the sheet's presentation at the exhibit (what is displayed beside the sheet); (5) the one-line story the label's back carries.

Evaluation: Two Class 6 sections keep specimen cupboards. Section A's cupboard is magnificent — sixty jars and sheets, glossy, but its register has many blank habitat columns and its fresh lots are never closed out. Section B's cupboard holds eighteen items, every one fully labelled, every register row complete, audit pages filled each term. The science fair asks each section to send ONE exhibit 'that shows what a specimen collection is for'. Evaluate: which section's cupboard better serves the chapter's purpose, the two registers' difference in one sentence each, and the exhibit each section should send.

Apply: Match each feature to the desert bill it pays and its owner: (1) the fleshy green stem; (2) the long double eyelashes; (3) the burrow under the sand; (4) the broad padded foot; (5) the dry scaled skin; (6) the spine where a leaf should be.

Create: Design the "Desert Bank Audit" — a Class 6 one-period activity that prices the class's own day against the desert's two bills: the three ledgers the class fills about itself, the two design changes the audit inspires (a school adaptation), and the closing comparison sentence linking the audit to the chapter.

Application: The class is gifted a live cactus for the classroom. Design the "Desert Tenant Protocol" — the care sheet that keeps it healthy for years: one line each for (1) the placement; (2) the watering calendar; (3) the soil; (4) the two dangers of a monsoon-term classroom; (5) the quarterly health check with its three signs.

**HOTS:** A mountain plant species is found at 2,500 m and 4,000 m. At the higher site, individuals have 30 % smaller leaves and 20 % thicker cuticles. Propose a hypothesis for this phenotypic plasticity and design a simple experiment to test it.
Given a bird with a wing span of 30 cm and a wing area of 150 cm², calculate its aspect ratio (wing span² ÷ wing area). Show your steps.
Apply the concept of wing loading to predict which of two birds — a swift (mass 40 g, wing area 180 cm²) and a pigeon (mass 300 g, wing area 250 cm²) — is more maneuverable in tight spaces.
What is the primary purpose of an observation sheet during a Class 6 field visit on adaptations?
Compare the data‑collection approach of a field visit (direct observation) with that of studying preserved specimens (node 004). Identify two advantages and two limitations of each method.

Apply: Match each PPT fault to the rule it breaks and the one-line correction: (1) slide 7 carries four organisms with a paragraph on each; (2) the title slide names the topic but no group members or date; (3) a slide's photograph has no caption; (4) the deck runs camel, cactus, duckweed, fish, with no claims between; (5) the final slide says 'Thank You' over a sunset clip-art.

Apply: Match each clip usage to the rule it invokes and the one-line reason: (1) an animated gill-diagram cited as proof that "fish breathe water in this rhythm"; (2) a time-lapse of a wilting lotus leaf presented as "what one hot afternoon does"; (3) a borrowed clip played without naming its source; (4) the same pond clip watched a third time with a third question; (5) the heron's strike slowed to a tenth of speed for the strike-count.

Application: The class must teach the nursery section (age 5) something true about the pond using video, in ten minutes. Design the "Small Eyes Session": the one clip chosen and why, the two protocol steps kept and the three steps adapted for age, the one hands-on anchor beside the screen, and the one sentence the five-year-olds must leave able to say.

Apply: Match each picture-use to the picture-kind it needs (photograph / diagram / either with caption) and the one-line reason: (1) proving the school pond had a kingfisher on 14 July; (2) teaching where the lotus leaf's stomata sit; (3) the wall display of the four habitat addresses; (4) recording that the class's seedling grew a curved root this week; (5) showing how the three layers of a leaf are arranged.

Application: The class must build the picture bank's newest section: "OUR TISSUES" — a preview wall for next chapter's work, using what the class can make without a microscope: one line each for (1) the three pictures the class can photograph itself; (2) the two diagrams the class will draw and from what observation; (3) the one borrowed window it may bring and its licence; (4) the claim-card grammar the section adopts; (5) the question the section ends on, to be answered next chapter.
A Class 6 student writes: “Tissue is a group of different cells working together.” Identify the error and explain why the correct definition requires “similar cells”.

Apply: Sort each described tissue to its branch and name the question-answer that placed it: (1) cells at the growing tip of a balsam shoot, dividing daily; (2) soft thin-walled cells filling a potato, storing starch; (3) long thick-walled dead cells forming the gritty threads of a mango; (4) a stem pipeline of several differently-shaped cells carrying water upward; (5) living cells with thickened corners in a young bean stem, letting it bend.

Application: The class microscope club receives three prepared slides labelled only 1, 2, 3 — no names. Slide 1: a solid mass of small, thin-walled, box-like cells, several rows deep. Slide 2: one flat sheet of transparent, brick-like cells, a single layer thick. Slide 3: long cells with extremely thick walls and almost no inside space left, scattered strands among softer cells. For each slide, decide the branch of the tree the tissue sits on, name the tissue, and state the visible clue that settled it.

Evaluation: Two charts hang in different classrooms. Chart 1 sorts plant tissues by JOB: "making food / holding the plant / carrying things / storing / covering". Chart 2 is the chapter's tree: meristematic vs permanent, then simple vs complex. Judge which chart sorts better for a biology student, name the test you applied, and give one tissue that chart 1 misplaces or double-lists — with the reason.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Choose the correct option: The tissue responsible for growth in length at a root tip is (i) parenchyma (ii) meristematic (iii) xylem (iv) sclerenchyma. (b) Match the columns — Column I: parenchyma; collenchyma; sclerenchyma; xylem; phloem. Column II: (1) water conduction upward; (2) food conduction; (3) flexible corner-thickened support; (4) storage and packing; (5) rigid dead strength. (c) State one way in which simple permanent tissues as a group differ from complex permanent tissues as a group, with one example from each group. (d) Why does the classification tree never ask "one kind or several?" about meristematic tissue?

Apply: A micrograph of a growing shoot tip is described as follows: at the dome's surface, cells are tiny, square, gapless, nuclei enormous; three rows deeper, cells are larger with small bubbles appearing; at the edge of the view, cells are round, large, each with one clear centre and a rim of cytoplasm. (1) Name what the three regions show. (2) State the two structural changes that mark the journey between them. (3) Give the one-line reading of the whole micrograph.

Apply: For each event, name the meristem address involved and predict the plant's growth outcome: (1) a lawn-mower passes over doob grass; (2) a radish crop is harvested, roots and all; (3) a wire tied tightly around a young mango stem cuts into the bark as the stem tries to thicken; (4) a cook cuts spring onions an inch above the soil and leaves the bases in the bed.

Application: The class keeps three pots on the same sill: pot 1 grass, pot 2 a bean seedling, pot 3 an old money-plant cutting with a woody base. The class's cat nibbles pot 1 to the soil weekly, a friend's elbow snaps pot 2's tip once, and pot 3 is never touched. Predict each pot's form after a month, with the address reasoning for each.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Choose the correct option: Growth in the thickness of a tree trunk is due to (i) apical meristem (ii) intercalary meristem (iii) lateral meristem (iv) permanent tissue. (b) Match the columns — Column I: root tip; grass-leaf base; beneath the bark of an old stem; shoot tip of a branch. Column II: (1) intercalary meristem; (2) apical meristem; (3) lateral meristem; (4) apical meristem. (c) State whether True or False, correcting the false ones: (i) Meristematic tissues are found scattered at random throughout the plant. (ii) Intercalary meristem helps in the regrowth of grass after grazing. (d) A cook harvests spring onions by cutting the leaves an inch above the soil; the bed yields again in a fortnight. Name the tissue responsible and its position. (e) Why does pruning the top of a hedge make it bushier rather than shorter for long?

Apply: For each event, name the meristematic function at work (multiplication / staffing / healing — more than one may chain) and one sentence of reasoning: (1) a radish push es its swollen root deeper each week; (2) a mango seedling's first true leaf expands behind the shoot tip; (3) a lawn repairs a bald patch worn by a football goalpost; (4) a tree seals a broken branch stub with smooth wood in a few seasons.
CISCE past-paper pattern: “Name the meristem responsible for the increase in girth of a dicot stem. State its location.” Provide the answer in the format expected for a 2-mark question.

Apply: A cross-section of a young sunflower stem shows: an outer single layer of flat skin cells; beneath it, 3–4 layers of elongated cells with extra wall material piled at their corners, nuclei visible, green dots present; deeper, large loose thin-walled cells; at the centre, pipelines in a ring. (1) Name the corner-thickened layer. (2) State two visible clues from the description that identify it. (3) Predict the stem's behaviour in a gust of wind. (4) State what would change if the corner deposits were replaced by full uniform thick walls.

Apply: A described microscopic field shows, scattered in soft pulp: short cells with extremely thick dark walls, tiny pinpoint centres, no visible contents, and small unpainted dots in the thick walls; nearby runs a bundle of very long narrow taper-ended cells with the same thick walls and pinprick lumens. (1) Name the tissue and its two forms as seen. (2) State what the pinprick centres and the unpainted dots are. (3) Name the everyday fruits this field could have come from. (4) State the one feature that would have to change for the long cells to be called collenchyma.

Application: The class must verify a market claim — "our pear orchard's fruit is 100 percent grit-free by a new spray". Design the verification: the two tests to run (bite and scrape-and-stain of a thin peel section under the class microscope), the expected observation if the claim is TRUE, the expected observation if FALSE, and the one honest limitation of a spray-based claim to state on the certificate.

Apply: Assign the tissue (and form, where relevant) to each region, with the job that decided it: (1) the crisp body of a cucumber; (2) the ridge just under a young okra's skin; (3) the hard click of a pepper seed's coat; (4) the green body of a spinach leaf; (5) the strands pulled from a sugarcane stick's crush.

Application: A herbarium press holds a 30-year-old specimen: the leaf is paper-brittle and brown, but the midrib still runs the blade's length as a firm thread, and a seed glued to the sheet still clicks when tapped. State which tissue regions have survived as themselves and which have decayed, reason from each tissue's living state, and write the one-line conservation moral.

Apply: Address each market-and-garden item with its tissue and one-line job: (1) the red body of a watermelon slice; (2) the angular ridge of a cucumber vine; (3) the husk pulled off a coconut; (4) the coat of a soaked rajma bean that slips off the seed; (5) the gel squeezed from an aloe leaf; (6) the stringy strands left after crushing a sugarcane stick.

Application: A school kitchen garden reports three observations in one week: (1) the radish pulled on Monday was crisp; by Friday in the sun the same bed's radishes turned rubbery-soft; (2) the young gourd vine's new tendrils bend freely but its week-old main stem only sways; (3) the fallen mango under the tree has a bruised soft patch but a stone that no bruising touched. Explain each observation by naming the tissue behind it.

Apply: Identify the xylem showing through each observation, and the property on display: (1) the grain pattern polished on a teak tabletop; (2) the net of "veins" in a fallen banyan leaf's skeleton; (3) the strings that snap when a palak-leaf stalk is peeled; (4) the drinkable-rise proof that a white petunia flower turns coloured when its twig stands in coloured water (what will the colour have climbed in?).
If a leaf produces 12 g of sucrose per hour and 75 % is loaded into phloem, how much sucrose enters phloem in 2 hours?

Apply: Predict and justify the outcome of each variation of the experiment: (1) a twin twig stood in PLAIN water beside the experimental one; (2) a twig whose base was crushed with a hammer before placing; (3) the experimental twig left for TWO days instead of a few hours; (4) a twig with its petals carefully removed before placing.

Create: Design "THE OBSERVATION LOG" — the one-page record sheet the class fills during the experiment: its five fields, the time-interval plan for a 3–5 p.m. sitting, and the one-line conclusion sentence the log's last field must force the writer to compose.

Application: A village science fair asks for a zero-cost version of this demonstration using only local materials. Design the version: the local white-flowered twig (and the acceptable substitute if no flowers are in season), the household stain, the two recycled items of apparatus, and the fair-goer's 20-second takeaway the young demonstrator must deliver. State one safety-and-courtesy rule for cutting twigs in a village setting.

Apply: Predict and justify the outcome of each variation: (1) seedling B's roots are cut but its stump is sealed in wax before standing in water; (2) HALF of A's roots are trimmed; (3) both seedlings are moved to a dark, cool cupboard overnight after a fresh watering; (4) B is instead placed in a humid chamber (a covered jar, leaves never touching drops) with its roots cut.

HOTS: A nursery packs saplings for dispatch by the thousand. Three packing rules are proposed: (1) wrap root balls in damp moss; (2) strip ALL leaves off before packing to "reduce thirst"; (3) punch air holes and keep the boxes cool and shaded. For each rule, state the station of the water line it protects, and judge which rule is the odd one out — protecting a DIFFERENT side of the ledger than the other two — with the reason.

Application: A city balcony gardener loses three plants in one week and brings the cases to the class clinic: (1) a jade plant watered daily, soil always soaked; (2) a mint pot left during a hot weekend, soil bone-dry on return; (3) a tomato seedling repotted at noon whose fine roots fell away with the old soil. For each case, state the broken station and the one corrective habit.

Apply: For each exam question, name the chart or model that answers it fastest and the one element from it that must appear in the answer: (1) "Differentiate xylem and phloem"; (2) "Show with an experiment that roots absorb water"; (3) "Give two examples each of the three simple permanent tissues"; (4) "Why is xylem called a complex tissue?"

Application: Your exam-hall strategy is the margin-sketch. For each of these four CISCE-style questions, state the sketch you draw in the margin and the FIRST sentence of the answer that walks it: (1) "Draw a labelled chart of the classification of plant tissues"; (2) "How does the structure of xylem suit its function?"; (3) "An experiment shows a rootless seedling wilting in water — explain"; (4) "Compare the three simple permanent tissues".

Evaluation: Two members propose the club's chart-quality checklist. Farhan's checklist: (1) colourful headings; (2) all chapter facts present; (3) neat handwriting; (4) drawings everywhere. Ira's checklist: (1) one claim stated in the title; (2) every element serves the claim; (3) labels exam-sayable; (4) reproducible from memory in a minute. Evaluate both checklists: which produces displays that RAISE exam answers, what each of Farhan's four criteria actually measures, and the merged checklist's five items in priority order.

Evaluate: A borrowed internet clip teaches plant transport with these claims: (1) "food moves only downward from the leaves"; (2) it names several individual cell types of xylem and phloem as must-learn lists; (3) its xylem arrow points downward "because gravity helps". Run the accuracy checklist on all three claims: verdict on each, the chapter fact each violates, and the standing rule for out-of-syllabus detail.

CISCE past-paper pattern: "What is chemistry? State its importance with two examples from daily life." Write the short model answer, of the kind an ICSE Class 6 examiner expects, in about five sentences.

Design a two-page "Visit Diary" for the class trip: page 1 with four observation columns, page 2 with a personal conclusions box. Fill the columns with sample entries for the quality control laboratory station.

Evaluation/critique: A student pins a card that reads: "Scientist X (a name the class cannot trace in any book) discovered the cure for all fevers in 1732." The teacher moves the card to the "to check" corner. Defend or critique the teacher's action, and state the rule it enforces about the gallery's content.

The advertisement's claims about immunity building, 100% natural safety, and universal suitability without doctor supervision are scientifically misleading because herbal syrups do not replace vaccines, natural sources still obey dosage rules, and every child requires individualized medical evaluation. The working evaluates each sentence by contrasting marketing exaggeration with chemical reality regarding plant-based preparations and clinical oversight. A wrong critique outright dismissing herbal chemistry rather than addressing safety claims reveals the opposite misconception of rejecting valid plant properties.

Evaluate: "Since only about 118 elements exist, the number of different substances in the world must also be limited to about 118." Examine the hidden assumption in this claim and give a reasoned verdict using substances you know.

Answer in ICSE examination style, in six to eight lines: "What is an element? Name two metals and two non-metals, give one property of each family, state one element that is liquid at room temperature, and explain in one line why about 118 elements are enough to build millions of substances."

HOTS: Ancient Indian and Greek thinkers spoke of five elements — earth, water, air, fire and sky — while modern science says about 118. Build the reconciliation: in what sense were the ancients pointing at something real, what test their "elements" fail and why, and what the modern definition adds that makes 118 exact where the old five were loose.

Evaluation/critique: An advertisement for a health drink proclaims: "Contains 25 natural elements your body needs!" A rival label says: "Made with pure elements only." Using this node's definition, critique both labels: what the first claim might honestly mean and how it misleads, why the second label is either meaningless or dangerous, and the one sentence an honest label for a health drink could write.

Application: A packet of "electrolyte drink mix" lists in tiny print: "Contains: Na, K, Mg, Ca, Cl, C6H12O6 (glucose), flavouring." Decode the packet for a Class 6 buyer: the five single-letter symbols with element names and the family of each, what the longer string "C6H12O6" shows about buildability (letters combining with numbers to write a whole compound), and the one line telling the buyer which listed item is NOT an element and why that is no cause for alarm.

Evaluate this sentence written by a Class 6 student in his notebook: "When we heated the grey iron powder with the yellow sulphur powder, the two mixed and formed iron sulphide, which is just iron and sulphur lying together, so we could still pull the iron out with a magnet." Find every language error in the sentence, explain what each wrong word claims, and rewrite the sentence correctly in the language of chemistry.

Evaluation/critique: A student argues: "Since chemistry insists on exact words, the everyday words should be banned from the science classroom altogether — no 'salt', no 'burnt', no 'mixing'. Only sodium chloride, combined with oxygen, and so on." Evaluate the argument: what it gets right about the laboratory's needs, where it fails about learning, and state the balanced policy for a Class 6 classroom in two sentences.

Apply: Using the periodic table, answer as a table-lookup exercise: (a) the name and atomic number of the element with symbol S; (b) the symbol of the element numbered 11 and its family-neighbour directly above it in the table; (c) whether the element with symbol Cl is a metal or non-metal and which named family it belongs to; (d) the two lightest noble gases; (e) which of iron (Fe) and sulphur (S) sits in the metals region and which in the non-metals region.

Answer in ICSE examination style: "(a) What is the periodic table? (b) Name the horizontal rows and vertical columns of the table. (c) Write the symbols of the elements with atomic numbers 1, 6, 8 and 11. (d) State, with reason, whether potassium is placed closer to metals or non-metals in the table. (e) Name the family of very unreactive gases and one member of it."

Application: The city science museum installs an interactive periodic table where touching a box lights up the element's story. You are hired to write the light-up story for FOUR boxes: carbon (6), oxygen (8), sodium (11), and argon (18). Each story: two lines maximum, first line the element's table-position and family/region, second line its most vivid everyday Indian presence. Write the four stories, keeping the table-geometry (position, region, column) as the first line's spine.

Comparison: Compare the periodic table and the alphabetical element-list as two tools, on four counts: (1) what question each answers fastest, (2) what each shows about sodium-potassium kinship, (3) what each shows about metals versus non-metals as a whole, (4) which one could have predicted a missing element's properties and why. Present as a two-column comparison table, then state the one-sentence verdict on when a chemist reaches for which.

CISCE past-paper pattern: "(a) State the principle on which the modern periodic table arranges the elements. (b) Write the symbols of the elements with atomic numbers 3, 11 and 19, and name the family they form. (c) Give the name and symbol of the element whose atomic number is 6, and state its region of the table. (d) Name the family of gases in the last column and state their signature property. (e) Why is hydrogen's position called special? Answer in one sentence." Write the five-part answer exactly as demanded.

Application: The school is choosing its first model kit on a limited budget, and the supplier offers three options: Kit A — large balls (4 cm), one colour only, 60 balls and 60 sticks; Kit B — standard size, six-colour casting per the world convention, 120 balls and 100 sticks, holes drilled 1-to-4 per ball; Kit C — cheap pre-glued fixed models (water, carbon dioxide, oxygen ready-made; cannot be dismantled). Write the purchase recommendation: evaluate each kit against the three teaching needs (cast must be readable; builds must be student-made; grips must reflect fixed hands), declare the winner with the reason, and state the one upgrade that would make the losing kits serviceable.

Apply: A friend builds four assemblies and asks you to identify them. Assembly 1: one black with four whites, stool-shaped. Assembly 2: one blue with three whites, tripod. Assembly 3: one white joined to one green. Assembly 4: two whites and one red — but the whites are joined to EACH OTHER, and the red hangs off one end of the pair. For each: name the substance (or diagnose the fault), give the recipe, and — for Assembly 4 — state exactly what is wrong and rebuild it in words.

Application: The city water-board's mobile van visits your school with a demonstration: "Is this water?" They show three sealed vials. Vial 1: pure water. Vial 2: water with common salt dissolved. Vial 3: a liquid that is NOT water but is built of hydrogen and oxygen in a DIFFERENT whole-number ratio (hydrogen peroxide — two hydrogens to TWO oxygens). Using your model-knowledge, write the van-visit note: what each vial is at particle level (builds, recipes, sticks-or-no-sticks), why vial 2 is still "water-based" but is a MIXTURE not a compound, why vial 3 is the fixed-proportion law's sharpest lesson — same elements, different recipe, different substance — and the one-line poster the van should carry.

Application: The school's sports day drinks-stall offers three containers: (1) ORS-style salt-sugar solution, (2) fresh lime water with sugar, (3) packaged "pure drinking water". The stall-in-charge wants the science club's display-card for each: at particle level, what is in the container (components, sticks-or-none, recipe-or-none); which laws each container obeys; and one property-retention proof a thirsty athlete could appreciate. Write the three display-cards.

HOTS: The retention law says properties survive in mixtures. But consider the salt solution's VOLUME: 50 ml of water plus 10 grams of salt dissolved does NOT give the volume naive addition predicts — the final volume is less than water-plus-salt-piled-dry would suggest. Does this shrinkage break the retention law? Unpack the HOTS: what volume is (a bulk, crowd-level property) versus what retention protects (component properties), why inter-particle settling can reduce total volume without any component losing itself, and what this case teaches about which observations can test the retention law and which cannot.

Create: Design "The Golden Jar Fair" — a class exhibit teaching honey-as-mixture to visitors through four stations: (1) The Component Shelf (model or picture of honey's parts), (2) The Bee's Evaporation Works (the wing-fanning demo or its model), (3) The Calling-Card Table (three honeys or their picture-cards for flower-reading), (4) The Winter Puzzle (granulation-versus-spoilage). For each station write the visitor-instruction, the chapter-connection (which earlier node's idea the station cashes), and the stamp-line for the fair passport.

Application: The state forest department runs a tribal honey-collection improvement programme and asks your class for the "chemistry-corner" of its training booklet — three do-and-don't cards for collection and storage, each grounded in the chapter's laws: Card 1 on COLLECTION (why the comb's sealed cells matter — what unsealed, unripe nectar is), Card 2 on STORAGE VESSEL (why the airtight dry jar, and what monsoon air does to an open jar), Card 3 on HEAT (why gentle warming rescues grain but strong cooking ruins honey — the scorch-guard principle). Write the three cards in trainer's language with the law-citation under each.

Evaluate: "Common salt and a salt solution are practically the same thing — salt in water — so both should be classified alike." Examine the claim: classify each correctly, run the decisive rows of the table over both, name the one operation that separates the solution's components and why no such operation could ever part the compound, and state the one sentence a Class 6 student should write to settle the confusion.

Evaluate: "The iron-sulphur tube proves its union only if the flame is withdrawn while the glow continues — otherwise the demonstration proves nothing, since a flame can make anything look changed." Examine the claim: what the withdrawn-flame glow establishes (self-sustained energy release, change reaching the whole mass), what it does NOT establish by itself (identity of the product — hence the magnet and the other tests to come), and whether the carbon demonstration carries an equivalent self-evidence; finish with the one sentence that states what a Class 6 demonstration must show to witness a chemical change.

Reasoning with working: A student mixes 14 g of iron powder with 12 g of sulphur powder and heats the heap till the glow finishes the marriage. Using the 7:4 recipe, work out step by step: how many grams of iron sulphide form, which element is left over and how many grams of it remain un-married, and what the magnet shows on the cooled mass.

Apply with working: Three heaps are prepared and fully reacted — HEAP P: 21 g iron + 8 g sulphur; HEAP Q: 7 g iron + 4 g sulphur; HEAP R: 10.5 g iron + 6 g sulphur. For each, state the mass of iron sulphide formed, the mass and identity of any leftover, and the magnet's reading on the cooled product. Show the working for each.

Answer in ICSE examination style: "(a) In what ratio by mass do iron and sulphur combine to form iron sulphide? (b) A mixture contains 14 g of iron and 8 g of sulphur. State the mass of iron sulphide formed on heating, giving your reason. (c) What will you observe if a magnet is brought near (i) the fresh mixture, (ii) the product formed from the mixture in (b)? (d) Why is the magnet-test done on the mixture BEFORE heating as well as on the product after? (e) A student's product leaves grey particles that respond to a magnet. What does this indicate about the mixture's composition? Answer in one sentence each."

CISCE past-paper pattern: "(a) Why is iron powder chosen as the standard substance for demonstrating separation by a magnet? (b) A mixture of 7 g iron powder and 6 g sulphur powder is heated strongly. Calculate the mass of iron sulphide formed and name the substance left over. (c) The product in (b) is treated with a magnet — state and explain the observation. (d) Why must the mass-ratio of the reactants be 7:4 for the magnet to be silent? (e) State one similarity and one difference between the iron-sulphur heap before heating and the product after heating. Answer in one sentence each."
Critique the following claim: "Since iron sulphide is made of iron and sulphur, its density should be the average of the densities of iron (7.87 g/cm³) and sulphur (2.07 g/cm³)."

Your school's water filter dispenses into a steel tumbler placed on a wobbling stool, and 250 mL of water spills onto the floor daily. The class monitor claims: "If we freeze the 250 mL of water into ice first, no volume of water will be lost on the floor, because solids have definite volume." Critically evaluate the monitor's plan and the science in the claim.

Design a 3-step demonstration using a water bottle, a balloon and a transparent jar to prove to the class that (i) a liquid takes the container's shape, (ii) a gas fills the entire container, and (iii) a solid is needed only as the container, not as a shape-keeper for fluids. Write each step with its exact expected observation.

During Diwali cleaning, your grandmother fills three containers for storage: (1) a steel tin with besan, (2) a plastic bottle with groundnut oil, (3) an airtight jar she puffs with a little extra air before sealing (as for papad). For each, state what happens to the contents' shape and arrangement over the months it stands untouched, and justify with the classification.
A rectangular metal block measures 8 cm in length, 4 cm in breadth and 3 cm in height. Calculate its volume in cm³ and in mL.
Convert 2.5 L of milk into millilitres and cubic centimetres.
You have a 500 mL beaker and a 250 mL measuring cylinder. Which instrument gives a more accurate volume of a liquid? Why?
A past CISCE paper asks: “Define volume. State its SI unit. Convert 3.75 L into cm³.” Provide the answer as expected in the exam.
You have 150 mL of milk in a measuring cylinder. You pour it into a wide shallow dish. What is the volume of milk in the dish? Show your reasoning.
You have a balloon partially inflated at room temperature. Predict what happens to its size when you place it in a refrigerator for 10 minutes, and explain why.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Which of the following phenomena best demonstrates that gas particles are in constant random motion? (a) A balloon expands when heated. (b) A perfume scent spreads in a room. (c) Water boils at 100 °C. (d) Ice melts at 0 °C.” Choose the correct option and justify.
A 250 mL sample of milk at 20 °C is heated to 60 °C. If the coefficient of volume expansion of milk is 0.0007 °C⁻¹, calculate the increase in volume.

Apply the concept of definite volume to a real‑life situation: a milkman delivers 1 L of milk in a flexible plastic pouch. The pouch is squeezed into a smaller box for transport. What happens to the milk’s volume and why?
**HOTS:** If a balloon is taken from a warm room (30 °C) to a cold air‑conditioned room (18 °C), what will happen to its size? Explain using particle motion.

Design a two-minute classroom demonstration titled "The water's round trip" using only a glass of hot water (poured in class from a flask), a cold steel plate, a spoon and a mirror-strip — no open flame, keeping Class 6 safety. Specify each step, the action the class performs or watches, and the one takeaway sentence per step — covering three ideas: invisible particles leave hot water; a cold surface brings them back as droplets; the material is water at every address.

Four glasses of water stand on the bench, each to receive one spoon of sugar: (1) hot water, stirred; (2) hot water, left still; (3) cold water, stirred; (4) cold water with a sugar lump instead of grains, stirred. Arrange the four in order of finishing, name the lever that decides each position, and state what a fifth glass — cold, stirred, and given a fifth spoon after four — would show at its bottom.

A street-side sharbat stall mixes its concentrate each dawn: sugar into warm water, stirred, then cooled and iced through the day. By 4 pm the last glasses are poured and a sediment of sand-like grains shows in the empty vessel. The stall owner's boy says: "The sugar turned back to sand — the ice frightened it." Write the corrective note for the boy: what the dawn's warm water did, what the day's cooling did and did not do, where the evening grains came from, and the one practice that keeps the vessel sweet to the last glass.
A student reads the liquid level in a 250 mL beaker at the 180 mL graduation. The meniscus is curved upward. Should the student record 180 mL or a different value? Explain.
Evaluate the statement: “A beaker can be used to measure exactly 50.0 mL of hydrochloric acid for a titration.”
During an experiment, you need to heat 100 mL of water to boiling. Which beaker capacity would be most appropriate, and why?
A CISCE Class 6 exam question asks: “State two safety precautions to observe when heating a liquid in a beaker.” Provide the answer as per board expectations.
A student claims that a beaker can replace a measuring cylinder for all volume measurements in Class 6 experiments. Critique this claim using the concepts of accuracy and calibration.
During a lab session, you have a 100 mL beaker, a 250 mL beaker, and a 500 mL beaker. You need to heat 180 mL of a solution that tends to foam vigorously. Which beaker would you choose and why?
Compare a beaker and a test tube for the task of heating a small volume (10 mL) of a volatile liquid. Which is more appropriate and why?
Why must a person drink about 2–3 litres of water every day even in winter when there is no sweating and no thirst? Give the underlying reason and two signs the body shows when this need is not met.

A municipal tanker supplies 4,000 litres once a week to a lane of ten families. Evaluate whether this supply can meet the lane's household need, using the estimate of roughly 270 litres per family per day, and state clearly what the shortfall implies for conservation behaviour.

Estimate and compare: a family of four uses about 270 litres per day. A mid-size factory uses 500,000 litres per day. Calculate how many families' daily household demand equals the factory's single day, and state the lesson this comparison teaches for city water planning.

A village panchayat objects that a new plant "will drink the river." The plant replies: "We circulate 40 lakh litres a day but consume only 4 lakh." Evaluate the plant's defence: compute the percentage consumed, state whether the panchayat's fear is fully answered, and name the one further assurance the plant must give.

Estimate: producing 1 kg of rice takes over 1,000 litres of water through the growing season. A family of four eats about 1.5 kg of rice per day. Calculate the weekly rice-water cost of the family, express it in 250-litre tank loads, and state the conservation conclusion this calculation supports.

A district has water for either 200 hectares of flooded paddy or 800 hectares of drip-irrigated vegetables (same total water). Each hectare of paddy earns a family ₹30,000 per season; each hectare of vegetables earns ₹12,000 but supports two families' employment. Evaluate both options on earnings and employment, and state which you would recommend and on what single condition.

A village has 40 wells. After three years of poor monsoon and dozens of new motor pumps, many wells stand nearly dry in May. Explain, step by step, what happened to the water table, and predict what the same wells will show in the October after a strong monsoon — with the reason.

Two villages lie 10 km apart on the same plain. Village A keeps its fields open and porous with traditional tanks; Village B paved its fields into a new industrial estate last decade. Both receive identical rain. Compare the two villages' wells after ten years in depth of water table, colour/quality of storm flows, and drought behaviour — one sentence each.

A village draws 150 L of water per day from a nearby river for drinking and cooking. If the river’s flow at that point is 2 m³/s, what fraction of the river’s flow is used by the village each day? (Assume 1 day = 86 400 s.)

A city must choose between two water projects at equal cost: (A) restore a silted lake beside the old town (dredge, divert drains, fence catchment); (B) lay a pipeline from a river 40 km away. Compare the two on supply reliability, groundwater side-effect, and long-term maintenance, and give your recommendation with its one risk.

A city's water board must rank four actions by how much they protect the resource map: (1) fixing leaking public taps; (2) building percolation ponds on the city's last open ground; (3) tarring the remaining fields to ease traffic; (4) protecting the lake's inlet streams from encroachment. Rank them from most to least protective, with one sentence of reasoning each.

A panchayat has a fixed fund and must choose one first step for its fouled pond: (1) divert the two lane drains that run in; (2) dredge the silted bed; (3) fence the buffer and build a separate washing ghat. Sequence all three correctly and justify the order; state what happens if the order is inverted.
Calculate the day's waste of a tap dripping twice per second at about 0.25 millilitre per drop, and state, with one other habit, the two cheapest litres a household can save.

A colony of 100 families adopts three habits: bucket baths (saving 50 L per person per day, 4 persons a family), repaired leaks (saving 40 L per family per day), and rooftop pits refilling 200 L per family per monsoon-day of rain. Calculate the colony's daily fresh-water saving and its daily recharge, and state which of the two numbers the town's rivers and wells feel first.

A municipal garden is watered by hose every noon for an hour; a proposed switch is drip lines at dawn for the beds and harvested-roof water for the fountains. Compute the weekly saving: hose 12 L/min × 60 min × 7 days versus drip 300 L/day × 7 days plus roof harvest 900 L/week credited. State which change saves by *method* and which by *source*.

A student records 3 buckets for bathing, 2 buckets for washing clothes, and 1 bucket for cleaning the floor each day. If one bucket holds 15 L, what is the total daily water use for these three activities?

After a week of audit, a student finds that toilet flushing accounts for 35 % of total household water use. Evaluate whether replacing the existing single‑flush cistern (12 L per flush) with a dual‑flush system (6 L/3 L) would significantly reduce overall consumption, assuming 8 flushes per day.
Design a one‑page water‑audit table template that a Class 6 student can use at home. List the column headings and explain the purpose of each column.

Create a brief “Water‑Saving Pledge” for a family of four based on an audit showing bathing (40 %), toilet (30 %), washing clothes (15 %), others (15 %). Include three specific actions with estimated litre savings per day.
In the CISCE Class 6 examination, a question asks: “Explain how a household water audit helps in water conservation.” Write a concise answer suitable for 3 marks.
Evaluate the effectiveness of using a “bucket‑count” method versus a “tap‑flow‑rate × time” method for estimating water use in the audit. Which is more appropriate for Class 6 students and why?

A past CISCE Class 6 paper asked: “Describe the steps you would take to conduct a water audit at home and how you would use the results to reduce water consumption.” Outline a model answer covering all key steps.

A cook salted soup too heavily and proposes three fixes: (1) add more water; (2) boil the soup hard to "drive the salt out"; (3) add a raw potato to "absorb the salt." Using solution science, evaluate each fix and state which works and why.

A municipal laundry boils 200 kg of cotton uniforms weekly. Plain-water boiling leaves the collars grey with embedded grease-washed dirt; a soda solution boils them clean but costs ₹40 of soda per week. The alternative — replacing all uniforms monthly — costs ₹8,000 monthly. Weigh the soda option against the replacement option and justify the laundry's choice.

A past-paper style question: "A packet of washing soda crystals weighing 250 g is left open in air and loses 50 g in weight as its water of crystallisation escapes. (a) Calculate the mass of water lost and the mass of the remaining powder. (b) The powder is dissolved in water and the solution evaporated to dryness — what mass of solid returns, and why is it not 250 g? (c) State one household and one industrial use of this substance." Give the full answer with working.

A student weighs 100 g of fresh sodium sulphate crystals into an open dish and 100 g of fresh common salt into another. After a month in dry air, one dish reads 100 g and the other reads less. Which is which, why did one lose weight, and what would happen to the loser's weight if the dish were moved to a damp store?

Two identical dishes hold 50 g of fresh sodium sulphate crystals each: dish A goes into a closed box with a sachet of drying agent, dish B sits open on the windowsill in the same room. Predict each dish after a week and explain which observation would change if the week were the wettest week of monsoon.

A school laboratory has budget for exactly one of two purchases: 5 kg of sodium sulphate for the three-salt demonstration, or 5 kg of extra common salt for the same demonstration. The chemistry teacher argues the sulphate; the storekeeper argues "salt is salt." Weigh both arguments and justify a decision, using what each salt contributes to the demonstration.

A past-paper style question: "A jar holds 400 g of fresh sodium sulphate crystals. (a) In dry air they lose 25% of their weight. Calculate the loss and the remaining mass. (b) The remaining mass is dissolved in water and the solution evaporated to dryness — state the mass recovered and account for every gram of the original 400 g. (c) The recovered crystals are moved to a damp store — state and explain the change in their weight." Give the full answer with working.

A district agriculture office must advise 200 farmers whose stored seed-grain has dampened and moulded, and whose pond has choked with slime. The office holds 50 kg of copper sulphate. Weigh its use for the pond against its use for the seed, state why the salt suits one job and not the other, and write the warning line that must accompany the advice.

A past-paper style question: "A student heats 25 g of blue copper sulphate crystals in a dry test tube until no further change occurs, and 16 g of white powder remains. (a) Calculate the mass of water of crystallisation lost, and what fraction it was of the original. (b) A drop of water is added to the cooled powder — state the observation and the mass of blue crystals finally present if all the water is returned. (c) State the test-for-water use of the white powder and one safety rule for the whole experiment." Give the full answer with working.

A past-paper style question: "(a) State why water is called the universal solvent and why the name is not literally true. (b) A salt pan holds 25,000 kg of sea water of 3.5% salt content — calculate the harvest when all water evaporates, and the litres of water lost (1 kg = 1 L). (c) A drain leaks 3 kg of soluble waste into the ground above a well field every week; calculate the waste carried into the groundwater in a year (52 weeks), and state why household cloth filters cannot stop it. (d) Name the dissolved gas fish depend on and state one human act that keeps it available in a tank." Give the full answer with working.

A past-paper style question: "(a) Define the atmosphere and state the two properties that make air matter, with one observation proving each. (b) A room of 40 cubic metres holds air of density 1.2 kg per cubic metre — calculate the mass of air in the room, and compare it with a 36-kg student. (c) A 10-litre closed drum is filled completely with water and capped — state the volume of air inside and the volume of oxygen that was lost with it (air is one-fifth oxygen). (d) State the two components of air that vary from day to day." Give the full answer with working.
If the bottle has a capacity of 500 mL and after tilting water rises to the 200 mL mark, what volume of air escaped?

**APPLICATION:** You have a 1 L plastic bottle and a bucket of water. Describe how you would modify the activity to measure the volume of air that escapes without using a graduated scale on the bottle.
**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** A textbook diagram shows the bottle tilted at 90° (horizontal) with water filling the entire bottle. Is this diagram accurate? Explain.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “When an empty bottle is inverted in water and tilted, bubbles are seen. What do these bubbles indicate? (1 mark)”

A past-paper style question: "(a) A 2-litre jar is used in the candle-jar demonstration — calculate the oxygen spent, the nitrogen left, and the water rise. (b) State the confirmatory test performed on the jar's remaining gas and its result. (c) A chip packet of 300 mL volume is flushed with pure nitrogen before sealing — calculate how much oxygen was kept out, and state why that protects the contents. (d) Name the structures on pulse roots that add nitrogen to soil and state what they take nitrogen from." Give the full answer with working.
If a legume plant fixes 5 g of nitrogen per square metre per season, how many kilograms of nitrogen are fixed in a 2‑hectare field? (1 hectare = 10 000 m²)
Create a one‑paragraph conclusion for an experiment where you measured the mass of a stone (30 g) and the volume of water it displaced (12 mL). Use the format taught in this node.

A student's observation table for three samples (salt, sand, sugar) reads: "salt — small, tasty, lots of it; sand — yuck, gritty, weight maybe 10; sugar — sweet like the canteen's, half the jar." Rewrite the table obeying the four recording rules, inventing reasonable measurements where the student should have taken them, and state what was wrong with each original entry.

Two students measure the same stone. Student A records "mass: 52 g" in the table. Student B writes in her notebook "this stone is heavier than yesterday's — maybe around half a kilo?" — and yesterday's stone is not available. Evaluate both entries against the register, state which belongs in the observation table and why, and write the honest entry for the comparison if the class wants to compare stones across days.

A student argues: "The register wastes time — 'the milk is hot' tells everyone what they need, so why write 70 °C?" Answer the student with the purpose of the register, giving two situations where the bare feeling-word fails and the measured entry succeeds — one from daily life and one from the science room.

A past-paper style question: "(a) Rewrite as scientific entries: 'the bottle holds a bit less than half a litre'; 'the room was very warm'; 'the powder weighed nearly 40'. (b) A table row reads: Salt — 10 — dissolves; Sugar — 15 — sweet. State the three register faults and rewrite the row. (c) State two science-room rules with the reason each exists. (d) A student writes 'the liquid is safe because it looks like water.' Name the rule this breaks and the test that should have been run." Give the full answer.

State the formula for the volume of a rectangular solid, name the unit of the answer, and calculate the volume of a brick measuring 20 cm by 10 cm by 8 cm, showing every step and writing the conclusion line for the observation table.
Convert, writing the unit at every stage: (a) 250 g into kg; (b) 1.5 L into mL; (c) 2 kg into g; (d) 750 mL into L; (e) state the bridge between mL and cm³ and use it on 60 mL.
