Three students measure the same cuboid duster and report: A — "Volume: 120"; B — "Volume: 120 cm"; C — "Volume: 120 cm³, sides 6 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm." Judge each answer against the register, state what B's unit claims about the duster, and write the one entry a stranger can check.

A shop sells juice in two bottles: bottle P holds 1.5 L and costs ₹90; bottle Q holds 500 mL and costs ₹40. Using the register's conversions, calculate which bottle gives more juice per rupee, showing the unit at every stage, and write the conclusion line the comparison table would carry.

A measuring cylinder's water reads 65 mL. A stone is lowered and the reading becomes 92 mL. The stone is removed, dried, and lowered again with an air bubble unnoticed on its base; the reading becomes 94 mL. Calculate the stone's volume from the first pair, the false volume from the second pair, the bubble's billed volume, and the percentage by which the bubble overstated the stone. Then write the honest table entry.

A village handpump's outlet fills a 500 mL bottle in 10 seconds. A family needs 60 L of water daily. Calculate the pump's delivery rate in mL per second, the time to fill 60 L (in seconds and in minutes), and the number of 500 mL bottles that make the daily need — all in register, units at every stage. Then judge: if the family's audit (the chapter's opening) showed bathing takes one-third of the day's water, how many bottle-minutes does bathing alone consume?

A past-paper style question: "(a) A metal cube has sides of 5 cm — calculate its volume. The cube is lowered into a cylinder and the water rises from 200 mL to 325 mL — calculate the volume by displacement and reconcile the two results. (b) Convert 4.2 kg to grams and 850 mL to litres. (c) A brick of volume 1800 cm³ has a base of 15 cm by 10 cm — calculate its height. (d) State two precautions for the displacement method." Give the full answer with working.

A program is fed to a translator which converts and executes it line by line. While entering data the student makes a mistake in line 10; the program stops right there. Which style of translation is at work, and why did the program stop at that exact line?
Design a classroom chart with three columns — Level, Sample instruction for "add 5 and 3 and show it", Human comfort (low/medium/high). Fill it, and justify the comfort ratings.
A program contains an error on line 7 of 20. Describe exactly what happens under a compiler and under an interpreter, and state the practical benefit each behaviour gives the programmer.

Your QBASIC-style program is: line 1 CLS, line 2 LET T = 5 + 3, line 3 PRINT "Total ="; T, line 4 END. Trace what happens from typing RUN to seeing output, naming the translator's action at each step.

A student claims: "My program has 3 errors, but the interpreter showed only 1, so the interpreter hides errors." Critique the claim precisely, stating what the interpreter was actually doing at the moment it reported the single error.

A past-paper style item asks: "An interpreter is translating a 9-line program. It has just executed line 5 successfully. State exactly which lines have been translated so far and which are untouched, and what would happen if line 6 contained an error." Give the model answer.
A large insurance company must process 20 lakh policy records every night without failure. Which category serves it, and which two characteristics of computers does this scenario chiefly depend on?

Match each workplace to its most suitable computer category and name the deciding characteristic for each: (a) a weather centre issuing a cyclone alert; (b) a single-shop billing counter; (c) a hospital's 30 counters sharing patient records; (d) a national bank's head office processing crores of transactions.

An office replaces its minicomputer with a single microcomputer, expecting the same service for 30 counters "since both can store records". Predict what will go wrong within an hour of opening, and identify the misjudged factor.

Design a five-step plan (plain-words algorithm) for this problem: "A shop gives a discount of ₹20 on any bill above ₹500. Given the bill amount, find the final payable amount." Then mark which of your five steps the computer will find easiest and hardest to translate.

A program prints the average of 60 and 20 as 80 instead of 50. State the faulty operation most likely present, the error type, and the journey stage at which the mistake actually entered — explaining why the translation stage let it through.

Apply the chapter to a fresh scenario: a district plans (i) 100 school computers, (ii) one records machine for 40 counters, (iii) monsoon modelling access, (iv) the state's exam-results processing for 20 lakh students. Assign a category to each and name the chapter rule you used at every step.
Create a 6-item mixed quiz card that tests the whole chapter — at least one item per theme — and supply its answer key. Keep each item answerable in one line.

In one exam hall, 60 students write a computer exam, and the school's results software will process 2 lakh answer-sheets tonight, while the meteorological centre refines the onset date of the monsoon. Assign one computer category to each of the three tasks, and in one sentence state the theme of this chapter that all three assignments obey.

Design a checklist card titled "Safe Transfer — 6 Checks" that a Class 6 student could pin beside the computer. Each check must be one line, and together they must cover the whole journey from before-plug-in to after-unplug.

A student copies a 2 GB video to a pen drive, watches the progress bar reach half, and unplugs the drive "to save time". Predict the exact state of the pen drive's file and of the original, and state which chapter habit was skipped.

Design the naming scheme: your class will save 40 homework files across the year and must be able to fetch, in one search each, (a) all homework of Term 1, (b) all homework you yourself submitted, (c) any single week's file. Propose the file-name format, give two example names, and write the three search patterns.

A student runs these searches on the folder (sci1.pdf, sci22.pdf, maths1.pdf, sci_notes.docx, art.jpg) and records the counts: * = 5, sci?.pdf = 2, sci*.pdf = 2. One of the three counts is wrong. Identify it, correct it, and justify character by character.

A past-paper style question asks: "A folder contains 60 files. (a) Write the search pattern to list all files whose names begin with 'science' and end with '.pdf'. (b) Write the pattern to list files whose names are exactly 8 letters long ending in '.txt', if all such names start with 'story'. (c) State which wildcard you used in (b) to fix the length and why." Provide the model answer.

Design the "photo hand-off" plan: your camera's memory card has 200 JPEG photos; your teacher needs ALL of them on her computer by tomorrow, the card must return home with you tonight, and the class computer has limited free space. Write the ordered plan, naming at each step the skill from this chapter it uses, and state why JPEG's compressed size matters to this plan twice.
A camera photo weighs 4 MB before formatting and saves as a 1.5 MB JPEG. State what compression did, what "lossy" means here, and why the phone manufacturer chose this trade for photographs.

A past-paper style question asks: "Ravi's folder has 30 photographs named pic1.jpg through pic30.jpg. (a) Write the wildcard pattern to select them all. (b) His friend renamed one to pic31.docx 'so it opens in the word processor and prints inside an essay'. State what will actually happen and give the correct procedure. (c) Name the part of the file name that decided the search in (a)." Provide the model answer.

Design the record-keeping plan: your class must track library books — one row per student, columns for book title, issue date and return date, with a count of books currently out updated automatically. State the correct file format with two reasons, give the file a suitable name, write the pattern to find this file among 200 mixed files later, and name the application family that opens it.
A spreadsheet file is called a ______, its grid page is a ______, and the box at column B row 3 is addressed as ______; the box can hold text, a number, or a ______ that recalculates automatically.

A past-paper style question asks: "The school office keeps Library.xls. (a) Name the format and the application family that opens it. (b) The office wants a copy the printers can read; a clerk renames the file to Library.pdf. State what results and give the correct procedure. (c) Write the pattern that finds every spreadsheet file in a folder containing 200 mixed files, and state the assumption about names your pattern makes." Provide the model answer.

Apply: Given the search patterns below on a drive containing `essay1.docx`, `essay2.docx`, `essay_draft.docx`, `photo1.jpg`, `photo2.jpg`, `song1.mp3`, state exactly which files each pattern returns and why: (a) `essay?.docx` (b) `*.jpg` (c) `*1.*`.
CISCE exam-style: A pen drive contains 40 files with scattered names. Describe, in order, the five steps you would perform to organise it completely, naming the Topic 2 skill used at each step.

Reasoning: Your class monitor wrote the library schedule as a paragraph: "On Monday the library opens at 10 am; on Tuesday at 12 noon; on Wednesday at 9 am; on Thursday at 1 pm; on Friday at 11 am." Explain, with two distinct reasons, why a table serves the reader better here.
Evaluate: Ravi typed his marks chart using spaces to push names and marks into lines: "Aarav 92 88 79". He says, "It looks like a table, so why learn table tools?" Evaluate his claim.

Application: The sports teacher emails you a daily-practice schedule as plain sentences ("Hockey on the ground at 6 am; athletics on the track at 6 am; ..."). You must pin a printed version on the sports room wall where students glance at it while running past. Rebuild it: which chapter stage list applies, what dimensions do you choose, and what single formatting decision matters most for a running-past reader?

Evaluation: A textbook chapter presents the rivers of India as a 2-page table (river, origin, length, tributaries, cities) and the story of the Independence movement as prose. The school decides to convert BOTH into tables "for easy revision". Write the evaluation: which conversion succeeds, which fails, and why the failure is principled rather than a matter of taste.
Reasoning: A friend has typed "Science 92" into a single cell of the marks chart. Using the anatomy — cell, row, column — explain precisely what breaks and why each later reader's job gets harder.

Apply: In a table with a header row and 5 data rows and 4 columns, give the addresses of (a) the top-right cell, (b) the bottom-left cell, (c) the cell exactly in the middle of the grid, and (d) state how many cells the table holds in all.

Create: Design the anatomy of a "Class 6B Birthday Chart" — state the rows family, the columns family, the header contents, the number of cells for 35 students and 12 months, and the one rule you would set so no cell ever holds two facts.

Application: You are handed a torn printout of the library issue register; only columns 3–5 of each row survive: "…— R.K. Narayan — 12 Mar — …", "…— Panchatantra — 14 Mar — …". The register is known to have 6 columns. (a) Name which column families are lost and which survive, given the standard register layout (S.No., Student Name, Book Title, Issue Date, Due Date, Remarks). (b) Which surviving cell lets you still answer "who has Panchatantra?" — or is it unrecoverable? (c) What does this exercise teach about columns and self-contained data?

Evaluation: A design teacher claims: "For scanning, borders matter more than shading: lines guide the eye, colours merely please it." A second claims the reverse. Judge both using three reader tasks — finding today's row in a 40-row canteen chart, distinguishing header from data, reading a borderless magazine grid — and deliver a verdict that assigns each feature its true role.

Past-paper pattern: (a) State the address of the cell at the intersection of the third row and the fourth column, using the standard order. (b) A table has 1 header row and 9 data rows with 6 columns; how many cells does it hold, and which address does its bottom-right cell carry? (c) In the anatomy, what is the difference between the active cell and a selected row? (d) A classmate insists "the header row is not a real row — it is a title". Correct the error with the counting rule it breaks.

Evaluate: Vijay says, "Counting rows and columns on paper before Insert is a waste — if the table is wrong, I'll just type into more cells and the computer will add rows." Evaluate his workflow for a 13-column by 30-row marks chart where he needs one extra SUBJECT column, not row.

Apply: You must insert a table for the Class 6 library issue register: title band, header row (Accession No., Book Title, Student, Issue Date), and 25 data rows. (a) State the exact dimensions to enter in the Insert dialog and why the title band is NOT part of them. (b) List the exact keystroke sequence (keys only) from the moment the grid appears to reaching row 3, column 2.

Create: Design the creation plan (not the formatting) for a "Week A / Week B" tiffin menu wall chart: 2 weeks x 5 days each, every day showing tiffin item and fruit, with day names shown once per week. State the columns and rows you would enter, the first five keystrokes after creation, and the one planning decision that saves you from restructuring later.
CISCE exam-style: Write the steps to insert a 5-column, 7-row table in a word processor document, and state what Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and the arrow keys each do inside a table.

Application: The lab clock gives your team 12 minutes to enter 60 names into a fresh grid (6 columns x 11 rows including header). The typist's average is one cell per 8 seconds. (a) Compute whether the fill fits, showing the arithmetic. (b) The typist says, "I'll skip Tab sometimes and press Enter — it feels faster." Compute the true cost of that habit in this session and prescribe the keystroke discipline that fits the clock.

Past-paper pattern: (a) Name the two numbers required by the Insert Table dialog. (b) A 6-column, 9-row table is created; give the address of the last cell and state what happens when Tab is pressed with that cell active. (c) A student wants the insertion point in the cell one row directly above a filled cell; name the two keys that achieve this and the one key that does NOT. (d) State the one-line contract card for Enter inside a table and the mishap it prevents.

Apply: The sports chart needs three uniform changes: the header row made bold and centred; the "Points" column's numbers right-aligned; the champion house's entire row made italic. For each change, write the selection made (target + technique) and the command(s) applied, and state how many mouse/keyboard actions the selection saves compared with formatting each cell individually (header row = 5 cells, points column = 8 cells, champion row = 5 cells).

Past-paper pattern: (a) Name the selection technique for choosing three adjacent columns at once. (b) State the two different outcomes of pressing Delete versus applying Delete Columns on a selected column. (c) A register row was cleared by Delete in error; name the fastest recovery and its limitation. (d) Write the exact steps to make a 4-cell header both bold and centred in the minimum number of user actions, and count the actions.

Reasoning: A 5-column marks chart must gain a "Grade" column between "Marks" and "Remarks". State the exact aim-selection and command, then trace every column's new position and address, and state what would have happened if the operator had selected the Remarks column instead of the Marks column before commanding insert.

Evaluate: A register holds 30 students. The clerk says: "New admissions came in alphabetical order in the middle of the list — I'll insert 2 rows after row 15, so I'll select row 15 and command Insert Rows twice." Evaluate the clerk's aim and count, state the correct procedure, and name the addressing consequence for the rows that follow.

Apply: The exam timetable (header + 6 exam rows x 5 columns: Date, Day, 9 am, 11 am, Invigilator) receives three changes: a new exam inserted between the 3rd and 4th exams; the "Invigilator" column deleted (duty moved to a separate chart); and the 11 am column widened because paper names wrap. For each change, write the aim-selection, the command (or drag), and the resulting dimensions — then give the final table's full dimensions.

Create: Design the growth plan for the Class 6 monitor's "Library Borrowers" chart across a full term: it begins with header + 20 rows and will gain roughly 1 borrower a fortnight and one new column ("Fine Paid") mid-term, and its "Book Title" column will need widening by month two. State, as a procedure the monitor can follow without help: the per-growth operation with its aim, the mid-term column operation with its aim, the resize by drag, and the one re-count habit that keeps later instructions valid.

CISCE exam-style: Write the steps to insert a new row between rows 4 and 5 of an existing table, and the steps to delete the 3rd column. State what happens to the addresses of the rows below the insertion and the columns right of the deletion.

Application: The half-yearly time table (header + 8 exam rows x 4 columns) must be updated after paper shuffling: exam 3 moves to the end of the list; exam 6 is cancelled (delete its row); a new exam is announced for the gap where exam 3 used to be. The clerk says: "Three operations, any order — the grid ends the same." Verify or refute the clerk's claim by computing the final row order under the clerk's implied plan and under a planned order, and state the operation-order principle for MIXED insert-delete on ROWS.

Evaluation: A design teacher claims: "Column widths should be decided by content length — the widest entry sets the width." A second claims: "By scanning importance — the most-read column gets the width." Judge both claims on a timetable where "Wednesday" (9 letters) is the widest day but the SUBJECT columns are the most-read, the total width is fixed by the page, and printing is in portrait. Deliver a verdict with a width-allocation procedure.

Past-paper pattern: (a) State the aim-selection for inserting a row between rows 6 and 7. (b) A 9-row x 4-column table loses its 2nd column and gains two rows at position 5; give the final dimensions and the new address of the cell that was at row 8, column 4. (c) State the mouse action that widens a column WITHOUT changing the table's total width, and the action that changes it. (d) Give one-line contracts for Insert Rows and Delete Columns as aim-and-effect sentences.

Apply: Dress the class library register (columns: S.No., Name, Book, Issue Date, Return Date; 30 data rows) for maximum scan efficiency. Write the exact dressing scheme — merges, borders, shading, alignment per column — with the selection each command needs, and justify each choice with the reader question it answers.

Application: The office photocopier renders grey shading as dark blotches, and the notice-board chart (header + 25 rows) must survive photocopying. Re-plan the dressing: which signals stay on shading, which migrate to borders/weight, and write the photocopier-proof scheme with selections. State the general principle for dressing under a degraded-print constraint.

Evaluation: Two students dress the same 30-row attendance register. Aditi shades alternate rows AND every column boundary gets a thin border. Vijay uses white rows with thin horizontal rules only, no vertical inner borders, shaded header. The register is read aloud by a monitor calling names down the page while a clerk ticks columns. Judge both dressings against the actual two-reader workflow (vertical name-scan by the monitor, horizontal tick-path by the clerk), declare the better dressing, and generalise: whose reading path should dictate the borders' directions?

Past-paper pattern: (a) Name the command that fuses selected cells and the command that reverses it. (b) State the alignment rule for a column of money amounts and the reason. (c) A chart's header row is bold but unshaded and its bottom border is thin; name the two dressing upgrades that mark the legend most clearly. (d) A merged title band spans 5 columns; a 6th column is inserted at the far right. State what happens to the band and to the addresses of columns 1-5, and the safe session order that avoids the problem.
You have a 3 × 3 table. You want the numbers in the last column to align to the right while the headings stay centred. Describe the exact steps.
Create a small table (2 rows, 3 columns) that shows a “Weekly Fruit Plan” with the top row merged across all three columns for the title. Sketch the steps you would take in the word processor.

In a CISCE Class 6 practical exam, you are asked to “Format the given table so that the header row has a dark blue background, white text, and thick bottom border; all data rows have light grey shading and thin inside borders.” Outline the sequence of actions you would perform.
A student claims that merging cells is the same as deleting a column. Using a 4 × 4 table example, explain why this is incorrect.
Compare the effect of applying “Outside Borders” versus “All Borders” on a 3 × 3 table. When would you choose each?
In a word processor, you have a table with 5 rows and 4 columns. You select the second column and press Delete. What happens to the table structure?
A teacher wants to create 30 certificates with each student’s name and grade. Outline the three main steps she must perform in Mail Merge.
Apply the Mail Merge concept: You have a list of 50 parents’ email addresses and want to send each a personalized PDF report card. Outline the steps from start to finish.
Critique the statement: “Using Mail Merge for a class of 20 students is overkill; typing each certificate manually is faster.”
Compare Mail Merge with the “Find and Replace” feature for personalizing 100 letters. Which is more appropriate and why?

Apply: A shown main document reads: "Dear ______, The sports day of Sunbeam School will be held on 14 December. Your ward of ______ house must report by 8 a.m. — Signed, Sports Secretary." A shown list beside it has columns: S_No, Ward_Name, House, Report_Time. State which component each fragment is, mark every place that needs a merge field with its correct field name, and state what should be done about the S_No column.

Create: Design the complete mail-merge set-up (main document outline, data source fields, and the merge fields marked in place) for a library overdue notice to students: it must greet the student, name one overdue book, state the days overdue, and name the returning fine. Refuse one tempting field with a reason, and state the one-record-one-copy consequence for a library of 300 students of whom 45 have overdue books.

CISCE exam-style: (a) What is a merge field? (b) Distinguish between a field and a record in a data source. (c) 60 records are merged with one main document — how many copies result, and what principle fixes the number?

HOTS: "One record in, one copy out" is stated as a virtue. Reverse it into a design question: a school must send notices to guardians EXCEPT those who have already paid (40 of 240). Two designs are proposed: (A) merge the full 240-record master list and let the office discard the 40 paid copies; (B) maintain the merge list as only the 200 unpaid records. Compare both designs against the count rule, error visibility, and maintenance cost, and give the verdict a systems designer would give.

Evaluation: A teacher claims: "Building the data source is 80 per cent of a merge project's work; the merge itself is the easy part." Evaluate the claim as a planning principle: on what facts about lists, letters and runs is it grounded, when does it break down, and what should a project plan therefore spend its time on?

Past-paper style: The main document reads "Dear «Student_Name», your project «Project_Title» was judged in «Judge_Group»." The data source: Student_Name | Project_Title | Judge_Group, with 5 records. (a) State what the merged output contains in total. (b) Record 3's Judge_Group cell is empty — describe copy 3 exactly. (c) After the run, the teacher edits record 5's group and wants all copies corrected — state what must be re-run and what must not.
Apply the wizard steps to create a set of address labels for 30 families using a CSV file *Families.csv* with columns *FamilyName, AddressLine1, City, PinCode*. List the actions for steps 3 and 4.

Create a new mail‑merge scenario: a teacher wants to email individual “Project Feedback” messages to 25 students. Outline the six wizard choices you would make, specifying the output option at the final step.

Apply the wizard to produce a set of personalized certificates for 12 competition winners. The data source *Winners.xlsx* has columns *Rank, Name, Event, School*. Which document type should you choose and why?
Critique the following workflow: A user selects “Envelopes” as document type, then in Step 3 chooses “Type a new list” and manually enters 50 addresses. Identify two inefficiencies.

Evaluate: A main document for the annual report circular contains 22 merge fields, including «School_Name», «Academic_Year», «Term», «Principal_Name» and «Reporting_Date» — all identical across every guardian. Evaluate the design on three grounds: what each copy actually receives, the risk profile of slotted fixed facts, and where each of those five fields truly belongs.

Apply: A shown draft sentence reads: "Dear ______, your ward of class ______ has been selected for the ______ on ______ at ______." The data source columns are: Student_Name, Guardian_Name, Class_Section, Event_Name, Event_Date, Event_Time. Perform the slotting: state which blanks take which fields, which blank (if any) should NOT be a slot, and run the reading test with the record Diya's father | Diya | 6B | Science Exhibition | 14 March | 10 a.m.

Create: Write the complete main document (full text, slots marked) for a library overdue notice using the list built in the previous node's worked example — fields Student_Name, Class_Section, Book_Title, Days_Overdue, Fine_Amount — and annotate beside it: each slot's rule justification and the reading-test line with a sample record (Ravi | 7A | "Tales of Panchatantra" | 6 | ₹20).

Past-paper style: A main document contains: "Dear «Guardian_Name», your ward «Ward_Name» of class «Class_Section» is hereby informed that the PTM will be held on «Date» in the school premises." The data source has columns: Guardian_Name, Ward_Name, Class_Section (all complete across 250 records). (a) Identify the one slot that will fail and classify it. (b) Give the correct repair and the sentence after repair. (c) State what would have printed if the repair were not made, and how the preview would have shown it.

Apply: A merge of the 40-record invitation list runs; the count check reports 40 letters, but the count of records in the list file is 41. State the two possible explanations, the diagnostic that distinguishes them, and the action for each — then state why distributing 40 letters when 41 records exist could still be correct.

Create: Write the run-sheet (the ordered checklist a pair of students follows) for merging the 40 invitation letters in a 35-minute lab period: each step with its time budget and its abort condition (the finding that stops the run for teacher help). Include the three verification artefacts the pair must produce before printing.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Name the step that must be completed before merging and state what it checks. (b) Distinguish between merging to a new document and merging to the printer. (c) After merging 60 records, the output holds 60 copies — state what this confirms and what it does NOT, and name the check that supplies the missing assurance.

Evaluation: A clerk merges 800 notices, samples copies 1, 400 and 800 (all correct), and ships. A guardian with initial 'Z' (record 797) received a letter with a blank name. Evaluate the sampling failure precisely: what three correct samples can and cannot promise, why the failure cluster sat at the END of the list, and the sampling design that would have caught this one — and what the only complete guard remains.

Comparison: Compare merge-to-new-document and merge-to-printer as output routes across four demand scenarios — a paper jam at copy 200, the principal's audit question, a correction discovered after the run, and a repeat print next month with an updated list. State for each which route serves, which fails, and conclude with the routing rule as a function of batch size and proof status.

Past-paper style: A clerk attaches a 60-record list, previews all 60 copies cleanly, merges to a new document, and the status bar reports 60 pages. The distribution clerk then finds the list file was never saved after the last 3 students were appended — they exist in the open list (and in the merged file) but not on disk. (a) Are the 60 printed copies complete and correct? (b) What is actually at risk? (c) State the immediate remedial action and the habit that prevents this class of incident.
A student previews 15 merged letters and notices that the 7th letter has an extra blank line before the address. Evaluate whether fixing this in the preview is the best approach.
You have a main document with merge fields «Name», «City», «Pincode». The data source contains 20 records. Describe the steps to print only records 5 to 10.
A teacher merges 30 student certificates. In preview, record 17 shows the «Grade» field as “A+” but the data source has “A”. The student claims the merge changed the data. Evaluate this claim.

You need to send 50 personalized emails using mail merge. After previewing, you realize three recipients should not receive the email. Describe how to exclude them without deleting rows from the data source.

Apply: A merged batch of the 40 invitations shows these four findings. For each: give the component, the specific defect, the repair at source, and the re-verification scope. (i) Every copy prints "Sunbeam School, Rampur" correctly EXCEPT the school name, which prints as "«School_Name»" on all copies. (ii) Copy 31's greeting is blank. (iii) Copies show 39 letters; the list has 40. (iv) Copy 9's house reads "Neem" but the register says "Peepal".

CISCE exam-style: (a) A merged letter prints "Dear «Name»" literally on every copy. Name the cause and the repair. (b) Another batch prints the greeting blank for 6 of 60 recipients. Name the cause and the repair. (c) State the ONE checking stage that would have caught both before printing.

Evaluation: An office measures its merge quality by "complaints received per month" (it was 3, then 1, then 0 — declared fixed). Evaluate the metric on three grounds: what complaints measure, what they systematically miss, and the metric pair an office should dashboard instead. Conclude with what the 3→1→0 trend could mean besides improvement.

Past-paper style: (a) Distinguish, with one example each, a data error and a design error in mail merge. (b) A merged output of 120 copies shows: copies 1–118 perfect; copy 119 prints "«House»"; copy 120 has an empty name slot. Diagnose each of the two defective copies, name the component, and give the repair and re-verification scope for each. (c) State the single rule whose observance would have prevented BOTH defects.

Reasoning: A submitted merge project shows: a letter whose greeting reads "Dear «Name»" on all copies; three copies with blank house slots; and a merged file holding 38 copies for a 40-record list. For each finding, name the owning checkpoint, the exact repair, and the checkpoint's own verification that should have caught it.

Create: Write the complete production plan (checkpoints, key decisions, checks — not keystrokes) for the school's "Reading Challenge" mailings: a monthly personalised progress letter to 42 students (handed in class), ONE term-end posted circular to guardians (so envelopes), and a year-end certificate batch. The plan must state the one-time survey and list design, the monthly maintenance rhythm, and the single design decision that prevents the most future work.

Evaluation: Two offices merge the same 800-guardian notice. Office A merges straight to the printer after a three-copy check. Office B runs the full six-link chain. Office A finishes 25 minutes earlier. On three grounds — error cost, error detectability, and total time including rework — evaluate which office has the better procedure, and state what the 25 minutes actually bought.

Past-paper style: (a) Define the term "merge field" and state its role in the main document. (b) A school merges a 120-record list to produce certificates; 118 are perfect, one shows "«Name»" literally, one has an empty name line. (i) Classify both defects by component with the output signature that identifies each. (ii) Give the repair and re-verification scope for each. (iii) State the checkpoint at which each should have been caught, and the single habit that keeps both nets in place. (c) The corrected batch must now also produce address labels for the 120 certificate envelopes — state the additional main document required and the checks specific to it.

In a CISCE ICSE Class 6 practical exam, you are asked to “apply a transition to all slides and an animation to the title of the first slide.” Write the exact menu steps you would follow in a typical presentation program (e.g., LibreOffice Impress or MS PowerPoint).

CISCE past‑paper pattern: In a practical exam, you are given a 4‑slide file with no transitions and no animations. The instruction: “Add a ‘Fade’ transition of 1 second to all slides. Add a ‘Float In’ animation to the title of slide 2, starting after previous.” Write the concise step‑by‑step procedure you would follow.
If a student sets a transition duration to 0.5 seconds and another to 5 seconds, how will the audience experience differ?
In a CISCE ICSE Class 6 exam, a question asks: “Name two transition categories and give one example of each.” Provide the answer.
Evaluate the effectiveness of using a **Morph** transition between two slides that have completely different content (e.g., a chart on slide 1 and a photo on slide 2).
A past CISCE ICSE Class 6 paper asks: “List three transition properties you can customize.” Provide the answer.

Apply: Build the animation plan for the "Rivers of India" show's five content slides. For each slide state: which objects (if any) get animations, which type and start condition, the sequence order, and the reason — including at least one object deliberately left static and one effect deliberately refused. The slides: (1) Title "Rivers of India"; (2) "The Ganga" — heading + 4 points; (3) "The Ganga's Journey" — heading + map; (4) "Rivers and Us" — heading + 4 points + 1 small photo; (5) closing "Every River Matters" — heading + pledge line.

Create: Design the animation plan for a 30-second self-running kiosk slide (school reception, no speaker): "Library Week — 5 events" (five event lines + one poster image). State type and start condition for each object, the sequence with delays, and the two rules that change when the click disappears — including what the plan must NOT rely on.

HOTS: "The animation pane is the score; the speaker is the conductor." Reverse this into a notation rule: the class must write, on paper BEFORE touching software, a one-line score for each animated slide using the grammar OBJECT[TYPE, START, ORDER]. Write the score for a four-slide section (title; 3-point slide with an attached photo; full-map slide; closing pledge), then state two faults the paper notation catches that are hard to see on screen, and the one fault it cannot catch.

Evaluation: A colleague grades student shows partly on "number of effects used", arguing that a show with 15 effects demonstrates more skill than one with 4. Evaluate the metric on three grounds: what effect count actually measures, what it predictably does to student work, and what a skills-honest metric would count instead.

Reasoning: A group's show is allotted five minutes but its first timed rehearsal reads 7 minutes 40. One member proposes: "We will simply talk faster and click quicker on the day." Another proposes cutting the show. Work out the arithmetic both plans imply, explain why the speed plan fails as a matter of attention arithmetic, and state the trim procedure with its order of cuts.

Apply: Write the run sheet for presenting the six-slide "Save Water" show in assembly: the pre-show checks (three), the sequence of control actions from start to finish mapped to the talk's moments (greeting, four content slides with reveals, the pledge, the question round), and the recovery actions for two live faults — a click that reveals the wrong point, and a jump request for slide 4 from the floor.

Create: Design the rehearsal protocol for a four-member group with one 40-minute lab period and a 5-minute slot: the number of timed runs, what each run measures and fixes, the fault log format, and the readiness test the group must pass before the period ends. Include what the group does if run one exceeds the slot by more than half.

CISCE exam-style: Your group's five-slide show is complete and must be presented in a five-minute slot followed by questions. (a) List the live control actions from starting the show to ending it, in order. (b) The first timed rehearsal reads 8 minutes — state the correct responses and the one response to reject, with reasons. (c) During the question round a teacher asks to see slide 3 again — state the control action, and state why paging back slide by slide is the wrong method.

Application: The group must present the same six-slide show three times in one day — hall assembly (500 students, 3-minute compressed slot, remote clicker), classroom lesson (40 students, 15 minutes with a discussion inside, mouse on the laptop), and a corridor kiosk loop between the two (no operator, 40-second cycle). Plan the day: which settings are shared across the three, which are re-set per venue, the per-venue control plan, and the file-handling rule that prevents one venue's re-settings from leaking into the next.

Reasoning: A slide carries eight bullet points in 20-point light-yellow text over a photograph of a river, set in three different fonts. The builder says each choice was reasonable alone: "yellow matches our water theme, the photo makes it lively, 20-point fit all eight points, and different fonts mark different speakers." Trace EACH choice to the physical fact of the room or the audience that defeats it, and restate the slide under the four clusters.

Apply: Run the full design audit on this described slide and write the fix list. Slide: "Water Scarcity in India" — heading in 40-point Comic-style font (the other six slides' headings are 36-point in the show font), positioned lower than the other headings; body: nine points, 22-point dark-blue text on a light-grey background, two points in bold italic, one point eight words long, one point a full sentence of 14 words; a small spinning water-drop clip-art in the corner; body text left-aligned except one point accidentally centred. Number each fault, name the cluster and rule it breaks, and give the fix and its level (layout-level or slide-level).

HOTS: "Design is measured at the last bench." Stress-test the rule with the accessible-design extension: a colour-blind viewer (about 1 in 12 males) cannot distinguish red from green; a low-vision viewer needs larger-than-standard text; a noisy hall defeats quiet audio. For each of the four design clusters, state whether its rules already serve these viewers, where they fall short, and the one addition per cluster that makes the show serve the whole room, not just the average eye.

HOTS: "The style sheet is decided before the slides." Reverse this into a fork-prevention rule: two sections must merge their shows for the inter-section final (Section A: serif show font, navy accents, Fade; Section B: sans-serif font, maroon accents, Push transitions). Predict the naive merge's failure modes slide by slide; then state the merge protocol that produces ONE style with BOTH sections' content intact in under 30 minutes, and the single decision that must be made BEFORE any merging begins.

Application: The show must now serve THREE outputs from one design system: the projected class show (dark lab, small screen), a printed handout (paper, one page per slide, possibly on a photocopier that loses light greys), and a corridor poster of the title slide (viewed at 2-4 metres while walking). Design the adaptation: which style-sheet rules hold across all three, which rule is re-tuned per medium and why, and the test each output must pass (in place of the last-bench test).

Evaluation: A designer proposes replacing the numeric rules with a single aesthetic: "Teach students one principle — make it beautiful — and trust their taste; numbers like '24 point' are training wheels." Evaluate the proposal on three grounds: what taste actually optimises for in a novice, whether the numbers are training wheels or load-bearing, and what the classroom loses if the numbers go — including the exam-context cost.

Past-paper style: (a) State the two acceptance tests for a designed show. (b) A show's slides look uniform on the builder's screen but the review finds three heading styles and 20-point body text on some slides — state the most likely CAUSE in how the show was built, the fix, and the level of the fix. (c) The same show has a different transition on every section's slides — state the fault, the rule, and the exact two-step repair. (d) Name the production stage at which the acceptance tests should have been run, and the person's-eye view they require.

Create: Design the workflow variant for a show that must be produced in ONE 40-minute period from a topic the group receives at the start of it (slot: 3 minutes, four slides, two members). State what the compressed workflow keeps, what it compresses, what it explicitly DROPS with its risk accepted, and the minute-by-minute schedule — then state which single dropped item the group must compensate for by habit rather than process.

Application: Your school's presentation team must deliver the SAME topic three times in one week to three audiences: Class 6 (40 students, 15 minutes, discussion inside), parents' evening (200 adults, 6 minutes, formal), and an inter-school contest (judges, 8 minutes, hard on-time landing). Design the multi-venue production: which workflow stages re-run per venue and which run once, how the plan sheet forks (one master, venue sheets), the venue-specific provisions each audience forces, and the rule that keeps the three shows one production instead of three.

Apply: Match each of these game behaviours to its block category (by name and colour) and its big idea: (a) the game starts when the green flag is clicked; (b) the mango keeps falling until caught; (c) the basket checks whether it is touching the mango; (d) the score increases by 1 on every catch; (e) the mango tumbles down the screen.

Application: The lab has 25 working machines but the Scratch installation on five of them shows a palette with NO Events category visible, and on two machines the stage area is missing entirely. For each fault class, state the most likely cause, the check that confirms it, the fix, and the teaching decision for the period — because the class must build version 1 today.

Evaluation: A parent argues: "Children should learn typing-based programming from the start; Scratch will teach habits they must unlearn." Evaluate the claim on three grounds: what the block environment actually trains that transfers, what genuine gaps block-based learning leaves (state them honestly), and the bridge that closes those gaps at the right time — including why Class 6 is the right year for Scratch specifically.
If a sprite has a "forever" loop containing "move 10 steps" and "if on edge, bounce", what will happen when the green flag is clicked?
A student uses a "repeat 10" loop to increase the score each time the cat touches the mouse. Is this correct? Why or why not?
Write the sequence of blocks (in words) to make a sprite say "You win!" when the variable "Score" reaches 5.
Which block category contains the "set [variable] to [0]" block? (a) Variables (b) Control (c) Operators (d) Events
If a sprite has three costumes named “walk1”, “walk2”, “walk3” and a script runs `repeat 6 [ next costume ]`, which costume will be shown at the end?

In a CISCE ICSE Class 6 practical exam, a student is asked to “make the cat sprite animate walking using three costumes”. The student writes: `when green flag clicked → repeat 10 [ switch costume to [walk1] → wait 0.2 secs → switch costume to [walk2] → wait 0.2 secs → switch costume to [walk3] → wait 0.2 secs ]`. Identify one flaw and suggest a correction.

A student places *move 10 steps* directly under *when green flag clicked* and complains the sprite "barely moves". Explain exactly what the script does and give the corrected structure for continuous movement.
What is the difference between *repeat 10* and *forever*? State what each does and name one situation where each is the right choice.
Write the full script (block by block) that makes a sprite switch to its next costume every 0.5 seconds, forever, when the green flag is clicked.

Design (in block outline) a two-sprite scene: a Teacher sprite that, 5 seconds after the green flag, announces "Line up!"; and a Student sprite that glides to the Teacher the moment the announcement is made.

Which ONE block is missing from this intended behaviour — "the sprite keeps moving right until it touches the edge, then stops" — and where does it go? (a) *forever* wrapping *move 10 steps*; (b) *repeat until <touching edge?>* wrapping *move 10 steps*; (c) *if <touching edge?>* wrapping *move 10 steps*; (d) *wait until <touching edge?>* placed before *move 10 steps*.

Write the complete script (block by block) for a "penalty whistle": when the green flag is clicked, the Referee sprite must say "Ready..." for 2 seconds, then "Whistle!" — and AT THE INSTANT "Whistle!" appears, the Striker sprite must start moving right. The Referee must then stop all scripts 3 seconds later.

Evaluate two competing designs for the same goal — a sprite that must blink (switch costume) exactly 20 times and then stop. Design A: *repeat (20)* → [*next costume* → *wait (0.5) seconds*]. Design B: *forever* → [*next costume* → *wait (0.5) seconds*] with *stop (this script)* planned "later". Which design meets the goal as specified, and what is the strongest argument AGAINST the other — in terms of what the marker (and the player) would actually observe?

[Past-paper pattern] Study the script: *when green flag clicked → go to x:(-200) y:(0) → repeat (4) [ glide (1) secs to x:(200) y:(0) → glide (1) secs to x:(-200) y:(0) → wait (0.5) seconds ]*. (a) How many total seconds pass before the script ends? (b) How many times does the sprite reach x = 200? (c) Rewrite ONE block so the crossing continues until the player presses any arrow key, and name the block used. Show your reasoning for each part.
If you set a variable *Score* to 0 at the start of a script and then use *change Score by 1* inside a *forever* loop that runs when the green flag is clicked, what will happen to the score?
A student uses two variables *Score* and *Lives* but forgets to set *Lives* to 3 at the start. Predict the effect on the game.
Design a script that adds 10 points to *Score* when the sprite *Player* touches *Coin*.

In Scratch, which of the following statements about variable scope is correct? (a) A variable created for this sprite only can be read by other sprites. (b) A variable for all sprites can be read and changed by any sprite. (c) Variables cannot be used inside broadcast scripts. (d) Variables are automatically reset to 0 when the project is shared.
Critique a script that sets *Score* to 0 inside a *forever* loop.
Compare the effect of *set Score to 0* vs *change Score by 0*.
Which block would you use to make a variable visible on the stage? (a) *hide variable [Score]* (b) *show variable [Score]* (c) *set Score to 0* (d) *change Score by 1*
In a nested structure — a *repeat 5* placed inside a *repeat 3* — how many times do the innermost blocks run in total, and how is the total worked out?

Predict the output: a sprite runs *when green flag clicked → set Count to 0 → repeat 4 → [ repeat 2 → [ change Count by 1 ] ] → say Count*. What EXACTLY does the sprite say when the script ends, and what monitor values does Count pass through?

Here is a faulty game script (Mango sprite): *when green flag clicked → go to x:0 y:180 → forever → change y by -5 → if <touching Basket?> then change Score by 1*. A tester reports: "the score shoots up by 60 while the mango is still near the basket, then the mango keeps falling off-screen and never returns." Identify the fault(s) and give the corrected script.

Write the complete block outline for a *level up* mechanism: when the Score variable reaches 10, the game must announce "Level 2!", increase the fall Speed variable by 2, and this must happen only once (not repeatedly) as the score keeps rising.

Design, in outline only, a complete 3-level "Catch the Mangoes" variant: level 1 needs 5 catches, each level raises speed, level 3 adds a second falling sprite, and 3 missed mangoes (not lives) end the game. List every sprite's scripts by name of hat and control blocks used — no exact numbers needed except the stated ones.

HOTS: "A game bug is a lie the project tells about itself." Stress-test the assembled project's honesty: the Score monitor reads 25 but the player only saw about 12 catches. List TWO distinct mechanisms by which an assembled project can display a score that no honest count of catches would produce, state the diagnostic probe for each, and explain why the five-step method — not guess-and-edit — is required when TWO faults produce ONE symptom.

Write the complete script pair for a "two-minute warning": the game runs with TimeLeft counting down from 120; at exactly 30 seconds left, a whistle sprite must switch to its *alert* costume and say "Hurry!" ONCE, and this must not repeat on later passes. Then state what goes wrong in each of these two broken attempts: (A) the if has no guard variable; (B) the guard variable is set but the costume is switched OUTSIDE the if.

[Past-paper pattern] Study this assembled fragment from a Catch-the-Mangoes project: *Basket — when green flag clicked: set Score to 0; set Speed to 4; go to x:0 y:-140. when green flag clicked: forever [ if <key (left arrow) pressed?> change x by −10; if <key (right arrow) pressed?> change x by 10 ]. Mango — when green flag clicked: forever [ change y by (0 − Speed); if <touching Basket?> [ change Score by 1 ]; if <y position < −160> [ go to x:(random) y:180 ] ].* (a) Name TWO assembly faults in the fragment. (b) State the player-visible symptom of each. (c) Write the minimal corrected version of the faulty blocks. (d) Explain why the Basket needs TWO separate green-flag scripts rather than one.

Where should the catch sound block go inside this catch branch, and why: *if <touching Basket?> then [ (A) start sound Pop (B) change Score by 1 (C) go to random top ]* — choose the order of A, B, C and justify.

Write the complete script that gives the project a "quiet mode": pressing the Q key lowers the stage's background-music volume by 10 (not below 10), and pressing the W key raises it by 10 (not above 100). Outline only the conditions that enforce the limits.

Write the complete script (all blocks) for a "heartbeat" effect in a maze game: a soft thump every 0.8 seconds while the player sprite is touching the wall, and silence otherwise — the heartbeat must start and stop smoothly and must NOT use *play sound until done* in a way that stalls movement. Then explain why your construction avoids both the stall trap and the machine-gun trap.

Your exhibition machine runs the game for 6 hours. Name THREE long-run audio failures that short testing misses, give the mechanism for each, and the preventive construction — one of which must involve a volume property drifting over time.

Evaluate two audio designs for the same 10-second award moment where the winner sprite must cross the stage, receive a trophy, and the words "Champion!" must appear. Design A: trophy sprite — *when I receive Winner → play sound [Fanfare] until done → say "Champion!"*. Design B: *when I receive Winner → start sound [Fanfare] → say "Champion!" for 5 seconds → wait (5) seconds*. Both "end" with the fanfare over the words. Which design is defensible, and what is the decisive observable difference in (i) the timing of the words, (ii) behaviour if the project is stopped mid-way, and (iii) what happens to anything scripted after the moment?

[Past-paper pattern] The stage of a project carries: *when green flag clicked → set volume to 20 → forever [ play sound [Song1] until done ]*. Sprite Ball carries: *when green flag clicked → forever [ if <touching Paddle?> then [ start sound [Boing] → turn 180 degrees ] ]*. (a) After 3 minutes of play, how many times has Song1 STARTED, and what determines the exact count? (b) The Ball's Boing is heard as a clean single boing per paddle-hit. State the two properties of the placement that make this clean. (c) The M key is wired: *when M key pressed → if <volume = 0> then set volume to 20 else set volume to 0* ON THE STAGE. A tester presses M during the song and reports "the music stopped and then started from the middle". Assess the report: which half is mistaken, and why? (d) Give one change that would make the song ACTUALLY restart from its beginning on each flag click, and name the concept that guarantees it.
To which layer of the Topic 6 map does each block belong — *when I receive [message]*, *repeat until*, *touching [sprite]?*, *change [Score] by 1*, *start sound*?

Predict the output exactly: *when green flag clicked → set Total to 0 → repeat 3 → [ repeat 4 → [ change Total by 2 ] ] → change Total by 10 → say Total*. State the final value, the value of Total at the end of each outer pass, and why the +10 lands where it does.

Spot and fix, with reasons: (a) a stack of five perfect blocks lies loose in the script area and "does nothing"; (b) a *set Score to 0* placed inside the forever that also contains *change Score by 1*; (c) a *say "Done!"* placed after a *forever* in the same script.

HOTS: "The syllabus taught Scratch, but the syllabus was really teaching three portable ideas." Identify the three PORTABLE ideas (valuable in ANY programming language, typed or block-based) that Topic 6 actually delivered, match each to the Scratch feature that carried it, and give one concrete symptom in a student who learnt the SCRATCH version but not the PORTABLE idea.

HOTS: Two students are given the same task ("sprite dodges falling raindrops for 30 seconds") and produce IDENTICAL correct scripts, but Student A's finishes in one attempt and Student B's takes nine attempts. What does this contrast prove about where difficulty actually LIVES in this topic — and what would you examine, beyond the final script, to distinguish A from B fairly? Design the three-part fairness check.

APPLICATION: Your school's computer lab runs Class 6 practical examinations on Scratch with this rule: "Any project that cannot explain itself is incomplete." Build the self-explanation apparatus INTO a submitted game project using only taught blocks: the project must, on pressing a special key, display a spoken-and-audible guided tour of its own scripts (what each sprite's job is). Write the tour sprite's script outline and state the discipline this rule enforces on how the ORIGINAL scripts must have been written.

[Past-paper synthesis, multi-part] A past-paper-style task presents this script: *when green flag clicked → set Score to 0 → set Speed to 4 → go to x:0 y:-140 → forever [ if <key (right arrow) pressed?> → change x by 10 → if <key (left arrow) pressed?> → change x by -10 → if <touching Mango?> → change Score by 1 ]* (Basket sprite). The Mango separately: *when green flag clicked → go to x:0 y:180 → forever [ change y by (0 - Speed) → if <y position < -160> → go to x:0 y:180 ]*. (a) State TWO behaviours in the intended game this script pair CANNOT produce, naming the missing construct for each. (b) The tester reports "score jumps by many per catch". Give the mechanism and the minimal one-block-class fix with its placement. (c) The game must speed up every 5 catches, exactly once per speed-up. Write the additional script (or addition) using a guard, and name the pattern. (d) Marks: identify which part of this task is Layer 5 (assembly craft) rather than Layers 2–4, and justify the classification.
Write the HTML code to display a heading “My School” and a paragraph “I study in Class 6”.

[Past-paper synthesis, multi-part] The skeleton quiz: a page must satisfy ALL of: (a) tab reads "Green Allies 2026"; (b) background palegreen with darkgreen text; (c) top of page: centred top-importance line "Our Green Allies"; (d) a divider exactly 200 pixels thick... — identify the impossible requirement, correct it to the nearest legal form, then write the complete page satisfying the rest; (e) finally, state the total count of opening tags in your page and justify why the count is exact. (Marks guide: (a)-(c) placement/attribute application; (d) attribute-value reasoning; (e) structural accounting.)

Write the exact HTML for each: (a) the chemical formula of water with its correct subscript; (b) 10 raised to the power 6; (c) the date "26th January" with the ordinal letters in proper position; (d) the word "Caution" both bold and italic.

A chemistry page needs the line: "Sulphuric acid is H2SO4 — handle with care!" where the formula's 2 and 4 are proper subscripts and "handle with care" is bold. Write the full line as HTML and account for every container you opened.

Find the error(s) and give the corrected code: `

The value of g is 9.8 m/s2, approximately.

` — intended rendering: "9.8 m/s²" with the 2 as a superscript, "approximately" in italic, and nothing else styled.

HOTS: A student proposes writing every chemical formula once, bold, at size 1 — "so it looks like a formula (small digits) and stands out (bold)". Dismantle the proposal using the structure/appearance division and the exact-wrap rule: what does each chosen effect actually communicate, what should communicate the formula-ness, and what would a chemist say the page now CLAIMS (wrongly)?

APPLICATION: The school is printing a certificate page for 200 students from ONE HTML template: name in script-style italic, class in bold, a Roman-numeral section number as superscript (e.g., "Section VI" style is fixed — the numeral stays full-size), and the date "15th August" with a true ordinal superscript. Write the template fragment with placeholders, and state the two requirements that make `<font>` the WRONG tool here (and what to use instead for each).

EVALUATION: A textbook from an older edition teaches `<center>...</center>` and `<font>` for all visual design; a newer syllabus chapter mentions that modern practice moves appearance out of HTML into stylesheets ("CSS — not in your course"). Evaluate, at this course's level: what `<font>`/`<center>` still DO teach correctly, what idea they teach badly, and deliver the verdict on how a Class 6 student should hold them — with the one sentence to remember.

[Past-paper synthesis, multi-part] The task: (a) Write the HTML line that renders "The 26th January parade was held at 10 a.m. sharp." with "26th" carrying a true superscript ordinal, "10 a.m." bold, and the whole line in darkred. (b) A classmate writes the same line as `The 26th January parade was held at 10 a.m. sharp.` — state whether their rendering differs from yours and why. (c) Give the total count of containers opened in the classmate's version and match each close. (d) State which single character error in (c)'s counting would produce a rendering fault visible as green-less text, and name the fault class. (Marks guide: (a) construction; (b) scope reasoning; (c) structural accounting; (d) fault-class link.)
Write the HTML for an ordered list that starts at 3 and uses uppercase Roman numerals.

A student writes
  1. One
  2. Two
and expects the list to start at 1. They then change type to "A" and claim the list will now start at "A". Is the claim correct? Explain.

Critique the following markup for a table of contents:
  1. Chapter 1
    • Section 1.1
  2. Chapter 2
. Identify any semantic or accessibility issues.

A student writes `
  1. First
  2. Second
` but sees numbers 1 and 2. How can she make the list start at 5?
Apply your knowledge: Write the minimal HTML to display a recipe with an ordered list of steps, where step 2 has two sub‑steps shown as an unordered list.
A past CISCE paper asks: “Write HTML code to create a list that displays the following output: 1. First item • Sub‑item A • Sub‑item B 2. Second item” Provide the exact markup.

APPLICATION: Design the class's 45-minute lab session plan that teaches the full cycle fault-first: minute-by-minute, what students DO, which two faults are staged on purpose, at which minutes, and what the closure artefact is — such that a student who has never saved a page before leaves with a working page AND the diagnosis reflex.

EVALUATE: "Modern editors with live preview make this node obsolete — the page updates as you type, so save-refresh discipline and .txt traps are history." Give what the claim gets right, what it hides (two things the discipline still teaches that live preview cannot), and the verdict for a Class 6 course specifically.

[Past-paper synthesis, multi-part] A board-style practical: (a) Write the full Save As decisions to store a page "My Best Friend" correctly. (b) The page must show its tab name and one image from the same folder — write the complete body code skeleton with the img placed. (c) After editing, a student presses F5 twice and sees nothing new; state the two cheapest checks in order and the fault each clears. (d) The examiner asks: "Name the ONE step in the whole cycle at which a wrong decision becomes invisible in the folder but fatal in the browser." Answer with the step and the mechanism. (Marks guide: (a) dialog decisions; (b) integration of nodes 2–7; (c) triage order; (d) the single-point-of-failure insight.)
Apply the concept of search operators to find a PDF of the ICSE Class 6 Computer Studies syllabus on the official CISCE website.
State the effect of each refinement: (a) putting `"solar system"` in quotes; (b) typing `jaguar -car`; (c) adding `for class 6` to a search about photosynthesis.

Rank these three sources for a school report on the Taj Mahal's history, best first, with a one-line reason each: (a) an anonymous blog "tajafacts.blogspot.in" with pop-up advertisements; (b) the official Archaeological Survey of India website's Taj Mahal page; (c) a question-and-answer site where users comment "I think it took about 20 years".
Arrange the search refinement in increasing order of results-narrowing, and justify: (S1) `mango`; (S2) `mango vitamin c`; (S3) `"mango vitamin c content" per 100 grams`.

APPLICATION: The class has 25 minutes of lab time for the "River Ganga" project — four facts needed (source city, length, two states it flows through, one pollution measure) with every fact cited from a named source. Design the time-boxed search plan: per-fact query (keywords stated), the refinement each may need, the source target type, and the assembly rule at minute 20 — such that no fact is uncited at submission.

EVALUATE: "Search engines have made memorising facts pointless — why remember anything when the answer is always one search away?" Give what the claim gets right, the three things that remain valuable to hold in memory (one must be from this node's craft), and the verdict as a sentence a Class 6 student can use.

[Past-paper synthesis, multi-part] (a) Write the field entries and body for a mail from a student account (`rahul.6a@school.edu`) to the headmaster (`head@school.edu`), CC the class teacher (`miss@school.edu`), requesting permission for a class visit to the science museum on 18 December, with a meaningful subject. (b) The headmaster asks: "Why was the teacher CC'd?" — answer in his terms. (c) The signed permission FORM must reach him — name the mechanism and its two requirements. (d) His reply arrives marked from an address `head-replies@school-edu.info` asking for the students' address list — state the two red flags and the safe action. (Marks guide: (a) composition; (b) CC semantics in social terms; (c) attachment requirements; (d) safety reasoning.)

Match each action to its broken netiquette rule: (a) forwarding "Forward this to 20 people for good luck!" to the whole class; (b) "ur such a loser, u know nothing about football"; (c) posting a classmate's phone number in a public group; (d) replying to a typo with "can't even spell, wasted my time". Rules available: spamming; flaming; privacy violation; being unforgiving/public correcting.

[Past-paper synthesis, multi-part] The composite: (a) A message reads: `FYI I cc'd everyone including ur email on this. FORWARDED the chain too. GREAT meeting u!!!` — identify the three netiquette problems with their rules. (b) Rewrite it correctly. (c) The forwarding in (a) exposed 15 classmates' email addresses to a stranger's chain-mail — state which TWO parties violated whose rights, and the immediate repair steps. (d) State the one permanent consequence that cannot be repaired even after (c), and the habit that would have prevented it. (Marks guide: (a) rule-tagging; (b) repair writing; (c) rights analysis; (d) the unrecoverable harm.)

Match each red flag to its meaning: (a) "CONGRATULATIONS! You won a free laptop — click in 10 minutes!"; (b) "I am 13 too! Let's chat — but keep our friendship secret from your parents"; (c) an email from your own account that you never sent; (d) a page asking to "re-enter your password to confirm your prize". Flags: urgency bait; secrecy demand; account compromise; password harvesting.

[Past-paper synthesis, multi-part] The composite: A student's account receives: (1) a mail "Your account will be deleted in 24 hours — verify your password HERE"; (2) a chat from an unknown account: "I have your class photo, want to see?"; (3) a group forward: "Send this to 15 friends or your account closes." (a) For each, name the flag currency (urgency/secrecy/free-stuff or a combination) and the pillar it attacks. (b) Write the single uniform response routine applied to all three, with the exact first sentence the student says to the adult. (c) For mail (1) specifically: state how the address-reading habit (previous node) exposes the fake before any password is typed. (d) State the one sentence summary of the whole safety chapter the student should carry — containing the words 'adult', 'same day', and 'never'. (Marks guide: (a) flag-pillar mapping; (b) uniformity of the routine; (c) URL forensics; (d) synthesis sentence.)
Critique the following netiquette rule: “Never use emojis in any online communication.” Is this rule appropriate for Class 6 students? Justify.

Past‑paper style: “Arrange the following steps in the correct order to send an email with an attachment using a web‑mail service: 1. Click ‘Compose’ 2. Log in to your email account 3. Click ‘Attach files’ and select the file 4. Enter recipient, subject, and message 5. Click ‘Send’”

In an ICSE-style classroom assessment you are asked: "Describe how you would prepare for and participate in a ten-minute group discussion on a topic given to you. Write your answer in about 150 words." Outline the key points your answer must contain.

In the style of an ICSE classroom assessment, answer in about 120 words: "You will participate in a group discussion next week. State any four rules of GD etiquette you will follow, and explain how one of them improves the quality of the discussion."

In an ICSE-style assessment you are asked: "Write a paragraph of about 120 words presenting ONE argument for the motion 'Sports period should be increased to one hour daily,' with a reason and an example, ending with a signposted conclusion." Write the paragraph.

In the pattern of an ICSE classroom assessment, answer in about 120 words: "Your team lost a debate though you felt your side was correct. State any three things you would check about your team's performance before blaming the judges, and explain why one of them matters most."
In an ICSE-style assessment you are asked: "Write the concluding paragraph (about 80 words) of a speech on 'Books are our best friends', ending with a call to action." Write it.

In the style of an ICSE classroom assessment, answer in about 120 words: "You must deliver a two-minute speech on 'Kindness to animals' next week. Describe the three parts of your preparation — planning, drafting, rehearsing — naming one specific activity in each part."

Design a complete two-minute classroom staging plan for this scene brief: "Two students find a lost purse in the corridor and decide what to do with it." List your cast (2–3 roles), the plot beats in order, one prop and its convention, and the freeze position for the ending.
In an ICSE-style assessment you are asked: "How is reading a play different from reading a story? Answer in about 100 words, mentioning dialogue, stage directions and the reader's imagination."

Apply the no-narrator rule: this prose sentence must become pure drama — "Arjun was terrified of the dark corridor but pretended to be brave in front of his sister." Write the exchange (3–5 lines with stage directions) that shows both the fear and the pretence, without any narrator.

In the style of an ICSE classroom assessment, answer in about 120 words: "Your class will perform a short play at the annual day. State any four stage conventions your class must follow so the audience stays 'inside' the story, and explain why one of them is the most important."

Design a one-week graded reading plan for a Class 6 student reading below level: the student can read short paragraphs but abandons chapter books after two pages. Include text choice, the daily routine, the Friday check, and the rule for moving up a level.

Design a reading plan for a Class 6 student meeting their first full one-act play (six pages, three scenes): what to do before reading, during the first pass, during the working pass, and the final check. Name one specific tool for each stage.

Design a one-week "poem-a-day" self-training plan for a Class 6 student that drills all four rungs of the reading ladder: what to do each day, how the difficulty rises across the week, and what the Sunday review checks.

In the pattern of an ICSE unseen-poem assessment, read this stanza: "The night train whistled like a lost bird, / And the platform slept beneath the fan; / A chai-glass rang its small tin word, / And the last porter rolled his shoulder, man by man." Answer: (a) Name the two figures in line 1 and the sound device in line 3. (b) What mood do the four lines build, and which two words or phrases most carry it? (c) Reference to context: explain "rang its small tin word" in your own words.
In an ICSE-style assessment you are asked: "Explain, in about 120 words, why a first draft should be written quickly and without stopping to correct mistakes." Write the answer.

Apply the stage-separation test to real behaviour: during a 15-minute draft, a student (a) rewrites her opening line four times, (b) circles "necessary" as unsure-spelt and continues, (c) stops to check whether her second paragraph is needed, deletes it, then rewrites it twice, (d) after finishing, reads aloud and fixes three verb tenses. Which behaviours follow the process approach, and which violate it?

In the style of an ICSE classroom assessment, answer in about 120 words: "Your friend writes only one draft and loses marks for unfinished endings. Describe, in order, the four stages of the writing process your friend must add before the final copy, saying what each stage would have caught in a typical unfinished-ending story."
Why should a 200-word narrative describe ONE small event rather than a whole day or trip? Show what goes wrong with the big choice, using a example.

A student's 200-word narrative opens: "Hello, my name is Ananya. I am twelve years old and study in class six. I live in Pune with my parents and my small brother. Last Sunday, I woke up at seven o'clock and brushed my teeth. Then I had my breakfast of poha. My mother told me to get ready because we were going to my grandmother's house." Evaluate this opening as a narrative beginning and state the correct opening strategy with a rebuilt first two sentences.

Apply the chain test to these five events from a draft: (1) Kabir forgot his lines; (2) the play started late; (3) the teacher gave the class a holiday; (4) the audience clapped; (5) Kabir's friend whispered his first line from the wings. Arrange them into a cause-and-effect chain, state which event is out of place, and explain the fix.

Design a prewriting-to-draft plan for this ICSE-style task: "Write a story of about 200 words beginning with: 'The power went off for the second time that evening.'" Show the planning notes (event choice, chain of five links, planned last line, word budget) and the drafting rules you would follow.

In an ICSE-style assessment you are asked to write the closing 40–50 words of a narrative whose complication — a lost school blazer on the coldest day of the year — has just been resolved by finding it on the wrong hook in the prayer hall. Write the ending.

A writer reasons: "Suspense means hiding information from the reader until the last line — so a good 200-word story shouldn't reveal what the trouble is until word 180." Test this against how short narratives actually build suspense.

Apply the proportion test: a 200-word narrative has a 90-word beginning, a 60-word middle and a 50-word ending. Diagnose what has happened to the story's body, name the two cuts that fix it, and state the correct budget with reasons.
Compare a 200-word narrative with a diary entry about the same event on four grounds: audience, structure demanded, role of feelings, and the treatment of the ending. Four rows.

In the pattern of an ICSE past-paper task, write a complete 200-word narrative on: "Write a story that ends with the words: '…and the least expected person taught me the most.'" Include one dialogue line and show, do not tell, the lesson.

Design the slab-splitting revision routine for a one-block 350-word fast draft: the four pencil-mark signals for boundaries, the two checks at each new seam, and the final read that verifies the whole operation.

In an ICSE-style assessment you are asked: "The middle of your 350-word narrative must be TWO paragraphs. State what the two paragraphs will each contain in a story about a frightening night power cut at your uncle's village farm, and write the transition sentence that opens the second paragraph."

Apply the skeleton read to these five first sentences from a student's five-paragraph story and diagnose the organisation fault they reveal: (1) "The Katputli colony fair opened at six." (2) "By eight, the string of my kite had tangled with a stranger's." (3) "Kites have been flown in India for centuries." (4) "Because the stranger was an old man with steady hands, we untangled it together." (5) "So that evening taught me that patience unties more knots than tugging."

In the style of an ICSE past-paper task, you must write the FIRST and LAST paragraphs only (about 60 words each) of a 350-word narrative titled "The Missing Tiffin". Your first paragraph must plant the mystery; your last must resolve it with one shown clue and land the meaning without stating a moral. Write both.

Apply the full pre-planning stage to this task: "Should mobile phones be allowed in school? Write an argument of about 300 words." Produce: the claim (one sentence), three reasons each with its specific evidence, the strongest counter-argument in its fair form plus your one-line rebuttal, and the planned last sentence.
Design the revision checklist for an argument draft — six questions in checking order — and state which single question catches the most marks in Class 6 exams, with reason.

In an ICSE-style assessment you are asked to write the OPENING paragraph (about 60 words) of an argument on "Every child should learn a musical instrument." It must hook, state the issue, and end with the claim. Write it.

Apply the claim-sizing test to three claims an exam might tempt, and select the best-arguable one for a 300-word piece, with reason: (a) "Mobile phones are the root of all evil among students."; (b) "Schools should teach mobile-phone etiquette alongside their use."; (c) "Some students use phones badly sometimes."

Compare the written argument with the spoken debate (Chapter 01) on four grounds: what the other side can do to you, the role of evidence, how the audience is reached, and what the "win" consists of. Four rows.

In the style of an ICSE past-paper task, write a complete 250-word argument on: "School bags are too heavy. Schools should act." Include a hook, the claim, two welded reasons, one fair counter-argument with rebuttal, and a landing last line.

(CISCE exam-style) Choose the correct words to complete the passage, as in an ICSE Language paper: "The library of our school (keep/keeps) its doors open till six. Everybody in Class 6 (borrow/borrows) at least one book a week. The students of the reading club (has/have) made a corner for junior readers. Anybody who damages a book must replace (it/them) with a new copy."

(Application) Your school's WhatsApp group message reads: "Attention: The list of holiday homework are out. Every student of Class 6 are requested to submit their project by Monday. Neither of the two gates is open before 7:30." Find the real-world consequence of each error, fix the message, and explain why a notice with concord errors damages the school's image more than a spoken slip would.

(Comparison) Compare the present perfect and the simple past as two ways of reporting a finished action: (i) the time-link each builds, (ii) the time words each accepts (already, just, yet, so far versus yesterday, last week, in 2019), (iii) one Indian-classroom sentence pair where the choice changes the message, and (iv) why CISCE grammar papers test the pair so heavily.

(Recall) List the four grammar question formats of a CISCE Class 6 paper and state the correct checking procedure for each in one or two lines. Then state the universal checking order used across all of them.

(Create) Design a five-sentence error-spotting drill for a Class 5 junior: exactly one planted fault per sentence, covering five different rules from this chapter (agreement with indefinite pronoun, compound-subject case, earlier-of-two past perfect, transitive verb object-case pronoun, tense anchor consistency). Write the faulty drill, the full answer key with rule names, and one line of advice your junior should read before attempting.

(HOTS) Three lines: (1) "The downpour hammered the tin roof." (2) "The downpour was a drummer on the tin roof." (3) "The downpour fell like a hammer on the tin roof." All three describe the same rain, yet they distribute THREE different devices.
