(c) The tanker driver claims "150 L a minute is 9 kL an hour, so exactly one hour". Audit the rate claim with the opened arithmetic. (d) The secretary must tell residents when the motor stops: state the lawful announcement line.

EVALUATION: A student claims: "capacity is the easiest node of the quartet because its rung equals mass's — nothing new except the liquids." Assess: name the ONE genuinely new trap this node adds (the litre's dot places versus money's, with the 4.08 L line), name one habit that transferred unchanged (with the line), and state what the quartet as a whole should have left in the student's hands.

PAST-PAPER PATTERN: A cold-drink plant fills 250 mL cans from a 6 kL batch. (a) Compute the number of cans filled. (b) The plant's filler loses 2 L an hour to froth; the batch fills in 40 L... the filling line runs 500 L an hour: compute the filling duration and the froth loss over that duration. (c) Compute the drink actually canned, and reconcile with (a). (d) A supervisor claims "6 kL at 500 L/h is 12 h, so 24 h for two batches". Audit both halves against your numbers.

State the fence law and the carpet law with their formulas and units. Then classify each job as fence-kind or carpet-kind: (a) ribbon around a gift box; (b) whitewashing a ceiling; (c) one lap of a rectangular field; (d) 1 m tiles covering a corridor floor; (e) neon strip along a hoarding's edge.

The coincidence hunt: for squares of side 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 cm, compute the perimeter and the area in two columns. (a) Circle every side where the two numbers coincide. (b) A student claims "for a square, the perimeter always equals the area — we proved it with side 4". Audit the claim with your table and with the units.

EVALUATE: A student writes: "A rectangle of perimeter 20 cm — I take length 15 cm and width 5 cm, since 15 + 5 = 20." Audit the claim: compute the real perimeter of the proposed rectangle, state the half-perimeter rule, and list ALL whole-number designs that truly have perimeter 20 cm with their areas.

APPLY: A bed of 2 m × 5 m is enlarged to 4 m × 10 m. (a) Compute the perimeter and area of both beds. (b) Fencing costs ₹12 per metre: compute the fence cost for both. (c) Grass seed costs ₹10 per sq m: compute the seed cost for both. (d) The gardener budgets "double the bed, so double all the money". Audit.

CISCE exam style: complete the table (both numbers WITH units), then answer (ii)–(iv): | Design | Perimeter | Area | | A: 8 cm × 3 cm | ? | ? | | B: 4 cm × 6 cm | ? | ? | | C: 9 cm × 1 cm | ? | ? | | D: 5 cm × 5 cm | ? | ? | | E: square, side 4 cm | ? | ? | (ii) Name a pair with the SAME area but DIFFERENT perimeter. (iii) Name a pair with the SAME perimeter but DIFFERENT area. (iv) Name the row where the two numbers coincide and state why that equality may not be used.

HOTS: A 6 cm × 4 cm sheet of paper loses a 2 cm × 3 cm square-corner piece (a corner notch). (a) Compute the perimeter and area of the remaining L-shape. (b) Instead, a 2 cm × 1 cm rectangular bite is taken from the MIDDLE of a long side. Compute the new perimeter and area. (c) Explain why the corner notch left the perimeter unchanged while the middle bite grew it. (d) Audit: "any cutting must reduce the perimeter."

HOTS: Twelve 1 cm × 1 cm tiles are arranged as whole rectangles: 1 × 12, 2 × 6 and 3 × 4. (a) Verify the area of each and compute each perimeter. (b) The border of the finished rectangle is decorated with ribbon: which layout needs the least? (c) Explain why no square layout exists for 12 tiles. (d) Audit: "the 1 × 12 layout covers more ground because it is longer."

APPLICATION: A kitchen garden gets 24 m of fence; whole-metre sides; four designs on the table: 1 × 11, 3 × 9, 5 × 7, 6 × 6 (in metres). (a) Verify the fence of each design. (b) Compute all four areas. (c) Choose the design for the largest harvest and compute how much more ground it holds than the worst design. (d) The owner insists on 1 × 11 "because long rows suit spinach" — restate the audit as a fair compromise the class can offer (what the owner gains, what it costs).

PAST-PAPER PATTERN: A wire 36 cm long is first bent into a rectangle 12 cm × 6 cm, then rebent into a square. (a) Verify that the rectangle uses exactly 36 cm and compute its area. (b) Compute the side and area of the square. (c) Which shape encloses more area, and by how much? (d) A classmate says: "the square gains area because rebending stretches the wire." Audit, and complete the audit with the 1 × 17 rectangle to show where the enclosed area bottoms out.

RECALL: (a) List four pieces of previous learning this chapter has already banked that this node spends. (b) Write the four-side total for a rectangle of 8 cm × 6 cm, then rewrite the same sum as a doubled pair. (c) State both totals.

REASONING: Run the fold ladder for three rectangles, writing every rung: (a) 8 cm × 6 cm; (b) 9 cm × 3 cm; (c) square of side 5 cm. At each, show the four-side sum, the paired sum, the doubled-packet form, and confirm all three agree. (d) State what makes the pairing lawful each time.

EVALUATE: A student computes the perimeter of an 8 cm × 6 cm card as "2 × 8 + 6 = 22 cm" and defends it: "I doubled the length and added the width — doubling and adding are both in the rule." Audit the working, name the exact defect, and rebuild the line correctly with both routes.

APPLY: An L-shaped mat is made from a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle with a 2 cm × 3 cm corner notch. (a) Explain which previous-learning route must be used and why the twin fold is not licensed. (b) Walk the boundary: list the six edge lengths in order and compute the perimeter. (c) State the mat's area using 005's product and the notch.

CREATE: Design the "Grow-a-Rule" chart for a desk mat of 30 cm × 20 cm: (a) the concrete shelf — what is walked/threaded and what it reads; (b) the pictorial shelf — what the grid drawing labels; (c) the abstract shelf — the four-side sum, the paired sum and the folded form, all shown; (d) the licence line printed at the foot of the chart.

CISCE exam style: (a) Ravi's notebook measures 24 cm by 18 cm. Write the perimeter as a four-side sum AND as a doubled pair, and state the total. (b) His handkerchief is a square of side 15 cm: write its perimeter as a four-side sum, as a doubled pair, and as a four-times form. (c) State, in one sentence, what the two shapes share that licenses both folds.

HOTS: A child asks: "WHY are opposite sides equal? You keep saying it, but why?" Answer with the grid: (a) On a grid drawing of an 8 cm × 6 cm rectangle, explain what the top edge and the bottom edge each count, and what the left and right edges each count. (b) Hence state why the four-side sum always folds into two equal packets. (c) State one shape where the fold would NOT be lawful, with side numbers.

HOTS: The class meets two cut-outs. Cut-out 1 has sides 5 cm, 6 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm in order. Cut-out 2 has sides 5 cm, 8 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm in order. (a) Compute each perimeter by the lawful route. (b) A student applies 2(5 + 6) = 22 to Cut-out 1. Diagnose. (c) The SAME student applies 2(5 + 8) = 26 to Cut-out 2, and the thread agrees with 26. Was the method licensed this time? Explain the difference. (d) State the general rule about the fold and its licence.

APPLICATION: The classroom blackboard frame measures 3 m by 1.5 m. (a) Compute the frame's perimeter by both routes. (b) Border tape is sold in 2 m rolls: how many rolls does the job need, and what length is left over on the last roll? (c) The monitor buys 4 rolls "since 4 × 2 = 8 and the board is about 9". Audit the purchase. (d) State the purchase line the monitor should have written.

PAST-PAPER PATTERN: A rectangular park measures 60 m by 40 m. (a) Compute its perimeter by the four-side route and the folded route, showing agreement. (b) A jogger completes 3 full rounds: compute the distance covered. (c) The municipality fences the park at ₹15 per metre: compute the fencing cost. (d) A watcher claims: "3 rounds is about 3 × 60 = 180 m, so the jogger has run under 200 m." Audit the claim against your figures.

RECALL: (a) State the formula in words and in symbols. (b) Name what each part of the symbols means (the 2, the bracket, l and w). (c) Run it on a rectangle of 13 cm × 6 cm, and show the four-side walk underneath once to confirm.

REASONING: For a 10 m × 4 m bed, compute: (a) P = 2(l + w); (b) 2l + w; (c) l + w. (d) Exactly one of these is the bed's perimeter — state which and explain in boundary-walk language what each of the other two counts.

EVALUATE: A rectangle has perimeter 36 cm and one side 14 cm. A student writes: w = 36 − 14 = 22 cm. (a) Audit: what does 22 actually equal, and what would the rectangle's perimeter be if w were really 22? (b) Do the job lawfully and verify. (c) State the size-check that flags the student's answer before any rebuild.

APPLY: (a) A photo measures 18 cm × 12 cm: compute the frame strip needed. (b) Strip costs ₹2 per cm: compute the bill. (c) A gift box is 22 cm × 13 cm and a ribbon of 70 cm wraps it exactly with no overlap: verify the fit by the formula. (d) A second photo measures 24 cm × 18 cm: state whether one 70 cm ribbon can also wrap it, with working.

CISCE exam style: complete the table (all figures with units; backward rows must show the half-perimeter line; rebuild each row): | Given | Find | Answer | | l = 14 cm, w = 9 cm | P | ? | | P = 48 cm, l = 15 cm | w | ? | | l = 11 cm, w = 11 cm | P | ? | | P = 30 m, w = 7 m | l | ? | | l = 25 m, w = 12 m | P, then cost at ₹5 per m | ? |

HOTS: A student reads "sum of the measures of its two adjacent sides" loosely and uses "the two sides I happen to have": for a 12 cm × 7 cm rectangle he computes 2(12 + 12) = 48 cm. (a) Audit with the walk. (b) State precisely what "adjacent" requires and why 12-with-12 fails it here. (c) For WHICH rectangles would his habit accidentally give the right answer, and why is the habit still condemned?

HOTS: P = 40 m is fixed for a whole family of rectangular plots. (a) Write the machine that produces every member (w in terms of l). (b) Tabulate the members l = 4, 9, 10 with their widths and areas. (c) Verify the machine's two boundary claims — "every l from 1 to 19 gives a lawful plot" and "l = 20 gives none". (d) State what this machine is, in the language of 010.

APPLICATION: A rectangular park measures 90 m by 60 m. (a) Compute its perimeter. (b) A morning-walker completes 5 full rounds: compute the distance. (c) Fencing costs ₹12 per metre: compute the cost of fencing the whole boundary. (d) A 4 m gate replaces part of the fence: recompute the fenced length and the bill.

EVALUATION: A student says: "Now that I have P = 2(l + w), the walk and the licence of 011 are baby things — the formula does everything." Assess: (a) name one job the formula cannot do without the walk; (b) name one error the formula's grammar itself prevents, and one it cannot; (c) verdict in one sentence.

PAST-PAPER PATTERN: A rectangle has perimeter 64 cm and one side 20 cm. (a) Find the other side. (b) Compute the rectangle's area. (c) The same 64 cm wire is rebent into a square: compute the square's side and area. (d) Compare the two areas and state the shape-law the comparison displays.

REASONING: Two groups measure the same notebook's perimeter. Group A (ruler on both adjacent sides, then formula): sides 22 cm and 15 cm. Group B (thread): 58 cm. (a) Compute A's perimeter. (b) State the gap between the groups and test it against the tolerance (half-unit per reading, cm scale → ±1 cm on the perimeter of a small notebook, allow ±2 cm for two sides... state the tolerance you adopt). (c) Group B's thread was found slack by one finger along each side: explain how slack manufactures extra length, and give the lawful repair.

EVALUATE: A group measures a round pot's rim by stepping a ruler around it, edge to edge in little chords, and reports "about 39 cm". A second group lays thread around the rim, straightens it, and reads 41 cm once. (a) Which method is lawful for a curve and why? (b) Diagnose the chord-stepping ruler's error direction (over or under, and why). (c) What should the second group still do before reporting 41?

APPLY: A corridor is too long for rulers. Group A calibrates its pace against the metre rod: 40 cm. It counts 18 paces. (a) Compute the corridor length in cm and in m. (b) Group B's pace calibrates at 48 cm and it counts 15 paces: compute and compare. (c) A rod-walk gives 7 m plus one 20 cm hand-span: reconcile all three. (d) State the rule that let two different paces report one corridor.

CREATE: Design the group's "Method Card" for measuring the school garden bed (a rectangle, roughly 3 m by 1.5 m): (a) chosen method and why the edge type licenses it; (b) role assignment for four members; (c) the two-reading plan with the tolerance line; (d) the rebuild/report line the card ends with.

CISCE exam style: complete the survey table — choose the best method, then compute or take the measure as indicated: | Object | Best method | Measure | | Notebook, 22 cm × 15 cm (rectangle) | ? | perimeter = ? | | Bangle (round rim) | ? | thread reads 38 cm twice | | Blackboard ledge, 3 m × 1.2 m (rectangle) | ? | perimeter = ? | | Tree trunk (round) | ? | thread reads 90 cm twice | | Gift box, 25 cm × 10 cm (rectangle) | ? | perimeter = ?, ribbon at ₹4 per cm... per m state cost |

HOTS: Two groups measure the same blackboard's perimeter. Group A reads 92 cm... (scale: the board's sides are 30 cm and 16 cm by rod). Group A (rod + formula): 2(30 + 16) = 92 cm. Group B (thread): 96 cm, twice, readings agreeing with each other. (a) Compute the gap and test against tolerance (±2 cm on this perimeter). (b) Both of B's readings agree with each other — can agreement within one method establish truth? (c) The defect hunt finds B's thread laid ACROSS the board's face at the corners instead of along the edges: explain the error's direction and size (two corners, each adding about 2 cm of diagonal shortcut-replacement). (d) Re-measure: B reports 92 cm. State the report.

HOTS: The school's T-shaped display board: top bar 6 dm × 2 dm, centred stem 2 dm × 3 dm below. A group proposes: "treat it as its bounding box 6 × 5 and fold: 2(6 + 5) = 22 dm." (a) Walk the true boundary (eight edges) and compute. (b) The bounding-box fold happens to give 22 too — is the group's method therefore licensed? Explain using the conservation idea. (c) The board is redesigned with the stem shifted to the LEFT edge (an L): does the bounding-box fold still agree? Compute both routes for the L (bar 6 × 2, stem 2 × 3 at the left end). (d) State the lesson in one line.

APPLICATION: The compound-wall paint job: the school compound is 60 m by 45 m (rod-verified). (a) Compute the perimeter by the formula. (b) Group A paces the compound: 120 paces along, 90 across, pace 50 cm — compute both sides and the perimeter from paces. (c) Group B paces 118 and 92 with the same calibration — compute its perimeter. (d) The paint rate is ₹9 per metre of wall: compute both groups' bills and explain why the perimeter (unlike the sides) survived the pace errors.

PAST-PAPER PATTERN: A rectangular card is measured by ruler: adjacent sides 16 cm and 9 cm. (a) Compute the perimeter by the formula and confirm by the four-side walk. (b) Compute the card's area. (c) A second group's thread reads 51 cm: test against tolerance (±2 cm on this perimeter) and state the verdict. (d) The teacher erases the width and keeps "P = 50 cm, l = 16 cm": recover the width by the backward formula and rebuild.

EVALUATE: A class ruler's zero mark is worn away. A student measures a crayon by placing its end "about where zero used to be" and reads 6.8 cm. A second student places the crayon's end exactly at the 1 cm mark and reads the far end at 8.2 cm. (a) Compute the second student's answer. (b) Audit the first student's procedure. (c) State the general reading rule both should follow on any scale.

APPLY: A corridor is measured with a 2 m tape in butted spans: three full spans and a tail of 90 cm. (a) Compute the length, writing the span column as the recorder would. (b) A calibrated pace (50 cm) gives 14 paces: compute and apply the tolerance test (±25 cm, half a pace). (c) State the butting rules that keep the span column lawful. (d) The same corridor by an unbutted tape dragged in one pass reads 7.1 m: audit.

CISCE exam style: complete the kit table — tool, protocol, and the reading it yields: | Job | Tool | Protocol | Reading | | Pencil length | ? | ? | far end at 8.2 cm, start at 1 cm (worn zero) → ? | | Desk edge, 1.8 m | ? | ? | one flat pass → ? | | Corridor, long | ? | spans 2+2+2+0.9 | total = ? | | Bangle rim | ? | closed thread, straightened | 26.4 and 26.6 cm → ? | | Rectangle cover, 6 cm × 4 cm | ? | grid AND tiles | grid 24 sq cm, tiles 24, formula 6 × 4 = 24 → ? |

HOTS: A card cut from the chart has sides 8 cm and 6 cm, but its corners are visibly slanted (a parallelogram look). A student measures with the kit: both long sides exactly 8, both short sides exactly 6. (a) Compute the perimeter and state which licence covers it. (b) The student then claims A = 8 × 6 = 48 sq cm. Use the set square and the tiles to audit. (c) State, with the kit's evidence, the TWO different licences one shape-family can hold or lose. (d) One line: what does the slant do to the height, and hence to area?

APPLICATION: The display-board beading job: board 1.5 m by 0.8 m; beading strips of 50 cm at ₹6 per strip; the school already owns one 20 cm offcut. (a) Compute the perimeter. (b) Compute strips needed after using the offcut, the bill, and the unused length on the last strip. (c) The vendor offers strips at ₹6.50 for exact 40 cm cuts "no offcut needed": compute that bill and compare. (d) State which order the bursar should place and the one-line reason.

PAST-PAPER PATTERN: A rectangular school signboard measures 2 m by 50 cm. (a) Open both sides to centimetres and compute the perimeter by the formula. (b) The board's edge is bound with ribbon at ₹3 per 25 cm: compute the bill. (c) The tape used had been reading 2% long (unnoticed); the sides were recorded as 204 cm and 51 cm: compute the billed perimeter and the excess charged at the ribbon rate. (d) Audit: which single care rule, applied on kit day, would have prevented the over-billing?

REASONING: Before measuring the blackboard, the class estimates: (a) Using floor tiles of 50 cm as the anchor, explain how the class estimates the board's width at "between 2.5 and 3.5 m". (b) The tape then reads 3.0 m — state the estimate's two jobs in this outcome. (c) A team records 3.02 m; another reads the same board as 302 cm and a third writes 3.2 m: audit all three as reports of one board.

EVALUATE: The wall behind the blackboard is to be painted. The wall is 6 m by 3 m; the board covers 3 m by 1.2 m. A student computes: "6 × 3 = 18 sq m — paint the whole wall; the board's face gets painted too, it is on the wall." (a) Audit: compute the lawful paint area. (b) Name the exact defect in the student's line. (c) The paint rate is ₹12 per sq m: compute both bills.

APPLY: The 6 m × 5 m floor is re-tiled with 50 cm square tiles. (a) Compute the tile count by the grid (tiles across, tiles down). (b) The supplier adds 5% for breakage: compute the order. (c) At ₹80 per tile, compute the bill. (d) A mason says "order 100 — six by five is thirty square metres, and 30 sq m at 1 tile per sq metre". Audit with (a).

CISCE exam style: complete the fixture table (both kinds' answers, units attached): | Fixture | Measures | Perimeter job | Area job | | Chart | 60 cm × 40 cm | border = ? | face = ? | | Door | 90 cm × 200 cm | frame = ? | face = ? | | Blackboard | 3 m × 1.2 m | frame = ? | face = ? | | Desk top | 1.2 m × 0.6 m | edge beading = ? | top cover = ? | | Floor | 6 m × 5 m | skirting (no door deduction) = ? | tiles of 50 cm: count = ? |

HOTS: The window is 1.2 m × 1 m, divided by its grille into four panes of 60 cm × 50 cm. (a) Compute the glass area by the pane split, and the face area by the single rectangle — confirm they agree. (b) Compute the grille members' total length (one vertical member of the full height, one horizontal of the full width). (c) A decorator offers ribbon "along every pane's edge": compute that length and explain its relation to the members' length. (d) Which number does the PAINT-THE-MEMBERS job need, and why not the ribbon length?

HOTS: The 12 × 10 tile grid of the floor re-lays its edge row in black (one tile wide). (a) Count the black tiles by the inner-rectangle method. (b) A student claims 2(12 + 10) = 44 black tiles "the perimeter in tiles". Diagnose. (c) State the corrected general rule for a one-tile border. (d) Black at ₹95, white at ₹80: compute the exact-grid bill by colour.

APPLICATION: The four walls (3 m high) of the 6 m × 5 m room; door 0.9 m × 2 m; two windows 1.2 m × 1 m each. (a) Compute the walls' area by the perimeter-times-height route, writing the perimeter line. (b) Compute the paintable area. (c) At ₹12 per sq m, compute the bill. (d) The painter quotes "66 sq m, ₹792, openings painted around free". Audit line by line.

EVALUATION: A student says: "Estimates are guesses, and maths does not guess — why estimate before measuring?" Assess: (a) the two jobs the estimate performed on the blackboard's 3.0 m reading; (b) one fixture the class cannot reach, and what an anchored estimate honestly provides there; (c) the verdict in one sentence.

PAST-PAPER PATTERN: The class chart measures 60 cm by 40 cm. (a) Compute the border length and the face area. (b) Frill at ₹2 per 10 cm: compute the frill bill. (c) Lamination at 5 paise per sq cm: compute the lamination bill. (d) The monitor bills "₹40 + ₹120 = ₹160": verify each line and the total, naming the kind of each bill.

RECALL: (a) State the rectangle's perimeter rule in words and symbols. (b) State the square's rule and show how it follows from the rectangle's when l = w = s. (c) Compute the perimeter of a square of side 12 cm by BOTH routes, and of a rectangle 15 cm × 9 cm — state the two totals.

REASONING: Derive the square's rule in full: (a) write the four-side walk for a square of side s; (b) fold it to the doubled packet; (c) simplify to 4 × s; (d) verify all three forms for s = 9 cm. (e) State WHY the square earns a shorter rule while the rectangle does not.

EVALUATE: A student computes the perimeter of a 12 cm × 8 cm rectangle as "4 × 12 = 48 cm", explaining: "4 × s is the short rule, and 12 is the longer side, so I used it." (a) Audit with the walk. (b) State exactly which condition the short rule demands. (c) Compute the true perimeter by both lawful routes.

APPLY: (a) A square photo is 8 cm on a side: compute the frame strip by both routes. (b) Strip costs ₹2 per cm: compute the bill. (c) A square frame is sold with 44 cm of strip already fitted: compute its side. (d) Rebuild to verify (c).

CISCE exam style: complete the table (both routes where the shape is square; units everywhere): | Given | Find | Answer | | Square, side 15 cm | P | ? (both routes) | | Square, P = 80 cm | side | ? | | Rectangle 18 cm × 12 cm | P | ? | | Square with the SAME P as the 18 × 12 rectangle | side, then area | ? | | Square handkerchief, side 30 cm | hem length | ? |

HOTS: Fixed fence 40 m. (a) Tabulate the family 19 × 1, 14 × 6, 12 × 8, 10 × 10 with areas. (b) State the ladder's direction and the square's position on it. (c) The gardener keeps 12 × 8: compute what the square would add. (d) Explain in product language why equal sides win at a fixed sum.

HOTS: P = 40 m fixed. (a) How many whole-metre rectangles does the family hold? Name three besides the square. (b) How many squares? Explain the uniqueness. (c) Compute the square's side two ways. (d) Assess: "the square is just one more member, no special status."

APPLICATION: A square courtyard of side 4 m is tiled with 50 cm square tiles, the edge row black, the rest white. (a) Compute the grid. (b) Black tiles by the border rule; white by subtraction. (c) Black at ₹95, white at ₹80: compute the bill. (d) The mason offers "5 m × 3 m instead — same 16 sq m, only 10 × 6 = 60 tiles". Audit the tile count, the border claim, and the swap.

EVALUATION: A student says: "Two perimeter rules now — 2(l + w) and 4 × s — two formulas to memorise separately." Assess: (a) what the derivation shows about the "two" rules; (b) what the identity check guarantees; (c) the memory rule that replaces double memorisation.

PAST-PAPER PATTERN: A wire 48 cm long is bent into a square, then rebent into a 14 cm × 10 cm rectangle. (a) Compute the square's side and area. (b) Verify the rectangle's perimeter; compute its area. (c) Which encloses more, and by how much? (d) A classmate: "the areas differ because the wire stretched differently." Audit and name the true source of the difference.

A class of 40 collects the going-to-school data. The raw lines give: walk 19, cycle 6, bus 9, car 4, auto 2. (i) Check the total. (ii) Compute the share of walkers and test the hypothesis "most students walk to school". (iii) State the full verdict sentence. (iv) The class then claims "walking is the most popular single way": test that claim too, and explain why the two verdicts differ though they use the same data.

Design the class survey project end to end for the hypothesis "More than half of Class 6 drinks milk at breakfast": the fixed answer list, the collection plan (who asks, the class-list checklist, the one-line record), the two data crimes and the checkpoint that catches each, the share computation template, and the verdict sentence frame. State what changes if the class has 43 students, not 40.

Compare two collection routes for the same hypothesis — "the school gate sees more two-wheelers than cars": Route A — count vehicles for 10 minutes at morning entry; Route B — copy the staff parking register's monthly totals. State which is primary and which is secondary, one strength and one weakness of each for THIS hypothesis, and the one design decision (the counting window) that decides whether Route A's data can settle the claim at all.

Answer as in a CISCE-style paper: "(i) What is raw data? (ii) A survey of 50 students on favourite fruit gives: mango 21, banana 12, apple 9, guava 8. State whether the hypothesis 'most students choose mango' is confirmed, with the working. (iii) Why must the answer list be fixed before collecting? (iv) State one difference between primary and secondary data with an example of each."

**APPLICATION:** The school's project fair hosts the class's "How do we come to school?" stall. Visitors challenge the exhibit: a parent asks "Why only 40 students? The school has 900 — your numbers are wrong for the school." Write the stall's answer kit: the precise statement of what the class data CAN claim (the group named in the hypothesis) and what it cannot, the sampling logic in one honest sentence a ten-year-old visitor can repeat, the two extensions the stall offers (a whole-school version: what it costs, and a parallel class-to-class comparison: what it shows), and the stall-board line that pre-empts the challenge for every visitor who reads before asking. **COMPETENCY:** Defending the scope of a small survey honestly while showing what a scaled version would require.

**APPLICATION:** The class must examine the hypothesis "The school's water break queue is longest just after the lunch bell" with a TIME-LOG method instead of a question survey. Write the method sheet: the operational definition (what counts as queue length and when observations are taken), the observation plan (which days, which windows, who watches, the two-minute record line), the two noise sources and the control for each, the verdict rule for "longest just after lunch" (what it must beat), and the full verdict sentence written for the sample data: after-lunch windows average 14 students, mid-morning windows average 6, home-time windows average 9. **COMPETENCY:** Converting a timing claim into an observation protocol with operational definitions, noise controls, and a comparative verdict rule.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "(a) Define a hypothesis in data handling and name its three parts. (b) Distinguish raw data from organised data in one sentence each. (c) A survey of 60 students on lunch preference gives: home lunch 26, canteen 24, both 10. Test the hypothesis 'Most students bring home lunch' with the doubling method and state the verdict. (d) The collector lost 3 lines and estimates them 'as canteen, since canteen looks popular' — state the correct treatment and the crime avoided. (e) For the SAME data, write one claim the data confirm and show its test." Answer as expected in a Class 6 CISCE-style paper.
What is the correct way to represent a count of 7 using tally bars?
A student draws tally bars for the data set {2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4} and writes the frequency of 3 as 2. Explain why this is incorrect.
Given the raw data: 5, 1, 5, 2, 5, 3, 5, 4, 5, 5. Construct the tally bars and frequency table, then state the mode.
Create a new data set of 8 observations where the tally for the value 2 shows exactly one complete group of five and two extra vertical lines. Write the raw data list.

In a CISCE Class 6 exam, a question asks: “The tally marks for the number of pencils each student has are shown. How many students have exactly 3 pencils?” The tally column for 3 shows |||| /. What is the answer?
A student claims that tally bars can only be used for numbers up to 10. Critique this claim with an example.
Evaluate the following frequency table for errors: Value | Tally | Frequency 1 | |||| / | 6 2 | ||| | 3 3 | |||| / | 5 4 | || | 2
Compare the use of tally bars versus a simple list for recording the colours of 20 marbles drawn from a bag. Which method allows faster identification of the most common colour? Explain.

A past CISCE paper asks: “The tally marks for the number of books read by students in a month are given. If the tally for 3 books is |||| / ||, how many students read exactly 3 books?” Provide the answer and show the reasoning.
A pictograph uses a symbol of a book to represent 5 books. If there are 4 symbols for Class 6, how many books did they read?
A student draws a pictograph where each symbol represents 2 items, but the data values are 3, 5, 7. Is this scale appropriate? Explain.
Given data: Apples 12, Oranges 18, Bananas 24. Choose a suitable scale and describe the pictograph (number of symbols for each).
Create a pictograph for the number of students in four houses: Red 30, Blue 45, Green 25, Yellow 35. Use a scale of 5 students per symbol. How many symbols for each?
In a pictograph, one symbol of a tree represents 10 trees planted. The pictograph shows 3 symbols for School A and 5 symbols for School B. How many more trees did School B plant than School A?
If a pictograph uses a scale of 8 items per symbol, what is the maximum data value that can be represented with 5 symbols without using half symbols?
A survey of favourite fruits shows: Mango 30, Apple 22, Banana 18, Orange 26. Design a pictograph with a suitable scale, explain your choice.
A pictograph uses a symbol of a car to represent 3 cars. The data values are 4, 7, 10. The student draws 1, 2, 3 symbols respectively. Critique this representation.
In a pictograph, one symbol of a book represents 6 books. The pictograph for Class 6 shows 4 symbols and a half symbol. How many books did Class 6 read?
A student draws a bar graph where the vertical axis scale jumps from 0 to 10 to 30. Evaluate this graph.
Given the frequency table: Apples 20, Bananas 35, Oranges 15, choose a suitable scale (1 cm = ? units) for a bar graph that fits within a 10 cm height.
Create a bar graph for the following data: Monday 12, Tuesday 8, Wednesday 15, Thursday 10, Friday 13. Describe the steps you would take.

In a CISCE exam, a bar graph shows the number of students in four clubs: Science 40, Maths 30, English 25, Art 20. The vertical axis is marked 0,10,20,30,40. What is the difference between the Science and Art clubs?

A teacher asks students to represent the number of different types of trees planted in a school garden: Neem 18, Peepal 12, Banyan 9, Mango 15. One student draws a bar graph with a scale of 1 cm = 3 trees but makes the Neem bar 5 cm tall. Is the bar height correct? Justify.
You have a frequency table of favourite sports: Cricket 30, Football 22, Hockey 18, Badminton 14. Choose a scale that allows the tallest bar to be exactly 8 cm on graph paper. What scale do you use?
Compare a bar graph and a pictograph for representing the same data set of 5 categories with frequencies up to 50. Which is more efficient and why?

A CISCE past paper question: “The bar graph shows the number of students in Class 6 who like different colours. The scale is 1 cm = 4 students. The bar for Blue is 3.5 cm tall. How many students like Blue?”
Find the mean and median of the following data set (number of books read by six students in a month): 3, 5, 2, 7, 4, 6.
Create a data set of five whole numbers (each ≤10) whose mean is 6 and median is 5.
In a CISCE Class 6 exam, a question asks: “The marks of 7 students in a test are 42, 38, 45, 40, 44, 39, 41. Find the mean and median marks.” Provide the solution as expected in the exam.
A data set of nine numbers has a mean of 12. If one number, 20, is removed, what is the new mean of the remaining eight numbers?
The ages (in years) of six cousins are: 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15. If a seventh cousin aged 8 joins the group, how do the mean and median change? Calculate both before and after.
Compare the mean and median of the following two data sets and explain which measure better represents the “typical” value in each case. Set A: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 Set B: 10, 11, 12, 13, 100
A past CISCE paper asks: “The weights (in kg) of 8 students are: 32, 35, 30, 34, 33, 36, 31, 37. Find the mean weight and the median weight.” Write the solution steps as per board expectations.

Define the mean and the median for a dataset of up to ten observations. State the two verification checks for a computed mean and the one identity check for an odd-count median. Compute both for the scores 6, 8, 4, 9, 5, 7, 3 (seven students), showing all working.

The even-count median: for the ten observations 7, 5, 8, 5, 9, 4, 6, 5, 7, 4 — (i) order the data and state the two middle positions and values; (ii) compute the median; (iii) compute the mean; (iv) the median 5.5 is not a value anyone scored — explain why that is still correct, and what the even median means on the number line.

Run the crocodile experiment on paper: start with the six values 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 9 — compute the mean and the median. Then the champion scores and the 9 is replaced by 91: recompute both. State exactly what each measure did in response, and give the one-sentence choosing rule this experiment proves.

Read both measures from a frequency table: the class's cups-of-milk data — 2 cups: 4 students; 3 cups: 1 student; 4 cups: 5 students (ten observations). (i) Unpack the table into the ordered run. (ii) Compute the median. (iii) Compute the mean. (iv) A student takes the median of the three VALUES (2, 3, 4) and gets 3 — show the correct answer, and state the general rule the trap teaches.

State the choosing rule between mean and median, then apply it to three datasets with reasons: (i) daily auto-fare over ten days: 30, 30, 32, 30, 31, 30, 29, 30, 32, 30; (ii) the same ten fares with one airport-day fare of 450 replacing one 30; (iii) the ages of players in a family cricket match: 11, 12, 13, 12, 40, 11, 13, 12 (father and son both play). For each, give both measures (compute), name the better summary, and give the reason in one sentence.

Answer as in a CISCE-style paper: "(i) Find the mean of 8, 12, 7, 9, 14 (five observations), showing the sum. (ii) Find the median of 15, 8, 11, 20, 13, 9. (iii) The mean of five numbers is 12; four of them are 10, 14, 9, 15 — find the fifth. (iv) The median of seven ordered values is the ___-th value; the median of eight ordered values is the average of the ___-th and ___-th."

**HOTS:** A school brochure prints: "Our students average 91% in the board-mock test" — computed from ten toppers' scores (88, 90, 91, 92, 93, 89, 90, 94, 92, 91) while the full class of 40 (toppers included) has a mean of 71 and a median of 74. Write the full critique: what the sentence claims, the two separate deceptions (the selection and the word "average"), the arithmetic that exposes each, the honest brochure line that uses the same 91% truthfully, and the reader's two-question defence against any future "average" claim.

**APPLICATION:** The class must present ONE summary number for the school's "reading week" — ten classes report books read: Class 6A's data are 8, 9, 9, 10, 9, 8, 10, 9, 9, 42 (one teacher-parent read-alongathon counted 42), while the school-wide dataset (all ten classes' means) is 8.5, 9, 9, 9.5, 8, 8.5, 9, 9, 9, 9. Write the presentation decision: the two candidate numbers for 6A (compute) and the recommendation with the crocodile reasoning; the school-wide choice (compute the mean of the ten class-means and the median) and why the school-wide dataset is calmer; the one-slide summary showing both numbers for both levels with labels; and the anticipated question ("why does 6A's number differ from its contribution?") answered in one sentence. **COMPETENCY:** Choosing and labelling summary measures at two levels of a real dataset, with honest presentation of an outlier's effect.

**APPLICATION:** The maths lab builds the "fair share machine": a physical model where n towers of blocks (the data) are levelled into n equal towers (the mean) by moving blocks one at a time. Write the machine's operating sheet: the construction (tower heights for the dataset 7, 3, 8, 6 — where the blocks come from), the levelling protocol (which towers donate, which receive, the stopping condition), the two facts the machine makes visible (the share value and the balance), the fractional case (dataset 4, 4, 7 — what the machine shows that whole blocks cannot, and the honest reading), and the one question the machine CANNOT answer (with the median's claim to it). **COMPETENCY:** Specifying a physical model of the mean that demonstrates sharing and balance, including its fractional limitation.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "(a) Define the mean of n observations. (b) Find the median of 14, 9, 17, 6, 11, 13, 10. (c) The mean of 8 numbers is 13.5 — find their sum; if seven of them sum to 91, find the eighth. (d) The runs of ten batsmen: 0, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 107 — which measure describes the typical score, and why? Compute it. (e) The mean of five observations is 8 and each observation is increased by 3: state the new mean with the reason." Answer as expected in a Class 6 CISCE-style paper.

A student uses a maths kit to record the favourite sport of 12 classmates. She places one counter per response but forgets to group them into tally sticks. What is the immediate effect on the data organisation step?

When constructing a bar graph on the grid mat, a learner decides that one cube represents 3 votes. If a category received 11 votes, how many cubes should be stacked, and what does the remainder indicate?
Evaluate the statement: “Using a maths kit to find the median of 9 observations is more reliable than calculating it on paper because you can see the middle cube.”
A teacher asks students to represent the data set {2, 5, 5, 7, 9} using the maths kit and then find the mean. Describe the kit‑based procedure and compute the mean.

Create a data‑handling task for a Class 6 peer that uses the maths kit to test the hypothesis “More students bring a steel tiffin box than a plastic one.” Outline the steps from collection to bar graph, specifying the scale you would choose.

In a CISCE‑style question, a bar graph made with the maths kit shows three bars of heights 4, 6, and 5 cubes. The scale is 1 cube = 4 students. What is the total number of students represented, and which category has the highest frequency?
Critique the following statement: “Because the maths kit makes data handling concrete, students do not need to learn the abstract symbols (tally marks, bar graphs on paper) until Class 8.”

A past CISCE paper asks: “Using a mathematics kit, a student recorded the number of books read by 9 classmates in a month. The data (in books) is: 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6. Construct a frequency table, draw a bar graph with a suitable scale, and find the median and mean.” Provide the complete solution as expected in the exam.
A student cuts out the following maximum temperatures (°C) from a newspaper for five consecutive days: 34, 36, 35, 37, 33. What is the median temperature?
The same five‑day temperature data (34, 36, 35, 37, 33) is to be shown in a pictograph where one symbol represents 2 °C. How many symbols should be drawn for the day with 37 °C?

A bar graph drawn from newspaper onion prices (₹/kg) for four weeks shows bars of heights 30, 28, 35, 32. The vertical axis is marked in steps of 5 kg. Evaluate whether the graph correctly represents the data.
Using the newspaper data set of daily milk prices (₹/litre) for six days: 48, 50, 49, 51, 50, 48, compute the mean price.
Create a frequency table and a scaled pictograph (1 symbol = 3 runs) for the following IPL scores taken from a newspaper: 45, 60, 30, 75, 55.

A CISCE‑style question: “The table below shows the number of newspapers sold by a vendor over five days. Day | Papers sold Mon | 120 Tue | 135 Wed | 110 Thu | 140 Fri | 125 Draw a bar graph to represent the data. Choose a suitable scale and label the axes.”

A newspaper publishes the following daily rainfall (mm) for a week: 12, 0, 5, 8, 0, 3, 10. If a student draws a pictograph with scale 1 drop = 2 mm, how many drops (including half drops) represent the day with 5 mm?
Using the same rainfall data (12, 0, 5, 8, 0, 3, 10), a student constructs a bar graph but forgets to label the vertical axis with units. Explain why this omission makes the graph ambiguous.

Compare a scaled pictograph (1 symbol = 3 runs) and a bar graph for the same set of five IPL scores (30, 45, 60, 55, 75). Which representation allows quicker comparison of the highest and lowest scores, and why?

A past CISCE paper asks: “The table shows the number of newspapers sold each day from Monday to Friday. Draw a bar graph using a scale of 1 cm = 20 newspapers. Day | Papers Mon | 100 Tue | 140 Wed | 80 Thu | 160 Fri | 120 What is the height of the bar for Thursday in centimetres?”

One survey, two pipelines: explain what the TYPE column and the HOURS column each become in the report. For the class results — types: cartoons 14, serials 9, sports 6, news 4, films 4, music 2, other 1 (40 students); hours: total 312, ordered middle pair 7 and 8 — compute every summary the report will print: the type ranking with its share, the pictograph's icon plan at 1 icon = 2 students, the mean and median of hours, and state which hypotheses each number feeds.

The newspaper cross-check: from the day's TV grid (96 programmes), the class counts — serials 22, cartoons 18, news 16, films 12, other 14, sports 8, music 6. The class's own choices: cartoons 14 of 40, serials 9 of 40. (i) Compare each type's offer share with its choice share. (ii) State the mismatch finding and the agreement finding in full sentences. (iii) Explain the choose-versus-offer distinction and why the mismatch is a finding, not a mistake.

The hours dataset carries a crocodile: 39 students report 282 hours in total, and one student reports 30 (a festival week). (i) Compute the mean of all 40 and the mean excluding the 30. (ii) The median of all 40 is 7; state whether it moves when the 30 is excluded, with the reasoning. (iii) The hypothesis bar was "our class averages more than 7 hours": test it twice — with all 40, and on the typical-student reading — and state how the report should present both answers.

Answer as in a CISCE-style paper: "(i) A class of 40 reports 312 total TV hours. Find the mean viewing time. (ii) The ordered middle pair of the 40 hours is 7 and 8 — find the median. (iii) The newspaper grid offers 18 cartoon programmes of 96 total. Express the cartoon offer share as a fraction and compare it with the class's cartoon choice share (14 of 40). (iv) State the choose-versus-offer distinction in one sentence each."

**APPLICATION:** The school's annual day needs a one-minute data segment on stage: the TV project's findings, delivered live. Write the stage plan: the three numbers that go on screen (chosen for audience impact AND honesty, with the caveat each carries), the 60-second script skeleton (four beats with timing), the one live-audience interaction (a show of hands that becomes data in real time — what is asked, how it is counted, what is done with it), and the two stage-safety rules for statistics (the claims the script is forbidden to make). **COMPETENCY:** Translating a statistical report into a live one-minute performance that stays honest under the pressures of stagecraft.

**APPLICATION:** Next term the class inherits the project and must IMPROVE it: this year's weak points (from the teacher's audit) were — the hours self-reports were guesses; the grid count used one day; three students' answers were never recorded; the pictograph's half-icons confused visitors. Write the improvement brief: one fix per weak point (with the mechanism and the check that proves the fix worked), the one weak point that CANNOT be fully fixed at Class 6 (and the honest workaround), the revised instrument's two new fields, and the one-line note the new team adds to the report's method section crediting this year's audit. **COMPETENCY:** Auditing a completed data project and specifying mechanism-level fixes with verification, including the honest limits of the class's instruments.

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** A student's revision card reads: "The capstone proves surveys always match newspapers if both are done carefully. The biggest type is the class's average programme. The grid's 96 slots mean 96 viewers. If the mean (7.8) and median (7.5) are close, the data have no crocodile. The report's verdict section may restate the hypotheses as confirmed because the class worked hard." Write the critique: each claim corrected with the project's mechanism, and the one-line rule that separates verdicts from effort.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "(a) Name the two kinds of data (by source) the TV project uses, with one example of each. (b) A class of 40 reports a total of 332 TV hours; the largest single entry is 45 hours (an exam-week binge), and the ordered middle pair is 7 and 9. Compute the mean and median, and state which the report should headline, with the reason. (c) The grid offers 20 cartoon slots of 100 and the class's cartoon choice share is 30%: compare the shares and state the finding. (d) A teammate proposes deleting the 45-hour entry 'because it is abnormal': state the correct treatment with the rule. (e) The project's four stages in order are claim, record, organise, and summarise — name the tool each stage uses and the one check that closes it." Answer as expected in a Class 6 CISCE-style paper.

A newspaper page carries five figures: (i) "The metro carries 12,40,000 riders daily"; (ii) "Chapter VII of the rulebook"; (iii) "The budget rose to ₹2,36,487 crore"; (iv) "About 50,000 attended"; (v) "Gold at ₹62,415 per 10 g". Match each figure to the chapter region it exercises, and state which one figure is ALREADY rounded (the tell-tale word) and which numeral system the Roman figure belongs to.

The chapter's ten nodes wear numbers 001–010. (i) Place nodes 002–010 into their regions. (ii) State what each of 06_005 and 06_006 adds beyond the other. (iii) State the two things the final synthesis node (06_010) does that no earlier node does. (iv) A student claims "06_001 and 06_010 are both overviews, so one must be redundant" — write the correction.

**APPLICATION:** The school's alumni newsletter wants a "Chapter 06 in adult life" column: five Indian adult contexts, one per region, each with the region's skill doing real work and one sentence of adult stakes. Write the column: the five contexts (with the specific skill and the stakes sentence), the one context that uses TWO regions jointly (named with the joint mechanism), and the closing line that tells the alumni why Class 6 was not a warm-up. **COMPETENCY:** Writing for an adult audience about junior mathematics, with each context carrying a genuine skill use and real stakes.

**APPLICATION:** The class must design the chapter's "passport" — a two-page foldable the student fills AS the chapter progresses (one stamp per node) and re-reads at exam time. Write the passport design: the two-page layout (what the left page carries, what the right carries), the per-node stamp format (what the student writes when a node is completed — the exact three fields), the pipeline strip along the fold (how the arrows are drawn and updated), and the exam-week ritual the passport serves (the 10-minute final walk). State what makes the passport a MAP rather than a contents page. **COMPETENCY:** Designing a progressive self-documentation artefact that encodes the chapter's structure for revision.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "(a) Name the chapter node that teaches the Indian and International systems and state one difference between the two ladders. (b) A figure in the news reads 'about 2,40,000 pilgrims' — name the region at work, the signal word, and one exact figure this could truthfully stand for. (c) The HCF–LCM link-formula: state it and verify it for 12 and 18. (d) A student computes 6,408 × 25 and reports 1,60,020 — use the estimate-guard to assess the answer before any exact check. (e) Arrange the chapter's ten nodes as a flow diagram with labelled arrows, and state the one arrow that will be reused most in the next year's fraction work." Answer as expected in a Class 6 CISCE-style paper.
What is the face value of the digit 7 in the number 7,65,432 (Indian system)?
In the number 4,56,789 (Indian system), what is the place value of the digit 5?
A student writes the expanded form of 3,21,045 as 3,00,000 + 20,000 + 1,000 + 40 + 5. Is this correct? Explain.
Write the number 6,78,901 in the International system and give the place value of the digit 8.
Create a 7‑digit number (Indian system) in which the digit 3 has a place value of 30 000 and a face value of 3.
If the place value of digit 6 in a number is 60 000 in the International system, give two possible numbers.
**HOTS:** Without writing the full expanded form, determine which is larger: 9,87,654 (Indian) or 987 654 (International). Explain your reasoning.

**APPLICATION:** A school library has 12,34,567 books. The librarian wants to write this number in the International system for a global report. Write the number and state the place value of the digit 2.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** In the number 4,56,789 (Indian system), if the digit 6 is replaced by 9, by how much does the number increase?
State the HCF of 24 and 36.
If the LCM of two numbers is 60 and their product is 360, what is their HCF?
Find the LCM of 15 and 20 using the prime factorisation method.
Create a pair of two‑digit numbers whose HCF is 9 and LCM is 108.
A school has 144 pencils and 96 erasers. They want to pack them into identical sets with no items left over, using the greatest possible number of items per set. How many items will each set contain?
If the HCF of two numbers is 1, what can you say about their LCM?
Two ropes are 180 cm and 240 cm long. They are to be cut into pieces of equal length with no rope left over. What is the greatest possible length of each piece?
Compare the HCF and LCM of the pairs (8,12) and (9,15). Which pair has a larger HCF? Which pair has a larger LCM?

A rectangular floor measuring 3.6 m by 4.8 m is to be tiled with square tiles of the largest possible size without cutting any tile. What is the side length of each tile, and how many tiles are needed?
Critique the method: “To add 2/3 + 1/4 , add numerators (2+1=3) and denominators (3+4=7) to get 3/7 .”
Round 6 842 to the nearest hundred.
A student rounds 9 560 to the nearest thousand and writes 9 000. Identify the error and give the correct rounded value.
Estimate the difference 7 438 – 2 189 by rounding each number to the nearest hundred before subtracting.
Which of the following numbers rounds to 3 000 when rounded to the nearest thousand? (a) 2 499 (b) 2 500 (c) 3 499 (d) 3 500
Create a 5‑digit number that rounds to 45 000 when rounded to the nearest thousand, but rounds to 44 900 when rounded to the nearest hundred.
In a CISCE exam, a question asks: “Round 1 04 987 to the nearest lakh.” Explain why this question is outside the Class 6 scope and what the correct answer would be if it were asked in Class 7.
A classmate claims that rounding 5 500 to the nearest thousand gives 5 000 because “the hundreds digit is 5, exactly halfway, so we stay.” Critique this claim.
Apply rounding to estimate the product 387 × 52 by rounding each factor to the nearest ten, then multiply. Compare with the exact product.
Evaluate the statement: “Rounding a number to the nearest hundred always produces a multiple of 100.” Is it always true? Justify.
Compare rounding 4 999 to the nearest ten, hundred and thousand. List the three results and explain the pattern.
A past ICSE paper asks: “Round 6 78 912 to the nearest thousand.” Provide the answer and show the steps a Class 6 student should write.
Round 5,846 to the nearest hundred.
A student rounds 9,999 to the nearest thousand and writes 9,000. Is this correct? Explain.
Estimate the sum 4,276 + 3,849 by rounding each addend to the nearest hundred. Then state whether the estimate is greater or less than the exact sum.
Use rounding to estimate the product 2,345 × 6. Show the rounded factor and the estimated product.
Create a 5‑digit number that rounds to 70,000 when rounded to the nearest thousand. Explain your choice.
A CISCE sample paper asks: “Round 8,49,372 to the nearest lakh.” Provide the answer and the reasoning.
A number rounded to the nearest hundred gives 6,700. What is the smallest possible original number? What is the largest possible original number?
A farmer harvested 12,345 kg of wheat and 9,876 kg of rice. He wants to report the total harvest to the nearest thousand kilograms. What should he report?
Compare the estimates obtained by rounding 4,567 to the nearest hundred and to the nearest thousand. Which estimate is closer to the original number? Explain.
CISCE past paper: “Round 7,84,592 to the nearest lakh and to the nearest ten thousand. Find the difference between the two rounded numbers.”
Which property allows you to rewrite (-4) × (6 + -2) as (-4)×6 + (-4)×(-2)? Justify your answer.
Simplify using properties: (-5) × [(-3) + 7] + (-5) × (-3). Show each step and name the property used.
A CISCE-style question: "Verify the associative property of addition for the integers -8, 5, and -3 by evaluating both (-8 + 5) + (-3) and -8 + (5 + -3)."
HOTS: Prove that for any integer a, a × 0 = 0 using only the distributive property and additive identity.

Application: The temperature in Shimla drops from 5°C to -3°C overnight. Next day it rises by 7°C. Use integer properties to find the final temperature and explain which property lets you add the changes in any order.
CISCE past-paper pattern: "Simplify: (-12) × [(-5) + 3] + (-12) × (-5) using suitable properties."

Recall-level: state the alignment rule for column work and the check for subtraction. Then compute 25,79,630 + 21,84,396 and 4,93,78,602 − 47,64,026 with the commas guiding the alignment, and verify both answers structurally.

Reasoning-level: state the shift law and WHY appending zeros works. Apply it: (i) 4,386 × 100; (ii) 9,08,000 ÷ 1000; (iii) 76 × 900 using the split (76 × 9 × 100). Then explain why the ×800 partial product of 1,248 × 1,865 must end in two zeros.

Reasoning-level: state the long-division cycle and the division identity. Divide 87,624 by 144 showing every cycle step, state quotient and remainder, verify by the identity, and state which quotient digit is zero and why it must be written.

Apply-level: a district's population is 4,93,78,602; males number 25,79,630 and females 21,84,396. (i) Write the children-count as one bracketed expression. (ii) Compute it exactly with the intermediate sum labelled. (iii) Run the estimate-guard. (iv) Verify structurally.

Create-level: from the raw data — a printer charges ₹185 per notebook, a school has 1,248 students, the school's budget is ₹2,50,000 — design a three-step word problem whose answer requires multiplication, addition and a comparison, solve it with labelled steps, and state the guard.

Answer as in a CISCE-style paper: "(i) Multiply 3,406 by 259. (ii) Divide 12,04,848 by 24 and verify. (iii) Find the number which when multiplied by 1000 gives 7,05,00,000. (iv) 350 travellers, buses of 48 seats — how many buses? Show the division and the decision."

**HOTS:** A student argues: "Checking division by the identity is circular — Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder is just the definition of the parts, so of course it fits. A check that cannot fail is not a check." Write the evaluation: the kernel in the claim (the identity IS the definition), why the check still works (the independence-of-road argument: the identity re-assembles the parts by MULTIPLICATION, a different operation from the division cycle that produced them), what the identity actually catches (with this node's own 68-versus-608 example), and the settled principle about when a verification is worth running.

**APPLICATION:** The school's Bal Mela committee holds ₹1,84,500. It rents 28 stalls at ₹3,250 each and spends ₹46,780 on decorations. (i) Write the money-left plan as one bracketed expression. (ii) Compute it exactly with labelled steps. (iii) The remaining money buys prizes at ₹499 each — how many prizes, and what is left? (iv) Guard both answers. **COMPETENCY:** Running a three-stage budget computation — plan, exact, purchase with remainder judgment, guard.

**APPLICATION:** A state transport depot must move 1,02,400 festival passengers on buses of 64 seats each, then handle a last-day rush of 8,530 more passengers with the same buses. (i) How many bus-trips does the main movement need, and why is the arithmetic clean? (ii) How many trips does the rush need, with the division and the remainder decision shown? (iii) Each trip costs ₹2,850 in fuel — compute the TOTAL fuel bill for both movements with a second-split verification. (iv) Guard the fuel bill. **COMPETENCY:** Chaining two divisions with opposite remainder verdicts into a multiplication with commercial stakes.

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** A student's revision card reads: "Alignment is optional if you're careful. Multiplying by 100 means writing two zeros at the end of whatever you had. In long division you can skip a zero quotient digit if the next digit is big. Remainders are always discarded. The identity check is extra work with no value." Write the critique: each claim corrected with this node's mechanism, and the one-line principle the whole card violates.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "(a) Multiply 4,806 by 309, showing the partial products. (b) Divide 24,05,760 by 144 and verify with the division identity. (c) Find the number which, when multiplied by 100, gives 3,06,700. (d) The same division 5,000 ÷ 63 = 79 remainder 23 answers three stories — 5,000 passengers in 63-seat buses; 5,000 pamphlets to 63 colonies; ₹5,000 buying saplings at ₹63 each. State the answer to each story. (e) A shop's bill claims 6,094 × 27 = 1,64,358 — assess the claim with the estimate-guard, then settle it exactly." Answer as expected in a Class 6 CISCE-style paper.

Recall-level: define the natural numbers and the whole numbers, state the smallest member of each and the exact difference between the two sets. State zero's three powers with one example each. Then give the successor of 99,99,999 and the predecessor of 10,00,000, with the comma reading of each answer.

Reasoning-level: explain why 0 has no predecessor in the whole numbers but every whole number has a successor. Then explain, with the jump picture, why a × 0 = 0 and why a ÷ 0 has no answer. State what each of these two asymmetries announces about the family's future extensions.

Reasoning-level: draw (or describe) the number line from 0 to 12 with equal marks, place the numbers 6 and 9 on it, and state which is greater by position. Then arrange 8,40,912; 8,04,912; 8,40,219; 8,90,412 in ascending order, and state how many whole numbers lie strictly between 3,406 and 8,041.

Apply-level: a game token starts at 6 on a floor number line. It moves: +8, then −5, then ×3 (three equal jumps of its current value), then −20. Write the whole journey as ONE bracketed expression, compute the landing mark step by step, and state whether every move stayed on the whole-number street.

Create-level: design a two-player number-line board game for Class 5 visitors — the board 0 to 30, two tokens, one dice-like deck of move-cards (+4, −6, ×2, ÷2, "swap with 0", and one FALL card) — write the rules, two solved sample turns (one using a ×2 card, one where a token falls off the left edge), and the one rule that keeps the game finishable.

Answer as in a CISCE-style paper: "(i) State the smallest whole number and the smallest natural number. (ii) Write the successor of 48,09,999 and the predecessor of 5,00,000. (iii) How many whole numbers lie between 1,046 and 2,046? (iv) What does the arrowhead on a number line mean?"

**HOTS:** A student argues: "Zero is overrated. The natural numbers did all the counting for centuries — zero is just a placeholder with a mythology built around it. Remove it and the line simply starts at 1." Write the evaluation: what the student gets right (counting precedes zero historically), the three collapse-points if 0 is removed (the line's origin, the place-value seats, the additive identity — each with a concrete failure), and the settled statement of what zero actually is — with the one asymmetry (no predecessor in W) that keeps zero interesting even after its case is won.

**APPLICATION:** A highway toll is the origin for a line of kilometre stones; a bus travels the highway. (i) The bus is at stone 84 — state its distance and direction from the toll in line-language. (ii) The bus moves from stone 84 to stone 132 — write the movement as an expression and compute the distance travelled. (iii) At stone 132 the bus turns back and travels 150 km — write the expression, attempt the landing, and state what the attempt reveals about the highway's line. (iv) A second bus starts at the toll and makes equal trips of 45 km, six times — at which stone does it stand, and which operation's jump model is this? **COMPETENCY:** Reading a real Indian highway as a number line with origin, direction and movements, including the failed landing.

**APPLICATION:** The school's maths club builds a 0–30 number-line mat for the junior classes and writes an instruction booklet. Write the booklet's three core pages: (i) the STANDING page — how to find your address on the mat (origin, one mark per number, right means greater), with the worked example of standing "at 17"; (ii) the WALKING page — how to add and subtract by walking, with two worked moves (9 + 13 and 22 − 15) and the left-edge rule; (iii) the JUMPING page — how to multiply by equal jumps and divide by the reach question, with one worked pair (4 × 7 and 28 ÷ 4) and the between-marks warning for 29 ÷ 4. **COMPETENCY:** Writing instructional material that teaches the line's three skills — standing, walking, jumping — to younger students, with worked examples and honest warnings.

**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** A student's revision card reads: "0 is not a number. The number line ends at the arrowhead. There is always a whole number between any two whole numbers. Successor of any number n is n + 10 if you jump by tens. Subtraction always has an answer." Write the critique: each claim corrected with this node's mechanism, and the one-line principle the whole card violates.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "(a) Write the successor of 9,99,99,999 and the predecessor of 10,00,00,000, and state the relationship between the two answers. (b) How many whole numbers lie strictly between 10,046 and 10,946? (c) A token walks: 12 + 9 − 17, then doubles its address (×2). Where does it land? Write one bracketed expression for the whole journey. (d) Complete the closure table: 8 + 0; 8 × 0; 0 ÷ 8; 8 − 8; 8 − 11; 8 ÷ 0 — answer or 'no whole-number answer'/'forbidden', one line of reason each. (e) State the two gaps of the whole-number line that the next lesson's synthesis fills, naming the families that will fill them." Answer as expected in a Class 6 CISCE-style paper.
A student says 0.333… is not a rational number because it never ends. Evaluate this claim.
Solve: (-5) + 3/4 - 1.25. Express answer as a fraction in simplest form.
If a number is both a terminating decimal and a fraction with denominator 8, what can you say about its numerator?
A recipe needs 2.5 kg flour. You have 5/2 kg. Do you have enough? Explain.
Simplify: (3/4) ÷ (-2/5) + 1.2. Express as a decimal.

You must carry to school (a) 200 g of sugar and (b) 200 mL of water. Explain, using the characteristics of solids and liquids, why the sugar goes in a paper packet but the water needs a leak-proof bottle.
Three students measure the width of the same blackboard by handspan and report 14, 16 and 15 spans. Explain fully why the answers differ and what this demonstrates about body-based units.

A student writes: "My science book is 24 units long." State the two separate defects in this statement as a measurement, and rewrite it into a proper measurement of a typical Class 6 science book, explaining each addition.

A doctor's tape measures a baby as "50 cm at birth" and the health card of an older child reads "1.25 m". Convert both to centimetres, and state why the health-card system uses cm for newborns and m for school children — connecting the choice to the unit-ladder principle of this node.

In the past-paper pattern: (a) Define measurement. (b) Why must a measurement carry a unit? (c) A wall is measured as 5 m 40 cm. Express this in centimetres and in metres (as a single figure). (d) State two qualities of a standard unit, with one line on how the metre shows each quality.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) Define mass. (b) Name its SI unit. (c) Convert 3.75 kg into grams and 4500 mg into grams. (d) Give one example each from daily life of a mass naturally stated in kg, in g and in mg.

A sealed steel flask contains 200 g of water. The water is frozen into ice, and later melts back to water, all inside the sealed flask. State the flask-plus-contents mass at each of the three stages with reasons, and identify the one everyday circumstance in which the reading *would* change.

A courier parcel is priced by slab: up to 2 kg, 2–5 kg, and above 5 kg. The parcel contains a books bundle of 1 kg 700 g, a cloth bundle of 900 g and a steel box of 2 kg 100 g. Find which slab applies, showing all conversions, and state what single arithmetic discipline decided the slab.

In the past-paper pattern: (a) Define mass and name its SI unit. (b) A water bottle holds 1 L of water of mass 1000 g. Express the mass in kg and in mg. (c) A shopkeeper's mixed stock shows 2 kg 400 g of tea and 850 g of coffee. Find the total in grams and in kilograms. (d) State one reason each why medicines are dosed in mg and vegetables sold in kg.

A student measures a pencil with a plastic ruler and reports 16 cm, but the pencil laid against a better scale reads 15 cm. The student insists the reading was taken carefully. Diagnose the most likely cause of the extra centimetre and state the alignment discipline that prevents it.
Evaluate the claim: "The centimetre should be abandoned for the millimetre, since millimetres give more exact answers — 150 mm is more precise than 15 cm."

In the CISCE examination style: (a) How many centimetres make one metre? (b) How many millimetres make one centimetre? (c) Convert 3 m 45 cm into centimetres. (d) Name the two alignment precautions to observe while measuring an object in cm with a ruler.

A tailor's tape is stretched slightly by years of use, so every "centimetre" on it is really 1.02 true centimetres. A customer orders "200 cm" of ribbon from this tape. How many true centimetres of ribbon arrive, and what does the case teach about certification of instruments?

A wall calendar is 45 cm tall and 30 cm wide, and it hangs with its bottom edge 110 cm above the floor. Using cm throughout, find the height of the calendar's top edge above the floor, and then decide — with reasons — which rung (mm, cm, m) each of three follow-up questions about the same wall should use: (i) how far the top edge is from the ceiling, (ii) whether a 60 cm shelf fits under the calendar, (iii) the thickness of the calendar's hanging wire.

In the past-paper pattern: (a) State the relation of the centimetre to the metre and to the millimetre. (b) A strip is measured as 2 dm 8 cm; express it in cm and in mm. (c) During measurement, why must the eye be directly above the final mark? (d) A student measures a notebook as 24 cm with a ruler whose lead-in is 1 cm; state the true length and the rule the student violated.
State the fixed relation between the inch and the centimetre, and convert: (i) 4 inches to cm, (ii) 12.7 cm to inches.

A shop advertises a "32-inch TV". Explain what the 32 inches measures, convert the figure to centimetres, and state why the shop keeps inches while the carpenter building the TV cabinet works in centimetres.

A bangle-maker sizes bangles in inches, and a customer's wrist measures 22 cm around. The maker's size chart says: size "2-4" means 2.5 inches inner diameter. Decide which chart size comes closest to fitting, showing the full translation, and state the precaution the customer should insist on.

Design a classroom activity in which students discover the 2.54 relation themselves using a dual-marked ruler and a table of paired readings, and state the expected table, the students' inference and the teacher's closing correction.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) Define the inch by its exact metric relation. (b) Convert 6 inches to centimetres. (c) Convert 25.4 cm to inches. (d) Name two Indian goods commonly sized in inches.

A student measures a doorway with a dual tape and writes: "Width = 36 in = 91.44 cm; Height = 78 in = 198.12 cm." A new sofa is listed as "90 cm wide, 195 cm high". Will it pass through? Show all working and identify the one trap the student's figures invite.

Evaluate the statement: "Because 1 inch = 2.54 cm exactly, converting a list of inch measurements to cm and then adding them gives exactly the same result as adding them in inches first and converting the total."

Compare the centimetre scale and the inch scale of a dual ruler under three heads: (a) how each unit divides into its own subdivisions, (b) which trades anchor to which scale in India, and (c) what fixed relation converts between them. Then state why a "15 cm" line on the cm edge is not found exactly under any inch number on the inch edge.

In the past-paper pattern: (a) State the exact inch–centimetre relation. (b) A door frame is 6.5 ft high — given 1 ft = 12 inches, express the height in inches and then in cm. (c) Why do Indian markets continue to use inches for some goods? (d) A student translates 10 inches as 25 cm. Compute the true figure and the size of the error as a percentage.
State the exact relations of the foot with the inch and the centimetre, and convert: (i) 4 ft to inches, (ii) 4 ft to cm, (iii) 91.44 cm to feet.
A cousin says she is "5 foot 3". Write this in the ′ ″ notation, unpack it into total inches, translate it into centimetres, and explain what the figure 5.3 ft would wrongly claim.

A tailor measures a school uniform shelf as 6 ft 4 in long. The storeroom wall space marked for it is 195 cm. Decide with full working whether the shelf fits, and state the clearance or shortfall in cm.

Design a classroom activity in which students verify the relation 1 ft = 30.48 cm themselves using a dual-scale foot-rule and a height chart, and state the predicted table, the students' inference, and the teacher's correction for the pair whose row disagrees.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) Define the foot through its exact relations with the inch and the centimetre. (b) Convert 7 ft to cm. (c) Convert 182.88 cm to feet. (d) Name two Indian situations where feet are the natural unit, and one where centimetres are.

A door frame is 6 ft 9 in tall. Three boxes must pass through upright: Box A is labelled 200 cm, Box B is "78 in", Box C is "6 ft 6 in". Convert everything to centimetres, rank the boxes by ease of passage, and identify which single translation, if botched, would wrongly reverse the ranking of B and C.

State one situation where reporting a length in feet-and-inches (mixed form) is the right choice, one where a decimal in feet (e.g., 5.5 ft) is right, and one where centimetres are right. In each, say who reads the figure and what they do with it.

Evaluate: "Converting 5 ft 8 in to cm by (i) unpacking to inches then ×2.54, or (ii) converting the feet to cm and the inches to cm separately and adding, must give the same answer — and this stays true no matter how the steps are grouped."

Compare the inch and the foot under three heads: (a) what fixed number joins them and why the traditional ladder feels "un-decimal"; (b) which everyday Indian measures are said in inches versus feet; (c) how a length given in one converts to the other in each direction. Then explain why "6 ft 5 in" and "5 ft 6 in" must never be read as the same figure even though both use the digits 5 and 6.

In the past-paper pattern: (a) State the two exact relations of the foot. (b) A basketball player stands 6 ft 7 in; convert this height to centimetres. (c) A ceiling is 240 cm high; express its height in feet and inches, and state whether the player in (b) can stand upright under it. (d) A student computes (b) as 6.7 × 30.48 = 204.216 cm; compute the correct figure and the size of the error in cm, and name the misconception revealed.
Convert, showing the factor used at each step: (i) 7 m to cm, (ii) 540 cm to m, (iii) 3.06 km to m, (iv) 48 mm to cm.

A shopkeeper sells ribbon from a 12 m roll. A customer buys three pieces: 250 cm, 1 m 80 cm and 750 mm. Convert all pieces to centimetres, find the total sold, and state how much ribbon remains on the roll in metres.
Evaluate the claim: "Conversions only change the number, so a measurement expressed in a different unit is a different measurement — 2 m and 200 cm are two lengths that happen to be equal."

An NCC parade ground is 120 m long. A drill manual printed abroad says the cadets must march "a total of 1/4 km each morning". Convert the manual's distance to metres, express it as lengths of the ground, and state how many complete ground-lengths make up the morning's march and what leftover distance (in m) remains.
Design a 10-minute classroom drill that trains the direction rule, including its question format, its marking scheme, and the specific follow-up for a student who fails three items in a row.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) State the relations that connect kilometre, metre and centimetre. (b) Convert 4.5 km to cm, showing each step. (c) A ribbon is 127 cm long; express its length in inches. (d) Why must lengths be converted to a common unit before addition? Answer with one example.

A student solves "add 2 ft 9 in and 1 ft 8 in" by converting each to decimals (2.9 ft + 1.8 ft = 4.7 ft) and reports 4 ft 7 in. Find the correct sum, quantify the error, and explain exactly where the student's method went wrong.
Arrange in ascending order and convert each to millimetres first: 0.5 m, 40 cm 5 mm, 3 in, 0.04 km, 1 ft 1 in. Then state which pair was closest and how close.

Compare the metric ladder and the traditional bridges as conversion systems under three heads: (a) the numbers that join their rungs; (b) how mixed figures behave (3 m 45 cm vs 5 ft 6 in) when written as decimals; (c) which system the pencil prefers for chaining many steps. Then state the one habit that makes the traditional system as safe as the metric.

In the past-paper pattern: (a) State the exact relations between metre, centimetre and inch. (b) A curtain rod is 4 ft 2 in; find its length in cm. (c) Two shelves measure 95 cm and 1 m 8 cm; which is longer and by how many cm? (d) A student converts (b) as 4.2 × 30.48 = 128.016 cm; compute the correct length and the error in cm, and name and explain the misconception in one sentence.
Evaluate the claim: "The pencil is 15 cm long — that is a fact. So 150 mm and 0.15 m are also facts about the pencil, and all three statements are equally useful in every situation."

A new student's height is needed for four purposes: the clinic chart, the family's speech, the tailor's uniform record and the school's registration form. The nurse measures 148.6 cm. State the figure each register should carry, converting where needed, and explain why the registration form's blank labelled "Height (cm)" must not be filled as "1.486".

A student estimates the classroom's length as "about 8 strides" and, with a 70 cm stride, predicts 5.6 m. The tape later reads 7.42 m. Diagnose the estimate's failure precisely, then show how a second estimate built on a different reference would have caught it.

Three students report the same corridor: "12 m", "1200 cm", "1.2 km". At most one can be right. Convert all to one unit, identify which is honest, and reconstruct the specific slip each wrong reporter made.

In the past-paper pattern: (a) State, with one-line reasons, appropriate units for: the thickness of a cycle spoke, the length of a notebook, the height of a water tank, the distance between two villages. (b) A student reports the tank as "0.008 km". Re-express this in metres and comment on the choice. (c) Explain, with an example, why the same length may be correctly reported in two different units. (d) A carpenter estimates a shelf at "three hand-spans of 20 cm" but measures 55 cm. Compute the estimate and the gap, and name the reference discipline that would have prevented the drift.
Describe, step by step, how to measure the length of a pencil to the nearest millimetre with a 30 cm ruler whose ends are intact, and state the exact wording of the recorded result.

A key is measured with a ruler whose zero end is snapped off. The key's head starts at the 1.0 cm graduation and its tip ends at the 4.6 cm graduation. Find the key's length, and explain why the answer is as trustworthy as one from an intact ruler.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) State two advantages of a measuring tape over a ruler. (b) What is the smallest value a standard school ruler can measure reliably, and what is this property called? (c) A cloth strip is measured from the 2.0 cm mark and its far end lies at the 35.4 cm mark. State its length with the working. (d) Name the error caused by viewing a scale from the side and state its prevention.

Two students measure the same notebook with the same ruler. Student P reads 23.9 cm; Student Q reads 24.4 cm. The notebook's true length is 23.9 cm. Diagnose the most likely single cause of Q's excess, state the check that confirms it, and explain why "Q measured more carefully" cannot be the explanation.
