In the CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Define speed and state the formula relating speed, distance and time. (2 marks) (b) A boy cycles to school 4.5 km away in 18 minutes. Convert 18 minutes to hours (as a fraction of 60) and calculate his average speed in km/h. (2 marks) (c) On the return trip he averages 13.5 km/h. Find the return time in minutes. (2 marks) (d) The boy's total outing (both trips plus 20 min at school) spans 56 minutes. Compute his average speed for the whole outing and explain, using the totals law, why it is NOT 15 km/h. (2 marks) (e) A train must average 60 km/h to keep its slot but is delayed 10 min at a station partway. Explain, with the totals relation, what its running speed must do, and state the one quantity the driver cannot create more of. (2 marks)

A 100 mL cylinder holds water. (a) Describe, step by step, how a student should read the volume. (b) What is the meniscus, and which line of it is read for water — with the reason? (c) The student reads 46 mL; the teacher, reading the same cylinder correctly, says 44. Name the likeliest fault and explain the physics-free geometry behind it.

The class demonstration: 60 mL of water is measured in the cylinder and then poured into the beaker. (a) Predict, with the geometry of narrow and wide vessels, roughly how tall the water column stands in each (cylinder inner diameter about 2.4 cm; beaker inner diameter about 6 cm; use height ≈ volume ÷ cross-section area, with A = πr², π ≈ 3.14). (b) Explain from your numbers why the cylinder can carry fine marks and the beaker cannot. (c) State what each instrument may honestly claim about the same 60 mL.

A pharmacist must measure 8 mL of syrup, and a class monitor must prepare 500 mL of salt solution for a practical. (a) Which instrument serves each, and why — with the matching rule stated generally? (b) Estimate the worst error each would suffer if the WRONG instrument were used (beaker marks every 25 mL; cylinder marks every 1 mL), and what that error means for the syrup dose and the solution.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) Why is the cylinder preferred over the beaker for measuring a definite volume of a liquid? (2 marks) (b) State the three precautions for reading a graduated cylinder correctly. (3 marks) (c) A cylinder initially holds water up to 50 mL. Some water is poured out and the new reading, taken correctly, is 31 mL. Find the volume poured out. (1 mark) (d) The same pouring is done a second time by a student who reads the final level with his eyes well above the meniscus and records 35 mL. Explain what his error does to his computed delivered volume and in which direction it errs. (2 marks) (e) Name one measurement task for which the beaker is the RIGHT instrument, and justify the coarseness of its marks rather than apologising for it. (2 marks)

A narrow 50 mL cylinder and a wide 250 mL beaker both hold "50 mL" of the same coloured water — the cylinder read exactly at the 50 mark, the beaker read "about 50" between its 25 mL marks. (a) Compute the height of the column in each if the cylinder's inner radius is 1.2 cm and the beaker's is 3.5 cm (A = πr², π ≈ 3.14). (b) A drop of about 0.5 mL is added to each. Compute each level's rise and say which instrument CERTIFIES the addition and which cannot see it. (c) State the design rule this comparison proves about where fine marks are physically possible.

A chemistry practical needs 40 mL of dilute acid in EACH of six test racks. The storekeeper issues one 100 mL measuring cylinder (1 mL marks) and one 1 L reagent bottle with no marks, and the class has one 250 mL beaker (25 mL marks). (a) Write the full procedure the class should follow to set up all six racks, using each instrument for what it is best at. (b) Where exactly does the cylinder's precision get spent, and where is approximation acceptable? (c) A student proposes measuring 40 mL by filling the beaker to "one-third above the 25 mark". Evaluate the proposal with numbers.

Design the school's "measuring mela" stall for younger visitors: three stations where a Class 6 docent teaches visitors to (1) read a meniscus correctly, (2) feel parallax physically, and (3) choose the right instrument. Specify each station's apparatus, the 30-second script, the visitor's hands-on action, and the take-home token (a sentence on a card) each station awards. Keep every script line free of jargon a 7-year-old would not own.

Evaluate each claim TRUE or FALSE with the reason: (i) A 500 mL single-mark flask is more precise than a 500 mL beaker for delivering exactly 500 mL. (ii) Reading the meniscus from above always inflates the volume. (iii) Two students reading the same still cylinder at the same eye level must get the same number.

In the CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Name the instrument you would use to measure exactly 45 mL of water, and state TWO precautions for reading it. (2 marks) (b) A graduated cylinder contains 62 mL of water. A stone is lowered in and the reading becomes 71 mL. Find the volume of the stone, and state the principle used. (2 marks) (c) Why does the same 30 mL of oil look "bigger" in a wide beaker than in a narrow cylinder, and which instrument's reading of it is more trustworthy? (2 marks) (d) A student records a beaker reading as "27 mL". State what is wrong with this record and write the honest form of the same observation. (2 marks) (e) The lab's 100 mL cylinder is dropped and its base cracks invisibly; it now leaks 1 mL per minute. Describe a quick test with timing that exposes the leak, and state what the test must hold constant. (2 marks)

A graduated cylinder holds water up to 60 mL. A stone tied to a thread is lowered in fully; bubbles are tapped off; the new reading, taken correctly, is 73 mL. (a) Find the stone's volume. (b) The stone is replaced by three SMALLER stones whose combined volume you expect to be the same; predict the final reading if they are all immersed in the same water, and justify with the principle. (c) State the unit of the answer in two equivalent forms.

A group reports a key's volume as 9 cm³ by immersion. On repeat, done slowly and carefully, it reads 6 cm³. For each of these faults — (i) the key was lifted partially out while the final reading was taken, (ii) water had splashed out during the first lowering, (iii) a visible bubble clung to the key's bow through the first reading — say whether it could EXPLAIN the first (larger) reading, the second (smaller) reading, neither, or both, with the direction each fault pushes.

(a) Write, as a numbered process, the graph-paper method for the area of a leaf — compact, but complete enough that a student who missed the earlier lesson could execute it. (b) A traced leaf sorts as F = 18, M = 7, H = 4, L = 11. Finish the process and give the area. (c) State the one deep similarity and the one deep difference between the water-rise process and the grid-count process.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) How is the volume of an irregular solid, insoluble in water, determined in the laboratory? State the principle involved. (2 marks) (b) A cylinder reads 40 mL before and 49 mL after a glass marble is immersed. Find the marble's volume. (1 mark) (c) A cork floats; describe the two-reading procedure that measures its volume, with the arithmetic of a worked set of readings. (3 marks) (d) Two errors gave a stone's volume as 20 cm³ instead of the true 15: first attempt, water splashed while the stone was being dropped in; second attempt, the stone was not fully submerged. For EACH attempt state whether it explains the error, with the direction. (2 marks) (e) A 3 × 2 × 2 cm iron block is immersed instead of being computed by formula. Predict the rise, and state what the agreement of the two methods would demonstrate. (2 marks)

A class has no cylinder free for the day, only a 500 mL home-measuring jug (marks every 50 mL) and a small 50 mL medicine cup (marks every 5 mL). They must measure a 12 cm³ bolt. (a) Which vessel measures, and why does the jug's failure teach the same lesson as the beaker's did? (b) Write the two-reading procedure with the actual numbers if the cup starts at 25 mL. (c) The bolt is too long to lie fully under water in the cup — describe the lawful fix that keeps the method honest, and name the general principle it applies.

An ice cube floats in a cylinder of water; a student insists on the sinker method, but the ice melts slowly during the work. (a) Compute the ice's volume from: sinker alone 46 mL; sinker + ice 54 mL — taken quickly. (b) A second attempt is slow: by the time the pair-reading is taken, a part of the ice (2 cm³ of it) has melted. State the reading obtained and the volume the careless computer would wrongly report. (c) State the general rule about subject stability that this node's methods silently assume, with one other example of a subject that breaks it.

Design the school's "Volume Mela" event for Class 5 visitors (next year's students): four stations — a stone of secret volume, a floater (cork), a regular block handshake, and a leaf — where visitors MEASURE and the docents AUDIT. Specify each station's apparatus, the visitor's task, the docent's audit question, and the secret answer the stations keep sealed. State the one rule that keeps the mela honest when a visitor's number disagrees with the seal.

In the CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Describe how you would find the volume of an irregular solid, insoluble in water, using a measuring cylinder. State the principle of the method. (3 marks) (b) Initial reading 32 mL; after immersing a glass stopper the reading is 41 mL. Find the volume of the stopper. (1 mark) (c) The stopper is replaced by a cork of expected smaller volume. Explain why a DIRECT immersion of the cork cannot measure it, and outline the two-reading method that can, with a set of consistent readings and the arithmetic. (3 marks) (d) During the stopper's immersion, a student's final reading was taken (i) before bubbles were tapped off and (ii) in a repeat, after the stopper accidentally splashed water out while being dropped in. For each, state the direction of the error in the computed volume. (2 marks) (e) State ONE situation from daily life where measuring a volume by rise-of-level is used, naming the quantity the rise reports. (1 mark)

An aluminium block of edges 5 cm, 2 cm and 2 cm pulls 54 g on a balance. (a) Run the full three-step process with every intermediate line. (b) Predict the block's behaviour in water, with the comparison that decides it. (c) A second aluminium block of the same stock measures 10 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm — find its density WITHOUT new arithmetic beyond one multiplication, and name the property that permits the shortcut.

One laboratory bench reports the density of aluminium blocks as 2.9 g/cm³ all morning, while every other bench reports 2.7 ± 0.1. The bench group insists "our blocks are just heavier aluminium". (a) Diagnose with the constancy argument and name the two most likely bench faults. (b) For each fault, state the direction it pushes the density and a ten-second test that convicts or acquits it. (c) The teacher weighs the SAME block on a good bench: 50.0 g; the suspect bench says 54.0 g. Complete the diagnosis.

A wooden block measures 10 cm × 6 cm × 5 cm and masses 180 g. (a) Compute its density. (b) Predict its water behaviour with the comparison. (c) The block is sanded down evenly by 0.5 cm on EVERY face (each dimension loses 1 cm total): recompute mass and density of what remains, using the fingerprint law — and state which quantity changed and which did not.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) Name the two instruments needed to measure the density of a rectangular metal block and state what each provides. (1 mark) (b) A block measures 4 cm × 2.5 cm × 2 cm and masses 210 g. Calculate its volume and its density. (2 marks) (c) The reference table reads: iron 7.8, copper 8.9, silver 10.5 (g/cm³). Identify the metal of the block in (b), then find the mass of a second block of the SAME metal whose volume is 30 cm³. (2 marks) (d) The balance used in (b) had a +5 g zero offset. Recompute the true density and state the direction and size of the error in the reported value. (2 marks) (e) State two precautions for the scale-measurement of the edges and one for the balance. (3 marks)

A student measures a wooden block's edges as 10.0, 6.0 and 5.0 cm and its mass as 180 g, computing 0.6 g/cm³. Her partner, checking, measures the SAME edges as 10.2, 6.1 and 5.1 cm ("the block is a bit bigger than you think"). (a) Compute the partner's volume and density with the same mass. (b) Compute the percentage difference in volume and in density caused by that 2–3% edge spread. (c) State the honest conclusion about how edge-reading differences propagate into the final fingerprint, and what the pair should record.

The class must certify a dry pine block (reference 0.5 g/cm³) but the only free balance is the kitchen scale from the home-ec room, which reads in 5 g steps. The block's true mass is about 150 g; edges 10 × 6 × 5 cm (300 cm³). (a) What density values can the kitchen scale actually produce for this block (list the neighbouring possible readings and their densities)? (b) Compute the finest precision the scale allows here, and compare with a 1 g-step balance. (c) State the general rule about instrument fineness and the fingerprint's decimal, and decide whether the kitchen scale can certify 0.5 honestly.

In the CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Describe, in order, how you would measure the density of a rectangular wooden block, naming the instruments and stating ONE precaution for each instrument. (3 marks) (b) A block measures 12 cm × 4 cm × 2.5 cm and masses 72 g. Calculate its volume and density. (2 marks) (c) Using your answer, find the mass of a larger block of the SAME wood measuring 18 cm × 6 cm × 5 cm. (2 marks) (d) The balance used in (b) carried a +4 g zero offset. Recompute the true density, state the direction of the reported error, and express it as a percentage of the true value. (2 marks) (e) The block in (c) is dropped into water. Predict and justify its behaviour, and state what changes in your prediction if the wood is waterlogged after a long soak (absorbed water adds 40 g of mass at unchanged outer volume). (1 mark)

What does a speed value (like 5 km/h) physically state about a mover? Place these on the everyday speed ladder from slowest to fastest, with an approximate km/h for each: express train, brisk walk, jet aircraft, school bus in city traffic, garden snail, leisure cyclist.

A student claims: "5 km/h must be a slow speed — it's such a small number." Evaluate the claim by giving FOUR everyday settings where 5 km/h carries four different meanings, and state the general principle about speed values this comparison teaches.

During a school trip, the class watches three movers cover the same 300 m flyover: the bus they ride (15 s), a passing cyclist (45 s), and — alongside on the service path — a jogger (90 s). (a) Compute all three speeds in m/s and rank them. (b) Back in the bus, a student says "the cyclist is faster than us — he passed us while we were stopped at the toll". Write the speed-literacy verdict on this claim. (c) State the two-question test ("same kind? same stretch?") that settles any playground 'faster' quarrel.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) Define speed and name its common everyday unit for vehicles. (2 marks) (b) A school bus covers its 6 km morning route in 12 minutes. Express 12 minutes in hours (as a fraction) and compute the bus's average speed in km/h. (2 marks) (c) A student walks the last 500 m from the bus stop in 6 minutes. Compute the walking speed in km/h and state whether it matches the "brisk walking" rung of about 5 km/h. (2 marks) (d) The bus's speedometer showed values from 0 to 45 during the route. Reconcile this with your answer to (b). (2 marks) (e) Give one everyday situation where a person CHOOSES a lower rung of the speed ladder voluntarily, and the reason that makes the lower rung the right one. (2 marks)

An escalator carries standing riders at about 0.5 m/s (1.8 km/h). A student walks UP the same escalator at her normal 1.5 m/s walking pace relative to the steps. (a) Find her speed relative to the building and place both speeds on the ladder. (b) Her friend stands still on the escalator; another friend walks on the STAIRS beside at 1.5 m/s. Rank the three girls as seen from the building, with reasons. (c) A bystander says "the walker on the escalator and the walker on the stairs move at the same speed — both are walking". Give the speed-literacy verdict with numbers.

The school's "Green Route" project wants students to choose the lowest-carbon way to reach a museum 8 km away: walk (5 km/h), cycle (13 km/h), public bus (25 km/h including waits) or family car (30 km/h in traffic). (a) Compute the travel time for each mode. (b) The project's rule is "lowest carbon per student wins, ties broken by time". Write the ranking you would expect and justify without numbers for carbon (walk/cycle near-zero, bus shared, car highest). (c) A student proposes "the car wins — it's fastest". Give the project-rule verdict on the proposal and the one clause the rule would need if the museum visit were time-critical.

Evaluate each claim TRUE or FALSE with the reason: (i) A cheetah's top speed and a school bus's route average are the same KIND of number. (ii) If two movers have equal average speeds over a day, they must have been side by side at noon. (iii) On a one-way 5 km lane, riding at 10 km/h instead of 5 doubles your arrival earliness by exactly 2×.

In the CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Define average speed and write the relation used to compute it. (2 marks) (b) A delivery boy cycles 3 km to a society in 15 minutes, waits 5 minutes at the gate, and cycles back by a 4 km route in 24 minutes. Convert each riding time to hours (as fractions) and compute his average speed for the WHOLE outing. (3 marks) (c) His cycle's speedometer-style app shows bursts up to 18 km/h. Reconcile with your answer. (1 mark) (d) The society gate has a "cyclists dismount" board. In ladder language, state what pace the board demands and why a place may cap a mover below its capability. (2 marks) (e) If he must make the return trip in 20 minutes flat on the same 4 km route, compute the required average and say whether the "about 13 km/h" leisure-cycling rung can deliver it. (2 marks)

The notebook-cover station: edges measured 24 cm and 18 cm. (a) Compute the area by formula. (b) The count check samples three full rows across the cover on a laid centimetre grid — how many squares per row, and how does the sample extend to the full check? (c) A group reports the formula answer as "432" with no unit and a count check of "about 430 because we didn't count all rows". Mark their work: what is right, what is missing, and what does the count check honestly certify?

At the palm station, Group A traces and counts 61 cm² for Student P's palm; Group B, tracing the SAME hand an hour later, gets 64 cm². The groups suspect fraud. You are the checker. (a) List the four lawful causes of a 3 cm² spread between honest tracings. (b) Name the two unlawful causes worth ruling out, with the check for each. (c) Write the verdict sentence the class record should carry for Student P's palm.

Design a NEW station for the area activities: the school's footpath tiles. The square tiles are 30 cm on a side, and a section of path is 12 tiles long and 8 tiles wide, with one tile cracked diagonally in half (both halves still in place). (a) Compute the path's total area by the tile-count route, treating the cracked tile as one full tile plus a discussion. (b) Convert to m². (c) State what this station teaches that the notebook station cannot, and one question the checker should ask every group.

The class must compare the heat-absorbing readiness of two dark surfaces for a solar-oven corner: the trapezium-shaped flap (parallel sides 20 cm and 30 cm, distance between them 10 cm) and the rectangular flap (25 cm × 10 cm). The class owns only the treaty and the rectangle formula. (a) Devise the lawful comparison the class can actually run — including how to handle the trapezium with the tools allowed — and state the expected verdict. (b) A student proposes "measure their perimeters instead — same tools". Evaluate.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) A student measures a desk top as 1.2 m by 60 cm. Convert both to centimetres and find the area in cm² and in m². (3 marks) (b) On the laid grid check, three sampled rows of the desk's photocopied overlay each counted 120 squares. State what this confirms and compute the total. (2 marks) (c) The same desk is estimated by a group as "about 0.5 m²". Assess the estimate and name the systematic cause such under-guesses usually have. (2 marks) (d) A broken tile of 900 cm² nominal size has a corner chipped off — about one-eighth of its area. Find the remaining area, and state which measuring route on the activities' list would certify the chip best. (2 marks) (e) State ONE reason the activities make groups rotate the four roles rather than letting the best counter count every station. (1 mark)

At the circle station, the class traces a 10-rupee coin-sized lid (2 cm across) and treaty-counts 3 cm²; the mathematics-room hint says a 1 cm-radius circle "wants" about 3.1 cm². A second lid, 6 cm across (radius 3), counts to about 27 against a geometric hint of about 28.3. (a) Compute each lid's treaty shortfall in cm² and as a percentage. (b) The class notices the BIG lid's percentage shortfall is smaller. Give the boundary-geometry reason (think: slivers per cm of edge, and edge per area). (c) State the design rule this station writes for the treaty's honest use.

The class wants the area of the school's uneven asphalt quadrangle for a paint budget. A 1 m² string grid is laid on part of it; the far end is under stacked desks and unreachable. (a) The reachable part grid-counts to 38 m² with a wavy edge; the covered part is roughly rectangular, measured by offset rods as 6 m × 4.5 m. Compute the total and state which part carries which kind of uncertainty. (b) Paint covers 10 m² per litre. State the litre order with the tolerance clause a careful painter writes. (c) The contractor asks: "why not just measure length × breadth of the whole yard?" Give the class answer.

Evaluate each claim TRUE or FALSE with the reason: (i) If two students trace the same leaf and their treaty counts differ by 2 cm², at least one made a mistake. (ii) A rectangle's formula answer and its full square-by-square count must agree exactly. (iii) Cracking a tile into two pieces that stay in place changes the tile's area.

In the CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Describe how the area of an irregular leaf-shaped cut-out may be determined using a graph sheet. State the FOUR counting rules. (3 marks) (b) A student's trace gives: F = 40, M = 12, H = 6, L = 25. Compute the area. (1 mark) (c) A rectangular card measures 12 cm × 8 cm. Its area is first computed by formula and then checked by laying a centimetre grid: rows sampled at 12 squares each across 8 rows. State the check's conclusion and the reason such agreement is forced on rectangles. (2 marks) (d) The same card has a circular hole of radius 1 cm cut in its middle. Compute the card's remaining area, given π ≈ 3.14 — and state which part of the computation is formula-certified and which carries treaty-style uncertainty if the hole were jagged instead of round. (2 marks) (e) Give ONE reason the activities record an estimate column and ONE reason they rotate team roles. (2 marks)

The equal-volume station uses four 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm boxes filled with cotton, crumpled paper, water and sand, massing 80, 150, 1000 and 1500 g. (a) Compute all four densities. (b) A cotton box twice as large (20 × 10 × 10 cm) is added, massing 160 g. Does the density RANKING change? Does the mass ranking? (c) State the licence condition of the equal-volume shortcut, using your answers.

At the equal-volume cube station, a group's hand-feel ranking of the four painted cubes is: iron heaviest, then aluminium, then zinc, then wood lightest. The balance reads: wood 4.8 g, aluminium 21.6 g, zinc 56.8 g, iron 62.4 g (all 2 cm cubes). (a) Compute the four densities and the TRUE ranking. (b) Exactly which pair did the hand mis-order, and why is that pair the expected casualty? (c) State the division of labour between hand and balance this station certifies.

The cut-in-half station: a plasticine block 6 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm masses 43.2 g. (a) Compute its density. (b) Fill the station's table for each half (dimensions, volume, mass, density) and verify the invariance. (c) A student predicts before the cut: "each half will have density 0.6, since it's half the block." Write the verdict the tray of predictions earns this entry, with the arithmetic that teaches it.

The water-line tray presents: the wood cube (0.6), the iron cube (7.8), a sealed hollow plastic box (40 g, outer 10 × 8 × 4 cm), and a lidded tin of pins (90 g, volume 80 cm³). (a) Compute the average density of the box and the tin. (b) Write the four tray verdicts with the deciding comparison. (c) The surprise rows are the floating box and the sinking tin — state the law they jointly demonstrate, and the wrong rule they jointly kill.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) Two sealed identical-looking cubes, P and Q, of the same size (4 cm edge) mass 128 g and 499.2 g. Compute both densities and identify each from: wood 0.6, aluminium 2.7, iron 7.8 (g/cm³). (3 marks) (b) Cube Q is sawn into eight equal small cubes. State the mass, volume and density of each small cube, with the arithmetic that verifies the sawing conserved the material. (3 marks) (c) All nine objects (P, Q whole and Q's eight children) are dropped in water. Give the verdicts with the comparisons. (2 marks) (d) A student claims cube P "should weigh more because it is bigger than the small cubes". Name the confusion and answer it with one number. (2 marks)

The tray's final round uses two sealed tins of identical outer volume (300 cm³ each). Tin X floats with about two-thirds of its volume submerged; tin Y sinks. (a) State tin X's average density from its floating position (the sunken fraction equals the density ratio for water) and compute its mass. (b) Tin Y's mass lies somewhere above a threshold — state the threshold and explain why no exact mass follows from "sinks". (c) A student claims "X and Y are equally dense up to the waterline and then Y just has more stuff". Give the lawful restatement of what IS known about each.

A station extension asks: "the school's water tank floats a hollow sealed marker cube (side 20 cm, mass 960 g). (a) Compute its average density and its sunken fraction in fresh water. (b) Monsoon: the tank's water becomes salt-mixed at 1.1 g/cm³. New sunken fraction? (c) A leak lets 300 cm³ of tank water into the cube. New mass, new average, and does the line climb or fall? Compute and state the general rule for flooding hollow floaters.

Design the "Density Detective" corner for the school fete: visitors receive three sealed identical cubes (2 cm) — one wood, one aluminium, one iron — painted alike, plus a balance, a trough, and one prediction card. The visitor must identify all three WITHOUT computing any division. Specify the lawful procedure (sorting tricks only), the identification logic each step delivers, the one computation the docent performs at the end to certify, and the card's confession line every visitor writes.

Evaluate each claim TRUE or FALSE with the arithmetic or principle: (i) At the equal-volume station, the box with the most AIR inside must be the least dense. (ii) If tin A (500 g, 400 cm³) and tin B (450 g, 300 cm³) are dropped in water, B sinks and A floats. (iii) Two cubes of the same material but different sizes can be separated by the water tray.

In the CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Define density and state the formula. (2 marks) (b) A rectangular block measures 5 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm and masses 108 g. Calculate its volume and density. (2 marks) (c) The block is painted and sealed inside a wrapper of negligible mass and volume; state and justify whether the density, the float verdict in water, or the identification of the material changes. (2 marks) (d) Two identical jars are filled — one with oil (0.9 g/cm³), one with honey (1.4 g/cm³) — to the same 200 cm³ level. Compute the contents' masses and state which jar the hand finds heavier and by how much. (2 marks) (e) Both jars are placed in a large trough of water (jars sealed, walls thin). State the verdict for each with the comparison, and the one clause about what the trough actually measures. (2 marks)

Run the full protocol: (a) A block measures 8 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm and masses 432 g — find its density. (b) A bus covers 18 km in 36 minutes — find its speed in km/h. Show every move, including the check lines.

(a) An iron statue's volume is 250 cm³ (by the water method). Iron's density is 7.8 g/cm³. Find its mass. (b) A cyclist rides at a steady 12 km/h for 45 minutes. Find the distance. (c) State which mask each part wears and why the operation follows.

(a) A 390 g iron block (density 7.8 g/cm³): find its volume. (b) At a steady 15 km/h, how long does a 45 km journey take? (c) Both answers are PARTNER masks — state the common operation and the two unit disciplines each answer must honour.

Comparison round: (a) Two same-size cubes (8 cm³ each): cube X masses 43.2 g, cube Y masses 21.6 g. Which is denser, and by what factor? (b) A walker covers 2.5 km in 30 minutes; a cyclist covers 9 km in 45 minutes. Who is faster, and by what factor? (c) State the drill's rule for lawful comparison verdicts.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) State the formula linking density, mass and volume, and rearrange it to find (i) mass and (ii) volume. (2 marks) (b) A glass slab measures 10 cm × 5 cm × 2 cm and masses 250 g. Calculate its density. (2 marks) (c) Another slab of the same glass has volume 60 cm³; find its mass. (2 marks) (d) A train covers 210 km in 3 h 30 min. Express the time in hours (as a fraction) and compute the average speed. (2 marks) (e) At the speed found in (d), how far does the train travel in 2 hours? Verify your answer with a re-substitution check. (2 marks)

The ladder's trick round: a problem sheet prints "A metal cube of side 5 cm has density 2.7 g/cm³" and asks, in three parts, (a) the mass, (b) the mass of a SAME-METAL cube of side 10 cm WITHOUT reusing the density, (c) the side of a same-metal cube of mass 972 g. Solve all three with mask names, and state the scaling law that connects (a), (b) and (c) for same-metal cubes.

A family problem: "Appa drives 24 km to the office at a steady 48 km/h. Amma cycles the same route, leaving at the same time, at 12 km/h. Their child takes the school bus, which covers 30 km at 40 km/h with 10 min of stops." (a) Compute all three travel times (bus: driving + stops). (b) If all three must reach their destinations by 8:00 a.m., write each one's latest departure time. (c) Amma proposes leaving 10 min early "to buy flowers on the way". How many minutes of flower time can she buy without being late?

Evaluate each claim TRUE or FALSE with the arithmetic or principle: (i) If block A has twice the volume and twice the mass of block B, the two have equal densities. (ii) A trip's average speed can exceed its highest steady driving speed if the route is short. (iii) In the mixed problem, the trolley's 72 kg load makes the 3 km trip take longer than an empty trolley would take.

In the CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) A cubical block has side 6 cm and mass 756 g. Calculate its volume and density. (2 marks) (b) What mass of the same metal forms a cuboid of 9 cm × 6 cm × 4 cm? (2 marks) (c) A cyclist covers 8 km in the first half hour, stops 10 minutes, then covers 6 km in the next 20 minutes. Compute the average speed for the whole outing in km/h, with the time as an exact fraction. (3 marks) (d) At the average found in (c), how long would a 21 km trip take? Give the answer in hours and minutes. (2 marks) (e) State ONE check that would have caught each of these two classic slips: (i) dividing volume by mass in (a); (ii) using 30 minutes as the second leg's time in (c). (1 mark)

The delivery relay: one 100 mL cylinder is filled to 60 mL. The relay must deliver 25 mL into beaker A, then 10 mL into beaker B, then 40 mL into beaker C. (a) Write the three labelled rows (INITIAL, TARGET-FINAL, DELIVERED) for each delivery as they should appear on the record sheet. (b) The final reading after beaker C is 0 mL is impossible — compute the true final state and what remains. (c) The B-team pours past its target (final 23 instead of 25). What was delivered to B, what remains for C, and what does the relay's design do about the slip?

The shelf holds 10 mL (0.2 mL marks), 100 mL (1 mL marks) and 250 mL (5 mL marks) cylinders. Match each to its job and justify: (a) 6 mL of food colouring for a dye experiment; (b) 80 mL of water for a solution; (c) 220 mL of rinse water. (d) State the general matching rule and the cost of breaking it in each direction (too-fine cylinder for a big job; too-coarse for a small job).

The audit partnership rule: "no cylinder number enters the record until a second reader has called the mark." (a) Write the audit's three steps for a displacement reading. (b) The reader calls 47, the checker calls 48 on the same still level. State the lawful resolutions, in order, and the one resolution that is OUTLAWED. (c) Explain what the partnership rule trains that a solo reader never learns.

In the CISCE examination style: (a) State TWO precautions for reading a liquid level in a graduated cylinder. (2 marks) (b) A cylinder contains 40 mL of water. A glass marble is immersed fully; the new reading is 45 mL. State the volume of the marble. (1 mark) (c) 30 mL of dilute ink is required from a cylinder initially filled to 55 mL. State the reading at which pouring must stop, and the volume delivered. (2 marks) (d) The ink delivered is checked by a small measured beaker and reads only 28 mL. Give the two likeliest causes, and which reading would have revealed each. (2 marks) (e) A 100 mL cylinder is suspected of a hairline crack that leaks slowly. Describe the two-minute test that settles the suspicion and the observation that convicts. (3 marks)

The activity week's oddest job: the class must deliver 5 mL of a precious indicator solution, but only a 100 mL cylinder (1 mL marks) is clean. (a) Write the lawful delivery row and the honest precision claim. (b) The docent offers the alternative: use the UNCLEAN 10 mL cylinder (0.2 mL marks) after rinsing it three times with the indicator itself ("rinse with what you will measure"). Evaluate this alternative against the clean-but-coarse option, with the rinsing logic stated. (c) State the general rule for the fine-instrument-dirty versus coarse-instrument-clean choice.

The week's accident log records three near-misses: (1) a cylinder carried by its lip slipped and chipped the lip; (2) a group stirred dye in the cylinder with a pencil; (3) a group's "water" reading was 3 mL high — the cylinder still held last period's ink film. (a) For each, write the entry in the care poster's format (rule, accident prevented, record consequence prevented). (b) For near-miss 3, compute the error the film would have caused in a delivered-volume row (INITIAL 50, TARGET-FINAL 30) and state which honest habit surfaces it. (c) State why the poster is authored by the CLASS from the log, rather than issued by the teacher.

Design the "Cylinder Trials" — the activity week's certification event where every student earns a "Trusted Reader" badge through three stations: a blind reading (the docent pre-sets a level), a blind delivery (deliver 20 mL judged by the receiving vessel), and a displacement (a sealed tube of known volume 6 cm³). Specify each station's pass standard, the single attempt rule and its reason, the badge's wording, and the one re-test provision for a failed station.

Evaluate each claim TRUE or FALSE with the arithmetic or principle: (i) Delivering 25 mL in two 12.5 mL instalments is more accurate than one 25 mL pour on the same cylinder. (ii) A displacement reading taken with the solid resting on a thread (not touching the bottom) differs from one where it sits on the base. (iii) If the initial reading is taken with the cylinder still swaying from the fill, both readings (initial and final) being taken the same way cancels the error.

In the CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Name the instrument used to measure accurately 28 mL of a liquid and state the reading rule. (2 marks) (b) A measuring cylinder contains 52 mL of water. 28 small identical glass spheres are immersed fully; the reading becomes 70 mL. Find the volume of ONE sphere. (2 marks) (c) The class must deliver 15 mL of dilute acid from a cylinder filled to 40 mL. State the reading at which to stop, the delivered volume, and ONE precaution during the pour. (2 marks) (d) The class's 100 mL cylinder was verified by a certified 100 mL fill and took 96 mL to the brim; a recheck next term gives 96 again. Certify or convict the cylinder, with reasoning. (2 marks) (e) The class record shows a displacement row: INITIAL 45, TARGET-FINAL 60, DELIVERED 15. The teacher returns the sheet. State what is wrong with the row's structure for a displacement entry, and write the corrected row. (2 marks)

A 250 mL beaker (25 mL marks) holds liquid to a point clearly between the 200 and 225 marks, nearer the 225. (a) Write the honest reading and the honest record line. (b) A student records "218 mL". State what is wrong and what the marks CAN certify. (c) The same liquid is poured into the 100 mL cylinder in instalments and reads 210 mL total (read to 1 mL). State what this exercise demonstrates about the two instruments' claims.

The experiment protocol demands "250 mL of water, of which exactly 50 mL goes into the reaction cup". One group runs the whole job in the cylinder (three 100 mL fills to cover 250, then the 50 by difference). (a) Evaluate the group's plan against the coordination protocol, counting the cylinder-fillings spent. (b) Write the protocol's plan for the same job with the row labels (CARRIED / CERTIFIED) filled. (c) State the general division of labour and the one phrase from the record that proves the protocol ran.

Design the "Solution Bar" station: eight groups each need 250 mL of salt water (about 5 g salt per group), prepared at one tap with one cylinder, one balance and two beakers per group. Specify the station's flow plan (which instrument touches which step), the record row per group, the two queue-avoidance moves, and the safety clause about heating if the method says "warm water".

In the CISCE examination style: (a) Why is a beaker preferred over a measuring cylinder for stirring and warming a solution? (2 marks) (b) State the largest volume a 250 mL beaker (marks at 25 mL intervals) can honestly certify, and the form of words its readings must use. (2 marks) (c) A solution must be made with "about 200 mL" of water and exactly 8 g of salt. Name the instrument for each ingredient and the reading discipline for the water. (2 marks) (d) From the prepared solution, exactly 40 mL is required. Name the instrument, write the delivery row (initial 65 mL), and state one precaution. (2 marks) (e) A student warms the solution in the CYLINDER over the flame "because it was already measured in it". State TWO things wrong with this act and the vessel that should have been used. (2 marks)

The coordination protocol meets its edge case: the class must deliver an exact 50 mL of a solution, but the solution is ALREADY in the 250 mL beaker, mixed and stirred, and the only clean cylinder is the 100 mL. The group proposes: "pour from the beaker into the cylinder up to about 60, then fine-adjust to 50 by adding drops from the beaker." (a) Evaluate the proposal against the difference method's honesty and state the lawful delivery row. (b) The drops refuse to cooperate — the level jumps from 49 to 51. State the two lawful fixes. (c) State the general principle about fine-adjustment at coarse-to-fine boundaries that this edge case teaches.

The school fair's "Measurement Café" serves three orders, cooked with the chapter's instruments: Order 1 — "500 mL of lemonade, exact"; Order 2 — "a leaf's area, medium rare"; Order 3 — "the chef's marble's volume, to go". (a) For each order, name the instrument(s), the unit served, and the discipline that guarantees it. (b) A fourth order arrives — "the chef's speed, walking to the stove 8 m away in 6 s" — solve it and name the unit. (c) The café's menu footer reads "no order served without its unit and its vouch". Explain the footer as the chapter's summary in one sentence.

In the CISCE past-paper pattern — the chapter's closing synthesis: (a) Name the instruments you would use to measure: (i) the area of a leaf; (ii) the volume of a glass marble; (iii) the mass of a pencil. (3 marks) (b) A cylinder reads 50 mL; a stone tied to a thread is lowered in and the reading becomes 71 mL. State the stone's volume, and name the property of water that makes this possible. (2 marks) (c) The stone masses 156 g. Compute its density and predict its behaviour in water. (2 marks) (d) A beaker carries 1 L of water for the class and the teacher pours out four certified 150 mL portions by cylinder. State how much water remains in the beaker, and with what claim-size each number in your answer is spoken. (2 marks) (e) State ONE habit common to every measurement in this chapter — from the leaf trace to the trolley problem — and illustrate it in one sentence from any station you choose. (1 mark)
Evaluation: “The five‑kingdom system is outdated; the three‑domain system should be taught instead.” Evaluate this claim for a Class 7 curriculum.
If a culture of *E. coli* doubles every 20 minutes, starting with 200 cells, how many cells will be present after 2 hours?
An Amoeba engulfs a spherical food particle of diameter 5 µm. Estimate the volume of the food vacuole formed, assuming it is spherical (use π ≈ 3.14).

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Draw a labelled diagram of Amoeba showing the following: cell membrane, nucleus, contractile vacuole, food vacuole, pseudopodia. Write one function for each labelled part.” (5 marks)
Answer in CISCE short-answer style: What-are-pseudopodia?-State-any-two-functions-they-perform-in-Amoeba. (2-marks)
If an Amoeba consumes 0.5 µL of O₂ per minute, how many microlitres of O₂ does it consume in 1 hour?
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Describe how oxygen reaches the mitochondria in an Amoeba.” (3 marks)
If an Amoeba divides by binary fission every 20 minutes, how many Amoebae will be present after 1 hour starting from a single cell?
A student measures 12 mL of CO₂ produced by 0.5 g dry mass of *Rhizopus* mycelium in 2 h. Calculate the respiration rate in mL CO₂ h⁻¹ g⁻¹.
If a baker uses 10 g of yeast that doubles every 90 minutes, how many grams of yeast will be present after 4.5 hours assuming no loss?
A student writes 3 examples for Monera, 2 for Protista, 4 for Fungi, 5 for Plantae, and 3 for Animalia. How many total examples did the student write?
You have 10 minutes to make picture cards for 5 kingdoms with 2 examples each. If each card takes 1 minute, can you finish? Show calculation.
Compare the picture card project with the laboratory specimen observation (node 016) in terms of learning outcomes.
During a zoo trip, you record 30 animals: 10 mammals, 8 birds, 5 reptiles, 4 amphibians, 3 fish. Calculate the percentage of vertebrates that are mammals. Show your working.
What is the primary purpose of a kingdom classification chart in a Class 7 biology classroom?
A chart displays the five kingdoms with 3 example organisms per kingdom. How many total example organisms are shown on the chart?
If a teacher wants to add a new example organism to each kingdom on an existing chart that currently has 4 examples per kingdom, how many new organism entries must be added in total?
What is the primary purpose of a biological model in a Class 7 classroom?
A photograph of a bacterium is labelled “Magnification 500×”. If the image of the bacterium measures 5 cm on the photograph, what is the actual length of the bacterium in micrometres?

A student makes a picture card for a mould. The photograph on the card shows a colony diameter of 3 cm. The real colony measured in the lab is 30 mm. What is the scale of the photograph (image : real)?
In an ICSE Class 7 exam, a question asks: “Write the word equation for photosynthesis and name the pigment that captures light energy.” Provide the expected answer.
Design a simple word‑equation‑based story that a Class 7 student could use to explain photosynthesis to a younger sibling.
Answer in CISCE short-answer style: Why-is-light-called-the-energy-source-of-photosynthesis-and-not-a-raw-material? (2-marks)
**APPLICATION:** A farmer wants to boost yield in a greenhouse tomato crop. She considers enriching the air with CO₂ to 800 ppm. List two benefits and one risk of this practice.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain why the rate of photosynthesis does not increase indefinitely with increasing carbon dioxide concentration.” (3 marks)

A student sets up two identical Hydrilla sprigs in test tubes with water. One tube is kept in bright light, the other in darkness. After 30 minutes, the light tube shows many bubbles; the dark tube shows none. Explain the observation using the role of water.
**Application:** Design a fair test to compare the effect of three different watering regimes (daily, every 3 days, weekly) on the rate of oxygen evolution in Hydrilla over a 2‑week period.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Explain why a plant kept in a dark room for 48 hours and then exposed to light shows a delayed onset of oxygen evolution compared with a plant kept in light continuously.”
Multiple‑choice (CISCE past‑paper style): Which pair of wavelengths is most strongly absorbed by chlorophyll a? A) 430 nm and 660 nm B) 500 nm and 600 nm C) 550 nm and 700 nm D) 480 nm and 580 nm
Answer in CISCE short-answer style: State-two-ways-in-which-photosynthesis-is-indispensable-to-animals-that-never-eat-plants. (2-marks)

A student sets up the apparatus but forgets to add the dark control. After 10 minutes she sees bubbles in the collecting tube. She concludes that light is not necessary for photosynthesis. Evaluate her conclusion.
Answer in CISCE short-answer style: Distinguish-between-breathing-and-respiration. (2-marks)
Write the word equation for photosynthesis as taught in Class 7 ICSE Biology.
If a plant uses 12 molecules of carbon dioxide, how many molecules of glucose can be produced according to the word equation? (Assume the simple ratio 6 CO₂ → 1 glucose.)
State the word equation for aerobic respiration in plants as expected in an ICSE Class 7 exam.

If 180 g of glucose (1 mol) undergoes anaerobic alcoholic fermentation in yeast, how many grams of carbon dioxide are released? (Molar masses: glucose = 180 g mol⁻¹, CO₂ = 44 g mol⁻¹; reaction: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂)
Answer in CISCE short-answer style: Name-two-organisms-that-respire-anaerobically-and-state-one-useful-product-of-each. (2-marks)
A Hydrilla plant in a test tube produces 12 mL of oxygen gas in 30 minutes under bright light. Assuming the rate stays constant, how many millilitres of oxygen will it produce in 2 hours?
If a leaf consumes 5 mmol of carbon dioxide per hour during photosynthesis, how many mmol of oxygen are released in the same period, assuming the stoichiometric ratio from the word equation?
Predict the net gas exchange (oxygen and carbon dioxide) for a green plant kept in continuous bright light for 24 hours, assuming temperature and water are optimal.
**HOTS:** A plant is kept in an atmosphere enriched with 5 % CO₂ (normal ~0.04 %) under normal light. Predict how the rates of photosynthesis and respiration will change, and justify your answer.
State the word equation for photosynthesis as taught in Class 7 (no symbols).

**HOTS:** If a plant is kept in an atmosphere with 0.04 % carbon dioxide (current ambient) and then moved to 0.1 % carbon dioxide while light, temperature, and water remain constant, predict the short‑term effect on photosynthetic rate and justify using the concept of limiting factors.
A student runs for 30 minutes in 35 °C heat and loses 600 mL of sweat. If sweat contains 0.9 % NaCl by mass, calculate the mass of sodium chloride lost (assume sweat density ≈ 1 g/mL).
Application: A marathon runner in humid Kolkata loses 3 L of sweat but drinks only 1 L of water. Predict two physiological consequences related to sweat gland function and fluid balance.

If a person’s breathing rate increases from 12 to 20 breaths per minute while tidal volume stays at 500 mL, how does the volume of CO₂ exhaled per minute change, assuming each exhaled breath contains 4 % CO₂?
Apply your knowledge: If a person holds their breath for 30 seconds, what happens to the CO₂ level in their blood and why?
Answer in CISCE short-answer style: Name-the-blood-vessels-and-the-duct-connected-to-a-kidney-and-state-what-each-carries. (2-marks)
A student claims the urinary bladder can hold 2 litres of urine comfortably. Evaluate this claim.

If a person drinks 500 mL of water and the kidneys produce urine at 1 mL/min, approximately how long before the bladder reaches the urge‑to‑void volume of 200 mL? Assume the bladder was empty initially.
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Label the urinary bladder, ureters, and urethra in the given diagram of the human excretory system. State one function of the urinary bladder.” (3 marks)
If a boy’s urethra is about 20 cm long and urine flows at 10 mL/s, how many seconds does it take to pass 200 mL of urine?
A 12‑year‑old boy complains of burning urination and fever of 38.5 °C. List two immediate steps a teacher should advise.
A spherical kidney stone has a diameter of 6 mm. Calculate its approximate volume in cubic millimetres (mm³). Use π ≈ 3.14.

**Application:** A school health camp screens 200 students for kidney‑stone risk factors. 40 students report daily water intake <1 L, 30 report high salt intake, and 10 report both. How many students have at least one of these two risk factors?
Answer in CISCE short-answer style: Where-is-the-spinal-cord-located-and-how-is-it-protected-Name-one-situation-in-which-it-acts-without-awaiting-the-brain. (2-marks)
Answer in CISCE short-answer style: Name-the-three-kinds-of-nerves-according-to-the-work-they-do-stating-the-direction-each-carries-its-messages. (2-marks)
If the average adult brain weighs 1.4 kg and the cerebrum constitutes about 85 % of total brain mass, calculate the approximate mass of the cerebrum in grams.
If the cerebral cortex thickness averages 2.5 mm and the total cortical surface area is about 0.25 m², estimate the volume of grey matter in cubic centimeters.
A Class 7 student learns to play the tabla. After weeks of practice, the strokes become fluid and precisely timed. Which cerebellar process underlies this improvement, and how does it work?

Create: Design a "Flash-Route Corridor" for a class 6 classroom visit using floor chalk, two token lanes, and a far chair labelled BRAIN. It must let children physically run one reflex event with five stations in order, send the brain a second, slower messenger, and end with a chant that fixes the move-first-feel-later order.
Answer in CISCE short-answer style: Define reflex action. Name, in their correct order, the parts of the pathway a reflex message travels. (2 marks)

Application: A homework checker must mark four claims "use", "use with flag", or "reject": (1) a cricketer's sharp slip catch is a reflex action of the spinal cord; (2) the knee-jerk test can work even when the person is fully unaware of the tap; (3) vomiting is a reflex action; (4) reflex actions can be suppressed by strong willpower. For each give the verdict and one line of reason.

CISCE past-paper pattern: "The reflex is the body's bodyguard: untrained, unasked, and always on duty." Examine this statement with reference to (a) the definition and the arc's five stations in order (b) the timing — what moves first and what is felt later, with the reason (c) the centres — which reflexes belong to the cord and which lie higher (d) the verdict and one everyday scene showing the reflex guard at work. (5 marks)

**HOTS:** A researcher discovers a new type of nerve in a deep‑sea fish that conducts impulses at 150 m/s without a myelin sheath. Propose a plausible structural adaptation that could explain this speed.
Describe the role of pollen grains in seasonal allergic rhinitis as expected in a CISCE Class 7 examination answer.

Create: Design a "Mite Hotel Inspector" corner for a class 6 classroom visit using a giant craft mite, five item-cards, and an inspector's stamp. It must teach the three hotel demands, have children "inspect" household items and grant or refuse them a mite-hotel licence, and end with the inspector's sun-rule.
Answer in CISCE short-answer style: What are dust mites? Why are they important in the study of allergies? (2 marks)

Application: A homework checker must mark four claims "use", "use with flag", or "reject": (1) a child allergic to mites is safest sleeping in a friend's house whose bedding is newer; (2) mites themselves are more dangerous than their droppings; (3) freezing a soft toy in a freezer for a day can kill its mites; (4) a mite allergic student should avoid all exercise that raises sweating. For each give the verdict and one line of reason.

CISCE past-paper pattern: "The dust mite turns the world's most comfortable furniture into the allergy story's main address." Examine this statement with reference to (a) the creature defined in one line (b) the three needs it finds in a mattress (c) the mechanism by which comfort becomes allergy (d) the verdict and one practical consequence for a school dormitory in a humid city. (5 marks)
A student with fair skin has a safe UV dose limit of 7 200 UV Index·s. If the UV Index is 9, what is the maximum safe exposure time in minutes? Show your calculation.
If a child plays outside for 25 minutes when the UV Index is 7, calculate the UV exposure dose. Is it above the safe limit of 7 200 UV Index·s?

Create: Design a "Three Doors" wall corner for a class 6 classroom visit using three cardboard door-flaps (MOUTH, NOSE, SKIN), a bag of allergen-cards, and an "inside addresses" chart. It must let children post each allergen-card through its correct door, show that the doors lead to different alarm-places inside, and include at least one card that could use two doors.
Answer in CISCE short-answer style: Through which route do food allergens enter the body? Describe their journey in, and state two places where the reaction typically shows. (2 marks)

Application: A homework checker must mark four claims "use", "use with flag", or "reject": (1) thorough cooking makes every food allergen harmless; (2) a milk-allergic child may safely drink flavoured milk substitutes only if the label says "dairy-free"; (3) a child allergic to eggs reacted to a cake with no visible egg — this proves the label was wrong; (4) food-allergy reactions can involve breathing, not just the gut and skin. For each give the verdict and one line of reason.

CISCE past-paper pattern: "Three doors serve the intruder: the mouth carries its cargo slowly and silently." Examine this statement with reference to (a) the three doors and their cargoes (b) the mouth route's journey inside the body (c) the silence of the door and the loudness of the alarm, with the places it shows (d) the verdict and one practical consequence for the school tiffin break. (5 marks)
A classroom of 40 students has 30 % prevalence of dust‑mite allergy. How many students are likely to show nasal symptoms when the room is swept?
**HOTS:** If a new air‑purifier claims to remove 99 % of particles >0.3 µm, would it significantly reduce nasal allergy symptoms for a child allergic to *Aspergillus* spores (2–5 µm)? Justify.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Describe two structural features of the nasal cavity that help in trapping dust and pollen.” (2 marks)

A student applies a barrier cream before playing in a field with high pollen count. If the cream reduces the effective allergen concentration at the skin surface by 60 %, and the original pollen flux (without cream) is 2 × 10⁻⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹, what is the new flux? Assume flux is directly proportional to surface concentration.

A researcher claims that “since the stratum corneum is only 15 µm thick, any particle smaller than 15 µm will freely diffuse into the dermis.” Using your knowledge of skin structure, evaluate this claim.
A child with known dust mite allergy plays on a carpet for 30 minutes. Describe the sequence of events from allergen contact to visible skin reaction, naming the key cells and mediators involved.
Design a simple chart for a Class 7 student to track whether their allergy is seasonal or perennial over a year.

A student records sneezing episodes for 12 months and plots a bar graph. The graph shows peaks in March‑April and October‑November, low in other months. What type of allergy does this suggest? Name two possible allergens.

A bedroom has an initial dust‑mite allergen concentration of 12 µg/g of dust. After encasing the mattress and washing bedding at 60 °C, the concentration drops by 75 %. What is the new allergen concentration? (Give answer in µg/g.)

If a HEPA filter removes 99.97 % of airborne particles ≥0.3 µm, and the room air initially contains 50,000 particles per litre, how many particles remain per litre after filtration? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
A Class 7 student with photo‑allergy develops a rash after 20 minutes of midday sun exposure. Which precaution would be most effective for future outdoor activities?

Design a one‑week “Allergy‑Safe Routine” for a Class 7 student with perennial dust‑mite allergy and seasonal pollen allergy (peak in March). Include at least three daily actions and two weekly actions.
A teacher plans a 35‑minute lesson using a PPT with 14 slides. If the introduction and conclusion take 5 minutes total, how many minutes per content slide?

Compare a video that uses animated microscopic view of Aspergillus conidiophores releasing spores with a photograph slide of the same structure. Identify two advantages of the video for Class 7 learners.

You view a temporary mount of *Aspergillus* under 400× total magnification (40× objective, 10× eyepiece). On the digital screen a conidium measures 0.5 mm in length. Calculate the actual length of the conidium in micrometres.
A student observes a house dust slide at 400× and sees many small, spherical particles about 3 µm in diameter with a rough surface. Which allergen are these most likely to be, and why?

In a CISCE exam, a question shows a labelled photograph of a house dust slide with a scale bar of 50 µm. The image includes a dust mite (length 250 µm), a pollen grain (diameter 30 µm), and a cluster of *Aspergillus* spores (each 3 µm). The question asks: "Calculate the actual length of the dust mite if its image measures 25 mm on the photograph." Provide the answer with units.

HOTS: A researcher claims that "photographs of house dust are obsolete because modern molecular methods (PCR, immunoassays) can detect allergens more sensitively." Critique this claim from the perspective of a Class 7 biology curriculum.

CISCE past‑paper pattern: A question provides a photomicrograph of a house dust slide with a scale bar of 100 µm. The image shows a cluster of spherical particles (each ~5 µm) radiating from a central structure. The question asks: "Identify the structure and name the genus. State one health significance." Provide the answer as expected in the exam.
CISCE exam‑style: “State two factors that affect the rate of diffusion and explain how each factor influences the rate.” (2 marks)
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Define diffusion. State two factors that affect its rate. Give one example of diffusion in a plant.” (3 marks)
A student adds salt to one side of a U‑tube separated by a semipermeable membrane. Predict the water level change after 10 minutes.
In an experiment, a raisin of mass 2.0 g is placed in water for 2 hours. Its mass becomes 3.2 g. Calculate the percentage increase in mass. Explain the process responsible.
Assess whether root pressure alone can account for water rise in a 30 m tall mango tree.
A student cuts a balsam stem and attaches a manometer. The water column rises 12 cm. Calculate the root pressure in kilopascals (kPa). Use ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻².
A leaf loses 0.8 mL of water per hour through transpiration. How much water is lost in 5 hours?
If a plant’s transpiration rate doubles when temperature rises from 25 °C to 35 °C, and the original rate was 1.2 mL h⁻¹, what is the new rate?
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Define transpiration. State two functions of transpiration in plants.” (2 marks)
In a cross‑section of a dicot stem, vascular bundles are arranged in a ring. If you count 12 bundles in a young mustard stem, how many distinct xylem–phloem pairs are present?
CISCE exam‑style: “State two structural differences between xylem vessels and phloem sieve tubes that relate to their functions.” (2 marks)
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Describe the structure of a sieve‑tube element and its companion cell. Explain how they work together to transport food in plants.” (3 marks)

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** In a diagram of a transverse section of a mango stem, the xylem is stained red and phloem green. The question asks: “Which tissue would show accumulation of a radioactive potassium isotope applied to the roots after 24 hours?” Choose the correct tissue and give a brief reason.
A student places a balsam stem in eosin solution and covers the leaves with a transparent polythene bag. After 30 minutes the dye has risen only 2 cm. Explain the observation.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** In an experiment, a balsam stem is placed in a solution of radioactive potassium (⁴²K⁺). After 30 minutes, radioactivity is detected in the leaves. Which tissue transported the ion and what does this indicate about ion movement?

Answer in CISCE short-answer style: In the petunia-flower experiment, why is a white-flowered shoot chosen, why is the stem cut under water, and what exactly do the red veins on the petals prove? (2 marks)

CISCE past-paper pattern: "A white petal's red veins are the transport system's autograph — written in light, protected by a clean cut, and countersigned by a control." Examine this statement with reference to (a) the writing — how light produces the signature (b) the clean cut — the condition without which no ink flows (c) the countersignature — what the control adds that the experimental shoot cannot (d) the verdict and one line on why the experiment closes the chapter's demonstration series. (5 marks)
A CISCE past‑paper question: “In an experiment, a balsam plant is placed in eosin solution. After 2 hours the flower turns pink. Explain the process.”

Given the table below of transpiration rates (mL h⁻¹) at four temperatures, describe how you would construct a bar graph. | Temperature (°C) | Transpiration rate (mL h⁻¹) | |------------------|----------------------------| | 20 | 2.5 | | 25 | 3.8 | | 30 | 5.2 | | 35 | 4.0 |
In an ICSE Class 7 exam, a question asks: “Explain how a straw model of xylem helps understand the cohesion‑tension theory.” Write a concise answer.
**COMPARISON:** Compare a physical straw model of xylem with a diagrammatic model of the cohesion‑tension theory. Which is more effective for a Class 7 student and why?
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain how a model using a plastic bottle and a narrow tube can demonstrate root pressure. Mention two limitations of this model.” (3 marks)
A teacher plans a 20‑minute PPT lesson on transpiration. If each slide is allocated 2 minutes, how many slides should the teacher prepare?
**CISCE past-paper pattern:** “State two differences between a physical change and a chemical change. Give one example of each.” (2 marks for differences, 1 mark each for examples)
A CISCE exam question: “State two differences between physical and chemical changes and give one example of each.” Write a concise answer suitable for 3 marks.
CISCE past-paper pattern: “Give two reasons why the burning of a candle is considered a chemical change, while the melting of the wax is a physical change.” Write a concise answer for 2 marks.
Why does the temperature of melting ice stay at 0 °C until all ice has melted?

A student places 80 g of ice at 0 °C in a sealed insulated container and supplies heat until all ice melts. The final mass of water is measured. What is the expected mass of water? (Use the principle of mass conservation.)
During boiling, 150 g of water at 100 °C is converted to steam in a closed apparatus. The condensed steam is collected and weighed. What mass of liquid water should be obtained?
A teacher asks: “If you heat a sealed syringe containing 10 mL of water until it boils, the plunger moves outward. Does this prove that mass is not conserved?”
Critique the following experimental plan: “To show mass conservation during boiling, boil 100 mL of water in an open beaker for 10 minutes, then weigh the beaker.”

An ICSE past‑paper question: “A student heats 30 g of ice at 0 °C in a closed insulated flask until it becomes water at 0 °C. The mass of the flask and contents is measured before and after. What will be the mass reading? Explain.”
A textbook states: 'All colour changes in chemistry experiments are chemical changes.' Critique this statement with two counter‑examples from Class 7 experiments.
A copper rod 50 cm long is heated and its length becomes 50.08 cm. Calculate the percentage increase in length.
A student mixes equal volumes of 1 M HCl and 1 M NaOH in a polystyrene cup and records a temperature rise of 6 °C. Evaluate whether this observation alone proves a chemical change occurred.
A teacher claims that “any reaction that produces a temperature rise of less than 1 °C cannot be a chemical change.” Critique this claim using the concept of heat evolution.
A reaction in a test tube produces a steady blue flame with a power output of 0.8 W for 15 s. Calculate the total light energy emitted.
During caramelisation, sugar releases light of power 0.05 W for 40 s. How much energy is given off as light?

A teacher mixes 5 g of baking soda (NaHCO₃) with excess vinegar (CH₃COOH) and collects 1.2 L of carbon dioxide gas at room temperature. If the same reaction is performed with 10 g of baking soda under identical conditions, what volume of CO₂ would be expected? (Assume direct proportionality.)
A CISCE exam question: "State two observations that would help you decide whether a given change is chemical or physical." Provide a concise answer suitable for a Class 7 paper.
**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** A textbook states: "If a change produces a gas, it is a chemical change." Write a brief critique (3–4 sentences) pointing out the flaw and suggesting a corrected statement.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** "State two observations that indicate a chemical change has taken place when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to zinc granules." Provide the answer as expected in a Class 7 ICSE paper.

In a demonstration, 6 g of baking soda with excess vinegar fills the receiver at a steady rate of 0.5 L of gas per minute for 4 minutes. Predict the total volume of gas collected, and state whether this experiment shows a physical or a chemical change.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "Draw a labelled diagram of an experiment to show that a gas is evolved when dilute acid reacts with a carbonate, and state one observation in the receiver." Answer as expected in a Class 7 ICSE-style paper.

A piece of paper weighs 4.0 g before burning. After complete combustion, the ash weighs 0.6 g. Assuming the loss in mass is due to gases escaping, calculate the mass of gases produced. Show your working.
If 8 g of common salt is dissolved in 200 mL of water and the solution is completely evaporated, what mass of solid salt will be recovered?
Apply the concept of mass conservation to a real‑life situation: A household uses 200 g of table salt per month. If they buy a 1 kg packet, how many months will it last, assuming no spillage?
If 10 g of pure chalk (CaCO₃) is heated strongly until constant mass, what mass of carbon dioxide is evolved? (Molar masses: CaCO₃ = 100 g/mol, CO₂ = 44 g/mol)

Two iron nails are set up for a week: nail 1 in a dry covered dish, nail 2 half-dipped in open water. State where rusting occurs, where it is fastest on that nail, and what two conditions this experiment shows are necessary.
7 g of iron combines completely with 4 g of sulphur to form iron sulphide. How much sulphur is needed to combine completely with 14 g of iron, and what mass of iron sulphide results?

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "When iron filings are heated with sulphur powder, a new substance is formed. Name the product, state two properties in which it differs from iron, and identify the type of change with one reason." Answer as expected in a Class 7 ICSE-style paper.

In an experiment, 2 g of sulphur is heated in a closed container. After heating, the mass of the container and contents remains 2 g. Explain why this observation supports the law of conservation of mass for a physical change.
In an experiment, 2 g of sulphur is heated in a closed container. After the experiment, the mass of the container and its contents is found to be 2 g. Which law does this illustrate? State the law.
Calculate the mass percent of salt in a mixture containing 20 g of salt dissolved in 80 g of water.

In an experiment, 5.6 g of iron powder reacts completely with 3.2 g of sulphur to form iron sulphide. Calculate the mass ratio of iron to sulphur in the product and state whether this supports the law of definite proportions.

**Application:** You are given three unknown samples: (A) a clear liquid that boils at 100 °C at 1 atm, (B) a yellow solid that separates into two layers when mixed with water, (C) a grey powder that is attracted by a magnet. Classify each as element, compound, or mixture and justify.
If 4 g of hydrogen react completely with 32 g of oxygen, what mass of water is formed? Show your calculation.
What type of mixture is milk classified as in the ICSE Class 7 chemistry curriculum?
If 250 mL of cow milk contains 3.5 % fat by mass and the density of milk is 1.03 g mL⁻¹, calculate the mass of fat in the sample.

**APPLICATION:** A dairy technician needs to standardise milk to 3.0 % fat by mixing whole milk (4.5 % fat) with skim milk (0.1 % fat). How many litres of each should be mixed to obtain 1000 L of standardised milk?
If 56 g of pure iron completely rusts to form Fe₂O₃ (ignoring water of hydration), what mass of rust is produced? (Molar masses: Fe = 56 g mol⁻¹, Fe₂O₃ = 160 g mol⁻¹)
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Write the balanced chemical equation for the rusting of iron in the presence of water and oxygen. State one condition necessary for rusting.” (3 marks)
If the density of iron is 7.87 g/cm³, what is the mass of a solid iron cube of volume 12 cm³?
**Comparison:** Compare the density of iron (7.87 g/cm³) with that of aluminium (2.70 g/cm³) and explain why aluminium is preferred for aircraft bodies despite iron’s greater strength.
Given a piece of aluminium foil (mass = 5.4 g) and the molar mass of Al = 27 g mol⁻¹, calculate the amount of substance in moles.
A sample of pure water has a mass of 18 g. Using the mass ratio of hydrogen to oxygen in water (1:8), calculate the mass of hydrogen and oxygen in the sample.
If 10 g of gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) is heated to constant mass, what mass of plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O) is obtained? (Molar masses: gypsum = 172 g mol⁻¹, plaster of Paris = 145 g mol⁻¹)
During a demonstration, 15 g of gypsum yields 12.6 g of plaster of Paris. Calculate the percentage yield.

A student dissolves 5 g of salt in 100 g of water; a friend dissolves 20 g of salt in 100 g of water. Both then evaporate their solutions completely. State what each recovers, and use the results to classify (i) the solutions and (ii) the recovered solid.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "Sodium chloride is a compound, but salt solution is a mixture. Give two differences between them, and state what is recovered when the solution is evaporated." Answer as expected in a Class 7 ICSE-style paper.

A kiln charges 12 g of limestone and collects 5.3 g of carbon dioxide gas that escapes during heating. Assuming complete decomposition, calculate the mass of quicklime produced, and explain where the missing mass went.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "Limestone is strongly heated in a kiln. Name the solid product and the gas evolved. What happens when water is added to the solid product? Write the complete cycle that ends with the substance back as limestone-family material on a wall." Answer as expected in a Class 7 ICSE-style paper.
8 g of sodium hydroxide reacts completely with 9.8 g of sulphuric acid, producing 14.2 g of sodium sulphate. Calculate the mass of water formed, and state the law this calculation illustrates.
In 12 units of sodium sulphate, how many sodium atoms, sulphur atoms and oxygen atoms are present, and what is the total atom count?

**APPLICATION:** A detergent factory wants to prepare 40 kg of powder containing 12% sodium sulphate filler. Calculate the mass of Na₂SO₄ needed and the mass of other ingredients, and explain why the factory may lawfully vary this percentage in another product while a chemical plant CANNOT vary the proportion of sodium in Na₂SO₄.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "Write the formula of sodium sulphate and count the atoms in one unit. Name the reaction that prepares it from sodium hydroxide and sulphuric acid, give the products, and state one use of the salt." Answer as expected in a Class 7 ICSE-style paper.
A student heats 10 g of sodium hydrogen carbonate and collects 4.4 g of carbon dioxide. Does this result support the decomposition reaction 2 NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂?
**EVALUATION:** A textbook states “Sodium hydrogen carbonate decomposes at 100 °C to give sodium oxide, carbon dioxide and water.” Identify the error and write the correct decomposition products.
Element X has atomic number 11 and element Y has atomic number 17. Which element is more likely to form a positive ion in a reaction? Explain.
Write the atomic number and mass number of an element with 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Explain how the atomic number decides the element’s position in the periodic table.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "Define a molecule. Distinguish between a molecule of an element and a molecule of a compound with one example each. What is obtained when a molecule of water is split, and are the products water?" Answer as expected in a Class 7 ICSE-style paper.
What is the definition of a molecule according to the ICSE Class 7 curriculum?
Calculate the total number of atoms present in 2 molecules of carbon dioxide (CO₂).
Design a molecular formula for a compound containing 3 carbon atoms and 8 hydrogen atoms, and state its atomicity.
**APPLICATION:** A sample of carbon dioxide (CO₂) contains 5 molecules. How many oxygen atoms are present in the sample? Show your calculation.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** "Define molecule. Give one example each of a diatomic element molecule and a triatomic compound molecule." (2 marks)
A model-maker has 12 oxygen atoms and wants to build as many complete O₂ molecules AND O₃ molecules as possible with equal numbers of each. How many of each can be built, and how many atoms are used?
In one unit of Na₂SO₄, state the reading in words, the role of the subscript 2, the atomicity of the radical team, and the total atoms per unit.
**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** A classmate writes: "Ozone's atomicity is 3, so ozone is thrice as strong an element as oxygen." Write a four-sentence critique separating the count from the quality.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "Define atomicity. Give the atomicity of He, O₂, S₈ and the carbonate radical. In CaCO₃, state what is joined to what and count the total atoms per unit." Answer as expected in a Class 7 ICSE-style paper.
In the ICSE Class 7 exam, a question asks: “Identify the polyatomic ion among: Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, O₂, H₂O.” What is the correct choice and why?
**HOTS:** Explain why the symbol for iron (Fe) does not follow the first‑letter rule, even though iron is not among the first 20 elements.
**EVALUATION/CRITIQUE:** A textbook claims “All element symbols are derived from the first two letters of the English name.” Critique this statement using examples from the first 20 elements.
Write the formula of the compound of aluminium (valency 3) and oxygen (valency 2) by exchanging valencies, and verify the balance by the hands-product check.
An element X combines with exactly two hydrogen atoms per atom of X. (i) State X's valency. (ii) X forms a chloride with chlorine (valency 1). Write the chloride's formula and verify.
Why do helium, neon and argon have valency 0, and what does this explain about their atomicity and their usefulness?
Using radical valencies, write the formula of calcium carbonate (calcium valency 2, carbonate radical valency 2) and of sodium sulphate (sodium 1, sulphate 2), and verify both.
Iron shows valencies 2 and 3. Write the formula of its oxide in the valency-3 case and verify. Name the phenomenon demonstrated.
**HOTS:** A student reasons: "Carbon's valency is 4, so carbon must always combine with exactly four atoms of the other element." Critique this using carbon dioxide and the hands-product balance.

**APPLICATION:** A water-purifier filter uses "alumina" (aluminium oxide). Derive its formula from valencies, verify it, and then compute the total atoms per formula unit. The packet also lists "aluminium sulphate" as a coagulant — derive and verify that formula too (sulphate radical valency 2), noting the bracket rule.

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "Define valency. Write the valencies of the first twenty elements in order (grouping repeats is allowed). Using the table, write with verification the formula of the compound of magnesium and oxygen." Answer as expected in a Class 7 ICSE-style paper.
Given an element with atomic number 11, identify the element, its group, period, and expected valency.
In the periodic table, element X is in Group 17 and Period 2. Write its symbol and valency.
Write the symbol and valency of the element in Group 2, Period 3.
If an element is in Group 16 of the periodic table, what is its typical valency and why?
Evaluate the statement: “A valency card for neon should show valency 8 because it is in Group 18.”
Using valency cards, determine the simplest formula for the compound formed between aluminium (valency 3) and chlorine (valency 1). Show the steps.
**HOTS:** A student claims that because helium is in Group 18, its valency card should show valency 8. Critique this claim using the concept of chemical inertness.

**Application:** You have valency cards for sodium (1), magnesium (2), aluminium (3), and chlorine (1). Using only these cards, list all possible binary compounds (1:1, 1:2, 2:1, etc.) that can be formed and write their formulas.
**Evaluation/Critique:** A textbook shows a valency card for carbon with valency 2. Assess whether this is appropriate for Class 7 ICSE chemistry.
Why does oxygen typically exhibit a valency of 2?
Write the formula of the compound formed between nitrogen (valency 3) and hydrogen (valency 1).
Given the symbols and valencies: H = 1, O = 2, N = 3, C = 4. Write the formulas of water, ammonia, and methane.
