(iii) The command that sizes a column to its widest entry is ______. (c) State whether True or False, correcting the false ones: (i) Deleting a row leaves a blank row behind. (ii) A formula's range stretches automatically when a row is inserted inside it. (iii) A hidden column is excluded from all calculations. (d) A register's total reads =SUM(D2:D21). State the formula after a row is inserted at row 15, with the one-line reason. (e) Give the one sentence that states this node's discipline.

Apply: Build the register's totals column for forty students in the minimum authoring steps: students in rows 2–41, subjects in C, D, E. Write the exact sequence — the one formula authored, the copy operation, the anchor discipline, the verification, and the footprint warning if the paste accidentally targeted F2:H41 instead.

Application: Assign each person the copy-craft duty their role actually owns, with the one-line reason: (1) the Class 7 student; (2) the class monitor building the register; (3) the peer checker; (4) the teacher reviewing a submitted sheet.

Evaluation: The department debates the register's totals column. Option COPY-DOWN: one authored, verified formula copied to all forty rows. Option TYPED-EACH: each row's total typed individually by the data-entry student, "so the student learns every formula". Evaluate both for (1) the entry week, (2) December's error audit, and (3) what each teaches; award the better option per case with the reason, and state the principle about learning and leverage that the debate settles.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Choose the correct option: To relocate data so that the source becomes empty, use (i) copy and paste (ii) cut and paste (iii) autofill (iv) undo. (b) Fill in the blanks: (i) The staging area that holds a copied selection is the ______. (ii) Copying is done with Ctrl+______ and pasting with Ctrl+______. (iii) A copied formula's references ______ to face its new neighbourhood. (c) State whether True or False, correcting the false ones: (i) After a copy-paste, the source cells are emptied. (ii) A pasted block replaces whatever occupied its destination footprint. (iii) The formula =B2*2 copied one column right becomes =C2*2. (d) Meera copies =AVERAGE(C2:C31) from D32 down to D33. State what D33 now reads and whether it serves her purpose of showing the class average again below. (e) Give the one sentence that states this node's discipline.

Reasoning: A student selects the single cell containing 5 and drags the fill handle down five cells. Explain exactly what arrives and why — reasoning from what evidence the filler had — and state the selection that would have produced the series she wanted (5, 10, 15...).

Apply: Produce the following with the fewest keystrokes, stating the exact selection before each drag: (a) roll numbers 1 to 40 down a column; (b) all seven weekdays across a row starting Monday; (c) the months of the second half-year down a column starting July; (d) the totals column for marks in C3:E42; (e) the odd numbers 1, 3, 5 ... up to 19.

CISCE exam-style: (a) What is AutoFill? What is the fill handle? (b) State what fills when: (i) 10 and 20 are selected and dragged; (ii) only 15 is selected and dragged; (iii) "Friday" is selected and dragged. (c) Name the feature that continues days and months automatically. (d) A student drags =SUM(C3:E3) from F3 to F40. State what F40 holds and the one check that confirms the drag was true.

Application: Assign each person the autofill duty their role actually owns, with the one-line reason: (1) the Class 7 student; (2) the class monitor preparing next term's blank register; (3) the peer checker; (4) the teacher who assigns "build the register" as homework.

Evaluation: Two classes build the term's attendance sheet — 40 students × 22 weekdays. Class P types every roll, every day-name, every cell by hand. Class Q autofills the structure (rolls, weekday header, per-student totals) and types only the attendance marks. Evaluate both for (1) the sheet's correctness at submission, (2) the students' grip on the grid's grammar, and (3) the teacher's audit burden; award the better approach per case with the reason, and state the principle about human effort that the comparison prices.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Choose the correct option: The small square at the corner of a selection, used to extend patterns, is the (i) pointer (ii) fill handle (iii) name box (iv) scroll lock. (b) Fill in the blanks: (i) Selecting 4 and 8 and dragging produces the series 12, 16, ... with a step of ______. (ii) Dragging "May" fills the months ______, ______ next. (iii) Dragging a formula copies it with ______ references. (c) State whether True or False, correcting the false ones: (i) Dragging a single number fills a number series. (ii) AutoFill can continue the days of the week automatically. (iii) A formula dragged down ten rows appears in all ten rows with translated references. (d) Ravi needs roll numbers 1 to 45. He types 1 in A2 and drags. State what he gets and the two-step cure. (e) Give the one sentence that states this node's discipline.

Apply: For each of the three anchor institutions — school, library, railway — name one table, one record (with its contents), and three fields, and state which field could serve as the unique identifier each will need at station 4.

HOTS: The chapter's map promises that every station consumes the previous station's product. Test the promise at its weakest joint: station 5 (queries) claims to need station 4 (primary key) — yet one can obviously ask "list all students" of an unkeyed table. Reason out what the primary key contributes to querying that the objection misses, the query that FAILS without it, and the principle about identity that the joint reveals.

Application: Assign each person the chapter-project duty their role actually owns, with the one-line reason: (1) the Class 7 student; (2) the class monitor; (3) the computer teacher; (4) the school office staff who will use the finished database.

Evaluation: The chapter could be taught in two orders. Option TOOL-FIRST: every DBMS button and dialog in week one, real data later. Option QUESTION-FIRST: begin with the office's unanswerable questions, teach each station only when a question demands it. Evaluate both for (1) the first fortnight's retention, (2) the students' ability to choose the right DBMS tool unprompted in March, and (3) the risk each order carries; award the better order per case with the reason, and state the principle about tools and questions that the choice demonstrates.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Define a database. (b) What is a record and what is a field? Give one example of each in a Books table. (c) Name any two DBMS programs. (d) The school canteen keeps its stock on paper and asks, "Which items fall below 10 packets daily?" State whether a database would help, using the anatomy.

HOTS: The chapter's border gives spreadsheets the flexible page and databases the governed collection. Test the border's hard case: the school's ONE-class mark list (45 students, 5 subjects, totals, grades, a chart) lives happily in a spreadsheet — until the principal asks for "all 45 students' English marks across all four terms since Class 5, with each term's teacher." Reason out what breaks, why each term-sheet's design caused it, what the four-term demand really is (a query across collections), and the border principle the case sharpens.

Application: Assign each person the database-duty their role actually owns, with the one-line reason: (1) the Class 7 student; (2) the school office clerk who will use the class-built library database; (3) the computer teacher; (4) the principal.

Evaluation: The school must decide where the fee collection record lives. Option SPREADSHEET: one page per month, quick totals, printed for the notice board. Option DATABASE: a Payments table with typed fields, unique receipt numbers, and daily queries ("today's collection", "defaulters by class"). Evaluate both for (1) March's audit (the examiner asks for any receipt's details in ten seconds), (2) the clerk's daily comfort, and (3) five years of records; award the better tool per case with the reason, and state the principle about records and time that the choice demonstrates.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Choose the correct option: In a database table, a row holds (i) one field (ii) one record (iii) one table (iv) one DBMS. (b) Fill in the blanks: (i) A database is an organised collection of related ______. (ii) A ______ is one complete entry in a table. (iii) LibreOffice ______ and Microsoft ______ are two DBMS programs. (c) State whether True or False, correcting the false ones: (i) A field is one complete entry in a table. (ii) A spreadsheet is the better tool for the school's ten-year student memory. (iii) Banks, hospitals and railways all keep their working data in databases. (d) A shop's stock list holds 500 items with fields Item, Qty, Price, questioned daily at billing, where item names must not repeat. State whether it passes the anatomy test, with the count of yeses. (e) Give the one sentence that states this node's discipline.
What is the default file extension for a database created in Microsoft Access 2016 and later?
Design a short checklist (maximum five items) a Class 7 student should follow each time they create a new database.
In a CISCE ICSE Class 7 exam, a question asks: “State one reason why a primary key cannot contain NULL values.” Write a concise answer suitable for the exam.
A student writes `SELECT * FROM Students WHERE Class = '7' OR Sport = 'Cricket'`. Evaluate whether this query will show a Class 6 student who likes cricket.
Write a query to display the names of all students in Class 8 sorted by admission number descending.
In the ICSE Class 7 Computer Studies exam, a question asks: “Write the SQL statement to list all fields of the table ‘Books’ where the price is greater than 200.” Provide the exact statement.

Apply querying to a real‑world scenario: a school canteen wants a list of students who have a lunch‑card balance below ₹50. The table **LunchCard(AdmNo, Balance)** exists. Write the query and explain each part.
Evaluate the following query for correctness: `SELECT Name, Class FROM Students WHERE Class = '7' ORDER BY Name DESC;` Assume Class is stored as a numeric field.
Compare a query that uses a visual query designer with one written in raw SQL. List two advantages and two disadvantages of each approach for a Class 7 learner.
Past‑paper style: “Write the SQL statement to display the names of students who are in Class 6 or Class 7 and whose sport is ‘Badminton’.” Provide the statement and explain the use of parentheses.

HOTS: The report's summary line "37 books overdue" is trusted by the principal without counting. Reason out what must be true beneath that trust: the chain of guarantees from table to summary, the one link a careless form could break, and the principle about dressed answers that the trust rides on.

Application: Assign each person the face-duty their role actually owns, with the one-line reason: (1) the Class 7 student; (2) the data-entry clerk; (3) the in-charge who designs forms and reports; (4) the principal who reads the reports.

Evaluation: The library must issue 800 books in the week before vacation. Option TABLE-RUSH: clerks type straight into the Issues grid — fast, wide, no forms in the way. Option FORM-FLOW: a query-bound issue form (book picked from list, member picked from list, date stamped). Evaluate both for (1) the rush week's throughput, (2) January's return season (every book must find its borrower), and (3) the clerks' formation; award the better option per case with the reason, and state the principle about speed and structure that the rush tests.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Choose the correct option: The database screen used for entering records one at a time is a (i) report (ii) form (iii) query (iv) table. (b) Fill in the blanks: (i) A report presents records in a ______ format for printing. (ii) Forms and reports usually take their records from a ______. (iii) The report part that shows counts and totals is the ______. (c) State whether True or False, correcting the false ones: (i) Deleting a form deletes the records it displayed. (ii) A report changes the data it presents. (iii) A well-designed report shows every field of the table. (d) The clerk must enter 200 records today. State the two form features that keep the entry accurate, and the one check she runs before starting. (e) Give the one sentence that states this node's discipline.

Reasoning: The result sheet of 250 students is in entry order. Explain, reasoning from what each reader must DO, why the principal's prize list is sorted on Marks descending, while the teacher hunting "who scored above 90?" reaches for a filter instead — and why neither operation changes any student's marks.

Evaluate: After the mid-term, a student's table "looks empty" and he says, "The filter deleted my failed records — I filtered for marks above 40 and now everything below is gone forever." Evaluate the claim: what actually happened, the two checks that prove it, and the corrected sentence he should say instead.

Apply (predict the result): The PE teacher's Runners table: | Bib | Name | House | Time (s) | | 7 | Dev | Nehru | 12.9 | | 14 | Aditi | Tagore | 11.8 | | 3 | Kabir | Nehru | 12.4 | | 21 | Meera | Gandhi | 13.1 | | 9 | Sara | Tagore | 12.4 | | 12 | Rohan | Gandhi | 11.9 | The final takes runners with Time ≤ 12.5, ranked fastest first. Predict exactly which rows remain after the filter, and the final ranking order after sorting — and state the tie-break rule you used.

HOTS: The sports list reads "Aditi 91st overall" — but Aditi's row was sorted while three filters were active, and her "rank" was read off the filtered view. Reason out what the number 91 actually counts, the two questions that expose the error, and the principle about reading ranks off views that the incident teaches.

Application: Assign each person the operation-duty their role actually owns, with the one-line reason: (1) the class monitor preparing the seating plan; (2) the PE teacher building the final's lane list; (3) the librarian answering "what came in this week?"; (4) the exam cell pinning the morning rule for all three.

Evaluation: The library's year-end stock-taking must produce (A) the full catalogue list for the audit — every book, accession-number order — and (B) the "lost books" list for the police complaint — only the 23 records flagged Lost, by title. The assistant proposes doing both by hand from one printout, marking and copying. Evaluate the hand method against the view method for each list, award the better method per list with the reason, and state the principle about views and originals that the stock-taking tests.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Choose the correct option: Temporarily hiding the records that do not satisfy a condition is called (i) sorting (ii) filtering (iii) formatting (iv) indexing. (b) Fill in the blanks: (i) Sorting arranges records in ascending or ______ order. (ii) The field chosen for sorting is called the sort ______. (iii) A filtered record is hidden, not ______. (c) State whether True or False, correcting the false ones: (i) Sorting changes the values inside records. (ii) A filter that hides rows has deleted them. (iii) Records always move one field at a time during sorting. (d) Given marks 72, 91, 68, 85 — write the order after sorting descending, and the survivors of filtering Marks > 70. (e) Give the one sentence that states this node's discipline.

Apply: Design the lost-property office's database end-to-end. Given: items are handed in daily, stored till claimed, and unclaimed items older than one month are donated. Produce the build-sheet — (1) the table's fields with the data type of each; (2) the primary key with its never-empty-never-repeated justification; (3) the query for the donation list with its exact condition; (4) the intake form's design in two craft rules; (5) the report's four dressing decisions.

HOTS: A Class 7 student says, "I understand each tool, but I cannot tell which one an exam question wants." Reason out the cure: the five-verb routing rule stated in full, its application to three mixed question-wordings, and the principle about questions and verbs that makes the rule reliable.

Application: Assign each person the station-duty their role actually owns across the school's fee system, with the one-line reason: (1) the clerk at the counter; (2) the DBMS itself; (3) the in-charge who designed the system; (4) the auditor who arrives once a year.

Evaluation: The school must choose its records future. Option PAPER-PLUS: registers stay authoritative, a computer list kept "when someone has time". Option VAULT-FIRST: the table authoritative from day one, entries by form, answers by query and report. Evaluate both for (1) the normal term, (2) the fever-wave June, (3) the audit and the transfer certificate years later; award the better option per case with the reason, and state the principle about authority and records that the choice tests.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Choose the correct option: The software used to create and manage databases is the (i) OS (ii) DBMS (iii) GUI (iv) URL. (b) Fill in the blanks: (i) A ______ is a field that uniquely identifies each record. (ii) A query returns a set of ______ that satisfy its condition. (iii) Sorting changes the ______ of records, not their values. (c) State whether True or False, correcting the false ones: (i) A report stores its own copy of the records it prints. (ii) A form must show all records on one screen. (iii) A filtered table has fewer records than before. (d) A school system must answer "Class 8 students of Gate 2 bus, roll order" every Friday. Name the object that stores the answer's question, the operation that orders the rows, and the object that prints the titled countable sheet. (e) Give the one sentence that states this chapter's discipline.
Create an ordered list that counts down from 5 to 1 using the `reversed` attribute.
In an ICSE exam, a question asks: "Write the HTML code to display a list of three programming languages as an ordered list starting at 10 with lowercase letters." Provide the exact code.
Write the complete `` tag to display `diwali.jpg` located in a subfolder `festivals` with alternative text “Diwali lamps glowing” and a display width of 400 pixels.
Design a minimal HTML snippet that shows two images side by side: `flag.jpg` (alt “Indian flag”) and `map.jpg` (alt “India map”). Each image should be 250 px wide. Do not use CSS.
You have an image `map.png` (1200 × 800) that you want to display at 600 × 400 on a page without distortion. Write the `` tag using only HTML attributes.
Compare the effect of using `` versus `` when the original image is 600 × 400 pixels.
Write the HTML code to embed an image `logo.gif` located in the parent directory of the current HTML file, with alternative text “Company logo” and a display width of 150 pixels.

Application: Assign each builder the link-duty their role actually owns on the school site team, with the one-line reason: (1) the page writer; (2) the picture editor; (3) the checker who tests the finished pages; (4) the adviser who approves the site for launch.

Evaluation: Two teams each built the school's five-page site. Team A wrote all internal links relative and external absolute; Team B wrote every link with full absolute addresses, "so nothing is ambiguous". The district now asks every school to move its site to the district server under a new address, and a reviewer reports Team B's site "works but every page flashes a delay before loading". Evaluate both sites for (1) the migration day, (2) the reviewer's delay report, (3) the year of routine edits that follow; award the better practice per case with the reason, and state the principle about conventions that the migration tests.
Write the HTML for a 2×2 table with header cells "Name" and "Age" and one data row "Asha" and "12".
Apply your knowledge: write the minimal HTML to show a 3×3 multiplication table for numbers 1 to 3, using only `<table>`, `<tr>`, `<td>`, and `<th>`. Include a header row and header column.

Evaluate: The principal rejects the club's banner — "It keeps sliding away before I finish reading. Make the message stay." The club proposes three fixes: (1) raise `scrolldelay` to 1000; (2) change `behavior` to "slide"; (3) change `behavior` to "alternate". Evaluate each fix against the principal's actual complaint, award the best, and state the principle about tuning dials versus changing manners.

Apply (predict the output): Predict exactly what a visitor sees for each of these three banners: (1) `<marquee direction="up" height="120" scrollamount="3">House Captains: Tagore — Aditi. Gandhi — Rohan.</marquee>` (2) `<marquee behavior="alternate" direction="right">SPORTS DAY — FRIDAY</marquee>` (3) `<marquee behavior="slide" scrolldelay="150">Fees close 15th</marquee>` State the motion, the direction, and where each message ends up.

Application: Assign each screen-owner their marquee-duty with the one-line reason: (1) the computer club that writes the banners; (2) the duty teacher who watches parents watch the screen; (3) the office that owns the deadline notices; (4) the principal who approves what the reception says.

Evaluation: Two proposals for the school screen's daily lineup. Proposal MANY-WALKERS: six banners run at once, one per message, each alternating direction for variety. Proposal ONE-STAGE: one marquee stage cycles the day's six messages slowly (direction up, generous height), with the urgent banner as the only second walker. Evaluate both for (1) a parent's 20-second wait at the desk, (2) the office's guarantee that each deadline notice is read at least once, (3) the screen's attention budget by term's end; award the better proposal with the reason, and state the principle about motion's budget that the lineup tests.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two things a listener should do before a passage is read aloud for the first time. (ii) Why are listening passages usually read twice in examinations? (2 marks)

A Class 7 student says: "I listen best when I close my eyes and just let the words wash over me — taking notes would distract me." Evaluate this claim as a theory of listening comprehension for an examination where ten questions follow a twice-read passage.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two courtesies a speaker must observe when joining an ongoing discussion. (ii) Why should disagreement in a discussion always be supported with a reason? (2 marks)

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two reasons why a presentation should be delivered from key-word cards rather than a full written script. (ii) What is meant by voice modulation, and why is it assessed in oral examinations? (2 marks)

Your school's assembly hall has a broken microphone, and your class's presentation hour proceeds anyway — 240 students, one open courtyard. Argue what changes in delivery technique and what does not: which of the four voice tools and three body tools need adjustment for this venue, and which principles hold unchanged?

Design a five-minute peer-feedback form for your class's presentation hour: five rating rows (structure, pace-pause, pitch-volume, eyes-body, congruence), each on a 1–5 scale, with one concrete observation the rater must write per row. Give the exact wording of the five rows and one worked example row filled in. COMPETENCY note: the form must turn ratings into evidence, not vibes.

A chart in a classmate's talk shows city temperatures "soaring" — the y-axis runs from 38°C to 42°C, and the line looks like a cliff. The data itself shows a rise from 38.5 to 41 degrees over twenty years. Evaluate the chart's honesty and prescribe the fix.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two faults that make a slide ineffective in a multimedia presentation. (ii) Why should a speaker plan the talk's words before designing its slides? (2 marks)

Your school plans to replace all Class 7 oral-assessment marks with "slide-deck marks" — the deck is submitted, the teacher reads it, no talk is delivered. Argue against the policy using the node's account of what a multimedia talk is, and propose the assessment compromise that keeps the fair part of the idea.
In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) Give one feature that marks a passage as literary and one that marks it as non-literary. (ii) Why must a retelling use your own words? (2 marks)

A publisher reissues a diary — a real family's dated entries from the 1947 months — with no changes to the text. A reviewer calls it "the finest novel of the year". Untangle the two errors a Class 7 reader should spot, and state what the diary can and cannot honestly be called.
What is the primary purpose of a community‑focused text in the ICSE Class 7 reading curriculum?

A Class 7 exam asks: “Identify two textual evidences that show the community’s collective decision‑making in the passage.” The passage describes a village council vote and a subsequent feast. Which evidences are most appropriate?

A past ICSE paper asks: “Read the passage about a neighbourhood library run by volunteers. Summarise the passage in 50 words and comment on whether the writer presents a balanced view of the library’s challenges.” Outline a step‑by‑step plan a student should follow in the exam.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two features that would mark a passage about the nation as literary rather than historical writing. (ii) Why must a reader identify whose voice a national text speaks in? (2 marks)

Your school magazine receives three reviews of the same national story and prints only one. Review 1: "A thrilling tale; five stars." Review 2: "The story's recurring train, described as carrying 'whole villages in one whistle', makes it the definitive history of Partition." Review 3: "The train — 'whole villages in one whistle' — and the kept neem tree make this story argue that roots outlast borders; a shaped experience, not a history, and moving precisely because it claims only feeling." Write the editor's note choosing Review 3: the specific failure of each rejected review, and the two tests Review 3 passes.

In a newspaper article about Delhi’s air‑quality index, the author writes, “The AQI crossed 400 yesterday, proving that government policies have failed.” Identify the claim, the evidence, and evaluate whether the evidence fully supports the claim.

You are given a 150‑word news report on a recent oil spill off the Mumbai coast. Design a three‑step classroom activity that helps students (1) extract facts, (2) identify the author’s tone, and (3) write a 40‑word summary.

A passage says: "The new panel's efficiency rose to 22 per cent." List the two questions that make this number meaningful, and show the difference between the checked and unchecked versions of the claim.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two features of language that mark a passage as an explanation of how something works. (ii) Why should a reader fix a technical term's meaning on first meeting? (2 marks)

Your school plans to let AI chatbots "summarise science passages" for Class 7 students before they read them. Using this node's account of what reading an explanation builds, argue what is gained and what is quietly destroyed, and frame the policy amendment that keeps the gain.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two ways a writer can show rising conflict without stating that people are angry. (ii) Why do peace texts often place a shared threat or shared task at the turning point? (2 marks)

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two ways a writer builds suspense in an adventure passage without introducing any villain. (ii) Why must the reader of an adventure track what is running out? (2 marks)

In this paragraph, identify the carrier-clause and the discards, naming each discard's kind: "Rainwater harvesting is the practice of catching rain where it falls and storing it for use — a practice as old as the stepwells of Gujarat and as new as last year's municipal circular. In one form, rooftop collection, rain from the terrace travels through pipes into a filtered sump. In another, the recharge pit, it is guided into the ground itself to raise the water table. My uncle in Nagpur installed one after the 2019 shortage and now washing water is free. Both forms answer the same problem: the rain that once refilled wells now runs off concrete into drains and is lost."

Why must a summary preserve the original's proportions, and what goes wrong when it does not? Show with a 100-word argument (60 words on one ground, 30 on a second, 10 on the conclusion) that gets summarised as equal thirds.

The same 300-word text must serve two readers: a classmate who missed the lesson (summary A) and your own revision file three months later (summary B). What differs between the two summaries, if the rules are the same?
In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two rules a summary must follow besides brevity. (ii) Why is the verification pass (re-reading summary beside original) essential? (2 marks)

Design the "Cut & Prove" workshop for your library period: the material (one 300-word text per pair, drawn from this term's themes), the three timed stages of the workshop (mark, draft, verify) with minutes and the exact deliverable of each, and the two-trade closing round in which pairs swap summaries and trade on them. COMPETENCY note: the design must make the verification pass physical and public.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two questions that test whether a piece of evidence supports a claim. (ii) Why should a written evaluation state the strongest point on the other side? (2 marks)

Design the "Verdict Court" session for your class: one live text per week (an editorial, circular, or speech extract from school life), the three courtroom roles rotated among students (Restate Counsel, Plank Examiner, Counter Counsel), each role's one mandatory output, and the judge's fixed two-sentence verdict formula. Show the roles firing on the wallet-editorial from Worked Example 1. COMPETENCY note: the design must make every evaluation a structured, checkable performance.

Name the four stations of the composition skeleton and state the one job of each. Then match them to this outline made for the topic "A Visit to a Book Fair": (1) "Crowd, smell of new books, lost between stalls." (2) "Finding the old Atlas stall; buying the book I still use." (3) "What the hour taught me about looking for one thing."
Why does the CISCE composition task set a band of 200–250 words instead of saying "write as much as you can"? Give two reasons — one for the writer, one for the examiner.

For a picture composition on "A Busy Market Scene", a student lists nine points: (i) crowd pushing to the vegetable stalls; (ii) history of the market since 1950; (iii) a hawker weighing chillies with brass weights; (iv) the definition of a market economy; (v) a cow wandering between carts; (vi) bus conductor ringing the bell; (vii) the municipal corporation's annual budget; (viii) a child crying for a balloon; (ix) prices rising every week. Select the points for a 200–250 word composition, arrange them in order, and name the rule each rejected point breaks.
In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two functions of the concluding paragraph of a composition. (ii) Why must each body paragraph contain only one main idea? (2 marks)

Your school's new AI writing assistant produces a complete 230-word composition on any topic in four seconds. The head of department proposes allowing it for practice but asks the class: "What exactly does the machine skip that you cannot afford to skip?" Answer her question — what the four seconds omit, what remains yours, and the one sentence you would put on the assistant's screen.

Design the "Composition Hour" for your class: the fixed 40-minute structure (minutes allocated to plan, draft, budget-check, and revise), the one mandatory written artefact each stage must produce, and the peer-review swap protocol with its fixed three-question review slip. Show the hour firing on the topic "A Morning at the Railway Station" using the outline from Worked Example 3. COMPETENCY note: the design must make the writing process a structured, checkable performance.

Compare the unplanned composition and the planned composition as two productions of the same 40 minutes under four heads: where the writer's decisions are made, what happens to mistakes, what the reader experiences, and what the writer takes away for the next piece. Then state why the chapter opens with composition before story, poem, and dialogue.

A CISCE past-paper-pattern question: "In a short composition, the writer's chief difficulty is not saying enough but saying almost too much." Explain with reference to (a) why abundance, not scarcity, is the real problem at 200–250 words, (b) the two instruments the craft supplies against abundance — the one-incident rule and the cutting protocol — and (c) what the examiner's marking of a banded script actually rewards — and close with what a writer who has mastered the budget can do that an unrival writer cannot. COMPETENCY note: the answer must run all three parts and end on the mastered writer.

Name the five stations of the story skeleton and the job of each. Then match them to this outline given for a story titled by the writer: (1) "Meera loses her father's stamp album while shifting house." (2) "She remembers the scrap dealer's truck that came that morning." (3) "She runs three streets, finds the truck at the vegetable market." (4) "The dealer turns the junk sack; the red album, corner-bent, is there." (5) "Her father says nothing, but that evening they fix the torn pages together."

Why must a short story contain trouble at all — a Class 7 story of 200 words cannot develop a deep conflict, so why is a quiet report of a pleasant day not acceptable as a story? Give the reason in terms of what makes a reader read.

A story outline reads: (i) Arun promises his grandmother to water her tulsi plant daily during her week away; (ii) his school holds special cricket practice all week; (iii) he waters the plant each evening, tired but faithful; (iv) Friday's match runs late, he returns after dark, exhausted; (v) the plant is drooping; (vi) he waters it and sits beside it till it lifts. The budget is 200 words. Decide which points you would join, which you would expand most, and which you would compress to a clause — with reasons.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two functions of the climax in a short story. (ii) A story's problem is solved by the words "suddenly, a policeman arrived and caught the thief." Name the fault and give one repair. (2 marks)

Your school's AI assistant completes any outline into a 200-word story in four seconds, and the head of department asks the class: "The machine's stories are competent. What are you training when you write yours badly first?" Answer her — what the machine skips, what the human draft practises, and the one sentence you would put on the assistant's screen.

Design the "Story Workshop" protocol for your class: the fixed steps from outline to marked draft, the one mandatory artefact each step produces, and the three-question peer-review slip. Show the protocol firing on the puppy outline from Worked Example 3, including where the seed-check happens. COMPETENCY note: the design must make story-craft a structured, checkable performance.

Compare the report and the story as two treatments of the same event — the flooded gully and the missed bus of Worked Example 1 — under four heads: the question each answers, the sentence-economy each practises, the place each allows feeling, and the exam task each serves. Then state why the Writing chapter needs both this node and the composition node before it.

Name the parts of the standard Class 7 poem skeleton and the job of each. Then read these four lines and mark their rhyme scheme in letters: "The bell rang out across the ground, / A thousand feet came at the sound; / The last one left still ties his lace, / And walks into the empty space."

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two functions of a poem's final stanza. (ii) A student writes: "The clouds so white, / A lovely sight, / The birds took flight, / All felt just right." Why does this quatrain fail, and what is the first repair? (2 marks)

A classmate argues: "Free verse must be easier — no rhymes to find, no scheme to keep. I'll write all my poems in free verse and save the effort." Diagnose the theory of poetic form on show, and answer with what the scheme actually does for a Class 7 poet, and when free verse is the right — and earned — choice.

Design the "Poem Workshop" protocol for your class: the fixed steps from topic to fair copy, the one mandatory artefact each step produces, and the three-question peer-review slip. Show the protocol firing on the topic "The Street Dog", using the plan from Diagnostic 5. COMPETENCY note: the design must make poem-craft a structured, checkable performance.

Compare the story and the poem as two vehicles for the same material — the arrival of rain from Worked Example 1 — under four heads: the build-unit, the economy, the work of sound, and the landing. Then state why the Writing chapter places the poem after the story, and what each form does for the writer who will one day write the other.
Why should a writer avoid long, uninterrupted speeches in a Class 7 dialogue?
A CISCE exam question asks: “Write a dialogue of about 150 words between two friends discussing a school trip to the Sundarbans.” Outline the key elements you would include to meet the rubric.
A past CISCE paper asked: “Write a dialogue of about 150 words between a librarian and a student who wants to borrow a reference book that is not for issue.” Outline a model response plan.
Critique the effectiveness of the analogy “A cell is like a factory” in a biology textbook for Class 7 students.

Apply the active–passive transformation to the following instruction for a school laboratory manual: “Add 10 mL of hydrochloric acid to the beaker.” Write the passive version suitable for a procedural text.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) Classify as simple, compound, or complex: "When the bell rang, the class fell silent." (ii) State the two changes that a verb undergoes in the active-to-passive transformation. (2 marks)

Design the "Error Clinic" protocol for your class: how a returned test paper is converted, in one fixed 20-minute session, into a routed re-practice plan — the fixed steps, the mandatory artefact each step produces, and the three-question self-audit slip. Show the clinic firing on a paper whose losses were: two voice-change items (both tense-changed), one clause classification (compound called complex), one analogy (topic-trap taken). COMPETENCY note: the design must make error-correction a structured, checkable performance.
Create a one‑sentence definition of the atmosphere that a Class 7 student could use in a quiz.
A student argues that “since nitrogen is 78 % of the atmosphere, it must be the main greenhouse gas.” Critique this claim using the properties of greenhouse gases.
Evaluate the claim: "Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of the air, so it cannot be important."
Write a single sentence, fit for a Class 7 quiz, that defines the composition of the atmosphere.
Imagine the atmosphere suddenly contained 50% oxygen instead of 21%. Critically assess what would change for fire, for life and for the landscape.

A mountaineer on an 8,000-metre Himalayan peak needs an oxygen cylinder, and says, "The air up here has less oxygen in it than the air in Dehradun." Critically correct the statement using both composition and structure.

A student concludes: "The Montreal Protocol banned CFCs in 1987, so the ozone layer must have healed within a few years — any continued talk of ozone depletion is scaremongering." Evaluate this reasoning.
Temperatures in the thermosphere can exceed 1,000°C, yet an astronaut's exposed hand would feel freezing cold. Explain the paradox.

A newspaper headline reads: "City sweats at 30 degrees!" The same day a desert town reports 40 degrees and no one sweats. Using the elements of weather, explain how the headline can be literally true and the desert town still more comfortable.

Every afternoon in coastal Andhra, the wind reverses: from the sea by day, toward the sea by night. Construct the full explanation of this daily reversal using the pressure-temperature link, and predict which direction the wind blows at 9 a.m.

A farmers' cooperative in Vidarbha must pick a sowing window using only five readings: (1) daytime temperature falling from 38°C to 31°C over a week; (2) humidity rising from 25% to 70%; (3) pressure at its lowest of the month; (4) clouds building from clear to overcast by evening; (5) wind shifting from dry inland to moist onshore. Advise the cooperative, naming the weather event these readings announce and the actions for the next 72 hours.

Two forecasters defend their methods. The village elder: "Termites swarming and a ring around the moon — rain inside three days; my fathers never needed instruments." The meteorologist: "Satellite cloud motion, pressure trend and humidity profile — rain probability 70% tomorrow evening." Evaluate both methods honestly: what each sees that the other misses, and the balanced conclusion for a district administration.

Kochi receives rain every April afternoon around 4 p.m., while Mahabaleshwar receives its heaviest rain in July with no fixed hour. Identify the type of rainfall at each place and explain why the timing differs so completely.

Delhi's January fog often swallows the airport at 6 a.m. and has thinned to haze by noon, even with no wind. Explain the fog's birth and its mid-morning retreat using condensation ideas, and say why flights are delayed at 6 but not at 12.

An airport operations manager in Lucknow faces a January morning: dense fog, visibility 150 metres, thirty flights waiting. Apply the knowledge of fog and precipitation to draft the morning's plan — which flights move first, what should be arranged for passengers, and which equipment decides the morning.

A quiz master reads: "Statement 1 — It never rains in November in Nagpur. Statement 2 — It did not rain in Nagpur this November." One statement isclimate, one is weather — but both are wrong as universal truths if a single November shower ever falls. Identify which is which, and explain why the two are judged by completely different standards of evidence.

A city's water board must decide this week whether to impose cuts, using: (i) the reservoir level at 40% of capacity; (ii) the seasonal forecast "normal rainfall expected"; (iii) the thirty-year record showing the city's reservoirs fill mainly in July–September; (iv) this month's rainfall 60% below normal. Apply the weather-climate framework to draft the board's decision logic — which readings govern this week's action, which govern the standing policy, and why confusing the two kinds of decision ruins either the city or the budget.
Evaluate this claim: "Two isotherms on the same map — one for 28°C and one for 30°C — may cross each other near a mountain range, because the mountains make temperatures change quickly."

An isotherm map is drawn from actual station temperatures instead of temperatures reduced to sea level. Predict exactly what will go wrong with the picture, using a coastal plain beside a 2,000-metre plateau as your test case, and state the principle the correction protects.

Two isohyets of different values can never cross — yet on an atlas a student finds what looks like the 100 cm isohyet appearing as two separate closed loops in two different parts of the map. Explain why this is not a violation of the non-crossing rule, and what each loop is asserting.

A horticulture department must site (i) a rain-fed mango orchard and (ii) a drip-irrigated vegetable cluster, using only an annual isohyet map on which a broad wet belt (over 100 cm) occupies the hills, a narrow crowded transition crosses the foothills, and a wide dry belt (under 50 cm) fills the plains. Using nothing but the map's lines, place each project and justify the placement from the spacing and values of the isohyets.

Every weather station in India measures its daily rainfall at the same fixed morning hour. A student calls this "an arbitrary tradition — each place could measure at midnight, since 24 hours is 24 hours". Examine the claim: what actually breaks if different stations used different measurement hours, and why is the common hour not arbitrary?

A new multi-storey car park is built 30 metres upwind of a weather station that has kept an unbroken 40-year record. The station's own instruments are untouched. Will the record stay honest? Identify which readings are at risk, the direction of each distortion, and what should be done about the 40-year archive.

A forward on a family chat shows a screenshot: "Heavy cyclone to hit Odisha coast tomorrow!!" with no date, no issuing office, no validity time. The official website shows a yellow warning for the same coast dated today, valid 48 hours, for "heavy rainfall, wind speed 50–60 km/h", with the storm still far at sea. Compare the two messages as sources, and state which one a family should act on and how.
Create a five-step checklist that a class 7 student could paste beside the computer for reading any weather report on the official website before a school picnic.

A coastal district's control room receives, in one hour: (i) the official website's orange cyclone alert, valid 36 hours, storm 300 km at sea; (ii) a fisher cooperative's report of sudden long swell at a village jetty; (iii) a viral video claiming the storm will strike "tonight". Rank the three inputs for the control room's next actions, justify each rank by the report-anatomy criteria, and state what action each input earns.

From a daily weather box you read: "New Delhi 41/27, Chennai 36/28, Mumbai 32/26, rainfall (24 hrs): Mumbai 44 mm, others nil." State every distinct conclusion this single line supports, and the one conclusion it does not.

A newspaper report states: "The city recorded 8 mm of rain against a normal of 30 mm for the date." Unpack this single sentence: what is an "observed against normal" comparison, which parts of the chapter's chain produce each number, and why can the same sentence honestly appear in a report that also says "the monsoon has been vigorous this week"?

Apply the passport test to this passage from a web page: "Scientists warn that this year's monsoon may fail completely. A study shows rains have dropped 40% over ten years. Share this before it is deleted!" State the verdict on each of the four questions, and the final verdict on the page.

A student claims: "The passport test is defeatist — no one can check everything, so we should just trust the biggest, most professional-looking sites and be done." Write the considered reply: what is right in the fatigue, why the conclusion fails, and the minimal checking discipline that a class 7 student can actually sustain.

Create a step-by-step classroom exercise that takes a student from a blank page to a complete weather report in one 40-minute period, using the school station's register and today's official bulletin.

A report reads: "The minimum temperature was 24°C." A classmate asks why the report bothers with the minimum at all — "everyone knows the day's heat is the maximum." Explain what the minimum records, when it occurs and why the pair of figures carries information that neither number holds alone.

A classmate draws the week's rainfall as a line graph, joining Monday (0 mm) through Wednesday (12 mm), Thursday (45 mm), Friday (20 mm) and Saturday (0 mm) with one smooth line. Explain precisely what falsehoods the line tells, and redraw the plan correctly, stating what the gaps in your version mean.

A student plots a day's hourly temperatures (8 a.m. 27°C, 10 a.m. 30°C, 12 noon 33°C, 2 p.m. 34°C, 4 p.m. 32°C) as a line graph, then claims: "The graph shows it was exactly 33.5°C at 1 p.m." Weigh the claim: what the joined line may honestly be used to read between plotted hours, what it may not, and the discipline sentence that keeps the two apart.

Two rainfall diagrams of the same district week hang in a corridor: one begins its value axis at 40 mm, so only Friday's 60 mm bar appears at all; the other begins at zero and shows five bars including three of 5–15 mm. Both use every figure correctly. Explain precisely how the first diagram misleads despite containing no wrong numbers, and write the two-sentence caption that would disarm the trick without redrawing it.
You are given a rock sample with visible quartz, feldspar, and mica crystals about 3 mm across. Identify the rock type and its cooling environment.
Past‑paper style: “Describe the formation of the Deccan Traps and name the dominant rock type.” (3 marks)

A state museum must choose one hall's theme: "Our Rocks at Work" (cement, coal, oil and groundwater from sedimentary rocks) or "Our Rocks as Archives" (fossils, strata and the story of ancient seas and climates). As the student member of the planning board, evaluate the two themes for a Class 7–8 audience, recommend one with reasons, and design the single exhibit that anchors it.
Design a simple field observation activity for Class 7 students to distinguish mechanical from chemical weathering on a local rock outcrop.

Given a soil profile description: “0‑20 cm dark brown, granular, high organic matter; 20‑55 cm reddish‑brown, blocky, clay accumulation; 55‑90 cm pale yellow, massive, weathered parent material; below 90 cm hard basalt.” Identify the horizons (O, A, E, B, C, R) present and justify each assignment.
Design a simple field activity for Class 7 students to create a miniature soil profile using locally collected materials (rocks, silt, clay, organic matter). List the steps and the learning outcome.
Explain why terracing is more effective than contour ploughing alone on steep slopes (>20°) in the Himalayan region.

A farmer in Rajasthan adopts mulching with paddy straw on a 2‑ha wheat field. After one season, soil moisture at 15 cm depth is 18 % higher than in an adjacent unmulched plot. Evaluate whether this outcome alone proves mulching is the best conservation method for that region.
Design a simple contour ploughing plan for a 100 m long, 12° slope field. State the approximate horizontal spacing between contour lines if the recommended vertical interval is 1 m.

Compare the effectiveness of strip cropping versus terracing on a 12° slope with moderate rainfall (1200 mm/yr). Which method would you recommend for a smallholder growing finger millet and pigeon pea, and why?

A farmer in the Deccan Plateau adopts mulching with sugarcane trash on a 3‑ha cotton field. After two years, soil organic carbon rises from 0.45 % to 0.62 %. Explain the biogeochemical pathway linking mulching to this increase, and state one limitation of relying solely on mulching for long‑term carbon sequestration.
A past CISCE ICSE question: “Explain how contour bunding and graded bunding differ in design and purpose.” Provide a model answer structured for 4 marks.

A student collects a soil sample from a local garden, performs a jar test, and gets 40 % sand, 40 % silt, 20 % clay. Which Indian soil type does this most closely resemble, and what crop would you suggest?
What is the primary educational purpose of a PPT in a Class 7 geography lesson on weathering and soil formation?
Evaluation/Critique: A PPT on “Soil Conservation” uses only government scheme logos (e.g., PMKSY, RKVY) without any field photographs or diagrams. Critique its effectiveness for Class 7 geography.

A student argues: "At 1 cm to 5 km a soil map must be almost exactly true — such a big scale factor means the surveyors measured everything. It is the class sketch map that is approximate." Weigh the argument: what the student has right about the class sheet, what is backwards about the two maps' relationship, and the one sentence that states how map scale and map truth actually trade against each other.

Which of the following is a defining feature of a large‑scale industry in India? A) Capital investment less than ₹1 crore B) Employment of fewer than 50 workers C) Use of advanced machinery and high capital (₹10 crore+) D) Production only for local village market
A Class 7 student argues that “since large‑scale industries need huge capital, only foreign companies can set them up in India.” Critique this claim using Indian examples.

Apply the chapter to a real decision: a state government has ₹100 crore to spend and two proposals — (A) subsidise one giant plant that will employ 2,000 workers directly; (B) support 400 small units with credit, power and marketing help, each employing 15–25 workers. Write the development board's reasoned note comparing the two on employment per rupee, spread, and risk, and state the recommendation.
A village has 30 families each running a cottage unit that makes 15 hand‑woven scarves per week. How many scarves are produced in a month (4 weeks)?
A government scheme provides a ₹50,000 grant to each cottage unit for buying a solar dryer. Explain how this could change the unit’s classification.

A textile mill in Surat employs 2,000 workers: 1,200 unskilled, 600 semi‑skilled, 200 skilled. If the mill adds a new automated dyeing unit requiring 50 skilled technicians, what will be the new percentage of skilled workers?
Create a short plan (3 steps) for a state government to improve the skilled labour pool for the automobile industry in Pune.
In a CISCE exam, a question asks: “Explain two ways in which the Factories Act, 1948 protects industrial workers.” Write a model answer.
A Class 7 student argues that “automation will completely replace labour in future factories.” Critique this view using the concept of labour‑technology complementarity.

Apply the concept of labour cost to decide: Should a new food‑processing unit be set up in Punjab (average daily wage ₹400) or in Bihar (average daily wage ₹250) if both have similar raw material access?
Your school plans to install a 5 kW rooftop solar panel system. Identify whether this uses a renewable or non‑renewable resource and list two advantages for the school.
Design a simple poster for a Class 7 science fair that shows the difference between renewable and non‑renewable resources using everyday Indian examples.
In the context of India’s energy mix, explain why increasing the share of renewable resources is essential for sustainable development. (3 marks)
If a new technology could extract energy from ocean currents with 90 % efficiency, would that make ocean‑current energy renewable? Justify.
A household replaces a 1.5 kW diesel generator with a 1.5 kW rooftop solar system. List two changes in the household’s energy profile regarding renewability and emissions.

‘Renewable energy resources are those which can be replenished naturally within a short period.’ Explain this definition with two examples from India and state one advantage of using such resources. (4 marks)
A village in Odisha plans to install a 5 kW solar PV system. If average daily insolation is 5 kWh/m²/day and panel efficiency is 18 %, calculate the minimum panel area required.

**Application:** A household in Bengaluru uses 300 kWh/month. They install a 3 kW solar system with 5 peak sun hours/day. Estimate the percentage of monthly consumption met by solar, assuming 80 % system performance.
A family uses 30 litres of petrol per month for their car. If they switch to a more fuel‑efficient vehicle that uses 20 % less petrol, how many litres will they save in a year?
If petroleum formation takes 100 million years, and current global consumption is 100 million barrels per day, estimate how many years of formation are represented by one day’s consumption.
A school bus runs 200 km per day and consumes 1 litre of diesel per 5 km. How many litres of diesel does it use in a 200‑day school year?
Write a short note (about 80 words) on the environmental impacts of petroleum combustion and suggest two measures to reduce them.

Match the following hydroelectric projects with their rivers and states: 1. Koyna 2. Salal 3. Sharavathi 4. Nathpa Jhakri Options: A. Chenab – Jammu & Kashmir B. Koyna – Maharashtra C. Sharavathi – Karnataka D. Sutlej – Himachal Pradesh

A household’s monthly electricity bill shows 300 kWh consumption. If they replace all incandescent bulbs (total 500 W) with LEDs (total 75 W) and use them 5 hours daily, estimate the new monthly consumption.
A city plans to replace all street‑lights (5,000 lamps of 150 W each) with 50 W LEDs. If lamps operate 12 hours nightly, calculate the annual energy saving in MWh.
A household decides to run the washing machine only with full loads, reducing cycles from 5 to 3 per week. Each cycle uses 1.2 kWh. What is the monthly energy saving?

Compare the energy‑saving impact of (a) replacing a 1.5‑tonne 3‑star AC with a 5‑star inverter AC, and (b) adding roof‑top solar panels of 2 kW capacity. Assume the AC runs 8 hours/day for 120 days/year; solar generates 4 kWh/day on average. Which saves more annual grid electricity?
Evaluate the policy proposal: “Provide free electricity up to 100 units/month for all rural households to eliminate consumption disparity.” Discuss two potential unintended consequences.
A past CISCE paper asked: “Explain how the distribution of energy resources influences regional development in India.” Provide a concise model answer structured for 4 marks.
If Monday’s meter reading is 15230 kWh and Tuesday’s reading is 15295 kWh, how much electricity was consumed on Tuesday?

A student draws a bar graph of daily electricity use but uses a vertical axis scale that jumps from 0 to 200 kWh in steps of 50, while the highest daily value is only 95 kWh. Evaluate the effectiveness of this graph.
Given the following daily consumption (kWh) for a week: Mon 60, Tue 55, Wed 70, Thu 65, Fri 80, Sat 85, Sun 50. Draw a line graph and identify the day with the highest consumption.
Create a pie chart to show the proportion of weekly electricity use attributed to three appliance groups: Lighting (140 kWh), Cooling (210 kWh), Others (150 kWh). Show the angle for each sector.

Apply the method of finding daily consumption to a scenario where the meter is read at 6 am on Day 1 (12000 kWh) and at 10 pm on Day 2 (12080 kWh). What is the consumption for the 40‑hour period, and how would you express it as an average daily (24‑hour) rate?

Reason from evidence: A family reads its meter every Sunday and plots units per week: Weeks 1–3 hold steady near 42 units; in Week 4 the family adopts door-handle cues and a last-out rule for three often-forgotten fans; Weeks 5–8 record 39, 38, 37, 37 units — through the same hot weather. Reason out what each phase of the graph demonstrates, why the steady weather matters to the argument, and what a Week 9 jump back to 41 would honestly indicate.

Apply: Your class of 40 students keeps leaving fans running after every period. Apply the habit's anatomy to design the classroom fix: name the cue, the action, the reinforcement, and the two verification instruments (the roster and the meter link), and state the one design error that would sink the scheme.

Create: Design a one-month "FAN GUARD" campaign for your home using the habit's full anatomy and the 05_008 measuring frame: the Week 0 baseline, the named cues for three rooms, the family roster, the weekly graph ritual, the reward that is NOT a new appliance, and the honesty rule. Present it as a campaign card a family could pin on the wall.

Answer in CISCE short-answer style: Why is the ceiling fan chosen as the target of the switch-off habit? State the formula for the energy a fan consumes and compute the units wasted by a 70 W fan left running 5 hours daily for 10 days. (2 marks)

Application: The school's summer bill is dominated by 120 classroom fans. The bursar will fund exactly one intervention before May: (a) replacing all fan regulators with five-speed efficient ones, (b) a trained Last-Outer roster across all classes with weekly wing-meter feedback, or (c) two school assemblies on energy saving. Apply the habit framework: state what each option actually changes, choose with reasons, and define the measurement that would prove the choice right by June.

CISCE past-paper pattern: "The last finger on the switch holds more power than the meter can measure." Examine this statement with reference to (a) the measured power — what the meter does and does not register about a switched-off fan (b) the unmeasured power — what the trained reflex produces beyond the units it saves (c) the reflex's passage from one finger to a generation — how a Class 7 habit scales into national arithmetic, with one named chain (d) the verdict and one line on what the switch teaches about the size of citizenship. (5 marks)
Name two major central government schemes launched after 2010 that aimed to provide electricity connections to all rural households in India.

A village 50 km from the nearest substation receives electricity at 11 kV. If the distribution transformer steps down to 230 V for household use, calculate the turns ratio of the transformer (assume ideal).
HOTS: If India aims to achieve 500 GW of non‑fossil fuel capacity by 2030, explain how this target influences the design of the transmission grid.
Application: A school wants to install a 5 kW rooftop solar system. If the average daily solar insolation is 5 kWh/m²/day and panel efficiency is 18 %, estimate the required panel area.
Comparison: Compare the objectives and implementation focus of DDUGJY (2015) and Saubhagya (2017) in a table with three rows: Objective, Target Beneficiary, Key Infrastructure.
CISCE past‑paper pattern: “Explain how the integration of renewable energy sources into the national grid supports the goal of 24×7 power for all. Mention two challenges and two solutions.” (4 marks)
Recall: Define a pie chart and state the comparison it makes. Write the sector-angle formula. List the four reading steps in order, and convert a 144° sector into a percentage share.

Reason from evidence: A home's summer pie shows: Fans 40%, Fridge 25%, Lights 10%, TV 5%, Others 20%. After the family's switch-off month, the new pie shows Fans 30%, Fridge 31.25%, Lights 12.5%, TV 6.25%, Others 20% — and the total fell from 200 to 160 units. Reason out why the fans' share fell while the fridge's share ROSE though the fridge was untouched, what the lights' rising share proves about the family, and why the "Others 20%" constant slice is the chart's quiet warning.

Apply: The class must draw the pie of the school lab wing's monthly units: Computers 90, Fans 40, Lights 20, Water system (pumps) 30, Others 20. Apply the full drawing protocol: compute every sector angle, run the sum-check, and state the one finding sentence the chart exists to deliver.

Answer in CISCE short-answer style: What is a pie chart? The home's monthly consumption of 150 units is divided: Fans 60, Fridge 45, Lights 30, Others 15. Calculate the sector angle for the fans and state the share of the lights as a percentage. (2 marks)

Application: The school office gives the eco-club the wing's month of 300 units: Computers 135, Fans 75, Lights 30, Water system 45, Others 15. The club may present ONE chart to the principal to win one intervention. Apply the decision discipline: compute the pie, choose between asking for (a) auto-shutdown timers for the lab computers or (b) a Last-Outer roster for fans, and justify the choice with the chart's arithmetic and the intervention's mechanism.

CISCE past-paper pattern: "The circle kept the family's secrets; the protractor made them speak." Examine this statement with reference to (a) the secrets — what the family bill concealed that the pie revealed (b) the speech — how the angle formula converts silent units into comparable testimony, with one computation (c) the limits of testimony — what the pie still could not say about the family's month (d) the verdict and one line on what the protractor teaches about evidence. (5 marks)
Create a short questionnaire (5 questions) to investigate the awareness of renewable energy among classmates.

Compare the use of a paper‑based questionnaire versus a mobile‑app questionnaire for collecting energy‑use data in a mixed urban‑rural Class 7 project. List two advantages and two disadvantages of each mode.
What is the primary purpose of constructing an energy model in Class 7 Geography?
Evaluate the effectiveness of using a cardboard model of a nuclear reactor to teach energy concepts at Class 7 level.
Compare a physical model of a wind turbine with a computer simulation of the same turbine in terms of learning outcomes for Class 7 students.

Apply: A wildlife documentary team has one shooting season and must film: (1) gorillas in rainforest, (2) the wildebeest river-crossing migration, (3) Victoria Falls at its mightiest, (4) desert oasis life, and (5) snow against an equatorial skyline. Apply the belt-map: state WHERE (country/feature) and WHEN (season/water condition) each shot is best taken, and the one country whose borders would let the team film three of the five with least travel.

Answer in CISCE short-answer style: Name the two headstreams of the Nile and the city where they meet. State the direction of the Nile's flow and explain briefly why a great river can cross the world's largest desert without drying up. (2 marks)

CISCE past-paper pattern: "Africa is the continent where the sun writes straight, and everything else runs to catch up." Examine this statement with reference to (a) the sun's straight writing — the latitude machine that lays the belts (b) the catching up — the two great interruptions (the Rift and the altitude of the peaks) that the sun's scheme does not write (c) the human reading of the belts — one crop and one way of life per belt, with named places (d) the verdict and one line on what the sentence teaches about geography's first principles. (5 marks)
In the outline map of the world provided, identify and label the capitals of the three sovereign nations of the Australian continent. (3 marks)
Application: Given a political outline map without labels, place the three capitals using the following coordinates: Canberra 35° S, 149° E; Wellington 41° S, 174° E; Port Moresby 9° S, 147° E.
CISCE past‑paper pattern: In the given map, identify the country whose capital lies at 35° S, 149° E.
Apply the case‑study method to a hypothetical European country “Alpia” located in the Alps with high peaks, glacial valleys, and a population of 2 million. Predict its dominant economic activities.

A research team plans to drill an ice core at 3 km depth in East Antarctica. Estimate the age of the ice at that depth if the average annual accumulation is 0.25 m water equivalent and the density of firn is 0.55 g cm⁻³.
Past‑paper style: “Explain two ways in which a mind map helps a Class 7 student locate European countries on a political outline map.” (2 marks)
On a political outline map of Europe with a scale of 1 cm = 500 km, the measured distance between Paris and Berlin is 1.8 cm. Estimate the real straight‑line distance.

Answer in CISCE short-answer style: Define population density and state its formula. Explain why Egypt's population clusters along the Nile while much of the rest of the country is nearly empty. Name Africa's most populous country. (2 marks)

Application: A class must plan a 15-minute "AFRICAN CITIES" segment for school assembly, countering the "no real cities" cliché with three city cards — Cairo, Lagos, Nairobi — each with location-and-water logic, one people-and-language line, one work-and-modernity line, and one belt tie-back. Apply the node's content to build the three cards and the opening sentence that frames them.

CISCE past-paper pattern: "The desert drew the emptiest map, and out of it came the busiest roads." Examine this statement with reference to (a) the empty map — why the Sahara holds so few people (b) the busy roads — what crossed it and why, naming the caravan trade and its goods (c) the roads' children — the cities and peoples the crossings built, with Timbuktu and the Swahili coast as cases (d) the verdict and one line on what the sentence teaches about emptiness and connection. (5 marks)
If a map scale shows 1 cm = 500 km, what is the approximate straight‑line distance between Berlin and Warsaw if they are 3.2 cm apart on the map?
On the outline map of Europe provided, shade the area representing the European Union member states as of 2020 and label any three.
Using a political outline map of Africa (scale 1 cm = 500 km), measure the straight‑line distance between Lagos (Nigeria) and Nairobi (Kenya) and convert it to kilometres.
A CISCE exam asks: “Describe how the Great Rift Valley influences the distribution of lakes and volcanic mountains in East Africa.” Provide a concise answer suitable for 3 marks.
A past CISCE paper asks: “Explain how the location of the Cape of Good Hope influenced early European sea trade routes to Asia.” Provide a structured answer for 4 marks.
Application: You have a political outline map of Africa and a completed mind map. Describe the step‑by‑step process to locate all 54 countries on the outline map using only the mind map.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** A 2023 ICSE Geography question asked: “Explain how a student‑made scrap book can be used as a revision tool for the ‘Study of Continents’ chapter.” Write a concise answer (≈60 words) that would earn full marks.

Reason from evidence: Two road routes must climb the same 300 metres to a hill station. Route A crosses contours that lie 50 metres apart on the ground; Route B crosses contours 400 metres apart. Both sheets carry a 20-metre contour interval. Reason out which route is the road and which is the staircase, compute both steepness fractions, and state why the gentle route is also the cheaper one to build and to drive.

Apply: A hiker's map carries 20-metre contours. Apply the height-reading rules to four positions: (1) a tent drawn exactly on a line labelled 180; (2) a spring a quarter of the way between the 160 and 180 lines; (3) a triangulation point inside the innermost ring labelled 220; (4) a bridge where a road crosses a stream between the 100 and 120 lines near their crowding. State each height or height-range with the rule used, and the one position whose figure is an estimate.

Answer in CISCE short-answer style: What is a contour interval? Two slopes cross contours of the same 20-metre interval; one slope's contours lie 40 m apart on the ground, the other's 200 m apart. Calculate both steepness fractions and state which slope is steeper. (2 marks)

HOTS: "The contour interval is a map's honesty setting — small enough to tell the truth, large enough to tell it simply." Unpack this line: what the interval's SIZE trades off (detail versus clutter), how the same hill is drawn twice with a 10 m and a 50 m interval and what each version is FOR (a planner's sheet versus a trekker's overview), why no single interval serves all purposes, and what the choice teaches about all map generalisation.

Application: A district's planners must choose between two reservoir sites. Site A sits in a gorge: contours at 20 m interval crowd to 80 m apart across the stream. Site B sits in a shallow valley: the same contours lie 600 m apart. Apply the contour system to the choice: compute both valley-side steepnesses, state which site holds more water per dam-length and why (in contour terms), name the site's extra advantage for hydro-power and the one investigation contours cannot settle.

Evaluation: "Children should learn relief from 3-D models and globes FIRST, and contour maps only after — flat contour sheets are an abstraction taught too early." Evaluate in four moves: what the model-first case gets right about the dimensional jump, what it misses about models' own limits and contours' own concreteness, the honest sequence, and the verdict on the order of teaching.

CISCE past-paper pattern: "The contour is the map's way of keeping its promise to the hills." Examine this statement with reference to (a) the promise — what the flat map would otherwise lose and the contour's exact commitment (b) keeping it — the fixed interval and the spacing rule as the promise's mechanics, with one computation (c) the promise's limits — what even the faithful contour cannot tell about the hills (d) the verdict and one line on what the sentence teaches about maps as promises. (5 marks)

A CISCE exam question shows a topographic extract with a closed contour loop labelled 300 m, 290 m, 280 m toward the centre and short hachures on the inner side. What feature is shown and what is its elevation trend?

On a topographic map you see a hill represented by concentric contours at 100 m, 120 m, 140 m, 160 m. The contour interval is 20 m. Calculate the relief of the hill and describe how the contour spacing would change if the hill were steeper.

A past CISCE paper asks: “On the given toposheet extract, identify the landform at grid reference 123456 and justify your answer using contour evidence.” Outline the steps you would take to answer this question fully.
On a contour map, you see concentric closed loops with elevation values increasing toward the centre (e.g., 300 m, 320 m, 340 m). What landform does this pattern represent?
Given a contour interval of 20 m and index contours every 100 m, how many thin contour lines lie between two consecutive index contours?

In a CISCE ICSE Class 7 exam, a toposheet excerpt shows a series of V‑shaped contours with the apex pointing toward a contour value of 450 m, while the arms open toward 400 m. Identify the landform and state the direction of stream flow.

A topographical map shows a series of concentric closed contours with hachures on the inner side of the innermost loop. The values decrease from 400 m (outer) to 350 m (inner). What landform does this represent, and how do the hachures help confirm it?

A past CISCE ICSE question shows a toposheet excerpt with a ridge line running northeast‑southwest. The contour interval is 20 m. The ridge is flanked by valleys on both sides. Sketch (describe) the expected contour pattern and indicate how you would identify the ridge crest on the map.
On a 1:50 000 toposheet, you see a series of black rectangles aligned with a red line marked “NH‑44”. What settlement pattern does this represent?

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Study the given toposheet extract (1:50 000). Identify the settlement pattern at grid reference 123456 and give two reasons for its development.” (Assume the extract shows a row of built‑up symbols along a river.) Write the expected answer.

Recall: State the standard scale of a toposheet as a fraction and convert it (what ground distance does 2 cm stand for?). Name the five colour classes and one feature family of each. List four items of margin information.

Reasoning: On a given sheet, a village of black rectangles stands on the end of a spur 30 metres above a river; yellow fields lie along the riverbanks below it; a cart track zig-zags from the village to the fields; a tank sits beside the fields with a bund across a small stream. Explain, step by step, why the village's SITE was chosen on the spur end rather than beside the river — using the evidence of the colours and symbols, and the monsoon behaviour of the river.

CISCE exam-style: (a) What is meant by the contour interval of a toposheet, and where is it found? (b) Name the colours used for (i) contours (ii) a tank (iii) reserved forest (iv) cultivated land. (c) Convert the scale 1:50,000 to a statement: 1 cm represents how many metres? (d) State one use of the margin's index of adjoining sheets.

Past-paper pattern: Study the description of a toposheet extract and answer the questions. EXTRACT: A 1:50,000 sheet, contour interval 20 m. A river flows south, certified by contour Vs pointing north; a railway line (with two flagged stations) runs east–west crossing the river on a bridge; at the west station a nucleated town of many rectangles with a post office and a police station; east of the river, scattered huts among yellow fields with tanks; a green block south of the railway with a straight northern edge. (i) State the scale conversion and the direction of flow with its evidence. (ii) Classify the two settlements by pattern and rank their likely functions. (iii) Name the occupation zone east of the river and the water devices supporting it. (iv) What does the straight northern edge of the green block represent? (v) Why does the railway's presence at the west station support the town's higher rank?

Application: Your class must document the school's neighbourhood for a heritage folder using ONLY this node's visual forms (no maps of their own making). Name which form you choose for each of the four tasks — (i) recording the present frontage of a 200-year-old temple, (ii) showing how the market street changes from morning to evening, (iii) capturing the whole ward's layout of lanes and rooftops in one frame, (iv) explaining, for the folder's caption page, how the step-well works — and give the one-line reason for each choice.
Given a toposheet excerpt with a contour interval of 20 m, calculate the height difference between two points separated by three contour lines.
On a 1:50,000 toposheet, the distance between two settlements measured on the map is 4 cm. What is the actual ground distance in kilometres?
On a toposheet, the contour interval is 20 m. The highest contour shown is 300 m and the lowest is 100 m. How many contour lines are there between them?
Using an atlas index, you find “Kolkata” on page 42, grid reference E‑12. Describe the steps to locate Kolkata on the map.
On a political map of India, the scale is 1 cm = 200 km. If the distance between Delhi and Jaipur measures 3.5 cm on the map, calculate the actual distance. Show your working.
A topographical sheet uses a scale of 1:50,000. On the sheet, a river measures 4 cm from source to mouth. What is the actual length of the river in kilometres?
A student uses a 2010 satellite image from Bhuvan to analyse the current settlement pattern of a village. Evaluate this approach.
A teacher wants to show change in coastline over 20 years. Which internet resource and method would you recommend?

परीक्षा-शैली: (क) सक्रिय श्रवण की परिभाषा एक वाक्य में दीजिए। (1 अंक) (ख) कहानी-कथन के छह अंग क्रम से लिखिए। (2 अंक) (ग) सुनावट में ठहराव की दो स्थितियाँ और उनका कारण लिखिए। (2 अंक) (घ) त्रुटि पहचानिए — प्रश्न: 'श्रोता-जागरूकता का काम क्या है'; उत्तर: "श्रोता-जागरूकता बहुत ज़रूरी है; इससे कहानी अच्छी लगती है।" (1 अंक)

परीक्षा-प्रारूप प्रश्न: (क) कथा-श्रवण के चार स्तरों के नाम क्रम से लिखिए। (1 अंक) (ख) 'प्रारंभ' और 'समापन' का काम एक-एक वाक्य में लिखिए। (2 अंक) (ग) संकेत-शब्दों 'बारिश', 'स्कूल-बस', 'बूढ़ी ताड़ी की छतरी', 'गीली वर्दी वाले दो बच्चे' से कहानी की रूपरेखा बनाइए — शीर्षक, मोड़ और संदेश अवश्य दीजिए। (3 अंक) (घ) मूल्यांकन कीजिए — "मोहन कहता है: 'मैं कहानी रटकर सुनाता हूँ, इसलिए मेरी सुनावट सबसे सुरक्षित है।'" (2 अंक) (च) यह नोड अगले कौशल 'घटना/चित्र वर्णन' की तैयारी कैसे करता है — दो बिंदु। (2 अंक)
आपने स्कूल की कैंटीन में दोपहर के भोजन के समय एक छोटी घटना देखी। उसे घटना वर्णन के पाँचों तत्वों (काल-क्रम, कारण-परिणाम, संवाद, आत्म-प्रतिक्रिया, पात्र) का प्रयोग करते हुए 6 वाक्यों में लिखिए।
