A past CISCE paper asks: “Define the term ‘Internet Service Provider’ and give two examples from India.” Write a model answer for 2 marks.
A small office has 8 computers and wants a low‑cost network that is easy to expand. Which topology would you recommend and why?
Design a hybrid topology for a school with three labs (each 12 PCs) and an admin office (4 PCs). Sketch the arrangement and label the topologies used.
A network engineer claims that a full mesh topology with 8 nodes requires 28 links. Verify this claim using the formula for full mesh connections.
Critique the statement: "For a small office of 5 computers, a ring topology is the best choice because it uses less cable than a star."
Compare the fault tolerance of a star topology and a partial mesh topology with 6 nodes where each node has at least two links. Which provides better resilience and why?
A past CISCE paper asks: "Draw a labelled diagram of a star topology with 4 computers and a switch. State one advantage and one disadvantage." Provide the expected answer.

Application: the full mock — answer this five-part section in strict examination form within the stated mark-budgets: (i) [1] Name the device that repeats every message out of every port. (ii) [2] A home's pages will not load, but the modem's light is steady and the TV's apps work on the same Wi-Fi — diagnose the most likely device and the reasoning. (iii) [2] State why the home combination box needs BOTH a router half and a switch half — with one job for each. (iv) [3] A 4 MB photo arrives as 32 packets; two are lost on the way. State what IP does about them, what TCP does, and what the sender's and receiver's ends each contribute. (v) [5] The composite: the trust joins two city campuses (each a switched star) to share one admissions database. Name every device in the full path (desktop to server), the protocol pair carrying the database traffic reliably, and the one decision at each of the three joining points — then state why the database's single-copy rule (one server, both campuses read it) is what makes the network worth building at all, with the 06_002 advantage named.

Evaluation: three network designs were submitted for the same brief — a two-storey school wing, 24 machines, one server, one broadband line, strict budget. A: one 24-port switch, star-wired, router at the edge. B: three 8-port hubs chained, router at the edge. C: two 12-port switches (one per storey) joined to the first's router, no server — files kept on the busiest machine. Evaluate each design on delivery behaviour, privacy, and the filing decision; rank them; name the failure each would show in month one; and state the design principle that ranks them — then identify which single change to C makes it defensible, and why the change is not "add more ports".

Name the nine parts of the social-issue presentation skeleton in order, and match each to this opening minute of a presentation: "Good morning everyone. A boy in Class 8 inhaled whitener behind the lab on a dare — and his memory never fully returned. I am here to speak about drug abuse among school students. Drug abuse means using harmful substances — tobacco, inhalants, drugs — to change how one feels. Why does it begin? Curiosity. Peer pressure. The wish to escape a failure at home or in an exam."
Why must a 2-minute presentation on a social issue end with a call to action at all — the audience already knows drug abuse is harmful, so what does the request add that information does not?

A presentation on drug abuse must fit 2 minutes (roughly 260–300 spoken words). The draft plan allocates: a 90-word history of narcotics across the world, a 40-word definition, three causes at 45 words, effects in widening circles at 60 words, no evidence, a call to action at 25 words, and a conclusion at 30 words. Identify the three budget faults and re-plan the 2 minutes with word arithmetic.

Build the complete nine-part plan — one line per station — for a 2-minute presentation titled "Road Safety Begins at Our Gate", to be delivered in your own school assembly. Mark which station will carry the call to action, and state the one sentence you would keep on the palm-card as the cue for that station.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two qualities of an effective hook in a short presentation. (ii) A speaker begins, "Today I will tell you about the very bad and harmful social evil of drug abuse which is increasing in our society." Name the fault and give one repair. (2 marks)

Your school's AI assistant writes a complete 2-minute presentation on any social issue in four seconds, and the teacher asks the class: "The machine's speeches are fluent. What are you training when you deliver yours badly first?" Answer her — what the machine skips, what the human delivery practises, and the one sentence you would put on the assistant's screen.

Two hooks were drafted for a 2-minute value-talk on honesty: (A) "Honesty is the best policy — it is the foundation of all good character, as our elders always tell us." (B) "I returned fifty rupees that were not mine, and it was the most expensive fifty rupees of my life." State which hook opens the better value-talk and give three reasons.

A value-talk on "punctuality" must fit 2 minutes (roughly 270–300 words). The draft plan allocates: a 60-word praise of punctuality quoting two proverbs, a 30-word definition ("punctuality means being on time and disciplined"), a 20-word list of four situations where punctuality matters, no personal story, a 40-word reminder that great leaders were punctual, a 25-word slogan-request ("let us all resolve to be punctual always"), and a 45-word conclusion restating the proverbs. Identify the four faults and re-plan the 2 minutes with word arithmetic.

Build the complete value-talk plan — one line per station — for a 2-minute talk on "Empathy", to be delivered to your own class. Mark which station carries the no-sermon rule most dangerously (the station where the speaker is most tempted to preach), and state the one sentence you would keep on the palm-card as the cue for the request station.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two differences between a value-talk and a social-issue presentation. (ii) A speaker begins a talk on honesty: "Students of today have no values; cheating is everywhere and only punishment can cure it." Name the fault and give one repair. (2 marks)

A life-skills talk on "managing exam-night panic" must fit 3 minutes (roughly 400–450 words). The draft plan allocates: a 90-word explanation of exam stress hormones, a 25-word definition ("staying calm during exams"), four steps described only as "breathe deeply, think positive, take breaks, sleep well" with no order or counts, no demonstration, a 40-word warning that panic ruins results, and a 30-word motivational close ("believe in yourself and success will be yours"). Identify the four faults and re-plan the 3 minutes with word arithmetic.

Build the complete procedural talk plan — one line per station — for a 2-minute talk teaching the skill "making a classroom apology that repairs" (after breaking something, or wronging a classmate). Mark which step is load-bearing and give its exact words, and state the one sentence you would keep on the palm-card as the cue for the request station.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two features that make a life-skills talk different from a value-talk. (ii) A speaker teaching refusal skills says: "You should just say no to such offers politely and move away from bad company." Name the fault and give one repair. (2 marks)
Evaluate the effectiveness of using a “clarification checklist” (listen, question, paraphrase, confirm) as a self‑assessment tool for Class 8 students.

Apply the critical‑evaluation steps to a short extract: “The new metro line will reduce traffic congestion by 30%,” from a city government press release. List the questions you would ask to assess credibility.
A Class 8 student claims that “critical evaluation is only for literature, not for science textbooks.” Using the concept of genre and purpose, critique this claim.

Apply the five‑step critical‑evaluation checklist to a 50‑word advertisement for a new brand of notebook: “BrightMinds notebooks — 200 pages, smooth paper, eco‑friendly. Toppers’ choice! Buy now at ₹120.” List the questions you would ask at each step.

A friendship essay and the bicycle story share the topic "trust between the young". The essay argues: "Trust among friends is built by small daily actions — showing up, keeping small promises — and once broken by gossip it rarely returns." The story argues (per Diagnostic 1): trust broken in concealment must be confessed before it rusts. Compare the two texts under three heads — the form of evidence each uses, what each hides — and state which text would better support an examination answer about CONCEALMENT, with reasons.

In the CISCE examination pattern, answer: (i) State two differences between the topic of a text and its theme. (ii) A student writes: "The theme of the bicycle story is that Meera got new books in the end." Name the fault and give one repair. (2 marks)

**CISCE PAST-PAPER PATTERN:** "(a) In one sentence each, define container scene and unity thread. (b) A passage mentions 'pookalam at the doorstep' and 'sadya on a banana leaf' — state the region, the festival, and the marker categories at work. (c) Compare, in two sentences, a Pongal courtyard and a Bihu courtyard as harvest texts. (d) You suspect a travel passage treats a region as a postcard — state the three audit questions you would put to it. (e) The Howrah passage ends 'nobody needed the second or third' — explain how that sentence converts a marker list into a unity argument." Answer as expected in a Class 8 CISCE-style paper.
What does the term “heritage” refer to when analysing a literary text in Class 8 English?
Create a 100‑word comparative paragraph that analyses how a Sri Lankan short story and an Indian newspaper editorial portray the 2004 tsunami’s impact on coastal communities.
Comparison: Compare the treatment of the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War in an Indian school textbook chapter and a Bangladeshi graphic novel.
A Class 8 student argues that “any story with a journey is an adventure.” Using the node’s definition, critique this statement.

Rewrite the following sentences into a coherent paragraph of about 80 words, adding appropriate transitional phrases: “The library is quiet. Students read books. The librarian helps them. New books arrive every month.”
A Class 8 exam asks: “Write a paragraph of 250‑300 words on ‘A memorable train journey’.” Outline the planning steps you would follow before drafting.

Identify the missing component in this formal letter draft: “12 Green Lane, Mumbai 400001 / 15 October 2025 / The Principal, St. Mary’s School, Mumbai / Subject: Leave Application / Respected Sir, / I am writing to request leave… / Yours faithfully, / Rohan”.

In a CISCE Class 8 exam, a question asks: “Write a formal letter to the Municipal Commissioner complaining about irregular garbage collection in your locality.” Outline the three essential body paragraphs.
CISCE 2023 paper: “Write a formal letter to the District Collector requesting a community library in your village.” List the four content points the marking scheme expects in the body.
Write a 60‑word advertisement for a weekend cricket coaching camp for Class 8 students in Mumbai, including headline, key details and a call‑to‑action.
A CISCE Class 8 exam asks: “Design an advertisement for a school library book‑donation drive.” Outline the plan‑draft‑revise‑edit steps you would follow.
Critique the ethical implication of an advertisement that claims “Our fairness cream guarantees 3 shades lighter in 7 days.”
Compare a classified newspaper ad (text‑only, 30 words) with a full‑page magazine ad (visual, 150 words) for the same coaching centre.
A past CISCE paper asked: “Write an advertisement for a ‘Clean Up Your Neighbourhood’ drive organized by the Residents’ Welfare Association.” Provide a model answer (70 words).
A student writes a diary entry dated 15 August 2025 but describes events from 14 August. Identify the error and its impact on the entry’s credibility.
Compare the effect of the idiom *‘break the ice’* versus the literal phrase *‘start a conversation’* in a speech welcoming new Class 8 students.
Describe the major factors that lead to high population density in the Nile Valley and the Indo‑Gangetic plain. (4 marks)

A planner is given data: Country X has 50 million people and an area of 1,000,000 km²; Country Y has 10 million people and an area of 50,000 km². Which country has the higher population density, and what does that suggest about over/underpopulation pressure?

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Define ‘optimum population’. Explain how it differs from ‘overpopulation’ and ‘underpopulation’. Give one example of a country close to its optimum population.” (4 marks)
Why is Australia considered underpopulated even though it has a population of over 26 million — more than many other countries?
Past-paper pattern: "What is meant by optimum population? Explain how overpopulation and underpopulation both represent departures from it, with one example each." [4 marks]

A town has a birth rate of 18 and a death rate of 6 per 1,000. Its population is 2,00,000. During the year 4,000 people emigrate and 1,500 immigrate. Calculate the town's population at the end of the year, showing every step.
HOTS: A country records zero population growth even though its birth rate (13 per 1,000) exceeds its death rate (8 per 1,000). Is this possible? Deduce what must be true about its migration.

Application: A hill town's population was 1,50,000. During a tourist-boom year, births were 2,700, deaths were 900, 6,000 workers arrived to build hotels and 2,000 retired residents left for the plains. Calculate the year-end population and state which flow dominated.

Past-paper pattern: "The table shows a town's vital statistics for a year: population 5,00,000; birth rate 19; death rate 7; immigrants 9,000; emigrants 14,000. (a) Calculate the natural growth rate. (b) Calculate the total population change and the year-end population. (c) State and explain the single most important action the town council could take to stabilise its population." [2 + 2 + 1 = 5 marks]
CISCE past‑paper pattern: “Explain the term ‘migration’ and state two factors that cause people to migrate from rural to urban areas in India.” (3 marks)

Classify each case by purpose and duration, naming the wave of Indian emigration it belongs to where applicable: (i) a labourer from Chhattisgarh on a five-year contract at a Malaysian palm plantation; (ii) a Gujarati trader's family settling permanently in Nairobi in 1920; (iii) a Hyderabad software engineer migrating to the USA on a skilled work visa with a green-card plan; (iv) a Kerala mason on a two-year UAE site contract, renewing it eight times.

Past-paper pattern: "Study the description and answer: A 30-year-old diploma holder from coastal Andhra paid an unregistered agent ₹80,000 to reach a Gulf construction job; his two-year contract pays triple his home wage; he sends 60% of it home monthly. (a) Identify the wave/type of emigration. (b) Name two risks visible in this case. (c) State one action the government could take to protect such workers." [1 + 2 + 1 = 4 marks]

A sending village shows the following changes over 15 years: men aged 20–45 mostly absent; 60% of farms managed by women; three new English-medium schools; a moneylender closing down; and a youth preference for "Gulf plans" over farming. Explain each observation as a specific impact of migration.

Past-paper pattern: "Study the description and answer: District K sends 3 lakh workers annually to metro construction; 55% of its farms are managed by women; remittances equal 40% of district income; enrolment in local industrial-training institutes has fallen by half in ten years. (a) Identify the dominant migration pattern and its stream. (b) Explain the fall in ITI enrolment as a migration impact. (c) State one measure to reverse the impact in (b)." [1 + 2 + 1 = 4 marks]

Past-paper pattern: "Study the description and answer: In a given year, 12,000 nurses from one developing country cleared foreign licensing examinations and emigrated; the same year, its own health ministry reported 30,000 vacant nursing posts and a new nursing college built entirely with public funds. (a) Name the phenomenon and the sector in which it is 'sharpest'. (b) Identify the two asymmetries the description illustrates. (c) State one measure the destination countries could adopt to reduce the damage without stopping the flow." [1 + 2 + 1 = 4 marks]
In the CISCE examination style: "Why do educated and skilled people emigrate from developing countries? Give three reasons." [3 marks]

Past-paper pattern: "Study the case and answer: Dr. Asha completes her medical degree at a government college where her education was heavily subsidised. Her district hospital lacks a functioning ICU and has no path to specialisation; promotion depends on retirements. A foreign hospital's recruitment team visits her city, offers a post at five times her salary, sponsors her licensing examination and work visa, and promises a research-track career in a fully equipped hospital. She emigrates within a year. (a) Identify two push factors and two pull factors in the case. (b) Explain which single factor you judge strongest, giving the mechanism. (c) State one home-side measure that would most likely have changed her decision, and why it matches the differential." [1 + 2 + 2 = 5 marks]
In the CISCE examination style: "Explain three effects of brain drain on developing countries." [3 marks]

Past-paper pattern: "Study the case and answer: Over five years, a developing country's information-technology sector sent 1,00,000 (one lakh) trained engineers abroad as permanent settlers. During the same five years, domestic software firms reported unfilled senior posts, two home-grown product companies folded for want of experienced leadership, and the country received large annual remittances alongside a growing diaspora that funded college laboratories and mentored student startups. By the decade's end, several thousand of the earlier emigrants returned to found firms in the home technology cities. (a) Name two positive and two negative impacts visible in the case, with the side each sits on. (b) Explain why the remittances could not save the two folded companies. (c) State what the returning founders changed about the country's long-run account, and name the term for their movement." [2 + 2 + 2 = 6 marks]

Classify each development as an instance of migration, natural increase, or reclassification driving urbanisation, with a one-line reason: (i) a village gains a thermal-power township and is notified a municipality; (ii) a metro's population rises as farm families from three states settle in its construction workforce; (iii) a city's own births exceed its deaths by 40,000 a year; (iv) a large village crosses 5,000 residents and 75 per cent non-farm male workers and becomes a census town; (v) a new expressway halves travel time to a megacity and weekend-van families relocate outward along it.
In the CISCE examination style: "What is meant by urbanisation? State three causes of urbanisation." [1 + 3 = 4 marks]

Application: A village of 3,800 people, 82 per cent farm-dependent, sits where a new expressway interchange and a cold-chain logistics depot are being built 2 km away. Predict its twenty-year trajectory through the cause-streams of urbanisation, stage by stage, and state the single indicator that will earliest reveal the turning point.

Past-paper pattern: "Study the settlement report and answer: Sunheri began the decade as a village of 4,200 residents at 320 persons per km², with 74 per cent of male workers in cultivation. It ended the decade with 6,400 residents at 470 persons per km², 78 per cent engaged in non-farm work after a food-processing unit and a polytechnic opened; the panchayat has petitioned for municipal status. (a) Show, using the census tests, that Sunheri now qualifies as a census town. (b) Identify which cause-streams operated during the decade, with evidence from the report for each. (c) State one likely impact of the notification on Sunheri's next decade." [2 + 2 + 1 = 5 marks]

Classify each impact by sign (positive/negative) and domain (economic, social, environmental, infrastructural): (i) a state capital's hospitals now offer cardiac and cancer care; (ii) the city's lake is filled for a housing layout; (iii) garment-factory employment draws 20,000 women into first-time wage work; (iv) evening water comes one hour a day in summer; (v) children of slum and tower study in the same government school; (vi) peak-hour traffic crawls at walking pace.
In the CISCE examination style: "Explain three problems that rapid urbanisation creates for a city." [3 marks]

Application: A city of 15 lakh, ringed by farmland and three shallow lakes, must absorb 5 lakh residents in twelve years. Forecast its impact ledger under "business as usual" (frozen water capacity, no transit plan, edge expansion over farms and lakes) across five domains — housing, water, transport, land, health — and mark which two entries will prove hardest to reverse once created.

Past-paper pattern: "Study the city report and answer: In fifteen years, Bharatnagar grew from 20 lakh to 34 lakh residents. Piped water capacity stayed at 300 MLD; bus fleet stayed at 1,200 while registered two-wheelers tripled; 60 hectares of lake and farmland were converted to housing; air-quality readings degraded every winter; one in four residents now lives in informal settlements. (a) Identify four impacts visible in the report, with each one's domain. (b) Compute the water deficit at 34 lakh using the 135 litres-per-person norm, and state its consequence. (c) Name the single measure that would most change the report's next edition, with its mechanism." [2 + 2 + 2 = 6 marks]

Given a map showing a metropolitan core and three surrounding settlements — Settlement A (population 50 000, only residential, no local industry), Settlement B (population 3 lakh, has an IT park, own municipal council), Settlement C (population 8 lakh, mixed land use, own municipal corporation, connected by metro) — identify which are satellite cities.

Trace one complete smart loop — a city's underground water pipe springs a leak at 2 a.m. — through the sense–analyse–act–verify stages, and state what the loop saves compared with the un-smart outcome.
In the CISCE examination style: "What is a smart city? State two of its features and give one example of such a city." [1 + 2 + 1 = 4 marks]

HOTS: A city floods on schedule every monsoon despite 3,000 new CCTV cameras watching its streets. Diagnose the failure using the loop framework, and redesign the system so the cameras earn their keep.

HOTS: A municipal service moves app-only; within months, complaint volumes fall 40 per cent and officials claim success. Construct the two rival readings of the same statistic, and design the measurement that would settle which is true.

Past-paper pattern: "Study the two-city note and answer: Twin-built riverside towns, A and B, both installed cameras, free Wi-Fi and an app. Town A housed everything in a control room staffed by police alone; departments learned of events from newspapers. Town B built an integrated command centre where water, drainage, traffic, health and waste data converged; each department was contractually bound to respond to alerts within set times; monthly public dashboards published response performance. After two monsoons, Town B's flooded hours fell by half; Town A's did not move. (a) Identify which town satisfies the smart-city definition and why. (b) Name the two design elements Town A lacked. (c) State the feature of Town B that most likely caused the flooded-hours fall, with its mechanism." [2 + 2 + 2 = 6 marks]
A Class 8 student is asked to create a Venn diagram comparing village and city life. Which two overlapping items should appear in the intersection?

Apply: A large automated textile park opens at the edge of a district town — 5,000 workers on site, most machines run by computer. Predict, step by step, the settlement changes over the following ten years, naming the mechanism behind each.

Create: Design a 30-minute classroom brainstorming session on "How does technology drive urbanisation?" — its question phrasing, the rules of the divergent phase, the clustering method, and the convergent ending. State one rule you would enforce hardest, and why.
In the CISCE examination style: "Explain how technological development promotes urbanisation. Support your answer with two examples from India." [4 marks]

Past-paper pattern: "Read the extract and answer the questions. *'When the broad-gauge line reached Balpur in 1998, it carried three things on schedule: the morning shuttle to the district city, wagons loading the new rice mill's output, and, by evening, the first daily returns of people who had begun working in the city while keeping their village homes. Within a decade, Balpur's grain traded wider, its harvest crews had shrunk to machine squads, its station bazar held two colleges and a hospital, and its emptying corners had filled instead with boys waiting for the 6:10 shuttle in ironed shirts.'* (a) Identify the two directions of movement the line created, with evidence for each. (b) Name the mechanism behind the shrinkage of harvest crews, and the wider chain it belongs to. (c) 'Balpur urbanised without becoming a city.' Justify or challenge this statement using the settlement criteria." [2 + 2 + 2 = 6 marks]

Reasoning: Why must a Class 8 project on smart cities begin by narrowing "smart cities in India" to a single question about a single city? What exactly goes wrong with the wide version at each later stage?

Evaluate: Two project proposals reach the teacher. Proposal A: "A study of smart cities in India — I will collect pictures and information from the internet and make a colourful chart of ten cities." Proposal B: "Which smart feature has most changed daily life in our town — the water metering, the new bus displays, or the waste-collection app? A survey of 30 households in Ward 4." Judge both: strengths, failures, and the one change that would most improve the weaker.

Apply: A student's Ward 4 survey of 30 households returns these results on which smart feature most changed daily life: water metering — 6 households; bus displays — 8 households; waste-collection app — 11 households; "nothing changed" — 5 households. (i) Convert this into a table with percentages. (ii) State the finding the data supports. (iii) State one follow-up question the student should now ask, and why.
In the CISCE examination style: "You have to prepare a project on a smart city being developed in India. State the steps you would follow, from choosing the topic to presenting the report." [5 marks]

HOTS: A student's survey finds that 80 per cent of respondents praise the city's new waste app — but every respondent was approached outside the mobile store on a weekday morning. Diagnose the sampling failure precisely, predict what a fair sample would likely show, and state the two sentences the student must add to the report once the flaw is discovered after submission of data.

HOTS: A Mission city's public dashboard claims "95 per cent of smart-city works completed". Your project's ten interviews in two wards find unpaved lanes, irregular water timing and no visible smart feature. Construct the rival readings of the dashboard figure, design the one table that would test between them, and state what the project should finally claim.

Evaluation: A classmate argues: "The project's findings cannot change anything — we are Class 8, the city will not read our report, so the marks are the only real output." Assess the claim: what it gets right, what it misses about who actually reads student work and how, and the refutation the chapter's own material supplies.

Past-paper pattern: "Read the extract from a student's project report and answer the questions. *'Question: Has the e-governance app changed how Ward 6 residents get municipal certificates? Method: I interviewed 12 households (6 app users, 6 non-users) during my winter vacation stay with my aunt. Findings: all 6 app users received their last certificate without visiting the office, in 3–7 days; 5 of 6 non-users visited the office twice on average and waited 2–4 weeks; the 6th non-user is my aunt's neighbour who cannot read and asked me to apply for her. Conclusion: the app works. Limits: I could not check official records.'* (a) Identify the project's strongest stage and justify with evidence from the extract. (b) The finding hides an exclusion. Name it, cite the extract's evidence, and state the analysis the student should have written. (c) Rewrite the conclusion in one sentence so that it is both true and complete." [2 + 2 + 2 = 6 marks]

Reasoning: On 26 January 2001 an earthquake of magnitude about 7.7 struck Gujarat. Explain why the same earthquake, occurring under an uninhabited part of the Rann of Kachchh, would not have been called a disaster — and what this tells us about where the word "disaster" actually lives.

Evaluate: A classmate classifies these five events all as "natural disasters": (i) the 26 December 2004 tsunami; (ii) the Mumbai floods of 26 July 2005; (iii) the Bhopal gas leak of December 1984; (iv) the annual floods of the Brahmaputra in Assam; (v) a fire that gutted a multi-storeyed factory because its staircases were locked and its fire extinguishers were expired. Judge each classification, correct the wrong ones, and state the single test you used.
In the CISCE examination style: What is a disaster? Distinguish between natural and man-made disasters, giving two examples of each from India. [4 marks]

HOTS: Two Indian coasts are struck in the same decade by cyclones of comparable intensity. Coast A's toll: thousands dead. Coast B's toll: dozens dead, after lakhs of people moved to shelters in the preceding 48 hours. Neither coast controlled the cyclone. Construct the full explanation of the toll difference using the hazard–vulnerability–capacity model, and state the lesson it forces about the word "preventable".

Past-paper pattern: Read the extract and answer the questions. *"The hill district's third cloudburst in five years sent a wall of water and debris through the market settlement below the new highway. Forty-two bodies were recovered; the district hospital was overwhelmed. Survivors said the slope above the highway had been stripped of trees during cutting, and no slope-protection work had followed. The district's early-warning siren, installed years ago, was found rusted and unconnected to any power source. 'The mountain has always been cruel here,' the pradhan said. Officials announced compensation for the families."* (a) Classify this disaster by family, justifying with two pieces of evidence from the extract. (b) Identify the three human amplifiers named in the extract and state what each converted a hazard into. (c) "The mountain has always been cruel here." Challenge the pradhan's framing in two sentences using the extract's own facts. [2 + 3 + 2 = 7 marks]

Evaluate: Two households in the same flood-prone mohalla receive the same first warning at 10 a.m. Household A: listens, decides to "wait and watch how serious it gets", packs documents at 2 p.m., and wades with belongings to the shelter at 5 p.m. through chest-deep lane water, carrying a steel trunk. Household B: on the first warning, switches off the mains, seals documents in plastic, shoulders a pre-packed kit, and walks to the shelter at noon through ankle-deep water. Audit both households phase by phase, state what each did right, and identify the single decision that most changed their outcomes.

Apply: A district issues its flood advisories in stages. Stage 1 (Yellow, "advisory"): heavy rain forecast, river rising, 48 hours expected. Stage 2 (Orange, "warning"): river above danger mark at the upstream gauge, 24 hours. Stage 3 (Red, "evacuation order"): breach reported 6 km upstream, water reaching the locality in 2–3 hours. State, for each stage, exactly what the Sarkar family of a low-lying locality should complete, and why each task belongs to its stage and no later.
In the CISCE examination style: What is meant by disaster management? State two safety measures that should be taken *before* a flood and two *during* a flood. [4 marks]

Application: Your school lies in a flood-prone town and the Principal asks you to draft the School Flood Protocol — the rules for the three stage-warnings and for the after-flood reopening. Draft it: (i) what the school completes at Yellow (48 h), Orange (24 h) and Red (evacuation), staff and students distinguished; (ii) the two absolute student rules during any flood emergency; (iii) the reopening checklist that must be completed before students re-enter.

Past-paper pattern: Read the extract and answer the questions. *"When the administration announced that the embankment upstream had given way, Tara's father moved the family's grain to the loft and went to the haat as usual. By midnight the lanes were knee-deep; the family climbed to the roof with two bags of clothes. Tara's mother waded back for the ration card and land papers at 2 a.m. In the relief camp, the children drank the tank water provided without boiling; four of them, including Tara, reported stomach cramps within the week. On return, the family slept in the house the same night. The village's school reopened the next morning, its tanks unflushed."* (a) Identify two correct acts and two dangerous acts in the family's conduct, naming the phase of each. (b) State the rule that Tara's mother broke and the rule the school broke; whose breach cost more, and why? (c) Rewrite the family's next-monsoon plan in four lines so that every breach above is closed. [2 + 3 + 2 = 7 marks]
A case study: In the 2001 Gujarat earthquake, many buildings collapsed due to non‑ductile construction. Explain two building design features that improve earthquake resistance.
Write a short note (about 80 words) on the role of community awareness in reducing casualties during earthquakes and fires.

Evaluate: After identical floods, two districts report. District P: control room opened on the first warning, 40,000 people moved to shelters pre-stocked in October, NDRF columns clearing roads by day two, relief registers opened within a week. District Q: warnings received but not disseminated below the block office, shelters locked with keys untraceable, boats requisitioned after the water rose, relief distributed three weeks late through an unverified beneficiaries' list. Judge the two responses against the four-phase cycle, identify the level at which each failure occurred, and state the two reforms that would most change District Q.

Apply: IMD names a severe cyclone expected to cross a coastal district in 72 hours. Write the countdown — what exactly happens at T-minus-72, T-minus-48, T-minus-24 and T-minus-0 to landfall — at each level of the ladder (national, state, district, local), with the one act at each stage that must not slip.

In the CISCE examination style: Describe the role of the government in disaster management, stating the four levels of its machinery in India and naming two national institutions with their functions. [5 marks]

HOTS: Between the Super Cyclone of October 1999 (nearly ten thousand dead on the Odisha coast) and Cyclone Phailin of October 2013 (fewer than fifty dead, nearly ten lakh evacuated from the same coast), the cyclones were comparable but the state was not. Identify precisely what the government built or changed in those fourteen years — categorising each item as hardware, software or law — and explain why the *software* items, the cheapest on the list, did most of the life-saving work.

HOTS: In a coastal evacuation, the control room's dashboard shows 70 per cent of a village moved to shelters — yet the panchayat had reported "warning received, all informed". Diagnose the gap between informing and moving: name the four populations that warnings routinely fail to reach or move, and design the two mechanisms that close the gap without waiting for the disaster to reveal it.

Past-paper pattern: Read the extract and answer the questions. *"As Cyclone 'Tej' strengthened over the Bay, the IMD bulletin at 11 a.m. warned of landfall near the Kavali coast in 60 hours. By 1 p.m., the district control room had opened; by nightfall, 11,000 of the coast's 26,000 residents were in shelters. Fishermen refused to beach their boats — 'the sea pays for the boat's loan'. On day two, the panchayat's loudspeaker van broke; three villages received no door-to-door visit. At landfall, 9,000 people were still unaccounted for in the surge zone; the NDRF, pre-positioned behind the line, pulled 1,200 from rooftops and trees. The final toll: 31. The Collector's dawn-after briefing began: 'The machine held at seven of its ten joints.'"* (a) Identify the two joints of the machine that failed, naming the level of the ladder at which each sits. (b) The fishermen's refusal is which of the four last-mile populations, and what machine feature addresses it? (c) "The machine held at seven of its ten joints" — explain how a 31-death toll and a 9,000-person accounting gap can be true together, and state the one reform the Collector's next October should fund first. [2 + 2 + 3 = 7 marks]
Which prior‑learning topic from Class 6 Geography best explains why the Brahmaputra River floods annually during the monsoon?

Compare the role of the fire triangle (fuel, heat, oxygen) taught in Class 7 Chemistry with the safety measure “remove fuel” during a kitchen fire. Which component of the triangle does this measure target?

In the ICSE Class 8 Geography exam, a question asks: “Explain how the concept of the water cycle helps in predicting flood‑prone areas.” Write a concise answer (3‑4 sentences) that would earn full marks.
Evaluate the effectiveness of using a KWL chart at the start of this chapter for a heterogeneous Class 8 class where some students have experienced a flood and others have not.

Evaluate: For the same flood, the class can watch a three-minute social-media clip (unattributed, dramatic music, 20 lakh views) or a thirty-minute documentary (archive footage, named officials and survivors, broadcast archive). Evaluate the two as learning sources using four criteria, and state the one thing the clip offers that the documentary does not — with the safeguard that makes it usable.

Apply: During a tsunami documentary's twelve-minute core segment, a student's note grid must stay current. Fill the four-column grid as the ideal student would at four timestamps — the beach's sudden withdrawal (minute 1), the scientist's explanation of the two-plate rupture (minute 4), the warden's megaphone evacuation of the lane (minute 8), the survivor's account of returning to the house (minute 12) — writing each cell in one line, and name which column the class most often fails to fill and why.

In the CISCE examination style: What is a documentary film? State three ways in which documentary films are useful in the study of disasters, and mention two precautions the class should take while using them. [5 marks]

Application: Design the complete one-period (40-minute) viewing lesson for a 22-minute preparedness documentary following an NDRF battalion's flood-rescue training — minute-by-minute plan, with the before-questions, the grid focus for this film type, the audit step sized to the time left, and the exit ticket. Verify the arithmetic closes at 40 with contingency.

Past-paper pattern: Read the extract and answer the questions. *"From the class's submitted review of a 2013 Kedarnath flood documentary: 'The film opens with pilgrims' phones recording the rising mandakini water. At minute six a hydrologist explains the extreme rainfall of that June on a data wall. At minute eleven a shopkeeper describes how he ran his family uphill on the second warning. At minute nineteen the film shows the rebuilt market and the new warning siren on the ridge. The narration at minute twenty says the valley 'learned its lesson forever'. Our grid's question column holds: the phones recorded but who received the recordings? Was the second warning official or the crowd? Who maintains the ridge siren — and when was it last tested?'"* (a) Identify the documentary type(s) and the timestamp that justifies each classification. (b) The class's three question-column entries share one property — name it, and explain why such entries are the grid's most valuable output. (c) Evaluate the minute-twenty narration claim ("learned its lesson forever") using the audit vocabulary, and state what evidence would be needed to earn it a place in the class's notes. [2 + 2 + 3 = 7 marks]
In the CISCE examination style: What are visual sources in the study of disasters? Name three kinds of visuals with one use of each, and state two precautions necessary while reading them. [4 marks]

Past-paper pattern: Read the extract and answer the questions. *"From the geography laboratory's incident file, Tuesday: 'Class 8-C was given Visual 1 — an aerial photograph, captioned "Bihar floods, this week" — and Visual 2 — a rainfall chart, titled "Our district, the monsoon of record". The chart's axes carried units and its source line named the district's records for a 30-year period. The photograph carried no source, no date; its caption was the only label. Task one asked for two facts extractable from each visual. Most pairs produced for Visual 2 the season's wettest month and its departure percentage, with working. For Visual 1, one pair wrote "the flood is severe" and "the water is deep"; another pair wrote "this proves our district floods"; a third pair refused the task and wrote: "Visual 1 yields zero facts — it is a picture with an assertion attached." The file notes the third pair's answer as the year's best."'* (a) What made Visual 2 productive of facts where Visual 1 was not? Name the property and the apparatus that carried it. (b) Assess the third pair's refusal: is "zero facts" strictly correct, what CAN an unlabelled photograph ever yield, and was the refusal still the best answer? (c) The file asks for a one-line rule to print above the laboratory's visual bench. Write the rule, and state the two student habits it is designed to build. [2 + 3 + 2 = 7 marks]
What is the primary purpose of using newspaper articles when studying natural and man‑made disasters in Class 8 Geography?

Given a newspaper clipping about a cyclone that lists “evacuation of 2 lakh people,” “opening of 150 relief camps,” and “distribution of 5 lakh food packets,” list three safety measures a student can infer for future cyclones.
Use a recent newspaper article (e.g., *The Hindu*, 15 July 2023, on Himachal Pradesh landslides) to identify the immediate relief measures announced by the state government.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define a periodical. (b) Distinguish a journal from a magazine. (c) Why are journals and magazines called secondary sources of disaster information? (d) Name one Indian magazine useful for disaster study. [5 marks]
Evaluate the usefulness of the 2018 Kerala flood case study for designing a flood‑preparedness plan in a coastal city like Mumbai.
Apply the five‑step framework to outline a case study of the 2001 Bhuj earthquake.
Create a one‑page case‑study template that a Class 8 student could fill for any disaster.
A student wants to include satellite imagery in a case study on the 2021 Maharashtra floods. Which step of the framework does this best support, and why?
Critique the following case‑study excerpt: “The 2018 Kerala floods were caused by heavy rain. Many people died. The government helped.”
Compare the role of community volunteers in the 2018 Kerala floods and the 2001 Bhuj earthquake.
Evaluate the usefulness of the Bhuvan portal (ISRO’s geoportal) for a Class 8 student preparing a flood‑risk map of their district.
Compare the Internet’s role in disaster management today with its role ten years ago (c. 2015) in India. Highlight two technological advances that have changed student‑level access.
Design a simple earthquake mock drill plan for a Class 8 classroom of 40 students, listing three key steps.
Write a short note (about 80 words) on the importance of debriefing after a mock drill, citing two benefits.
Why does the teacher use a documentary clip before opening a discussion on the 2018 Kerala floods?
Create a discussion prompt that integrates a newspaper article on the 2023 Uttarakhand flash floods with the government‑role node.

A past‑paper style question: “Describe how a teacher can use a case study of the 2013 Uttarakhand flash floods to structure a 30‑minute discussion that meets CISCE’s assessment objectives for disaster management.”
Name the six political entities that constitute East Asia as defined in the CISCE Class 8 syllabus.
**HOTS:** “If the Himalayas were 1 000 m lower, how would East Asia’s climate and vegetation change?”
**COMPARISON:** Compare the latitudinal climate gradient of East Asia (20° N–50° N) with that of eastern North America (25° N–50° N). Identify two similarities and two differences.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “On the outline map of Asia provided, mark and label: (a) the Gobi Desert, (b) the Yangtze River, (c) the Japanese island of Hokkaido, (d) the 40° N parallel.”
A student is given a climate graph for Yakutsk (62° N, 129° E) showing January mean –38 °C and July mean +19 °C. Identify the climate type and justify using the graph.
**HOTS:** How would a 2 °C rise in mean annual temperature affect the southern boundary of continuous permafrost in North Asia?
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain how the physical geography of North Asia influences its economic activities.” (4 marks)

**Application:** You are given annual temperature figures for a Central Asian town — July mean about 30 °C, January mean about −10 °C — and for a coastal Chinese city at the same latitude — July 28 °C, January 3 °C. Compare and explain the contrast.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) What is meant by a landlocked country? (b) Name the two great rivers of Central Asia and their terminal lake. (c) Why are the region's terminal lakes salty? (d) State one consequence of the Aral Sea's shrinkage. (e) Name the mountain hub from which Asian ranges radiate. [5 marks]

**APPLICATION:** A farmer in the Fergana Valley relies on Syr Darya water for cotton. Using knowledge of the Tian Shan’s glacial melt, propose one adaptation strategy if glacier volume shrinks by 30 % over the next 30 years.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define watershed. (b) Name the river called "China's sorrow" and explain the title in one sentence. (c) Which is Asia's longest river and into which sea does it flow? (d) Name the world's largest delta. (e) State one reason the Tigris–Euphrates basin became a cradle of civilisation. [5 marks]

In a CISCE‑style map‑based question, you are given a blank outline of Asia with only the equator and the 100° E meridian marked. Place and label the following: Japanese Archipelago, Philippine Archipelago, Indonesian Archipelago, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Sri Lanka, Maldives.
A weather station at 45°N, 85°E records an average January temperature of –20 °C, July temperature of 20 °C, and annual precipitation of 150 mm. Identify the climate type and justify.
A location at 30° N, 80° E lies at 2 500 m altitude in the Himalayas. Predict its natural vegetation type and justify.
Explain why the Tibetan Plateau experiences a cold, alpine climate even though it lies mainly between 28°N and 40°N (subtropical latitudes).

Given a north‑south transect along 100°E from the equator (0°) to 60°N, sketch a flow chart linking latitude, relief, climate, and natural vegetation for three locations: (a) Singapore (1°N), (b) Lhasa (30°N, 3,650 m), (c) Yakutsk (62°N).
Given a climate graph for a station at 45°N, 120°E (Harbin), identify the climate type and natural vegetation, and explain how latitude and continental interior position contribute.
Describe how the relief of Asia influences the distribution of its major river systems. (CISCE exam‑style, 5 marks)
“Explain how the relief of Asia influences the distribution of its major mineral resources.” (CISCE past‑paper pattern, 6 marks)
Derive the natural vegetation of a place at 25° N with 900 mm of summer-concentrated rainfall on a low coastal plain, showing the reasoning chain.
**Application:** A geography quiz gives three clues — "55° N, 400 mm precipitation mostly as snow, conifers everywhere" — and asks for the belt and one economic use. Solve and show the reasoning.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define natural vegetation. (b) Why is the monsoon forest called deciduous? (c) Name the largest forest belt of Asia and its chief trees. (d) What is the snowline? (e) State one adaptation each of a desert plant and a tundra plant. [5 marks]
Using a map scale of 1 cm = 200 km, calculate the actual distance between two cities that are 3.5 cm apart on the map.

A student measures 3 cm between two cities on an atlas map with a graphic scale of 1 cm = 150 km. What is the actual ground distance, and why might the measured distance differ from the true travel distance?
Using an atlas, you find that the city of Ulaanbaatar lies at 47.9° N, 106.9° E. Describe the steps you would take to locate it on the Asia political map.
Compare the use of a graphic scale bar versus a representative fraction (RF) scale for measuring distances on an atlas map. Which is more practical for a Class 8 student and why?
What is the primary purpose of using clay or papier‑mâché in a Class 8 geography lesson on Asia’s physical features?
Evaluate the statement: “A clay model of the Himalayas built at 1 cm = 100 km horizontal scale and 1 cm = 1 000 m vertical scale accurately represents the mountain range’s steepness.”

In a CISCE ICSE Class 8 geography exam, a question asks: “Explain how a three‑dimensional clay model of the Tibetan Plateau can help students understand the formation of the Asian monsoon.” Write a concise model answer (≈80 words).

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State one advantage of tabulating data. (b) Convert into a two-row table: "Siberia's rivers flow north to the Arctic Ocean; East Asia's rivers flow east to the Pacific." (c) Draw, in words, a four-box chain showing the fate of Central Asia's rivers. (d) Which tool — chain or table — suits "compare the climate belts of Asia"? (e) State one rule for wording table cells. [5 marks]
Why does India need a Standard Meridian despite its longitudinal spread of about 29°?
If it is 12:00 noon at the Standard Meridian (82°30′E), what is the local solar time at 68°7′E (western tip)?
If India adopted two time zones split at 82°30′E, what would be the maximum time difference between the easternmost and westernmost points? Show your calculation.

A flight departs from Mumbai (72°50′E) at 10:00 IST and lands in Kolkata (88°22′E) after 2 hours 30 minutes flight time. What is the local solar time at Kolkata on arrival, assuming no time‑zone change?

On the outline map of India provided, mark and label: (i) 82°30′E meridian, (ii) 23°30′N parallel, (iii) the northernmost point (Indira Col), (iv) the southernmost point (Indira Point). Write one sentence on the significance of each.
A past CISCE paper asked: “Describe how the location of India’s neighbours influences its climate.” Write a model answer for 4 marks.

परीक्षा-शैली में: (क) सक्रिय श्रवण के तीन काम लिखिए। (1 अंक) (ख) प्रस्तुति के तीनों अंगों के नाम और प्रत्येक का एक-एक काम लिखिए। (3 अंक) (ग) वाद-विवाद में दो शिष्टाचार-नियम लिखिए। (2 अंक) (घ) उच्चारण-स्पष्टता के अतिरिक्त मौखिक अभिव्यक्ति के तीन अन्य मानक बताइए। (2 अंक)

आपके विद्यालय की मोबाइल-नीति पर वाद-विवाद है। विपक्ष के तीन तर्क: (1) "मोबाइल से शिक्षा-ऐप्स पढ़ाते हैं"; (2) "सुरक्षा के लिए ज़रूरी है"; (3) "आज की पीढ़ी बिना मोबाइल अपंग है"। आपका पक्ष: विद्यालय के घंटे में मोबाइल-प्रतिबंध। (क) तीनों का शिष्ट, बिंदुवार उत्तर लिखिए। (ख) उत्तरों के क्रम की योजना बताइए — किस तर्क का उत्तर सबसे पहले और क्यों?

परीक्षा-पद्धति में: (क) प्रस्तुति 'स्वच्छ भारत अभियान' पर तीन-अंग रूपरेखा लिखिए — हर अंग में एक वाक्य। (2 अंक) (ख) श्रवण-अंश: "सूचना — कल सुबह नौ बजे सफ़ाई-अभियान, बगीचे के द्वार से शुरुआत; दस्ताने अपने; ग्यारह बजे शपथ।" तीन बिंदु और उनका क्रम लिखिए। (2 अंक) (ग) वाद-विवाद: "सफ़ाई की ज़िम्मेदारी सरकार की है, नागरिक की नहीं" — विपक्ष के पक्ष में आपका शिष्ट विरोध-पंक्ति युग्म (दो वाक्य) लिखिए। (3 अंक) (घ) निम्नलिखित आशुभाषण-रूपरेखा में एक बिंदु ग़लत क्रम में है — पहचानिए और सही क्रम लिखिए: "निष्कर्ष; क्या (विषय-परिभाषा); जैसे (उदाहरण); क्यों (महत्व)"। (2 अंक) (ई) बताइए कि (ख) के उत्तर में सक्रिय श्रवण के कौन-से काम का प्रयोग हुआ। (1 अंक)
प्रस्तुति की तैयारी के पाँच चरण क्रम सहित लिखिए। चरण 3 (सामग्री-संग्रह और छँटाई) में छँटाई किस कसौटी पर होती है, एक उदाहरण सहित बताइए।

परीक्षा-शैली में: (क) तैयारी के पाँच चरणों के नाम क्रम सहित लिखिए। (1 अंक) (ख) श्रोता-विश्लेषण के तीन पहलू लिखिए। (3 अंक) (ग) प्रस्तुति के दौरान ठहराव के दो उपयोग लिखिए। (2 अंक) (घ) मंच-भय को कम करने की दो पद्धतियाँ लिखिए। (2 अंक)

परीक्षा-पद्धति में: (क) प्रस्तुति की तैयारी के पाँच चरणों के नाम क्रम सहित लिखिए। (1 अंक) (ख) विषय 'मेरा विद्यालय' का दायरा विषय-विश्लेषण द्वारा दो पंक्तियों में स्पष्ट कीजिए — क्या लिया जाएगा, क्या नहीं। (2 अंक) (ग) चार-मिनट प्रस्तुति का समय-बजट सेकंडों में लिखिए और मुख्य भाग के चार बिंदुओं पर प्रति-बिंदु समय निकालिए। (2 अंक) (घ) निम्न आरंभ-वाक्य में दो त्रुटियाँ पहचानिए: "प्रिय अध्यापक महोदय, आज मैं जो कुछ भी बोलूँगा वह सब बहुत ही बढ़िया और महत्वपूर्ण है, इसलिए कृपया सभी लोग बहुत ध्यान से सुनिए, तो अब मैं अपनी बात शुरू करता हूँ।" (2 अंक) (ई) आत्म-मूल्यांकन की चार-स्तंभ सूची लिखिए। (2 अंक) (च) बताइए कि (घ) के सुधार में बोलने के कौन-से दो औज़ार लागू होंगे। (1 अंक)
“समय-सीमा 3 मिनट है” – एक वक्ता इस सीमा का पालन कैसे सुनिश्चित कर सकता है?

आपदा-वर्णन में तथ्य-अनुभूति का संतुलन कैसे रखा जाता है? निम्न दो विरोधी वाक्यों का मूल्यांकन कीजिए और बताइए कि प्रत्येक में क्या ग़लत है: (अ) "बाढ़ में 214 गाँव प्रभावित, 38 सड़कें टूटीं, क्षति का अनुमान आगे बताया जाएगा।" (ब) "हे भगवान! ऐसी विभीषिका! पानी ही पानी था! लोग तबाह हो गए, कुछ नहीं बचा, किसी की कोई गलती नहीं थी फिर भी सब बर्बाद!"
