(iii) The toy maker paints only the conical part red at ₹0.50 per cm² and the hemispherical part green at ₹0.40 per cm²: compute the total painting cost and state which colour covers the larger area.

Which of the following solids cannot have its volume found by simply counting whole unit cubes? (a) Cube of side 3 cm (b) Cuboid 4 cm × 2 cm × 3 cm (c) Sphere of radius 2 cm (d) Right prism with square base 2 cm and height 5 cm.
A rectangular tank measures 50 cm × 40 cm × 30 cm. How many litres of water can it hold?
A rectangular fish tank measures 60 cm × 30 cm × 40 cm. It is filled to 3/4 of its height with water. How many litres of water are in the tank?
Compare the volumes of a cube of side 4 cm and a cylinder of radius 2 cm and height 4 cm. Which has greater volume and by how much? (Use π = 22/7)

A past CISCE paper question: “A cuboidal box of internal dimensions 20 cm × 15 cm × 10 cm is to be packed with cubical packets of side 5 cm. Find the maximum number of packets that can be packed.” Solve.
State the volume formula for a cube of edge a with its unit, derive it from floor-counting, and list the cube's four edge-derived measures (frame, LSA, TSA, V) with their units for a = 3 cm.
A cube has volume 343 cm³. Find its edge, verify by re-substitution, and then compute its TSA. Explain which table makes the converse immediate.
A dice factory makes dice of edge 2 cm from blank plastic cubes of edge 20 cm, with no waste. How many dice per blank? Solve by BOTH the volume route and the edge route, and confirm the two agree.

A cube's edge grows from 3 cm to 6 cm. Compute both volumes and both TSAs, state each growth factor, and explain why the two factors differ — then evaluate the claim '216 is both the big cube's volume and its surface number, so area and volume converged'.
A water tank is a cube of edge 1.5 m. (i) Compute its volume in m³. (ii) Convert the edge to cm and compute the volume in cm³. (iii) Verify the conversion by computing 1 m³ in cm³ and multiplying.

Compare the cube's four measures for a = 5 cm (12a, 4a², 6a², a³) and for a = 10 cm. For each measure, state its growth factor between the two sizes, and arrange the four FORMULAS (not values) by how fast they grow with a.

HOTS: A student claims: "One cube of edge 12 cm holds MORE than twelve cubes of edge 4 cm, and the excess is 12³ − 12 × 4³." Set up both totals, evaluate the claim's arithmetic and its conclusion, and state the correct comparison with its simplest exact ratio.

Application: An ice-cube tray has 12 cubical cells of edge 2 cm. (i) Compute the volume of ice per cell and the tray's total ice volume. (ii) The tray freezes 90% of the water poured (10% loss to spillage/evaporation): how much water must be poured to fill all cells? (iii) A giant novelty cube of edge 6 cm is frozen in one cell of a different tray: how many standard 2-cm ice cubes equal its volume, and why is the answer not 3?

Evaluation/Critique: A student writes: "A cube of volume 216 cm³ has edge 36 cm, because a cube has 6 faces and 216 ÷ 6 = 36." Diagnose both errors (the operation and the divisor's origin), compute the true edge from the perfect-cube table, and repair the student's division into a CORRECT statement involving 216 ÷ 6.

Comparison: Compare the cube's volume formula a³ with its surface formulas, then compare three real cubes — dice a = 2, gift box a = 20, storage crate a = 200 (all cm): compute all three volumes, express each as a multiple of the previous, and connect the pattern to why storage is measured in m³ while dice are measured in cm³.

CISCE past-paper pattern: Three metal cubes of edges 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm are melted together and recast into a single new cube (no loss). (i) Compute each cube's volume and the total. (ii) Show the total is a perfect cube and find the new cube's edge. (iii) Compute by how much the new cube's TSA falls short of the sum of the three old TSAs, and explain the direction of the change (why melting SMALLER cubes into ONE BIGGER one must reduce total surface).
A student claims that a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 5 cm has volume 45π cm³. Evaluate this claim.
A cylindrical water tank has radius 0.5 m and height 2 m. How many litres of water can it hold? (Use π = 22/7)
Design a cuboid box with volume 240 cm³ using only integer dimensions. List all possible sets (length ≥ breadth ≥ height).
A solid cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm is melted and recast into a cuboid of length 14 cm and breadth 10 cm. Find the height of the cuboid. (Use π = 22/7)
A farmer has a cylindrical grain silo of radius 3 m and height 8 m. Grain bags each hold 0.5 m³. How many full bags can be filled from a full silo? (Use π = 22/7)
Compare the volume of a cube of side 10 cm with a cylinder of radius 5 cm and height 10 cm. Which is larger and by how much? (Use π = 22/7)

A rectangular tank 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and 1 m deep is full of water. The water is poured into a cylindrical vessel of radius 0.5 m. Find the height of water in the cylindrical vessel. (Use π = 22/7)
Define capacity, state the exact conversions among mL, cm³, L, m³ and kL, and derive 1 L = 1000 cm³ from the litre's definition as one cubic decimetre.

A fish tank measures 60 cm × 40 cm × 50 cm (outside measurements; walls thin enough to ignore). (i) Compute its capacity in litres. (ii) The owner fills it only to 40 cm: how many litres then? (iii) State the convert-order discipline the computation followed.
An overhead cylindrical tank has radius 70 cm and height 1.5 m. Compute its capacity in litres (π = 22/7), showing the convert-order discipline explicitly.
(i) How high will 500 L of water stand in a tank whose base is 50 cm × 40 cm? (ii) How many 250 mL glasses can be filled from a 5 L jug? (iii) State the division logic each answer uses.

A family uses 900 L of water daily. Its underground sump measures 3 m × 2 m × 1 m. (i) Find the sump's capacity in litres and kL. (ii) How many days does a full sump last? (iii) A tanker of 12 kL refills the empty sump: how much overflows, if the sump's usable capacity is only 6 m³ (half filled with sediment)?

Build the capacity ladder in one table: express 1 mL, 1 L, 1 kL, 1 m³ in cm³; then place these everyday items on the ladder with plausible figures — a teaspoon, a milk pouch, a bucket, a bathtub, a home overhead tank, a municipal tanker — and state the rung each is naturally spoken at.

HOTS: A student claims: "A 1.2 m × 1 m × 0.5 m sump holds 0.6 kL, so three such sumps hold almost 2 kL — and since 1 kL is 'about a thousand buckets', the family never needs a tanker." Compute the sump exactly, evaluate the three-sump total, and dissect the 'about a thousand buckets' figure: what bucket size makes it true, and is the figure honest at a standard 15 L bucket?

Application: A village panchayat builds a rectangular storage tank 6 m × 4 m × 1.5 m, filled by a hand pump delivering 12 L per minute. (i) Compute the tank's capacity in litres. (ii) Find the filling time in hours. (iii) The panchayat must give each of 60 families 40 L daily from this tank once full: how many FULL days does one filling serve, and does the pump — run 4 hours a day — keep pace with that daily draw?

Evaluation/Critique: A student writes: "Our tank is 240,000 cm³, so it holds 24 L — and since 24 L is 24,000 mL, it also holds 24,000 sugar-cubes of space." Diagnose each clause (the ÷1000, the mL chain, the cubes), give the corrected readings, and state the one check that would have caught the error before it propagated.

Comparison: Two drums stand side by side: Drum A is a cuboid 50 cm × 50 cm × 80 cm; Drum B is a cylinder r = 35 cm, h = 90 cm (π = 22/7). (i) Compute both capacities in litres. (ii) Which holds more, and by how many litres? (iii) Compare their footprints (floor areas) and state which drum is 'space-efficient' per floor area, with the ratio.

CISCE past-paper pattern: A municipal water bill charges ₹6 per kL. A household's tank is 2.5 m × 2 m × 1.2 m, filled fully twice in a month from the mains (assume no other use). (i) Compute the tank's capacity in litres and kL. (ii) Compute the monthly consumption in kL and the bill. (iii) The household installs a 5000 L rainwater sump expected to harvest 9 kL across the month's rains: compute the new mains requirement and the saving on the bill; then state the percentage saving exactly.
A student claims that the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 8 cm and 12 cm and height 5 cm is 8 × 12 × 5 = 480 cm². Evaluate this claim.
A parallelogram has base 9 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm. If you cut it along the height and rearrange, what are the dimensions of the resulting rectangle and its area?
In an ICSE‑style question, a trapezium has parallel sides 10 cm and 14 cm, and its area is 72 cm². Find its height.
A trapezium has parallel sides in the ratio 3:5 and height 12 cm. If its area is 288 cm², find the lengths of the parallel sides.

A carpenter needs to cut a parallelogram‑shaped piece of wood with base 40 cm and area 600 cm². What must be the perpendicular height? If the carpenter mistakenly uses a slant height of 20 cm, what area would they calculate and by how much would it be off?

An ICSE past‑paper question: “The area of a trapezium is 210 cm². Its parallel sides are in the ratio 3:4 and the distance between them is 10 cm. Find the length of the longer parallel side.” Solve it.
List any five components of the maths kit used for mensuration in Class 8.
Design a step‑by‑step activity using unit cubes from the kit to find the volume of a cuboid of dimensions 5 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm.

A student uses the maths kit to find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 9 cm and 15 cm and height 6 cm. She arranges two trapezium cutouts to form a rectangle. What is the area of the trapezium? Show the steps she would follow with the kit.

A question from a previous ICSE paper: "Using a maths kit, a student finds the total surface area of a cube of side 4 cm. She unfolds the cube net and measures each face. What is the total surface area?" Provide the solution steps as the student would do with the kit.
You have a rectangular carton of length 20 cm, breadth 15 cm, height 10 cm. How many 1 cm³ cubes are needed to fill it completely?
Design a classroom activity using only readymade items (like matchboxes, ice‑cream cups) to help a Class 8 student discover the formula for volume of a cuboid.
A water tank is in the shape of a cuboid of dimensions 2 m × 1.5 m × 1 m. If water is poured into it using a 10 litre bucket, how many bucketfuls are required to fill the tank? (1 m³ = 1000 litres)
If you have a set of identical cubes of side 2 cm, can you exactly fill a cuboid of dimensions 7 cm × 6 cm × 5 cm? Justify your answer.
A farmer stores grain in a cylindrical silo of radius 2 m and height 5 m. He uses sacks of capacity 50 kg each, and 1 m³ of grain weighs 800 kg. How many sacks can he fill from a full silo?
A textbook suggests using sand to measure the volume of an irregular stone by displacement. Critique this method for a Class 8 student.
A rectangular tank 4 m long, 3 m wide and 2 m high is full of water. Water is pumped out at a rate of 500 litres per minute. How long will it take to empty the tank? (1 m³ = 1000 litres)

A carton measures 30 cm × 18 cm × 12 cm; a matchbox measures 6 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm. (i) Count the matchboxes that fill the carton exactly. (ii) Compute the carton's volume in cm³ two ways: via the matchbox's own volume, and via lbh directly. (iii) State why the two must agree.

A bucket is estimated at 12 L. It is filled from a mug calibrated at 300 mL, taking exactly 50 mugs. (i) Compute the bucket's true capacity. (ii) Compute the estimate's error in litres and as a percentage. (iii) Explain what the estimate-measure-audit cycle teaches for the NEXT estimate.

Two kitchens measure the same 3 L jug with their own cups: Kitchen A's cup takes 20 pours, Kitchen B's takes 15. (i) Find each cup's size. (ii) Compute what the two 'cup-counts' would imply about a 6 L drum if each kitchen divided 6000 mL by its own cup. (iii) State the communication failure and the standard-unit fix.

Comparison: Container P is a tall glass 6 cm × 6 cm × 20 cm; Container Q is a wide bowl 12 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm. (i) Compare them by the TRANSFER test — describe the experiment and its possible outcomes. (ii) Compare them by COMPUTATION in cm³. (iii) State what each method delivers, and which is decisive when they seem to disagree.

HOTS: A student claims: "We can measure this jar's volume with marbles — fill it, count the marbles, multiply by a marble's volume. Counting is counting, so it's exact." Set out the claim's hidden premise, refute it with a concrete gap demonstration (a 1000 cm³ box, 2-cm cubes versus 2-cm marbles), and state precisely what the marble-count DOES measure.

Application: A household's water needs: drinking 6 L, cooking 8 L, bathing 4 buckets (15 L each), utensils 2 mugs of 1.25 L, and a 250 mL-per-plant watering of 40 plants. (i) Compute the day's total water use in litres. (ii) The roof tank holds 150 L: how much remains after all uses if it starts full? (iii) The family wants a 2-day independence from supply: audit whether a 200 L tank suffices, and state the minimum tank size for exactly 2 days.

Evaluation/Critique: A student writes: "We measured the carton with matchboxes and got 180 — so the carton's volume is 180." Diagnose the three defects (missing unit, missing calibration, missing standard conversion), repair the statement completely with the matchbox at 6 × 3 × 2 cm, and state the general rule for reporting any filler-count measurement.

Comparison: Compare the two great measurement cultures — the daily filler culture (cups, mugs, buckets, matchboxes) and the standard unit culture (cm³, L, m³): what each does well, where each fails, and how the calibration act (filler volume in mL) lets them interoperate. Use the 3 L jug, the 150 mL cup and the 250 mL mug as the running example.

CISCE past-paper pattern: A water tank measures 90 cm × 60 cm × 50 cm. (i) Compute its capacity in litres. (ii) It is filled from 15 L buckets: how many full buckets fill it exactly? (iii) If one bucket is poured every 90 seconds, find the total filling time in minutes. (iv) A student estimates the tank at 'half a drum of 100 L': audit the estimate's percentage error, and state which single dimension the student most likely misjudged.
A student draws a pie chart with four sector angles: 100°, 80°, 120°, and 70°. Is this a valid pie chart? Explain.
In a survey of 50 students, 20 like cricket, 15 like football, 10 like hockey, 5 like badminton. A pie chart is drawn with the cricket sector measuring 150°. Evaluate whether this angle is correct.
Draw a pie chart for the following data: Favourite fruit — Mango 12, Apple 8, Banana 6, Orange 4 (total 30). Calculate each angle and list them.
Create a simple data set of 4 categories with total frequency 20 that yields whole‑degree angles for a pie chart. Provide the frequencies and the resulting angles.
A pie chart represents 360 students in four houses with sector angles: Red 60°, Blue 90°, Green 120°, Yellow 90°. How many students are in Green house?

A pie chart has five sectors. The largest sector measures 150°. What is the maximum possible angle for the second‑largest sector if all angles are whole degrees and the remaining three sectors are at least 1° each?
A survey of 40 students records their favourite festival: Diwali 15, Holi 10, Eid 8, Christmas 7. Draw a pie chart and state which festival occupies the largest sector.
In a survey of 180 students, the pie chart shows the following angles for modes of transport: Walk 72°, Cycle 108°, Bus 90°, Car 90°. How many students use the Bus?

Two fair coins are tossed together. List the sample space, and compute P(two heads), P(exactly one head), P(at least one head) and P(same faces); show the events' probabilities sum to 1 across the full list.

A coin is tossed 300 times and shows heads 175 times. (i) Compute the empirical probability of heads. (ii) State the theoretical probability for a fair coin. (iii) Comment on the gap, and on what 30,000 tosses showing 58% heads would suggest.

HOTS: A student claims: "If I toss a coin until heads appears, the game must end within four tosses on average... no — within four tosses for SURE, because five tails in a row is too unlucky to happen." Set out the exact distribution: compute P(heads on toss 1), P(first heads on toss 2), on toss 3, on toss 4, and the probability the game runs FIVE OR MORE tosses; evaluate the claim with the exact figure.

Application: A KBC-style phone contest gives a contestant a 50-50 lifeline implemented as a coin toss for each option: the computer hides behind 'heads = option A, tails = option B'. The contestant has eliminated nothing and must pick between two options. (i) Compute the chance the coin's suggestion is correct. (ii) The contestant then reasons: 'the coin said A; last night's episode the coin said A and it was wrong — so I switch to B.' Evaluate the switch with the relevant probabilities. (iii) The show runs this lifeline 500 times a season: about how many of the coin's suggestions are correct, and what does that say about trusting the lifeline?

Comparison: Compare the theoretical and the empirical routes to probability — their sources, their formulas, their guarantees, and their meeting point — by running both on one coin: the list-route giving P(H) = 1/2, and a 30-toss experiment giving, say, 17 heads. State what each route can tell you that the other cannot, and the rule for which to trust in which situation.

CISCE past-paper pattern: A coin is tossed three times. (i) List the 8-outcome sample space and state each outcome's probability. (ii) Find P(exactly two heads), P(at least two heads), and P(heads on the first and last toss). (iii) Compute P(all three same) and its complement's probability, verifying the pair sums to 1. (iv) In 160 rounds of this triple toss, about how many rounds would show exactly two heads, and why is the actual number allowed to differ?
A student says the probability of rolling a 7 on a standard die is 1/6 because there are six faces. Evaluate this claim.
In a game, you win if you roll a number greater than 4. What is the probability of winning?
A fair die is thrown once. Find the probability of getting a number which is a factor of 6.
Explain why the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die remains 1/6 regardless of previous rolls.
A teacher uses a die to randomly select a student from a group of 6. If the die shows 4, the 4th student is chosen. What is the probability that the 3rd student is chosen?
A student argues that since a die has six faces, the probability of rolling a 1 is 1/6, but if you roll the die 6 times you are guaranteed to get a 1 exactly once. Critique this argument.
A die is thrown once. Find the probability of getting a number which is not a factor of 6.
A student rolls a die 60 times and gets frequencies: 1:12, 2:8, 3:10, 4:11, 5:9, 6:10. She claims the die is biased because the frequencies are not all 10. Evaluate her claim.

Create a chance experiment using a spinner with 5 equal sectors numbered 1–5. Write a procedure to collect data for 40 spins and show how to calculate the sector angle for outcome 3 if it occurs 9 times.

A Maths Kit contains a standard die and a coin. In an experiment, the die is rolled 120 times and the coin is tossed 120 times. The die shows a ‘6’ 22 times. The coin shows heads 58 times. (a) Calculate the relative frequency of getting a 6 on the die. (b) Calculate the relative frequency of heads. (c) Which experiment’s relative frequency is closer to the theoretical probability? Justify.

**HOTS:** A Maths Kit contains a biased coin that lands heads 60% of the time. Without knowing the bias, a student tosses it 200 times and gets 115 heads. She concludes the coin is fair because 115 is close to 100. Critique her reasoning and suggest a better statistical approach appropriate for Class 8.

**Application:** You have a Maths Kit with a 6‑sector spinner (numbers 1–6). Design a game where two players each choose a different set of three numbers. They spin the spinner 50 times; a player scores a point when the outcome is in their set. Explain how to use the kit to test whether the game is fair before playing.
**Evaluation/Critique:** A textbook states: “After 10 tosses of a coin, the relative frequency of heads will be 0.5.” Evaluate this statement and explain why it is misleading for Class 8 learners.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** In an experiment, a student uses a Maths Kit to roll a die 180 times. The frequency of getting a prime number (2, 3, 5) is 96. (a) Calculate the experimental probability of getting a prime number. (b) What is the theoretical probability of getting a prime number on a fair die? (c) Is the die likely fair? Give a reason based on your calculations.
Design a simple experiment using two ₹1 coins to estimate the probability of “both coins show the same face”. Describe the steps and how you would compute the experimental probability.
In a CISCE‑style question, a bag contains 3 fair coins. One coin is chosen at random and tossed. What is the probability that the result is Head?
A teacher asks: “If you toss a fair coin 100 times, will you definitely get exactly 50 Heads?” Choose the correct response.
Critique the statement: “Since a coin has two sides, the chance of Head is always 50 % even if the coin is bent.”
State the single-die sample space and each face's probability; compute P(even), P(prime), P(greater than 4), P(7) and P(a number from 1 to 6); and verify the six face-probabilities sum to 1.

Explain why the two-dice sample space has 36 outcomes and why the eleven possible sums (2 to 12) are NOT equally likely — illustrating with the rows owned by sum 7 and sum 2, and computing both probabilities.
A fair die is rolled once. Find P(a multiple of 3), P(not a multiple of 3), P(a number between 2 and 5 inclusive), and P(a number less than 1). Verify the complementary pair in the first two.
Two fair dice are rolled. Compute P(doubles), P(sum at least 10), P(sum not equal to 7), and P(both dice show the same OR the sum is 7). Verify your last answer by listing its rows.

A die was rolled 600 times with these counts: face 1: 106, face 2: 94, face 3: 101, face 4: 98, face 5: 105, face 6: 96. (i) Verify the counts. (ii) Compute all six empirical probabilities. (iii) Compare with 1/6 and state whether the die is suspect, with your criterion.

Comparison: Compare the single-die space (6 outcomes) and the two-dice space (36 pairs) with the coin spaces (2 and 4): for each, state the list size, one event with probability 1/2, and the recurring trap. Then identify which of the four spaces first shows an event with probability 1/36, and what that event is.

HOTS: A student claims: "Sum 7 is most likely because 7 is a lucky number in every culture — and anyway, P(sum 7) = P(sum 6) = P(sum 8) because they are all 'near the middle'." Test the claim numerically (exact diagonal counts and probabilities for sums 6, 7, 8), state what actually determines a sum's probability, and evaluate the student's two justifications separately.

Application: A snake-and-ladders-style race: a counter climbs a ladder if the roll shows a multiple of 3, slides if it shows a prime, and stays otherwise (a roll is judged once). (i) Compute P(climb), P(slide), P(stay) for one roll, treating the events as assigned in that order of priority (a multiple of 3 that is also prime — the face 3 — counts as climb). (ii) Verify the three probabilities sum to 1. (iii) Over 120 rolls, give the expected counts of climbs, slides and stays, and explain why the actual tally may differ.

Evaluation/Critique: A student writes: "I rolled a die six times and got 1, 3, 5, 2, 6, 4 — each face once. So the die is 'perfectly fair', and my friend's die showing 3, 3, 4, 1, 6, 2 (no 5, two 3s) must be loaded." Diagnose the reasoning's defects (sample size, what fairness predicts, what a single batch proves), state what six rolls CAN and CANNOT show, and design the corrected experiment.

Comparison: Compare the coin space (c8_math_icse_05_002) and the dice space as scaling steps of one framework: list sizes (2, 4, 36), the recurring trap (collapsed descriptions), the events that stay 1/2, and the diagonal structure unique to two dice. State the framework's three fixed commands that survive every scaling.

CISCE past-paper pattern: Two dice are rolled together. (i) Construct the sum table (which sums occur, with how many pairs each) and verify the total is 36. (ii) Find P(sum divisible by 3), P(sum divisible by 4), and P(sum divisible by 3 AND by 4). (iii) Find P(sum divisible by 3 OR 4) using the inclusion of the overlap. (iv) In 180 rolls, about how many give a sum divisible by 3, and why may the actual count differ?

State the three-step framework for any random experiment, and apply it to: (i) a spinner with 8 equal sectors (2 red, 3 blue, 3 green); (ii) a bag with 3 red, 2 blue, 3 green balls; (iii) the letters of PROBABILITY face down. Give P(blue or green) in each case.

A spinner claims 'four equal chances: red, blue, green, yellow'. Inspection shows the circle divided into 8 equal sectors: 2 red, 2 blue, 1 green, 3 yellow. (i) Compute the TRUE probabilities of the four colours. (ii) Which colour is most likely, and by what factor over an equal-share claim? (iii) What design would make the label honest?
A bag holds 3 red, 2 blue and 3 green identical balls. One ball is drawn at random. Find P(red), P(not blue), P(red or green), and P(yellow); verify the partition red + blue + green = 1.

From the same bag (3 red, 2 blue, 3 green), one ball is drawn and NOT returned. (i) If the first ball was red, compute P(second is red) and P(second is blue). (ii) If instead the ball is REPLACED and the bag shaken, recompute both. (iii) State the principle the pair of answers displays.

The letters of PROBABILITY are placed face down and one card is drawn. Find P(vowel), P(B), P(consonant), and P(vowel or B); explain why P(vowel) + P(consonant) = 1 but P(vowel) + P(B) < 1, and what the difference equals.

Comparison: A first ball is drawn from the bag of 3 red, 2 blue and 3 green. Compare the SECOND draw under replacement (ball returned, bag shaken) and without replacement (ball kept out), given the first ball was GREEN in both worlds: the outcome list for the second draw, P(second is red) in each, and the independence status. Then state which world the coins and dice of this chapter lived in.

HOTS: A student claims: "A bag with 6 red and 4 blue balls is 'a 60% bag'. After you draw a red and keep it out, it becomes 'a 6/9 bag' — so reds get MORE likely, and you should always bet red second." Test the claim with exact fractions: compute P(red second) after one red is removed, after one BLUE is removed, and before any removal; state what actually happens to red's probability in each case, and correct the betting rule.

Application: A school's cultural committee draws names from a bowl for three performance slots — slot 1, slot 2, slot 3 — with each drawn chit KEPT OUT (no one performs twice). The bowl holds 20 chits: 8 from Class 8, 7 from Class 7, 5 from Class 6. (i) Compute P(Class 8 sings in slot 1). (ii) Given a Class 7 chit was drawn for slot 1, compute P(Class 8 for slot 2). (iii) Compute the probability that ALL THREE slots go to Class 8 (draws in sequence, nothing replaced), listing the shrinking numerators and denominators, and state why the fraction is so small compared with (1/2)³ or similar intuitions.

Evaluation/Critique: A student writes: "P(vowel) + P(B) in PROBABILITY is 4/11 + 2/11 = 6/11, which is less than 1, so 5/11 of the cards are missing from my list — the framework must be broken." Diagnose the student's inference (what the sub-1 total actually means), repair the accounting with the correct partition, and state the general rule for interpreting sums of probabilities that land below 1, at 1, and above 1.

Comparison: The chapter met three families of chance devices — symmetry devices (coin, die, equal spinner, full bag), stateful devices (the bag under removal), and record-worlds (weather, next-day events). Compare them on: how the outcome list is built, whether probabilities are exact or estimates, whether trials change the device, and what each family contributes to the framework. Use rain-tomorrow, the 8-sector wheel, and the 12-marble bag as the running examples.

CISCE past-paper pattern: A lucky draw uses a drum with 30 tickets: 12 marked A (apron), 10 marked B (book), 8 marked C (cap). Tickets are drawn one at a time and NOT returned. (i) Find P(first is A). (ii) Given the first was A, find P(second is B). (iii) Given the first two were A and B, find P(third is C). (iv) A spectator claims: 'Since A had the most tickets, every draw is most likely to be A.' Evaluate the claim for draws 1, 2 (after A drawn), and 3 (after A, B drawn), with exact fractions, and state the general lesson about 'majority' under removal.
An irregular solid of mass 150 g is lowered into a graduated cylinder containing 50 mL of water. The water level rises to 80 mL. Calculate the density of the solid in kg m⁻³.
A piece of metal of mass 200 g is lowered into a graduated cylinder containing 100 mL water. The water level rises to 125 mL. Calculate the density in kg m⁻³ and state whether it will float in water.

A piece of wood of mass 30 g is placed in a graduated cylinder with 50 mL water. The water level rises to 65 mL. Calculate the density of wood in kg m⁻³. Will it float in water? (Density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³).
A block of ice has a volume of 200 cm³. Taking the density of ice as 0.92 g cm⁻³, calculate its mass in grams and state whether it will float or sink in water (ρ_water = 1.0 g cm⁻³).
An object of density 850 kg m⁻³ is placed first in water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³) and then in kerosene (ρ = 800 kg m⁻³). Predict its behaviour in each liquid with reasons.

The same closed steel flask is filled with exactly 1 kg of water, then sealed and frozen so the water becomes ice. (a) Does the mass change? (b) Does the volume change? (c) Does the density change? Answer each part with a reason.

A hot air balloon rises. Explain the rise using density, and calculate the approximate mass of air displaced by a balloon whose volume is 3000 m³ (density of cool outside air = 1.3 kg m⁻³; density of hot air inside ≈ 1.0 kg m⁻³). What is the mass difference that helps lift the balloon?

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** Given the densities — cork 240 kg m⁻³, ice 920 kg m⁻³, iron 7800 kg m⁻³, kerosene 800 kg m⁻³, water 1000 kg m⁻³, mercury 13600 kg m⁻³ — answer: (a) Which of the three solids float on water? (b) An iron cube measures 2 cm along each edge. Taking 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³, calculate the mass of the cube (density of iron = 7.8 g cm⁻³). (c) State what happens to this cube when placed in mercury, with a reason.
Convert: (a) kerosene's density 0.8 g cm⁻³ into kg m⁻³; (b) iron's density 7800 kg m⁻³ into g cm⁻³. Show the conversion factor used in each direction.
A student writes: "The density of the liquid is 250 g / 200 mL = 1.25 mL/g, so it floats on water." Identify and correct every error in this statement.
The mass of a rectangular wooden block is 456 g and its dimensions are 12 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm. Calculate its density in g cm⁻³ and in kg m⁻³, and state whether it floats on water.
Rearrange ρ = m/V to find (a) mass and (b) volume. Then use the correct form: find the mass of 40 cm³ of glycerine of density 1.26 g cm⁻³.

Three liquids are poured into one tall glass and settle as three layers: bottom layer density 1.4 g cm⁻³, middle layer 1.0 g cm⁻³, top layer 0.8 g cm⁻³. A small solid of density 1.2 g cm⁻³ is dropped in. State where it comes to rest and explain using the sinking/flating rule at each stage of its fall.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define density and write its SI unit. (1) (b) The mass of an empty graduated cylinder is 80 g; with 50 cm³ of liquid X in it, the total mass is 135 g. Calculate the density of liquid X in g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³. (2) (c) Liquid X is poured into water. Predict, with reason, where it settles. (1) (d) State one prior-learning skill, other than calculation, that must be correct for the measurement in (b) to be trustworthy. (1)

An irregular metal piece has mass 54 g. A cylinder reads 40 mL of water before and 60 mL after immersion. Calculate the density in g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³, and state whether the piece floats or sinks in water.

The density of mustard oil measured by a group is 0.92 g cm⁻³. Convert to kg m⁻³ and predict what happens when mustard oil is poured into a glass of water; then predict where a crystal of density 1.15 g cm⁻³ dropped into the same glass settles.

A practical exam records this data for an irregular solid: mass 81 g; cylinder readings 50 mL before, 80 mL after immersion. (a) Compute the density. (b) The solid is known to be aluminium (2.7 g cm⁻³). Evaluate the group's work: is the discrepancy consistent with a specific procedural slip? Identify the most likely one and the corrected reading set.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Name the apparatus used to collect displaced water when the solid is too large for a graduated cylinder. (1) (b) A large metal knocker displaces 88 mL of water collected from this apparatus; its mass is 704 g. Calculate its density in kg m⁻³. (2) (c) Will this metal sink or float in mercury (ρ = 13600 kg m⁻³) and in water? Justify both. (2)

Given the following densities, predict which objects float in which liquids. Objects: A (0.6 g/cm³), B (1.2 g/cm³), C (0.95 g/cm³). Liquids: Water (1.0 g/cm³), Oil (0.8 g/cm³), Salt solution (1.2 g/cm³).
An object of mass 200 g and volume 250 cm³ is placed in a liquid of density 0.8 g/cm³. Will it float or sink? Justify with calculation.

A teacher gives students three liquids of unknown densities and three solids of known densities (0.5, 1.0, 1.5 g/cm³). Describe a method to determine the unknown liquid densities using only floating/sinking observations.
A student wants to separate a mixture of sand (density 2.6 g/cm³) and plastic granules (density 0.9 g/cm³) using a liquid. Which liquid density would achieve separation, and why?

A past ICSE question: “State the condition for a body to float in a liquid. A body of density 0.8 g/cm³ is placed in a liquid of density 1.2 g/cm³. Will it float or sink? Give reason.” Provide the answer as expected in the exam.

A matrix cell reads: plastic toy (950 kg m⁻³) — floats in saturated salt solution (1200 kg m⁻³). Justify this cell completely, and state whether the toy rides higher or lower in the salt solution than in plain water, with reasoning.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** The investigation matrix records: object X floats in water but sinks in kerosene; object Y sinks in both water and brine (1200 kg m⁻³). (a) Write the density inequality that each object's behaviour gives. (2) (b) Object X has mass 153 g and its measured density is 850 kg m⁻³. Calculate its volume in cm³. (2) (c) If brine's density is raised by adding more salt, state and explain what happens to a floating object's submerged fraction. (1)
What is the least count of a graduated cylinder, how is it calculated, and what is the least count of a 100 mL cylinder whose scale has 100 divisions?
A student reads a water level with the eye above the mark and records 52 mL in a 1 mL least-count cylinder. Explain the error, its direction, and the two reading habits that eliminate it.

You must measure 8 mL of a liquid as accurately as possible. Available: a 10 mL cylinder with 0.1 mL least count, a 50 mL cylinder with 1 mL least count, and a 100 mL cylinder with 1 mL least count. Which do you choose, and what percentage precision does each offer for this measurement?

A cylinder reads 40.0 mL of water. A stone is lowered in; the level reads 47.5 mL. The stone's mass, from the balance, is 60 g. Calculate the stone's density and state whether it will float or sink in the water it was measured in.
A student claims: "If I read the top of the meniscus every time, the errors cancel out when I subtract V₁ from V₂." Evaluate this claim with numbers, using a bias of 0.4 mL per reading.

A group reports the volume of the same stopper as 8.5 mL (cylinder, least count 1 mL) and, using a denser reference trick, claims 8.500 mL. Evaluate the second claim's honesty and state what the extra digits assert.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Name the error that occurs when a liquid level is read with the eye above the surface, and state whether it makes the recorded volume too large or too small when the scale is on the far side of the liquid. (1) (b) A cylinder holds water to the 45 mL mark. An irregular solid is added; the level rises to 52 mL. The solid's mass is 35 g. Calculate its density in g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³. (2) (c) State whether this solid will float or sink in the water of the cylinder, and give one reason tied to a density comparison. (2)

A large stone tied with thread is lowered into a full Eureka can; 250 mL of water collects in a measuring cylinder. The stone's mass is 675 g. Calculate its density in g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³, and state whether it sinks or floats in water.

The Eureka can is filled with kerosene (0.8 g cm⁻³) instead of water for a stone that reacts with water. The stone's mass is 156 g; the kerosene overflow is 60 mL. (a) Find the stone's volume and density. (b) State whether the change of liquid affected the volume found, and why the kerosene's density never entered the calculation.

A group's Eureka-can result for a metal cube (true edge 4.0 cm) is 61 mL of overflow; direct geometry gives 64 cm³. Evaluate which reading is right, what the can result's most likely cause is, and why the cube is the ideal test object for catching exactly this error.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Why is this instrument named after the exclamation "Eureka"? (1) (b) A large metal ornament displaces 145 mL from a full Eureka can; its mass is 1276 g. Calculate its density in kg m⁻³. (2) (c) The ornament is lowered into a full can of brine (1200 kg m⁻³): state the overflow volume and the mass of brine displaced. (2)

A 250 mL beaker has an internal diameter of 6.4 cm. Calculate the level rise when 50 mL of water is poured in, and compare it with the rise in a graduated cylinder of 2.5 cm bore. What does the comparison explain about the two vessels' scales?

For each task, choose the vessel — graduated beaker, graduated cylinder, or Eureka can — and justify: (a) measuring 9 mL of glycerine for a density determination; (b) heating 150 mL of water for a solubility demonstration; (c) finding the volume of a stone the size of a lemon; (d) quickly checking that roughly 400 mL of salt solution was prepared.

A group measures 200 mL of kerosene in a 250 mL graduated beaker (least count 50 mL) for a density determination. The accepted density of kerosene is 0.8 g cm⁻³. Estimate the best and worst density the group could compute if their poured volume is out by one full mark (50 mL), given the measured mass is 160 g.

A beaker carries marks every 50 mL, and a group records "167 mL" of a liquid read from it. Evaluate the record and restate it honestly. Then state what the group should have done if 167 mL was genuinely required for the practical.

A student argues: "The beaker's ±5% is small — for kerosene at 0.8 g cm⁻³ the density error will also be about 5%, which is acceptable." Evaluate the claim with the chapter's own flotation stakes, and state the error budget that would actually be acceptable.

Two beakers on the shelf look identical, but A is a "laboratory beaker" with printed marks and B is a plain beaker. A group uses B to prepare "200 mL" of solution by eye. What systematic problem does this create for the investigation discussion, and what one habit fixes it?

A sales catalogue offers a "precision beaker, class A, ±1% at 100 mL" at ten times the price of the cylinder. Evaluate whether it replaces the graduated cylinder on the school shelf: compare bore geometry, least count, displacement use, and duty.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Why does a graduated beaker give only approximate volumes? Give the geometrical reason. (1) (b) A beaker of diameter 8 cm contains liquid to a height of 3.0 cm. Calculate the approximate volume of liquid (π ≈ 3.14). (2) (c) The same volume is required to an accuracy of 1% for a density determination: name the vessel and justify. (2)

A group fills a 100 mL graduated cylinder exactly to the 100 mark with water and finds the increase in mass over the empty cylinder is 100.8 g. Compute the density they measured, compare with the reference value, and decide whether the instrument or the technique deserves the 0.8% discrepancy.

A fresh egg has mass 60 g and volume 55 cm³. (a) Compute its density. (b) Predict and justify its behaviour in fresh water. (c) Predict its behaviour in saturated brine of density 1.2 g cm⁻³. (d) State the one kitchen action that flips the egg from sinking to floating.

Design a single-page classroom wall chart, "Lighter or heavier than water?", that a Class 8 student can use to predict flotation at a glance. Specify its two columns, at least eight entries from the chapter's material list, and the one-line rule printed at the bottom.

A 2-litre water bottle is labelled "2 L". A student weighs it on the balance (c8_phy_icse_01_013) and gets 2.06 kg for the water alone. The label is accused of being wrong. Evaluate the accusation with an error budget, and state what measurement would settle the question properly.

A lake in Himachal Pradesh freezes at its surface in January while fish survive in the water beneath. Using the densities of ice (about 920 kg m⁻³) and water (1000 kg m⁻³), explain the floating of the ice sheet, and state what would happen to lake life if water behaved like most liquids (solid denser than liquid).

An old inland cargo boat has a load line painted for river water. The owner proposes loading it identically for a sea voyage "since the line is the line". Evaluate the proposal with the two densities (river 1000, sea 1030 kg m⁻³), state the direction and rough size of the error, and name the deck-level consequence if the error is ignored on a fully loaded hull.

Assemble the reference-liquid idea into a comparison table with three columns — medium (fresh water, seawater, saturated brine), density (1000, 1030, about 1200 kg m⁻³), and the fraction of an ice cube (920 kg m⁻³) submerged — and write the one-sentence rule the table teaches. Then state what fraction of the cube is above the surface in brine and why the cube rides higher there than in fresh water.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State the density of water in CGS units and express it in SI units, showing the conversion. (2) (b) A sealed hollow plastic ball of mass 45 g and volume 60 cm³ is placed in water, then in a liquid of relative density 1.1. State and justify its behaviour in each. (2) (c) 1 litre of seawater of density 1030 kg m⁻³ is evaporated to dryness and leaves 30 g of salt. Estimate the density of pure water recovered in the condensate and justify the value. (1)

A glass marble of mass 15 g is dropped into a graduated cylinder and the water level rises from 50 mL to 55.7 mL. Calculate the marble's density, state which material class it matches, and predict its behaviour in water and in a dense liquid of 3000 kg m⁻³.

A bead of density 900 kg m⁻³ is dropped into a tall jar in which kerosene (800 kg m⁻³) floats as a layer over water (1000 kg m⁻³). State exactly where the bead ends up, and justify each stage of its journey. What would change if the bead's density were 750 kg m⁻³?

A sealed steel tin of mass 1.2 kg has an outer volume of 1400 cm³. Show the full calculation that decides its fate in water, state the verdict, and explain what the tin's material density (about 7800 kg m⁻³) has to do with — or not do with — the answer.

A carpenter's scrap box holds a block of teak (about 700 kg m⁻³) and a block of ironwood-style hardwood (about 1100 kg m⁻³). Both are called "wood". State each block's behaviour in water, and explain why "wood floats" is a false generalisation while "iron sinks" survives almost every test — with the one classic exception.

A raft is built from 20 dry wooden logs, each of mass 30 kg and density 600 kg m⁻³, lashed to a light wooden deck carrying two adults of total mass 120 kg. Show whether the loaded raft floats, and how much of the logs' volume remains above water when it floats in equilibrium.

Build the one-object-five-liquids verdict table for an aluminium cube (2700 kg m⁻³): liquids are kerosene (800), water (1000), brine (1200), glycerine (1260) and mercury (13600). For each liquid give "sinks" or "floats", and for one floating case the submerged fraction. Then write the single sentence that generates every row.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define density of a substance and state its SI unit. (2) (b) A solid of mass 54 g, when lowered into a Eureka can filled to the spout, displaces water which is collected in a measuring cylinder and reads 20 cm³. Calculate the density of the solid and state which of the following it most likely is, with reason: glass (2.5), aluminium (2.7), iron (7.8). (2) (c) State whether this solid will float or sink in a liquid of relative density 2.0, giving the comparison that decides it. (1)

Define the relative density of a liquid, and use the liquid density ladder to state, with reasons, the final arrangement when petrol (700), water (1000) and mercury (13600 kg m⁻³) are poured into one tall jar and left to settle.

A laboratory group weighs an empty beaker (60.0 g), runs 50 mL of glycerine into it from a graduated cylinder, and reweighs: 123.0 g. Calculate the glycerine's density in g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³, its relative density, and state where it would sit in a jar layered with water and mustard oil (920 kg m⁻³).

When mustard oil is poured into water it forms a permanent top layer, but when alcohol (about 790 kg m⁻³) is poured into water the two blend into one uniform liquid. Explain the difference in terms of miscibility, and state what determines the density of a blended liquid. Why can no permanent oil-on-water layer be formed by waiting for oil and water to "settle apart" after vigorous shaking — and what actually happens overnight?

A customer claims: "Milk always floats on water — everyone knows cream floats — so milk is lighter than water." Evaluate the claim with the densities (milk about 1030 kg m⁻³, cream about 930, water 1000), state what actually floats on what, and give the consequence for detecting watered-down milk.

You must build a five-layer "liquid tower" for the science exhibition from: honey (1420), water (1000), kerosene (800), mercury (13600) and mustard oil (920 kg m⁻³). State the pouring order that guarantees the tower forms, the final arrangement, and the fate of (a) a candle-wax ball (950), (b) an iron nut (7800), (c) an ice cube (920) dropped in. Give one safety rule the design must respect.

An oil tanker accident spills 200 tonnes of crude oil (about 900 kg m⁻³) into a harbour. Explain, with densities, why the oil remains at the surface where booms and skimmers can collect it, and state what would change if the spill were of a "heavy" crude of density 1010 kg m⁻³ in the brackish harbour water (1015 kg m⁻³).

A jewellery workshop's rinse jar holds water over a layer of honey. A gold ring (19.3 g cm⁻³), a silver chain (10.5), a glass bead (2.5) and a plastic button (1.2) are dropped in together during cleaning. State where each comes to rest, and explain what the jar is quietly doing to the workshop's mixed small items.

A cook thickens a syrup and notices the raw egg (about 1.09 g cm⁻³) that sank in it yesterday now floats. No new ingredient except sugar entered the pot. Explain the change in terms of the liquid ladder, and state the cook's two options to bring the egg back under — with the one that preserves the sweetening.

Assemble the node into a comparison table with three columns — liquid (kerosene, water, honey), relative density (0.80, 1.00, 1.42), and one duty it performs in this chapter or the kitchen — and write the single sentence that generates every layering answer. Then state where a bead of relative density 1.20 rests in a kerosene–water–honey tower, and why "heavier liquid" and "thicker liquid" must not be confused.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define relative density of a liquid and state why it has no unit. (2) (b) 20 mL of a liquid weighs 25 g. Calculate its density in g cm⁻³ and its relative density. (1) (c) This liquid, water and kerosene are poured into one jar. State the final arrangement with reasons, and state where a solid of density 1.2 g cm⁻³ comes to rest. (2)

From a standard weight box containing 200, 100, 50, 20, 10, 5, 2 and 1 g pieces, state the combination that balances a mass of 387 g, and show the addition. Why does the box contain 1-2-5 pieces in each decade rather than, say, ten 10 g pieces?

A student weighs a beaker of boiling hot liquid immediately on the beam balance and obtains 195.4 g. The same beaker is reweighed after cooling and reads 197.1 g. Explain the discrepancy, evaluate the student's claim that "the first reading was fine because the balance was already levelled and zeroed", and state the correct procedure.

Complete the density measurement the chapter has been building: a dry beaker weighs 60.0 g; 50 mL of glycerine is poured in from a graduated cylinder and the beaker plus glycerine weighs 123.0 g. Compute the glycerine's mass and density, name the balance rule that made the mass trustworthy, and state the result as a rung on the liquid ladder of c8_phy_icse_01_012.

An electronic balance calibrated on Earth reads "154.6 g" for a brass block. The same block is placed on the same instrument inside a lunar station. A classmate claims: "It still reads 154.6 g — grams measure grams." Evaluate the claim, state what the instrument actually reads there and why, and name the one instrument among beam, spring and electronic whose lunar reading remains a true mass.

A kirana shop's beam balance reads 1.000 kg for a bag of sugar only when the shopkeeper leans a finger on the sugar pan. Another shop's digital scale shows 1.000 kg exactly, but its pan carries a hidden scrap of metal taped underneath. Diagnose both frauds, state which side loses in each, and give the one inspection that catches both instantly.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define mass and state its SI unit. (2) (b) State the combination of weights from the box (200, 100, 50, 20, 10, 5, 2, 1 g — one each) that balances 275 g, and the final reading if the rider then sits at 0.8 g on a rider scale whose smallest division is 0.1 g. (2) (c) A student weighs a liquid twice by difference and gets 63.0 g and 63.4 g. State the value to report and one likely cause of the spread. (1)

A classroom door can be pushed at three places: 5 cm from the hinge edge, at the middle of the door, and at the handle near the far edge. With the same push at each place, arrange the three cases by how easily the door opens and explain the pattern using the two factors of turning effect.

A student claims: "A bigger force always produces a bigger turning effect, no matter where it is applied." Evaluate this claim using the spanner-and-nut situation: Appu applies 12 N at 0.8 m from the nut, his apprentice applies 20 N at 0.4 m from the same nut. Which effort turns the nut more, and what does this do to the claim?

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Name the turning effect of a force and state the two factors on which it depends. (3) (b) A gate is pushed with 24 N at 0.5 m from the hinge line in one trial and with 12 N at 1.2 m in another. Form the force-and-distance products, state which trial turns the gate more, and by how much. (3) (c) Explain why a force applied exactly through the pivot cannot turn the body, whatever its size. (2)
A force of 20 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.25 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment and state its direction if the force tends to rotate the body anticlockwise.
Two forces act on a light rod pivoted at its centre: 10 N at 0.3 m on the left side (downward) and 15 N at 0.2 m on the right side (downward). Is the rod in rotational equilibrium?
A student uses a 0.4 m long spanner to apply a force of 60 N at an angle of 30° to the spanner. What is the effective perpendicular distance, and what moment is produced?
In a CISCE board question, a uniform beam 4 m long is pivoted at one end. A force of 30 N acts vertically downwards at the free end. Calculate the moment about the pivot.
A 0.8 m long uniform rod is pivoted at one end. A force of 25 N is applied at the midpoint, perpendicular to the rod. Calculate the moment about the pivot.

Critique the following experimental method: “To verify the principle of moments, a student places a 50 g mass at 20 cm from the pivot on a balanced ruler and then adds a 100 g mass at 10 cm on the same side, observing that the ruler tips.”
Compare the turning effect of a 30 N force applied at 0.2 m perpendicular distance with a 15 N force applied at 0.5 m perpendicular distance. Which produces a larger moment?
A CISCE past‑paper question: “A uniform beam 5 m long weighs 200 N and is supported at its ends. A 300 N weight is placed 1 m from the left support. Calculate the reaction forces at the supports.”
In a water tank, pressure at 2 m depth is measured as 20 kPa. Assuming constant density, what is the pressure at 5 m depth?

Design a simple experiment to show that liquid pressure at the same depth is the same in all directions. Include a numerical prediction: if pressure at 1 m depth is 10 kPa, what pressure would a sensor read at 1 m depth facing sideways?

A rectangular tank 2 m deep is filled with water. The pressure at the bottom is P. If the tank is replaced by a conical tank of same depth and base area, will the pressure at the bottom change? Justify.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State the principle of communicating vessels and explain it using equal pressure at equal depth. (2) (b) A tall bottle has holes at 8 cm and 24 cm below the water surface. Compare the two jets and give the law. (2) (c) An even-thickness garden tank cracks near its base; a neighbour proposes fixing it by "making every wall twice as thick". Evaluate the proposal and give the better repair. (2)
If a 10 N force is applied at a perpendicular distance of 0.2 m from a pivot, and the same force is applied at 0.5 m, which application produces a larger turning effect?

In an ICSE exam, a question shows a uniform rod pivoted at its centre with a 5 N force applied at 30 cm from the pivot on one side and a 3 N force applied at 40 cm on the other side. State which side will rotate downward.
A cyclist applies a force of 30 N on a pedal that is 0.18 m from the crank axle. Calculate the turning effect produced.

Critique the following experimental design: “To show turning effect depends on distance, hang a 200 g mass at 10 cm, then at 20 cm, then at 30 cm from the pivot, but keep the pivot at the 0 cm end of the ruler.”
Compare the turning effect produced by a 5 N force at 0.6 m with that produced by a 3 N force at 1.0 m. Which is larger and by how much?

An ICSE past‑paper question: “A uniform rod of length 1 m is pivoted at its centre. A force of 8 N is applied perpendicular to the rod at a point 20 cm from the pivot. Calculate the moment of the force about the pivot.”

A force acts at the handle of a door, directed at 45° across the door's face instead of squarely at right angles to it. Compare the turning effect with a square push of the same strength at the same point, explaining using the line of action and the perpendicular distance, and state the extreme case of pushing direction that gives no turning at all.

A cycle pedal is at the end of a crank 17 cm long. A rider pressing the pedal squarely downwards when the crank is horizontal produces a strong turning effort about the axle; state what happens to the turning effect as the crank rotates to point straight up with the same downward press, and explain using perpendicular distance. Why do riders naturally "stand on the pedals" when climbing?

Design a two-part classroom demonstration, using a centre-pivoted metre rule and two identical 1 N hanger weights, that shows (a) that opposing turning effects on the two sides can balance each other, and (b) that the balance is destroyed by moving one weight, with the sense of tipping predicted in advance. State the observations and the prediction logic.

A railway crossing barrier (a long light beam pivoted at one end near the road) is lowered by a porter pressing down on its free end, 3 m from the pivot. The porter can press with at most 250 N. A counterweight fixed 0.5 m on the other side of the pivot presses down with a steady 600 N. (a) Show, with standings, whether the porter can lower the barrier. (b) State the minimum distance from the pivot at which the porter must press to win, with working. (c) Explain the counterweight's purpose in the design.

Evaluate this student's experimental conclusion: "I hung 200 g at 20 cm left of a centre pivot and 200 g at 20 cm right; the rule stayed level. Therefore balance depends only on equal forces at equal distances — distance is not a separate factor." Identify the valid part, the invalid leap, and the one additional trial that destroys the leap.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State what is meant by the turning effect of a force and name the two factors on which it depends. (2) (b) A light rod is pivoted at its centre. A 6 N force acts squarely downwards at 25 cm left of the pivot, and a 5 N force acts squarely downwards at 30 cm right of the pivot. Form the two standings, state the sense of the net turning, and state what additional downward force at 10 cm left of the pivot would level the rod. (4) (c) Explain, with the idea of perpendicular distance, why a force can act on a body and produce no turning at all. (2)

Calculate the moment of a 12 N force applied squarely at a point 15 cm from a pivot. State the unit carefully, and state the moment of the same force applied at the same point if the distance is instead quoted as 0.15 m.

A student computes a moment and announces "30 N·m — so the force must be 30 N." Evaluate the claim: is the force fixed by the moment alone? Give two different force–distance pairs that both produce a moment of 30 N·m to settle the question.

A 4 m long see-saw is pivoted at its centre. Ravi, weighing 400 N, sits 2.0 m left of the pivot. Sita, weighing 500 N, wants to balance him. (a) Calculate the moment of Ravi's weight about the pivot. (b) Calculate how far right of the pivot Sita must sit. (c) If the see-saw's seats are only at 1.0 m and 1.6 m marks on the right, state which seat she should take and what happens at the other.

Design a laboratory task, using a uniform metre rule balanced on a knife edge at its 50 cm mark, a 50 g hanger and a sealed unknown mass, by which a student can measure the unknown mass. State the procedure, the equation, and a worked numerical route for the case where the unknown hangs at the 30 cm mark and balances a 200 g hanger at the 75 cm mark.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) State the principle of moments. (1) (b) A spanner's pivot is a nut; a force of 40 N acts squarely at 25 cm from the nut's centre. Calculate the moment, in N·m. (1) (c) State two different changes, each of which alone would double this moment. (1) (d) A second force of 30 N acts squarely at 20 cm on the opposite side of the nut. State, with totals, which way the spanner turns. (1)

A bicycle's pedal crank is 0.18 m long. A rider's foot presses down with a steady 250 N. (a) Compute the moment about the crank axle when the crank is horizontal. (b) Compute the moment when the crank has rotated so that the foot's line of action passes 0.09 m horizontally from the axle (crank at 60°). (c) The rider claims the second position gives "half the exercise". Evaluate: which quantity has halved, and what does the bicycle lose?

A portico's uniform horizontal beam is held up by a support pillar at 3.0 m from the wall hinge-point; the beam's far end carries a hanging flower-basket of weight 200 N at 4.5 m from the wall. Taking the wall hinge as pivot: (a) compute the basket's moment; (b) compute the upward force the pillar must exert; (c) the gardener moves the basket to 3.0 m (above the pillar) — recompute the pillar's force and state what the beam's far end now tends to do.

Critique this student's marked solution: "Problem: balance a 6 N weight at 0.30 m right of a pivot with a 9 N weight on the left. Student's answer: 'The 9 N goes at 0.30 m too, because balance means the same distance on both sides.' The teacher marked it wrong." Was the teacher right? Give the correct distance and the check, and state the principle the student's answer violated.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State the principle of moments and name its unit-bearing quantities. (2) (b) A light rod is pivoted at its centre. A 12 N weight hangs 0.25 m left of the pivot; an unknown weight W hangs 0.30 m right of it and the rod is level. Calculate W. (2) (c) The 12 N weight is moved to 0.40 m left. Calculate the new right-side distance for W to still balance, and state the general pattern of the movement. (3) (d) State one precaution while performing the metre-rule experiment for the principle of moments. (1)

A brick weighing 30 N is laid on soft clay soil. (a) Calculate the pressure under it when it lies flat on its 0.20 m × 0.15 m face. (b) Calculate the pressure when it stands on its 0.15 m × 0.075 m end face. (c) State how many times larger the second pressure is, and why the brick's weight did not have to change for this to happen.

A drawing pin is pressed into a wooden board with a thumb force of 20 N. The pin's tip has an area of 0.5 mm² and its flat head an area of 1.0 cm². (a) Calculate the pressure under the tip in Pa. (b) Calculate the pressure on the thumb under the head in Pa. (c) State the ratio of the two pressures and explain in one sentence what the pin accomplishes by its shape.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Define pressure and state its SI unit. (1) (b) A metal cube of weight 200 N stands on a floor on a face of side 0.2 m. Calculate the pressure it exerts. (1) (c) State two changes, each of which alone would halve this pressure. (1) (d) Explain why a school bag is fitted with wide straps rather than thin strings. (1)

A hospital stretcher's two handles each carry half of a 800 N patient over a nurse's palm of contact area 0.004 m² per handle. (a) Calculate the pressure on each palm. (b) A padded sling replaces the handles, spreading each half over 0.02 m². Calculate the new pressure and the factor of relief. (c) The head nurse says "the sling is kinder because it shares the load". Refine her sentence into physics.

A rectangular metal sheet of weight 480 N can stand on any of three faces with areas 0.6 m², 0.3 m² and 0.2 m². (a) Compute the three pressures. (b) The sheet is laid on wet clay that dents above 2500 Pa. State which positions are safe. (c) A second sheet of the same weight and face areas is placed on top of the first (doubled weight, same footprint). Recompute the pressures for each position and state the doubled-weight law.

Assemble the chapter's final audit table — for the turning-effect strand and the pressure strand — with rows: what a force is multiplied by to give the effect, the effect's name and equation, its unit, and one designed device from daily life. Then state the one-sentence summary of the whole chapter that a Class 8 student should carry out of the examination hall.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define pressure and write its equation with units for each symbol. (2) (b) A storage drum weighing 900 N stands upright on its circular base of area 0.15 m². Calculate the pressure on the floor. (2) (c) The drum is rolled onto its rounded rim so that it contacts the floor along a strip of area 0.003 m². Calculate the new pressure and state the factor of increase, with the one-line reason. (3) (d) State one design on the drum's trolley that would let the 900 N be moved across a soft wooden floor without denting it, given the floor dents above 20 000 Pa, and show the minimum area arithmetic. (2)

A boy pulls a toy cart with a force of 60 N and the cart moves 15 m along the direction of the pull. (a) Calculate the work done by the boy. (b) He then lifts his school bag of weight 40 N and places it on a shelf 1.2 m higher. Calculate the work done against gravity. (c) State the unit of each answer.

Design a two-column classification table for eight everyday actions — (1) pushing a stalled scooter that moves, (2) pushing a stalled truck that does not move, (3) lifting a bucket from a well, (4) holding the bucket at rest at the top, (5) walking with the bucket on level ground, (6) a bullock pulling a cart forward, (7) pressing a heavy trunk sideways but it stays put, (8) climbing a staircase with your bag — sorting each into "work done" or "no work done" by the named main force, with the deciding reason in one line each.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Define work and write its equation with the unit. (2) (b) State two situations in which the work done by a force is zero. (1) (c) A force of 25 N moves a box 4 m along the force. Calculate the work done. (1) (d) Why is work done when a load is lifted, even if it is lifted very slowly? (1)

A space probe drifts through empty space at constant velocity, engines off, nothing touching it. (a) Is any force doing work on the probe during the drift? Justify with the definition. (b) Earlier, its engine fired for 10 minutes and accelerated it from rest. During which phase was work done, and by what? (c) A classmate argues "the probe must be having work done on it because it covers millions of kilometres." Refute him precisely, distinguishing the two locks of the definition.

A cycle-rickshaw puller starts from rest and pedals a passenger 2 km along a level road at steady speed. (a) Name every force doing work during the steady-speed phase and every force doing no work, with one-line reasons (consider: pedal/pedalling force on the cycle, gravity on rickshaw plus rider, upward road push on the wheels, air resistance and friction opposing motion, the puller's upward support on the seat). (b) During the initial acceleration from rest, which forces were doing work that stopped doing work once steady speed was reached? (c) Why is the puller exhausted after 2 km even though his vertical support force did no work throughout?

Evaluate this claim: "A crane always does more work than a man, because a crane is stronger." Test it with invented but consistent numbers: a man lifts a 100 N load through 3 m; a crane lifts a 2000 N girder through 0.1 m. Compute both works, judge the claim, and state the general rule the test exposes about which quantity decides work.

Compare the two "work recipes" met in this node — the sliding/pulling recipe (force × distance along the ground) and the lifting recipe (weight × height) — in a two-row table: what force each needs, what distance each counts, one identical-numbers example where both give the same work, and one sentence on how the same total work can be bought by a big-force-short-distance deal or a small-force-long-distance deal. Use a 100 N crate: lifted 2 m vertically versus hauled up a smooth incline needing a 50 N pull over 4 m of incline.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define work and state its unit. (2) (b) Give one example each of: a force doing positive useful work; a force acting with zero work done. (2) (c) A horse pulls a cart with a horizontal force of 300 N through 60 m of road. Calculate the work done by the horse. (2) (d) The same cart, fully loaded, now needs 500 N and the horse manages only 40 m before resting. Calculate the new work and state which trip cost the horse more work, with the comparison arithmetic. (2) (e) State, with a reason, whether the horse's upward push on the ground (through its hooves) does work on the cart. (2)

Define the joule. Write the identity connecting joule and newton-metre, and name the two multiples of the joule used for larger quantities with their values. Express 2500 J in kilojoules and 0.36 kJ in joules.

A drawer is pulled with a force of 12 N through a distance of 40 cm. (a) Convert the distance to metre and calculate the work done in joules. (b) The same force now pulls the drawer through 80 mm. Calculate the work done. (c) Express answer (a) in kilojoules.

(a) A shop shutter of weight 600 N is raised steadily through 2 m. Calculate the work done and express it in kilojoules. (b) A 500 N load is lifted using 1000 J of work. Calculate the height gained. (c) A force does 90 J of work while acting through 6 m. Calculate the force.

Build a "day of joules" estimate table for a Class 8 student: three activities — (1) lifting a 40 N school bag from the floor to a 0.75 m desk, (2) climbing a staircase of 12 steps, each 0.18 m high, where the student's weight is 300 N, (3) drawing a 150 N bucket up a 8 m well — each row showing the working W = F × d and the answer in J, then the column total in kJ. State the one conversion habit that keeps every row trustworthy.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Define the joule. (1) (b) Convert 0.75 kJ to joules and 350 J to kilojoules. (1) (c) A force of 65 N moves a box 80 cm along the force. Calculate the work done in joules. (1) (d) Why is the same unit, the joule, used for both work and energy? (1)

A physics chapter claims: "The joule is small, so scientists invented the kilojoule to make work look bigger." Untangle the claim: (a) what actually changes when a work value is re-expressed from J to kJ — the work, the number, or both? (b) Rewrite 2500 J in kJ and state which of the three (work, number, unit) changed and which stayed. (c) Why do scientists bother with prefixes at all, if the quantity never changes?

A gym trainee presses a 150 N exercise sled through 60 cm per repetition and completes 20 repetitions. (a) Calculate the work per repetition in joules. (b) Calculate the total work for the set, in J and kJ. (c) The trainee doubles the sled's resistance to 300 N but manages only 10 repetitions of the same 60 cm. Compute the new total and state whether the two sets are equal, and which factor traded against which.

Evaluate this shop-floor claim: "Our 2 kJ hydraulic press does more work than your 1500 J floor jack, and kJ proves it — kilojoules are the bigger unit." Compute both works in the same unit, judge the claim's verdict and its reasoning separately, and state the general rule for comparing any two quantities quoted in mixed prefixes.

Compare the joule with the newton in a two-row audit: what each measures, the defining equation behind each, one everyday magnitude of each, and one sentence on why the work unit could not simply have been "the newton". Then close with the pairing: express the work of lifting a 1 N apple through 1 m in (i) N m and (ii) J, and state what the two answers say about the unit names.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define the joule and express it in terms of the newton and the metre. (2) (b) A boy drags his school trunk 1.5 m with a horizontal force of 120 N. Calculate the work done in J and kJ. (2) (c) The trunk is then lifted by two men onto a 0.9 m platform; the work done against gravity is 540 J. Calculate the trunk's weight. (2) (d) A quoted "0.045 kJ" third task is offered to the boy instead of the drag. Compute it in joules and state, with the comparison, whether it exceeds his drag's work. (2) (e) Give one reason why all three answers above are unchanged if each task is performed twice as slowly. (2)
A girl carries a 5 kg school bag horizontally across a 10 m corridor at constant speed. How much work does she do on the bag against gravity? Explain.
Compare the work done in two cases: (a) lifting a 2 kg book 1 m vertically; (b) pushing the same book 1 m horizontally with a force of 5 N. Which involves more work? Assume g = 10 m/s².
A man pulls a sled with a force of 40 N at an angle of 30° to the horizontal. The sled moves 6 m horizontally. Calculate the work done by the man. (Use cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866)
A 3 kg block is lifted 2 m and then lowered back to its starting point. What is the total work done by gravity during the complete round trip? (g = 10 m/s²)
A force of 15 N acts on a body at an angle of 120° to its displacement of 2 m. Calculate the work done and state whether it is positive or negative.
A child pulls a toy car with a force of 8 N at an angle of 45° to the horizontal. The car moves 3 m horizontally. How much work does the child do? (cos 45° = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707)
Critique the statement: "If a person holds a heavy box stationary for 10 minutes, he does a lot of work because he gets tired." Use the physics definition of work.
Compare the work done in these two scenarios: (i) Lifting a 5 kg mass 2 m vertically. (ii) Pushing the same mass 2 m horizontally with a force of 30 N. Which requires more work? (g = 10 m/s²)
A 200 g ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial speed of 15 m/s. Calculate the work done by gravity when the ball reaches its maximum height. (g = 10 m/s²)

(a) Calculate the kinetic energy of a 0.5 kg football moving at 8 m/s. (b) Calculate the kinetic energy of the same football at 16 m/s. (c) State how many times the energy grew and why the growth is more than double for a doubled speed.

A truck driver says: "My loaded truck weighs four times your car, so at any speed it carries four times the destructive energy — size is everything." Evaluate: at the same speed is his proportionality claim right? Then test his "size is everything" conclusion with numbers: his 8000 kg truck at 10 m/s versus a 1000 kg car at 40 m/s, computing both kinetic energies and the verdict.

(a) A hammerhead of mass 2 kg strikes a nail at 5 m/s and is brought to rest. Calculate its kinetic energy just before impact, and state what becomes of it. (b) A cyclist slows from 6 m/s to rest and the brakes grow hot. Which earlier work reappears here, and how? (c) Why does a body at rest have zero kinetic energy even if it is very heavy?

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Define kinetic energy and write its formula with units. (2) (b) A 40 kg girl runs at 5 m/s. Calculate her kinetic energy. (1) (c) State, with the reason, what happens to her kinetic energy if her speed doubles to 10 m/s. (1) (d) Name the form of energy a moving bus possesses and the unit it is measured in. (1)

A goods lift accelerates a 500 kg crate from rest to 4 m/s. (a) Calculate the kinetic energy imparted. (b) State, with the work–energy identity, how much work the lift's motor spent on this acceleration (ignoring height gain and friction). (c) The crate is later brought to rest over 0.5 m by a buffer. Calculate the average force the buffer exerts, and state the energy's final fate. (d) Why is no kinetic energy question answered in newton?

Evaluate this driving-school poster: "Braking distance grows with the SQUARE of speed — doubling your speed needs four times the distance to stop." Using the work–energy identity (brakes do work F_brake × distance = KE to remove, at roughly constant braking force), derive the square-law for distance, and test it with numbers: a car needing 20 m to stop from 40 km/h — compute the stopping distance from 80 km/h, and state what assumption about the braking force the derivation uses.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define kinetic energy and write its formula, naming the units of every symbol. (2) (b) A 900 kg car moves at 20 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy in kJ. (2) (c) The car's speed falls to 10 m/s. Calculate the new kinetic energy and the energy given up, and name the process that absorbed it. (2) (d) A 0.02 kg pellet at 100 m/s and a 4 kg ham at 5 m/s are compared. Compute both kinetic energies, rank them, and identify which law makes the tiny fast pellet competitive. (2) (e) State one situation from daily life where a small increase in speed produces a disproportionately large increase in the energy to be managed, with the square-law arithmetic stated. (2)

(a) Calculate the potential energy of a 2 kg water pot resting on a shelf 3 m above the floor (g = 10 m/s²). (b) The pot is moved to a shelf 6 m high. Calculate the new PE and state the law the change illustrates. (c) Express both answers in joules and state the reference level used.

(a) An archer draws a bow, doing 80 J of work against its elasticity, and holds it drawn. Name the energy now stored, its form, and its amount. (b) The arrow is released. State what becomes of the 80 J in the first instants of flight. (c) Two water tanks serve a building: tank A of 500 kg on a 6 m stand, tank B of 250 kg on a 12 m stand (g = 10 m/s²). Compute both PEs and state whether either tank holds more stored energy, with the comparison used.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Define potential energy and state its unit. (1) (b) A 5 kg box is lifted onto a platform 2 m high (g = 10 m/s²). Calculate its potential energy there. (1) (c) State two everyday examples of elastic potential energy. (1) (d) Why does the same book have different potential energies when measured from the floor and from the street below the window? (2)

A mountaineering textbook says: "Climbing the same route by the steep face or the gentle zigzag path deposits exactly the same energy in you — the path's shape is irrelevant." (a) Verify the claim with numbers: a 60 kg climber and a 120 m height gain (g = 10 m/s²), computing the PE gained — does the route shape enter m g h? (b) Why, then, does the zigzag feel easier? Distinguish the physics quantity from the body's delivery rate without using the word reserved for rate-of-working (that concept lives in later classes). (c) State what the claim implies about two different summits of heights 120 m and 120 m on different mountains.

A hotel installs a dumbwaiter (small food lift). Loaded cabin: 40 kg, raised from ground floor (0 m) to third floor (9 m) at steady speed, g = 10 m/s². (a) Calculate the PE gained by the cabin. (b) Calculate the tension force in the cable during the steady rise and the work the cable does over the 9 m, and compare it with (a). (c) At the third floor the cable is released by mistake and a safety spring stops the cabin after a 1.5 m fall inside the shaft. Calculate the cabin's PE loss in the fall and state what the spring absorbed. (d) Why did the cabin's kinetic energy stay out of parts (a) and (b)?

Evaluate this claim by a warehouse manager: "Stacking cartons higher is free storage — same floor space, more cartons." From the physics side, compute the extra PE stored per 10 kg carton when the stack grows from 2 m to 6 m (g = 10 m/s²), and evaluate the claim's hidden cost: state what the higher stack has bought (more stored energy) and what now stands to be released in an accident, comparing the 2 m and 6 m stacks' energy content per carton column.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define potential energy and write the expression for gravitational PE, naming each quantity's unit. (2) (b) A 0.5 kg mango falls from a 4 m branch. Calculate its PE on the branch (g = 10 m/s²). (2) (c) On the ground it rests in a basket 0.5 m above the ground. Calculate its PE there, and state the energy given up in the fall and one thing it became. (2) (d) A 2 kg jackfruit on a neighbouring 4 m branch is compared with the mango. Compute both PEs and identify which law makes the jackfruit's store four times the mango's. (2) (e) State, with a one-line reason, whether the mango's PE values in (b) and (c) would change if the tree stood on a hill 100 m above the sea and both parts were re-measured from sea level. (2)
