State the four-step discipline for solving an energy numerical. Then apply steps 1 and 2 to this data: "a 700 g stone thrown at 90 km/h, from a 150 cm high wall" — writing the converted inventory and naming which energies the stone's situation can involve.

(a) A 0.2 kg stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from a 10 m tower (g = 10 m/s²). Calculate its kinetic energy and its potential energy at the instant of release. (b) State the stone's total (KE + PE) at that instant. (c) Another stone of the same mass is thrown at the same speed from ground level: compute its KE and PE there and state what changed and what did not.

A 1500 J raise: a crate was lifted 3 m (g = 10 m/s²). (a) Find the crate's mass. (b) Find the crate's weight. (c) A second crate of mass 50 kg is raised 3 m — find its PE gain, and use the two answers to verify PE ∝ m.

(a) A 1200 kg car has 150 kJ of kinetic energy. Calculate its speed. (b) A 0.5 kg ball has 40 J of potential energy on a ledge (g = 10 m/s²). Calculate the ledge's height. (c) A falling coconut hits the ground at 20 m/s. From what height did it fall from rest (g = 10 m/s², air ignored)?

A school geography-and-physics trip reports three sights with data: a 2500 kg temple chariot parked at rest; a 0.1 kg sparrow flying at 6 m/s at 8 m height; a 60 000 kg jet at 200 m/s at 3000 m. For each, compute every energy the situation involves (g = 10 m/s²), and rank the six values. State the one lesson the sparrow teaches about small bodies at height.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Write the formulas for kinetic and potential energy, with units. (2) (b) A 4 kg body moves at 5 m/s at a height of 3 m. Calculate its KE, its PE, and their sum (g = 10 m/s²). (2) (c) The body now comes to rest on the ground. State its KE and PE there (ground as reference). (1) (d) Name the unit in which both answers are expressed and the quantity common to both formulas. (1)

A physics puzzle: "A 1 kg bag of sugar sits on a 2 m shelf in Bombay and on an identical 2 m shelf in Shimla. Are its energies the same?" (a) Compute its PE in each kitchen using g = 10 m/s² as the course convention and note the answer. (b) The purist objects: g actually varies slightly with location (it is a little smaller on high ground). State what the objector is claiming about the shelf-PE in the two cities, while affirming the course convention's purpose. (c) Compute the sugar's KE in both kitchens as it sits still, and state the one situation that would make the two cities' KE differ.

A warehouse robot lifts a 12 kg parcel from the floor to a 4 m rack, then slides it along the rack at a steady 0.5 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). (a) Compute the parcel's PE on the rack. (b) Compute the work done by the lift (steady rise) and compare with (a). (c) Compute the parcel's KE during the steady slide. (d) The robot lowers the parcel to a 1 m picking bench. Compute the parcel's PE there and the energy the lowering gave up, and state one place that energy went.

Two students audit a pendulum-style ride data sheet and disagree. Sheet: "car of 300 kg at 15 m/s at the lowest point; at the highest point of its arc, 10 m above the lowest, momentarily at rest (g = 10 m/s²)." Student 1: "the highest point holds more energy — it is higher." Student 2: "the lowest holds more — it is faster." Compute the car's KE and PE at both points (lowest point as the PE reference) and evaluate both students against the totals; state which single condition would make their disagreement real.

Assemble the node's decision card as a table with rows: situation type (moving; raised; both; falling from rest), formula(s) chosen, one worked micro-example with numbers, and the audit check for that row. Then close with the three-line summary of the workshop: the conversion receipt, the selection test, and the free-fall cross-check, each in one sentence a Class 8 student could reproduce in the examination hall.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State the formula and unit for each of kinetic energy and potential energy. (2) (b) A 0.8 kg ball is thrown upward at 10 m/s from a 3 m terrace (g = 10 m/s²). Calculate its KE and PE at the instant of release. (2) (c) The ball momentarily stops 5 m above the terrace. Calculate its PE at that highest point (terrace as reference) and its KE there. (2) (d) Using the free-fall identity arithmetic, calculate the speed the ball would hit the ground with if it simply fell from the terrace edge (3 m drop, from rest). (2) (e) State why the mass does not appear in the final formula used in (d). (2)

Define an energy transformation. Name six forms of energy a Class 8 student should be able to identify. Write the transformation chain of a torch, naming the form that enters and the forms that leave.

A student claims: "A mixer-grinder uses 100 J of electrical energy and delivers 100 J of blade motion — so where is the heat you keep talking about? If the motor warms up, some energy must have been destroyed." Resolve the claim: state the correct chain, allocate the 100 J consistently with the no-destruction principle, and name the everyday evidence the student is ignoring.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) State the principle governing all energy transformations. (1) (b) Write the transformation chain for: (i) an electric iron; (ii) a boy climbing a ladder. (1) (c) In the chain for a falling mango, name the two mechanical stores involved and the direction of the change. (1) (d) A table fan runs for an hour and its motor is warm. Name the transformation responsible for the warmth and state why this does not mean energy was wasted out of existence. (2)

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State the law-like principle governing energy transformations. (1) (b) Write the transformation chains for: (i) a photovoltaic garden lamp (sun by day, glow by night); (ii) a pressure cooker on a lit gas burner. (2) (c) A school's water tank on its 10 m tower feeds a tap at ground level: name the two mechanical stores involved in the descent and the direction of the change; compute the PE per kilogram of water at the tank (g = 10 m/s²). (2) (d) The tap's stream turns a small toy paddle-wheel glued to a cheap dynamo, lighting one LED. Write that final chain and state the one transformation whose heat share you would check by touch. (2) (e) A student summarises: "every chain ends in heat eventually." State whether the summary is acceptable as a first approximation and justify it against the principle in (a) in two sentences. (3)

An integrative scene: a 20 kg sack of rice is hauled 6 m along a floor, then lifted onto a 1.5 m loft (g = 10 m/s²). The hauling force is 60 N; the lift needs the sack's weight. (a) Compute the work done in the haul. (b) Compute the work done in the lift and the PE the sack gains. (c) State the chapter connection that makes (b)'s two numbers equal, and give the sack's total mechanical energy at rest on the loft (floor as reference).

One scene, all chapter ideas: a 0.5 kg stone is thrown straight up at 10 m/s from a 2 m wall (g = 10 m/s², air ignored). (a) Compute the KE at throw and the work the thrower's arm did on the stone. (b) Compute the stone's PE at the wall-top instant. (c) The stone rises to its highest point 5 m above the wall: compute its PE there (ground reference) and state its KE there. (d) Write the throw in transformation-chain notation.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) State the chapter definition of energy, with its unit. (1) (b) A 60 N force moves a box 4 m along itself. Calculate the work done. (1) (c) That box is then lifted 2 m; its mass is 9 kg (g = 10 m/s²). Calculate the lifting work and the box's PE gain, and state why they are equal. (2) (d) Name the two mechanical stores the chapter has given bodies, with one example of each. (1)

A revision session hears four one-line claims. Audit each against the map, quoting the row and the anti-slip rule: (a) "I lifted my bag slowly, so I did less work than if I had lifted it fast." (b) "The falling coconut hits harder from 8 m than from 2 m — nine or so times harder." (c) "The wound toy's spring stores the same energy whatever the winding." (d) "The fan's warm motor proves some electricity is destroyed." For each, state right or wrong, the correcting rule, and — for any wrong claim — the corrected version of the statement.

Evaluate this parent's complaint after seeing the chapter: "My child used to say force moves things — simple. Now you have work, joule, KE, PE, transformations — four new words for what a push does. Isn't this complexity for its own sake?" Answer with the three-sentence bridge plus the added-power argument: name one question the child's old vocabulary cannot answer at all that the new vocabulary answers with a number, and compute that number for a concrete case (a 30 kg child on a 40 cm step, g = 10 m/s²).

Assemble the chapter-so-far audit table with rows: concept; formula or notation; unit; the anti-slip rule; and one integrative link to another row (how it feeds or is fed). Cover all four rows (work, KE, PE, transformation). Then close with the chapter's one-sentence story as a Class 8 student should be able to tell it in the examination hall — no formula in the sentence, the whole structure in it.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define work and energy, and state the relation between their units. (2) (b) A 12 kg body is pushed from rest to 5 m/s on level ground and then lifted 2 m onto a shelf (g = 10 m/s²). Calculate: (i) the work done in accelerating it; (ii) the work done in lifting it; (iii) its total mechanical energy at rest on the shelf (ground reference). (3) (c) The body falls off the shelf: calculate its KE and speed just before landing (air ignored). (2) (d) After landing it lies still and slightly warm: account for the missing mechanical energy in transformation language, and state the principle the account obeys. (2) (e) State one way this consolidation differs from re-learning: what should a student carry forward into the pendulum node that single-topic revision would miss? (1)
A force of 15 N acts on a box at an angle of 60° to the horizontal. The box moves 4 m horizontally. Calculate the work done by the force.
Evaluate the statement: “If a person holds a heavy suitcase stationary at a height of 1 m, they are doing work on the suitcase.”

A girl pushes a 10 kg crate across a smooth floor with a constant horizontal force of 40 N for a distance of 6 m. Calculate the work done by the girl and state whether the work is positive, negative, or zero.

A 5 kg block is pulled up a smooth incline of length 3 m making an angle of 30° with the horizontal by a force parallel to the incline of 30 N. Calculate the work done by the pulling force. (Take g = 10 m/s²).
A force of 25 N acts at 37° to the horizontal on a block that moves 10 m horizontally. Without using a calculator, estimate the work done (use cos 37° ≈ 0.8).
A porter carries a 30 kg suitcase up a flight of stairs of vertical height 4 m. Calculate the work done by the porter against gravity. (Take g = 10 m/s²).
Compare the work done in two cases: (i) lifting a 5 kg mass vertically 2 m; (ii) pushing the same mass horizontally 2 m with a force of 20 N on a frictionless surface. Which involves more work?

A 2 kg block is pulled up a rough incline of length 5 m at 30° by a force of 30 N parallel to the incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. Calculate the work done by the applied force. (Take g = 10 m/s²).
In the video, a vendor pushes a handcart horizontally with a force of 50 N for 10 m. What is the work done by the vendor on the cart?
A girl lifts a 5 kg school bag vertically upward by 1.2 m. The video states the work done by the girl is 60 J. Verify this using g = 10 m/s².
The video shows a boy pulling a sled with a force of 40 N at an angle of 60° to the horizontal over 5 m. He claims the work done is 200 J. Evaluate his claim.
A cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg is hit by a bat. The video says the bat does 30 J of work on the ball during contact. If the ball starts from rest, what is its speed immediately after being hit?
A CISCE exam question: “A force of 30 N acts on a body at an angle of 30° to the horizontal. The body moves 4 m horizontally. Calculate the work done by the force.” Show the steps as the video would.

A video clip shows a coolie carrying a 20 kg load on his head while walking horizontally at constant speed for 50 m. He claims he does 10,000 J of work on the load. Using the concept of work, evaluate his claim.
Compare the work done in two video scenes: (A) pushing a cart horizontally with 50 N for 10 m, (B) lifting a 5 kg bag vertically 2 m (g = 10 m/s²). Which involves more work? Show calculations.

A past CISCE paper asks: “A force of 20 N acts at an angle of 60° to the horizontal. The body moves 3 m horizontally. Calculate the work done by the force.” Provide the solution as expected in the exam.

A student times a pendulum for 20 oscillations and the stopwatch reads 50 s. (a) Calculate the time period. (b) Calculate the frequency, with its unit. (c) Why time 20 oscillations instead of just one? (d) A second pendulum of the same length but a heavier bob is timed the same way — state its time period relative to the first, with the rule used.

A pendulum's bob of mass 0.2 kg is pulled aside so that the extreme position is 0.05 m vertically above the mean position (g = 10 m/s²). (a) Calculate the bob's PE at the extreme relative to the mean position. (b) State its KE there. (c) State its KE and PE at the mean position, and the total at both stations in the ideal pendulum. (d) The bob is replaced by a 0.4 kg bob pulled to the same amplitude: state the new PE at the extreme and the new timing, with rules.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Define the mean position and one oscillation of a simple pendulum. (1) (b) A pendulum completes 30 oscillations in 45 s. Calculate its time period and frequency. (2) (c) State where in the swing the bob's kinetic energy is maximum and where its potential energy is maximum. (1) (d) Name one factor that changes the time period and one that does not. (1)

A temple's brass lamp hangs from a long chain and swings gently in the evening breeze. A child times 10 complete oscillations at 35 s. (a) Compute T and f. (b) The breeze gives the lamp a slightly larger small amplitude; state the effect on T and justify with the regularity. (c) A devotee ties a second identical lamp-and-chain alongside (same length); state the new lamp's timing relative to the first and the rule. (d) The lamp's 2 kg body swings through an extreme 0.03 m above the mean level: compute the PE at the extreme and the KE at the mean (ideal, g = 10 m/s²), and the speed at the mean. **Hint check:** timing rules + station energies in one temple scene.

A toymaker proposes a "mass-tuned metronome": a pendulum whose period you change by sliding weights ONTO the bob — "heavier bob, slower, more dignified tick." (a) Evaluate the proposal with the timing rule: what actually changes when the bob is loaded? (b) Redesign the toy so the dial truly changes T, naming the construction change and its direction rule. (c) The toymaker's prototype is timed: 50 oscillations in 75 s at one setting and 50 in 150 s at another. Compute both periods and state which setting used the longer string, with the ratio.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define amplitude and one oscillation of a simple pendulum. (2) (b) A pendulum has T = 2 s. Calculate its frequency, and the time for 15 oscillations. (2) (c) State the energy condition (KE and PE) at the mean position and at an extreme, and name the exchange running between them. (2) (d) A 0.25 kg bob is released from an extreme 0.16 m above the mean level (g = 10 m/s²): calculate the PE at the extreme, the KE at the mean, and the speed at the mean. (3) (e) The pendulum eventually stops swinging. Name the agencies responsible and state, in one sentence each, (i) what happened to the mechanical energy and (ii) why this does not contradict the transformation principle. (3)

State the law of conservation of energy as this chapter establishes it. Name the three demonstrations the video uses to stage it, and write the one-sentence version of the law a Class 8 student should reproduce in the examination.

A 0.5 kg ball is released from rest at 4 m above the ground (g = 10 m/s², air ignored). (a) Compute its PE at release and its KE there. (b) Compute its PE, KE and speed at 2 m (mid-fall). (c) Compute its KE and speed just before the ground. (d) State the total at all three stations and the law it demonstrates.

The video's pendulum uses a 0.1 kg bob whose extreme positions are 0.2 m above the mean-position level (g = 10 m/s²). (a) Compute the total mechanical energy of the ideal pendulum. (b) State the KE and speed at the mean position. (c) At a station 0.1 m above the mean level, state the PE and KE split. (d) In the real video the same pendulum's amplitudes shrink over the minutes: state what the shrinking measures and where the "missing" joules are, with the law's wording.

A classmate watches the spring-mass toy segment and says: "The spring made the block move, so the spring created kinetic energy." (a) Correct the claim, naming the store the spring held and the work that filled it. (b) The toy's block of mass 0.4 kg leaves the spring at 3 m/s: compute the KE delivered, and state the spring's stored energy just before release (ideal). (c) After several bounces the block rests and the spring lies quiet: write the toy's whole story as a transformation chain with the final forms, and state the law the story obeys.

Design the video's closing segment yourself: a 60-second classroom demonstration that makes the constancy of the total visible to the back bench, using a pendulum, three chalk marks (top, middle, bottom of the arc) and a call-and-response script. State the setup, the three marks' call-outs (energy wording), the one number the class should chant at every mark, and the 10-second closing sentence of the segment.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) State the law of conservation of energy. (1) (b) A 2 kg stone falls freely from rest from 10 m (g = 10 m/s², air ignored). Calculate its KE and speed just before the ground. (2) (c) State the stone's PE and KE at half the fall. (1) (d) After hitting the ground the stone rests. Account for the 200 J in transformation language. (1)

A mountain stream feeds a water-wheel grinder. (a) Trace the water's energy from the high stream to the turning wheel in a chain with the stores named. (b) The stream drops 12 m; compute the PE released per kilogram of water (g = 10 m/s²) and the speed the water would reach in a free fall through that drop. (c) The miller says "the wheel turns all day for free." Refine the sentence into physics: what is actually paying, and why is the bill invisible at the mill? (d) State where the water's remaining mechanical energy goes after the wheel, and complete the account with the law.

Two students dispute the video's falling-ball table. Student 1: "At half-height the speeds must be equal at the two halves of the fall — the table shows symmetric halves." Student 2: "No — the second half must be faster; the ball is falling longer distances per second." Adjudicate using the constant total: compute the ball's speeds at 1 m and 3 m of a fall from 4 m (g = 10 m/s²), state who is right, and identify the exact quantity that stays symmetric while speeds do not.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State the law of conservation of energy. (1) (b) A 0.6 kg ball is thrown straight up at 8 m/s from the ground (g = 10 m/s², air ignored). Calculate its initial KE and the height it reaches (all KE converted to PE at the top). (3) (c) Compute the ball's PE and KE at 2 m on the way up, and verify the constant total. (2) (d) The ball falls back and strikes the ground, coming to rest with a thud. Account for the energy at the impact, naming the final forms. (2) (e) A classmate proposes "a perfectly bouncy ball could bounce forever, giving free entertainment." Judge the ideal case against the law and the real case against friction, in one sentence each. (2)

Two diagrams of a ray meeting an air–water surface are proposed. Diagram P: the ray strikes the surface at 40° to the surface, and the underwater ray continues at 25° to the normal. Diagram Q: the ray strikes at 40° to the normal, and the underwater ray continues at 50° to the normal. Evaluate each: state whether the angles are quoted from the correct reference line, whether the bend direction obeys the rules, and deliver the verdict on which diagram (if either) a CISCE examiner would accept.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Define refraction of light and state its cause. (2) (b) A ray passes obliquely from water (speed ≈ 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s) into air. State, with the rule, whether the refracted ray bends towards or away from the normal. (1) (c) Complete: light travels along the normal from air into water — its direction ______ and its speed ______. (1) (d) Give one everyday observation that refraction explains, and name the direction of bending responsible. (1)

A student claims: "If light slows down in glass, then a ray aimed at a thick glass block must come out the far side later AND at a different place than a ray aimed through the same width of air — so two side-by-side rays, one through glass, one through air, should arrive visibly separated." Set up the fair test: (a) state whether the claim's physics is right about timing, and compute the arrival lag over a 12 cm width (glass ≈ 2 × 10⁸ m/s, air ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s); (b) state what else the claim ignores about the glass ray's path that affects where it emerges; (c) judge the "visibly separated" promise for a classroom bench.

Build the comparison table: reflection versus refraction, four rows — (1) what happens to the light, (2) the medium situation, (3) the pair of angles and their rule, (4) one everyday signature. Then add a fifth row the two share, and state which of the two this chapter's glass slab and water tumbler stage.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define refraction of light. (1) (b) Copy the sentence and fill the blanks: "When a ray of light passes obliquely from a rarer medium to a denser medium, its speed ______ and it bends ______ the normal; the angle of refraction is ______ than the angle of incidence." (1½) (c) A ray in air strikes a water surface at an angle of incidence of 45°. Inside the water the refracted ray lies closer to the normal. State whether r is greater or less than 45° and name the rule used. (1) (d) State what happens to a ray that strikes the same surface along the normal, and give its speed in water. (1) (e) Explain in two sentences why a swimming pool looks shallower than it is. (1½) (f) The teacher replaces the water with clear oil in which light travels even slower than in water. State, with the rule, whether the refracted ray for the same 45° incidence now bends more towards the normal or less. (2)
A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. What is its focal length? A convex mirror has the same radius of curvature. Compare their focal lengths.
A student measures the distance from the pole of a concave mirror to its focus as 12 cm. What is the radius of curvature of that mirror?

**HOTS:** A concave mirror and a convex mirror have the same numerical focal length of 15 cm. An object is placed 30 cm in front of each mirror. Without drawing ray diagrams, predict the nature (real/virtual) and relative size of the images formed. Justify using the concept of focus.

**APPLICATION:** A driver’s side mirror on a car is convex with a radius of curvature of 2 m. Calculate its focal length and explain why this mirror provides a wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size.

**COMPARISON:** Compare the focal lengths of two concave mirrors: Mirror A has radius of curvature 40 cm; Mirror B has radius of curvature 60 cm. Which mirror converges parallel rays more strongly? Explain.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “A spherical mirror has a focal length of 12 cm. An object is placed 24 cm in front of the mirror. State the type of mirror (concave/convex) if the image formed is real and inverted.” Choose the correct answer and justify.

Explain, using the compass or ball picture, why a mirror cut from a sphere of radius 20 cm curves more sharply than a mirror cut from a sphere of radius 40 cm, and state which of the two has its centre of curvature nearer its pole. Then state what happens to the curvature and to C as the parent sphere's radius grows without limit.

A torch's reflector cup curves sharply and holds its bulb at one particular point on its axis; a large gently curved metal bowl could in principle do the same job but badly. (a) Name the point where the bulb must sit and the relation it has to the mirror's geometry (use f = R/2 from c8_phy_icse_04_002). (b) A reflector's parent sphere has R = 6 cm: compute f and state how far in front of the cup's pole the bulb sits. (c) A second cup has R = 24 cm: state without computation whether its bulb sits nearer or farther from the pole than the first, and what happens to the emerging beam's spread if the bulb is mounted at the wrong cup's focus.

Design a five-minute "curvature safari" for your class using only kitchen steel: a spoon, a katori, a thali and a flat steel plate. Script three stops — (1) sorting the four by curvature with a stated criterion students can apply by eye, (2) the bulb test that shows the sharpest member forming a tiny inverted image, (3) the closing question you pose that links the safari to why a torch cup is a tight dish. State the one sentence you want every student to carry out of the safari.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Define centre of curvature of a spherical mirror. (1) (b) Copy and complete: "The ______ is the centre of the mirror's reflecting surface, and the straight line joining it to the centre of curvature is called the ______ ______." (1) (c) State where C lies for a concave mirror and for a convex mirror, with one clause of reason for each. (1½) (d) A plane mirror is sometimes called a spherical mirror of infinite radius. State what its curvature and its centre of curvature are taken to be. (1½)

The school workshop must pick a reflector for a new solar cricket-light — a device that gathers morning sunlight into a small heating spot to toast paper crisp for a demonstration. Stock: cup P (R = 20 cm), cup Q (R = 100 cm), plate (flat). (a) Name the point where sunlight must be gathered and compute it for P and Q. (b) Which cup toasts faster at its focus, and why does curvature decide it? (c) Why is the plate useless here, and what does this same uselessness make it good for elsewhere in optics? (d) The builder asks if the reflector's diameter matters as much as its curvature. Answer with the role each plays.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Draw a concave mirror as an arc, marking P, C, F and the principal axis, given that its radius of curvature is 10 cm. Label distances PC and PF. (2) (b) State the relation between f and R and compute f for this mirror. (1) (c) A second mirror has four times the radius of the first. State the effect on (i) its curvature, (ii) the position of C, (iii) its focal length. (1½) (d) A convex mirror has R = 16 cm. Compute f and state on which side of the mirror F and C lie, with the term used for such a focus. (1½) (e) A student says, "a plane mirror is not a spherical mirror at all." Judge the statement with the limit argument and give the plane mirror's curvature and C in that reading. (2) (f) Name one situation where sharp curvature is essential and one where gentle curvature is preferred, with one clause of reason each. (2)

Define the radius of curvature of a spherical mirror. On which side of the mirror is C marked for each type, and what single relation then locates the principal focus? State the relation and use it: for R = 18 cm, compute f.

Two mirrors, P and Q, are drawn on the board with their construction arcs. P's arc was swung with the compass at C₁, 12 cm in front; Q's arc was swung with the compass at C₂, 40 cm behind. (a) Identify each mirror as concave or convex with the clause that decides it. (b) Compute f for each. (c) State which mirror bends parallel rays more strongly and how the figures' arc shapes betray it. (d) For each, write the label you would put beside its F (real or virtual) and why labels matter to the examiner.

A torch manufacturer needs its reflector to send the bulb's light out as a near-parallel beam, and the bulb's mounting collar can be fixed anywhere from 3 cm to 9 cm in front of the reflector's pole. (a) Name the seat the bulb must occupy and state the parallel-beam fact that justifies it. (b) Compute the range of R values the reflector may have for the bulb to sit exactly at F somewhere in the mounting range. (c) Two stock reflectors are available: R = 8 cm and R = 20 cm. Which is usable as-is, with the bulb at what collar setting, and what must be said of the other?

Design the class's one-period practical: measuring R of three polished dishes (a spoon bowl, a katori, a shaving dish) by the distant-window method. Script: (1) the data table you draw on the board beforehand (name its columns), (2) the two safety and accuracy rules you announce, (3) how teams handle a dish whose image never sharpens, (4) the closing board summary that fills the table's last column with R values and one pattern sentence.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Copy and complete: "The radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is the distance between the ______ and the ______ ______." (1) (b) State the relation between focal length and radius of curvature. (1) (c) A concave mirror has f = 7 cm. Compute R. (1) (d) A convex mirror has R = 30 cm. Compute f and state whether its focus is real or virtual, with one clause of reason. (2)

The school's annual fair includes a "guess the R" stall: three polished dishes, and a card that reads "closest guess to the true R wins". You may not touch the dishes to measure them, but the stall-keeper allows the window test. (a) State the one test and the single reading that decides your guess for a concave dish. (b) Your readings: dish 1 sharpens at 2.5 cm, dish 2 at 30 cm, dish 3 never sharpens. Write your three entry-form answers (with computed R where possible) and the honest note for dish 3. (c) The stall-keeper objects: "dish 1's focus is too close to read accurately with a school scale — does the win still count?" Answer with the practical remedy.

A car's convex wing mirror carries the moulded marking "R = 30 cm" (a simplified label). (a) Compute the labeled mirror's focal length and state its position and character (real/virtual). (b) Explain in two sentences why traffic mirrors are made convex with long-ish R rather than concave — name what the driver needs and which focus behaviour would sabotage it. (c) The label's R is the parent sphere's radius; state what doubling or halving it would do to the view, and name the direction a designer would go to widen the view further. (d) State the one everyday convex-mirror fact that proves no paper test is ever run on traffic mirrors.

Two teams measure the SAME katori and report different R: Team 1 says 22 cm, Team 2 says 28 cm. (a) Name the two most likely procedural causes of a 6 cm disagreement in the window method. (b) State the refined protocol (three clauses) that removes each cause. (c) If both teams' refined readings settle at f = 12.0 cm, write the final R with the relation shown. (d) The katori's maker specifies R = 24 cm. Judge the teams' refined result against the specification and name the agreement quality this class practical should be graded on.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define radius of curvature and state its relation to focal length. (1½) (b) A concave mirror produces a sharp image of a far-away tree on a screen held 11 cm from its pole. Find f and R. (1½) (c) Another mirror has R = 50 cm: compute f and state whether it could have produced the same 11 cm reading, with the reason. (2) (d) A convex mirror has f = 8 cm: compute R and state the positions of F and C relative to the reflecting face. (2) (e) Describe in two sentences how the class verifies f = R/2 for the mirror in (b) by construction with compass and scale. (2) (f) A student reports measuring a convex mirror's f by the window method as 6 cm. Give the verdict with the physical reason. (1)

In the coming activity, a ray will strike a glass surface at 35° to the surface. (a) Convert this to the angle from the normal, showing the arithmetic. (b) State why the activities insist on normals rather than surface angles. (c) A student records "angle of incidence = 35°" from this setup. Diagnose the error, correct the entry, and state which previous-learning habit would have prevented it.

The bridge rehearsal drill: (a) Convert to normal angles: a ray at 20° to the surface; a ray at 62° to the surface. (b) Convert R to f and f to R: R = 26 cm; f = 7.5 cm. (c) State the normal-incidence exception that the drill must not let the class forget, and give the refraction behaviour in that case.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) State the law of reflection used as previous learning in this chapter. (1) (b) A ray strikes a plane mirror at 40° to the mirror's surface. Calculate the angle of reflection, showing the conversion. (1½) (c) State how the corresponding angles behave when the same ray passes INTO water instead, and name the rule. (1½) (d) State one respect in which the reflection and refraction behaviours are alike, as the bridge's table records. (1)

A colleague proposes deleting the bridge period and "revising during the activity whenever needed". Audit the proposal: (a) name the two activity moments where a mid-activity revision halts the whole bench, and why pairs cannot absorb them; (b) the colleague concedes angles but asks why the straight-line belief needs re-arming — after all, "no one disbelieves it". Answer with the prediction-sheet logic; (c) state the compromise the colleague would accept: the single 90-second element of the bridge that must never be cut, with its reason.

The bridge wall-chart must carry a "wrong turns" panel: the four most common errors students bring from previous learning into the refraction activities, each with its origin and its on-the-spot correction. Write the four entries — (1) the surface-angle habit, (2) the reflected-everywhere habit, (3) the "bends because water pushes" folk physics, (4) the inversion habit in R = 2f.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) A ray strikes a water surface at 25° to the surface. Calculate its angle of incidence. (1) (b) State what happens to this ray on entering the water — towards or away from the normal — with the rule. (1½) (c) State the angle relation for the small part of the same ray that reflects at the surface, with the law's name. (1½) (d) The class prediction sheet asks, for the bent pencil, one entry in each of its three columns. Write the model entries. (3) (e) Explain in two sentences why the eye sees the underwater pencil displaced, using the straight-line belief. (2) (f) A classmate records "angle of refraction = 65°" for part (b) and calls it "bending away from the normal". Verify or correct the entry with arithmetic. (1)

Design the pair-rotation chart for a class of 8 pairs running three activities (bent pencil, coin-in-tumbler, glass-slab-over-arrows preview). (a) State the swap schedule and how the chart guarantees every student operates at least once and observes at least once. (b) State the complementary-readiness pairing rule with one example pairing from the bridge's shelf results. (c) One pair finishes early and starts admiring their reflection in the tumbler. Write the protocol-legal redirection that converts their free minutes into sanctioned physics.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) In a paired experiment on refraction at a water surface, name the quantity the observer records and the two columns filled before the apparatus is touched. (1) (b) An operator pours water to the marked line while the observer times the settling of the surface. State why the observation is recorded BEFORE any explanation is attempted. (1) (c) A student's entry reads: "The light refracted because the medium changed." Convert it to a lawful observation entry. (1) (d) State one duty of each role that cross-checks the other, and why the record is signed by both. (2)

Two pairs reach different verdicts on the same activity. Pair 1's record: empty-tumbler control entry, pour to mark, apparent-bend entry, amended rule, both signatures. Pair 2's record: one sentence — "the pencil bent when we poured water; refraction." (a) State which record can survive cross-pair comparison at the board meeting, and why the other cannot. (b) The teacher proposes a "record minimum standard" of four clauses. Write them. (c) Pair 2 protests: "our physics was right!" Adjudicate with the evidence clause.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) In a paired experiment, state the two columns completed before the apparatus is touched and the language in which observations must be recorded. (1) (b) A pair's margin note reads: "Disagreement: A expects appearance (surface re-routes light); B expects hiding (straight-line law)." The coin appears. State which prediction is confirmed and what becomes of B's law, with the amendment's wording. (2) (c) State why the record is signed by both partners. (1) (d) Convert to camera-language: "The beam bent towards the normal because glass is denser." (1) (e) The SWAP rule made a reluctant student operate. State the failure the rule prevents and the product the class gains. (2) (f) A pair proposes recording on one shared sheet "since we agree on everything". Rule on the proposal with the two-clause reasoning. (2)

In the beam-tracing activity, a group records these two lines: "Entry point at the marked dot on the near face; exit point at the dot on the far face; the straight line joining entry to exit passes under the slab." (a) State what geometry this line already establishes about the ray's path under the slab. (b) The Measurer adds: "entry dot at 30° from the normal at the near face; the exit dot lies on the line at 30° from the normal at the far face." State what the two equal readings suggest and what the group CANNOT yet claim. (c) Write the EXPLAIN-stage entry that states the pattern without overclaiming.

Design the evidence-pool board for four teams after the beam-tracing activity. (a) State the board's three columns and what each holds. (b) Two teams report 30°-30°, one reports 30°-31°, one reports 28°-28°. Write the pooling entry the class adopts, distinguishing reading error from contradiction. (c) State the one question the teacher asks that converts the pool from a table into a pattern, and the answer the class should give.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) In a group of four running a refraction activity, name the role that quotes the angles and the line the angles must be quoted against. (1) (b) State TWO advantages group work has over pair work in this chapter's activity strand. (1) (c) A group claims "light always emerges parallel from a glass slab" after one trial at one angle. State what is missing before the claim can be written as a rule. (1) (d) State the mechanism that prevents a "passenger" student in a group of four, and name what a group with an unfilled role cell cannot do. (2)

A school inspector watches the pool and asks: "If four teams agree, why is that better than one team being right?" Write the group's three-part answer: (1) independence (what must differ across teams for agreement to mean anything); (2) error-width (what agreement within ±1° shows that a single 30° cannot); (3) the fourth team's role (what a disagreement contributes to the same pool). Then state the inspector's strongest possible counter and the class's reply.

The beam-tracing protocol requires dots to be fixed where the ray actually crosses each face. (a) State why the dot's position is the measurement's foundation, using the normal's dependence on it. (b) A dot is fixed by eye 4 mm from the true crossing point; the face-point is 6 cm from the sheet's edge and the reading claims 30° from the normal. Estimate the reading's error and state whether the pool's ±1° width absorbs it. (c) State the two fixes the protocol prescribes for dot-fixing precision.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Name the role responsible for keeping the protocol sequence in a group of four. (½) (b) State the two entries the Recorder is forbidden to write, with the stage where each belongs instead. (1½) (c) Four teams read 30-30, 30-31, 28-28, 32-26 degrees (entry/exit, from the respective normals). Classify each reading-pair as error-width, in-pattern, or construction-fault, with the criterion. (2) (d) State the three clauses of the board form used at the evidence pool. (1½) (e) A group writes "light always emerges parallel" after one trial. State the level-of-claim fault and the lawful wording for this stage. (2) (f) The tick cells show Meera has held Coordinator twice and Observer never. State what the chart prescribes and why. (2)

(a) Explain why the normal at the pole of a spherical mirror is the principal axis itself, and why the normal at any other point of the mirror is the radius through that point. (b) A ray strikes the pole making 25° with the principal axis. State the angle of reflection, the direction of the reflected ray, and the angle between the incident and reflected rays. (c) State why the reflected ray is drawn solid while a line drawn from the point of incidence through F behind a convex mirror is drawn dashed.

A student's concave-mirror diagram is described as follows: the arc is drawn with hatching on the hollow (inner) side; F is marked 8 cm in front of P; C is marked 4 cm in front of P (beyond F); a parallel incident ray reflects along a line drawn solid, passing through C; and one reflected ray continues as a solid line 2 cm behind the mirror. (a) Identify each fault and state the convention each violates. (b) State the corrected specifications for R = 24 cm. (c) Which single fault would most mislead a reader about the mirror's identity, and why?

Draw (as a specification, step by step) the complete concave-mirror skeleton for R = 30 cm at the scale 1 cm on paper = 5 cm actual. State every measured distance on paper, the compass setting for the arc, and on which side of the arc the hatching falls if light comes from the left.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) State what serves as the normal at the pole of a spherical mirror. (½) (b) Copy and complete: a ray parallel to the principal axis, after reflection from a concave mirror, passes through ______; after reflection from a convex mirror, it appears to diverge from ______. (1) (c) A student draws a reflected ray continuing 3 cm BEHIND a convex mirror as a solid line. Name the fault and state the rule violated. (1) (d) For a convex mirror of radius of curvature 30 cm, state the distance of F from P, the side of the mirror on which F and C lie, and how they are drawn. (1½)

A torch has a concave-metal reflector with its small bulb placed exactly at the principal focus F. (a) Represent the reflector as a diagram and use the standard rays to show what the beam leaving the torch is like, naming the rule and the principle that carry the argument. (b) The bulb slips and sits 1 cm in front of F (towards the mirror). State, from the diagram rules, what changes about the beam. (c) Separately, a calibration ray strikes the reflector's pole making 25° with the axis: compute the angle between the incident and reflected rays, with working.

A scooter's rear-view mirror is a convex mirror. (a) Represent it as a diagram and draw TWO rays arriving parallel to the axis (one above, one below) showing their reflected paths and all constructions, with every line's status named. (b) From your figure, state why the driver's eye — placed near the axis — receives light from a WIDE fan of directions behind, which is the mirror's whole point. (c) The mirror's R = 40 cm: state f, and where F sits in the figure.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State what serves as the normal at the pole of a concave mirror. (½) (b) A convex mirror has f = 12 cm. State PC and PF with their sides, and the style of each mark. (1½) (c) Draw (as a labelled specification) the complete figure for the mirror in (b) showing standard ray one for a parallel ray 2 cm above the axis at scale 1 cm = 4 cm. (2) (d) State the rule that lets the SAME figure be used for a ray LEAVING the focus, and name the principle behind the rule. (1½) (e) A drawn figure shows a concave mirror with the parallel ray reflected through a point midway between F and C. Name the fault, the convention violated, and the corrected line. (2) (f) State TWO differences between the drawings of a real focus and a virtual focus. (2)

(a) Show, step by step, why the emergent ray from a parallel-faced slab is parallel to the incident ray. (b) A student says: "if the ray comes out parallel, the slab did nothing at all." State what the slab DID do, with the two bendings and their sites. (c) State what happens to a ray that strikes the slab at 0° (square on), and why.

A student's slab-tracing figure is described: "entry ray drawn meeting the slab and bending AWAY from the entry normal inside the glass; the inside ray drawn as a gentle curve; at the exit face the ray bends towards the normal and leaves at 30° when the entry incidence was 45°." (a) Identify each of the four faults and the rule each violates. (b) State the corrected inside angle and exit angle if the true inside reading is 28°. (c) Which fault would most damage the measured lateral shift, and why?

A tracing gives these readings: angle of incidence at the entry face, 45° from the entry normal; the ray inside the glass at 28° from the entry normal. (a) Compute the ray's angle with the exit normal inside the glass, with justification. (b) Compute the exit angle and state the direction of each bending with the rule named. (c) The measured lateral shift is 3 mm for a slab 12 mm thick. Predict, with reasons, the shift for (i) a 24 mm slab of the same glass at the same incidence, (ii) the same 12 mm slab at a smaller incidence of 20°.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) State what happens to a ray of light when it enters a glass slab obliquely, and when it leaves it. (1) (b) Define lateral displacement. (1) (c) A ray emerges from a slab travelling in a direction 5° off its incidence direction. State what this reading indicates about the slab's faces. (1) (d) State TWO changes that increase the lateral displacement produced by a given glass slab. (2)

Your bench must measure how the lateral shift depends on the incidence angle, using one slab. (a) Design the series: the angles to use, what is held fixed, and what is measured each trial. (b) Predict the shape of the result (shift versus angle) including the endpoint at 0°. (c) A partner wants to include a 75° trial "for drama". State the two practical objections from the bench's own apparatus and record rules.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State the direction rule for light entering glass obliquely. (½) (b) A ray inside a slab meets the exit face at 30° from the exit normal. The entry incidence was 45°. State the exit angle and show the step that licenses it. (1½) (c) For the same slab: state what change in the slab would increase the lateral shift without touching the angles, and what change in the RAY would do so. (2) (d) The emergent ray is measured 2 mm from the incident line along a slant at 60° to the lines. Convert to the lawful shift figure. (1½) (e) State why a student who draws the bend once, mid-slab, will also inevitably misquote the inside angle. (2) (f) Complete the record line: "At ______° incidence, the ray inside ran at ______° from the normal at the ______ face; it left at ______° from the normal at the ______ face, ______ to the incident ray, displaced ______ mm ______ between the incident and emergent lines." (2)
What is the primary reason a laser pencil is preferred over a torch for ray‑tracing experiments in Class 8?
A student shines a laser pencil at a glass slab at an angle of incidence of 30°. The measured angle of refraction inside the glass is 19°. Calculate the refractive index of glass relative to air.

During the activity, the emergent ray from the glass slab is displaced laterally by 2.3 cm. If the slab thickness is 5 cm and the angle of incidence is 40°, evaluate whether this displacement is consistent with the refractive index found in Question 2 (n ≈ 1.54).

A student uses a laser pencil to trace a ray through a water‑filled tumbler (refractive index 1.33). The angle of incidence in air is 45°. Compute the angle of refraction in water and the lateral displacement if the water depth is 10 cm.

In a CISCE‑style question, a diagram shows a laser pencil beam entering a glass slab at 35° to the normal and emerging parallel to the incident ray but displaced. The slab thickness is 6 cm and the refractive index is 1.5. Calculate the lateral displacement of the emergent ray.

A student argues that a laser pencil can be used to determine the focal length of a concave mirror by reflecting the beam off the mirror and measuring the distance to the focal spot. Critique this method for a Class 8 lab.
Compare the use of a laser pencil versus a ray box (multiple slits) for demonstrating refraction through a glass slab in a Class 8 classroom.

A past CISCE paper asks: “A laser beam is incident on a rectangular glass slab of thickness 5 cm at an angle of 30°. The refractive index of glass is 1.5. Calculate the lateral displacement of the emergent ray.” Provide the full solution as expected in the exam.

A laser pencil emits a beam of 1 mm diameter with a divergence of 0.5 mrad. The beam travels 50 cm before hitting a white sheet of paper. Calculate the approximate diameter of the laser spot on the paper.

A ray from the pencil's immersed tip strikes the water surface at 40° from the normal and refracts into the air at 55° from the normal. (a) Verify that this refraction is lawful and name the rule it follows. (b) By how many degrees does the ray's direction change at the surface? (c) The eye receives this ray and back-projects it straight. State where the tip's apparent position lies relative to its true position, and why. (d) State what the ray does between the tip and the surface.

The comparative pour is run at two levels with these described readings: at 40 ml, the immersed part (about 6 cm of shaft) appears slightly raised and kinked; at 80 ml (about 11 cm immersed), the kink is plainly visible and the raised part seems longer. The tumbler and pencil are unmoved; the eye was at the same side position. (a) State the one variable of this comparison and why the rest had to be pinned. (b) Explain why the kink grows with the level, using the four-link chain. (c) The Operator reports: "I let the pencil float free for both readings — it stood upright anyway." Rule on the report.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) A pencil standing in a tumbler of water appears bent at the water surface. Name the phenomenon responsible and state the rule the light follows at the surface. (1) (b) State why the pencil's straightness matters to the demonstration. (1) (c) A wooden pencil released in the tumbler floats. State what this shows about its density and what the Operator must therefore do. (1) (d) State TWO rules the pencil obeys as the record instrument on a tracing sheet. (2)

The pencil's kink appears exactly at the water-surface line — not above it, not below it. (a) State why the kink's position is fixed at the surface, using the four-link chain. (b) The tumbler is filled to the brim so the surface sits 2 cm higher: state where the kink now appears and what stays fixed. (c) A student proposes oil floating on the water (two liquid layers) and predicts "two kinks". Rule on the prediction with the chain.

Assemble the mark-quality audit for the pencil's instrument costume: for each of four marks — a 0.5 mm sharp dot, a 2 mm blob, a single ruled thin line, a line drawn twice — state (a) the position-uncertainty it carries, (b) its effect on any angle quoted from it, and (c) the one-word verdict (LAWFUL or FAULTY). Then state the single principle that generates all four verdicts, and what the audit says about pressing pressure.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State the rule followed by light passing from water into air. (½) (b) A ray from an immersed point meets the surface at 35° from the normal and refracts at 48°. Compute the direction change and state the apparent effect at the eye. (1½) (c) State why the kink in the pencil's image sits exactly at the surface line. (1½) (d) The pour's record must name three data besides the observation itself. State them. (1½) (e) A sheet carries a 3 mm blob dot at the exit point and an exit angle of 31° quoted from it. State what the angle's honest description is, and the lawful repair. (2) (f) Complete the discipline sentence: "The pencil is trusted twice — as the object because its ______ is beyond doubt, and as the pen because its ______ can be ______ by every reader." (2½)

(a) State the scale's two costumes and the one-line rule for each. (b) List the four clauses of a lawful reading. (c) Convert and quote: a paper distance measures 34 mm on a drawing made at 1 cm : 5 cm. Write the lawful record line.

A student measures the lateral shift of a slab tracing as follows: holds the scale slantwise across the gap between the incident and emergent lines because "the gap is wider there", reads 6 mm at an oblique eye, and writes "shift = 6" on the sheet. (a) State each fault against its clause. (b) State the lawful measurement and the lawful record line. (c) State why "6" is worse than no entry at all.

A mirror skeleton was drawn at 1 cm : 5 cm. Measured on the paper: PF = 30 mm, PC = 62 mm. (a) Convert both to actual distances and quote them lawfully. (b) The figure claims f = R/2. Check it from your measurements and state the verdict with the honest wording. (c) State which clause of the reading discipline makes this check meaningful, and what the verdict would be worth if the two paper measurements had been taken by different students at different eye angles.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) State the measurement the lateral shift requires, and the direction in which the scale must lie. (1) (b) A reading falls between two 1 mm divisions. State what the reader writes. (1) (c) State TWO faults that make a quoted length untrustworthy. (2)

The datum clause says a length must be quoted against its defining reference. (a) State the defining reference for each of: the lateral shift, the slab's thickness, a mirror skeleton's PF. (b) A student measures the slab thickness "across a corner" — diagonally from a top-face edge to the opposite bottom-face edge — and quotes 13.2 mm for a 12.0 mm slab. State what the 13.2 measures, and the minimum repair. (c) State why the datum clause and the perpendicular clause are one clause in two costumes.

A bench must measure the shift for five trials at increasing incidence angles, and the Measurer proposes reading all five shifts "at the widest visible gap" for speed, then halving them all "since slants read about double". (a) Rule on the proposal clause by clause. (b) State the lawful fast protocol that respects the Measurer's time concern. (c) The five lawful readings come out 0.0, 1.5, 2.5, 4.5, 6.0 mm for angles 0°, 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°. State what the series shows, quoting the endpoint with its special status.

The school workshop cuts a new glass slab for the class, and the sheet from the workshop says only "THICKNESS: 10 mm". (a) State what the class must do before the slab is trusted for measurements, and write the two record lines the check produces. (b) The workshop's value proves to be the corner-diagonal (11.2 mm for a 10.0 mm slab). State what this reveals about the workshop's datum and the clause it violated. (c) State the certification sentence the class writes on the slab's seat card.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State the two costumes of the bench scale. (½) (b) A shift reading falls between the 3 mm and 4 mm divisions, nearer 3. Write the lawful record line. (1½) (c) A skeleton drawn at 1 cm : 4 cm has paper PF = 20 mm. State the actual f, showing the written conversion. (1½) (d) The zero edge of a scale is chipped. State the lawful reading method and its record form. (1½) (e) A student reads the shift at a slant as 6 mm and writes "≈ 4.5 mm after correction". State the two faults and the one lawful action. (2) (f) Complete: "A length becomes a measurement when it carries its ______, its ______, its ______ and its declared ______." (2) (g) State why the scale is not used to read the angle between the incident ray and the normal. (1½)
What is the primary function of an eraser in a Class 8 Physics optics activity?
A student draws an incident ray at 30° to the normal on a white sheet, then realises the angle should be 40°. Describe the correct steps to correct the diagram using an eraser and scale.
Design a simple checklist a Class 8 student could use before starting a refraction experiment to ensure their drawing tools (pencil, scale, eraser, white sheet) are ready.

In a CISCE ICSE Class 8 practical exam, a student is asked to “draw the path of a ray through a glass slab.” The student’s diagram shows smudged lines and multiple overlapping rays. Which tool misuse most likely caused this, and how should it be corrected?
A past CISCE ICSE Class 8 practical paper asks: “State one precaution to be taken while using an eraser during a ray‑diagram experiment.” Provide a model answer.

(a) State why the free surface must be FLAT for the pencil's kink to form as one clean line. (b) State what a brim-full tumbler does to the demonstration, and why the brim rule exists. (c) The tumbler is filled to the 80 ml mark but sits on a folded cloth; the bench under one side is 3 mm lower. State what happens to the surface and to the kink, with the reason.

The pour runs 40 ml mark to 80 ml mark. (a) Compute the water added and write the two level data lawfully. (b) State what changes optically between the two levels and what must NOT change. (c) The supply bottle's mouth is wider than the tumbler's — pouring splashes the record area. State the two lawful responses.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Name the two media whose boundary is the working surface of the pencil-in-tumbler demonstration, and state which is denser. (1) (b) State the datum against which a water level is quoted. (½) (c) State why the free surface is always flat and horizontal, and what this guarantees for the demonstration. (1½) (d) A student wipes the sweating outer wall with a cloth and the view of the pencil blurs into moving streaks. State what happened and the lawful alternative. (1)

The tumbler is to be filled for the deepest lawful demonstration. (a) State the highest lawful fill and the reason it stops short of the brim. (b) The tumbler's highest printed mark is 200 ml and the brim is ~20 mm above it. A student proposes filling to the halfway point between mark and brim "for a longer pencil immersion". Rule on the proposal with the datum clause. (c) State the two gains the demonstration actually gets from a higher level, and the one gain it does NOT get.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State which is denser: air or water — and name the rule that governs light crossing between them. (½) (b) A pour runs from the 50 ml mark to the 150 ml mark. State the water added, written lawfully. (1) (c) State why the free surface is level even on a tilted bench, and what must then be read with care. (1½) (d) The demonstration's kink is claimed; the through-the-wall widening is parked. State the difference between the two claims' status in one sentence each. (2) (e) A visitor fills the tumbler to the brim "so nothing more can spill". State the two failures this causes and the lawful maximum. (2) (f) Complete the seat card's clause: "The wall is ______, never ______; the level is a ______, never a guess; the record area stays ______." (1½) (g) State the one sentence in which the tumbler-water apparatus earns its place as the chapter's final node. (1½)

(a) Explain, using the behaviour of molecules, why evaporation causes cooling. (b) Explain why the temperature of boiling water stays at 100 °C even over a fierce flame. (c) A wet handkerchief placed on the forehead of a person with fever brings relief. Explain with the mechanism in (a).

(a) An electric kettle raises the water's temperature by 6 °C every minute. The water starts at 24 °C. Compute the time to reach the boiling point, and state the temperature 3 minutes after that. (b) Two identical wet handkerchiefs are drying in the same room: one is folded to a quarter of its area, one is spread full. State which dries faster and the factor, with the lever named. (c) State the four factors that quicken evaporation.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Define boiling point. (1) (b) State TWO differences between evaporation and boiling. (1) (c) Why does evaporation cause cooling? (1½) (d) Give one everyday example each of evaporation and of boiling, naming the clause of the definition each example displays. (1½)

A covered pot of water and an open pot of the same water sit on the same warm shelf. After a day, the open pot has lost 50 ml; the covered pot has lost nothing measurable, but a farmer claims "the covered pot is evaporating too — its vapour just stays inside". (a) Rule on the claim with the molecular picture: what happens INSIDE the covered pot? (b) State what the closed space reaches, and why the net loss is zero. (c) The farmer then says "so a matka's pores are a mistake — they let the water escape". Rule on this second claim, with the matka's design purpose.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Define boiling point of a liquid. (1) (b) Water at 96 °C in a beaker: state which of the two processes can occur and where. (1) (c) A student says: "wet clothes dry faster if we spread them because they get more sun." Re-write the claim lawfully with the correct lever. (1½) (d) Explain why you feel cool after a swim even on a hot day, and why the feeling is stronger in wind. (2) (e) Two pots of water on identical flames: a wide shallow kadhai and a tall narrow patila, each holding one litre at 30 °C. State which reaches the boil first, with the two rates at work. (2½) (f) State one observation in a kitchen that shows the plateau (constant temperature during boiling) WITHOUT a thermometer. (1)
Calculate the increase in length of a 10 m steel rail when the temperature rises from 20 °C to 40 °C. (α_steel = 1.2×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹)
A 2 m aluminium rod (α = 23×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) is heated from 15 °C to 35 °C. Find the change in length.
Calculate the increase in length of a 1.5 m copper rod (α = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ °C⁻¹) when heated from 25 °C to 75 °C.
A steel bridge is 200 m long at 10 °C. If the temperature rises to 35 °C, find the change in length. (α_steel = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ °C⁻¹). Show all steps.
A metal rod of length 2 m expands by 2.4 mm when heated through 60 °C. Calculate its coefficient of linear expansion.
In an experiment, 50 g of water at 100 °C is converted to steam at 100 °C. Calculate the heat supplied. (Latent heat of vaporization = 2260 J/g)
Compare the energy required for boiling 100 g of water at 100 °C versus evaporating 100 g of water at 25 °C. (Latent heat at 100 °C = 2260 J/g, at 25 °C ≈ 2440 J/g)
A beaker contains 200 g of water at 80 °C. It is left to cool to 20 °C. Calculate the heat lost. (Specific heat of water = 4.2 J/g°C)

(a) Compute the maximum water for boiling in a 250 ml flask under the one-third clause. (b) The flask's base is 8 cm across (area ≈ 50 cm²) and its neck opening is 2 cm across (area ≈ 3 cm²). Estimate how many times slower the water level falls by evaporation through the neck than it would from an open base-sized surface, and name the lever. (c) State why the evenness of the wall thickness matters as much as the thinness.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Why is the flask used — and not a metal pot — for the class boiling demonstration? (1) (b) State TWO precautions while heating water in a flask. (1) (c) A 300 ml conical flask is used for boiling. State the maximum volume of water it may hold for the task. (1) (d) Why does a flask of water lose less water overnight than an open basin of the same water? (1)

A flask task must show, in one session: (1) bubbles forming in the bulk; (2) that the temperature holds at the boiling point; (3) that steam carries the water away. (a) State what the flask setup needs for each of the three shows. (b) State which show the NECK threatens and how the setup manages the threat. (c) State the show that needs the clock, and write its two lawful time readings.

The school's flask kit shrank: only a 100 ml flask and a 500 ml flask remain, and the class of five groups must each run the 10-minute boiling watch. (a) Assign flasks to groups with the fill arithmetic shown for each. (b) Two groups must share one mount: state the lawful sharing protocol (three steps). (c) The 500 ml flask's base is cracked at one edge — state the certification decision and the honest record line.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Name the flask feature that lets boiling be identified as a bulk phenomenon. (½) (b) A 360 ml flask: state its lawful boil-fill with the rule. (1) (c) State two reasons the flask sits on wire gauze and not directly in the flame. (1½) (d) A stoppered flask with a delivery tube is heated; the tube's end is under water in a beaker. State the event that threatens when the flame goes out, with the mechanism. (2) (e) State why the neck's small opening is a benefit during heating but a drawback when filling and cleaning. (2) (f) Complete: "The flask is heated only with ______ and ______ inside, moved only by ______, and refilled only when ______." (1½) (g) State one observation through the flask wall that proves the water is boiling and not merely hot. (1½)

A mount is described: the mesh rests on the tripod's ring but one edge is bent down 5 mm; the burner stands 10 cm off to one side because "the flame reaches anyway"; the flask sits centred. (a) Identify each fault with its clause. (b) State what the off-centre flame does to the mesh's delivery at the flask's base. (c) Rewrite the mount as a three-line lawful specification.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) State the purpose of the wire gauze used while heating a flask. (1) (b) Why does a tripod stand have three legs? (1) (c) State where the burner is placed relative to the mesh, and why. (1) (d) State ONE precaution while handling the tripod and mesh after heating. (1)

The mesh's spread clause has a quantitative heart: the flame delivers its heat through a tip-region of about 1 cm², and the mesh delivers it over a flask base of about 50 cm². (a) Compute the spread factor and state what it means for the heat delivered per cm² of glass. (b) State why the ceramic centre matters most at the START of heating. (c) A student argues "the wires alone would do — the centre is decoration". Rule with the two materials' roles.

The mount must serve two sessions back-to-back with no cool-down time between: Session 1 boils water in the flask; Session 2 is a junior class's demonstration. (a) State what the mount's clauses forbid about back-to-back use, and what they permit. (b) Design the handover protocol: five steps with the clause each protects. (c) The junior teacher proposes "we will just use the mesh from Session 1 hot — it saves five minutes." Rule on the proposal with the clause and the real cost.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Name the two pieces of the mount on which a flask is heated. (½) (b) State the wire gauze's purpose in one sentence. (1) (c) A burner stands 6 cm off the mesh's centre with the flask centred: state which region of the flask's base runs hotter and why. (1½) (d) State why the tripod's legs are iron and the mesh's centre is ceramic — one reason each. (2) (e) The flame is off and the bench is being cleared. A student picks up the mesh by its centre with bare fingers. State the outcome, the clause broken, and the lawful handling. (2) (f) Complete: "Heat is received at a ______ and delivered as a ______; the flask, the mesh and the flame share one ______." (1½) (g) State one observation during the boil that tells you the axis has drifted mid-session. (1½)

**CISCE exam style:** (a) State the use of the air hole in a Bunsen burner. (1) (b) Name the hottest region of a non-luminous flame. (1) (c) State TWO differences between a luminous and a non-luminous flame. (1) (d) Why should a burner be turned off at the tap and not by folding the rubber tube? (1)

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Name the part of the Bunsen burner that regulates the air supply. (½) (b) State the colour and one other property of a non-luminous flame. (1) (c) The flame of a properly set burner shows a light blue cone: state where the temperature is greatest and where the gas is unburnt. (1½) (d) A burner's flame strikes back: state TWO signs the student would notice and the FIRST corrective action. (2) (e) State why a luminous flame blackens a heating vessel, and what that blackening costs the heating itself. (2) (f) Complete the lighting order: "Strike the ______ first; hold it at the top of the ______; then turn on the ______; finally set the ______." (1) (g) State the one check that tells you, from across the room, that a burner is burning at the jet inside the barrel. (1½)

**CISCE exam style:** (a) State the boiling point of pure water at normal atmospheric pressure. (½) (b) State TWO properties of water that make it suitable as the heating liquid in school demonstrations. (1) (c) Why should the flask be no more than two-thirds full for the boiling demonstration? (1) (d) Name the process by which droplets form on the cooler inner walls of the flask during heating, and the process that put the vapour there. (1½)

The sister school in the hills reports its watch plateauing at 94°C; the city school's plateau is 100°C. The hill teacher wants to "fix the water" by adding salt. (a) Rule on the fix: what salt actually does to the boiling point and why it cannot repair the 6-degree gap. (2) (b) State the true lever for the plateau value and its two everyday demonstrations (one in each direction). (2) (c) Write the hill school's corrected record line, and state why the 94°C plateau is BETTER teaching than a broken-instrument cover-up. (3)

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) State the boiling point of pure water at normal atmospheric pressure. (½) (b) State TWO reasons water is chosen as the working substance for the boiling watch. (1) (c) A student heating water sees small bubbles clinging to the inner walls at 65°C: state what they are and whether the water is boiling. (1½) (d) During the watch, droplets form on the cooler upper walls: name the two processes involved and state where the vapour came from. (1½) (e) Give TWO reasons the flask is not filled to the brim. (1) (f) Complete the clause: "Pour cold water only into a ______ flask; fill to about ______ of its capacity." (1) (g) A hill-station school records a steady plateau at 94°C: state the reason and name the kitchen device that pushes the boiling point the other way. (2) (h) State why a steam scald is more severe than a scald by boiling water at the same temperature. (1½)

A setup uses a roller of radius 4 mm touched by the bar 1 mm from the pivot, and a pointer 20 cm long. During three minutes of heating the pointer tip sweeps 10 mm across the card. (a) Show that the bar's extension is about 0.2 mm, with the full working. (b) State the amplification factor and why the setup needs it. (c) The unamplified truth: state what the class would see at the bar's free end with bare eyes, and why the demonstration still counts as measurement, not trickery.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Name the demonstration that shows a solid expands on heating along its length, and name its amplifying part. (1) (b) State what is observed when a heated ball is placed on a ring at room temperature. (1) (c) A metal ring is heated and a cold ball that previously just passed through is now placed on it: state the observation and the inference. (2)

The bar-and-pointer setup's far end may rest on a knife EDGE pivoting the pointer, instead of a roller. (a) State what the two variants share — the single geometric idea that makes both work. (b) The pivot-to-touch distance is 2 mm and the pointer is 30 cm: compute the factor and the swing for 0.4 mm of growth. (c) State the one way the long thin pointer BETRAYS the demonstration if made carelessly (too heavy or too whippy), and the two properties the ideal pointer needs.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Name the experiment that demonstrates the expansion of a metal along its length on heating. (½) (b) In that experiment, state the work of the long pointer. (1) (c) A ball passes through a ring when both are cold. The ring alone is now heated. State the observation and the conclusion. (1½) (d) State why the flame is moved along the bar's length instead of being held at one point. (1) (e) A setup's pointer swings 24 mm; its amplification factor is 40. Calculate the bar's extension. (1) (f) Complete: "One end of the bar is held against a fixed ______ so that expansion is directed along its length; on cooling the pointer returns, showing that the bar ______." (1) (g) State ONE everyday observation that shows a metal hole or rim expands on heating. (1½) (h) A student heats the bar for a minute and sees no pointer motion: state the TWO most likely mechanical causes and the first check for each. (2)
A steel rail of length 12 m at 20 °C is heated to 45 °C. Given α_steel = 12×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹, calculate the increase in length.
In a CISCE ICSE exam, a question shows a graph of length vs temperature for a metal rod, which is a straight line passing through (0 °C, 1.000 m) and (100 °C, 1.0012 m). Determine α for the metal.
An overhead power line made of aluminium (α = 23×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) is 200 m long at 15 °C. If the temperature rises to 40 °C, how much longer does the line become?
Compare the fractional volume change of 1 L of mercury (γ = 180×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) and 1 L of air (γ ≈ 3400×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) for a 30 K temperature rise.
A past ICSE paper asks: “A metal rod of length 50 cm at 0 °C expands to 50.06 cm at 100 °C. Calculate its linear expansivity.”

(a) Define vibration, frequency, and time period, with units. (b) State the relation between frequency and time period, and use it both ways: find f when T = 0.004 s, and find T when f = 250 Hz. (c) State the pitch-frequency rule in one line.

A mosquito's wings vibrate about 550 times per second; a housefly's about 200 times per second; a honeybee's about 250 times per second. (a) Arrange the three insects' hums from deepest to shrillest, with the rule used. (b) State each insect's time period for the mosquito's value only (T = 1/f, to three decimal places). (c) The bee and the fly sound confusingly similar on a hot afternoon: state which is slightly shriller and by how many vibrations per second they differ.

A pet shop sells a "silent dog whistle" that blows a note at about 25,000 Hz (25 kHz). (a) State why a human hears nothing from it, using the audible range. (b) State why the dog responds. (c) A student proposes testing the whistle by blowing it in class: state what the class would and would not perceive, and the one sound-event in the room they should still watch for.

**CISCE exam style:** (a) Define frequency and state its unit. (1) (b) A tuning fork completes 1200 vibrations in 4 seconds. Calculate its frequency and its time period. (2) (c) State whether the note of a 512 Hz fork is of higher or lower pitch than that of a 256 Hz fork, with the reason. (1)

A fork's stamped frequency and its felt pitch are said to be "the cause and the heard effect". (a) State what a frequency counter would report for a 440 Hz fork and what the listener reports, in one line each. (b) Explain why physics keeps the two in separate chairs rather than defining pitch as frequency. (c) A listener with a cold reports the fork "sounds duller" though the counter still reads 440 Hz: state what this pair of readings demonstrates about the two chairs.

The school's corridor has three "voice clocks": the school bell (struck, about 500 Hz), the recess drum (about 150 Hz), and a mosquito in the stairwell (about 600 wingbeats per second). The corridor also has a forbidden dog whistle (22 kHz) someone has hung as a prank. (a) State which two sounds the corridor hears simultaneously at any moment and which one it never hears at all, with the range argument. (b) Arrange all four by pitch and state the deepest-to-shrillest span in kilohertz. (c) The prank is reported as "there is a sound driving the dogs mad in the corridor": state what is physically true in the report and what is wrong in the wording.

**CISCE past-paper pattern:** (a) Name the phenomenon that is the source of all sound. (½) (b) Define time period and write its relation with frequency. (1) (c) A body vibrates 4500 times in 9 seconds: calculate its frequency and time period. (1½) (d) State the approximate frequency range of hearing of the human ear, and classify 15 Hz and 25,000 Hz. (1½) (e) A mosquito's wings and a bee's wings beat at 550 Hz and 250 Hz respectively: state which produces the higher-pitched hum and why, and calculate the bee's time period. (2) (f) Complete: "The number of vibrations made in one second is called ______; its unit is ______; the time for one vibration is called ______." (1½) (g) A student says: "A sound of 100 Hz is twice as high-pitched as a sound of 50 Hz." State what is right and what is loosely wrong in this, and give the lawful sentence. (1½)

A sitar string of length 0.8 m, tension 80 N, and linear mass density 0.005 kg/m is plucked. If the length is shortened to 0.6 m while tension and mass density remain unchanged, what happens to the fundamental frequency?
A rubber band of length 0.30 m and linear mass density 0.002 kg/m is stretched with a tension of 10 N. Calculate its fundamental frequency. (Use f = (1/2L)√(T/μ))

A CISCE exam question: “A closed organ pipe of length 0.5 m produces a fundamental frequency of 170 Hz. If the speed of sound in air is 340 m/s, verify whether the pipe is indeed closed or open.” (Show calculation)

A past CISCE paper asks: “A stretched string of length 1 m and mass 0.01 kg is under a tension of 100 N. Calculate its fundamental frequency. If the length is reduced to 0.5 m by pressing a fret, what is the new fundamental frequency?” (Show all steps.)
If a sound wave has a frequency of 256 Hz and travels at 340 m/s, calculate its wavelength. Is this sound necessarily a monotone? Explain.
A musician uses a tuning fork of 440 Hz to tune a guitar string. Explain the principle behind this using the concept of monotone.
A sound wave is represented by the equation y = 0.02 sin(2π × 512 t). Identify the frequency and amplitude. State whether this wave represents a monotone. Justify.

A wave sketch shows Sound P with crests 3 mm above the rest line and 30 crests arriving each second; Sound Q shows crests 1 mm above the rest line and 90 crests arriving each second. Compare P and Q on pitch and loudness, and justify each comparison from the sketch numbers.

From a CISCE past-paper pattern: (i) Copy and complete: "The maximum displacement of a vibrating body from its ______ position is called its ______." (ii) The amplitude of a sound wave is increased from 0.5 mm to 2 mm. Calculate the factor by which its loudness increases. (iii) The same sound is then heard by a student who walks from 5 m to 20 m from the source. State, with reason, whether the calculation in (ii) still describes what this student notices.
