Compare the 7 Cs with the “KISS” principle (Keep It Short and Simple). Identify two similarities and two differences.
Write a short note on “Principles of Effective Communication” as per the ICSE Class 9 Commercial Studies syllabus.

Apply the channel‑richness decision rule: A startup founder must communicate a strategic pivot (high ambiguity, high emotional impact) to 15 employees working remotely. Choose the best primary channel and justify.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “A regional sales manager in Lucknow sends a quarterly target revision via a formal letter to 50 distributors across Uttar Pradesh. Only 60% meet the new target. Using the communication process, identify two barriers and suggest one specific strategy for each to improve compliance.” (4 marks)
Create a short policy guideline (3 bullet points) for using video‑conferencing in a mid‑size Indian firm.
CISCE exam‑style: “Explain how cloud‑based document collaboration supports the principle of ‘clarity’ in business communication.” (3 marks)

Application: A retail chain with 50 stores uses a shared Google Sheet for daily sales reporting. Store managers edit simultaneously. One manager accidentally deletes a column of GST‑taxable amounts. How does the tool’s version history mitigate this error, and what step should the admin take immediately?
CISCE past‑paper pattern: “State three advantages of using video‑conferencing for inter‑branch meetings in a banking organisation. (3 marks)”

Create a set of minutes for the agenda in Question 4, assuming the following decisions: (a) Project on track, (b) Critical bugs assigned to developers with 48‑hour deadline, (c) Two additional developers approved for next sprint.
Critique the following agenda item: “Discuss marketing — 30 min — All.” State why it is ineffective and rewrite it properly.

CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern: “Draft the minutes of a Board Meeting of XYZ Ltd. held on 15th July 2025 at 11:00 a.m. to consider and approve the annual budget for 2025‑26. The meeting was attended by all directors. The CFO presented the budget highlighting a 10% increase in marketing spend. After discussion, the budget was approved unanimously. The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chair.” (5 marks)
List the seven Cs of effective communication as prescribed in the ICSE Class 9 Commercial Studies syllabus.

Case Study: M/s Patel Electronics receives a written complaint from a dealer about defective goods. As the Sales Manager, draft a reply letter addressing the complaint, offering replacement, and assuring quality improvement. (10 marks)
Create a brief narrative showing how a transaction — purchasing goods worth ₹15,000 on credit from M/s Gupta & Co. — flows through the accounting cycle up to trial balance.

**APPLICATION:** A trader in Delhi records a sale of ₹25,000 on credit but forgets to post the entry to the debtor’s ledger. Describe the impact on the trial balance and on the financial statements if the error remains undetected.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “State the accounting equation. Explain how the double‑entry system ensures that the accounting equation remains balanced after every transaction.” (4 marks)
Journalise: (i) Bought goods on credit from Suresh ₹45,000; (ii) Sold goods for cash ₹28,000; (iii) Paid Suresh ₹25,000. Show account classification and rule applied for each.
Find the error: An entry records — "Furniture A/c Dr. 15,000; To Purchases A/c 15,000 (Being furniture bought for cash)". State two errors and the corrected entry.

Journalise as a compound entry: Purchased machinery for ₹80,000; paid carriage inward on it ₹2,000, installation charges ₹6,000; and, separately on the same day, paid factory rent ₹5,000 — all in cash. Justify the treatment of carriage and installation.

A trader's day: opened the business with cash ₹3,00,000; bought goods ₹70,000 for cash; sold half the goods for ₹55,000 cash; paid shop rent ₹10,000. Journalise all four and prove the day's debit total equals the credit total.

Application: A trader's 15th March: (i) received an order for goods worth ₹30,000 from Kavita; (ii) dispatched the goods to Kavita the same day; (iii) Kavita paid ₹30,000 by cheque on 20th March. Which of the three events are journalised, when, and with what entries? Justify the treatment of the event not journalised.

Evaluation: A proprietor argues: "My drawings — ₹25,000 this year for family expenses — should be debited to family welfare expenses, so my business shows genuine costs." Evaluate the accounting treatment he proposes and state the correct entry with its effect on capital.

Past-paper pattern: Read the case and answer. "A stationery trader's journal for the week shows: (1) Cash Dr 90,000; To Capital 90,000 — started business. (2) Purchases Dr 35,000; To Cash 35,000 — goods bought. (3) Furniture Dr 15,000; To Purchases 15,000 — old shop racks bought. (4) Cash Dr 40,000; To Sales 40,000 — cash sales. (5) Rent Dr 6,000; To Cash 6,000 — rent paid. (a) Identify the wrong entry and rewrite it. (b) State whether the week's totals would agree before the correction, and what this proves. (c) Journalise the corrected week's totals proof."
A student posts a journal entry debiting Cash ₹2,000 and crediting Sales ₹2,000, but in the ledger she credits Cash and debits Sales. Evaluate the impact on the trial balance.
Record the following transaction in the journal and post it to the ledger: “On 12 May, paid rent ₹4,500 by cheque.”

Create a ledger account for “M/s Sharma Traders” given these journal entries: 1) 3 Jun – Purchases from M/s Sharma Traders ₹7,000 (credit). 2) 10 Jun – Paid M/s Sharma Traders ₹3,000 by cheque. 3) 18 Jun – Returned goods to M/s Sharma Traders ₹1,000.
A firm records a transaction debiting Machinery ₹25,000 and crediting Cash ₹25,000. Later it discovers the payment was made by cheque. Evaluate the effect on the ledger if the entry is not corrected.
Apply the journal‑ledger process to this scenario: On 20 Sep, the proprietor withdrew ₹5,000 cash for personal use. Show journal entry, ledger postings, and the effect on the accounting equation.

CISCE 2023 Specimen Paper style: “Pass journal entries for the following and post them into the ledger of ‘M/s Gupta & Co.’: (i) Goods sold to M/s Gupta & Co. on credit ₹15,000. (ii) Received ₹14,500 from M/s Gupta & Co. in full settlement. (iii) Goods returned by M/s Gupta & Co. ₹2,000.”
Apply the Dual Aspect Concept to the following transaction: “Rohan starts a business with cash ₹2,00,000.” Show the two accounts affected and the accounting equation after the transaction.
A small enterprise records a ₹10,000 donation to a charitable trust as a business expense. Identify the concept violated and explain the correct treatment.
A trader’s journal shows: “Cash A/c Dr. ₹8,000 To Sales A/c ₹8,000”. Show the posting in the Cash and Sales ledger accounts (use T‑format).

Create a ledger account for “Rent Expense” given these journal entries: (i) 5‑May Rent A/c Dr. ₹6,000 To Cash A/c ₹6,000; (ii) 20‑May Rent A/c Dr. ₹4,000 To Outstanding Rent A/c ₹4,000. Balance the account.

In a CISCE ICSE exam, a question asks: “Post the following journal entry into the ledger: ‘Furniture A/c Dr. ₹15,000 To Bank A/c ₹15,000’. Show the Furniture and Bank accounts with proper balancing.” Outline the steps you would write.

**Application:** M/s Verma Electronics, Bengaluru, sold goods worth ₹30,000 on credit to M/s Rao Traders on 12‑Jun‑2025. On 20‑Jun, M/s Rao returned goods worth ₹5,000. On 25‑Jun, M/s Rao paid ₹20,000 by cheque. Show the ledger accounts for M/s Rao Traders and Sales Return, and balance them.
**Evaluation/Critique:** A textbook states: “Balancing of nominal accounts is not required because they are closed at year‑end.” Critique this statement for a Class 9 student.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** The following journal entry appears in the books of M/s Singh & Sons, Lucknow: “Drawings A/c Dr. ₹8,000 To Cash A/c ₹8,000” (i) Post this entry into the Drawings and Cash ledger accounts. (ii) Balance both accounts assuming the following opening balances on 1‑Apr‑2025: Drawings ₹0, Cash ₹40,000 (Dr.). (iii) State the classification of each account.
In a transaction, a firm pays ₹10,000 to a creditor by cheque. Identify the two accounts affected, their classes, and the debit/credit for each.
Apply the debit/credit rules to the following: “Purchased furniture for office use paying by cheque ₹75,000.”
**Application:** A firm buys a delivery van for ₹8,00,000, paying ₹3,00,000 cash and taking a loan for the balance. Show the debit/credit for each account involved.
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “State the rule of debit and credit for: (a) Capital Account, (b) Drawings Account, (c) Rent Received Account.” (3 marks)
Record the following transaction in the journal: Paid rent ₹5,000 by cheque on 12 March 2025.
Create a compound journal entry for a transaction where a business receives ₹10,000 cash and ₹5,000 cheque from a debtor, Mohan, in full settlement of his dues of ₹16,000.
Give the journal entry for: Goods worth ₹20,000 sold to Rahul on credit, subject to 10% trade discount and 5% cash discount if paid within 15 days.
Record the journal entry for: Withdrew ₹10,000 cash for personal use on 15 August 2025.
Pass journal entries for the following: (a) Paid salaries ₹8,000 (b) Received commission ₹2,000 (c) Purchased furniture for ₹15,000 on credit from M/s Delhi Furnishers.
The proprietor takes goods costing ₹9,000 (selling price ₹12,000) for his household. Journalise, and justify both the account credited and the figure used.

Find the error and state its three-fold effect: the clerk recorded the proprietor's withdrawals for the year — cash ₹10,000 and goods costing ₹8,000 — as: "Family Welfare Expenses A/c Dr 18,000; To Cash A/c 18,000." Give the corrected entries and the net effect on profit and capital under both treatments.

From the following, compute the closing capital: opening capital ₹1,80,000; additional capital introduced during the year ₹40,000; net profit for the year ₹55,000; drawings ₹5,000 per month. Then state where each of the four items would sit in the final accounts.

Classify each event by its effect on capital and profit (increase/decrease/none, with reason): (i) owner introduces his family silver, valued ₹60,000, into the firm; (ii) firm pays the owner's life-insurance premium ₹12,000 from the cash box; (iii) firm earns ₹25,000 profit; (iv) owner takes a company printer home permanently.

Application: A firm's books show: opening capital ₹2,60,000; closing capital ₹2,88,000; drawings for the year ₹36,000 in cash plus goods costing ₹4,000; interest on capital allowed ₹12,000; interest on drawings charged ₹1,500. Profit has been reported as ₹69,500 AFTER the two interest adjustments. (a) Reconstruct the profit before adjustments. (b) Prove the closing capital by the full closing-capital statement. (c) State why the two interest items move profit and capital in opposite senses.

Past-paper pattern: Read the case and answer. "Nandini's books show on 31st March: cash ₹30,000; stock ₹78,000; debtors ₹52,000; machinery ₹1,40,000; furniture ₹26,000; creditors ₹44,000; bank loan ₹60,000. Her father reminds her she began the year with capital ₹2,50,000, drew ₹4,500 a month, took goods costing ₹6,500, and the firm paid her LIC premium ₹7,500 — none of which she ever recorded in a drawings account; all were debited to 'Miscellaneous Expenses'." (a) Compute her capital from the balance-sheet data. (b) Compute her true drawings for the year. (c) Compute the profit implied for the year, and state the correction needed in Miscellaneous Expenses.
A firm forgets to record prepaid insurance of ₹3,000. Evaluate the effect on profit and the balance sheet.
Pass the journal entry for accrued interest of ₹2,500 on a fixed deposit.

A CISCE board question: “From the following trial balance, pass adjustment entries for (a) outstanding wages ₹2,000, (b) prepaid insurance ₹1,500, (c) depreciation on furniture @10% on ₹50,000. Show the effect on the Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet.” Outline the steps.

A company pays ₹24,000 on 1 July for a one‑year insurance policy. Show the adjustment entry on 31 March and the amounts to be shown in the Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet for the year ending 31 March.
Evaluate the impact on net profit if depreciation on a delivery van is overstated by ₹5,000 due to an incorrect useful life estimate.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “From the following balances, prepare the necessary adjustment entries and show their effect on the Trading and Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet: (i) Closing stock ₹30,000; (ii) Outstanding rent ₹2,000; (iii) Prepaid salaries ₹1,500; (iv) Depreciation on plant @10% on ₹80,000.” Provide the journal entries and the extracts of the affected accounts.

A year-end extraction gives: gross profit ₹68,000; indirect expenses ₹41,500; indirect incomes ₹3,500; opening capital ₹1,45,000; drawings ₹28,000. Compute net profit and closing capital, then state the balance-sheet side each result occupies.

Match each error to the earliest stage that MUST catch it, with one-line reasons: (a) a credit purchase omitted entirely; (b) sales book overcast by ₹200; (c) furniture purchase debited to Purchases; (d) a customer's receipt posted to his debit instead of credit; (e) carriage outward entered in the Trading Account.

Application: A colleague hands you four mid-chain figures with one missing each time — compute the missing figure: (i) Net sales 2,00,000, COGS 1,44,000, GP = ? (ii) GP 56,000, indirect expenses 39,000, indirect incomes 4,000, NP = ? (iii) Opening capital 1,10,000, NP 21,000, drawings 18,000, closing capital = ? (iv) Assets 3,40,000, liabilities 1,52,000, capital = ?; and then (v) the consistency test: do (iii) and (iv) describe the same firm if its only assets are stock 80,000 and cash 80,000?

Past-paper pattern: Read the case and answer. "Pintu's first year: opened with cash ₹2,00,000; bought goods ₹1,40,000 (cash ₹1,00,000; ₹40,000 credit from Ghosh); sold goods ₹1,80,000 (cash ₹1,25,000; ₹55,000 credit to Neha); Neha returned goods ₹5,000 and settled the balance by cheque; paid Ghosh in full by cheque; shop rent ₹12,000 cash; wages ₹9,000 cash; carriage inward ₹3,000 cash; closing stock ₹26,000; machinery bought for cash ₹50,000 is also on hand, valued at ₹50,000." (a) Compute cash-in-hand at year end. (b) Prepare the Trading Account result (gross profit). (c) Compute net profit, closing capital, and the balance-sheet total, proving equality. (d) Pintu's uncle says the machinery should appear as an expense "since it was bought this year" — resolve the uncle's claim by naming the error class and the correct account path through the cycle.
A customer writes a cheque for ₹5,000 but the account has only ₹3,000. What will the bank do?
Design a simple flowchart showing the flow of money when a depositor places ₹10,000 in a fixed deposit and the bank lends ₹8,000 to a borrower.
A customer wants to transfer ₹2 lakh to a supplier in another city within minutes. Which banking service should they use and why?
A new bank, “Greenfield Bank”, is promoted by a group of Indian entrepreneurs with 100% private capital. It obtains a licence from RBI and starts operations. Classify Greenfield Bank and justify.
In the ICSE Class 9 Commercial Studies exam, a question asks: “Distinguish between scheduled and non‑scheduled banks on any three points.” Write a concise answer.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain the term ‘Scheduled Bank’. State any two conditions a bank must fulfil to be included in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934.”
A customer wants to deposit ₹10,000 every month for 5 years and earn compound interest. Which account should she choose?

**HOTS:** A bank introduces a “Flexi‑Deposit” that combines features of Savings and Fixed Deposits: funds above ₹25,000 automatically sweep into an FD for 180 days at 6 % p.a., while the balance stays in savings at 3 % p.a. If a customer maintains an average balance of ₹1,00,000 for a year, estimate the annual interest earned.

**Application:** A freelance graphic designer receives irregular payments totalling ₹8,00,000 annually. She wants an account that offers some interest, allows unlimited withdrawals, and provides a cheque book. Which account type should she open and what additional facility might she request?
**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** *Question:* “State three points of distinction between a Savings Bank Account and a Fixed Deposit Account.” (3 marks)

A student deposits ₹10,000 in a Savings Account offering 3 % p.a. simple interest calculated on daily product basis. If the balance remains unchanged for 30 days, what is the interest earned for that month? (Assume 365 days a year.)
Create a scenario where a Recurring Deposit is more appropriate than a Fixed Deposit for a 25‑year‑old salaried employee earning ₹40,000 per month.

ICSE 2023 pattern: “Distinguish between Savings Account and Current Account on the basis of (i) interest payment, (ii) withdrawal restrictions, (iii) target customers.” Write the answer in a tabular form.

**HOTS:** “A bank introduces a ‘Flexi‑Deposit’ that combines features of Savings and Fixed Deposits: it pays savings‑account interest on balances up to ₹1 lakh and FD rate on the excess, with automatic sweep‑in/out. Analyse how this product changes the liquidity‑return trade‑off for a small business owner.”

**Application:** A college student receives a scholarship of ₹50,000 annually. She wants to keep the money safe, earn some interest, and withdraw for hostel fees each semester. Which account type should she open? Provide two reasons.

**Comparison:** Compare the maturity proceeds of a ₹1 lakh Fixed Deposit for 1 year at 6 % p.a. simple interest versus a Recurring Deposit of ₹8,333 per month for 1 year at 6 % p.a. compounded quarterly. Which is higher and by how much?
**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “Distinguish between Fixed Deposit and Recurring Deposit on any four points.” (ICSE 2022, 4 marks)
A student writes a cheque for ₹5,000 but forgets to sign it. The bank returns it with the remark "Drawer's signature missing". Identify the legal consequence under the Negotiable Instruments Act.
CISCE past‑paper pattern: "Define 'cheque' as per the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. State two differences between a cheque and a bill of exchange."
A customer wants to transfer ₹8 lakh to a vendor at 11:30 pm on a Sunday. Which channel should they use to ensure immediate credit? A) NEFT B) RTGS C) IMPS D) Cheque deposit

Arjun’s father transfers ₹25,000 to a relative via NEFT at 4:15 pm on a Wednesday. The bank’s NEFT batch schedule is every half hour starting at 8:00 am. When will the beneficiary’s account be credited? A) 4:30 pm same day B) 5:00 pm same day C) Next working day 8:30 am D) Instantly
Design a one‑page infographic for a school fair that explains the three main e‑banking channels (NEFT, IMPS, UPI) to Class 8 students. List the four key elements you would include for each channel.

**Application:** A freelancer receives ₹75,000 from a foreign client via SWIFT into their Indian bank account. The bank offers to credit the amount via NEFT or RTGS to the freelancer’s savings account. Which channel should the freelancer choose if they need the money by 10 am next working day and the amount is below ₹2 lakh?
Explain why IMPS is preferred over NEFT for an urgent ₹2 lakh transfer on a Sunday evening.

A customer wants to transfer ₹50,000 from her savings account to a vendor’s account on a Saturday 10 PM. She has access to internet banking, UPI app, and a debit card. Which channel should she use and why?
In the ICSE Class 9 Commercial Studies exam, a question asks: “State two advantages of electronic banking over traditional branch banking.” Write a model answer.

A customer tries to transfer ₹2 lakh via UPI at 11 PM on a Sunday but the transaction fails with “Daily limit exceeded.” The customer’s bank sets a per‑transaction limit of ₹1 lakh and a daily limit of ₹2 lakh. Explain why the transaction failed and propose a correct approach.

Compare the transaction charges for a ₹10,000 transfer via NEFT (₹2.50 per ₹10,000 + GST) and UPI (zero charge for customers). Calculate the cost difference and discuss why banks still promote UPI despite zero direct revenue.
ICSE 2023 Commercial Studies paper asked: “Explain the role of NPCI in the Indian payment ecosystem.” Write a concise answer suitable for 3 marks.

A firm’s cash book shows a debit balance of ₹ 50,000. The pass book shows a credit balance of ₹ 55,000. The only difference is a cheque of ₹ 5,000 deposited but not credited. Evaluate whether the cash book needs any correction entry.

Prepare a Bank Reconciliation Statement as on 31 March 2026 using the following data (start from pass book balance): Pass book balance ₹ 80,000 (credit); Cheques issued but not presented ₹ 12,000; Cheques deposited but not credited ₹ 7,000; Bank charges ₹ 400 not in cash book; Interest credited by bank ₹ 250 not in cash book; Direct deposit by customer ₹ 3,000 not in cash book.

A CISCE specimen paper asks: “From the following particulars, prepare a Bank Reconciliation Statement as on 31 December 2025, starting with the cash book balance.” The data includes: Cash book balance ₹ 40,000 (debit); Cheques issued but not presented ₹ 8,000; Cheques deposited but not credited ₹ 5,000; Bank charges ₹ 300; Interest allowed by bank ₹ 200; Direct deposit ₹ 1,500. Outline the steps and give the final adjusted pass book balance.

A business finds that its cash book shows a debit balance of ₹ 2,00,000 while the bank statement shows a credit balance of ₹ 2,10,000. The only reconciling item is a cheque of ₹ 10,000 deposited but not yet credited. The student concludes the cash book is overstated by ₹ 10,000. Evaluate this conclusion.

Apply the BRS procedure to a real‑life situation: You receive an SMS alert that your savings account was credited with ₹ 2,500 interest, but your personal cash book (expense tracker) does not show it. Show the adjustment needed in a BRS starting from the bank statement balance.

CISCE 2024 Specimen Paper Question: “From the following particulars, prepare a Bank Reconciliation Statement as on 31 March 2024, starting with the cash book balance: Cash book balance ₹ 1,20,000 (Dr.); Cheques issued but not presented ₹ 15,000; Cheques deposited but not credited ₹ 10,000; Bank charges ₹ 500; Interest allowed by bank ₹ 300; Direct deposit by customer ₹ 4,000; Cheque dishonoured ₹ 2,000 (not recorded in cash book).” Provide the final adjusted pass book balance and list the cash book correction entries.
A bank holds total deposits of ₹80 crore. The CRR is 4%. Calculate the cash it must keep with the RBI, and the fall in its lendable funds if the CRR is raised to 4.5%.
Inflation has been running at 6.5%, above the RBI's target band. Evaluate what the Monetary Policy Committee should do to the repo rate and the CRR, and what each change does.

Route these six examination questions to their home slices, and state in one line what each answer must contain: (i) "Distinguish between crossing general and special." (ii) "State any two functions of the Reserve Bank of India." (iii) "Prepare a BRS from the pass book balance." (iv) "Which account suits a trader with daily high-volume collections?" (v) "Which rail moves ₹5,00,000 the same day?" (vi) "What is KYC? Name two documents."

A new trader, Anita, starts a provisions business: she expects 40+ daily collections, must pay one supplier ₹3,00,000 today, and wants her bank's figures verified monthly. Advise on the three needs, naming the slice behind each advice.

From a cash book balance of ₹40,000, run the reconciliation: cheques issued not presented ₹6,200; cheques deposited not credited ₹8,900; bank charges ₹140; interest credited ₹260; a customer's direct UPI ₹1,150. Show the pass book balance.
A tenant must pay ₹50,000 monthly rent to a landlord in another city. Evaluate cheque versus UPI for this recurring payment and give a reasoned choice.

Five payments, five right answers — name the correct mode each time with the deciding rule: (a) ₹250 to the vegetable vendor; (b) ₹90,000 to a hospital at 11 p.m. on a holiday; (c) ₹3,40,000 builder instalment needing same-day proof; (d) ₹15,000 monthly salary to one cook, standing order; (e) ₹28,000 to a supplier who insists on a signed instrument for his records.

[CISCE past-paper pattern — mixed paper] Answer briefly, each part from its own slice: (i) Define a bank in one sentence. (ii) State any two functions of commercial banks. (iii) Name the parties to a cheque. (iv) Expand and define RTGS. (v) From cash book ₹30,000: cheques issued not presented ₹4,500; cheques deposited not credited ₹6,800; bank charges ₹120 — find the pass book balance.
A retailer buys 200 units of a product from a wholesaler and sells them to consumers. Identify the trade type and list two functions the wholesaler performed before this sale.
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Distinguish between ‘Import Trade’ and ‘Entrepôt Trade’ on any three bases.” (3 marks)

A spice wholesaler in Kochi buys 500 kg of pepper at ₹400/kg, incurs ₹15,000 in grading and packing, and sells to retailers at ₹500/kg. Calculate the wholesaler’s gross profit and gross profit margin percentage.

**Application:** A retailer in Patna buys 200 units of a product from a wholesaler at ₹300/unit on 45‑day credit. The retailer’s selling price is ₹400/unit. If the retailer sells 150 units within 30 days and the remaining 50 units after 60 days, calculate the retailer’s cash‑flow advantage from the credit term, assuming a 15 % annual cost of funds.
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Explain the role of a wholesaler in the distribution of agricultural produce in India. Give two functions with examples.” (4 marks)
Why is "breaking the bulk" called the retailer's most basic service? Explain with the journey of one 50-kg sack of sugar.
A chain store cuts prices 10% below the kirana store on identical branded goods. Evaluate whether the kirana store should match the price cut, and what it should do instead.

[CISCE past-paper pattern] (i) Name the retailer described: "moves door to door on foot with a basket of bangles and combs". (ii) State two features of a co-operative store. (iii) A shop sells ONLY sports goods with expert advice — name its class. (iv) Give two merits of a mail-order house for customers in small towns. (v) From the following, compute the retailer's net profit: purchases from wholesaler ₹2,40,000; sales ₹3,00,000; expenses ₹45,000.

**APPLICATION:** A dairy cooperative in Gujarat produces pasteurised milk (shelf‑life 48 hours). It currently sells through a two‑level channel (cooperative → distributor → retailer). Propose a channel modification to reduce spoilage and justify with two factors.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain the factors a manufacturer of consumer durables should consider while selecting a channel of distribution. (4 marks)”

Case study: M/s Sharma Exports, Mumbai, contracts to sell 20 tonnes of spices to a buyer in Dubai under CIF Jebel Ali. The goods are damaged during sea transit due to rough weather. Who bears the loss? Explain.
If a country’s Export Price Index is 120 and Import Price Index is 100, what is its Terms of Trade index?
A country’s Terms of Trade index falls from 110 to 95 over two years. Explain two possible causes and one likely consequence for the country’s current account.

From the following annual figures (₹ lakh crore), compute the balance of trade and classify it: goods exports 32; goods imports 44; software and other services exports 25; services imports 12; remittances received 9.

Classify each transaction into the current account or the capital account of India's BOP: (i) export of basmati rice; (ii) a Japanese company builds a car factory in Gujarat; (iii) software services billed to a US client; (iv) an NRI deposits ₹20 lakh in an Indian bank; (v) a French tourist spends in Jaipur; (vi) the government repays a foreign loan; (vii) workers' remittances from the Gulf.

[CISCE past-paper pattern — mixed] (i) Define balance of payments. (ii) Name the two accounts of the BOP and one item in each. (iii) State the full form and founding year of the WTO and its headquarters. (iv) What is duty drawback? (v) Goods exports ₹18 lakh crore, goods imports ₹24 lakh crore, services surplus ₹7 lakh crore — compute the BOT and the current account balance, and classify each.

An Indian exporter ships machinery worth ₹50 lakh to Germany. The buyer opens an irrevocable letter of credit. List the three documents the exporter must present to the negotiating bank to claim payment under the LC.
A CISCE Class 9 exam question: “State any two consequences of not obtaining a ‘Let Export’ order from customs.” Write a concise answer as per board marking scheme.
**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern Question:** “State the sequence of documents required for exporting goods from India. Explain the importance of any two documents.” (4 marks)
India’s exports in a quarter are ₹ 2,50,000 crore and imports are ₹ 3,10,000 crore. Calculate the balance of trade and state whether it is a surplus or deficit.
ICSE 2022 Paper: “Distinguish between a bill of exchange and a bill of lading in the context of foreign trade.” Provide two points of distinction.

ICSE 2023 Specimen Paper: “A Mumbai based company exports machinery to a buyer in Kenya. The payment is to be made through a letter of credit. List the documents the exporter must present to the bank for negotiation. (4 marks)”
Why is CSR spending under Section 135 of the Companies Act 2013 considered mandatory rather than voluntary charity?

A mid‑size Indian electronics manufacturer with a net profit of ₹10 crore decides to allocate ₹15 lakh for a village school. Does this meet the CSR requirement under Section 135? Show your calculation.
**APPLICATION:** A startup in Bengaluru with net profit ₹3 crore wants to design a CSR initiative. It is not legally mandated. Propose a low‑cost initiative that aligns with all three dimensions.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain the concept of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) as per the Companies Act 2013. State any two activities that can be undertaken under CSR.” (4 marks)
List the three dimensions of social responsibility as defined in the CISCE Class 9 Commercial Studies syllabus.
In the CISCE ICSE 2023 Commercial Studies paper, a 4‑mark question asked: “Explain two arguments in favour of social responsibility of business.” Write a concise answer that would earn full marks.

**HOTS:** “A firm can be economically responsible but socially irresponsible.” Construct a brief Indian scenario (max 60 words) that illustrates this paradox, naming the firm type and the specific irresponsible act.

**Application:** You are the owner of a small spice‑grinding unit in Kerala. The local Panchayat proposes a new rule requiring all food‑processing units to install dust‑extraction systems within six months. The system costs ₹3 lakh, which is 15 % of your annual profit. Decide whether to comply early, wait for enforcement, or challenge the rule. Justify using the three dimensions.

**Evaluation/Critique:** Critique the view that “mandatory CSR spending under Section 135 of the Companies Act 2013 has made the ethical dimension of social responsibility redundant for large companies.”
**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “Explain, with two examples, how a commercial organisation can fulfil its ethical responsibility towards the environment.” (4 marks)
Evaluate the effectiveness of mandatory CSR spending (Section 135) in improving social outcomes in India.
CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern: “Explain three arguments against social responsibility of business. (3 marks)” Write a model answer.
Which layer of Carroll’s pyramid is satisfied when a company merely complies with the Environment Protection Act 1986?
**Evaluation/Critique:** Critique the argument: “Mandatory CSR (Section 135) undermines voluntary ethical behaviour because firms treat it as a tax.”

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “Explain the concept of ‘Corporate Social Responsibility’ with reference to the Companies Act 2013. State any three arguments in favour of CSR and two arguments against it.” Provide a model answer outline.

A plant manager finds that a conveyor guard, fitted properly, slows the line by 6%. He removes it; the law's annual inspection is months away. Evaluate his act and state the responsibility test he is failing.

Kavita earns ₹18,000 per month and is covered by the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The firm declares bonus at the minimum rate. Compute her annual minimum bonus, the maximum it could have been, and the difference; show the working.
The board must split ₹2 crore of discretionary money: a dividend top-up to shareholders or a workers' housing block near the plant. Argue BOTH claims and construct the responsible split.

[CISCE past-paper pattern — mixed] (i) Name the Act that provides for a share of profits to eligible employees, with its minimum rate. (ii) State two responsibilities towards employees that go BEYOND legal compulsion. (iii) Which law protects equal pay for men and women, and what does it order? (iv) A firm saves costs by hiring a 14-year-old at half wages — state the legal position and the responsible verdict. (v) Compute: salary ₹15,000/month, bonus declared at the maximum rate — annual bonus payable?
A mobile phone manufacturer advertises “5G ready” on a model that only supports 4G. Identify the specific unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the regulator that can act.
Evaluate whether a company’s “no‑questions‑asked return policy” for 30 days fully satisfies the consumer’s right to redressal.
A CISCE board‑style question: “Explain how the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 strengthens the right to redressal compared to the 1986 Act.” Provide three distinct improvements.

A consumer buys a refrigerator with a 10‑year compressor warranty. After 3 years the compressor fails. The manufacturer refuses repair, saying the warranty covers only “manufacturing defects” and the failure is due to “voltage fluctuations”. The consumer has no voltage stabiliser. Using the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, decide who bears the burden of proof and what the likely outcome is.

A company launches a “green” detergent claiming “100% biodegradable in 7 days”. Independent lab tests show 60% degradation in 30 days. The company argues the claim is based on “ideal laboratory conditions”. Apply ASCI guidelines and CPA 2019 to determine the violation and penalty.
Critique the statement: “Small businesses with turnover below ₹20 lakh are exempt from consumer protection laws.” Provide legal reasoning.
Compare the redressal mechanism under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 and the 2019 Act for a complaint valued at ₹5 lakh. Highlight two procedural improvements in the 2019 Act.

CISCE past‑paper pattern: “Explain the concept of ‘product liability’ introduced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. State any three parties who can be held liable.” Provide a concise answer as expected in the board exam.
State the three Section 135 thresholds at which CSR obligations attach to a company, and the three institutional duties the section then imposes.

A company's net profits were ₹46 crore, ₹58 crore and ₹76 crore over the last three financial years. Compute the minimum CSR budget for the coming year, showing every step, and state TWO Schedule VII areas it could fund.
Section 135 is called "trusteeship made mandatory". What did Gandhian trusteeship originally ask for, what does the section actually command, and what gap remains between the two?

A firm's accountant proposes booking ₹50 lakh of speed-money paid to clear a stalled pollution consent as 'community facilitation expense'. Unpack every layer of wrong in the proposal, and state what the firm should have done and should now do.

[CISCE past-paper pattern — mixed] (i) State the CSR applicability threshold in terms of net profit. (ii) Name any four Schedule VII activity areas. (iii) What does the CSR committee consist of? (iv) Profits of the last three years: ₹11, ₹13, ₹16 crore — compute the minimum CSR spend. (v) A firm spends its CSR budget on scholarships for employees' children only — decide and justify in two lines.

A company claims its CSR plantation drive planted 50,000 saplings. An auditor finds 60% survival after two years. The company argues the audit should only count saplings planted, not survival. Critique this argument using social audit principles.
Compare the social audit requirements under the Companies Act, 2013 (Section 135) with the voluntary BRSR framework.

CISCE 2023 Specimen Paper style: “A large retail chain has implemented a CSR programme to reduce plastic packaging. Describe the steps the company should take to conduct a social audit of this programme, and explain how the audit findings would be disclosed in the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report.”

A bottling plant draws 5,000 kilolitres of fresh water monthly. It installs rainwater harvesting that recharges 800 kl and a recycling loop that reuses 1,500 kl of process water. Compute the new fresh-water draw and the percentage saving; verify the arithmetic.

Evaluate the owner's argument: "Effluent treatment costs ₹40 lakh a year. If I discharge raw at night into the drain, I save it — the stream is big and the check is rare." Give the true cost accounting of the ₹40 lakh 'saving' and your verdict.

A firm's complete shift to solar power costs ₹6 crore and cuts energy bills by ₹1 crore a year. The CFO says the payback of six years is too slow. Evaluate with the payback arithmetic, the hidden ledgers the CFO has not opened, and your advice.

[CISCE past-paper pattern — mixed] (i) Define pollution in one line and name its four kinds. (ii) Which Indian statute is the umbrella environment law, and what year followed the Bhopal gas tragedy? (iii) State the two natural rates that sustainability balances. (iv) A plant needs 6,000 kl/month; harvesting gives 900 kl, recycling 1,100 kl — compute fresh draw and saving %. (v) Why is "the cheapest effluent is the one never created" the smartest line in environmental management?
Define the term "social responsibility of commercial organisations" as per the ICSE Class 9 syllabus.
Evaluate the statement: “A company that spends 2 % of its profits on CSR activities automatically fulfills its social responsibility.”
Create a short‑answer question (3 marks) that tests a student’s ability to distinguish between ethical and philanthropic responsibilities, and provide a model answer.
Evaluation/Critique: “Mandatory CSR spending (2 % rule) has improved social outcomes in India.” Critically evaluate this claim with two arguments for and two against.
State Adam Smith’s definition of economics and list the four main economic activities he identified. (2 marks)
Define economics according to Adam Smith. Mention any two limitations of this definition. (3 marks)

A farmer in Maharashtra has 5 hectares of land. He can grow sugarcane (profit ₹1,20,000/ha) or cotton (profit ₹90,000/ha). Using Robbins’ framework, identify the opportunity cost of choosing sugarcane on all 5 hectares.
In the ICSE 2023 Economics paper, a question asked: “Distinguish between Robbins’ and Marshall’s definitions of economics.” Outline the answer structure a student should follow to score full marks.

**APPLICATION:** A startup in Bengaluru has 10 developers. They can build a fintech app (projected revenue ₹50 lakh) or an edtech platform (projected revenue ₹40 lakh). The developers’ time is the scarce resource. If the startup chooses fintech, what is the opportunity cost? Show the calculation.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Define economics according to Lionel Robbins. Explain how his definition leads to the concept of opportunity cost. Give one example from the Indian context.” (4 marks)
State the exact wording of Keynes’s definition of economics as given in the ICSE Class 9 syllabus.
**APPLICATION:** The RBI cuts the repo rate by 50 basis points. Using Keynes’s definition, trace the expected chain of effects on income and employment.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Define economics according to Keynes. How does it differ from Robbins’s definition? (3 marks)”

(HOTS) "The national income is ₹300 lakh crore" and "this firm's revenue is ₹300 crore" — a student says both are macro because both are large numbers. Correct the student and derive a rule that survives every such case.
A freelance graphic designer creates a logo for a startup and receives ₹15,000. Classify this activity and justify using the three criteria.
A Class 9 student writes: “Economic activities are only those done by businesses; individuals cannot perform economic activities.” Identify the flaw and correct it.

(Application) A district collector must rank four unmet wants for one year's budget: (i) a mobile medical unit for 12 remote hamlets; (ii) street lights for one town's market road; (iii) a sports stadium for the district headquarters; (iv) clean drinking water taps for three flood-prone villages. Rank the wants with reasons from the urgency and classification angle, and justify why the lowest-ranked want is still a legitimate want.

(Application) A school's economics club prepares a "wealth audit" of one student's household: scooter, rented flat, solar panel bought under subsidy, gold chain, pending electricity bill of Rs 4,000, and a leased shopfront for the family business. Prepare the audit — include/exclude each item with its test or category — and compute net wealth in symbolic terms.

A consumer’s total utility from eating mangoes is: 1 mango = 40 utils, 2 mangoes = 70 utils, 3 mangoes = 90 utils. Calculate the marginal utility of the 2nd and 3rd mangoes and state whether diminishing marginal utility holds.

If the price of a samosa is ₹15 and a student’s marginal utilities (in ₹ equivalent) for successive samosas are 25, 20, 15, 10, 5, how many samosas will the student buy to maximise utility? Show the reasoning.

Create a short ordinal‑preference ranking for three bundles: (A) 2 apples + 1 banana, (B) 1 apple + 3 bananas, (C) 3 apples + 0 bananas, assuming the consumer prefers more apples to bananas. Indicate the ranking and justify.

A consumer’s total utility from listening to songs on a streaming app is: 1 song = 15 utils, 2 songs = 28 utils, 3 songs = 39 utils, 4 songs = 48 utils, 5 songs = 55 utils. Calculate the marginal utility of the 4th song and comment on whether the law of diminishing marginal utility holds up to this point.

If the price of a movie ticket is ₹200 and a viewer’s marginal utilities (in ₹) for successive movies in a month are 300, 250, 210, 180, 150, how many movies will the viewer watch? Show the marginal‑utility‑price comparison.

A marigold garland travels: farmer grows flowers in Hosur; van carries them to Bengaluru's KR Market at 4 a.m.; trader stores part of the stock overnight for the next day's festival; shopkeeper strings the garlands; the priest performs the puja service. Identify who produces and what utility each creates.

"A moneylender who charges 60 per cent annual interest, lends only for wedding celebrations, and seizes the borrower's land on default is engaging in production." Evaluate this claim using the utility criterion.

A wedding celebration serves 500 plates of which about 150 return barely touched, and fireworks are burst for an hour. Using the concepts of consumption, wasteful consumption and opportunity, evaluate the evening's economics.

(Application) A campus of 3,000 students wants to reduce its consumption footprint without cutting learning or nutrition. The audit shows: 40 per cent of canteen food wasted, all lights burning in empty classrooms, single-use cups and packaged water, and bus idling at stands. Classify each as wasteful consumption, over-consumption, or efficient final consumption, and prescribe one intervention of each of the two kinds (reduce-waste; shift-the-satisfier) with the consumption concept it exploits.

(Application) Your household's monthly consumption audit shows: 900 units of electricity (two ACs at 22–24 °C, old geyser, all-incandescent backups), 40 kilolitres of water (long showers, hose-washed car), 25 kg of food waste, and weekly online purchases individually courier-packaged. Design a sustainable-consumption plan with six actions, each tagged with its operating idea and its expected effect on a named resource; state which want each action explicitly refuses to cut.

(Past-paper pattern) "Sustainable consumption satisfies present wants without foreclosing future ones. Apply the framework to a small-town river that serves, in order of current draw: a paper mill's process water, irrigation for 400 hectares, and the town's drinking supply, while untreated sewage returns to the same river. (i) Identify the unsustainable features of present use. (ii) Allocate the river's sustainable budget across the three uses, with reasons. (iii) Name two operating-idea interventions that raise the budget itself." (ICSE-style.)

(HOTS) Two neighbouring districts grow the same potato variety. District A sells through a single commission agent who also publishes the only price information; District B runs an electronic auction where hundreds of lots trade on screen. The same truckload fetches 15 per cent less in A. The agent protests: "The market is the same for both — same variety, same buyers' region." Using the market definition's elements, explain what differs between the districts' markets and where the 15 per cent goes.
If the market price of tomatoes rises from ₹20/kg to ₹30/kg, describe the likely effect on quantity demanded and quantity supplied.

**Application:** A new electric scooter is launched at ₹1,20,000. The manufacturer expects to sell 5,000 units in the first year. If the price is reduced by 10 %, estimate the new quantity sold assuming a price elasticity of demand of -1.5.
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** “Explain how price functions as a signal, a rationing device, and an incentive in a market economy. Illustrate each function with a suitable Indian example.” (5 marks)
Why can the same good's exchange-value change drastically — an umbrella from Rs 100 in March to Rs 350 in August, a candle from Rs 10 to Rs 100 in a blackout — while its usefulness is unchanged?

(Past-paper pattern) "Value-in-exchange requires utility, scarcity and transferability together; price is value-in-exchange in money terms. Apply the framework: (i) A Chennai household owns: a flat in a demanded locality; the family's old Maruti in working order; the grandmother's recipes known by heart; a reserved railway berth certificate for tonight; and the sea breeze on the Marina. For each, state value-in-use (high/low), value-in-exchange (present/absent), and the decisive condition. (ii) The berth certificate's holder cannot travel — state what happens to its exchange-value at 8 p.m. against the 9.14 p.m. departure, and name the characteristic of services responsible. (iii) State which single item would move OUT of exchange-value's world if transferability were withdrawn — and why the others would remain." (ICSE-style.)

(Application) Your district reports: per capita income rising 7 per cent yearly; two new private colleges; government hospital beds per thousand unchanged; farm incomes up in the command area, stagnant in the hills; a new expressway bypassing the hill block. Prepare a two-column development audit — GROWTH EVIDENCE and DEVELOPMENT GAPS — and prescribe the single intervention with the largest development return, with reasoning.

(Application) A city's market economy shows three simultaneous signals: rent in the tech corridor up 40 per cent; enrolment in industrial-training institutes for hospitality down; a boom in food-delivery gig work with no contracts. Advise the city government: which of these signals should it let the market answer alone, which need public response, and what is the ONE public response with the highest long-term return? Give reasons in terms of the model's machinery.
Evaluate whether India’s mixed economy has succeeded in reducing poverty since 1991.
In a hypothetical mixed economy, the public sector contributes 30 % of GDP and the private sector 70 %. If total GDP is ₹200 lakh crore, calculate the public sector’s output.
Evaluate the impact of the 1991 liberalisation on the balance between state and market in India’s mixed economy.
“Explain two reasons why the Government of India continues to own a majority stake in public sector banks.” (CISCE 2023 pattern)

Compare the following two hypothetical countries and decide which is more likely to be classified as developed. Country A: GNI per capita $38,000; HDI 0.92; services 78 % of GDP; life expectancy 82 years. Country B: GNI per capita $5,200; HDI 0.68; agriculture 30 % of GDP; life expectancy 68 years.

Given the data below, classify the country as developed or developing and justify using at least three indicators. GNI per capita: $12,500; HDI: 0.78; Industry share of GDP: 35 %; Agriculture share of GDP: 12 %; Life expectancy: 75 years.
**HOTS:** “A country’s real GDP grows 5 % annually for five years, yet its Gini coefficient rises from 0.35 to 0.42. Discuss the implications for development.”

**APPLICATION:** The state of Odisha plans a new aluminium smelter expected to add 1 % to state GDP. Propose two specific development‑oriented conditions the state should attach to the project approval.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “Read the following case and answer the questions that follow: Country Z is a mixed economy where the government owns 30% of industrial assets, sets minimum wages, and provides free healthcare. Private firms operate in all other sectors. Recently, the government proposed selling its stake in the national telecom company to a private consortium. (a) Identify two parameters of the comparative framework that will change due to this disinvestment. (b) Explain one possible positive and one possible negative effect on equity. (c) Explain one possible positive and one possible negative effect on efficiency. (d) State whether this move shifts Country Z toward the market or planning end of the continuum.”

A case description reads: 'The state owns the railways, banks and power grid; consumer electronics, textiles and agriculture are private; food and fuel carry administered prices beside market prices; the economy's per capita income is rising while literacy climbs from 74 to 81 per cent.' Classify the economy on both grids, filing every datum.

A middle-class family has a monthly income of Rs 30,000. Its wish-list for the month: groceries Rs 12,000, school fees Rs 6,000, medicines Rs 4,000, a new mixer-grinder Rs 3,500, a weekend trip Rs 6,000, savings Rs 3,000 — total Rs 34,500. Show how this family's situation contains the economic problem and name the choice it must make.
"India's population of over 140 crore is its greatest liability, not its resource." Evaluate this claim using the human-resource idea.

(HOTS) A state government announces: "We will create resources — 10,000 new trained plumbers, two new industrial estates, and a canal." Using the four-factor frame, explain in what sense each announcement 'creates' a resource and what each creation costs.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Define the four factors of production. (ii) Classify with reasons: a brick kiln's clay pit; its fired-brick stockyard shed; its 30 moulders; its owner who bids for contracts. (iii) State why the clay pit is a different kind of scarce from the fired bricks in the shed. (iv) A candidate writes: 'The kiln's scarcest resource is its cash balance.' Assess the claim in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)

A family's monthly surplus is Rs 5,000. Rival claims: extra tuition for the daughter preparing for boards, a mixer-grinder, a contribution to the temple renovation, better groceries. Using intensity and urgency of wants, rank the claims and state what the ranking forgives and forgoes.

A district must split a fixed development fund between two schemes: a food-processing park (400 permanent jobs, mechanised lines) and a handloom cluster (1,200 jobs on looms, lower output per worker). Identify which basic problem each scheme's construction raises, and state the technique choice the district is making.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) State the two basic problems this node teaches, with one line each. (ii) For each decision below, name the problem (what / how) and the specific choice made: (a) a power board builds a hydel plant instead of raising coal output; (b) a garments exporter buys 50 stitching machines and hires 30 workers instead of 150 hand-tailors; (c) the state spends festival-season grain on a nutrition scheme rather than exporting it. (iii) State one merit and one demerit of the capital-intensive choice in (b). (iv) A candidate writes: 'the problems of what and how arise only in capitalist economies; socialist economies have plans, so no problem'. Correct the candidate in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) State the three basic problems of an economy in the order they are decided. (ii) For each case, name the problem illustrated and the specific decision or rule: (a) the state shifts its investment from a new stadium to a rural grid; (b) the public distribution system supplies grain at half the market price; (c) a textile mill adopts powerlooms and releases 400 handloom weavers. (iii) For case (c), state one distributional consequence beyond the released weavers themselves. (iv) A candidate writes: 'the three problems are solved by the government in India because India is a mixed economy'. Correct the candidate in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)

A student has Rs 500 and one free Sunday. Option one: buy a reference book; option two: a day trip costing Rs 500; option three: save the money and revise at home. She chooses the book. State the opportunity cost, and explain why it is NOT 'the trip plus the savings'.

From the data, compute the opportunity costs: a weaver family can weave, per week, either 12 saris or 18 dhotis (not both fully). (i) The opportunity cost of one sari in dhotis; (ii) the opportunity cost of one dhoti in saris; (iii) if demand fixes output at 6 saris, how many dhotis are forgone in all, and what does the remainder of the week's capacity produce?

A shopkeeper computes her yearly 'profit' as sales of Rs 12,00,000 minus shop expenses of Rs 9,00,000, and reports Rs 3,00,000. She owns the shop premises (which could be rented out for Rs 1,20,000 a year) and works full-time herself (her wage elsewhere would be Rs 2,40,000 a year). Compute the implicit costs and reassess her true gain.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Define opportunity cost and state why it arises. (ii) A factory floor assembles either 200 radios or 120 torches a day. Compute the opportunity cost of one radio and of one torch. (iii) The owner considers hiring his son at Rs 0 'since family helps free'. State the economic objection and the term for the cost ignored. (iv) The state diverts a river to a plant; a farmer loses the fishing the river supported. State whose opportunity cost this is and how it should enter the plant's cost." (ICSE-style.)

From the schedule — combinations A to E: (20 machines, 0 grain), (18, 3), (15, 5), (10, 7), (0 machines, 8 lakh tonnes grain) — compute the opportunity cost of grain in machines for each successive step, and state the pattern the steps display with its reason.

Two economies, same curve. Economy X produces at point M (4 lakh tonnes grain, 8 machines); the curve through M's neighbourhood allows (6 grain, 15 machines) and even (7, 10). Economy Y produces at point N on its own curve. State what each economy's position indicates and what advice the geometry gives each.

A state's frontier allows (12 thermal plants, 0 canals) to (0 plants, 9 canals), with combinations in between. The state currently operates 8 plants and 3 canals, and proposes to move to 10 plants and 2 canals. State, with working, (i) the opportunity cost of the extra plants, (ii) whether the new point lies on the old frontier given it allowed (10 plants, 2.5 canals), and (iii) what kind of move the proposal is.

(Application) Your school must allocate its 40-interact-student volunteer force between two events this month: the district science exhibition (stall-building duty) and the blood-donation camp (registration and aftercare duty). Experience says the full force could staff either a top-grade exhibition or a smooth camp; splits are possible but volunteers are better at one duty each. Design the planning sheet: a five-combination possibility table (with plausible numbers), the frontier sentence, the recommendation with its opportunity cost, and the note on which volunteers should be moved LAST as demands change.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Define production possibility curve. (ii) An economy's schedule: A(0 sugar, 40 cloth), B(5, 36), C(9, 28), D(12, 12), E(13, 0) — sugar in lakh tonnes, cloth in million metres. Compute the opportunity cost per lakh tonne of sugar for each move A→E, and state the pattern. (iii) The economy produces 9 lakh tonnes sugar and 20 million metres cloth. Name the position's class, compute its shortfall against C, and state one policy to cure it. (iv) A candidate claims: 'since the economy can produce E(13 sugar, 0 cloth), it should — sugar is sweeter.' Identify the two economic errors in the claim." (ICSE-style.)

A case description reads: 'A state with a fixed budget must choose between a mechanised dairy project (200 jobs) and a milk-collection cooperative network (1,100 jobs, lower output). Farmers' incomes in the district are among the lowest; the state funds the cooperative and simultaneously expands the ration quota in its villages.' File every datum in its grid — which problems and which cost concepts appear, and what each decision forgone.

(Evaluation) "Chapter 3 is the syllabus's operating system; Chapters 4–6 are programs that run on it." Evaluate the computing metaphor: what it captures about the relationship, where the metaphor strains, and the corrected formulation for a quiz banner.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Define opportunity cost and state the two properties that give rise to it. (ii) A weaver's week yields either 10 saris or 15 shawls; she weaves 6 saris and the rest shawls. Compute her opportunity costs and her output mix. (iii) For the economy: schedule M(0 steel, 100 food), N(10, 90), O(18, 70), P(24, 40), Q(28, 0); compute the opportunity cost of steel across successive moves and state the pattern. (iv) A candidate writes: 'since points inside the curve are safer, economies should produce there'. Identify and correct the two errors." (ICSE-style.)
Given Agriculture GVA = ₹28 lakh crore and Total GVA = ₹180 lakh crore, calculate agriculture’s GVA share.

**APPLICATION:** A state government plans to shift 5 % of its agricultural workforce to manufacturing by offering skill training. Using the employment‑share formula, estimate the new agricultural employment share if the total workforce remains 4 crore and current agricultural workers are 1.6 crore.

A farmer owns 1.5 hectares split into four strips, irrigates none of them, borrows from a moneylender at harvest-failure, and sells his wheat within days of the harvest. Show how the four facts interlock into one system, and state which two single changes would most loosen the knot.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Name any four problems of Indian agriculture, one line each. (ii) A farmer has 2 hectares in 4 strips, one tube-well serving 2 strips, sells paddy a week after harvest at 18 per cent below the season's later peak, and owes a moneylender Rs 60,000 at 5 per cent per month. (a) Name the problems the case displays. (b) Compute the yearly interest rate on the loan and state what it implies against a typical farm profit. (iii) State the single first measure you would advise, with the strand it unties. (iv) A candidate claims: 'irrigation alone would fix everything here'. Assess in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)
A farmer in Punjab switches from traditional wheat (yield 1.2 t/ha) to an HYV wheat (yield 3.5 t/ha) using the full input package. Calculate the percentage increase in yield.

**Application:** A farmer in Haryana wants to adopt a new HYV rice variety that promises 6 t/ha but requires 250 kg/ha of nitrogen fertiliser. Current practice yields 3.5 t/ha with 120 kg/ha nitrogen. If nitrogen costs ₹30/kg and rice sells at ₹15,000/tonne, should the farmer switch? Show calculations.
What does the National Food Security Act 2013 change about the status of food in India, and what are its headline entitlements?

(HOTS) "The NFSA's 67 per cent coverage is an admission of failure — a rich country would not need to subsidise two-thirds of its people." Critically examine: what the coverage figure actually reflects, what the criticism gets right about the destination, and why universal-coverage schemes are NOT automatically the better design.

(HOTS) Two states receive identical central grain allocations. State A delivers 92 per cent of entitlements to genuine card-holders; State B delivers 60 per cent, the rest leaking. Trace THREE upstream causes of the divergence and TWO downstream consequences — using the chain's language throughout.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Define food security and name its pillars. (ii) A district's fair-price shop receives 100 quintals monthly and issues 74 quintals against genuine cards; 20 quintals are found sold in the open market; 6 quintals spoil. (a) Compute the leakage and spoilage shares, and name the pillar-failure each represents. (b) State one instrument against each. (iii) The NFSA entitles a priority household of six to how much grain monthly, and at what prices? (iv) A candidate writes: 'with buffer stocks full, the district is food secure.' Correct in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Name the four families of adverse impacts of industrialisation. (ii) A leather-tanning cluster discharges untreated effluent into a river used downstream for irrigation and drinking. (a) Name the impact and the externality. (b) State two harms with their bearers. (iii) The same cluster employs 3,000 workers whose town council opposes a treatment-plant order fearing job losses. Assess the council's position in three sentences. (iv) A candidate writes: 'pollution is the price of progress; nothing can be done.' Identify the two errors." (ICSE-style.)

(Application) Your school is adopting an industrial neighbourhood for a service project. Design the ONE-PAGE 'Green Watch Card' — a pocket checklist a student pair can complete in a 30-minute walk: six checks (two water, one air, one waste, one worker-visible, one community) each with what-to-look-for and what-to-record; then the escalation line telling students what to do with a failed check.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) State the three environmental Acts with their years. (ii) A proposed cluster of 80 dyeing units awaits clearance near a river town. (a) Name the two pre-clearance instruments and the two operational instruments the cluster must carry. (b) For each, state the failure it prevents. (iii) The cluster promises 'self-regulation by members'. State the condition under which self-regulation can substitute for part of external monitoring. (iv) A candidate writes: 'treatment plants encourage pollution because they make polluting cheap.' Assess in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)
A rural household of 4 spends ₹3,200 per month on consumption. The official rural poverty line is ₹816 per capita per month. Determine if the household is below the poverty line.
Explain the concept of poverty line and describe how it is used to estimate the number of poor in India. (4 marks)

State the Head Count Ratio formula, compute it for a village with 2,000 people of whom 550 live below the poverty line, and interpret the result in one sentence each on the absolute and relative readings.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Define absolute poverty. (ii) A block has 40,000 people; 8,800 are below the poverty line. (a) Compute the poverty ratio showing all steps. (b) After five years, the block's incomes rise 20 per cent for every household. State and justify the effect of this rise on (1) absolute poverty, (2) relative poverty in the block. (iii) Name and draw the instrument that would reveal whether the block's income distribution has grown more unequal, labelling both axes and the reference line. (iv) A student claims: 'The block now has zero poverty since everyone's income rose.' Correct the claim in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)

Define unemployment through its three conditions, and classify as unemployed / out of the labour force / underemployed: (i) an 18-year-old registering at the employment exchange and searching daily; (ii) a 60-year-old retiree tending a garden; (iii) a farm hand who got only two days of paid work last week and sought more; (iv) a married woman who says she is not looking for paid work.
State three identifying features of seasonal unemployment, and explain how each distinguishes it from structural unemployment (node 005's subject, named here only by contrast).
Why do annual employment statistics understate seasonal unemployment, and how does daily-status measurement capture it? Illustrate with a labourer employed 240 days of a 365-day year.

Compute: a block has a labour force of 12,000, of whom 10,560 are working and 1,440 are unemployed and seeking. State the unemployment rate and the workforce; then explain in one sentence why the rate would rise if the same survey moved from annual status to daily status.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Define unemployment, stating its three conditions. (ii) A block's labour force is 20,000; 17,600 are working. (a) Compute the unemployment rate. (b) Of the unemployed, 1,200 are idle only between harvest and sowing. Name their type and the two features that identify it. (iii) Explain why an annual-status survey would record the 1,200 as employed. (iv) A candidate writes: 'Seasonal unemployment will end when the rains become regular.' Assess in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)

State the zero-marginal-product test for disguised unemployment, apply it to a family farm whose output by worker-number runs 0, 20, 34, 42, 44, 44 quintals for one to six hands, and identify the disguised-unemployed hands.

Compute and interpret: a district's labour force is 50,000; 6,000 are openly unemployed. The district's farms employ 30,000 workers, and a marginal-product survey finds 4,800 of them add zero output. State the open unemployment rate, the disguised unemployment on the farms, and the combined underutilised-labour share of the labour force.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Distinguish between seasonal and structural unemployment, one line each. (ii) The table shows output on a plot: 1 hand — 15 quintals; 2 — 28; 3 — 36; 4 — 40; 5 — 40. (a) Compute marginal products. (b) Which hands are disguised unemployed, and by what test? (iii) State two reasons why disguised unemployment is common on Indian family farms. (iv) A candidate writes: 'Removing the fifth hand will raise the farm's efficiency.' Assess in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)
A factory replaces 200 manual packers with an automated packing line that requires 20 technicians. Explain why this change represents capital‑labour substitution.

Apply the concept: A bank in Mumbai installs AI‑driven chatbots that handle 80 % of customer queries, reducing the need for call‑centre agents from 1,000 to 200. Identify the type of unemployment created and suggest one policy measure to mitigate it.

**Application:** A small‑scale food‑processing unit in Punjab plans to install a fully automated packaging line costing ₹2 crore, which will replace 30 manual packers earning ₹12,000 per month each. The machine’s annual operating cost (maintenance, electricity) is ₹15 lakh. Assuming a 10‑year machine life and a discount rate of 8 %, should the unit adopt the machine purely on labour‑cost savings? (Ignore taxes and salvage value.)

Compute and interpret: an economy enters the year with 40 million unemployed; the labour force grows by 8 million during the year; the economy creates 5.5 million jobs. State the year-end unemployment stock and the year's job-gap, and explain the accumulation logic across a decade of similar arithmetic.

(Application) A new district collector inherits a district with: (a) 30,000 farm families holding a disguised surplus; (b) two dying craft clusters; (c) a polytechnic graduating 400 a year with 60 placements; (d) public-works budget for one season. Design the ONE-PAGE Employment Compact: the four lines of spending matched to the four problems, each with its cause-target and its measurable one-year indicator; and the two-line sequencing rule that keeps the compact honest.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Name the two 'clocks' whose divergence explains persistent unemployment. (ii) An economy: labour force grows 9 million a year; jobs grow 6 million; stock 45 million. (a) Compute the job-gap and the stock after two years. (b) State the two conditions under which the stock begins to fall. (iii) Match each to its cause and face: silent handloom society; automation-heavy new mill; graduates without placements. (iv) A candidate writes: 'Since India's growth rate is now high, unemployment must be falling.' Assess in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)
A beneficiary receives a ₹30,000 loan at 4 % interest with a 25 % capital subsidy on the loan amount. Calculate the effective loan amount the beneficiary must repay.
Explain two major limitations of IRDP that led to its restructuring into the Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) in 1999.

**Application:** A district planner wants to allocate ₹50 lakh for a new IRDP‑style programme targeting 200 beneficiaries. Each beneficiary needs a ₹20,000 loan and a 30 % subsidy. Determine if the budget is sufficient and, if not, the shortfall.
Compare PKVY with IRDP (node 008) on three dimensions — unit of action, instrument, and income logic — and state what the comparison shows about the evolution of anti-poverty scheme design.

Compute and interpret: a 50-acre (20-hectare) PKVY cluster receives assistance of about Rs 50,000 per hectare over three years, with around Rs 31,000 per hectare directly to farmers for organic inputs. State the cluster's total assistance, the direct-to-farmer share, and the share retained for mobilisation, training and certification; then state one reason the direct share is deliberately the larger.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) What is the full form and objective of PKVY? (ii) A 20-hectare cluster: (a) compute total assistance at about Rs 50,000 per hectare over three years, and the direct-to-farmer amount at Rs 31,000 per hectare; (b) state what the remainder finances. (iii) State two features of PGS certification that suit small farmers. (iv) A candidate writes: 'Organic farming is useless because yields fall.' Assess in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)
Evaluate whether HRIDAY’s exclusive focus on 12 cities limits its impact on India’s overall heritage conservation.
A city planner in Ajmer receives ₹30 crore from the Centre under HRIDAY. How much must the State contribute, and what is the total project fund for that city?
A Gram Panchayat receives a demand for 30 workers for 20 days each. If the current wage rate is ₹250 per day, calculate the total wage bill the Panchayat must request from the Centre.
If a state government decides to increase the wage rate under MNREGA by 10% above the notified minimum wage, discuss the possible impact on the scheme’s budget and employment generation.
What were the three main pillars of India’s 1991 economic reforms?
Why did the Indian government pursue liberalisation in 1991?
**Evaluation/Critique:** “Digital India has failed because internet penetration in rural India is still below 40 %.” Critique this claim using two counter‑arguments.
**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** “Explain how the LPG reforms of 1991 contributed to the emergence of the Indian IT services industry. Give two specific policy changes and their impact.”

State the 1991 crisis conditions that forced the New Economic Policy, naming the trigger events and the reserve position, and explain why the response was structural reform rather than merely emergency borrowing.
Define the licence Raj and state its three costs; then name the 1991 measures under which each cost was buried.

Compute and interpret: before reform, an imported machine cost Rs 1,00,000 at world price with a 150 per cent customs duty; after liberalisation the duty fell to 30 per cent. (a) Compute the landed price before and after, and the percentage fall. (b) State one gain and one pressure the fall creates, and name the strand the measure belongs to.

(Application) Your school's commerce society mounts an exhibition: '1991 — The Year of the File'. Design the exhibit for one hall — FIVE stations, each dramatising one liberalisation strand through a BEFORE/AFTER artefact pair (what the citizen or producer held in 1990 versus 1995); then the one-panel epigraph panel whose single sentence the visitor should carry out.

(Evaluation) "India liberalised the FACTORIES but not the FACTORY ACTS; the 1991 package freed capital and left labour frozen." Evaluate this asymmetry doctrine: the case that labour-law rigidity is the unfinished liberalisation, the counter-case that labour protection is not a control but a floor, and the balanced formulation a policy examiner would mark.
Name any two methods of privatisation used by the Government of India since 1991.
In the context of the 1991 economic reforms, explain the role of the Disinvestment Commission and give one example of a strategic sale completed after 2014.
Explain the term ‘strategic disinvestment’ and illustrate with a recent Indian example. (3 marks)

Define the Balance of Trade and compute: a year's merchandise exports Rs 30 lakh crore, merchandise imports Rs 50 lakh crore; services exports (mainly software) earn Rs 25 lakh crore; remittances Rs 10 lakh crore. State the BOT, the effect of services and remittances on the external position, and the policy meaning of the financing pattern.

Compute and interpret: a special economic zone unit exports goods worth Rs 500 crore using imported inputs worth Rs 300 crore. State the value added retained in India, and explain why SEZs were designed as enclaves with special rules — the two design purposes — and the one criticism they attract.

(HOTS) "The border did not merely open; it THINNED." Examine: the three thicknesses the old border had, how each thinned after 1991, and the one border-thickness that remains by design — with the reason the design is right.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) Define globalisation, naming two of its flows. (ii) A year's data: goods exports 35, goods imports 48, services exports 22, remittances 8 (Rs lakh crore). (a) Define and compute BOT. (b) Compute the overall position (goods + services + remittances) and interpret. (iii) Name the world trade organisation India joined in 1995 and state one discipline membership imposes. (iv) A candidate writes: 'Globalisation means foreign companies buying Indian public-sector firms.' Assess in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)

Compute and interpret: the Mission provides Rs 500 crore per city from the Centre over five years, matched equally by the state. (a) Find the per-city total and the average annual outlay per city from both sources together. (b) For 100 cities, state the combined mission outlay. (c) State why the per-city sum is deliberately modest, and name the two levers the design expects the city to pull.

How do Digital India and Skill India complete the chapter's arc — what does each inherit from the 1991 pillars, and what does the 2015 trio (with the Smart City) add that the pillars alone never delivered?

Compute and interpret: a subsidy of Rs 300 per cylinder reaches 4 crore beneficiaries monthly. Under the old channel, leakage was estimated at one-fifth; under DBT, leakage is eliminated. (a) State the monthly leakage before DBT and the annual saving. (b) State one reason official cumulative DBT savings estimates run high across schemes, and one caveat to read them with.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) State Digital India's launch date and any two vision areas. (ii) Explain the JAM trinity with each component's role in DBT. (iii) A district pays 40,000 trainees a Rs 1,000 certification reward under PMKVY; the old informal route certified one-tenth of them. (a) Compute the total reward outgo; (b) state which PMKVY feature the reward is tied to and why. (iv) A candidate writes: 'Skill India will end unemployment by training everyone.' Assess in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)

Compute and interpret: an economy grows at 3.5 per cent per year (pre-reform trend) and then at 6.5 per cent (reform trend). Using the rule of thumb that doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate, (a) compute both doubling times; (b) state how many doublings separate a generation (say 35 years) under each trend; (c) interpret the gap in one sentence.

(Application) Your school must present a 'Thirty Years' exhibition corridor: five panels, one per chapter-node era (licence era, 1991 pillars, IT-globalisation decade, 2015 missions, the open road ahead). Design each panel's ONE artefact and ONE caption line (what it shows, what it teaches); then the corridor's closing panel — the single exhibit that summarises the whole walk.

(Evaluation) "India should now write a SECOND 1991 — for the state's own delivery machinery." Evaluate this second-reform doctrine: the diagnosis of the delivery gap, the two design principles a '1991 for the state' would carry, and the one danger of transplanting market vocabulary into state functions that the doctrine must avoid.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) State the trend growth shift the reforms achieved. (ii) A generation is 35 years. (a) Compute doubling times at 3.5% and 6.5% (rule of thumb 70 ÷ rate). (b) State the multiple of the starting size reached under each trend. (iii) Name two achievements and two unfinished areas of the reform era, one mechanism each. (iv) A candidate writes: 'Since inequality rose, the reforms failed the poor.' Assess in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)
Recite the chapter spine — each node's one-line contribution from 001 to 008 — and expand the chapter sentence with its four agenda items.

Compute and interpret the chapter's summary arithmetic: an economy of nominal GDP growing 6.5 per cent a year doubles in about 11 years; a scholarship flow of Rs 2.5 crore a month leaks one-eighth under the old channel and zero under DBT; a trade account shows goods exports 40, imports 55, services 20, remittances 9 (Rs lakh crore). State the three results and the one lesson each contributes to the chapter's verdict.

(HOTS) "Every generation writes its own definition of 'reform'; your syllabus carries two and is about to need a third." Examine: the 1991 definition of reform (removal), the 2015 definition (platform-building), and the third definition the chapter's open agenda demands — deriving it from the four agenda items, and stating the examinable test of whether a policy qualifies as reform under each definition.

(Past-paper pattern) "(i) State the chapter spine in one sentence. (ii) A mock paper: (a) classify with reasons — tariff cuts under WTO, a state hotel chain's sale, an Aadhaar-seeded pension credit; (b) compute — BOT with goods exports 30, goods imports 44, services 18, remittances 7 (Rs lakh crore), and the overall position. (iii) Name the four answer-skeletons this chapter teaches and match one chapter topic to each. (iv) A candidate writes: 'I know everything; the exam is just writing it out.' Assess in two sentences." (ICSE-style.)
