(Apply) In a circle with centre O, chord AB carries ∠OAB = 32°. (a) Find ∠AOB. (b) Find the angle subtended by AB at a point P on the major arc. (c) Find the angle at a point Q on the minor arc, and verify the two rim angles against each other.
(Create) Design a 4-mark question chaining the isosceles radii triangle, T-N1, and the same-segment transfer; give the scheme.

(CISCE exam-style) Prove that an angle in a semicircle is a right angle. Hence, AB is a diameter of a circle with centre O and radius 5 cm; C lies on the circle with AC = 6 cm. Find BC and the area of triangle ABC. [6]

(Application) A football coach marks a semicircular shooting arc of radius 9 m on the goal line's centre as diameter's midpoint — the goal posts are 7.2 m apart at A and B on the arc's base line? — clean: goal mouth AB = 7.2 m on the boundary circle of radius 9 m; a striker runs along the arc AB's segment. (a) At the arc's midpoint, what angle do the posts subtend at the striker? [3] (b) Does the angle change along the run? Name the theorem. [1] (c) The rival striker stands at the mirror point on the opposite arc: what angle, and what is the sum? [1] Marking scheme: (a) central angle: half-chord 3.6 ⟹ half-central = arcsin? — Class 9 route: the striker at the arc midpoint sits at distance 9 from centre O, and the perpendicular from O to AB meets its midpoint M with OM = √(81 − 12.96) = √68.04 ≈ 8.25 m — angle computation needs trigonometry, which Class 9 lacks; REPLACE numeric (a) with: striker S at the arc's midpoint of the MAJOR arc AB? — the honest fix: the question wants the THEOREM not the number: the angle is constant along the arc (C-N2), equal to half the central angle; numeric evaluation deferred to trigonometry. Accept: (a) angle = ½ × central ∠AOB, constant along the arc [1 T-N1 halving, 1 C-N2 constancy, 1 statement that the exact value needs the central angle from chord data]. (b) No — same segment ⟹ equal [1]. (c) The mirror point sees the supplement; sum 180° [1]. Design lesson: applied questions must respect the toolkit — theorems give relations, and lengths need Pythagoras-compatible data.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) In a circle with centre O, chords AB and CD are parallel and on opposite sides of O; M is the midpoint of arc AB? — clean: A, B, C, D lie on a circle with centre O; ∠AOB = 100° (arc AB), and C, D are points on the opposite arc with ∠COD = 60°. (a) Find the angle subtended by arc AB at a point P on the opposite arc. [2] (b) Find the angle subtended by arc CD at a point Q on arc AB's side. [2] (c) If P and Q are joined to form quadrilateral? — instead: state ∠APB + ∠CQD and justify with the arc bookkeeping. [2]
A chord of length 16 cm is at a distance of 6 cm from the centre of a circle. Find the radius of the circle.
A circular track has radius 25 m. A straight shortcut (chord) is made at a distance of 15 m from the centre. Find the length of the shortcut.
Create a problem where the chord length is 24 cm and the radius is 13 cm, and ask for the distance of the chord from the centre. Provide the solution.
In a circle of radius 17 cm, a chord is 30 cm long. Find its distance from the centre. Hence, find the length of another chord which is at a distance of 8 cm from the centre.
**QUESTION:** In a circle, two parallel chords of lengths 24 cm and 10 cm are on the same side of the centre. The distance between the chords is 7 cm. Find the radius of the circle.

**QUESTION:** A circular fountain of radius 10 m has a straight walkway (chord) at a distance of 6 m from the centre. Find the length of the walkway. If the walkway is widened to a strip of width 1 m on each side of the chord, approximate the area of the strip as a rectangle.
**QUESTION:** A student writes: “For a circle of radius 5 cm, a chord at distance 3 cm has length 2√((5² - 3²)) = 2√((25-9)) = 2√(16) = 8. Therefore the chord length is 8.” Critique this solution.

**QUESTION:** In the given figure, O is the centre of the circle. AB is a chord of length 24 cm. OM ⟂ AB. If OM = 5 cm, find the radius of the circle. Hence, find the length of chord CD which is at a distance of 12 cm from the centre.

(Evaluate) In radius 10, chords 16 and 12 are drawn. A student finds distances 6 and 8, then answers "separation = 14". Assess: is 14 ever right? What does the answer depend on? What additional datum would settle it, and what would the two full answers be?

(Apply) A circle of radius 13 cm carries two parallel chords, 10 cm and 24 cm, on opposite sides of the centre. (a) Find their separation. (b) Find the areas of the two radii-triangles and comment. (c) The same two chords moved to the same side: new separation?
(Create) Design a 5-mark question combining a cyclicity proof with a length computation; give the scheme.

(CISCE exam-style) In a circle of centre O and radius 13 cm, two parallel chords AB = 24 cm and CD = 10 cm lie on opposite sides of O. (a) Find the separation of the chords. [2] (b) AB is shifted (staying parallel, same length) until it passes through O: state its new identity and the new separation from CD. [2] (c) Find the area of triangle OCD and verify it against triangle OAB's area. [2]

(HOTS) Two chords of a circle, not parallel, intersect inside at X. The products XA·XB and XC·XD are claimed equal "because both equal r² − OX²". For Class 9: prove the special case where one chord is a diameter, and state what the general proof needs that Class 9 has not built.

(Application) A round tandoori roti of radius 9 cm is cut by two parallel chords of 14.4 cm? — clean: radius 9, chords 14.4? — use 9√? — keep triple-friendly: radius 15 cm, two parallel equal cuts of 24 cm, symmetric about the centre. (a) Find each cut's distance from the centre. (b) Find the middle strip's width and identify its shape. (c) A guest claims the two edge segments (beyond the cuts) are equal in area. Assess and justify.

(Evaluation) A student claims: "In the angle–length chain, after finding ∠ABC = 90°, the 30–60–90 ratios are needed; but since trigonometry comes later, exact lengths like 5√3 are not legitimately available at Class 9." Evaluate: what Class 9 instrument DOES certify BC = half-hypotenuse in a 30–60–90 triangle? Is AB = 5√3 certified without trigonometry? Where does the boundary of legitimacy lie?

(Comparison) Compare solving a two-chord problem by pure computation versus by theorem-verdict-first in four rows: the first written line, the error surface, the marks at risk, and the figure-type where each wins. Then write the hybrid script for a 6-marker.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) In a circle of centre O and radius 5 cm, AB is a chord with ∠OAB = 30°? — instead, the classic: ABCD is cyclic; AC is a diameter of 13 cm; ∠BAC = 30°? — with the 5–12–13 family: AC diameter 13? — set: AC = 26 cm diameter, ∠BAC = 30°. (a) Find ∠ABC and ∠ADC. [2] (b) Find BC and AB exactly. [2] (c) Given D is the mirror of B across AC (AB = CD? — with BD ⊥ AC), find the quadrilateral's area. [2]

(Reasoning) Assemble the full solution: in a circle of radius 20 cm, parallel chords 24 cm and 32 cm lie on opposite sides of the centre. Find their separation, identify the quadrilateral formed by joining the four endpoints in order IF the chords were equal, and state what figure the UNEQUAL pair actually forms.

(Evaluate) A question states: "A circle carries three chords whose minor arcs have central angles 150°, 140°, and 120°." A student begins computing chord lengths. Evaluate: what should happen BEFORE any computation, what is the arithmetic verdict, and what would make the data realizable?

(Apply) In a circle of radius 13, ∠OAB = α for chord AB, with the right triangle 5–12–13 at the chord's midpoint. (a) Express ∠AOB in terms of α. (b) Express the rim angle ∠APB (P on the major arc) in terms of α. (c) Given α is the angle of a 5–12–13 triangle at the 5-side? — state what more is needed for a numeric α, and why Class 9 stops there.
(Create) Design a 6-mark mixed question that chains the right-triangle engine, the angle family, and the cyclicity test; give the scheme with every mark mapped.

(CISCE exam-style) In a circle of centre O and radius 10 cm, chord AB = 16 cm is placed on one side of O, and chord CD = 12 cm on the opposite side. (a) Find both distances and the separation. [2] (b) AB and CD are each shifted toward O by 1 cm (lengths unchanged): state their new distances and the new separation. [2] (c) A student claims the shifted configuration has the chords "meeting at the centre" — assess. [2]

(HOTS) A question-setter proposes: "Chords AB, BC, CA of a circle have lengths 10, 10, 16 with radius 9? — radius 10. Verify realizability by the angle budget: compute the three arcs' central angles' FEASIBILITY without trigonometry, using only the distance ordering."

(Application) In a 30-minute window: Q1 "find the distance of a 16 cm chord in a circle of radius 10" [2]; Q2 "prove equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre" [3]; Q3 "two parallel chords 16 and 12 on opposite sides, radius 10 — separation?" [3]; Q4 "prove the angle in a semicircle is 90°" [3]; Q5 "cyclic quad ∠A = 2∠C — find both" [2]; Q6 "radius 5, ∠OAB = 30°, AC diameter — find BC" [3]. Allocate minutes; name engines.

(Comparison) Compare the chapter's two verification stamps — the 2r collapse (a computed length landing exactly on the diameter) and the 180° budget (angle sums landing on the total) — in four rows: what each certifies, the configurations each fits, a failure each can MISS, and the cost of running each. Then write the audit-selection rule for a 6-marker with both lengths and angles.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) ABCD is cyclic with centre O; AC is a diameter of 26 cm; chord AB = 24 cm. (a) Find BC. [2] (b) Find the distance of AB from O. [2] (c) Find the distance from O to chord BC. [2] (d) ∠BAC? — instead: given ∠BAC satisfies sin ∠BAC = BC/AC? — final: express ∠BOC as twice ∠BAC and state what extra tool yields its degree value. [2]

A teacher records the heights (cm) of 25 students: 140, 142, 145, 147, 148, 150, 152, 152, 153, 155, 156, 158, 160, 162, 163, 165, 165, 167, 168, 170, 172, 173, 175, 178, 180. Construct a grouped frequency distribution with class width 10 starting at 135.
Create a scenario where arrayed data is more useful than grouped data for a Class 9 project.

In a CISCE ICSE Class 9 exam, a question asks: “The following data shows the number of books read by 20 students in a month: 3, 5, 2, 7, 4, 6, 5, 3, 8, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 3, 4, 5, 6, 2, 3. Prepare an arrayed data set and then a grouped frequency distribution with class intervals 1‑3, 4‑6, 7‑9.” Provide the final grouped frequency table.

A data set of 50 students’ marks (out of 100) is to be grouped. The teacher proposes class intervals 0‑10, 11‑20, 21‑30, …, 91‑100. Identify the flaw in this proposal and suggest a corrected set of class intervals.

A researcher records the number of pages in 30 novels: 120, 135, 142, 158, 167, 173, 180, 195, 210, 225, 230, 245, 260, 275, 280, 295, 310, 325, 340, 355, 370, 385, 400, 415, 430, 445, 460, 475, 490, 505. Construct a grouped frequency distribution with 6 classes of equal width.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** The marks obtained by 40 students in a Mathematics test are given below: 42, 35, 48, 50, 44, 38, 45, 40, 47, 41, 39, 43, 46, 49, 37, 44, 42, 45, 48, 50, 36, 40, 41, 43, 44, 46, 47, 49, 38, 39, 42, 45, 48, 50, 37, 40, 41, 43, 44, 46. (i) Arrange the marks in ascending order. (ii) Form a grouped frequency distribution with class intervals 35‑39, 40‑44, 45‑49, 50‑54. (iii) State the modal class.

(Evaluate) A student's table for the 12 scores shows: 6 → 2, 7 → 3, 8 → 4, 9 → 3, 10 → 1, claiming Σf = 13 "because the raw data had twelve entries and one must have been double-counted in the tally". Diagnose fully: what does Σf = 13 prove, what is the correct response, and is "one must have been double-counted" an acceptable conclusion?
(Apply) Convert to a frequency table: the shoe sizes of 18 boys: 6, 7, 6, 8, 7, 6, 9, 7, 8, 6, 7, 8, 6, 9, 7, 6, 8, 7. Include the tally column and the Σf audit.
(Create) Design a 4-mark question that tests tally construction AND table reading in one data-set; give the scheme.

(CISCE exam-style) The number of absentees over 25 school days: 0, 2, 1, 0, 3, 2, 0, 1, 4, 0, 2, 1, 0, 2, 3, 0, 1, 5, 0, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0. (a) Tabulate with tally marks. [3] (b) State Σf and the number of days with at least 2 absentees. [2]

(Application) A railway counter logs ticket refunds per hour: 0, 1, 0, 2, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 2, 1, 0, 3, 0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0. (a) Tabulate with audit. (b) The stationmaster wants "at least half the hours refund-free" verified: use the table. (c) The peak hour is double any other single-hour count? — instead: state whether any hour had more refunds than the modal count, from the table alone.

(Evaluation) A student claims: "Tallying is obsolete — computers count instantly, so the skill has no value." Evaluate: what does the tally discipline train that survives automation, where does the human tally still operate in real Indian settings, and what is the correct status of the skill in a Class 9 course?

(CISCE past-paper pattern) The daily wages (rupees) of 30 workers: 150, 200, 150, 250, 150, 200, 300, 150, 200, 250, 150, 200, 150, 250, 200, 150, 300, 200, 150, 250, 200, 150, 200, 150, 250, 200, 150, 200, 250, 150. (a) Tabulate with tally and audit. [3] (b) State the modal wage and the number earning at least ₹200. [2] (c) What fraction earns below ₹250? [1]

(Reasoning) Apply the in-between probe to classify: (a) number of rooms per house; (b) daily maximum temperature; (c) shoe sizes including halves; (d) the exact times (in seconds) of 100-metre races recorded to two decimals. Justify each in one line.

(Evaluate) A student builds a grouped distribution for the 20 family-size entries: classes 1–2 (11), 3–4 (7), 5–6 (2). The arithmetic checks (Σf = 20 ✓), yet the presentation is wrong for the purpose "how many families have exactly 2 children?" Evaluate: what is lost, what data support the exact answer, and when WOULD the grouped form be right for a discrete variate?

(Apply) Heights (cm) of 20 seedlings: 23, 27, 31, 25, 28, 34, 22, 29, 26, 30, 24, 32, 27, 21, 33, 26, 28, 25, 30, 29. (a) Classify the variate. (b) Build classes 20–25, 25–30, 30–35 by counting entries (count 25 in the class that Announces its upper end — the 25–30 class takes it). (c) Audit Σf.
(Create) Design a 4-mark question that tests classification AND the matching rule on four variates; give the scheme.

(CISCE exam-style) The number of wickets taken by a bowler in 30 matches: 1, 2, 0, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 4, 1, 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 0, 2, 1, 2, 1, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2. (a) Classify the variate and name the distribution you will build. [1] (b) Build it with audit. [3] (c) State the matches with at least 2 wickets. [2]

(HOTS) A data file records journey times only as whole minutes (12, 14, 17 …), yet a student classifies the variate as discrete "because every entry is an integer". Another says "continuous — but then why do no half-minutes appear?" Resolve both, and state the general principle about recorded data that resolves the tension.

(Application) A ration shop logs daily sugar sales in kg with decimals: 42.5, 38.0, 51.2, 45.75, … over a month. (a) Classify and choose the form with classes 35–40, 40–45, 45–50, 50–55 (shared values UP). (b) Given frequencies 4, 9, 11, 6 — audit against 30 days. (c) The shopkeeper asks "did we ever sell exactly 45 kg?" — answer from the grouped table, and state what the ungrouped record could answer.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) The weights (kg) of 25 cartons: 41.2, 47.8, 43.5, 52.1, 45.0, 49.3, 44.7, 51.6, 46.2, 48.9, 42.8, 50.4, 45.9, 47.3, 43.1, 49.8, 46.5, 52.7, 44.2, 48.1, 47.0, 45.4, 50.8, 46.9, 43.9. (a) Classify the variate and state the form. [1] (b) Tabulate into classes 40–44, 44–48, 48–52, 52–56 with the shared-value-UP convention and audit. [3] (c) State the modal class and the number of cartons below 48 kg. [2]

(Reasoning) The wickets table of a bowler over 30 matches: 0→6, 1→9, 2→10, 3→4, 4→1. (a) Compute the mean with the frequency form. (b) Compute the median by cumulative positions. (c) Both came out 1.5 — explain why that coincidence is unremarkable for discrete count data.

(Evaluate) A shop's daily sales (₹ hundreds): 42, 45, 41, 44, 43, 46, 42, 130. The manager reports "average sales ₹4,912" (mean) to the bank. Evaluate the report: compute both measures, state what each claims, and judge which is the defensible "average day" for a loan officer deciding repayment capacity.

(Apply) (a) The mean of six observations is 18; five of them are 15, 20, 16, 19, 22. Find the sixth. (b) Every observation is then increased by 5 — state the new mean and new median without recomputing, with reasons. (c) Each observation is doubled — state both new measures.
(Create) Design a 4-mark question that tests the combined-mean trap and its correction on two sections of a class; give the marking scheme and the distractor the wrong answer falls into.

(CISCE exam-style) A batsman's scores in 10 innings: 0, 5, 8, 12, 20, 24, 31, 45, 58, 107. (a) Find the mean score. [2] (b) Find the median score. [2] (c) The batsman claims "my average is 31" while the coach reports 22 — decide which figure better represents the innings and justify. [2]

(HOTS) The mean monthly rainfall of a city computed from 12 monthly values is 8 cm. A geography textbook reports "the median monthly rainfall is also 8 cm". A student argues: "If the mean is 8, the median must be 8 — the centre is the centre." Assess the argument: exhibit a 5-value data set with mean 8 and median different from 8, and state the correct general relationship between the two measures.

(Application) A battery plant quality log records cell lifetimes (hundreds of hours): 46, 48, 44, 47, 45, 46, 48, 47, 46, 240. (a) Compute mean and median. (b) The marketing team wants a number for "typical life" — advise which to publish and why. (c) The 240 entry is traced to a data-entry slip (should be 24): recompute both and state the lesson about medians and single-value errors.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) Seven plants' heights (cm): 12, 18, 9, 15, 21, 10, 20. (a) Find the mean height. [2] (b) Find the median height. [2] (c) Each plant grows exactly 5 cm in the next month; state the new mean and new median with reasons. [2]

(Reasoning) For the classes 10–20, 20–30, 30–40, 40–50 (exclusive): (a) state the width and all four class marks; (b) verify the spacing identity; (c) a value of exactly 30 is recorded — state which class receives it and why a convention is needed at all.

(Evaluate) A student tabulates daily temperatures (a continuous variate) into the classes 10–20, 21–30, 31–40, claiming "gaps prevent double-counting, so this form is safer". Evaluate the claim: what the gap form breaks for continuous data, when gaps are legitimate, and what the correct safeguard against double-counting is.

(Apply) Marks of 30 students (out of 50): 23, 31, 27, 42, 36, 25, 44, 29, 38, 22, 33, 27, 41, 35, 26, 30, 37, 24, 46, 28, 32, 39, 25, 43, 34, 21, 36, 31, 47, 30. Build classes 20–25, 25–30, 30–35, 35–40, 40–45, 45–50 with shared values going UP; tally with audit; compute all six class marks.
(Create) Design a 4-mark question that gives class marks and requires backward reconstruction of classes plus a width statement; give the scheme and the check that certifies the reconstruction.

(CISCE exam-style) The heights (cm) of 40 students are grouped as: 140–145: 4, 145–150: 9, 150–155: 13, 155–160: 8, 160–165: 4, 165–170: 2. (a) State the class width and write the class marks. [2] (b) A student is exactly 155 cm tall — name her class and justify with the convention. [1] (c) How many students are below 155 cm? What percentage measure at least 160 cm? [2]

(HOTS) A data set of 60 wages spans ₹120 to ₹980. A student proposes "10 classes of width 86" to use the exact trial width 860/10, producing classes 120–206, 206–292 … A second proposes "8 classes of width 110" starting at 100: 100–210, 210–320 … Evaluate both designs against the construction rules and state which is the better table and why.

(Application) A weather station must tabulate 90 daily maximum temperatures (a continuous variate, °C) spanning 18.4 to 39.7. (a) Choose the number of classes and a workable width with reasons. (b) Write the classes in the correct form. (c) The station's report template asks for "the mean temperature" — state exactly what the grouped table can and cannot supply, and which node's machinery the honest answer defers to.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) The weights (kg) of 60 parcels are grouped: 2–4: 8, 4–6: 15, 6–8: 20, 8–10: 12, 10–12: 5. (a) Write the class marks and verify the spacing identity. [2] (b) A parcel weighs exactly 6 kg — name its class under the up-convention, and state how many parcels are lighter than 8 kg. [2] (c) The dispatcher claims "the modal class means most parcels weigh about 7 kg" — assess. [2]

(Reasoning) The inclusive table: 0–9: 5, 10–19: 8, 20–29: 15, 30–39: 9, 40–49: 3. (a) Compute d and write all five boundary pairs. (b) Verify all three invariants. (c) State, in half-open notation, exactly which values the class 20–29 contains.

(Evaluate) A student computes the width of the inclusive class 31–40 as 40 − 31 = 9, uses 9 as the class width for every class, and proceeds to later computations. Evaluate: what the true width is, which computations silently mis-scale if 9 is used, and why the error survives a Σf audit.

(Apply) Working on the boundary grid of DQ2 (−0.5–9.5 … 39.5–49.5; frequencies 5, 8, 15, 9, 3): (a) Which class contains a score of exactly 29.5, and which a score of 29? (b) How many observations are below 29.5? (c) How many lie in [9.5, 29.5)? (d) Can the table answer "did any student score exactly 24.5"?
(Create) Design a 4-mark question that gives an inclusive table and requires conversion, invariant verification, and one boundary-based count; give the scheme and the most valuable single mark.

(CISCE exam-style) The weights (kg) of 50 cartons: 20–24: 7, 25–29: 13, 30–34: 18, 35–39: 9, 40–44: 3. (a) State the adjustment factor and write the boundary pairs. [2] (b) State which class holds a carton of exactly 29.5 kg and justify. [1] (c) How many cartons weigh at least 29.5 kg? What percentage is that? [2]

(HOTS) A student converts the exclusive height table (140–145: 4, 145–150: 9 …) by the inclusive recipe "subtract 0.5 from lower limits, add 0.5 to upper limits", producing 139.5–145.5 etc., and defends it: "conversion is always the same recipe." Diagnose the error precisely: what the recipe assumes, why it fails here, and what the correct boundary statement for this table is.

(Application) A school's record system stores marks (integer percentages, 0–100) and must produce, for a government proforma, (a) a grouped table suitable for median interpolation, (b) the count of students "below 33" (a pass-boundary report), given raw marks. Design the table: state the class form you choose, the boundaries, and the exact fence whose class-count answers "below 33" without convention ambiguity — and state what you do about the student with exactly 33.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) Marks of 50 students: 0–10: 6, 11–20: 12, 21–30: 18, 31–40: 10, 41–50: 4. (a) Write the boundary grid and verify it meets. [2] (b) State the class containing the 25th observation's class WITHOUT computing the median, with the cumulative reading shown. [2] (c) How many students scored below 30.5, and why can the table not tell whether anyone scored exactly 30? [2]

(Reasoning) On the heights table (4, 9, 13, 8, 4, 2 across 140–145 … 165–170): compute the mean by BOTH routes and explain algebraically why they cannot disagree; state what the 0.625 correction term in the assumed-mean route represents.

(Evaluate) A student computes the mean of the heights table as (142.5 + 147.5 + 152.5 + 157.5 + 162.5 + 167.5)/6 = 930/6 = 155 cm. Evaluate: the error, what the 155 happens to measure, and the reason the unweighted average drifts from the weighted one here.

(Apply) The wages table (₹): 151–200: 8, 201–250: 17, 251–300: 21, 301–350: 10, 351–400: 4 (n = 60). With boundaries 150.5–200.5 … 350.5–400.5 and marks 175.5 … 375.5: (a) compute the mean; (b) name the modal class; (c) locate the median class and compute the interpolated median.
(Create) Design a 6-mark question chaining construction, conversion and all three statistics on one data set; give the scheme with every mark mapped to a named move.

(CISCE exam-style) For the heights table (140–145: 4, 145–150: 9, 150–155: 13, 155–160: 8, 160–165: 4, 165–170: 2): (a) State the modal class and the number of students below 155 cm. [2] (b) Compute the estimated mean height. [2] (c) A summary claims "half the students are taller than 153.1 cm" — assess using the interpolated median. [2]

(HOTS) The class 150–155 (f = 13) in the heights table: exhibit a within-class configuration of the 13 heights for which the true mean of those 13 differs from the class mark 152.5 by nearly h/2, compute the resulting shift in the FULL table's estimated mean, and state the bound that confines any such configuration.

(Application) A city bus authority must publish ONE number for "typical waiting time" from a grouped table of 200 waits (0–2 min: 44, 2–4: 62, 4–6: 48, 6–8: 30, 8–10: 16). (a) Compute the estimated mean and the interpolated median. (b) Choose the publication number and defend it against the alternative. (c) The authority also wants "90% of waits are under X minutes" — compute X from the table, stating its exactness tier.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) Marks of 50 candidates: 0–10: 6, 11–20: 12, 21–30: 18, 31–40: 10, 41–50: 4. (a) Write the boundary grid and the class marks. [2] (b) Estimate the mean marks. [2] (c) Estimate the median marks by interpolation and verify that it lies inside the median class's fences. [2]

(Reasoning) Route each one-liner to its region and node, naming the formula that opens it: (a) "Find the area of the triangular park with sides 40 m, 41 m, 9 m." (b) "How much sheet metal makes a closed cylindrical drum of radius 30 cm and height 1 m?" (c) "A metallic cube of edge 6 cm is melted and recast into a cuboid 8 cm × 9 cm × h cm; find h." (d) "Find the cost of fencing a circular garden of radius 21 m at ₹50 per metre."

(Evaluate) Three student answers arrive: (i) "Volume of the cuboid = 2(8×6 + 6×5 + 8×5) = 236 cm³"; (ii) "Area of the circle = 2πr²"; (iii) "The tank holds 60000 litres." Each contains one specific error — identify the error, the correct statement, and the fastest audit that catches each.

(Apply) One taste per region, executed: (a) Heron for sides 12, 12, 12. (b) Sector preview: the cost of turfing a circular field of radius 14 m at ₹45 per m². (c) A closed cuboidal box 25 cm × 20 cm × 10 cm: total sheet area and capacity in litres.
(Create) Design a 4-mark "map" question that tests routing and unit discipline across all three regions without heavy arithmetic; give the scheme.

(CISCE exam-style) A rectangular card 18 cm × 12 cm carries a design made of a circle of radius 7 cm at its centre. (a) Name the region(s) engaged. [1] (b) Find the area of the card NOT covered by the circle. [3] (c) State the perimeter of the card and the circumference of the circle, and verify both are 1-D quantities. [2]

(HOTS) The chapter's three solids (cube, cuboid, cylinder) all admit "hollow" versions, and hollow problems flip which formula is priced. Take a hollow cylindrical tube open at both ends, r = 10, h = 21: state which surfaces exist, compute the metal used, and explain why the volume formula πr²h answers the WRONG question for a hollow tube (and what the right 3-D question even is at this stage).

(Application) A 3-hour exam carries this chapter as: Q1 Heron 3 marks, Q2 circle cost 3 marks, Q3 cube-cuboid table 4 marks, Q4 cylinder capacity 4 marks, Q5 composite solid 5 marks (19 marks total). Allocate minutes at ~1.2 min/mark, name each question's region, and state which two questions most need the two-route audit and why.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A cuboidal water tank is 6 m long, 5 m wide and 4.5 m deep, open at the top. (a) Find the capacity of the tank in litres. [2] (b) Find the area of the iron sheet required for the tank (base and four walls), ignoring overlap. [2] (c) The tank's water surface drops 0.5 m after a day's use; how many litres were drawn? [2]

(Reasoning) For the 13-14-15 triangle: (a) compute the area by Heron; (b) reconstruct the altitude on the 14-side and verify the area by ½bh; (c) find where the altitude's foot falls on the 14-side and state what the two flanking right triangles prove.

(Evaluate) A student computes the area of the 3-4-5 triangle as s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c) = 6 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 36 cm², quoting "the formula's job is done — the root is decoration since 36 is already nice". Evaluate: the exact error, the dimension argument that convicts it, and what the missing root would have returned.

(Apply) An isosceles triangle has equal sides 12 cm and base 8 cm. (a) Compute its area by Heron. (b) Verify by the altitude route. (c) The triangle is scaled by 3 (all sides ×3): state the new area without recomputing, and explain the scaling law.

(Create) Design a 4-mark question where a quadrilateral's area must be assembled from one right triangle and one Heron triangle, with a fence-cost rider; give the scheme and the distractor built into the data.

(CISCE exam-style) A triangular wall has sides 122 m, 120 m and 22 m. (a) Find its area. [3] (b) Turfing the wall's face costs ₹9 per m² — find the total cost. [1] (c) Verify the area by an independent route or state the strongest internal check available. [1]

(HOTS) Heron's formula is sometimes written without s as 16A² = (a + b + c)(−a + b + c)(a − b + c)(a + b − c). (a) Verify this identity on the 13-14-15 triangle. (b) Explain what each bracket is, relative to s. (c) Use the identity to prove the triangle inequality's necessity: show that if one side equals the other two summed, the area MUST be zero — and what that degenerate "triangle" is.

(Application) A traffic island is the 13-14-15 triangle (area 84 m²). (a) The council paints the island's border strip first: find the PERIMETER and state its unit class. (b) The island's longest side borders the main road; compute the altitude onto it. The council places a lamp at the altitude's foot on the 14 m side — how far is the lamp from each end of that side? (c) Resurfacing the whole island costs ₹350 per m² — find the cost.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A quadrilateral field ABCD has AB = 24 m, BC = 7 m, CD = 26 m, DA = 17 m and diagonal AC = 25 m. (a) Find the area of the field. [4] (b) Find the cost of fencing it at ₹12 per metre. [1] (c) The owner instead claims the diagonal should be fenced too "for strength" — find the extra cost and state whether the original (a) changes. [1]
A student calculates the circumference of a circle of radius 5 cm as 15.7 cm. Evaluate the answer.
Find the radius of a circle whose area is 154 cm² (use π = 22/7).
A circular running track has inner radius 20 m and outer radius 25 m. Find the area of the track (use π = 3.14).
A square and a circle have the same perimeter of 44 cm. Which figure has the larger area, and by how much? (Use π = 22/7)
A wheel of diameter 70 cm makes 200 revolutions per minute. Find the speed of the vehicle in km/h (use π = 22/7).
Critique the following solution: “Area of a circle of radius 5 cm = 2πr = 2×3.14×5 = 31.4 cm².”
Compare the results of calculating the area of a circle of radius 14 cm using π = 22/7 and π = 3.14. Which is more accurate for ICSE examinations?
ICSE 2023 pattern: “The circumference of a circle exceeds its diameter by 30 cm. Find the radius of the circle (take π = 22/7).”

(Reasoning) A cube has edge 6 cm. (a) Produce all five measures. (b) One face is left unpainted — state which formula changes and recompute the paint. (c) Two such cubes are glued face-to-face into a 6 × 6 × 12 box — state the new surface WITHOUT recomputing from scratch, with reasoning.

(Apply) An open-top cubic water tank has edge 2 m. (a) Find the tin sheet for its five faces. (b) Find its capacity in litres. (c) Painting the sheet (inside only) costs ₹15 per m² — find the bill, and state why "inside only" does not double the area here.
(Create) Design a 5-mark question that gives one measure of an unknown cube and demands two other measures plus a cost rider; give the scheme and name the inversion each mark tests.

(CISCE exam-style) Three solid metallic cubes of edges 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm are melted and recast into a single cube. (a) Find the new edge. [3] (b) Compare the new total surface with the sum of the three old surfaces, and state the change with its amount. [2]

(HOTS) A cube's body diagonal and its face diagonal differ by exactly 2 cm (body − face = 2). (a) Show that a√3 − a√2 = 2 forces a = 2/(√3 − √2) and rationalise to find a exactly. (b) Compute the cube's volume in exact surd form. (c) State why the answer, though surd-edged, is a perfectly valid cube.

(Application) A cold-storage room is a cube of edge 5 m. (a) Its walls and ceiling are insulated (floor not): find the insulated area. (b) Vinyl flooring is laid on the floor only at ₹250 per m² — find the cost. (c) The room's air-conditioning spec is quoted per cubic metre — state the volume figure and its litre equivalent. (d) A wire must run along the body diagonal from a floor corner to the opposite ceiling corner — find that length exactly.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A closed cubical box has total surface area 726 cm². (a) Find its edge. [2] (b) Find the length of the longest stick that fits inside it. [2] (c) Find the cost of painting it inside and out at ₹5 per 100 cm². [2]

(Reasoning) On the box 10 × 8 × 6: (a) produce all four measures; (b) explain why TSA − LSA = 2lb here and what that difference MEANS; (c) verify the diagonal by the two-step route with both intermediate values.

(Evaluate) A student, told the box 10 × 8 × 6 is "almost a cube", computes TSA as 6 × 8² = 384 cm² "since 8 is the average-ish edge". Evaluate: the correct TSA, the source of the student's error, the size of the miss, and the general lesson about approximating cuboids by cubes.

(Apply) A hall 8 m × 6 m × 4 m is white-washed on its four walls and ceiling. It has one door 2 m × 1 m and two windows each 2 m × 1.5 m, which are excluded. (a) Find the white-washed area. (b) At ₹12 per m², find the cost. (c) The hall's air volume in litres, as a facility-size check.
(Create) Design a 5-mark question: a cuboidal tank (open top) with capacity, sheet area, and fill-time riders; give the scheme and the unit traps planted.

(CISCE exam-style) A cuboidal box measures 60 cm × 40 cm × 30 cm. (a) Find its total surface area and capacity in litres. [3] (b) Find the length of the longest rod it can contain. [1] (c) How many cubes of edge 5 cm can be packed in it? [2]

(HOTS) A cuboid's three dimensions are in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1 and its volume is 162 cm³. (a) Find the dimensions. (b) Find its TSA. (c) Explain why the ratio-plus-volume data fix the box completely, while ratio alone (or volume alone) does not.

(Application) A water tank is 3 m × 2 m × 1.5 m, open at the top. (a) Its capacity in litres. (b) The sheet for its five faces. (c) It fills through a pipe at 50 litres per minute; a family draws 300 litres daily — find the minutes of inflow needed per day, and the water level (depth) after exactly one hour of inflow into the EMPTY tank.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A cuboidal box is 50 cm long, 35 cm wide and 20 cm high. (a) Find its capacity in litres and its total surface area. [3] (b) State the length of the longest pole that can be placed inside the box. [2]

(Reasoning) For the cylinder r = 14 cm, h = 5 cm: (a) compute CSA, TSA and V exactly with π = 22/7; (b) verify the TSA by the two-piece route (wall + lids); (c) state the cylinder's TSA − CSA and match it to its geometric meaning.

(Evaluate) A student computes the sheet metal for a closed cylindrical drum (r = 7, h = 10) as πr²h = 1540 cm², quoting "area is area — the volume formula just happens to use the same letters". Evaluate: what the student computed, what the drum needs, why the letters mislead, and the one-question test that prevents the swap.

(Apply) An open-top cylindrical water tank has radius 3.5 m and depth 2 m. (a) Find the sheet for its base and curved wall. (b) Find its capacity in litres. (c) Water enters at 700 litres per minute — find the filling time from empty.
(Create) Design a 5-mark question on a road roller: sheet, revolution coverage, and a cost rider; give the scheme and the unit bridge the middle mark tests.

(CISCE exam-style) A closed cylindrical tin has radius 21 cm and height 5 cm. (a) Find its capacity in litres. [2] (b) Find the sheet metal in it. [2] (c) An open pan is made to the same dimensions — how much LESS sheet does it use? [1]

(HOTS) Two closed cylinders are compared: A has r = 7, h = 10; B has r = 14, h = 5 — B's CSA alone (2π × 14 × 5 = 440) exactly matches A's, but its lids differ. (a) Compute both cylinders' volumes and sheet areas exactly. (b) Explain, through the r versus r² structure, why the wider-flatter cylinder holds double the capacity at equal WALL area, and what the sheet budget actually equalises between them. (c) State the boundary of this reasoning: what it does NOT claim about optimality.

(Application) A factory must ship 1000 closed cans, each r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm. (a) Sheet metal for one can and the total order (in m²). (b) The cans ship packed upright in cuboidal cartons 42 cm × 42 cm × 10 cm: how many cans per carton, and why does the carton's height matching the can's matter? (c) One can's paint (outside, closed) at ₹0.02 per cm² — find the per-can and total bill.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A cylindrical vessel of height 40 cm holds 6.16 litres. (a) Find its radius. [2] (b) Find its curved surface area. [1] (c) It is to be made as an open vessel — find the sheet required. [2]

(Reasoning) The pipe: h = 14, R = 5, r = 4 (cm). (a) Compute the material volume and the outer and inner curved surfaces. (b) Compute the end-ring area and the pipe's total surface. (c) Verify the material volume by computing both cylinders separately and subtracting — and state why the two routes must agree.

(Evaluate) A student computes a drilled block's remaining volume (20 × 20 × 10 with an r = 7 hole through) as 4000 + 1540 = 5540 cm³ "the block plus the drilled cylinder — drilling adds material". Evaluate: the error's direction, what drilling actually does to volume and to surface, and the sentence that separates the two.

(Apply) Complete the drilled-block run: block 20 × 20 × 10, hole r = 7 through the 10 cm dimension. (a) Remaining volume. (b) Total surface after drilling. (c) The hole is then plugged with a cylindrical stopper fitting exactly (r = 7, h = 10) — state the block's volume and surface AFTER plugging.
(Create) Design a 6-mark question chaining thickness, recasting and a rate; give the scheme with each mark mapped to a named move.

(CISCE exam-style) An open cylindrical cistern has radius 7 m and depth 2 m. (a) Find its capacity in litres. [2] (b) Water flows in at 700 litres per minute; find the filling time from empty, in hours and minutes. [2] (c) Find the masonry surface to be cemented (base + inner wall). [2]

(HOTS) A hollow pipe's material volume is πh(R² − r²). (a) Derive the formula from two full cylinders. (b) Show what happens as r → R (the wall thins to nothing) and as r → 0 (the hole closes): do both limits return sensible solids? (c) The formula's shape suggests a shortcut: material volume = cross-section ring area × length — state why this is not a shortcut but a restatement, and when it becomes the FASTER route (long pipes, tabulated ring areas).

(Application) A tank is a cuboid 4 m × 3 m × 2 m with an open top; it fills from a pipe at 400 L/min while a cleaning drain leaks 40 L/min. (a) Find the tank's capacity in litres. (b) Find the NET filling rate and the time to fill from empty. (c) After filling, the inlet is closed and the drain is opened fully (now 60 L/min): find the depth after 5 hours of draining.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A cylindrical well has an inner radius 3.5 m and depth 10 m. (a) Find the capacity of water it can hold, in litres. [2] (b) The inner curved wall and floor are to be cemented at ₹45 per m² — find the cost. [2] (c) Water stands at a depth of 4 m; find the volume of water in litres and the empty height remaining. [2]

(Reasoning) Assemble the full solution: a triangular plot has sides 33 m, 44 m, 55 m. (a) Find its area by Heron. [2] (b) Recognise the cheaper engine available and recompute — state both values. [2] (c) The plot's longest side fronts a road; find the altitude onto it and the cost of fencing the whole plot at ₹20 per metre. [2]

(Evaluate) A question states: "A closed cube has volume 216 cm³ and total surface area 500 cm². Find its edge." A student begins solving 6a² = 500. Evaluate: what should happen BEFORE any computation, the audit verdict on each given, and the two consistent corrections the question could have carried.

(Apply) One chain, three engines: a cuboidal godown is 12 m × 8 m × 6 m. (a) Find its capacity in kilolitres. [1] (b) How many crates of 2 m × 1 m × 1 m stack in it (upright, aligned)? [2] (c) Its four walls are repainted at ₹5 per m² — find the bill. [1] (d) State the audit linking (a) and (b). [2]
(Create) Design a 6-mark mixed question that chains Heron, a cylinder, and a rate; give the scheme with every mark mapped.

(CISCE exam-style) A wooden block 24 cm × 12 cm × 6 cm has a cylindrical hole of radius 3 cm drilled through its 6 cm dimension. (a) Find the remaining volume. [2] (b) Find the total surface area after drilling. [2] (c) The drilled cylinder (the removed piece) is melted and recast into a cube — find the cube's edge, exact or to two decimals. [2]

(HOTS) A question-setter proposes: "A cylinder of radius 7 cm has CSA equal to its volume — numerically, 2πrh = πr²h. Find h." Verify realizability: solve the equation, interpret the solution geometrically, and state the unit crime hiding inside the question's premise.

(Application) A 30-minute window: Q1 "Heron: park 13-14-15" [3]; Q2 "cost of fencing a circle r = 21 at ₹50/m" [3]; Q3 "cube table: a = 4, 9, 12 rows" [4]; Q4 "open tank sheet + capacity r = 3.5, h = 2" [4]; Q5 "pipe R = 5, r = 4, h = 14: metal + total surface" [4]; Q6 "drilled block 20 × 20 × 10, hole r = 7: volume + surface" [6]. Allocate minutes; name engines; state where the two-route stamps go.

(Evaluation) A student's revision claim: "This chapter is just formula memorisation — 15 formulas on one sheet and I am done." Evaluate: what fraction of the chapter's archetypes the formula sheet actually covers, what the routing/audit layer contributes, and what the correct balanced plan looks like.

(Comparison) Compare the chapter's three verification stamps — the two-route agreement (two engines, one answer), the unit stamp (dimension check on every line), and the conservation check (volume in = volume out) — in four rows: what each certifies, the configurations each fits, a failure each can MISS, and the cost of running each. Then write the audit-selection rule for a 6-marker with mixed engines.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A cylindrical jar of radius 7 cm contains water to a depth of 12 cm. (a) Find the volume of water. [2] (b) A solid metal cube of edge 6 cm is dropped in and sinks fully; find the new water depth (no overflow). [3] (c) How many such cubes would make the jar overflow, if the jar's full height is 20 cm? [2]

In a right‑angled triangle, the side opposite a 40° angle measures 7 cm and the hypotenuse measures 10 cm. Without using a calculator, decide whether sin 40° is greater than, equal to, or less than 0.7, and justify your reasoning.
A student claims: “If sin θ = 0.8 , then θ must be 53° because sin 53° ≈ 0.8.” Evaluate this claim.
A right‑angled triangle has hypotenuse 13 cm and one acute angle θ such that sin θ = 5/13 . Find the length of the side opposite θ and the length of the remaining side. Show all steps.
Design a right‑angled triangle (give all three side lengths in centimetres) for which sin θ = 0.6 for one acute angle θ . Explain why your triangle works.
ICSE 2023‑style: In △ PQR , right‑angled at Q , PQ = 9 cm and PR = 15 cm. Find sin R .

**Application:** A surveyor stands 30 m from the base of a tower and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 35° . Using sin 35° ≈ 0.574 , estimate the height of the tower. Assume the surveyor’s eye level is 1.5 m above ground.
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** In △ ABC , right‑angled at B , AB = 5 cm, BC = 12 cm. Find sin A and sin C .
In a right‑angled triangle, the side adjacent to angle θ is 8 cm and the hypotenuse is 10 cm. What is cos θ?
A student claims that cos 45° = 0.5 because “half of 90° is 45°”. Evaluate this claim.
A 5 m long ladder rests against a vertical wall. The foot of the ladder is 3 m from the wall. Find the angle the ladder makes with the ground.
Create a right‑angled triangle where cos θ = 3/5 and the hypotenuse is 15 cm. State the lengths of the other two sides.

**HOTS:** In a right‑angled triangle, cos θ = 0.8. Without using a calculator, determine whether θ is greater than, less than, or equal to 45°. Justify your answer using the behaviour of the cosine function.
**APPLICATION:** A kite string is 50 m long and makes an angle of 30° with the ground. How far horizontally is the kite from the person holding the string? (Assume the string is taut and straight.)
**COMPARISON:** Compare the values of cos 20° and sin 70°. Which is larger, or are they equal? Explain using the complementary angle relationship.
**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** In a right‑angled triangle ABC, right‑angled at B, AB = 7 cm, BC = 24 cm. Find cos A. (ICSE 2019, 2 marks)
Evaluate the statement: “tan 45° = 1 because the opposite and adjacent sides are equal in a 45°‑45°‑90° triangle.” Is this reasoning correct? Explain.
A right triangle has an angle θ such that the side opposite θ is 7 cm and the side adjacent to θ is 24 cm. Compute tan θ and the angle θ (to the nearest degree) using a calculator.
CISCE exam‑style: In ΔABC, right‑angled at B, AB = 5 cm, BC = 12 cm. Find tan A and tan C.
**HOTS:** Prove that for any acute angle θ, tan θ · tan (90° − θ) = 1.
**Evaluation/Critique:** A textbook states: “tan θ increases as θ increases from 0° to 90°.” Critique this statement for completeness.
**Comparison:** Compare the values of tan 30°, tan 45°, and tan 60°. Which is the largest? Explain using the opposite/adjacent ratio in a 30‑60‑90 triangle.
**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** In ΔXYZ, right‑angled at Y, XY = 9 cm, YZ = 12 cm. Find tan X and tan Z. Hence, verify that tan X · tan Z = 1.

(Recall) Reproduce the full standard-angle table (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°) for sin, cos and tan; state which single entry is undefined and why; give both accepted forms for the 45° sine and the 30° tangent.

(Reasoning) Derive, with the triangles fully drawn in words: (a) the three 45° values from the isosceles right triangle; (b) the six 30°/60° values from the bisected equilateral triangle of side 2; (c) state the role-swap that connects the 30° and 60° readings and what it previews.

(Evaluate) A student claims: "sin 0° = 0 must be wrong — a 0° angle means no triangle exists, so all three ratios at 0° should be undefined, like tan 90°." Evaluate: what a 0° angle does to the right triangle's three sides, which ratios therefore have honest values, and why the 0° and 90° columns are degenerate but not symmetric in tan.
(Apply) Evaluate exactly: (a) (tan 45° × cos 60°)/(sin 30° + cos 0°). (b) sin²60° + cos²60°. (c) Evaluate 2 tan 30° × sin 60°.
(Create) Design a 4-mark question where a composite expression evaluates to a clean number only if the exact table values are used; give the scheme and the distractor the decimal-user falls into.
(CISCE exam-style) Prove that sin²30° + sin²45° + sin²60° = 3/2. [3] Hence or otherwise evaluate cos²30° + cos²45° + cos²60°. [2]
(HOTS) Without evaluating any surd, arrange in ascending order: sin 20°, cos 20°, sin 70°, tan 45°, cos 80°. Justify every comparison using only the monotone laws and the 45° crossover.

(Application) A drone ascends on a straight cable making 60° with the ground; the cable is 50 m. (a) Exact height gained. (b) Exact horizontal distance covered. (c) The pilot then shortens the cable to 40 m at the same angle — state the new height WITHOUT recomputing from scratch, with the scaling reason. (d) At what standard angle would the SAME 50 m cable reach exactly 25 m of height?

(Comparison) Compare the three ratios' behaviour across 0° → 90° in a four-row table: direction of travel, starting and ending values, the angle where each equals 1 (or its notable equality), and its 90° status. Then state the two structural facts about the table that survive every angle (not just the five celebrities).

(CISCE past-paper pattern) Evaluate, showing all substitutions: (a) 2 tan 30° sin 60° + tan 45°. [2] (b) Evaluate (cos²30° − sin²30°) ÷ (sin 60° × cos 60°). [3] (c) State, with one line of reason, the angle θ (0° < θ < 90°) for which tan θ is not defined. [1]
What is the value of tan 45°?
A right triangle has an angle of 30° and the side adjacent to this angle measures 8 cm. Which trigonometric ratio should be used to find the hypotenuse, and what is the hypotenuse length?
Evaluate the statement: “In a right triangle, if sin θ = 0.6 then cos θ must be 0.8.”
A flagpole stands vertically on level ground. From a point 20 m away, the angle of elevation to the top is 30°. Find the height of the flagpole.
ICSE 2023 style: In ΔABC, ∠B = 90°, AB = 6 cm, ∠A = 30°. Find AC and BC.
A right triangle has sides 5 cm, 12 cm, 13 cm. Which acute angle has sine = 5/13?

A tree stands on a hill inclined at 10° to the horizontal. From a point 50 m down the hill, the angle of elevation to the top of the tree is 35°. Explain why the simple tan 35° = height/50 is incorrect, and describe the correct approach.
Critique the statement: “If tan θ = 2, then sin θ = 2/√5 and cos θ = 1/√5.”
ICSE 2022 past‑paper pattern: In ΔPQR, ∠Q = 90°, PQ = 8 cm, ∠P = 30°. Find QR and PR.

(Reasoning) Prove sin A = cos(90° − A) from a labelled right triangle, and then derive, from the same figure: (a) cos A = sin(90° − A); (b) tan A × tan(90° − A) = 1; (c) the special case that makes 45° self-paired.
(Evaluate) A student simplifies sin(90° − A) as sin 90° − sin A = 1 − sin A. Evaluate: the exact error, its algebraic species, the correct conversion, and a numerical refutation.
(Apply) Evaluate exactly, no tables: (a) sin 20°/cos 70°. (b) sin 26° sin 64° + cos 26° cos 64°. (c) tan 7° tan 23° tan 45° tan 67° tan 83°.
(Create) Design a 4-mark question mixing a find-the-angle equation with one pairing evaluation; give the scheme and the check that certifies the angle found.
(CISCE exam-style) Prove that sin θ · cos(90° − θ) + cos θ · sin(90° − θ) = 1. [3] Hence state the value of sin 35° cos 55° + cos 35° sin 55°. [2]

(HOTS) The grand product tan 1° tan 2° … tan 89° = 1 generalises: replace tan by sin — is sin 1° sin 2° … sin 89° likewise 1? Decide, with full reasoning, what the sine chain actually equals IN STRUCTURE (no tables), and what property of tan makes its chain special.

(Application) A surveyor's theodolite at a point P sights a tower top at an elevation of 64°. (a) State the angle the sight-line makes with the vertical, and express the tower's height h in terms of the horizontal distance d using BOTH angles. (b) The surveyor's report says "height = d × tan 64°"; the client's engineer writes "height = d × cot 26°" — reconcile the two with the identity. (c) If d = 30 m and tan 64° is not tabulated in the client's sheet (which lists only angles up to 45°), state how the client computes h using their sheet, exactly.

(Evaluation) A student claims: "The complementary identities are useless — with a calculator, sin 25° and cos 65° both come from buttons; why learn a swap?" Evaluate: what the identity does that the calculator cannot (three distinct jobs), and the honest residual value of the calculator in this territory.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) (a) Prove that cosec²A − cot²A = 1, using the complementary identities and the definition of the reciprocal family. [3] (b) Hence evaluate cosec²52° − cot²52°. [1] (c) A student evaluates cosec²38° − cot²38° as "1 also — by the same rule"; assess whether the rule genuinely covers 38°, and state the general theorem just discovered. [2]

(Reasoning) Route each one-liner to its engine and execute the taste: (a) "Plot P(−3, 4) and state its quadrant." (b) "Solve graphically: x + y = 5, x − y = 1." (c) "Find AB for A(−1, 2), B(2, 6)." (d) "Find the centre of AB."

(Evaluate) A student plots (2, 3) as "2 up, 3 right" and claims "the pair is called ordered because you must write it neatly". Evaluate: the double error, the correct convention with its reason, and the fastest self-audit that catches the first error every time.

(Apply) One taste per engine, executed: (a) Build a 3-row table of values for y = 2x − 1 and name the line's crossing with the y-axis. (b) Solve graphically by reasoning: y = 3x and y = 3 (state the intersection). (c) Find the distance from P(2, −3) to the x-axis. (d) Find the midpoint of the segment joining (−4, 5) and (6, −1).
(Create) Design a 4-mark "map" question testing routing plus one micro-execution per engine; give the scheme.

(CISCE exam-style) A(1, 2), B(4, 6), and C(4, 2) are three points. (a) Plot-descibe the triangle ABC's shape by computing its sides. [3] (b) Find the midpoint of AB and verify it is equidistant from A and B. [2] (c) State, with reason, what kind of angle the triangle carries at C. [1]

(HOTS) A student claims: "Since (2, 5) satisfies y = x + 3, and (5, 2) is just the same numbers, it must satisfy the equation too." Refute with the substitution engine, exhibit the geometric meaning of both points relative to the line y = x + 3, and state the exact relationship between a point and its swap with respect to this particular line.

(Application) A robotic drill moves on a grid: it starts at A(0, 0), moves to B(6, 8), then to C(6, 0). (a) Total path length A→B→C. (b) The drill's straight-line return C→A. (c) The workshop wants a maintenance point exactly halfway along AB — give its coordinates and its distance from B. (d) State, with one audit line, what shape the triangle ABC is and which angle carries the right angle.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A(2, 3), B(6, 11), and M(4, 7) is claimed to be the midpoint of AB. (a) Verify the claim with the midpoint formula. [2] (b) Find the length AB and the lengths MA, MB, and state the three-way relation that must hold if M truly is the midpoint. [3] (c) The point N(4, 6) is proposed as an alternative "midpoint" — refute or accept, with the audit that decides. [2]
In the equation y = 3x + 7, which variable is independent and which is dependent?
Given the rule “Cost (₹) = 20 × Number of notebooks”, identify the domain and range if the number of notebooks can be 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5.
A car travels at a constant speed of 60 km/h. Write the ordered pairs for the first 4 hours of travel, taking time (hours) as the independent variable.

In a CISCE‑style question: “The temperature T (in °C) of a cooling cup of tea after t minutes is given by T = 80 - 2t. State the independent and dependent variables, and give the domain if the tea is observed until it reaches room temperature (25 °C).”
A teacher asks: “If y = 5x - 3, what happens to y when x increases by 2?” A student answers “y increases by 2”. Identify the error and give the correct change.
A recipe uses 250 g of flour for every 2 eggs. Write the rule linking number of eggs e (independent) to flour f (grams, dependent). If a baker uses 7 eggs, how much flour is needed?
Critique the statement: “In the equation x = 4y + 1, x is the independent variable because it is isolated on the left.”

CISCE past‑paper style: “The cost C (in ₹) of hiring a bicycle for t hours is given by C = 30 + 10t. (i) Identify the independent and dependent variables. (ii) Write the domain if the bicycle can be hired for a maximum of 5 hours. (iii) Find the cost for 3.5 hours.”
(Reasoning) Solve with full working: (a) (x + 1, 2y) = (4, x − 1). (b) (x − 3, y + 2) = (2y + 1, x − 4). (c) For (b), verify the solution by rebuilding both pairs.

(Evaluate) A student writes "(4, 9) lies on y = 2x + 1 because 4 + 9 = 13 and both are positive integers in the first quadrant". Evaluate: what the membership test actually requires, execute it, and classify the student's reasoning by what it would wrongly admit.

(Apply) For the points A(3, 1), B(3, −2), C(−1, −2): (a) state which pairs share an abscissa and what that means geometrically; (b) same for the ordinate; (c) name the quadrant or axis home of each point; (d) find the pair that would complete the rectangle with A, B, C.
(Create) Design a 4-mark question mixing one coupled-equality solve with one membership test; give the scheme and the distractor built into the numbers.

(CISCE exam-style) The points P(2a − 1, 3) and Q(5, a + b) are given. (a) If P = Q, find a and b. [2] (b) Write the common pair and state its quadrant. [1] (c) Find the distance of the point from the x-axis. [2]

(HOTS) How many ordered pairs of positive integers (x, y) satisfy x + y = 7? List them, state the pattern of the list, and describe geometrically where these pairs sit. Then answer: what changes if REPEATED pairs are forbidden (they are not) or if the integers must be DISTINCT?

(Application) A theatre's seat code is (row, seat-number) with row 1 nearest the screen. (a) Interpret S(5, 12) and explain why (12, 5) is a different (and possibly invalid) seat. (b) Two friends hold (5, 12) and (5, 14): who sits closer to the aisle at seat 0, and by how many seats? (c) A third friend at (7, 13) — find the seat-code distance components to each friend and state, with one audit line, whether the third friend is "between" them in the seat-map sense.

(Comparison) Compare the ordered pair with the two-row table and the two-member set as carriers of "two numbers" — four rows: what each preserves (order? repetition?), the equality rule each obeys, and one use for which each is the RIGHT carrier. Then write the selection rule: given data "x = 3 with y = 3", which carrier honours the data best and why.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) (a) Find a and b if (a + b, a − b) = (2c, c) and c = 3. [2] (b) State the quadrant of (a + b, a − b). [1] (c) A point R(t, t² − 4) for integer t: list the members of this pair-family for t = 0, 1, 2, 3 and state which of them lie in Quadrant IV. [3]

(Reasoning) Plot-in-words (trace the moves) for: (a) (4, −3); (b) (−5, 0); (c) (0, 0); (d) (−2, −2). Then state each flag's home (quadrant or axis) and explain why (c) is in no quadrant and on both axes simultaneously.

(Evaluate) A student plots (−2, 3) as "2 down, 3 right", defending it: "minus means down, and I read the numbers in the order I like — the point is near enough." Evaluate: the two errors separately, where each misplaced the flag, and the fastest self-audit protocol that catches both before inking.

(Apply) A data set: hourly temperature H(t) = (0, 16), (1, 18), (2, 22), (3, 24), (4, 23), (5, 21). (a) Choose and state a workable scale for both axes given graph paper of 20 × 20 squares. (b) Describe plotting the point (3, 24) under that scale. (c) Which plotted flag sits on neither axis and in which quadrant — all of them? State the general reason. (d) Reading back, which time had temperature 22?
(Create) Design a 4-mark question where plotting reveals a geometric pattern the student must name and justify; give the scheme and the certification the justification needs.

(CISCE exam-style) On a unit grid: (a) Plot and label A(2, 5), B(2, −1), C(−3, −1). [2] (b) Name the figure ABC suggests and give the missing fourth vertex D. [2] (c) State the lengths AB and BC by coordinate subtraction. [2]

(HOTS) A student plots five points and finds they all sit on one straight line through the origin. The pairs are lost, but one survives: (4, −6). (a) State the relation y = mx that all five must satisfy and determine m. (b) Name two more pairs that MUST be among the plotted set if integer coordinates were used and x ran from −4 to 4. (c) Explain why exactly ONE line through the origin passes through (4, −6) — the uniqueness that makes m the point's fingerprint.

(Application) A courier's route on the city grid passes the flags A(0, 0), B(2, 5), C(4, 10), D(6, 15). (a) Plot-describe the four flags' alignment. (b) Certify by the slot test with the candidate y = (5/2)x. (c) The depot is at E(8, 18) — is it on the same route line? Adjudicate. (d) The courier claims "each parcel handover is exactly 2 grid-identical steps along the line" — assess using the flag sequence's structure.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) On a unit grid, P(−1, 2), Q(3, 2), R(1, k) are plotted, with k an integer, and the three are to be collinear. (a) P and Q share ordinate 2; state the line PQ and the value of k that puts R on it. [2] (b) With k = 2, name the figure PQRS if S(1, −1) completes it, and give its sides. [3] (c) Instead the question-setter wants R strictly OFF the line PQ — list all integer k that achieve it. [2]

(Reasoning) Build the tables and solve graphically-by-arithmetic: x + 2y = 8 and x − y = 2. (a) Give three-point tables for each with well-spread x's. (b) Find the intersection arithmetically from the tables' shared pair. (c) Verify the crossing in both equations and state the solution.

(Evaluate) A student reads the crossing of two lines as (3.2, 1.8) on a question whose equations are x + y = 5 and 2x − y = 1, and reports "the solution is approximately (3.2, 1.8)". Evaluate: what the exact solution is, why the designed data forbid the decimal reading, and what the mismatch indicts in the drawing.
(Apply) Classify each system without drawing, then confirm in one line geometrically: (a) x + y = 4, x + y = 1. (b) 2x + 2y = 8, x + y = 4. (c) x − y = 1, x + y = 5. (d) 3x + 2y = 6, 6x + 4y = 10.
(Create) Design a 6-mark word problem that translates into two linear equations solvable graphically with an integer crossing; give the scheme and the translation traps.

(CISCE exam-style) Draw the graphs of y = 2x and y = 6 − x for x from 0 to 4, using a table of values. [4] (a) Read the solution of the simultaneous pair from the graph. [1] (b) Shade-and-state the region where BOTH y ≥ 2x? — state where y = 2x rises above y = 6 − x, and for which x-values. [1]

(HOTS) Two lines are drawn: L₁ through (0, 1) and (2, 5); L₂ through (0, 4) and (3, 3). (a) Derive both equations from the tables these points generate. (b) Solve the pair exactly. (c) The crossing is claimed to be "outside both drawn segments" — assess whether that matters for the solution's validity, and state the drawing discipline it dictates.

(Application) A movement planner has two vehicles: Van A's position y (km) after t hours is y = 40t; Van B started 60 km ahead and moves slower: y = 60 + 25t. (a) Draw both motion lines for t = 0 to 4 (tables). (b) Read when and where Van A overtakes B. (c) Verify. (d) The planner asks: "for which hours is A still behind?" — answer from the drawn lines.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A test has 20 questions: +5 marks for each correct answer and −3 for each wrong; no marks for skipped. A student scores 44 after attempting 12 questions. (a) Frame the two equations in c (correct) and w (wrong). [2] (b) Solve the pair graphically with tables. [3] (c) State how many the student skipped, and verify the score. [1]

(Reasoning) Compute with full working: (a) the distance A(−2, 3) to B(4, −5); (b) the distance C(7, −2) to D(7, 9); (c) the distance of E(−6, 8) from the origin and from the x-axis; (d) state why (a)'s answer survives reversing the points.

(Evaluate) A student computes the perimeter of the triangle A(1, 1), B(4, 5), C(5, 1) as AB + BC + CA = 5 + 5 + 4 = 14 and calls it "a right isosceles triangle since two sides are 5". Evaluate: the side computations, the correct classification with its right-angle vertex, and whether the student's perimeter survives.

(Apply) The points A(1, 2), B(4, 6), C(7, 2) are a park's corners. (a) Compute all three sides. (b) Classify the triangle fully (side-class AND angle-class with proof). (c) Compute the distance from B to the x-axis and state which side's length that equals, with the geometric reason.

(Create) Design a 5-mark question: given three points, compute the sides and prove a specific triangle type with the distance engine; give the scheme and the fingerprint discipline the proof mark requires.

(CISCE exam-style) The points P(0, 1), Q(2, 5), R(4, 9) are given. (a) Compute PQ, QR and PR in exact surd form. [3] (b) Determine whether P, Q, R are collinear, with the theorem stated. [2] (c) State what fraction of the way from P to R the point Q sits. [1]

(HOTS) The formula's order-independence: (a) Prove (x₂ − x₁)² = (x₁ − x₂)² algebraically. (b) Exhibit the one place in coordinate geometry where point order MATTERS (the ordered pair itself and the differences inside a SIGNED reading). (c) A classmate computes AB with A(5, −2), B(−1, 6) as √((−1 − 5)² + (6 + 2)²) and another as √((5 + 1)² + (−2 − 6)²) — reconcile the two answers without computing.

(Application) Two delivery points are A(1, 2) and B(7, 10) on a grid where 1 unit = 50 m. (a) The crow-flight distance in metres. (b) The courier must travel the grid streets (east/west/north/south only): compute the stair-path length in metres. (c) The courier claims "the stair path is never shorter than the crow flight, and here they differ by 40 m" — audit the claim. (d) A third point C(7, 2): state which of the two routes A→C→B equals the crow flight AB, with the reason.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A(4, 2), B(−2, 2) and C(k, 2) lie on the horizontal line y = 2, with B between A and C, and AC = 10. (a) Find k. [2] (b) Find AB and BC, and state their relation. [2] (c) A drone flies the straight route from A to C while a van drives the stair A→B→C along the grid streets — compute both distances and the drone's saving. [2]

(Reasoning) (a) Compute the midpoint of A(−3, 4) and B(5, −2). (b) Verify it with the distance engine (both half-lengths and the full length). (c) The point (1, 1) is proposed as the "true centre" since "it looks central" — adjudicate with one distance.

(Evaluate) A student computes the midpoint of (2, 3) and (4, 7) as (6, 10), showing work "(2 + 4, 3 + 7) = (6, 10)" — and defends it: "the centre must be past both points since it combines them." Evaluate: the error, where the true midpoint sits and why, the geometric meaning of the student's point (6, 10), and the one-line self-check that catches the missing halving.

(Apply) (a) Find the midpoint of the segment joining (−5, 8) and (3, −4). (b) M(2, −3) is the midpoint of PQ with P(−6, 1): find Q. (c) For the quadrilateral A(1, 2), B(5, 1), C(6, 4), D(2, 5), test the diagonals and classify.
(Create) Design a 4-mark question where the midpoint formula and the distance formula compose (midpoint found, then a distance FROM it); give the scheme and the composition slip the design catches.

(CISCE exam-style) The point (3, k) is the midpoint of the segment joining (1, 2) and (5, 6). (a) Find k. [2] (b) State the midpoint's quadrant or axis home. [1] (c) The point (3, 4.5) is proposed as an alternative midpoint lying "above the true one on the same vertical" — adjudicate. [1]

(HOTS) A right triangle has vertices O(0, 0), A(6, 0), B(0, 8). (a) Compute the hypotenuse AB and its midpoint M. (b) Compute MO, MA, MB. (c) State the discovered law (the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equidistant from all three vertices) and what it predicts about a circle drawn through O, A, B.

(Application) Two colony gates stand at G₁(−4, −2) and G₂(10, 6) (grid units = 100 m). (a) The builder promises a fountain "exactly halfway along the straight path between the gates" — give its coordinates and its distance to each gate in metres. (b) A resident at R(3, 2) claims the fountain is the midpoint of the segment G₁R — adjudicate with the distances. (c) State the total walking path length G₁ → fountain → G₂.

(Comparison) Compare the midpoint engine with the upcoming general SECTION formula it prepares — four rows: the division ratio each handles, the formula shape, one question each answers, and what the 1 : 1 mastery already provides for the general case. Then write the readiness rule: what a student should be able to do cold before meeting ratios other than 1 : 1.

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A(2, 3), B(8, 9) and M(5, 6) are given, with M claimed as the midpoint of AB. (a) Verify with the formula. [2] (b) Compute MA, MB and AB, and state the three-way law the numbers exhibit. [3] (c) The point N(6, 7) lies on segment AB? — N(6, 7): compute AN and NB, and determine whether N also qualifies as "a midpoint", with the general sentence your verdict teaches. [2]

(Reasoning) Assemble the full run: A(−1, 2) and B(5, 10). (a) Find the midpoint M and certify it with distances. [3] (b) Find the length AB and state AM's length without recomputation. [2] (c) The point C(2, 5) is claimed as "another midpoint of AB" — audit and verdict. [2]

(Evaluate) A question gives P(1, 1), Q(4, 5), R(7, 2) and asks "show that PQR is isosceles". A student computes PQ = 5, QR = 5, PR = 6 and writes "isosceles because two sides are equal — done, no more proof needed". Evaluate: whether the proof is complete for the side-class claim, what a "show that PQR is a RIGHT triangle" variant would demand, and the general proof standard the distance engine sets.

(Apply) One chain per engine pair, executed: (a) The midpoint of (2, 1) and (8, 7), then its distance to each endpoint. (b) Solve graphically-by-tables x + y = 8, y = 2x and verify. (c) Classify the triangle (0, 0), (5, 0), (0, 12) fully. (d) The endpoint D so that (1, 3) is the midpoint of CD with C(4, 7).
(Create) Design a 6-mark composite that chains the crossing engine and the ruler engine with a classification verdict; give the scheme with every mark mapped.

(CISCE exam-style) A(0, 0), B(8, 6) and M is the midpoint of AB. (a) Find M. [1] (b) Show that MA = MB = 5. [2] (c) A circle is drawn with centre M through A and B: determine whether C(11, 3) lies on it. [2] (d) State the radius and the diameter. [1]

(HOTS) A triangle has vertices A(2, 3), B(8, 5) and C. The specimen C = (4, 9) is proposed. Determine whether ANY point C can make the midpoint M of AB equidistant from A, B and C simultaneously, and describe the set of all such C.

(Application) A drone-survey maps four landmarks: A(0, 0), B(12, 0), C(12, 5), D(0, 5) (1 unit = 10 m). (a) Name the landmark figure and its dimensions. (b) Two surveillance posts must stand at the midpoints of AD and BC: give both, and the distance between them. (c) A cable must run from post-to-post (the segment of (b)) — state its length in metres and its direction relative to AD and BC. (d) A fifth landmark E(6, 2.5) is claimed as "the exact centre of the whole rectangle" — audit with both a midpoint argument and a distance argument.

(Evaluation) A student claims: "Audits double the work — verifying a midpoint with distances recomputes what the formula already did." Evaluate: what the formula computation certifies by itself, what the distance audit adds beyond it (two things), and the risk profile of an audited versus an unaudited script on a 6-mark composite.

(Comparison) Compare the chapter's two solution cultures — the DRAWN solution (graphical, 16_005) and the COMPUTED solution (formulas, 16_006–16_007) — in four rows: what each returns, its exactness ceiling, its evidence type, and its failure mode. Then write the routing rule for a question that could be answered either way (e.g., "where do the lines y = x + 1 and y = −x + 5 cross?").

(CISCE past-paper pattern) A(2, 3), B(8, 9), M(5, 6), and a circle centred at M through A and B. (a) Verify M is the midpoint of AB. [2] (b) Compute the circle's radius. [1] (c) Determine whether C(8, 3) lies on the circle, with full audit. [3]

Reasoning: Your friend says, "The length of my notebook is 25." Explain in three steps why this statement is scientifically incomplete, and show how each step is answered by a different part of this chapter.

Apply: A stack of 250 identical sheets of paper measures 2.5 cm in total thickness. Estimate the thickness of one sheet in mm and in µm, state which instrument from this chapter could measure it directly, and give one reason why the estimate-by-division method is still taught alongside direct measurement.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Define zero error and distinguish positive from negative zero error. (b) The period of a pendulum is 2.0 s — state its frequency. (c) Why must a zero error be corrected even when it is small, if the same correction applies to every reading?

HOTS: A student argues: "Since the screw gauge has the finest least count (0.01 mm), the whole chapter should just teach the screw gauge and skip the metre rule and vernier callipers." (a) Unpack the two hidden assumptions in this argument and show where each fails. (b) State the general selection principle this chapter actually teaches. (c) Give one CISCE-examination situation where the rule or vernier is not merely acceptable but the required answer.

Application: Your class is setting up a "measurement help-desk" at the school science fair for visitors from Classes 6–7. Design the help-desk around this chapter: (a) three measuring problems you will offer visitors, each solved with a different chapter instrument or method, with the teaching line you would speak (3 marks); (b) one question a visitor is likely to ask that the help-desk must route to an older class's physics ("we will learn that later") and why routing it is the honest answer (3 marks); (c) one way the help-desk will demonstrate zero error using the fair's own materials (2 marks).

Evaluation: Two laboratory groups reported values of g from the pendulum experiment (effective length 1.00 m): Group A reported g = 9.81 m s⁻² from timing 20 oscillations five times and averaging, with the metre rule's least count recorded. Group B reported g = 9.52 m s⁻² from timing a single oscillation three times, noting the bob's mass as 100 g. (a) Evaluate both records against the chapter's completeness standard (quantity, unit, instrument, least count, averaging, correction) with a point-by-point verdict table. (b) Identify the most likely numerical source of Group B's low value, showing the arithmetic. (c) Give the one-line verdict a CISCE examiner would write for each group.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Define the second in terms of the mean solar day. (1 mark) (b) A screw gauge has pitch 0.5 mm and 50 circular divisions; its negative zero error is 0.02 mm. For a wire, the main-scale reading is 0 mm and the 24th circular division coincides with the reference line. Calculate the corrected diameter. (2 marks) (c) The same wire's diameter is re-measured as 0.252 mm by a laboratory of higher precision. Express the percentage error of your (b) result relative to 0.252 mm, and state one conclusion about the screw gauge's suitability for this wire. (2 marks) (d) State the one property of the simple pendulum that made it historically valuable as a timekeeper. (2 marks)
Convert 4.2 GW (gigawatts) into watts and express the answer in scientific notation.
A student measures a wire length as 0.0035 km. Express this length in millimetres.
An experiment requires a mass of 0.0045 kg. The laboratory balance reads in grams. What reading should the student set, and how many significant figures are appropriate?
Compare the SI unit of energy (joule) with the commercial unit of electrical energy (kilowatt‑hour). Express 1 kWh in joules.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** A question asks: “Define the SI unit of force. A force of 10 N acts on a body of mass 2 kg. Calculate the acceleration produced.” Provide the definition and the calculation.

Recall: name the five parts of vernier callipers and the measuring job of each; state the least-count formula and evaluate it for a vernier whose 10 divisions equal 9 main-scale divisions of 1 mm each; state the sign of the zero error when the vernier zero lies to the left of the main-scale zero on closing the jaws.

Reasoning: A student claims, "The vernier scale is finer because its divisions are smaller and closer together than the main scale's." Untangle this: state what actually makes the vernier finer, show why the 0.9 mm design (not smaller engraving) produces 0.1 mm resolution, and explain why 20-division verniers reach 0.05 mm.

Analyse: Three objects must be measured — (i) the internal diameter of a glass test tube (about 2 cm), (ii) the thickness of a notebook's cover (about 3 mm), (iii) the diameter of a steel wire (about 0.4 mm). For each, decide whether the vernier callipers is the right instrument from this chapter's ladder (metre rule — vernier callipers — screw gauge), and justify via least count, range and accessibility.

Apply: With vernier callipers of least count 0.01 cm, the main-scale reading for a coin's diameter is 2.4 cm and the 7th vernier division coincides with a main-scale mark. On closing the jaws, the 3rd vernier division coincides. Compute the zero error with sign, the observed diameter, and the corrected diameter; then state the coin's diameter the way a complete laboratory record should read.

Create: Design and justify a one-page laboratory instruction card, "Using the vernier callipers correctly", for your school's Class 9 lab. It must contain: the four-step reading ritual, the closed-jaw zero-error check with the sign rule, one worked numerical (choose your own numbers and carry them through), and one WARNING box describing the most damaging mistake and its consequence for the final result.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Define the vernier constant (least count) of vernier callipers and write its SI value for the standard 10-division instrument. (b) State TWO measurements for which vernier callipers is preferred to a metre rule, with one reason each. (c) The zero of a vernier scale lies to the left of the main-scale zero by 4 divisions on closing; the least count is 0.01 cm — the observed reading for a cylinder's length is 3.42 cm. Find the corrected length and justify the sign of the correction.

HOTS: A manufacturer offers two vernier callipers at the same price: Model X has 10 vernier divisions spanning 9 mm (LC 0.1 mm); Model Y has 50 vernier divisions spanning 49 mm (LC 0.02 mm). Your school stocks Model X. (a) Show that Model Y's least count is 0.02 mm and explain why its longer vernier scale does not make it harder to read in principle. (b) Argue two genuine reasons a school might still prefer Model X for Class 9 use. (c) State the design limit: why can this trick not be extended indefinitely to make a 0.001 mm "vernier" for a school lab?

Application: Your school is digitising its lab records: every measurement must be entered as one line in a spreadsheet with columns [quantity, value+unit, instrument, LC, observed, zero error, corrected]. (a) Write the complete row for this measurement: a beaker's internal diameter taken with inside jaws, MSR 3.1 cm, 9th division coinciding, LC 0.01 cm, closed-jaw reading 2nd division coinciding (vernier zero right of main zero). (b) The spreadsheet applies an auto-correction formula; state the formula the "corrected" column must implement in terms of the other columns, and explain what breaks if a student types the zero error's magnitude without its sign.
