(c) Give one validation rule the spreadsheet could run on every row to catch sign mistakes automatically.

Evaluation: A dealer sells "school vernier callipers" with a certificate claiming LC = 0.001 cm (0.01 mm) — the same as a screw gauge — from a 100-division vernier scale. A student buys it and measures a coin as 2.4653 cm. Evaluate the purchase on three grounds: (a) physical plausibility of the claimed resolution for a line-scale instrument at school price; (b) statistical honesty of the reported value given a 0.01 mm claimed LC; (c) pedagogical suitability against the chapter's actual ladder (vernier 0.1 mm → screw gauge 0.01 mm). Conclude with the one-line advice you would give the school.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) A vernier callipers has its 10 divisions equal to 9 mm. A student measures the diameter of a cylinder: MSR = 2.8 cm, 7th division coinciding. On closing the jaws, the zero of the vernier scale lies to the right of the zero of the main scale, the 4th division coinciding. Calculate the corrected diameter. (3 marks) (b) The cylinder's true diameter (measured by a calibrated instrument) is 2.83 cm. Find the percentage error of the corrected result and comment on whether the vernier is a suitable instrument for this cylinder. (2 marks) (c) State one measurement for which this vernier is NOT suitable within the chapter's instrument set, naming the correct instrument. (1 mark)

Recall: name the six labelled parts of a screw gauge a diagram must show, state the function of the ratchet in one line, define pitch and least count, and write the least-count formula with its result for a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 circular-scale divisions.

Reasoning: Why does the screw gauge achieve 0.01 mm resolution while a millimetre-marked rule cannot, even though both are made in the same workshop with the same tools? Answer through the transmission principle, and show the arithmetic that connects a comfortable human action to the fine measurement.

Analyse: For each observation below, decide the sign of the zero error, compute it, and state the correction to be applied — the screw gauge has pitch 0.5 mm and 50 circular divisions. (i) On closing the jaws, the reference line coincides with the 3rd circular division. (ii) On closing, the reference line coincides with the 46th division. (iii) On closing, the reference line coincides exactly with the circular zero. Then justify the single algebraic rule that handles all three cases.

Apply: A screw gauge has pitch 1 mm and 100 circular divisions. For a copper wire: main-scale reading 0 mm, 52nd circular division coinciding; zero error determined as +0.02 mm (reference line at the 2nd division on closing). Another student reports the same wire as "0.52 mm" without correction, and a third reports "0.50 mm" claiming the zero correction was negative. Give the correct certified diameter and diagnose each wrong report.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Define back-lash error and state how it is avoided. (2 marks) (b) The pitch of a screw gauge is 0.5 mm and its circular scale has 50 divisions. While measuring the diameter of a wire, the pitch scale reading is 1 mm and the 20th division of the circular scale coincides with the reference line. Find the diameter. (2 marks)

HOTS: A designer proposes a "super gauge": pitch 0.1 mm with 100 circular divisions (least count 0.001 mm), claiming it should replace all ordinary screw gauges in the school laboratory. (a) Evaluate the claim with at least two physics-based objections. (b) State the design trade-off the finer pitch creates with the instrument's range. (c) Give the school-laboratory selection principle the proposal violates.

Application: Your school's astronomy club received a kit with a brass rod, a fine copper wire, a thin aluminium foil, and a Vernier-calliper-and-screw-gauge pair, and must label each item with its measured dimension for the exhibition. (a) Assign instruments and write the one-line teaching caption for each measurement (3 marks). (b) A visitor asks: "Why not measure the foil's thickness at ten different places and average?" — answer as the club member, distinguishing when averaging helps and when it is wasted effort (3 marks). (c) The visitor then asks: "My grandfather says old clocks used pendulums — is that the same trick as your screw?" — give the two-line answer connecting the transmission principle of this node to the next node's averaging principle (2 marks).

Evaluation: Two entries for the same wire, gauge of pitch 0.5 mm and 50 divisions, jaw-closed line at the 49th division. Entry P: "Diameter = 0.68 mm (LC 0.01 mm; zero error −0.02 mm corrected; mean of 3 readings)." Entry Q: "Diameter = 0.66 mm (mean of 3 raw readings)." The true certificate value, checked later against a gauge set, is 0.68 mm. (a) Reconstruct each entry's arithmetic and locate Q's defect. (b) Explain why Q's number is close to P's and why closeness does not rescue the entry. (c) Write the examiner-style verdict for each entry.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) State one functional difference between the pitch scale and the circular scale of a screw gauge. (1 mark) (b) The pitch of a screw gauge is 1 mm and its circular scale has 100 divisions. When the jaws are closed, the 97th division coincides with the reference line. For a wire, the pitch-scale reading is 0.5 mm and the 8th division coincides with the reference line. Calculate the corrected diameter. (3 marks) (c) The wire's true diameter, measured by a laboratory of higher precision, is 0.612 mm. Calculate the percentage error of the corrected value and state whether the instrument-plus-protocol performance is acceptable for a 0.01 mm least-count gauge, with one reason. (2 marks)
A pendulum of length 0.25 m is taken to a planet where *g = 4.0 m s⁻²*. Calculate its period.
A student measures the time for 30 oscillations of a 1.00 m pendulum as 60.0 s. Determine the experimental value of *g*.
A pendulum of length 0.50 m is used to measure *g* on a planet. The measured period is 1.20 s. Calculate *g* on that planet.

Compare the periods of two simple pendulums: Pendulum A has length *L* and is on Earth (*g = 9.8 m s⁻²*). Pendulum B has length *4L* and is on a planet where *g = 9.8/4 m s⁻²*. Which has the longer period, or are they equal?
CISCE past‑paper style: “A simple pendulum of length 1.21 m makes 30 complete oscillations in 66.0 s. Calculate the acceleration due to gravity at that place. (Take π = 3.14)”

Reasoning: A student argues: "My stopwatch reads to 0.01 s, so timing a single oscillation and averaging five single timings is just as good as timing 20 oscillations in one run." Examine the claim quantitatively: compare the two designs' reaction-time contamination, and state the additional failure mode of hand-timing single swings that repetition cannot cure.

Analyse: Four students measured g with the same pendulum (L = 1.00 m). A: timed 1 oscillation once → T = 2.1 s, g = 8.95 m s⁻². B: timed 20 oscillations once → 40.4 s, T = 2.02 s, g = 9.68 m s⁻². C: timed 20 oscillations three times (40.2, 40.4, 40.0 s) → T̄ = 2.01 s, g = 9.76 m s⁻². D: used four lengths and the T²–L graph, slope 4.04 s²/m → g = 39.48/4.04 = 9.77 m s⁻². Rank the four results by trustworthiness, assigning a reason to each ranking move, and state what single feature of D's design makes it the strongest.

Apply: A pendulum has effective length 0.81 m. A student times 50 oscillations in 90.0 s. (a) Compute T and f. (b) Compute g (4π² = 39.48). (c) Predict the new period if the length is increased to 1.21 m, using the ratio method and then verifying by direct substitution.

Create: Design the observation table and analysis plan for the school's g-experiment practical file, to be executed in one 40-minute period with a metre rule, a stopwatch, string and two bobs (brass 50 g, wooden 100 g of the same size). Your design must produce BOTH a single-length value of g and a T²–L graph value, and must include the two comparison tests (mass, amplitude). Specify: the columns of each table, the lengths you would choose and why, the number of repeats, and how the two g-values will be compared at the end.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Define the seconds pendulum and state its period and approximate length at a place where g = 9.8 m s⁻². (b) A pendulum completes 30 oscillations in 54 s; find its time period and frequency. (c) A student records the bob's length as "string length = 98 cm" and uses it as L in g = 4π²L/T² — state and justify the error, given the bob is a 2 cm diameter sphere.

Application: The school wants a "gravity map of the building" — g measured on the ground floor and on the terrace (about 10 m higher). A senior argues the difference is real but tiny: g decreases with height approximately as Δg/g ≈ 2h/R with Earth's radius R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m. (a) Estimate Δg/g for h = 10 m and the expected ΔT/T for the same pendulum. (b) Given the experiment's realistic timing precision of about 0.5% in g, state honestly whether the terrace difference is measurable, showing the comparison arithmetic. (c) The team still wants a display: design the honest version of the exhibit (what CAN be shown varying g measurably with the same apparatus?).

Evaluation: A coaching institute's "rapid g-lab" advertises: "Determine g in 60 seconds: time ONE oscillation with our digital stopwatch (0.01 s), and our app computes g instantly." A school evaluates the kit. (a) Compute the best-case percentage error in g from reaction-time timing of one 2 s swing, and the same for a 20-oscillation run, comparing with the kit's 60-second claim. (b) Evaluate the kit's design on three grounds (physics, statistics, pedagogy). (c) Give the one modification that would make the kit honest at the same speed.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Copy and complete: "The time period of a simple pendulum does not depend on ____ of the bob and, for small oscillations, hardly on ____; it depends on the ____ and on the ____ at the place." (2 marks) (b) A pendulum of length 1.00 m has its 20-oscillation time measured five times: 40.2, 40.4, 40.2, 40.6, 40.6 s. Compute the mean period and g (4π² = 39.48), quoting g to an honest number of figures. (3 marks) (c) The same pendulum is moved to a hill station where g = 9.78 m s⁻². Find the new 20-oscillation time to one decimal place. (2 marks) (d) State ONE reason why the timing is started when the bob passes the mean position rather than at an extreme. (1 mark)
How many significant figures are in the measurement 0.00450 kg?
Why are the trailing zeros in 1500 ambiguous without a decimal point?
A student records the diameter of a wire as 0.25 mm using a screw gauge of least count 0.01 mm. Is the recorded value correct in terms of significant figures?
Add 12.11 m, 18.0 m, and 1.013 m. Express the sum with correct significant figures.

Design a measurement procedure to determine the density of a metal cube using a vernier calliper (least count 0.01 cm) and a digital balance (least count 0.1 g). State how many significant figures the final density should have.
The time period of a simple pendulum is measured as 2.45 s, 2.48 s, 2.43 s, 2.46 s, 2.47 s. Calculate the mean time period and express it with appropriate significant figures.
A digital balance displays mass as 12.345 g. The manufacturer states the uncertainty is ±0.005 g. How many significant figures are justified? Explain.
A rectangular sheet has length 15.2 cm and breadth 10.1 cm measured with a vernier calliper (least count 0.01 cm). Calculate its area with correct significant figures.

A student writes the value of g as 9.8 m/s² in a lab report. Another writes 9.81 m/s². Which is more appropriate for Class 9 experiments using a simple pendulum and stopwatch of least count 0.1 s? Justify.

The diameter of a spherical ball is measured using a screw gauge of least count 0.001 cm. The main scale reading is 0.5 cm and the circular scale reading is 25 divisions. If the zero error is –0.002 cm, find the corrected diameter and express it with appropriate significant figures.
What is the least count of a vernier caliper if 10 vernier divisions coincide with 9 main scale divisions of 1 mm each?

A student measures the diameter of a wire using a screw gauge with least count 0.01 mm. The main scale reading is 2.5 mm and the circular scale reading is 45 divisions. If the zero error is +0.02 mm, what is the corrected diameter?
In a simple pendulum experiment, a student plots T² vs L and obtains a straight line passing through the origin with slope 4.0 s²/m. The student claims g = 9.87 m/s². Evaluate this claim.

You have a vernier caliper with 1 MSD = 1 mm and 20 VSD = 19 MSD. You measure the internal diameter of a cylindrical pipe and get MSR = 2.3 cm, VSR = 8. The zero error is –0.02 cm. Find the corrected internal diameter in cm.

A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on the circular scale. The zero of the circular scale is 2 divisions above the reference line when the jaws are closed. A student measures the thickness of a glass plate and records MSR = 3.0 mm, CSR = 28. Calculate the corrected thickness. (ICSE 2022 pattern)

A vernier caliper has 1 MSD = 0.1 cm and 20 VSD = 19 MSD. A student measures the thickness of a coin and gets MSR = 0.3 cm, VSR = 12. The zero error is –0.02 cm. The student claims the thickness is 0.42 cm. Is the student correct? Justify.

You need to measure the internal diameter of a thin glass tube (~2 mm) with high precision. Which instrument would you choose: vernier caliper (LC 0.01 cm) or screw gauge (LC 0.001 cm)? Explain your choice considering the size and fragility.
A student determines g using a simple pendulum and obtains g = 10.2 m/s². The accepted value is 9.8 m/s². The student says the difference is due to air resistance. Critique this statement.

Compare the least count and typical measurement range of a vernier caliper (LC 0.01 cm, range 0–15 cm) and a screw gauge (LC 0.001 cm, range 0–2.5 cm). Which is more suitable for measuring the diameter of a human hair (~0.007 cm)?

ICSE 2023 Physics Question: A screw gauge has a pitch of 1 mm and 100 divisions on the circular scale. When the jaws are closed, the zero of the circular scale is 4 divisions below the reference line. A wire is placed between the jaws and the readings are: Main scale reading = 2 mm, Circular scale reading = 72. Calculate the diameter of the wire. (3 marks)
A car travels 30 km north in 0.5 h, then 40 km south in 1 h. Calculate its average speed and average velocity. Show all steps.

On a velocity‑time graph, a straight line with positive slope passes through the origin. What does the slope represent, and what does the area under the graph from t = 0 to t = 4 s represent if the velocity at 4 s is 8 m s⁻¹?
A particle starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration a = 3 m s⁻². Using the appropriate equation, find its displacement after 5 s.
A typical ICSE question: “A body moving with uniform acceleration covers 20 m in the 2nd second and 30 m in the 4th second. Find the acceleration and the initial velocity.” Solve it step by step.
A particle moves along a straight line with velocity v(t) = 4t – 2 (m s⁻¹), where t is in seconds. Determine the acceleration at t = 3 s and the displacement between t = 1 s and t = 4 s.
A car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ applies brakes and decelerates uniformly at 5 m s⁻². How far does it travel before stopping? Which equation of motion is most direct?

**ICSE 2023 pattern:** A body starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration. It covers a distance of 120 m in the 6th second of its motion. Find its acceleration and the total distance covered in the first 6 seconds.

Reasoning: A student's diary records "Cycling: 10 km" for a ride that went 6 km south, then 8 km east. The student claims: "My displacement was also 10 km, since that's how far I cycled." Reconstruct the correct calculation for both quantities, explain exactly which step of the student's reasoning confuses the two categories, and state what the ride's numbers would be if instead the student had cycled 6 km south and then 8 km NORTH on a parallel road.

Analyse: Four journeys all end 100 m north of the start: (i) a straight 100 m walk north; (ii) 100 m north, 30 m east, 30 m west (a bulge); (iii) 100 m north then 100 m south then 200 m north; (iv) one and a half laps of a circular track arranged so the finish point lies 100 m north of the start. For each, compute distance and displacement (magnitude and direction), arrange the four distances in order, and state what stays fixed across all four — and why that fixed item is the "verdict".

Apply: On a long straight canal tow-path, a cyclist rides 2.4 km east, rests, rides 1.8 km west, then finally rides 0.9 km east. Taking east as positive, compute (a) the total distance; (b) the net displacement with sign and direction; (c) the displacement after just the first two legs; (d) state in one line why the rest period contributes to neither quantity.

Create: Build the "journey decoder" card: a three-question routine that takes any raw journey description ("drove 5 km to the mall, then 3 km to the gym") and outputs the complete physics record. Specify the three questions, the record format, and run the routine on two journeys of your own — one where distance and displacement agree, one where they differ — showing all outputs.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Can the distance travelled by a body be less than the magnitude of its displacement? Justify your answer. (b) A body moves 9 m east, then 12 m north. Find the distance covered and the magnitude of the displacement. (c) Under what single condition do the magnitudes of distance and displacement become equal?

Application: The school's geography department asks the physics club to certify two monsoon relief routes to the same shelter: Route P, straight 4.0 km along the embankment; Route Q, 2.4 km along the road east then 3.2 km along the bund north (perpendicular legs to the same shelter). (a) Compute distance, displacement magnitude and direction for each route, and verify both displacements agree (use the 3-4-5 family). (b) The relief team must also plan the RETURN to base along "any route" and wants to promise villagers "you will walk no more than X km and end exactly at base" — state X's minimum honest value and the route that achieves it, with reasoning. (c) The team's report draft says "both routes cover 4 km". Rewrite the sentence in complete chapter language.

Evaluation: An exam-prep app drills this node with 50 questions; an audit finds 44 of them are "add the legs" distance sums, 4 are Pythagorean displacements, and 2 mention direction. Evaluate the app against the chapter's examination weight: (a) estimate the app's training bias and name the two skills it under-trains most severely; (b) predict the specific mark losses a student drilled only on this app would suffer on a standard paper section (definition items, direction-marked displacements, closed-path conceptuals); (c) rewrite the app's question-mix prescription in one sentence with proportions.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Define displacement and state its SI unit. (1 mark) (b) A man walks 5 m towards east, then 12 m towards north. Calculate (i) the distance walked and (ii) the magnitude of his displacement. (2 marks) (c) He then walks 12 m due south from that point. Calculate his final distance walked and the magnitude and direction of his final displacement relative to the START. (3 marks) (d) State, with reason, which leg(s) of this journey could be removed while keeping the final displacement unchanged. (2 marks)
A car travels 30 km north in 0.5 h, then 40 km south in 0.5 h. What are its average speed and average velocity?
A particle moves along the x‑axis: at t = 0 s it is at x = 2 m; at t = 4 s it is at x = –6 m. Calculate its average velocity and average speed if the total path length covered is 12 m.
A CISCE‑style question: “A body moves 20 m east in 4 s, then 20 m west in 6 s. Find (i) average speed, (ii) average velocity.” Provide the answer with units.

A particle moves on a line such that its velocity is given by v(t) = 3t - 2 (m s⁻¹) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 s. Without integrating, argue whether the average speed over this interval equals the magnitude of the average velocity.
A delivery van travels 15 km north in 20 min, then 10 km east in 15 min, then 5 km south in 10 min. Compute its average speed and the magnitude of its average velocity for the whole journey.

**CISCE past‑paper pattern:** A car moves along a straight road. Its odometer reads 12 500 km at the start of a trip and 12 620 km at the end. The trip takes 2 hours. The car’s displacement is 80 km north. Calculate (i) average speed, (ii) average velocity. Express answers in km h⁻¹ and m s⁻¹.
A car moves at 15 m s⁻¹ for 8 s, then uniformly accelerates to 25 m s⁻¹ in the next 4 s. Sketch the velocity–time graph and calculate the total displacement.
Create a displacement–time graph for a particle that moves 10 m forward in 2 s, rests for 3 s, then moves 5 m backward in 2 s. Describe the key features.

A particle’s velocity–time graph is a straight line with negative slope intersecting the velocity axis at 20 m s⁻¹ and the time axis at 5 s. Determine the acceleration and the displacement between t = 0 and t = 5 s.
A car’s speed–time graph consists of a rectangle of height 10 m s⁻¹ from 0–4 s and a triangle on top of it from 4–6 s rising to 20 m s⁻¹. Find the total distance travelled in 6 s.

CISCE past‑paper style: “The velocity–time graph of a particle moving in a straight line is shown (describe: a trapezium with parallel sides 4 m s⁻¹ and 10 m s⁻¹, height 6 s). Calculate (a) the acceleration during the first 2 s if the velocity rises uniformly from 4 to 10 m s⁻¹, (b) the total displacement in 6 s.”

Reasoning: A car travelling at 10 m s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly and covers 150 m while reaching 40 m s⁻¹. A student writes: "v = u + at, so 40 = 10 + a·t — I have two unknowns, this problem cannot be solved." (a) Solve the problem fully with the correct equation, computing both the acceleration and the time. (b) Verify the distance by the equation the student attempted. (c) Name the selection error the student made, as a rule.

Analyse: Four problems share one journey (u = 6 m s⁻¹, a = 2 m s⁻², t = 4 s). For each question, name the ONE equation that answers it fastest and compute: (i) the velocity at t = 4 s; (ii) the distance covered in the 4 s; (iii) the distance covered had the body been observed only through its speeds, given it reached 14 m s⁻¹ (u and v known, distance wanted, time forgotten); (iv) the time at which the body was at 30 m from the start (set up only — state the equation form and why the answer needs the quadratic or factorisation, then factorise 30 = 6t + t² and give t).

Apply: A car moving at 22 m s⁻¹ brakes uniformly at 2.0 m s⁻² to a halt. (a) Find the time taken to stop and the total braking distance. (b) Find the distance covered during the FIRST 5.5 s of braking, and state what fraction of the total it represents. (c) Verify (a)'s distance by a second equation. (d) One line: why does the second half of the STOPPING TIME consume so little distance?

Create: Build the "Equation Picker" flowchart: a decision routine that takes any uniformly-accelerated problem and outputs the correct equation in one step. Specify the knowns-enumeration step, the three branches (with the omitted quantity that defines each), and a validity gate that can REFUSE a problem. Run the routine on three problems: (P1) from rest, a = 3 m s⁻², find v after 4 s; (P2) braking from 25 m s⁻¹ to rest over 100 m, find a; (P3) a bus whose acceleration varies stop to stop, find s in 10 s.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Define acceleration and state its SI unit. (1 mark) (b) A body moving at 5 m s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m s⁻². Calculate its velocity after 4 s and the distance travelled in that time. (3 marks) (c) State the condition under which the average velocity of a body equals (u + v)/2. (1 mark)

HOTS: On a road running east–west with EAST chosen positive, a bus is travelling WEST (toward the negative side) at 15 m s⁻¹ when the driver brakes; it halts in 5.0 s. A student writes: "Braking means negative acceleration, so a = −3.0 m s⁻², u = 15, and s = 15 × 5 − ½ × 3 × 25 = 75 − 37.5 = +37.5 m — the bus ends 37.5 m EAST of where braking began." (a) Write the correct sign translation and solve for a, t-check and s. (b) Show precisely where the student's signs self-contradict. (c) Compute the correct final position and state which of the student's two claims (the sign of a; the direction of s) was accidentally right — and why "accidentally" is the operative word.

Application: A car travels at 20 m s⁻¹ on a highway when a buffalo steps out 60 m ahead. (a) The driver's reaction time is 0.5 s (the car moves at constant 20 m s⁻¹ until the brakes bite). Compute the reaction distance and the braking distance at a deceleration of 5.0 m s⁻², and the margin remaining. (b) A drowsy driver has a 1.5 s reaction time; compute the total stopping distance and state whether the outcome differs qualitatively. (c) The highway authority's board reads: "Reaction distance grows linearly with speed; braking distance grows with the square." Verify BOTH clauses with the numbers at 20 m s⁻¹ and 10 m s⁻¹ (same 0.5 s reaction, same 5.0 m s⁻²), and state which clause explains why speed cameras protect buffalo best.

Evaluation: A marker returns three solutions of "a car braking from 72 km h⁻¹ stops in 5.0 s; find the deceleration and the braking distance." Solution A: u = 72, a = (0 − 72)/5 = −14.4, s = 72 × 5 − ½ × 14.4 × 25 = 360 − 180 = 180 m. Solution B: u = 20 m s⁻¹, a = −4 m s⁻², s = 20 × 5 − ½ × 4 × 25 = 100 − 50 = 50 m. Solution C: u = 20 m s⁻¹, a = −4 m s⁻², s = 0 − 400/(2 × (−4)) = 50 m. (a) Identify which solutions are correct and locate the exact step where any wrong one fails. (b) Compute the scale of the error in A as a ratio. (c) State the checking habit that catches A in one line, and rewrite A's first line correctly.

Comparison: Build a three-row comparison of the equations of motion — for each equation: the symbols it relates, the symbol it OMITS, and the canonical problem type it answers fastest — then state (i) which equation's omission makes it the forensic tool (skid marks: distance known, time never measured), and (ii) the one graph reading (c9_phy_icse_02_004) that equals equation 2's output, with the shape that carries it.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Define uniform acceleration and write its SI unit. (1 mark) (b) A body starts from rest with uniform acceleration 2.0 m s⁻². Calculate its velocity after 6.0 s and the distance covered in that time. (2 marks) (c) A car moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest with uniform deceleration 4.0 m s⁻². Calculate the distance it travels while stopping and the time taken. (3 marks) (d) State ONE situation in which the equations of motion CANNOT be applied even though the body moves in a straight line, and name the graph feature that would expose the situation on a velocity–time plot. (2 marks)
Evaluate: “If a stone is dropped from a height of 80 m, its velocity after 2 s is 19.6 m/s downward.” Assume **g = 9.8 m/s²** and downward positive.
A ball is projected vertically upward with **u = 15 m/s**. Taking upward as positive, calculate the maximum height reached. Use **g = 9.8 m/s²**.

CISCE exam‑style: A stone is dropped from a tower of height **h**. After **1 s**, another stone is thrown downward from the same tower with an initial speed of **20 m/s**. Both stones reach the ground simultaneously. Find **h**. (Take **g = 10 m/s²** for simplicity.)

HOTS: A ball is thrown upward from a height of **10 m** above ground with **u = 20 m/s**. At the same instant, another ball is dropped from the same height. Which ball hits the ground first? Justify using equations of motion.

Application: A construction worker drops a hammer from a scaffold 45 m high. At the same moment, a colleague on the ground throws a wrench upward at **25 m/s**. Determine if and where they meet. Use **g = 10 m/s²**, upward positive.

Comparison: Compare the time of flight for a ball thrown upward at **20 m/s** from ground level with that of a ball dropped from a height of **20.4 m** (the maximum height of the first ball). Use **g = 9.8 m/s²**.

CISCE past‑paper pattern: A stone is thrown vertically upward with a speed of **29.4 m/s**. Find (i) the maximum height reached, (ii) the time taken to reach the maximum height, (iii) the velocity of the stone after **4 s**. Take **g = 9.8 m/s²**.

Reasoning: A student argues: "The motor of our ceiling fan runs steadily, the blade takes the same time for every revolution, so the TIP of the blade is in uniform VELOCITY." (a) Refute with the two things the tip's velocity does that magnitude cannot capture. (b) Compute the tip's speed for radius 0.5 m at 300 rpm (use π = 3.14). (c) State what the tip's average velocity is over one revolution, and what surprising physical fact that zero corresponds to (the net change of position).

Analyse: A cyclist rides a circular track of radius 7 m at a constant speed, completing one lap in 8 s (use π = 22/7, √2 ≈ 1.41). For one FULL lap, HALF a lap, and a QUARTER lap from a fixed start point, tabulate: distance covered, magnitude of displacement, average speed, magnitude of average velocity, and the direction of the average velocity (where nonzero). Then state the trend the half-lap and quarter-lap magnitudes show as the arc lengthens, and what value the trend approaches.

Apply: A washing-machine spin drum of radius 20 cm spins at 600 rpm (use π = 3.14). (a) Find the time period and the speed of a point on the drum's wall. (b) The machine switches to 1200 rpm: state the new period and the new tip speed, and by what factor each changed. (c) Compute how many revolutions the drum completes in 15 s at 600 rpm. (d) One line: why does the drum's wall point never "slow at the corners" of its circular path?

Create: Design the "Circle Card" — a one-page routine for analysing ANY uniform circular motion: the four entries it must always produce (path fact, speed computation, velocity direction, acceleration direction), the one validity question it must ask first, and the two averages it must compute (full cycle and half cycle). Then run the card on a giant wheel: radius 15 m, one revolution in 60 s (π = 3.14), and write the two averages with their directions.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Why is the motion of a body moving with constant speed in a circle called accelerated motion? (1 mark) (b) A body moves in a circle of radius 7 m and completes one revolution in 4 s. Calculate its speed. (2 marks) (c) Name the direction in which the body moves at any instant, and the direction of its acceleration. (1 mark)

Application: A mela (fair) giant wheel of radius 15 m completes one revolution in 60 s at a steady rate (π = 3.14). A rider boards at the bottom point B. (a) Compute the rim's speed. (b) State the rider's velocity direction at the topmost point T and at the two side points, given the wheel turns so that the bottom moves in the +x direction. (c) Compute the rider's average velocity for the ride from B to T (the half revolution) — magnitude and direction. (d) The operator's board says: "Riders at the top and bottom move at different speeds." Evaluate the statement against this chapter's definitions, and write the one corrected sentence for the board.

Evaluation: A study-assistant AI generates five one-line "facts" for revision. Audit each: (1) "Uniform circular motion is uniform because the speed is constant." (2) "The velocity of a body in uniform circular motion points from the body to the centre." (3) "A fan's blade tip has zero average velocity per revolution, so it effectively goes nowhere — its displacement is zero." (4) "Uniform circular motion is an example of accelerated motion." (5) "The equations v = u + at etc. apply with a = 0 because the speed never changes." State CORRECT or WRONG for each, and for every wrong one, the minimal repair that keeps the line's spirit.

CISCE past-paper pattern: (a) Define time period and frequency of uniform circular motion, and state how they are related. (2 marks) (b) A body moves uniformly in a circle of radius 7 m, completing one revolution in 4 s. Calculate (i) the distance covered in one revolution and (ii) the speed of the body. (2 marks) (c) For the same motion, calculate the body's average velocity over one revolution, and over half a revolution (magnitude and direction). (3 marks) (d) State why this motion is accelerated even though the speed is constant, and name the direction of the acceleration. (2 marks)

Reasoning: A classmate's mock-test script contains five answers: (i) "The athlete's lap: speed 8 m s⁻¹, velocity 8 m s⁻¹ since she never slowed"; (ii) "First half of the journey at 30 km h⁻¹, second half at 60: average 45 km h⁻¹"; (iii) "The v–t graph is a straight line rising from 0 to 20 m s⁻¹ in 50 s: its slope is the speed, 0.4 m s⁻¹"; (iv) "Braking from 20 m s⁻¹ at 2.5 m s⁻²: a = +2.5 since braking speeds the stopping"; (v) "The stone on the snapped string flies outward, away from the centre." For EACH, name the error's node-home, give the correct answer, and state the one repair sentence that fixes the classmate's understanding.

Analyse: Six motions are described: (P) a metro train holding exactly 72 km h⁻¹ on a straight elevated track; (Q) the same metro braking evenly into a station; (R) a ceiling-fan tip at steady rpm; (S) a ball thrown vertically upward (air resistance ignored); (T) a bus in city traffic on a straight road, speeding and slowing irregularly; (U) a cyclist rounding a circular track at a steady 5.5 m s⁻¹. For each: classify the motion with the chapter's exact vocabulary, state whether v = u + at applies (with the validity reason), and name the tool that WOULD analyse it.

Apply: A metro line's station run: the train starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 0.5 m s⁻² for 30 s, cruises at constant velocity for 90 s, then brakes uniformly to rest in 30 s. (a) Find the cruise velocity and the distance covered in each phase. (b) Find the station-to-station distance and the journey time. (c) Compute the average speed in m s⁻¹ and km h⁻¹. (d) Verify the total distance by the v–t trapezium area.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Distinguish between distance and displacement, and between speed and velocity, stating the parent–child relation in each pair. (2 marks) (b) A car covers 36 m in 4 s and a further 24 m in 6 s. Calculate its average speed in m s⁻¹ and in km h⁻¹. (2 marks) (c) A body moves with constant speed in a horizontal circle. State, with reason, whether a force-like influence is needed to maintain the motion, and in which direction it must act. (2 marks)

Application: A car travels at 72 km h⁻¹ on a highway when a broken-down truck is spotted 95 m ahead in the lane. The driver's reaction time is 0.75 s (the car holds 72 km h⁻¹ until the brakes bite), and the brakes decelerate it uniformly at 5.0 m s⁻². (a) Compute the reaction distance, the braking distance, the total stopping distance, and the margin. (b) Compute the total time from sighting to halt. (c) A safety campaign poster claims: "At double the speed, the stopping distance doubles." Evaluate the claim with the 144 km h⁻¹ case (same reaction time and braking), and write the corrected poster line using this chapter's relation. (d) State which chapter tool answered (a)'s two distances, and why TWO tools were needed.

Evaluation: A classmate's revision plan for this chapter allots its 10 hours: 6 h re-reading the textbook, 2 h re-copying the three equations and the graphs' rules, 1 h on distance/displacement conceptuals, 1 h on one full numerical. Evaluate the plan against the section's demand profile — estimates: conceptual/distinction items ~40% of the marks, single-step numericals ~25%, multi-phase or graph numericals ~25%, circle/justify items ~10% — identify the plan's two biggest misallocations, predict the two most likely mark losses on exam day, and rewrite the 10-hour plan with proportions matched to the demand profile.

Comparison: Build the chapter's master comparison in one table — for each of the five tool-zones (quantity pairs, averaging rules, graph readings, straight-line equations, circle rules) state: what it answers, its validity gate, and its single most-examined item — then state which TWO zones share the same underlying parent distinction (name it), and why the exam can test that distinction once in Class 9 language and once in graph language without repeating itself.

CISCE past-paper pattern (full mini-section, 10 marks — solve all): Q1 (3 marks) (a) Define average speed. (1) (b) A car covers 36 m in 4 s and the next 24 m in 6 s. Find its average speed for the whole journey in m s⁻¹ and km h⁻¹. (2) Q2 (4 marks) A body's velocity–time data: t = 0, 10, 30, 40 s; v = 0, 15, 15, 0 m s⁻¹. (a) State the nature of motion in each of the three phases. (1) (b) Find the total distance by the trapezium area and verify by summing segment areas. (2) (c) Find the average speed for the 40 s. (1) Q3 (3 marks) A body moves uniformly in a circle of radius 7 m, completing a revolution in 4 s (π = 22/7). (a) Find the distance in one revolution and the speed. (2) (b) State the body's average velocity for one revolution with the reason. (1)
A 2 kg block rests on a horizontal wooden table. Take g = 9.8 m/s². Calculate the magnitude of the normal reaction force exerted by the table on the block.
A 5 kg box is pulled horizontally across a rough floor by a rope with tension 30 N. The frictional force opposing motion is 12 N. Determine the net horizontal contact force acting on the box.

A 10 kg crate is pushed across a horizontal floor with a force of 50 N at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. Calculate the normal reaction force on the crate. (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern Question:** A block of mass 2 kg is placed on a smooth horizontal table. A horizontal force of 6 N is applied to the block. (i) Draw a labelled free‑body diagram showing all forces acting on the block. (ii) Calculate the acceleration of the block. (iii) If the same block is now placed on a rough table with a frictional force of 2 N opposing the motion, what will be its acceleration?
Evaluate the statement: “Because 1 kg equals 1000 g, 1 newton must equal 1000 dyne.”
Convert 75 dyne into newtons.
A force of 3.2 newton acts on a surface of area 4 cm². Calculate the pressure in pascals.
Which of the following correctly relates the cgs and SI units of energy? A) 1 erg = 10⁻³ J B) 1 erg = 10⁻⁷ J C) 1 erg = 10⁷ J D) 1 erg = 10⁻⁹ J
The pressure of a gas is recorded as 1.2 × 10⁴ Ba. Convert this pressure to pascals and state whether the gas pressure is above or below atmospheric pressure (≈1.01 × 10⁵ Pa).
A past‑paper style question: “A force of 4.5 newton acts uniformly over a rectangular surface of length 8 cm and breadth 5 cm. Calculate the pressure exerted in pascals.”
A car of mass 1000 kg moves at a constant velocity of 20 m/s on a straight road. What is the net force acting on the car?
Compare the inertia of a 1 kg iron block and a 1 kg cotton bag.
A 500 g object moves with uniform velocity of 10 m/s on a frictionless surface. State the net force acting on it and justify using Newton’s first law.
A 5 kg block is pulled across a horizontal frictionless surface by a horizontal force of 20 N. What is its acceleration? If the same force is applied to a 10 kg block, what is the new acceleration?
Two forces, 30 N east and 40 N north, act simultaneously on a 10 kg object initially at rest. Determine the magnitude and direction of its acceleration.
A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates from rest to 20 m s⁻¹ in 10 s. Assuming constant acceleration, calculate the average net force acting on the car.
A 2 kg block rests on a smooth horizontal table. A horizontal force of 6 N is applied. After 3 s, what is the block’s velocity and how far has it moved?

A 4 kg block on a smooth horizontal surface is acted upon by two forces: 10 N at 30° above the horizontal and 6 N horizontally opposite to the horizontal component of the first force. Find the magnitude of the block’s acceleration.

A rocket of initial mass 500 kg ejects gas at a constant rate, producing a constant thrust of 10 000 N. Assuming mass loss is negligible over the first 2 s, calculate the rocket’s acceleration at *t = 1 s*.

Compare the acceleration produced by a 5 N force on a 1 kg mass in SI units with the acceleration produced by the same force expressed in cgs units (5 × 10⁵ dyne) on a 1000 g mass. Show that the numerical value of acceleration is identical in both systems.
**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** A 2 kg body moves along the x‑axis under a force *F = (6t) N*, where *t* is time in seconds. If the body starts from rest at *t = 0*, find its velocity at *t = 3 s*.

Reasoning: A 20 g bullet fired at 400 m s⁻¹ horizontally embeds in a wooden block of mass 3 kg hanging at rest. A classmate argues: "The bullet should win easily — it is enormously faster; the block has almost no speed at all." Use momentum to arbitrate precisely: compute the bullet's momentum, contrast it with the block's initial momentum, and explain what "quantity of motion" means in a way the speed comparison misses. Then compute what the CLASSMATE'S ranking (by speed) would have predicted and why the product-ranking differs.

Analyse: A 0.5 kg ball travels horizontally at 8 m s⁻¹, east-positive. Three interactions follow: (P) it is caught dead; (Q) it is returned along its line at 8 m s⁻¹; (R) it is returned along its line at 3 m s⁻¹. For EACH: write initial momentum, final momentum, Δp with sign, and interpret the sign in words; then rank the three by |Δp| and state why (Q) is the largest even though the speed barely differs from (P)'s case.

Apply: (a) Compute the momentum of a 1500 kg car moving at 72 km h⁻¹; state it in SI. (b) The car above is stopped by a crumple-zone in 0.5 s in one crash test and by a rigid barrier in 0.05 s in another. Find the average force in each case and the ratio between them. (c) A 50 N net force acts on a 4 kg body at rest for 2 s. Find the momentum gained and the final velocity, checking the velocity against F = ma kinematics.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Define momentum and state its SI unit. Is it a scalar or a vector? (2 marks) (b) A hockey ball of mass 200 g moves at 10 m s⁻¹ and is struck back along its path at 25 m s⁻¹. Find the change of momentum. (2 marks) — show the axis line the scheme pays for.

HOTS: The momentum form F = Δp/t is "more fundamental" than F = ma. Build the argument in three parts: (i) show the reduction (momentum form → F = ma) in one line; (ii) exhibit a physical situation the momentum form handles where the constant-mass shortcut has no purchase, and describe how the rate form still delivers an answer in principle; (iii) give the CISCE Class 9 verdict — which form should a Class 9 numerical be COMPUTED in, and which form should the LAW be STATED in — with the reason for the split verdict.

Application: A car's crash sensor records: mass 1000 kg, speed before 18 m s⁻¹, the crumple zone brought it to rest in 0.3 s. (a) Compute the average force the barrier exerted. (b) The same design goal restated: keep the average force below 60 kN. Compute the minimum stop-time the crumple zone must deliver at this speed. (c) At 36 m s⁻¹ (double), with the 0.3 s stop-time of (a), compute the force and state the general rule (in Δp language) for how force scales with speed at fixed stop-time. (d) The brochure claims "our crumple zone halves the crash force." Make the claim precise: halves compared to WHAT, and under which held-fixed quantities.

Evaluation: A textbook's solved example: "A 5 g bullet moving at 200 m s⁻¹ strikes a tree and penetrates 4 cm before stopping. Find the average resistive force. Solution: p = 5 × 200 = 1000; the bullet stops in distance 4 cm = 0.04 m; F = p/s = 1000/0.04 = 25,000 N." (i) Identify and repair every fault (units, the divided quantity, the route). (ii) Solve it correctly by TWO routes: via a time estimated from kinematics, and directly via the work-energy-free route using v² = u² + 2as for a; reconcile the answers. (iii) The book's answer (25,000 N) differs from yours by a factor — state the factor and trace exactly which steps caused it. (iv) State the general exam habit this example installs.

CISCE past-paper pattern (full mini-section, 10 marks — solve all): Q1 (2 marks) (a) Define momentum and give its CGS unit. (1) (b) Convert 5 kg m s⁻¹ into CGS units. (1) Q2 (4 marks) A 300 g ball moving at 8 m s⁻¹ is struck back along its path with 18 m s⁻¹, contact 0.06 s. (a) Find Δp. (2) (b) Find the average force with direction. (1) (c) State what the force would have been for a plain stop in the same 0.06 s, and the ratio of return-hit force to stop force. (1) Q3 (4 marks) A 800 kg elevator cage moving upward at 4 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest in 2 s by its brakes. (a) Find the change of momentum of the cage. (1) (b) Find the average net force producing this change, with direction. (1) (c) Explain in momentum language why a longer braking time (say 8 s for the same initial speed) is mechanically gentler on the cable, with the numbers. (2)
A 5 kg block A pushes a 3 kg block B on a frictionless horizontal surface with a force of 12 N. What is the magnitude of the force that block B exerts on block A?
A typical CISCE board question: “State Newton’s third law of motion. A gun of mass 2 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.02 kg with a velocity of 400 m/s. Calculate the recoil velocity of the gun.”

**HOTS:** Two identical balls collide head‑on on a frictionless surface. Ball 1 moves right at 4 m/s, ball 2 moves left at 2 m/s. After collision, ball 1 moves left at 1 m/s. Using Newton’s third law and momentum conservation, determine the velocity of ball 2 after collision.
**APPLICATION:** A firefighter holds a hose ejecting water at 20 kg/s with a speed of 15 m/s. Calculate the force the firefighter must exert to hold the hose steady.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “State Newton’s third law of motion. A 0.05 kg bullet is fired from a 2.5 kg rifle with a muzzle velocity of 300 m/s. Calculate the recoil velocity of the rifle. Explain why the rifle’s recoil velocity is much smaller than the bullet’s velocity.”
A student says that the gravitational force between two 1 kg masses placed 1 m apart is 9.8 N. Evaluate this statement.
Calculate the gravitational force between Earth (mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg) and a 70 kg student standing on its surface (radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m). Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²·kg⁻².

A satellite of mass 500 kg orbits Earth at a height of 400 km above the surface. Calculate the gravitational force acting on it. (Earth mass = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg, Earth radius = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²·kg⁻².)

Compare the gravitational force between two 1000 kg masses separated by 10 m with the electrostatic force between two 1 C charges separated by 10 m. (Use k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².) Which is stronger and by what factor?
A solid cube of side 5 cm and mass 250 g is fully immersed in water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³). Will it float or sink? Justify using densities.
A cylindrical block of wood (ρ = 600 kg m⁻³) of height 0.2 m and cross‑section 0.01 m² floats vertically in water. Calculate the length of the block submerged.
A CISCE exam question: “A hydrometer reads 1.020 in a liquid. What is the liquid’s density in kg m⁻³? (Take density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³.)”

A submarine at 200 m depth in seawater (ρ = 1025 kg m⁻³) experiences a pressure increase of 2 MPa relative to the surface. Verify whether this pressure increase is consistent with the hydrostatic formula.
A hollow steel sphere (mass 2 kg, outer radius 0.1 m) is placed in water. Will it float? If yes, what fraction of its volume is submerged? (ρ_water = 1000 kg m⁻³)
Compare the buoyant force on a 1 kg block of wood (ρ = 600 kg m⁻³) and a 1 kg block of iron (ρ = 7800 kg m⁻³) when both are fully immersed in water.

A past CISCE paper asks: “A solid cube of side 4 cm and relative density 0.8 is placed in a liquid of relative density 1.2. Find the fraction of the cube’s volume that remains above the liquid surface.”
What is the gauge pressure at a depth of 5 m in a liquid of density 800 kg m⁻³? (Take *g = 10 m s⁻²*.)
If atmospheric pressure is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, what is the absolute pressure at 12 m depth in seawater (ρ = 1025 kg m⁻³, *g = 9.8 m s⁻²*)?
A dam wall is 30 m high. Water stands at the full height on one side. Calculate the average pressure exerted by water on the wall. (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, *g = 9.8 m s⁻²*)

A submarine is at a depth where the gauge pressure is 3.0 × 10⁶ Pa. If the density of seawater is 1025 kg m⁻³ and *g = 9.8 m s⁻²*, what is the depth of the submarine? (Ignore atmospheric pressure for gauge pressure.)
A water tank has a square hole of side 10 cm at a depth of 3 m from the free surface. Calculate the force exerted by water on the hole. (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, *g = 9.8 m s⁻²*)

Compare the pressure at the bottom of two containers: Container A holds water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³) to a height of 5 m. Container B holds mercury (ρ = 13 600 kg m⁻³) to a height of 0.5 m. Which has greater gauge pressure at the bottom? (Take *g = 10 m s⁻²*.)
A CISCE past‑paper style question: “The pressure at a depth of 10 m in a liquid is 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. If the atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, find the density of the liquid. (*g = 10 m s⁻²*)”
A solid sphere of volume 2×10⁻⁴ m³ is fully immersed first in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) and then in oil (ρ = 800 kg/m³). Compare the buoyant forces in the two fluids.
Calculate the buoyant force acting on a rectangular block of dimensions 0.1 m × 0.05 m × 0.02 m when it is completely submerged in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²).
A solid cube of side 5 cm is completely immersed in water. Calculate the buoyant force acting on it. (Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s².)

A hollow steel sphere of outer radius 5 cm and inner radius 4 cm is fully immersed in water. Without calculating the exact buoyant force, explain whether the buoyant force on this sphere is greater than, equal to, or less than the buoyant force on a solid steel sphere of the same outer radius.
Compare the buoyant force experienced by a 1 kg block of wood (density 600 kg/m³) and a 1 kg block of iron (density 7800 kg/m³) when each is fully immersed in water.

A CISCE ICSE 2023 paper asked: “A solid cube of side 4 cm is completely immersed in a liquid of density 800 kg/m³. Calculate the buoyant force acting on the cube. Take g = 10 m/s².” Provide the solution as a student would write in the exam.
A solid cube of side 0.10 m and mass 0.80 kg is fully submerged in water (ρ_(water)=1000 kg m⁻³). Calculate the buoyant force and state whether the cube will sink or float when released.
A cylindrical piece of wood (density 600 kg m⁻³) of volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ floats in oil of density 800 kg m⁻³. Find the volume of wood submerged.

A CISCE past‑paper style question: “A body of mass 500 g and volume 400 cm³ is completely immersed in a liquid of density 1.2 g cm⁻³. Find the apparent weight of the body in the liquid. (Take g = 10 m s⁻².)”
A student argues that if a body is neutrally buoyant in water, its density must be exactly 1000 kg m⁻³. Critique this argument considering the possibility of the body being partially submerged.
An iceberg of density 917 kg m⁻³ floats in seawater of density 1025 kg m⁻³. What fraction of the iceberg’s volume is above water?
Compare the buoyant force on a 1 kg iron block and a 1 kg wooden block when both are fully submerged in water. Explain any difference.

CISCE past‑paper pattern: “A solid cylinder of height 0.20 m and cross‑sectional area 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² floats vertically in a liquid of density 800 kg m⁻³ with 0.12 m of its length submerged. Find the mass of the cylinder. (Take g = 10 m s⁻².)”
A solid sphere of density 800 kg/m³ is placed in a liquid of density 1000 kg/m³. Will it float? What fraction of its volume will be submerged?
A rectangular wooden block (density 500 kg/m³) of dimensions 0.2 m × 0.1 m × 0.05 m floats in water. Calculate the depth of submersion.

A body of volume V and density ρ_b floats in a liquid of density ρ_l. Derive an expression for the fraction of volume submerged. If ρ_b = 0.8 ρ_l, what percentage of the body remains above the liquid surface?
A hydrometer of mass 0.10 kg floats in a liquid with 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ of its stem submerged. Determine the density of the liquid.
Compare the fraction submerged for a body of density 0.6 g/cm³ in water (1 g/cm³) and in mercury (13.6 g/cm³).
A wooden block of density 600 kg/m³ and volume 0.002 m³ floats in water. Find the minimum external force required to completely immerse the block.

Recall: define density and relative density, state their SI (and CGS-practical) units, and write the two conversion bridges. Then compute the density and relative density of a copper block of mass 890 g occupying 100 cm³, expressing the density in BOTH g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³.

Reasoning: (a) A student asks: "If relative density is a ratio of two densities, why does everyone use WATER — and why water at exactly 4 °C?" Answer with the metrology in two sentences. (b) A second student computes the RD of mercury as 13.6 and writes "mercury is 13.6 kg m⁻³ heavier than water." Locate and repair the error. (c) An alloy is made by mixing 2700 g of aluminium (ρ = 2700 kg m⁻³) with 7800 g of iron (ρ = 7800 kg m⁻³), volumes adding. Compute the alloy's density and RD, and state why it lands between the two.

Analyse: Four substances with their relative densities: ice 0.92, kerosene 0.80, iron 7.8, mercury 13.6. (P) Rank their densities in kg m⁻³. (Q) For each, state float or sink in WATER, with the comparison made explicit. (R) A closed glass marble (RD 2.5) is dropped into each of the four substances — state its verdict in each, with the rule. (S) Ice is dropped into mercury and into kerosene — two different verdicts; give both and the single principle that generates them.

Apply: An irregular metal ornament is weighed (m = 456 g) and then lowered into a measuring cylinder holding water: the reading rises from 200 mL to 270 mL. (a) Find the ornament's volume and density (in g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³) and its RD. (b) Identify-plausible-or-not: is it consistent with pure copper (RD 8.9)? (c) The same ornament in a brine of RD 1.2 (if the cylinder held brine instead): predict the new reading rise and the apparent extra displacement error if a student forgets the cylinder already contained 200 mL. (d) State the one assumption about the ornament that the displacement method silently makes.

Create: Design a complete density-bottle determination of a UNKNOWN clearing fluid's relative density, to be executed by a Class 9 pair with a ±0.02 tolerance claimed. Specify: (i) the equipment list and the exact reading protocol (which masses, in which order, and why that order); (ii) a filled-in sample reading table with the RD computation landing inside the claimed tolerance; (iii) the two largest error sources in the protocol and the one procedural guard against each; (iv) the transfer sentence: what changes if the fluid is (contrary to assumption) volatile?

CISCE exam-style: (a) Define relative density of a substance. State TWO reasons why water is chosen as the reference substance. (3 marks) (b) A solid weighs 80 gf in air and 60 gf when fully immersed in water. Calculate the relative density of the solid and its density in kg m⁻³. (2 marks)

HOTS: A hydrometer-style test tube carries lead-shot and floats upright: 15.0 cm of its stem is submerged in water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³). In an unknown liquid the same tube floats with 18.75 cm submerged. (i) Explain why the SUBMERGED LENGTH ratio yields the liquid's RD, deriving the relation from floatation equilibrium. (ii) Compute the unknown liquid's RD and density. (iii) The tube is then placed in a third liquid and sinks to 12.0 cm; compute that liquid's RD, and state the general law the three readings display (length in water × RD_water = length in liquid × RD_liquid? — verify with the numbers).

Application: An iceberg floats in sea water (ρ = 1025 kg m⁻³) with ice's density 920 kg m⁻³. (a) Compute the fraction of the iceberg's volume submerged, and the fraction showing above the surface. (b) An iceberg calved into FRESH water (ρ = 1000) instead: recompute both fractions and state the direction of change with reason. (c) The iceberg melts partially, its remaining ice still at 920: state what happens to the water line of the un-melted part (qualitatively, with the one-line reason), and the maritime hazard this "roll-over" implies. (d) A 1000 m³ iceberg: compute the mass of ice and the volume of meltwater it will add to the sea.

Evaluation: A student's lab report on density contains five sentences: (1) "We found the stone's volume by dividing its mass by the water level in the cylinder." (2) "The relative density came out as 2.6 g cm⁻³, so the stone is glass." (3) "We weighed the density bottle empty, then with liquid, then with water — and computed RD as (liquid mass − water mass)/bottle mass." (4) "The iron block sank in mercury, confirming that iron is denser than every liquid." (5) "Since the alloy's density was between its two metals' densities, we concluded volumes added on mixing." Mark each right or wrong (half-credit for a right core with a wrong clause), locate each fault precisely, and rewrite all five as a correct methods paragraph.

CISCE past-paper pattern (full mini-section, 10 marks — solve all): Q1 (2 marks) (a) Define density and write its SI unit. (1) (b) Convert 0.9 g cm⁻³ into kg m⁻³ and state the RD of the substance. (1) Q2 (4 marks) A metal cube of side 4 cm weighs 499.2 gf in air. (a) Compute its volume and density (g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³). (2) (b) Predict its weight when fully immersed in water (gf), showing the loss-of-weight reasoning. (2) Q3 (4 marks) A density bottle weighs 20 g empty; with a brine fill it weighs 45 g; with a water fill it weighs 70 g. (a) Compute the brine's RD and density. (2) (b) A test tube floats at 16 cm in water and 20 cm in this brine: verify the consistency of the two independent measurements, and state the law your verification uses. (2)
A solid weighs 50 N in air and 40 N in water. What is its relative density?
A piece of metal weighs 200 gf in air, 180 gf in water, and 175 gf in a liquid. Find the relative density of the liquid.
A solid weighs 30 gf in air and 24 gf in water. When immersed in a liquid, it weighs 25 gf. Calculate the relative density of the solid and the liquid.
A jeweller has a gold ornament weighing 50 gf in air and 46.5 gf in water. Given relative density of gold is 19.3, comment on purity.
A body weighs 100 gf in air, 80 gf in water, and 75 gf in a liquid. Find (i) relative density of the body, (ii) relative density of the liquid.
A wooden block of volume 0.02 m³ and density 600 kg/m³ is placed in water (ρ_(water) = 1000 kg/m³). Calculate the buoyant force acting on the block and state whether it floats or sinks.
A body weighs 50 N in air and 30 N when fully immersed in water. Calculate its relative density. (ICSE 2019 pattern)

A cylindrical block of wood (density 600 kg/m³, cross-section 0.01 m², height 0.2 m) floats vertically in water. How much of its length is submerged? (HOTS: combine floatation condition with geometry)

A student uses a spring balance to weigh a stone in air (80 gf) and in a liquid (60 gf). The liquid's relative density is 0.8. Find the volume of the stone. (Application: use buoyant force in a liquid other than water)
Compare the pressure at the bottom of two containers: Container A has water height 1 m; Container B has water height 1 m but a larger base area. Both are open to atmosphere. (Comparison)

ICSE 2022 pattern: A solid weighs 300 gf in air. When immersed completely in water, it weighs 200 gf. When immersed completely in a liquid of relative density 1.2, it weighs 180 gf. Find (i) the volume of the solid, (ii) the relative density of the solid. (CISCE past-paper pattern)
A student claims that water contracts continuously as it cools from 10 °C to 0 °C. Evaluate this claim.
**APPLICATION:** A school installs a 5 kW solar array. On a clear day it receives 5 hours of peak sunlight. Estimate the daily electrical energy produced in kWh.

Recall: define heat and temperature in one sentence each with units; state the direction rule for heat flow; and convert (a) 25 °C to kelvin, (b) 293 K to °C, (c) 837.2 J to calories (1 cal = 4.186 J).

Reasoning: (P) Convert 68 °F to °C and to K. (Q) A weather report says Delhi touched 40 °C; express this in °F. (R) A deep-freeze holds ice cream at −4 °F; express in °C. (S) A student claims: "Since 1 °C = 1.8 °F, a rise of 10 °C must be a rise of 18 °F, and therefore 20 °C must equal 36 °F." Separate the true half from the false half and correct the false half.

Analyse: A geography field kit must measure: site A, a Siachen observation post at −50 °C; site B, boiling water for sterilisation at 100 °C; site C, a normal Delhi summer day near 45 °C. Available thermometers: mercury-in-glass (freezing −39 °C, boiling 357 °C) and alcohol-in-glass (freezing −117 °C, boiling 78 °C). (i) Assign a thermometer to each site and justify each with the freezing/boiling comparison. (ii) The kit's junior member suggests "just use alcohol everywhere, since it stays liquid over a bigger range." Audit the suggestion with site B. (iii) State the ONE temperature range over which BOTH thermometers work, with the arithmetic.

Apply: (a) A clinic in Chennai records a patient's temperature as 100.4 °F on a Fahrenheit clinical thermometer. Convert to °C and state whether the patient has fever (normal ≈ 37 °C, fever above 37.5 °C). (b) The same clinic's Celsius thermometer is marked 35 °C to 42 °C. Express this range in °F and explain why the range was chosen so narrow. (c) The nurse forgets to jerk the thermometer after a previous feverish patient read 40 °C. What will happen if the NEXT patient is normal (37 °C) and the reading is taken without jerking?

Create: Design a 5-minute classroom demonstration, "Two currencies: temperature decides, mass delivers," for this node, using only: one electric kettle, one steel spoon, two identical steel bowls, and a bucket. Specify: (i) the three steps with what students observe at each; (ii) the single sentence the demonstration proves, and the sentence it does NOT prove (a nearby trap); (iii) the two questions you would ask in the last minute to check transfer of the idea, each with the expected answer.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Define thermal equilibrium. (1 mark) (b) A substance is at 122 °F. Express this temperature in °C and in kelvin. (2 marks) (c) State two reasons why mercury is preferred as a thermometric liquid. (1 mark)

HOTS: Three bodies, one ledger. Body P: 2 kg of water at 30 °C. Body Q: 200 g of oil at 60 °C. Body R: 5 kg of sand at 25 °C. (i) Rank the bodies by TEMPERATURE and explain what the ranking does and does not tell us. (ii) If P, Q and R are brought into contact in that order, state the direction of heat flow at each contact and justify each with the direction rule. (iii) A student computes "total temperature" = 30 + 60 + 25 = 115 °C and calls it "the system's temperature". Audit this in three sentences, naming the property that CAN be added and the property that cannot.

Application: An Indian household in June (ambient 42 °C) owns: a mercury room thermometer, an alcohol thermometer salvaged from a cold-storage, and a clinical thermometer. (a) The family wants to verify a geyser's outlet water claimed to be "bathing-hot, about 50 °C": which instrument(s) can legally do the job? Justify against each liquid's limits and each instrument's range. (b) The alcohol thermometer is instead used for the deep-freezer (−18 °C) and the mercury one for the geyser test: state each instrument's verdict, with the arithmetic in °F as a cross-check for the geyser. (c) The child of the house measures his own temperature with the clinical thermometer after a rough-and-tumble game and reads 37.2 °C. The grandmother insists on jerking it and re-measuring. Explain, mechanically, why the re-measurement is good practice even though the kink guarantees the reading "sticks".

Evaluation: A textbook-summary draft contains five sentences about this node. (1) "Heat always flows from a body with more internal energy to a body with less." (2) "The Fahrenheit and Celsius readings coincide at −40." (3) "An alcohol thermometer is preferred over mercury for measuring the temperature of boiling water." (4) "When a thermometer is placed in contact with a body, it reads the body's temperature instantly." (5) "At thermal equilibrium, two bodies have equal temperature but generally unequal heat." Mark each RIGHT or WRONG (half-credit: right core, wrong clause), locate each fault precisely, and rewrite all five correctly.

CISCE past-paper pattern (full mixed mini-section, 10 marks — solve all): Q1 (2 marks) (a) State the direction rule for heat flow and name the condition at which flow stops. (1) (b) Convert −13 °F to °C. (1) Q2 (4 marks) (a) A mercury thermometer and an alcohol thermometer stand in a beaker of water at 60 °C. State, with the inequality lines, which column(s) respond and why. (2) (b) The water is then heated to 90 °C: state what each instrument reads and what happens to the non-responding one. (2) Q3 (4 marks) (a) A kitchen display shows an oven dial at 250 °C: express this in °F and in K. (2) (b) A body at 310 K is cooled until its kelvin reading halves. Express both temperatures in °C and state, in one sentence, what the halving means physically. (2)
Explain why the coefficient of volume expansion β of water is negative between 0 °C and 4 °C.
Calculate the volume change when 2 kg of water cools from 10 °C to 4 °C. Use β = +2.0 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹ for this range and ρ₁₀ ≈ 999.7 kg m⁻³.
Design a simple experiment to demonstrate that water has maximum density at 4 °C using a graduated cylinder, ice, and a thermometer.
In a CISCE board question, a lake in Ooty cools from 10 °C to 0 °C. Describe the sequence of density‑driven water movements and the final temperature profile.
Compare the thermal behaviour of water between 0 °C and 4 °C with that of ethanol over the same range. Which liquid shows anomalous expansion and why?
A student plots volume versus temperature for water from 0 °C to 10 °C and obtains a V‑shaped curve with the vertex at 4 °C. Explain why the curve is symmetric only approximately.

**CISCE Past‑Paper Pattern:** A 250 mL glass beaker is filled with water at 4 °C and placed in a freezer at –10 °C. The beaker cracks after 30 minutes. Assuming the water reaches 0 °C and 20 % freezes, estimate the total volume increase that caused the crack. Use β = –2.0 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹ for 0–4 °C, β = +2.0 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹ for 4–10 °C, and ice density = 917 kg m⁻³.

Recall: state the two laws of energy flow in one sentence each; name the roles in a food chain (four roles); and compute the energy stored at the third trophic level if green plants fix 50 000 J of solar energy, using the 10 % rule.

Reasoning: Match each device to its useful output, its degraded form, and compute its efficiency: (P) an electric bulb takes 200 J and delivers 16 J of light; (Q) a ceiling fan takes 300 J and delivers 210 J of moving air's kinetic energy; (R) a car engine takes 4 000 J of fuel energy and delivers 1 200 J of mechanical work; (S) a solar cell takes 1 000 J of sunlight and delivers 180 J of electrical energy. Then order the four from most to least efficient.

Analyse: A grassland ecosystem fixes 2 00 000 J per square metre per year in its grass. The chain runs grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk. (i) Compute the energy stored at each level (10 % rule) and state how much reaches the hawk. (ii) State what happened to the remaining energy at each step, naming the processes. (iii) A student asks: "Since the hawk gets so little, why don't hawks eat grass to cut out the middlemen?" Answer with the one biological fact and the one physics sentence.

Apply: A village school runs on a 300 W rooftop solar array feeding batteries to LED lamps. (a) Over one sunlit hour the array receives 6.0 × 10⁵ J of solar energy and delivers 9.0 × 10⁴ J to the batteries. Compute the array's efficiency. (b) The stored battery energy is then converted by the LEDs: 80 % becomes light (the rest heat in the drivers). Compute the light energy delivered if 9.0 × 10⁴ J is drawn from the batteries. (c) Express the overall pathway sun → light as a fraction and state, with one sentence, why this does NOT violate conservation of energy.

Create: Design a 5-minute classroom skit, "The Roti's Journey," that teaches one-way flow and the 10 % rule to Class 6 students, using five volunteers (sun, wheat plant, goat, child, decomposer) and paper counters worth "100 J" each. Specify: (i) the four scenes with the counters handed at each and who keeps what; (ii) the one physical prop or gesture that makes the one-way rule visible (energy never flows back); (iii) the closing question to the audience and its expected answer.

CISCE exam-style: (a) State the law of conservation of energy. (1 mark) (b) What is meant by degradation of energy? Give one example. (2 marks) (c) An electric geyser consumes 6.0 × 10⁵ J of electrical energy and delivers 4.5 × 10⁵ J as hot water. Find its efficiency and name the degraded form. (1 mark)

HOTS: A farmer proposes a "closed energy farm": crops → cattle → biogas digester → generator → electricity back to power the farm's lamps and pumps, with NOTHING leaving. (i) Trace the energy through the loop and state, with the degradation clause, why the loop cannot run forever without external input. (ii) The digester delivers 20 % of the cattle-waste energy as electricity. The farm needs 10 kWh of electricity daily and the cattle chain (fodder growth → cow → waste) retains 5 % of the fodder's captured energy as waste energy. Compute the daily solar energy the crops must capture. (iii) State the ONE input the loop still takes from outside even in the farmer's design, and why "closed" is the wrong adjective for ENERGY though right for MATTER.

Application: A hill school designs a zero-waste midday meal system: LPG cooking is replaced by (1) a solar cooker (direct sunlight → heat, 40 % capture of incident energy on its mirrors), (2) a biogas digester fed by the school's food waste (waste chemical energy → gas at 45 % capture; gas → cooking heat at 60 % burner efficiency), and (3) LED lighting powered by a small panel (15 % panel, 85 % lamp). (a) The school's food waste carries 4.0 × 10⁷ J of chemical energy per day. Compute the useful cooking heat delivered by route (2). (b) Compare route (2) with route (1) for a sunny day: state the sunlight-capture needed to match the route (2) output, and which route the school should trust for the MONSOON week and why. (c) Compute the overall efficiency of route (3) and one design change that would most improve it.

Evaluation: A revision-card draft carries five claims. (1) "Energy flows in a cycle through an ecosystem." (2) "At each trophic level about 90 % of the energy is lost as heat and to decomposers." (3) "A 100 % efficient machine is possible in principle if friction is removed." (4) "Fossil fuels are a fresh input of solar energy." (5) "Food chains with five levels are rare because the energy left is too small to support a sixth." Mark each RIGHT or WRONG (half-credit: right core, wrong clause), locate each fault, and rewrite all five correctly.

CISCE past-paper pattern (full mixed mini-section, 10 marks — solve all): Q1 (2 marks) (a) Name the trophic role of: (i) grass, (ii) fungi on a fallen log. (1) (b) A chain stores 900 J at the small-fish level; compute the big-fish (next) level. (1) Q2 (4 marks) (a) State the law of conservation of energy and give its one-line reconciliation with degradation. (2) (b) A pump lifts water using 500 J of electrical energy; 425 J becomes the water's potential energy. Find the efficiency and the degraded output. (2) Q3 (4 marks) (a) A three-level chain (grass → deer → tiger) stores 4 0 000 J at grass. Find the tiger's energy and the total energy lost to respiration/decomposers across all transfers. (2) (b) State why the flow is one-way, with the material-contrast clause. (1) (c) Express the tiger's share as a percentage of the grass's capture. (1)

A village in Rajasthan receives 300 sunny days per year. If a 2 kW solar panel system operates at 15 % capacity factor for 8 hours per sunny day, calculate the annual electrical energy produced in kWh.
In the context of India’s energy policy, discuss two reasons why the government promotes solar energy over coal‑based power. (3 marks)

A city plans to replace 20 % of its coal power with rooftop solar. If the coal plant capacity is 500 MW (capacity factor 0.8), calculate the required solar capacity assuming a solar capacity factor of 0.2.
Explain two advantages and two limitations of using biogas as a renewable energy source in rural India. (4 marks)
Using the simplified radiative‑forcing formula ΔF = 5.35 ln(C/C₀) (W m⁻²), calculate the increase in radiative forcing when CO₂ rises from 280 ppm to 420 ppm. Show all steps.
ICSE 2023 Physics paper asked: “State two consequences of global warming on the Indian subcontinent.” Write a concise answer as per board expectations.

**HOTS:** If the Earth’s average albedo increased from 0.30 to 0.32 due to expanded cloud cover, qualitatively describe how this would interact with the enhanced greenhouse effect. Would it amplify or dampen warming? Justify.

**APPLICATION:** A city plans to replace 50 MW of coal‑fired generation with solar PV. Coal emits 0.9 kg CO₂ kWh⁻¹; solar emits 0.05 kg CO₂ kWh⁻¹ (lifecycle). Assuming a capacity factor of 0.25 for solar and 0.75 for coal, calculate the annual CO₂ reduction in tonnes.

**COMPARISON:** Compare the greenhouse effect on Venus (surface temperature ~460 °C, atmosphere 96 % CO₂, pressure 92 bar) with Earth’s enhanced greenhouse effect. Identify two similarities and two differences.

**CISCE PAST‑PAPER PATTERN:** “Explain how the greenhouse effect leads to global warming. Mention two human activities that increase greenhouse gases and two consequences of global warming for India.” (4 marks)

Recall: distinguish "energy conservation" (the practice) from "conservation of energy" (the law) in one sentence each; state the two drivers of the energy crisis; and compute the daily energy in kWh of a 1.2 kW heater run 3 hours.

Reasoning: A household replaces five 60 W incandescent bulbs with five 9 W LEDs, each used 5 hours daily. (i) Compute the daily and yearly saving in kWh. (ii) At ₹8 per kWh, compute the yearly saving in rupees. (iii) The LEDs cost ₹4,500 in total. Find the payback period (time for savings to repay the cost), and state whether the swap is rational on pure economics.

Analyse: A school's summer electricity audit shows: 40 tube-lights of 36 W burning 6 h/day in daylight-lit classrooms; 12 fans of 70 W running 8 h/day in occupied rooms only half the time; 2 water coolers of 500 W running 8 h/day; and an idle 1 kW water heater left switched on 24 h/day "to keep it warm". (i) Compute each item's daily kWh and the total. (ii) Rank the items by WASTE (energy serving no purpose), with reasons — note the tube-lights' daylight overlap and the fans' empty-room hours. (iii) Propose the one change with the largest daily saving and compute it.

Apply: (a) Classify: solar cooker, diesel, biogas, coal, wind, natural gas — renewable or non-renewable, with the renewal-timescale clause for each class. (b) A state utility charges ₹6.5/kWh. A household cuts its monthly use from 180 kWh to 144 kWh by the audit's measures. Compute the monthly bill before and after, and the percentage reduction in energy. (c) State, in one physics sentence each, how the same reduction helps (i) the fuel reserve and (ii) the climate.

Create: Design a 6-minute "Energy Mela" stall for Class 7 visitors that teaches one demand-side measure with a live measurement. You have: one 60 W incandescent bulb and one 9 W LED lamp (both on demo stands), one hand-crank generator, paper and pencils. Specify: (i) the activity in three steps and what each visitor MEASURES (not just watches); (ii) the single sentence visitors write on their slip, and the neighbouring wrong sentence the stall must prevent; (iii) the take-home card's three lines.

CISCE exam-style: (a) Define energy crisis. (1 mark) (b) State two demand-side measures of energy conservation, each with its one-line physics reason. (2 marks) (c) A 2 kW geyser heats water 1 h daily. Its owner fits a timer and insulation, cutting use to 0.5 h daily at the same 2 kW. Compute the monthly (30-day) saving in kWh and in rupees at ₹7 per kWh. (2 marks)

HOTS: A state's power department faces a drought year: hydropower (usually 40 % of supply) will deliver half its normal output. (i) State, with the energy-flow vocabulary, why drought hits hydro first. (ii) The gap is proposed to be filled by diesel gensets. Compute the extra monthly cost to a 300 kWh/month household if the marginal diesel power costs ₹14/kWh for one-third of its consumption (the rest stays at ₹6). (iii) The department instead offers a "save 15 %" rebate scheme. For the same household (300 kWh baseline), compute its bill if it saves exactly 15 % and all its (reduced) consumption is billed at ₹6, and state the incentive sentence that makes the scheme self-reinforcing.

Application: A food court replaces its cooking line: three 2 kW electric hotplates (6 h/day) with two 2.5 kW induction hobs (which cook the same food in 4 h/day because they heat the vessel directly). (a) Compute the daily energy before and after. (b) Compute the percentage saving and the monthly (30-day) saving at ₹8/kWh. (c) The induction hobs cost ₹54,000 installed; state the payback in years, and give the ONE sentence explaining WHY induction is more efficient (the physics of the heating mechanism).

Evaluation: A policy-note draft makes five claims. (1) "Since energy is conserved, the energy crisis cannot really exist." (2) "LED lamps conserve energy because they destroy less energy than filament bulbs." (3) "Shifting the geyser to night hours saves the same energy as switching it off for unused hours." (4) "Renewable energy is called renewable because it renews on human timescales, unlike fossil deposits." (5) "A 20 % reduction in per-capita energy use with a growing population still raises TOTAL consumption." Mark each RIGHT or WRONG (half-credit: right core, wrong clause), locate each fault, and rewrite all five correctly.

CISCE past-paper pattern (full mixed mini-section, 10 marks — solve all): Q1 (2 marks) (a) Name the quantity measured by an electricity meter in "units", and state its relation to the joule. (1) (b) A 120 W fan runs 8 h. Compute its daily consumption in units. (1) Q2 (4 marks) (a) State two renewable and two non-renewable sources. (2) (b) A household uses 240 kWh/month. By fitting a solar water heater it cuts 60 kWh/month of electric geysing. Compute the new bill at ₹6.5/kWh and the monthly saving. (2) Q3 (4 marks) (a) Define energy degradation and connect it, in one sentence, to why conservation is necessary even though energy is conserved. (2) (b) Ten classrooms each leave one 36 W tube-light burning 4 h/day with no one inside. Compute the yearly (200 school days) waste in kWh and its cost at ₹7/kWh. (2)
Explain why water contracts when cooled from 4 °C to 0 °C, unlike most liquids.
A 2 kg iron rod (c = 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) absorbs 54 000 J of heat. Calculate its temperature rise.
